title: GitHub Pages builds fail for every gh-pages commit; PR previews are not being pruned
description:
Since 2026-10-21 07:53 UTC every GitHub Pages build of the gh-pages branch errors with the generic 'Page build failed' (pages/builds API), starting with a PR-preview deploy for another PR before this one. Each PR's 'preview' check then fails in scripts/ensure-pages-published.sh after 4 rebuild rounds, because Pages keeps serving the previous build. Earlier intermittent failures: 06:18 and 07:38-07:39 UTC.

Likely cause (inferred, not confirmed; the Pages error carries no detail): the published site is over GitHub Pages' 1 GB limit. The gh-pages tree API (truncated, so these are lower bounds) shows at least 45,813 files, at least 1,339 MB of blobs, and at least 263 pr-preview/pr-N directories, while only 45 PRs are open. So previews of closed PRs are not being removed, even though pr-preview.yml triggers on 'closed' with action: auto, and remove-approved-pr-preview.yml exists for the other close path.

Impact: every PR's preview check fails. Production currently serves master (built before the outage), but the next master deploy publishes through the same failing Pages build and would not go live.

Fix direction:
1. One commit on gh-pages removing pr-preview/pr-N for every closed PR. This is a destructive write to the shared branch, so it needs explicit approval.
2. Confirm Pages builds again, then re-run a failed preview check.
3. Find why the close handlers leave previews behind, and add a scheduled sweep of closed-PR previews so it can't silently recur.
4. Optionally squash gh-pages history, since repo size includes every preview ever deployed.
close_reason: Closed on GitHub (issue #1369); reconciled by bd-github-sync.

title: A device that has not received the properties flip yet writes cell-only property values, and nothing backfills them when the flip arrives
description:
The transaction layer chooses cell or children storage from THIS device's local workspaces.properties_migration. A device whose local row still reads 'cell' after the workspace was switched to property blocks elsewhere (it booted before sync delivered the row, or was offline) writes property cells with no field or value children. When the row later updates to 'children', nothing revisits the owners it wrote, and later ordinary edits add children only for the keys they change, so an untouched key stays cell-only indefinitely.

Observed in #1265: 5 of the 68 gaps (a daily note, a panel block, a layout-session block) came from one device session a few days after its workspace was switched, before that device had the new row. The other 63 were a cross-workspace transaction, which #1277 closed.

Today's mitigation is the runbook: re-run 'Migrate properties to child blocks' once every device has caught up, then confirm audit-properties' coverage section reads missing = 0. That matters most for the large-workspace switch, where boot-time writes on any lagging device (today's daily note, UI state) land cell-only.

Directions to weigh, none chosen: (a) when a device first reads its workspace as switched, materialize children for the owners it wrote while it read 'cell'; (b) hold property writes on a device whose workspace row is older than the server's; (c) keep the runbook step and document it at the gesture.
close_reason: Not fixing: coordinate devices around a flip and re-run the cell-to-children pass if a gap appears

title: A long read during a bulk write lets the write-ahead log grow by gigabytes, and the next open replays all of it
description:
Measured on a local copy of a large graph (Chrome, OPFS write-ahead VFS). A read that stays in flight during a bulk write stops the write-ahead VFS from reclaiming its log. Every commit appends a copy of each page it dirtied. Normally a checkpoint reclaims those copies, but a held read blocks that, so the log grows far faster than the database. The next page load reads, checksums and indexes every frame inside PowerSync's `init()`, before `repoReady`, and the user sees "Loading…" for that long. Copying into the main file happens at the first checkpoint after the open.

Measurements:
- A clean properties migration (1.12M blocks after) kept the log at about 13 MB or less. The first reload had `repoReady` at 1.2 s.
- One reader held for 127 s in the middle of the same migration grew the log from about 12 MB to 8.5-8.9 GB, about 70 MB/s, while the main file did not grow. Once the read ended and writes continued, the log drained within about 30-40 s.
- Opens with logs of 1.35 GB, 1.84 GB and 11.1 GB spent 11.3 s, 13.9 s and 72 s between `dbPrepared` and `dbOpened`, about 6.5-8.4 ms per MB. Below about 1 GB, the replay cost disappears into open-to-open variance: the same rig took 0.4-6.4 s with logs of a few MB. After the 11.1 GB open, the sidecars were drained (12 KB and 0 B). That matches the original report's after-state.
- During the real migration, batches did not slow while the log grew. They stalled once, for about 16 s, when the read ended and the checkpoint caught up. A synthetic write loop did see commits stall for up to 5.4 s each while its log grew past 1 GB.
- `PRAGMA wal_checkpoint=noop` returns a page count through `db.execute`. It is the VFS's approximate count of distinct pages in un-checkpointed transactions, not the file size.
- `PRAGMA wal_checkpoint=truncate` waits for a held reader, then checkpoints everything. It returned 7.5 s after the read ended. But it truncates only the INACTIVE log file. The 1.84 GB log was the active file and kept its bytes, so the next open still spent 13.9 s re-reading them. The active file is reclaimed only after the writer swaps away from it, which takes about 1000 pages of further writes with the inactive file empty, and then a later checkpoint.

The log survives to the next boot only if reads keep it from being reclaimed until the writes stop. The original 187 s boot (#1298) has the same signature. At the measured 6.5 ms/MB, though, 187 s implies a log of roughly 28 GB, which is about 6-7 minutes of blocked checkpoints at 70 MB/s. That session ran several 30-70 s full-scan agent-bridge evals during and after the migration, but its pre-boot log size was not recorded. This attribution is inferred, not measured. The startup record now captures the sizes (`dbFileBytes`).

Other risks: disk exhaustion (minutes of a held read during a migration means tens of GB of OPFS), and a long writer stall at the drain.

Proposed fix, in order of leverage:
1. Back-pressure in bulk writers. Between batches, read the log size (`PRAGMA wal_checkpoint=noop`). Over a threshold (say 256 MB worth of pages), run `PRAGMA wal_checkpoint=truncate` on the writer. It waits out the held read, so the writer pauses instead of growing the log. This needs a way for a `WorkspaceBackfill` pass (or its runner) to reach the writer between batches. The importer would use the same helper.
2. At the end of a bulk pass, drain so that a reload right after it does not re-read the log. One truncate is not enough, because it leaves the active file in place. The drain has to force a swap, for example by lowering `journal_size_limit`, making a small write and checkpointing again. Verify by file size.
3. When the sidecars recorded at boot are large, have the loading screen say it is applying pending database changes, so a long open does not read as a hang.
4. Upstream (wa-sqlite `WriteAhead`): the open re-reads frames an earlier checkpoint already copied, a truncate checkpoint never truncates the active file, and a held snapshot blocks both the checkpoint and the log swap with no bound.
close_reason: Closed on GitHub (issue #1341); reconciled by bd-github-sync.

title: Consistency audit's stranded-rows check is quadratic in the upload queue — pins a reader core for hours after large write bursts
description:
The data-integrity consistency audit's local_server_divergence check counts "stranded local-only" rows with a per-row NOT EXISTS over ps_crud that filters on json_extract(p.data,'$.type') and json_extract(p.data,'$.id'). Nothing can index that, so every candidate block (a live block with no blocks_synced row) rescans the whole upload queue: cost = candidates x queue length.

Measured on a local-only copy of a large graph after the properties migration (1.1M live blocks, 777k ps_crud rows): the original predicate took 263 s for a slice of 200 candidates (about 1.3 s per block), which extrapolates to days for the full count. A one-pass rewrite — collect the pending block ids once and anti-join with NOT IN — computed the full count in 4.5 s. The audit fires at deep idle about 70 s after every page load, so every session longer than a minute had one PowerSync reader worker pinned at 100% CPU for the rest of the session (DB-pool busy time equal to wall clock across 4-hour sessions), with reads falling back to the writer connection.

The copy amplified it (blocks_synced was emptied and a local-only client never drains ps_crud), but the real exposure is the same shape: the device that runs the cell-to-children migration holds roughly as many fresh rows without a blocks_synced echo as it has pending uploads (about 770k on this graph), and each of them scans the queue until it finds its own entry. Even a tenth of that backlog is hours of a pegged core, and the check reruns every session start and every 30 minutes while the backlog lasts. Any large upload backlog (offline editing, imports) hits the same path. Unverified but consistent: 2 of 16 long sessions on one real Android client show pool busy time equal to session length.

Fix direction: materialize the pending ids once and use NOT IN, filtering NULL ids so NOT IN's NULL semantics cannot drop rows, e.g. b.id NOT IN (SELECT json_extract(data,'$.id') FROM ps_crud WHERE json_extract(data,'$.type')='blocks' AND json_extract(data,'$.id') IS NOT NULL). The same pendingClause also guards localRicherWhere and serverAheadWhere in that check. syncObserver/reconcile.ts already selects the same pending-id set, so the predicate should have one owner rather than a second copy. Pin it with a test whose fixture has a non-trivial ps_crud and asserts the counts, plus a query-plan or timing guard so the quadratic form cannot come back.
notes: Implemented in c386db9fcd; ready-for-review PR https://github.com/Stvad/knowledge-medium/pull/1326 targets #1310. Shared NULL-safe pending-block ID SQL in core now serves audit/reconcile/materialize. Full pnpm run check passed (775 files, 11247 tests); audit file 35/35. Seven mutation checks pinned every pending-exclusion arm, NULL/type filters, original correlation, and correlated NOT IN. Awaiting merge; PR carries Fixes #1310.
close_reason: Closed on GitHub (issue #1310); reconciled by bd-github-sync.

title: Require complete property writes in children-backed workspaces
description: Ordinary local property writes in a children-backed workspace must resolve the actual field identity and write matching child rows atomically, or reject. Current HandleTrusting boundary resolution can supply only an encoding schema; setters skip missing identity and commit cell-only values. Separate from workspace admission issue #811. Separate read fallback from write admission, keep storage mode explicit, cover typed setters and raw property bags in create/update, preserve unchanged existing orphan data, and leave live data repair out of scope.
close_reason: Shipped in #1277 (with #1279); live repair done under #1265

title: Audit and repair registered property cells introduced after migration without field children
description:
A read-only production audit of an already children-mode workspace found 68 registered, codec-valid property cells across 17 live blocks with no live matching field child. Repeated scans retained the same gap while new ordinary writes continued to gain children. A completed cell-to-children claim predates these owners' creations or last relevant updates. The affected owner rows match their downloaded staging copies; none has tombstoned field rows explaining the gap. Most examples are place/location properties, plus a daily note and UI metadata. No private identifiers or content are included here.

The ordinary registration audit reports zero unregistered keys and no unreadable bags, so it does not detect this class. Absence of a field currently retains the cell read fallback; this is incomplete child backing, not evidence that those values have already been lost. A definition rename/retype or eventual cell retirement would make the gap more consequential.

Confirmed cause for 63 of the 68 missing fields: an agent used eval with the app on another workspace, calling the ordinary typed geo helper, block.set and addType against an explicit foreign target. The bridge's typed commands refuse such writes, but eval exposes Repo directly. TxEngine.checkWorkspace enforces one workspace per transaction, not that the workspace has its definition registry loaded. Code-owned handles can still encode foreign values without a resolved field identity, so the write becomes cell-only. The remaining five missing fields are separate cases and are not explained by this agent admission. The transaction-level guard is already tracked in #811 (km-lbtm). Build/use a read-only cell-to-field coverage report and a deliberate idempotent missing-only repair; preserve existing live child truth. Verify on a local-only workspace, then re-audit all fields and cells before larger migrations. Related existing consistency work: #1011. The recorded-completion/runbook tradeoff in #1050 was explicitly accepted for the current fleet; this finding is not permission to rebuild that lock.
acceptance_criteria: Identify and regression-test the reachable origin when established; distinguish intentionally cell-only UI state from shared content; report coverage gaps even when every key registers; repair missing backing without overwriting existing child truth; verify zero unintended gaps in a read-only post-repair scan.
close_reason: Repaired: 68 cells on 17 blocks re-materialized by a re-run of the existing operator pass; post-repair read-only audit reads zero gaps. Coverage report merged in #1356. Remaining open cause tracked in #1354.

title: sync: permanent cross-device content divergence when a drift bump lands on a peer's stranded local stamp (I1 violated for content)
description:
Found while triaging the nightly deep-fuzz failure #1162, by `src/data/test/twoRepoConvergence.fuzz.test.ts`. #1164 (merged) took the unsound `user_updated_at` comparison out of that suite's oracle, which is what exposed this; before it, the shrinker stopped at the display-stamp divergence and **masked** this one.

**Two devices end up permanently disagreeing on `content`, at zero clock skew, with no error and no rejection.** A reload does not heal it: the losing content is on the device's own disk.

## Status (2026-10-15)

- Still reproduces on master `4d678c7` (the #1164 merge).
- **Recommended fix: make the equal-stamp skip compare the row, not just the stamp** — see below. A throwaway prototype fixed this divergence and the #1162 display-stamp one, with no migration and no server change. Not built yet; four pieces are open.

## Root cause

The client treats *equal nonzero `updated_at`* as proof that its local row already is the server row (`reconcile.ts` invariant I1, `localHoldsStagedVersion`). That proof does not hold, because **the server merges each column independently**: `apply_block_patches` `COALESCE`s every column from whichever patch writes it, while `updated_at` is one number. A row at version *v* can therefore hold columns from two different authors' patches, and a device whose local row also sits at *v* can differ from it in any column the other author wrote.

Earlier versions of this issue (and #1164's carve-out) attributed the `user_updated_at` half to "metadata is excluded from the version bump by design". **That was wrong, and is not the cause.** `updated_at` advances on every client write (`txEngine.metadataPatch`: `max(now, before + 1)`, unconditionally; `skipMetadata` only skips `user_updated_at`/`updated_by`), and the client never emits a metadata-only patch (`updatePatchChangesBlock` returns before writing). The server's `content_changed` gate only decides whether a strict `+1` is *guaranteed* on the un-drifted path. In the reproduction both patches change content. Content and `user_updated_at` diverge through the same mechanism: they are simply the columns the second author happened to write. `updated_by`, `created_at` and `created_by` are exposed the same way.

## Mechanism

Both devices hold ROOT at server version `…006`.

1. **A** makes two quick edits. Its local `updated_at` bumps (`max(now, before + 1)`) to `…007`, then `…008` — *above* server-now. No clock skew needed.
2. **A's patch** (base `…006`) is **un-drifted**. That branch future-clamps the proposal, then floors it, so the server acks A's write at `…007` — **below A's local `…008`**. A now holds a version the server never issued.
3. **B's patch** (same base) is now **drifted**. The drift bump `greatest(server_now, OLD.updated_at, least(raw_proposed, server_now + max_trusted_skew_ms)) + 1` lands on **`…008` — exactly A's local stamp** — while `COALESCE` writes B's `content` and `user_updated_at` over A's.
4. The echo reaches A at `…008`. A's row is at `…008`, so the drain **skips it in Phase 1**, before decrypting, and calls `decide(false)`, clearing `needs_apply` on the stated premise that equal stamps "prove the content identical". The row is marked resolved, so no later rematerialize or gap pass revisits it — which is what makes this **permanent**.

The existing collision guard (`if NEW.updated_at = raw_proposed then +1`) clears the *current* patch author's (B's) proposed stamp, not a third party's (A's) stranded one, which the server no longer knows about after step 2.

## Recommended fix: content-aware equal-stamp skip

Skip only when the incoming row is actually identical to the local one, not merely equal in `updated_at`. Measured with a throwaway prototype (since reverted):

| check | result |
|---|---|
| this issue's replay | **converges** (A ends on B's content) |
| #1162's display-stamp divergence | **converges** — the "accepted residual" closes |
| uncontended echo of your own write (`concurrentEditConvergence.test.ts`, the cost-floor test) | still **not** re-materialized: no extra write, no FTS/alias/reference trigger re-fire |
| `pnpm run check` | 3 failures, 10 240 passes; all 3 encode the old rule (see below) |

Why the skip exists at all: **cost, not correctness.** Per `concurrentEditConvergence.test.ts`, it avoids re-materializing every echo of your own write and re-firing the triggers. A content-aware skip keeps exactly that: an echo of your own write *is* identical, so it is still skipped.

**It has to be done in both phases.** Changing only Phase 2 (`materialize.ts`, which already holds the full local `beforeRow` and the full staged row) does nothing, because Phase 1 reads only `id, updated_at, deleted` and drops equal-stamp rows before Phase 2 sees them. The prototype lets equal-stamp rows through Phase 1 and compares the 13 synced columns in Phase 2.

**Still open before it can ship:**

1. **Cost (unmeasured).** Every echo of your own write now gets a decrypt (e2ee workspaces) and a batched full-row read inside the write lock, where today it is filtered on the stamp alone. It still avoids the write. Measure it before shipping.
2. **The SQL restatements of I1.** `STAGED_VIEW_GAP_SQL`, `SEED_STAGING_NEEDS_APPLY_SQL` and `blocksAlreadyReflects` still encode stamp-equality = applied; `reconcile.ts` requires them to match the drain. The prototype left them alone and nothing failed, so nothing pins their agreement for this case. Gap detection would under-report a divergent equal-stamp row.
3. **The in-memory cache.** `applyIfNewer` also rejects `<=` snapshots, so disk would converge while an open view kept the stale content until reload. The fuzz oracle compares disk only and cannot see it. The drift-bump migration's own comment proposes the closure: fall back to `setSnapshot` when the cache rejects a sync echo (every row reaching that path has already cleared the in-tx `hasPendingUpload` check).
4. **Tests that encode the old rule**, which failed under the prototype as expected:
   - the `stranded display stamp` canary in `twoRepoConvergence.fuzz.test.ts` — designed to fail when this lands; remove it **and** the `user_updated_at` carve-out with it, so the oracle compares all 13 columns again;
   - `materialize.test.ts` › "skips when a racing write bumps the local stamp to EQUAL…" — its purpose (Phase 2 re-reads in-tx state) still stands, but its scenario asserts keeping divergent local content at an equal stamp, i.e. this bug; give it identical content;
   - `materializeStateful.fuzz.test.ts` — its model predicts the stamp-only rule.

## Other directions (from the first version of this issue)

Still possible, but each is larger and none is needed if the above lands:

1. **Let the un-drifted path trust the proposal up to the skew cap**, as the drifted path does, so no ghost stamp is created. Changes how every row version is assigned, server-side.
2. **Cache/disk gate falls back to `setSnapshot` on a rejected sync echo.** The cache half of this is item 3 above. Alone it would not fix this issue, because the disk gate rejects the row before the cache sees it.
3. **Return the assigned version from the patch RPC** so the author clamps its local stamp down on ack. Protocol change.

## Reproduce

On master:
```
FUZZ_SEED=340680830 \
FUZZ_PATH="30:4:3:3:4:3:4:6:5:7:7:8:7:8:8:13:14:14:17:17:17:17:18:19:18:20:19:19:19:19:19:20:20:20:20:20:20:20" \
pnpm vitest run --testTimeout=600000 src/data/test/twoRepoConvergence.fuzz.test.ts \
  -t "interleaved mutator sequences with random sync points converge to identical state"
```
End state for ROOT, all three at `updated_at=…008`: device A `"!"`, device B `""`, server `""`.

**How reachable:** rarer than the display-stamp divergence, because the two devices must also write *different* content on top of the stamp collision. A 50-minute random-seed deep run did not hit it, so the nightly will usually pass; the replay above reproduces it every time.

## Not verified

`fakeSyncServer` models the trigger rather than executing it. The real migration's un-drifted clamp-then-floor sequence matches, but none of this has been reproduced against real Postgres.
close_reason: Closed on GitHub (issue #1163); reconciled by bd-github-sync.

title: Re-verify the bd-github-sync guards against bd 1.3.0 before allowlisting it
description:
The workspace store is now on bd 1.3.0 (schema v66). `scripts/bd-github-sync.mjs` refuses any bd outside `VERIFIED_BD_VERSIONS` (`1.2.2`), so the beads↔GitHub mirror is stopped until each guard's premise is re-checked against the 1.3.0 engine. Checklist (see also #877):

- push: 1.3.0 short-circuits on content equality (a content hash bound to the external ref, consulted before the remote issue is fetched) rather than the strictly-newer timestamp rule. The pre-pull push filter, its comment and the dry-run wording assume the old rule.
- pull: the re-apply paths guard (5) exists for (doPull's skip guard, buildPullIssueUpdates, typeFromLabels) were byte-identical to 1.2.2 in 1.3.0-rc.2; confirm on the stable tag.
- new seams: doPull requires the store to implement IssueUpdater and stamps an external-authority close-policy marker on every pulled update. Check the first run for either.
- behaviour changes the wrapper could trip on: `bd update --status` enforces close policy; `bd search` includes closed issues by default.
- already confirmed: `bd list --json` / `bd show --json` keep stdout clean under 1.3.0 (warnings go to stderr), so the wrapper's JSON parsing holds.

Then add `1.3.0` to `VERIFIED_BD_VERSIONS`, and judge the first sync from a real run's output.
close_reason: Done in #1161: the sync guards were re-verified against bd 1.3.0 and 1.3.0 is allowlisted; the first 1.3.0 sync ran clean.

title: Operator property migration aborts on a transient sync transition and never automatically resumes
description:
Observed on the first small real-workspace rollout using deployed build 867a7176: the cell-to-children flip succeeds and some child rows are created, but the backfill aborts with the generic download-side sync refusal. Manual retries and a page reload reproduce the failure. The operator tab logs an undo-history-clear warning for a committed write, then the abort one millisecond later. Subsequent read-only inspection finds the workspace in children mode, persisted new rows, connected=true, downloading=false, no download error, and workspaceViewGap=null.

Confirmed code path: Repo.syncViewGap refuses when backfillSyncSettledNow sees disconnected, downloading, or a download error; assertBackfillMayWrite converts this into a transient abort at batch boundaries. The catch logs that it will retry when clear and calls scheduleWorkspaceBackfills, but that scheduler filters to trigger=workspace-open, so this operator-triggered pass is never resumed by that call. The UI tells the user to retry, and repeated manual attempts can hit the same transient window.

Still unverified: which exact download-side flag changed on the operator tab at the abort. The pass causing a download of its own upload echoes is the leading explanation, not yet a measured attribution. This differs from the earlier staging-queue self-echo bug: that predicate was narrowed to exclude equal-stamp echoes; this error comes from the separate download-status predicate.

Fix direction: retain the completeness guard but allow the explicitly invoked run to wait for transient sync to settle and resume under its existing operator claim, with bounded waiting and the existing workspace/session/read-only checks preserved. Durable materialization gaps must still stop rather than loop. At minimum correct the nonexistent automatic-retry promise. Test with a gate that transitions during a committed batch, not the test helper default that settles immediately.
close_reason: Closed on GitHub (issue #1132); reconciled by bd-github-sync.

title: Refuse the one-way flip while ANY cell cannot migrate, not just any KEY
description:
DECISION (Vlad, 2026-09-22): having any cell that cannot migrate should stop the migration proceeding, rather than being reported after the one-way step.

Today the gesture refuses on KEY-level hazards only. `flipBlockedBySynthesis` blocks an un-flipped flip when a key has no definition, can never be given one, is still undefined after synthesis ran, when property bags are unreadable, or when the survey ran during a sync gap. All of those come from `planPropertyDefinitionSynthesis`, which surveys the ~556 distinct KEYS — cheap.

It does not refuse on CELL-level hazards: a value its codec will not decode. Those are found during the backfill, after the flip, and reported as a repair worklist. The large workspace has ~65 of them (km-4zrq).

The asymmetry has no principle behind it — both mean "this workspace can never finish the migration while they exist" — and the cell class is the one the pre-flip audit cannot see, because the key IS registered and only its stored values disagree.

Why it matters more later than it looks now: at `children` the cell is still dual-written and still the read surface, so an unmigrated cell still READS correctly today. That is what makes the current tolerance survivable. It stops being survivable at the cell end-state (the follow-up that retires cells), where an unmigrated value becomes unreachable. Fixing the gate before that lands is much cheaper than fixing the data after.

SHAPE, and the one to avoid: do NOT thread a `dryRun` flag through the backfill pass. That puts two modes in one writer and a guard at every write site. The decision is already a pure function — the pass calls `propertyCellValueRejection(schema, encoded)` per cell — so extract a read-only survey that walks the same candidate SQL and calls the same predicate, and let the pass and the survey share the decision rather than the code path. One owner, two callers.

Behaviour to match the existing precedent: HARD refusal on the way IN (un-flipped), naming the keys and a capped sample of the offending blocks. Once already flipped it stays ADVISORY for the reason the current code documents — refusing there would withhold the backfill from every other key over a handful that can never migrate.

Known limit, worth stating rather than engineering around: the survey cannot be complete on a live workspace, since a bad cell can arrive between the survey and the flip. That is the same class `scanSyncGap` already handles by refusing when the survey was taken over a partial graph, and the pass is a fixpoint besides. This is a "no known bad cells" gate, not a proof.

COST: unmeasured. It adds a full scan plus a decode of every property cell (~365k on the large graph) before the flip. Strictly cheaper than the full migration, which took 613s on that graph including ~760k row inserts, since the survey does the same scan and decode with none of the writes — but measure before promising a number. Instant on a small workspace.

Relates to km-4zrq (the cells this would have caught) and to the post-run half already shipped in GitHub PR 1106, which counts and names cells the pass skipped.
close_reason: Closed on GitHub (issue #1122); reconciled by bd-github-sync.

title: Repair the cells that store a list under a scalar string codec
description:
A property in the large workspace is declared with a SCALAR string codec while ~65 of its cells hold a LIST. The migration refuses every one of them: they land in `failureCount`, they are named in the repair worklist, and they can never become child-backed until either the value or the declared preset is fixed. Measured on a full copy of that graph — the converged sweep reports 108,444 of 108,509 property-carrying blocks accepted, and the 65-block shortfall is exactly these cells.

BLOCKER for flipping the large workspace (Vlad, 2026-09-22). The flip itself would still complete, but it is ONE-WAY, and these cells would sit cell-only on the other side of it while every re-run keeps reporting them.

The trap worth recording: `audit-properties` does NOT catch this class. The key IS registered — it has a definition and resolves fine — so the audit reports the workspace clean while these cells are unmigratable. The pre-flip audit checks for keys with no definition; this is a key whose definition disagrees with its stored values, which only the migration run (or a decode) surfaces. Anyone treating a clean audit as "ready to flip" will be surprised by the failure count.

Two repairs, and which one is right depends on whether the list or the declaration is the truth:
- If the values are correct, WIDEN the definition to the list preset. A widening is the safe direction; narrowing throws on every cell that does not fit (see seedIdentityLedger.ts).
- If the scalar declaration is correct, repair the values. `setProperty` with a value the codec accepts is the right shape, and on a flipped workspace it dual-writes the machinery, so repairing and migrating that key are a single act.

Identifying the key: the migration names the failing keys in its own report (the pass console-warns the block ids and per-key reasons, capped), so run the gesture and read the worklist rather than guessing. Key name deliberately left out of this issue — it is user graph data and this tracker is public.
close_reason: Repaired: the pre-flip cell survey now reports 0 rejected cells

title: SQLite connection wedges for minutes during the properties migration, and a reload does not clear it
description:
During the one-time properties migration on a ~350k-block graph the SQLite
connection intermittently stops serving ANY operation for minutes, and a page
reload does not clear it.

SIGNATURE (this is how to recognise it)
`repo.metrics().dbContention.busyMs` grows 1:1 with wall clock while the deltas
for `calls`, `getAll`, `getOptional` and `execute` are all ZERO — one acquisition
held and never released, with 10-15 operations queued behind it. A bare
`select 1` then times out. Observed stalls: 90 s, 137 s, 316 s, 756 s.

REPRODUCTION
Import a ~350k-block graph into a local-only workspace, flip
`properties_migration` to 'children', run the palette migration, and leave it
alone. It commits batches steadily (~26 blocks/s) and then stops.

RECOVERY
A page RELOAD does not clear it — the next page's first queries queue behind the
same jam. Navigating every client off the origin for ~20 s does clear it, which
points at the PowerSync SharedWorker (`enableMultiTabs: true`) rather than the
page. After that the pass resumes normally.

WHY IT MATTERS MORE THAN THE PASS'S OWN COST
Steady-state the pass runs at ~26 blocks/s, which is ~70 minutes for 108k
candidate blocks. The stalls are what turn that into hours. Two operator-facing
consequences:
  - the progress banner says "If it looks stuck, reload it", and reloading does
    NOT unstick it;
  - while wedged the gate's own "Release the claim" button silently does
    nothing, because releasing the claim is a write. The operator is left with a
    modal, a button that appears dead, and no working instruction.

RULED OUT
  - Tab throttling. A 1 s `setTimeout` chain and a `MessageChannel` ping-pong
    running side by side both read p50 1000 ms / max 1004 ms straight through a
    stall, so timers are not clamped and the main thread is not blocked.
  - The OPFS access-handle pool. While wedged both `.ahp-*` pools show 10 of 10
    slots free and the `-journal` sidecar is 0 bytes, so nothing is mid-write at
    the file level.
  - The pass's own read/write pattern. It reproduces identically on two
    different implementations — the per-row one and a rewritten one that issues
    two batched reads and two multi-row inserts per batch.

SCOPE / CAVEAT
Seen so far only on an imported local-only copy driven through the in-app
browser pane, on one machine. Not yet reproduced against the production client,
and not yet attempted on a second browser. Worth confirming before assuming
every device will hit it, but the migration is exactly the workload that would.
close_reason:
Harness artifact, not a product defect. Every observation came from an automated browser tab that was not displayed. A hidden tab pauses requestIdleCallback, requestAnimationFrame and paint-driven IntersectionObserver while setTimeout keeps firing, and this app schedules through scheduleIdle/scheduleDeepIdle — so the pass crawled and its pauses looked like the connection wedging. My throttling check sampled setTimeout and MessageChannel, neither of which is rIC, which is why it came back clean and I read the stalls as a product bug.

Re-run in a headed, genuinely visible Chrome on the same ~350k-block graph: the pass holds 198-202 blocks/s with linear progress and ZERO stalls, across three runs. Same database, same machine. rIC and rAF sampled per run confirm they fire normally there.

The recovery observation that pointed at the SharedWorker ('a reload does not clear it, navigating every client off the origin does') is explained the same way: the new page was starved exactly as the old one, so nothing changed until the tab was actually looked at.

Lesson recorded in reference_measuring_a_bridged_tab_is_throttled. Anything perf-sensitive in this app must be measured in a visible browser, with rIC and rAF sampled so each run says for itself whether it was starved.

title: A broken list definition has no repair target the picker offers
description:
MEASURED 2026-09-19 reviewing PR #1060.

STATE. A property definition on a preset that no longer builds (extension not
installed on this device, or synced from a client that had it), whose codec
was member-wise with verbatim member text - codecs.list(codecs.string), the
shape the kernel's own string-list produces. One consumer holds two members.
The schema editor renders the 'plugin contributing preset ... is not loaded'
notice next to a LIVE type picker, so the app offers re-typing as the repair
for exactly this state.

MEASURED: every one of the nine pickable targets refuses.

  -> string  REFUSED (1 lost)      -> date    REFUSED (2)
  -> number  REFUSED (2)           -> url     REFUSED (1)
  -> boolean REFUSED (2)           -> enum    REFUSED (2)
  -> list    REFUSED (2)           -> ref     REFUSED (2)
                                   -> refList REFUSED (2)

The only preset that commits is string-list, which is hideFromPicker.

Threshold is exact: a ONE-member broken text-list still escapes, a broken
scalar is fine, a broken JSON-spelled list is fine. It is specifically
member-wise + verbatim member text + two or more members.

EACH REFUSAL IS CORRECT - narrowing a two-member list to a scalar does lose a
value, and #1024 says refuse. Before PR #1060 these committed and silently
dropped every member but the first, which is the bug that PR fixed. So this
is not a regression in correctness; it is a capability gap the correctness
fix exposed.

The refusal's advice is unachievable: 'Fix or remove those values first, or
choose a type that can hold them' - the values are in property-child rows the
outline does not surface as such, and the one type that can hold them is not
offered.

ROOT CAUSE, and why a real fix is not just unhiding a preset. The no-codec
branch is half converted: the COUNTING side trusts the cell it last published,
while the WRITING side still re-reads the children's text with no codec
(convertValueChildContent with a null from-schema can only take the text
route). Counting trusts the cell; converting does not.

FIX DIRECTIONS, in order of how much they buy:
1. when there is no old codec, re-materialize the value children FROM THE CELL
   under the new schema instead of re-reading their text. Any repair to a type
   that can hold the cell's values then succeeds, and the branch stops being a
   special case that can only refuse.
2. drop hideFromPicker from string-list so a lossless target exists at all.
3. at minimum, stop saying 'choose a type that can hold them' when the picker
   offers none.

ESCAPES THAT EXIST TODAY: restore the missing plugin, or delete the schema
(the button warns 'Their values stay; the editor falls back to an inferred
type', so the data survives but the definition does not).

WHERE. valuesLostBy / heldValueCount and applyToParent in
src/data/internals/propertyDefinitionChangeProcessor.ts;
selectablePresets in src/components/propertyEditors/.
close_reason: Closed on GitHub (issue #1077); reconciled by bd-github-sync.

title: [BUG] a JSON-spelled value child stores a span merely quoted, not escaped
description:
MEASURED 2026-09-18 while fixing the conversion route order (km-st17).

A value child whose codec spells values as JSON (the default branch of
encodedValueToContent in src/data/propertyChildren.ts: the generic list
preset, enum, anything not string/url/ref/date/number/boolean) stores a
span-shaped string member with its PARENS INTACT.

Measured: a generic list property set to ['((a-id))'] stores the value row
content as "((a-id))" - JSON.stringify and nothing else. reference_target_id
is null, so the WHOLE-BLOCK reader is not fooled.

WHY THAT IS NOT ENOUGH. The escaping rationale at SPAN_OPENERS_RE in the same
file says it explicitly: quoting alone only stops the whole-block parser, and
the INLINE reader (plugins/references/referenceParser) scans spans anywhere in
content, so a merely-quoted span is still an inline reference that a rename
rewrites - silently editing the value. That is the hazard escapeContent exists
to prevent, and it is applied only on the string/url branch.

So the two spellings disagree about a rule that is not spelling-specific:
needsEscape/escapeContent guard the string branch, and the JSON branch has no
equivalent.

NOT YET VERIFIED: the rename-rewrites-it half. The storage is measured; the
consequence is taken from that comment rather than reproduced, because it
needs the references plugin driven end to end. Worth reproducing before
picking a fix.

FIX DIRECTION. Either apply the opener-escape to the JSON branch too (the
envelope is already a JSON string literal, so escaping its openers keeps it
parseable and self-identifying, exactly as on the string side), or move the
verbatim-content-loses-value question above the per-codec switch so one owner
answers it for every spelling. The second matches the repo's one-owner shape
and is why this is filed rather than patched inline.

WHERE. encodedValueToContent / needsEscape / escapeContent in
src/data/propertyChildren.ts.

title: A peer device gives no sign the graph is locked until someone tries to write
description:
The migration write-lock refuses edits while the cell-to-children pass holds a workspace's claim.

The device RUNNING the migration is covered: the gesture reports into a blocking modal that cannot be dismissed until the run reports an outcome, and that says the workspace is not accepting edits.

A PEER device has nothing. It learns the graph is locked by attempting an edit and reading the refusal toast, which is reactive — the pass can run for minutes with no sign until someone types — and each attempt raises its own toast rather than replacing the last one.

WHAT IS MISSING: a surface on the peer that appears while a claim is in flight and says the graph is not accepting edits, with the release command beside it.

WHY IT DID NOT COME WITH THE LOCK: the peer has no gesture to hang it off, so it needs the claim WATCHED rather than read per transaction. The claim block does not exist when the workspace opens and arrives mid-session via sync, which is the shape that has already produced a bug in this area — a subscription that reads a value only at render never re-evaluates, and one that starts on an absent row may not fire when the row lands.

SHAPE: a reactive read of the claim (the predicate the pipeline uses is a point read and is not reactive), a mounted surface, and the refusal toast given a stable id so repeated attempts replace rather than stack.
close_reason: Closed on GitHub (issue #1058); reconciled by bd-github-sync.

title: Block graph writes for the duration of the properties migration, instead of guarding each what-if case
description:
DECISION (Vlad, 2026-09-17): stop handling "what if X happens during the flip" case by case. While the migration runs, the graph does not accept user writes. One rule, enforced once, instead of a growing set of per-gesture guards.

WHY THE PRIMITIVE ALREADY EXISTS. commitPipeline already has a read-only gate: `if (isReadOnly && !scopeAllowedInReadOnly(scope)) throw new ReadOnlyError(scope)`. Three properties make it the right seam:
- it sits at the TRANSACTION boundary, so it covers every gesture without any of them knowing about the migration;
- it is ABOVE the same-tx processor pass and above the `isReplay` skip, so it catches undo and redo REPLAY, which a same-tx refusal structurally cannot (#1052);
- `scopeAllowedInReadOnly` already lets UiState and UserPrefs through, so navigation, panels and view state keep working. The app is non-writing, not frozen.

WHAT THIS SUBSUMES, and what can then be deleted:
- #1029's definition-edit refusal, shipped in #1043, becomes redundant: a blanket block covers renames and re-types along with everything else. Its ~57 lines and the predicate beside the claim would go, keeping only the claim read the new gate needs.
- #1042 (deletion during the backfill) - blocked, no special case.
- #1052 (replay bypasses every same-tx refusal) - blocked, and this is the one that is otherwise hard: replay deliberately skips same-tx processors, so no processor-level guard can ever see it.
- #1050's third route (a definition created mid-run, invisible to the pass's frozen resolver) - blocked.

WHAT IT DOES NOT SUBSUME, and what gets HARDER:
- #1050's core question - when does the block LIFT - becomes load-bearing rather than a corner. Today a stranded or prematurely released claim blocks renames; under this policy it blocks the whole graph. "A recorded completion is not completeness" stops being a nicety.
- THE ESCAPE HATCH IS ITSELF A WRITE. The documented recovery for a claim nobody will release is "delete the claim block on the Migrations page". Deleting a block is a BlockDefault write, which the block refuses. The release gesture has to be exempt from the lock it releases, or a dead claimant bricks the graph with no way out from inside the app. This is the piece most likely to be discovered late; design it first.
- THE MIGRATION'S OWN WRITES need the same exemption. The pass writes under BlockDefault deliberately, to keep the read-only gate and the seed-definition guard, so flipping `repo.isReadOnly` would block the migration itself. The lock needs to be a distinct condition with an exemption for the pass's transactions, not a reuse of the read-only flag.
- LAGGING AND OFFLINE PEERS are unchanged. The claim is synced data, so a device that has not received it keeps writing. Inherent to enforcing through synced state; worth stating rather than solving.

A CONSEQUENCE WORTH TAKING: #1049 (a definition edit during the confirmation dialog, leaving the gesture on a stale plan) was awkward because taking the claim before the dialog was declined - "a claim held across a user-length pause blocks every other device". Under this policy, blocking every other device IS the intent, so starting the lock at the dialog becomes an ordinary choice rather than a design problem.

SHAPE TO BUILD: a workspace-scoped migration lock read from the same claim block, checked beside the read-only gate in commitPipeline, with exemptions for the pass's own transactions and for the claim-release gesture; plus a UI state that says what is happening and how to get out of it.
close_reason: Closed on GitHub (issue #1057); reconciled by bd-github-sync.

title: [BUG] list -> string-list re-type reads a JSON member as its own spelling, mangling the value
description:
The mirror of #1024, found while closing it, and NOT fixed there.

MEASURED (2026-09-17, on the #1024 branch). A `list` property (generic preset,
`codecs.list(codecs.unsafeIdentity())`) whose members are the strings x and y
stores them as JSON text ("x", "y"). Re-typed to `string-list`, the string
member codec reads that text VERBATIM, so the member becomes the 3-character
string "x" — quotes included — instead of x. Silent: no report, no refusal,
nothing unreadable. Round trip string-list -> list -> string-list does not
return the list it started with.

WHY THE #1024 FIX DOES NOT COVER IT. That fix converts a value child by reading
its TEXT under the new codec first and only falling back to the codec that WROTE
the text when the text will not read. Here the text reads — the string codec
accepts anything — so the fallback never runs. Emptying is loud enough to catch;
mangling is not.

WHAT MAKES IT A SEPARATE DECISION. Preferring the value route whenever both
routes succeed fixes this pair and CHANGES another that is deliberately pinned:
`refList` -> `string-list` currently keeps the visible ((a-id)) span as escaped
text (test: "re-encodes EVERY member, not just the first"), and the value route
would give the bare id a-id instead. Both are defensible and the two cases want
opposite answers, so the ordering rule is a judgement call rather than a bug fix.

WHERE. `convertValueChildContent` in src/data/propertyChildren.ts owns the route
order. A test asserting the current (mangling) behaviour sits in
src/data/propertyDefinitionChange.test.ts so a change to it fails loudly.
close_reason: Closed on GitHub (issue #1055); reconciled by bd-github-sync.

title: A replayed definition rename bypasses every same-tx refusal, and is not the self-healing case the multi-tab undo gap was accepted for
description:
Raised by review on PR #1043. This does NOT reopen #1007's decision; it puts a consequence on the table that the decision did not have.

WHAT WAS ACCEPTED. #1007 closed as accepted: UndoManager is per Repo, so a pass that drops a workspace's undo history clears it in the clearing tab only, and another tab keeps its pre-pass entries. The acceptance is recorded at both history-drop sites, and its stated consequence is that "a replayed pre-pass snapshot is a stale cell over live children, projected away by the next write to them" - self-healing, which is what makes accepting it reasonable.

WHY A DEFINITION ROW IS NOT THAT CASE. Replay is not an ordinary write: commitPipeline skips ALL same-tx processors when isReplay is true, by design, so a replayed row reaches the database with no fan-out and no refusal. For a content or cell row that is fine and self-healing as recorded. For a PROPERTY DEFINITION row it is not:

- the replay restores a previous name or preset on the definition, which moves what the registry publishes;
- core.migratePropertyDefinition never runs, so no consuming cell is re-keyed and no value child is re-encoded - the same half-applied state that processor exists to prevent;
- nothing projects it away, because the definition row is not derived from anything. A later write to a consuming block does not repair a definition's name.

DURING THE BACKFILL THIS IS THE #1029 HAZARD, REACHED AROUND THE LOCK. PR #1043 refuses definition renames and re-types while the cell-to-children claim is in flight, but that refusal is a same-tx processor, so a replay in another tab walks straight past it. The remaining batches then resolve cell keys against a registry the replay moved, the old name answers to nothing, and materializePropertyChildrenForExistingRow skips it as unregistered - permanently, for every parent the pass had not yet reached.

REACHABILITY. Two tabs of one device (or a peer device), the other tab holding an undo entry that renamed or re-typed a definition, and a cmd-Z there during the multi-minute backfill. Narrow, but the migration runbook expects other tabs to exist - its own dialog tells the operator to reload them afterwards, which is an instruction that lands after the window, not before it.

DIRECTIONS, none chosen.
- Refuse replays for a workspace while a cell-to-children claim is active. Small and targeted, but it makes cmd-Z silently do nothing for minutes across every tab, which is a product decision.
- Refuse replay of a PROPERTY DEFINITION row generally, claim or no claim, on the grounds that a definition row replayed without its fan-out is half a change at any time. Wider, and arguably the real rule - the same argument applies to a replayed rename with no migration running at all.
- Re-judge #1007's acceptance now that a non-self-healing consequence exists, e.g. adopt its option (a) shared clear epoch after all.
- Accept again, explicitly for this consequence too, and record it at the refusal.

The third and fourth are cheap; the point of this bead is that the choice should be made knowing the difference between a stale cell and a stranded key.
close_reason: Covered by PR #1059 (Vlad, 2026-09-18): every device holding the claim row runs an UndoManager history drop for the length of the claim, and undo/redo return false while a drop is in progress, so a replayed definition rename in another tab or on a peer is refused for the whole backfill. Residual accepted: an offline peer never receives the claim, and the window between the claim's write and its arrival. The #1007 consequence recorded here, that a replayed definition row is not self-healing, stays true.

title: The definition-edit lock lifts while cell-only consumers remain: a recorded completion is not completeness
description:
Raised by review on the #1029 work (PR #1043). That PR refuses definition renames and re-types while a properties:cell-to-children claim is IN FLIGHT. The claim is a proxy for "this workspace still has cell-only consumers", and this bead is the proxy's other edge: the claim can be gone while consumers remain, so the lock lifts over a half-migrated graph.

TWO WAYS IN, verified in the code rather than assumed.

(1) A RELEASED CLAIM AFTER A PARTIAL RUN. Repo.withOperatorBackfillClaim hands the claim back on every exit it controls, including a mid-run abort — a deferred batch, a workspace turned read-only, a throw. The graph is then flipped, partly backfilled, and unlocked.

(2) A RECORDED COMPLETION THAT IS NOT COMPLETE. A run whose outcome is 'ran' records completion even when individual values failed to convert; the operator is told to repair those values and run again, and the claim carries a completedAt from the first run. Both a completed claim and an absent one read as "not in flight", which is what the lock keys on.

(3) A DEFINITION CREATED MID-RUN. Related enough to live here rather than in its own bead, because it has the same ending. The backfill captures ONE property resolver for the whole run, deliberately (a per-call resolver cost a resolve per cell key over ~650k rows) — see the resolveNameSchema comment in Repo. That resolver is a snapshot, so a definition created after it froze is invisible: namesPendingMaterialization keeps excluding the key as unregistered, and the run can record completion having never migrated those cells. The definition-edit lock cannot catch this one either, and deliberately so: it lets CREATES through, because that is what allows the gesture's own orphan-definition synthesis to mint under the claim it holds. Telling a user create from the gesture's own would need an explicit signal threaded from the gesture into the processor, which is the kind of back door that ends up load-bearing.

WHAT IT COSTS. In every case the cells stay cell-only under a REGISTERED key in a child-backed workspace. Nothing is lost while the workspace is at 'children': the cell is still dual-written and still the read surface. What it costs is (a) a definition rename before the retry now strands those cells permanently, which is exactly the hazard #1029 exists to prevent, and (b) the cell end-state step cannot safely run until they are migrated. It is detectable — audit-properties finds unmigrated keys, and the end-state step is measurement-gated — so this is a correctness gap with a detector, not silent data loss.

DIRECTIONS, none chosen.
- Persist an "incomplete migration" marker distinct from the claim, cleared only by a run that migrated everything, and gate the lock on that instead. This is durable per-graph state, which #1013 deliberately removed elsewhere, and it needs an owner for the case where the operator decides the unconvertible values are junk and will never convert.
- Do not release the claim on an abort that has already written, leaving the documented "delete the claim block" recovery as the way out. Cheaper, but it changes the claim's mutual-exclusion story and strands claims by design rather than by accident.
- Re-read the resolver per batch instead of per run, which closes (3) alone, at a measured cost the original comment says was the reason for the snapshot.
- Accept, and say so at the refusal's declaration.

Worth deciding before the first flip on a real graph.
close_reason: Accepted: covered by the #671 runbook; reopen if the fleet grows

title: A definition edit during the migration confirmation dialog leaves the gesture running on a stale synthesis plan
description:
Raised by review on the #1029 work (PR #1043) and deliberately not fixed there: that PR refuses definition edits while the cell-to-children claim is ACTIVE, and this window is before the claim exists.

THE WINDOW. The properties-migration action computes its synthesis plan and its block count BEFORE opening the confirmation dialog, and takes the graph-wide claim only after the dialog returns (src/plugins/properties-migration/action.ts). Between those two points sits a user-length pause during which no claim exists, so #1029's refusal does not fire.

WHAT AN EDIT IN THAT WINDOW COSTS. A definition renamed or re-typed from another tab or another device in that pause leaves its old name's cells with no definition. Those cells are not in the plan, which was taken while the name still resolved, so orphan synthesis mints nothing for them. The flip then lands, and the backfill excludes unregistered keys from its work list — so the key is not migrated and is not even reported as unmigrated. Re-running the whole gesture later does recover it, by planning synthesis for the now-orphaned name, but it mints a SECOND definition rather than restoring the first, so the property is split in two.

WHAT SYNTHESIS ALREADY RE-CHECKS, AND WHY IT IS NOT ENOUGH. applyPropertyDefinitionSynthesis deliberately re-asks, inside its writing transaction, whether each planned key is still orphaned and whether the deterministic id is still ours to write through. That covers a key that GAINED a definition during the pause. It cannot cover a key that LOST one, because such a key is absent from the plan and nothing iterates over what the plan does not name.

WHY THE OBVIOUS FIX IS NOT OBVIOUS. Taking the claim before the dialog is already declined at the call site, for recorded reasons: a claim held across a user-length pause blocks every other device in the graph while a dialog sits open, and a tab closed at the dialog strands it. Re-deriving the plan under the claim is also declined at its own declaration, because it would ask a different question than the one the user answered.

FIX DIRECTIONS, none chosen:
- Re-plan under the claim and REFUSE (not silently proceed) when the candidate set differs from the one that was consented to. Preserves consent, fails loudly, costs one extra workspace scan per gesture, and needs its own message.
- Accept and record it, on the grounds that the pause is short, the edit has to come from another tab or device, and re-running the gesture recovers the key at the cost of a split definition.
- Narrow the plan's exposure by computing the counts pre-dialog but the candidate list post-claim, if the dialog can be phrased so the counts it showed stay true.

Worth deciding before the first flip on a real graph rather than after.
close_reason: Accepted: covered by the #671 runbook; reopen if the fleet grows

title: A definition edit during the cell-to-children backfill strands cell-only consumers
description:
The flip runbook is flip THEN backfill, so for the whole duration of the chunked backfill a workspace is `children` while many parents are still cell-only. `core.migratePropertyDefinition` finds consumers through their FIELD ROWS, so a rename or re-type during that window updates only the parents the backfill has already reached.

WHY THAT IS PERMANENT, not merely late. After the rename, subsequent backfill batches resolve each cell key against the CURRENT registry, where the old name answers to nothing. `materializePropertyChildrenForExistingRow` skips an unregistered key (deliberately — it never deletes), so those parents never get field rows for it, and the value sits under a dead key that nothing else will ever visit. An incompatible re-type is the same story through the decode branch: the cell value no longer decodes under the current codec, and the backfill reports and skips it.

NOT A REGRESSION. The pre-#1013 same-tx rename processor used the identical consumer probe — `reference_target_id IN (...) AND is_field_form = 1` — and so did the deferred batch it replaced. Neither ever reached a cell-only parent. What changed is that there is no longer a deferred pass running minutes later, but that pass had the same blind spot, so it never covered this either.

OPTIONS.

(a) REFUSE definition renames and re-types while a `properties:cell-to-children` claim is active for the workspace. The claim already lives in synced data (`graphBackfillClaim.ts`), so the check is cheap, and the processor already refuses for two other reasons. Heavy-handed — the backfill can run for a long time — but a once-per-graph migration window is exactly where that trade is normally accepted.
(b) Include cell-only owners of the old key in the atomic fan-out. Correct but expensive: finding them means a `json_each` scan over the workspace's bags, unindexed, inside the user's editing transaction.
(c) Make the BACKFILL tolerant instead: have it materialize a cell key whose name no longer resolves by looking for a definition that recently held it. Needs a record of recent renames, which is the durable state #1013 removed.

(a) looks right, and it belongs with the flip work rather than with the re-encode: the hazard is a property of the runbook's flip-then-backfill ordering, and the fix has to be paired with whatever the operator does when the refusal fires.

Raised by review on the #1013 work.
close_reason: Closed on GitHub (issue #1029); reconciled by bd-github-sync.

title: Preset change with an unchanged codec.type schedules no re-encode, silently emptying a list
description:
Switching a property between two presets that share a `codec.type` schedules NO
re-encode, so its existing value children stay in the old grammar and are then
read under the new codec. For the two list presets this silently EMPTIES the
list.

MEASURED (2026-09-16, on the km-h1hy branch): a `string-list` property with
members `x` and `y` republished as `codecs.list(codecs.unsafeIdentity())`
produced no migration at all — no child rewrite, no cell change. The detector
(`changedPropertyDefinitionFacts`) compares `codecType`, and both presets carry
`'list'`.

WHY IT BITES NOW. Before the multi-value value-child shape, both presets stored
the whole array as JSON text in ONE child, so switching between them changed
nothing on disk. At member grain they differ: `string-list` stores a string
member VERBATIM (`abc`), while the generic `list` preset's identity member codec
stores it as JSON text (`"abc"`). So after a switch, `abc` is read as JSON,
`JSON.parse` fails, and the projection drops the member. Every member of every
affected block, silently, on the next reprojection.

The same hole is open to any custom list preset that changes its inner codec
without changing that discriminator.

NOT A NEW CLASS. `seedIdentityLedger.ts` already records that `codec.type` alone
is the wrong key — it freezes `presetId` AND `codecType` precisely because "a
codec whose `type` string moved under a stable preset id" and "an optional preset
and its required twin sharing a discriminator" are both invisible to one column.
The migration DETECTOR never learned the same lesson.

FIX DIRECTION: put the preset identity (or the member encoding) into the
discriminator alongside `codecType`, mirroring the ledger's two columns.
`PropertyDefinitionMetadata` does not carry `presetId` today, so this is registry
plumbing — the projector builds the metadata from the definition row, which does
store `presetId` — rather than a one-line change, which is why it is filed
separately from the multi-value work that surfaced it.

Worth checking while in there: whether the deferred pass can even re-encode
across this change, since both sides decode the same `properties_json` array but
disagree about the CHILD text, and the pass re-encodes children rather than
cells.
close_reason: Closed on GitHub (issue #1024); reconciled by bd-github-sync.

title: Make the property-definition codec re-encode synchronous and same-tx
description:
DECISION (Vlad, 2026-09-16): make the property-definition CODEC re-encode
synchronous and same-tx, on the initiating client only, replacing the deferred
per-device pass. Other clients receive the already-re-encoded rows by sync. The
user always sees a coherent state, and the pass stops being a data migration at
all.

WHY THIS IS THE RIGHT SHAPE

The rename half already works this way: `core.migratePropertyRename` re-keys
every consuming parent's cell in the same `repo.tx` that edits the definition
block, as ONE undoable step. The codec half was deferred instead, and every
problem this pass has had comes from that deferral, not from the re-encode.

THE STATED BLOCKER IS WRONG. `propertyRenameProcessor.ts` says a codec change
"needs the NEW codec, which the same-tx registry snapshot can't build". True of
the REGISTRY, which is frozen at tx start — but the codec does not come from the
registry. `tryBuildSchema(row, presets, metadata)` in `userSchemasService.ts`
builds it from the definition block's own row plus the value-preset map, and
nothing else. The rename processor already reads old/new NAME from the block's
before/after for exactly this reason; the same move yields the before/after
CODEC.

SCALE. The deferred pass chunks at 100 parents because it must survive
interruption. Synchronously it touches only blocks that set that ONE property —
thousands at the outside, one SQLite write transaction, well under a second. The
~650k figure that motivated chunking belongs to the props-as-blocks
cell->children backfill, a different pass over the whole workspace.

PLAN

1. Fold the codec re-encode into the same-tx definition-change processor
   (rename `core.migratePropertyRename` accordingly — a combined rename+retype
   is one edit and wants one processor). Resolve the before/after schema with
   `tryBuildSchema` from the definition block's before/after rows; the preset
   map has to reach `SameTxCtx`.
2. Keep the processor LAST in `KERNEL_SAME_TX_PROCESSORS`. The rename half
   already depends on running after MATERIALIZE/PROJECT: otherwise MATERIALIZE
   re-reads the re-keyed cell, sees the dropped key as a user deletion, and
   tombstones the field rows. The codec half inherits that constraint.
3. Delete the deferred machinery: `propertyDefinitionBaseline.ts` and its
   tests, `schedulePropertyDefinitionMigrations` /
   `runPropertyDefinitionMigrations` / `runPropertyDefinitionMigrationBatch`,
   drift re-detection, the sync-gap gating on this pass, plan validation and
   supersession checks, re-detect coalescing, and the whole undo interaction
   this pass accumulated (clear, revision watermark, clear epoch,
   `invalidateReplays`, the record-time epoch check).
4. Leave the `WorkspaceBackfill` runner's own undo clearing alone — the flip IS
   an explicit once-per-graph migration and that is where Vlad's "discard undo
   forcefully and notify" applies.

ACCEPTED, AND ALREADY THE ANSWER FOR RENAMES

A device offline across the codec change, which created rows under the old
codec, is not re-encoded by anyone. That is what the durable baseline existed
for. `propertyRenameProcessor.ts` already records the same residual for renames
and leaves it to a content-driven reconcile; this makes codecs consistent with
renames rather than opening a new gap. The baseline was nearly cut before merge
on #788 for these reasons.

CONSEQUENCES FOR OPEN ISSUES

#1006 (a partially applied re-encode leaves no record a sweep is owed) and
#1007 (the undo clear does not reach other tabs) are both artifacts of the
deferred per-device pass and should close as no-longer-applicable once this
lands.

A completed implementation of the REJECTED alternative — suspending the
workspace's undo for the pass's duration — is saved at
`~/Downloads/km-999-suspension-approach.patch`. Parts of it (an
`UndoManager.suspend` and the backfill runner wiring) may be worth salvaging
for the flip; the rest is moot under this design.
close_reason: Closed on GitHub (issue #1013); reconciled by bd-github-sync.

title: Multi-value properties as N sibling value children, before the flip so the backfill builds the final shape once
description:
Settled direction (design doc §5/§9, owner's call): a multi-value property is N sibling value children under one field row, a refList is N `((id))` value children, and the projection is a list AGGREGATE over the siblings rather than scalar first-wins. Today the shipped materializer serializes any non-string encoded value into ONE value child as JSON text, and the doc defers the N-children shape to "a follow-up slice". This bead pulls it forward to BEFORE the first flip.

WHY BEFORE THE FLIP. The cell -> children backfill is the one pass that visits every property cell and builds its child rows; whatever shape it builds is what every workspace holds from then on. Landing N-children after the flip means a SECOND uploading data migration over every array-valued cell in every workspace: delete the JSON child, create N member children, and change the projection under a fleet that has already been reading the old shape (an un-upgraded device reads N plain siblings under a list codec as unparseable, and the key goes unset there until it upgrades). Measured on the largest live graph on 2026-09-16, over valid non-empty bags of live blocks: array-valued cells are roughly 128,000 of about 360,000 property cells (a third), carrying about 159,000 members. The two largest keys by far are the kernel's own `types` (about 57k cells) and `alias` (about 26k), followed by importer-namespaced keys; `block-type:properties`, the refList on every type block, is in the set too. That second migration would be the same order of work as the backfill itself. Doing it first costs a design pass and an implementation; doing it second costs that PLUS a claimed, chunked, undo-clearing migration and a transition period where both shapes must decode.

Two further reasons the JSON-text child is the wrong resting state, both already recorded elsewhere: value children are ordinary editable blocks, and JSON text in an editable block is the "stringified JSON inside a property" lock-in the properties-model-evolution doc names as the painful kind of migration; and a refList stored as JSON ids is bare-id storage, which the design rejects for scalars as unvalidatable by construction (no grammar, so no way to tell prose from a ref), and which the merge-retarget rewrite cannot reach the way it reaches a `((id))` span.

SCOPE. Three kernel presets are multi-valued: `list` (identity codec over unknown members), `string-list` (`types`, `alias`), `ref-list`. Materialize: one child per member, sibling order = list order. Project: aggregate the parsed siblings into the array in sibling order. Dual-write and the deferred re-encode pass follow the same rule.

DESIGN QUESTIONS the pass has to settle (do not decide them here):
- Order: sibling rank IS the list order; what a reorder gesture on value children means for the cell.
- Dedupe: the merge policy already collapses divergent siblings to a content-deduped set. For a list that is set semantics, which is what `types` and `alias` want; whether a `list` preset may hold duplicates, or is declared a set, decides whether divergence and multiplicity are the same shape (they collapse cleanly if it is a set).
- Unset vs empty: zero children under a live field row already reads as "key omitted / defaultValue"; for a list preset defaultValue is `[]`, so empty list and unset coincide, which is fine unless some reader distinguishes them.
- Member grain: a `list` member can itself be an object; that member child holds JSON text, still, but at member grain. Whether that is acceptable or whether object members want a different shape.
- `types`: a string-list of type ids today. Whether it becomes a refList to type blocks (then each member is a `((typeId))` span with backlinks for free, and the bare-id problem goes away), or stays string-list with id-shaped strings. Live-data-affecting; owner's call.
- The two derived-column and recognition paths that key on "value position plus owning codec being ref/refList" must read a member child the same way they read a scalar ref child.
- The alias-seat hazard filed as km-jpj2 (JSON-family values shaped like a wikilink mint a phantom alias seat) largely disappears for list members once they stop being JSON text; check whether anything of it survives at member grain.

FALLBACK, if the flip must go first for some other reason: exempt the three multi-value presets from materialize, dual-write and the pass's candidate query until this lands. The pass is create-only over "cell keys with no field row", so once the shape lands a re-run of the EXISTING pass builds the missing children; no new migration machinery. That still leaves a third of cells cell-only through the interval and adds a temporary predicate in four places, so it is the second-best option, recorded so it is not re-derived.

Blocks the flip bead (the gesture, #671). Related: km-jpj2.
close_reason: Closed on GitHub (issue #1010); reconciled by bd-github-sync.

title: A migration's undo clear does not reach other tabs, so their stale entries stay replayable
description:
The migration clears the workspace's undo history so its writes cannot be
reverted onto, but `UndoManager` is per Repo instance and every tab has its
own. The database and the codec baseline are shared across tabs, so:

1. Tab A runs the codec re-encode, clears ITS undo history, and records the
   baseline.
2. Tab B still holds pre-migration undo entries for the same workspace.
3. A cmd-Z in tab B replays a whole `before` row snapshot and restores the old
   encoding.
4. Every later prime compares the baseline against the registry, finds them in
   agreement, and schedules nothing. The stale encoding is permanent.

The in-flight-replay guard added alongside this does not cover it either: its
epoch is read from the clearing Repo's own manager, so it invalidates replays
in the tab that cleared and nothing in any other.

DIRECTIONS.

(a) A shared clear epoch in `client_schema_state`, which every tab already
    reads and writes through the same database — no broadcast channel needed.
    The replay transaction compares the stored epoch against one carried by the
    entry. The cost is deciding what an entry carries: recording the stored
    epoch per transaction is a database read on every write, and a per-Repo
    counter is not comparable across tabs.

(b) A broadcast on clear, so other tabs drop their stacks. Cheap and matches
    what a user would expect to see, but best-effort — a suspended or
    backgrounded tab can miss the message and still hold replayable entries.

(c) Accept, and record the residual: the migration is the only thing that
    clears history today, multi-tab plus a cmd-Z in the non-migrating tab
    inside the window is narrow, and the consequence is bounded to the rows
    that entry touched.

Raised by review on the property-definition migration PR. Not fixed there: it
is a cross-tab invalidation protocol, the codebase has no general primitive for
one (only `db-mirror` carries a BroadcastChannel), and (a) changes what an undo
entry stores.
close_reason: Closed on GitHub (issue #1007); reconciled by bd-github-sync.

title: A partially applied codec re-encode leaves no record that a sweep is owed
description:
A codec re-encode that commits a chunk and then aborts can strand those rows
permanently, because nothing records that the pass was partially applied.

REPRODUCTION (all four must hold, but the outcome is permanent):

1. A definition's codec changes `string -> number`. The deferred pass runs and
   COMMITS at least one chunk, so those parents' values and cells are now
   number-encoded.
2. The definition is changed back to `string` before the pass finishes.
3. The pass aborts — superseded, or on a transient view gap.
4. The pass scheduled by the revert also aborts before writing.

The re-detect that follows compares the durable baseline (still `string`,
because nothing was recorded) against the live registry (`string` again) and
finds no drift, so it schedules nothing. The rows the first pass already
rewrote stay number-encoded with no mechanism that will ever revisit them.

WHY THE EXISTING GUARDS DO NOT COVER IT. Run-time plan validation stops a
superseded pass from STARTING, but not from having already committed a chunk
before the revert. "Nothing recorded, so the drift stays visible" is the
invariant the pass relies on everywhere else, and it fails here precisely
because the drift is no longer expressible as baseline-vs-registry: the rows
are in a codec neither of them names.

TWO DIRECTIONS.

(a) Durable per-(workspace, fieldId) "sweep owed" state, set when a chunk
    commits and cleared when the pass records. Detection ORs it in, so a
    partially applied pass always gets a sweep to the live codec on the next
    prime. Correct across a crash or reload; costs a second store beside the
    baseline with its own lifecycle, and changes what the baseline means.

(b) In-memory only: on a transient abort where the pass had already written,
    synthesize changes for the batch's fieldIds at the LIVE codec and schedule
    that sweep directly rather than relying on baseline detection. Roughly
    fifteen lines, no new storage. Leaves a residual — if the session ends
    between the partial write and the sweep, the rows stay stranded, so it
    narrows the window rather than closing it. Also needs a bound, since a
    sweep that itself aborts after writing would otherwise schedule another.

Raised by review on the property-definition migration PR. Deliberately not
fixed there: (a) is a new durable store and a change to what the baseline
records, which is the same design question that PR opened on, and (b) is a
partial mitigation whose residual should be an explicit choice rather than a
default.
close_reason: Superseded by #1013 (PR #1018): the deferred, chunked re-encode pass no longer exists, so there is no partially applied state to record. The re-encode runs inside the transaction that edits the definition and commits whole or not at all. Verified on master 2026-09-17: the batch runner, the durable baseline and the registry-diff detector are all gone.

title: master is red: the new two-names block-type refusal rejects mergeTypeMembershipProcessor's fixtures
description:
Master has been red since PR #584 merged (commit 5b017c587, 2026-09-15 ~17:40 UTC). Its own Run Tests workflow fails, and every open PR inherits the failure through the merge commit CI builds.

Two tests fail, both in src/data/internals/mergeTypeMembershipProcessor.test.ts, suite core.retargetMergedTypeMembership:
- "retargets onto a non-type survivor instead of dropping membership"
- "registry ownership > does not sweep up a seeded type when its token is merged away"

Both die the same way, a ProcessorRejection thrown from src/data/internals/blockTypeTypeifyProcessor.ts:124 through commitPipeline applyProcessor:

  Can't make this block a type: its text ("Plain page") and its block-type:label ("Dancer") are different names, but a type has ONE name

That guard is new in #584 ("refuse a block-type tag whose content and label are two names"). The merge changed blockTypeTypeifyProcessor.ts without updating this test file, whose fixtures deliberately set a block's text and its block-type:label to different names — so the setup the merge tests never ran together before landing.

Fix direction: decide whether those fixtures are now an illegal shape (update them to share one name, or build them through a path the guard does not police, e.g. a raw write) or whether the guard is over-broad for a RETARGET, where the membership is being moved onto an existing survivor rather than a block being newly tagged. Read the guard's own comment at blockTypeTypeifyProcessor.ts:122 first: it already carves out a user-added alias equal to the label, which suggests the retarget path may want the same treatment.

Related: km-egz2 ("Merging a type block into a differently-titled page is refused outright") looks like the same guard seen from the user side.
close_reason: Fixed on master by PR #983 (fix(merge): let the surviving type keep its own name), merged as 443af814b. Verified: pnpm run check green on a branch rebased onto that master, 9488 tests.

title: Merging a type block into a differently-titled page is refused outright
description:
