master is red: `src/data/internals/mergeTypeMembershipProcessor.test.ts` fails two tests, and the cause is a product regression rather than a stale fixture.

The content/label refusal added in #584 (`blockTypeTypeifyProcessor.ts`, "its text and its block-type:label are different names") now fires during a MERGE. Merging a type block into a plain page with `contentStrategy: 'keepTarget'` carries the type's `block-type:label` onto the survivor while the survivor keeps its own content, so the pair the refusal forbids is produced by the merge itself — and the rejection takes the whole transaction, so the gesture fails with that message.

Failing tests (both one root cause):
- `core.retargetMergedTypeMembership > retargets onto a non-type survivor instead of dropping membership`
- `core.retargetMergedTypeMembership > does not sweep up a seeded type when its token is merged away`

Both pass before #584 and fail at its merge commit; #584 touched only `blockTypeTypeifyProcessor.ts`, `typeExtraction.test.ts` and `nameFieldBlur.test.tsx`, so its own gate never exercised the merge path — a semantic conflict its CI could not see.

Direction to weigh, not a decision: the refusal is right for a user TAGGING a block, which is the gesture it was written for; a merge is not that gesture, and the survivor's label is derived state the merge itself wrote. So either the merge should reconcile the label with the survivor's content instead of carrying it verbatim, or the refusal should not apply to a label the same transaction produced. Reproduce with `pnpm vitest run src/data/internals/mergeTypeMembershipProcessor.test.ts`.
close_reason: Fixed on master by "fix(merge): let the surviving type keep its own name" (PR #983). My filing had the diagnosis backwards: I read the #584 refusal as too broad for a merge path. It was not — it caught a real clobber. A merge unions properties name-agnostically, so a type source's block-type:label rode onto a survivor that kept its own text, and the typeify processor then retitled the survivor to the dead block's name, defeating keepTarget. The fix reconciles label with content in the fold, where the contentStrategy answer already lives.

title: db-mirror re-arms the mirror schedule after a refused status clear
description:
`DbMirrorSettingsDialog`'s re-grant handler treats "the write resolved" as "the write applied":

    const cleared = await saving(dbMirrorStore.recordStatus(userId, {
      permissionLost: false, lastError: undefined, lastErrorAt: undefined,
    }, {ifDirectoryEpoch}))
    if (cleared) dbMirrorSchedule.resume()

`recordStatus` returns `Promise<DbMirrorState>` and resolves with a state object whether or not its `ifDirectoryEpoch` guard applied the patch — on refusal it returns the state UNCHANGED. `saving()` only yields undefined when the promise rejects. So `cleared` is truthy on a refusal too, and the schedule is re-armed as though the failure had been cleared. The variable name states the opposite of what the value means.

Reachable exactly where the guard exists to help: another tab changes the mirror folder while the browser's permission prompt is open. The guard correctly declines to wipe the new folder's recorded failure — and the dialog re-arms anyway.

The test that should have caught it is green for the wrong reason. `DbMirrorSettingsDialog.test.tsx` > "does not clear a failure belonging to a folder chosen while it was asking" ends on `waitFor(status.lastError === 'the new drive is full')`, which was already true before its `release('granted')`, so both of its closing waits pass without the granted branch having run at all. It never observes the refusal.

That undrained chain is also the flake: its late `resume()` lands inside the next test, whose assertion is `expect(mocks.resume).not.toHaveBeenCalled()`. Confirmed by instrumenting the mock with `expect.getState().currentTestName` and forcing a full-suite run — the stray call is attributed to "a re-grant the browser refuses leaves the flag set", which mocks `requestDirectoryPermission` to 'denied' and therefore cannot reach `resume` through its own handler. Locally it fails roughly 3 runs in 4 under full-suite load and 0 in 5 in isolation; it also failed CI on an unrelated PR.

Two shapes for the fix:

1. Caller re-derives the verdict — `if (next && next.directoryEpoch === ifDirectoryEpoch) resume()`. Three lines, no API change, but it puts a second copy of the guard's condition in the caller, and copies drift.
2. `recordStatus` reports whether it applied (`{state, applied}` or `DbMirrorState | undefined`), so the decision has one owner. Touches store.ts, its tests, and this call site. Preferred.

Either way the test must be reworked to actually observe the refusal — prove the positive clear first, then assert the refusal against a fenced signal rather than a condition that was already true — and the guard mutated away to confirm the test fails without it.
close_reason: Fixed in PR 977 on branch claude/ref-list-suggestion-select-7bbe6f: recordStatus now resolves to undefined when its folder condition refuses, so the dialog no longer re-arms the schedule after a refused clear. The test that was green for the wrong reason now fences on the write the handler awaited, which also removes the cross-test leak that made the gate flake.

title: Interaction-metrics query timings conflate main-thread stall with data-layer latency
description:
Found while investigating a reported interaction-metrics degradation.

WHAT IS TRUE

A query's recorded p50/p95 is wall-clock from request to resolution, so it
includes any period the main thread was blocked. It cannot distinguish "the
data layer got slower" from "a render stalled the thread while this query was
in flight". The plugin exists to catch data-layer regressions, so this is a
validity problem, not a cosmetic one.

MEASURED (2026-09-12, prod workspace ~328k blocks, one device)

- core.ancestors recorded p50 582.6ms / p95 582.9ms over 95 calls.
- The same walk's SQL: 2-6ms for 70-120 ids, plan is a primary-key lookup
  (SEARCH parent USING INDEX ... (id=?)), no CTE-inversion.
- 100 cold handles through the REAL query path, end to end: 8.9ms.

So ~98% of the recorded figure was neither SQL nor resolve-pipeline work. In
the same session core.childIds p95 590.6ms and groupedBacklinks.forBlock
544.3ms cluster at the same magnitude - the signature of several queries in
flight across one stall, each billed for all of it.

WHY IT MATTERS

Every verdict this plugin produces about query p95 inherits the ambiguity. A
render-path change that blocks the thread reads as a data-layer regression; a
genuine data-layer regression can hide inside stall noise.

THE SECOND, RELATED DEFECT: NO OBSERVATION COUNT

A stored TimingSample carries calls / p50Ms / p95Ms / totalMs and no count of
distinct observations. MIN_CALLS assumes one resolve is one measurement, which
request coalescing breaks: N callers awaiting one statement each record the
same wall-clock, so calls counts callers.

This is NOT detectable after the fact. Percentiles are sorted[floor(n * q)],
so a collapsed tail (p50 == p95) is produced equally by coalescing and by any
bimodal split - ten 5ms calls beside ten 100ms calls give p50 = p95 = 100. The
sample above is itself bimodal (~48 calls at ~583ms, ~47 at ~243ms), i.e.
indistinguishable from a genuine regression. An attempt to refuse trending on
that signature was therefore withdrawn; the monitor now only REPORTS a
collapsed tail as a caveat and still compares.

DIRECTION (not yet decided)

Count observations where they are known rather than inferring them later, and
either exclude blocked-thread time from the resolve's measurement (e.g. via the
Long Tasks API the startup timeline already uses) or record stall exposure
beside the timing so a reader can separate the two.
close_reason: Closed on GitHub (issue #958); reconciled by bd-github-sync.

title: Ancestor walk: return the parent it stopped at, so three sites stop re-deriving it
description:
Fallout from the per-id ancestor work (PR #934). Two review agents on
different lenses found this independently, which is the design signal.

ROOT CAUSE
`ancestorWalk` carries the seed row purely so something can answer one
bit: did this walk reach a root, or stop at a parent it could not see
(soft-deleted, or not materialized yet)? `AncestorWalk.seed` has exactly
ONE production consumer, `dependOnUnreachableParent`, which reduces it to
that bit and throws the row away. `core.ancestors` then does not surface
the answer, so the same question is asked again, twice more, in different
shapes:

  1. `crumbsFromAncestors` (src/utils/blockCrumbs.ts) recomputes it as
     `chain.length === ancestors.length && (highest ? highest.parentId
     === null : parentId === null)` — structurally the same two-arm
     expression as `dependOnUnreachableParent`'s `chain.at(-1) ?? seed`.
  2. Because the query does not carry it, `parentId` has to be threaded
     in from OUTSIDE: `AncestorCrumbTarget.parentId` -> a parallel
     `seedHandles` array in `useAncestorCrumbs` -> `useHandles(...,
     {fetchMissing: false})` -> a payload fallback.

PROPOSED SHAPE
Replace `seed: AncestorChainRow | undefined` with
`stoppedAtParentId: string | null`, computed in the batcher where the
rows already are, and surface it on `core.ancestors`' result.

WHAT IT DELETES
- `dependOnUnreachableParent` collapses to one inline line
- `crumbsFromAncestors` drops its `parentId` option and the
  `highest ? ... : ...` arm
- `useAncestorCrumbs` drops `seedHandles`, the second `useHandles` call,
  `AncestorCrumbTarget.parentId`, and the comment justifying all three
- `UseHandlesOptions.fetchMissing` goes entirely, which is the point:
  three reviewers independently flagged its doc as false (it gates the
  ensure-load only, and `LoaderHandle.subscribe` self-loads, so it is a
  no-op for every handle type except `Block`). This makes that
  unrepresentable rather than documented around.
~50 lines across four files.

CHECK BEFORE BUILDING
- `parentId` must STAY on the search/recents row payloads: `resultItems`
  uses it synchronously to decide whether to reserve a crumb line, which
  is a different job from seeding the walk.
- This changes a kernel query's result type (`BlockData[]` ->
  `{ancestors, stoppedAtParentId}`), touching the `useParents` /
  `useManyParents` selectors. `core.ancestors` is NOT in
  `src/extensions/apiCatalog.ts`, so there is no extension surface to
  break.
- Mutation-test the new dep per clause: the current one is pinned on both
  the `ancestors` and `manyAncestors` paths, and both pins must survive.
close_reason: Built on branch claude/ancestor-stopped-at-parent; PR #947 open with CI green (preview + test). AncestorWalk now carries stoppedAtParentId instead of the seed row; core.ancestors returns it alongside the chain, which deleted the two-arm derivation at both consumer sites, crumbsFromAncestors' parentId option, useAncestorCrumbs' seed handles and AncestorCrumbTarget, and useHandles' fetchMissing option. Net -45 lines. Dep pinned on both the ancestors and manyAncestors paths (mutation-tested by deletion); both reachesRoot clauses pinned separately. Not merged - awaiting review.

title: Ancestor queries: per-id sub-cache, so an id-set change stops minting a cold handle
description:
Two hooks now independently work around one root cause. That is the design signal.

ROOT CAUSE
`core.manyAncestors` is keyed by the WHOLE sorted id list (`HandleStore` keys on
the args) and its resolver has no per-id sub-cache. So ANY change to the id set
mints a fresh, unresolved handle — `peek() === undefined` — and every id in it
reads as "no data", including the ids that were already resolved a moment ago.

THE TWO WORKAROUNDS
1. `useManyParents` (src/hooks/block.ts) — carries the last resolved chains while
   the newly keyed handle loads, so the backlinks panel stops dropping a
   breadcrumb line per entry on every refresh. PR #488, merged 51f06f896. Cost:
   a render-phase setState with two guards (a termination guard, and an
   `ids.length > 0` guard because an EMPTY request resolves trivially and would
   otherwise wipe the memory).
2. `useAncestorCrumbs` (src/hooks/useAncestorCrumbs.ts) — an accumulate-
   only-what's-missing cache for search results, with SNAPSHOT semantics (not
   live). Its own doc says it is deliberately not built on `useManyParents`
   because "a search whose result set shifts every keystroke would re-run the
   full batched SQL for every visible row each time".

Both are the same shape: keep our own memory because the handle layer throws its
memory away whenever the key changes.

PROPOSED SHAPE
Give the ancestor query a per-id sub-cache, so a set change only queries the ids
not already held. Then a shifting id set is cheap by construction and neither
consumer needs a private memory.

WHAT IT BUYS
- deletes the carry-over and BOTH its guards from `useManyParents`
- removes the empty-id-set edge case entirely (an empty request asks for nothing
  rather than resolving to an empty map that overwrites the memory)
- removes the reason `useAncestorCrumbs` had to be snapshot-only, so search
  breadcrumbs could go live if wanted
- entering ids stop gaining their chain a load late, which is the one residual
  PR #488 documented rather than fixed

CHECK BEFORE BUILDING
`keepPrevious` on `useHandle` was considered and rejected for this: it would
carry the last COMMITTED selection, so an empty id set would commit an empty map
and poison the carry — reintroducing the defect the `ids.length > 0` guard
exists for. A per-id cache does not have that failure mode; confirm that before
adopting.
close_reason: Landed in PR #934 (merge 630cb4250): core.ancestors is now the per-id cache + invalidation unit, with ancestorWalk coalescing same-microtask walks into one manyAncestorsSql statement. Both private caches deleted — useManyParents' carry-over and both its guards, and useAncestorCrumbs' accumulate-cache/claim-set/chunking. Follow-ups filed as km-cdfc and km-x3fb.

title: Restoring a page whose name was taken while it was deleted aborts, leaving the page unrestorable
description:
Deleting a page, then letting anything else claim its name, makes the page
**permanently un-restorable**: the restore aborts and the page stays in the trash.

No sync and no second device are involved — this is reachable on one client with
ordinary gestures.

## Reproduction (verified on master `66fe2905d`)

Two shapes, both measured; the second is the one that needs no deliberate act
from the user at all.

**A. Something else takes the name.**

1. Page P claims alias `Inbox`.
2. Delete P. `block_aliases` is live-only, so the claim is released — but P's
   `properties_json` still carries `aliases: ["Inbox"]`.
3. Any other live block claims `Inbox`.
4. Restore P → `ProcessorRejection: Alias "Inbox" is already used by another block`.
   P stays `deleted = 1`.

**B. The app takes the name on the user's behalf.** Same outcome with no third
party: one referrer holding both `[[Inbox]]` and `((P-id))` is enough.

1. Page P claims `Inbox`; a referrer reads `see [[Inbox]] and ((P-id))`.
2. Delete P. `inlineDeletedBlockRefsProcessor` inlines the blockref, which is a
   content write on the referrer, which re-parses it — and `[[Inbox]]` no longer
   resolves to the dead P, so a **fresh alias seat is minted claiming `Inbox`**.
   (Measured: referrer content becomes `see [[Inbox]] and My Page`, and the
   `Inbox` claimant is a new block.)
3. Restore P → same rejection, P stays deleted.

So a single delete can make its own page un-restorable, as a side effect of the
delete's own cascade.

## Mechanism

`restore` flips `deleted` 1→0, which re-inserts the row's stored aliases into
`block_aliases`; the uniqueness trigger sees the live claimant and
`RAISE(ABORT)`s the whole transaction.

The codebase already knows about this and has the fix pattern —
`restorePropertiesStrippingAliases` in `src/data/targets.ts`, whose docblock
states it exactly ("a tombstone can carry a claim some live block took while it
was dead, and re-inserting it trips the alias-uniqueness trigger, rolling back
the CALLER's whole tx"). `createOrRestoreTargetBlock` uses it, together with
`partitionClaimableAliases`, so every seat / daily-note / kernel-page revival is
safe.

The **user-facing restore path is not**: `core.restore` (`src/data/mutators.ts`)
is a bare `tx.restore(id)` with no patch, so it re-inserts the stale bag verbatim.

## Fix direction

Give the user restore the same treatment the target-block primitive already gets:
drop the aliases another live block now holds (`partitionClaimableAliases`)
instead of aborting. Yielding a contested name keeps the page reachable, which is
the trade `partitionClaimableAliases` already documents for #378. Whether the
user should be told the name was yielded is the open question.

## Relationship to existing issues

- #185 documents the same abort, but frames the precondition as a **cross-client
  sync-seeded duplicate** and calls it latent. The restore half needs neither:
  the tombstone's stale claim plus one ordinary local claimant is enough. #185's
  fix (V2 uniqueness semantics for sync) would not close this path.
- Found while comparing the three competing fixes for #706; **orthogonal to that
  choice** — measured identical on master and on all three PR branches.

title: Warm-boot first-paint regressed ~4-6s starting 2026-08-19/20, still live
description:
Found by querying the startupRecord history that the startup-metrics plugin has
been writing since June and that nothing has ever read.

## The measurement

Metric: `firstContentPaintMs - repoReadyMs` -- the bootstrap gap between "repo is
ready" and "workspace layout painted". Isolating it from repoReadyMs matters:
repoReadyMs is FLAT across the whole window (~900-1400ms), so this is not sync,
materialization or DB open getting slower.

Daily MINIMUM of that gap (min = the cleanest warm-start sample; all devices):

    2026-07-31 .. 08-19   314 - 388 ms   (20 days, 3 weeks, rock steady)
    2026-08-20            4519 ms
    2026-08-21            1514 ms
    2026-08-22            1035 ms
    2026-08-23            2404 ms
    2026-08-24             377 ms  (min over 22 samples -- see bimodality below)

Confirmed on two independent devices with the same step at the same date, so it
is not one machine's local state.

## It is bimodal, not build-determined

Per-boot gaps on 2026-08-24 run mostly 3000-6000ms with occasional fast boots,
and TWO BOOTS ON THE SAME BUILD SHA gave 474ms and 3882ms. So a build bisect
alone will not localize it -- the slow path is conditional on state or timing,
not on the code being present.

## Window

Last clean build observed: 1d4d8c1a (#585), gap ~350ms, 2026-08-19 03:51 UTC.
First clean slow build observed: 84501f6a (#587), gap 4334ms, 18:29 UTC.
36 commits in between, including #596 (the properties cell-to-children
migration pass + its command-palette entry point), #590, #595, #587.

## Hypothesis (NOT verified -- stated so it can be falsified)

Bimodality plus a flat repoReadyMs points at CONTENTION rather than added work
on the critical path: the boot's serialized bootstrap round-trips queueing
behind something else on the single SQLite worker. A catch-up pass that runs at
boot and has work to do on some boots and not others would produce exactly this
shape. #596 landed such machinery in the window. Equally consistent with any
other newly-scheduled boot-time job; needs a real profile to tell apart.

Note the workspace is still in `cell` mode (not flipped), so if #596 is
implicated it is via the pass/projector running, not via the flipped read path.

## Next step

Profile a slow boot directly (the gap is between repoReady and first paint, so
the bootstrap phase in workspaceBootstrap / App phase 3), and check what is
occupying the SQLite worker during that window. The bimodality is the lever:
capture both a fast and a slow boot on the same build and diff what ran.

Related: this is the second regression this week that was sitting in already-
collected data with no reader.

title: Readwise: re-parking a solely-named document onto a fallback RENAMES the document
description:
MEASURED, not reasoned. A document whose alias bag is exactly [title] and whose content is that same title gets its CONTENT rewritten to the fallback when the sync re-parks it.

Repro (drove the real writer against a real repo):
1. sync a book so the document holds content `Deep Work` and aliases `[Deep Work]`
2. land a sync-applied co-claimant of `Deep Work` (raw insert with a later created_at, the shape sync apply produces)
3. sync the book again

`ensureDocumentAlias` finds the title contested, resolves the fallback, and rewrites the bag `[Deep Work]` to `[Deep Work (Readwise)]`. Observed afterwards: `content = "Deep Work (Readwise)"`. The real title is gone from the block.

Mechanism: the kernel reads a bag rewrite whose replaced entry equals the content as a RENAME, and re-keys content to follow. It is narrow — measured NOT to happen when the bag has two entries (bag `[Deep Work (Readwise), Deep Work]` reduced to `[Deep Work (Readwise)]` leaves content alone), which is why the existing suite never caught it.

Why it matters beyond the mangling: content being the real title is what the duplicate-name banner reads and what the merge requires of its target, so the document also loses its route back.

Fix directions, none free:
- Do not take a name away from a document that already holds it as its sole alias — the co-claim ambiguity is the banner's business. Cheapest; means the sync offers nothing for that case, consistent with the scope line already documented.
- Release the bag in its own transaction before claiming the fallback, the way a contested re-title already does. More machinery, keeps re-parking.
- Re-assert content after any bag rewrite. Least principled.

Wider than this extension: any code that rewrites an alias bag containing the block's content can rename the block. Worth checking the other reconcile sites.

title: Proactive interaction-performance regression detection + historical metrics
description:
Today a performance regression is noticed subjectively and then reconstructed by hand from a live client. Startup already has a per-session timeline; interaction performance has nothing comparable, and there is no history to check an intuition against.

## What already exists to build on

- `repo.metrics()` is rich: per-query resolve timings (calls/mean/p50/p95/p99/max/total), per-DB-method timings, invalidation fan-out counters (`invalidations`, `handlesWalked`, `handlesMatched`, `loaderRuns`, `midLoadInvalidations`, `reloadsAfterSettle`), `slowestTx` + `txLog`, and `handleStoreInventory` (handle count, dep percentiles, `topHeavy` — explicitly designed to spot resolvers that over-register deps).
- The startup-metrics plugin stores a per-session record as its own block under the per-user UI-state subtree, `Automation` scope, block-per-session to avoid cross-device LWW clobber. That storage shape is directly reusable.

## Three layers, cheapest first

**1. A static guard (no telemetry, runs in the gate).** Assert that no query registering a workspace-wide invalidation channel is also expensive. The grouped-backlinks case would have failed such a test the day it was introduced. This is a unit test, not monitoring, and it catches the whole class rather than one instance.

**2. Per-session interaction record.** Mirror the startup record: sample `repo.metrics()` deltas around edits and store per-session aggregates — cost attributed to structural vs content edits, per-query p95, invalidation fan-out ratio (`handlesWalked / invalidations`), and the `topHeavy` handle list. Gives history to check intuitions against, which is the thing most missing during an investigation.

**3. Alarm on the trend.** Threshold on the stored series rather than on a single session (single sessions are noisy — cold start, graph size, which panels are open). Report which query and which channel regressed, since that is what makes a report actionable.

## Design notes

- Panel layout dominates the mounted handle set, so records must carry enough context (open surface types, handle count) or session-to-session comparisons will be noise.
- Attribute by edit KIND. Content edits and structural edits have completely different cost profiles (measured: content ~0 re-resolves, structural ~500ms), so a single blended number hides regressions in either.
- The fan-out ratio and `topHeavy` are the leading indicators — they move when a dep gets miswired, before the wall-clock does on a smaller graph.
close_reason:
All three slices merged: the kernel (PR 885), the recorder (PR 887), and the reader/perf-monitor plugin (PR 832, merged 2026-09-03). The feature is live end to end — both recorders write per-session history, the monitor compares this session against this device's own past, and the trend dialog shows the series behind the verdict.

Follow-ups tracked separately, none blocking: km-gcdd (comment share / design rationale into docs), km-j64c (recorder-off is not a RecordingBlocker), and PR 898 (a small comment consolidation that arrived after the merge).

title: Grouped backlinks re-resolves on every block create/delete in the workspace
description:
A grouped-backlinks query handle subscribes to the workspace-wide `typedBlocks.live` invalidation channel, so **every** block creation or deletion anywhere in the graph forces a full re-resolve.

## Measured (live client, ~328k-block graph, idle worker)

| Edit | tx | query re-resolve | DB work in settle window |
|---|---|---|---|
| Content-only (typing) | 11ms | none | ~9ms |
| Structural (one new block) | 15.5ms | groupedBacklinks.forBlock, 298ms | **508ms** (21 getAll) |

No long tasks fire — the main thread is idle. The cost lands on the single SQLite worker, so subsequent reads queue behind it. That is the "contention / unresponsive but not frozen" symptom.

Under contention (measured during startup) the same query averaged 1756ms with 511 registered deps.

## Mechanism

`collectWhereDeps` (src/data/internals/kernelQueries.ts, ~line 935) subscribes to `TYPED_BLOCKS_LIVE_CHANNEL` keyed on the workspace alone whenever a `where` predicate uses the `target:` operator with a **non-selective** inner predicate. An empty inner object (`{target: {}}`) is always non-selective: `Object.values({}).some(...)` is `false`.

A backlink filter containing an ancestor-scoped exclude of the shape `{<ref-typed prop>: {target: {}}}` therefore wires the whole grouped-backlinks query to workspace-wide liveness.

Verified by counterfactual on the live graph: the `{target: {}}` spelling registers the workspace-wide live dep; `{exists: true}` does not (1355 vs 1354 deps, live dep present vs absent).

## Why the dep is load-bearing

It is not simply removable. With `target: {}` a source row whose ref points at a not-yet-existing block starts matching the moment that target is created, and creating the target fires no channel the query otherwise depends on (it never writes the named property). Dropping the subscription would leave the view stale.

## Directions

1. **Narrow the channel.** The target ids the sources point at are known; depending on `typedBlocks.structure` per referenced target id is precise and bounded, instead of every create/delete in the workspace.
2. **Coalesce re-resolution for expensive handles.** A handle whose last resolve exceeded some threshold could batch invalidations over a short window. Holding Enter or pasting a subtree currently pays the full cost per block created.
3. **Selectivity at the predicate level.** `{target: {}}` is nearly always meant as "the property has a value"; that intent is expressible as `{exists: true}`, which is selective. Worth considering whether an empty target predicate should compile to the existence check rather than to a workspace-wide subscription.

Option 3 also works as an immediate user-side workaround: on the graph measured, the two predicates returned identical sets (1353 blocks each, zero difference).
close_reason: Fixed and merged: ancestor-scoped target predicates now name their target ids instead of subscribing to the workspace-wide typedBlocks.live channel. Measured on a 328k-block graph: structural-edit re-resolves 1 to 0, settle-window getAll 1064ms to 31-48ms. Review round moved the dep source from block_references (projected post-commit, so it lagged the property write) to properties_json.

title: Write-side property-machinery guards fail closed in a background workspace, inlining machinery they should retain
description:
Split off from a review of the #779 investigation, which confirmed the phantom-page half does NOT reproduce. This is the surviving half of the same root cause: a recognizer that depends on registry scope cannot answer for a workspace that is not loaded.

`isPropertyFieldRow` / `isPropertyValueRow` (src/data/propertyChildren.ts) resolve the definition through `tx.isPropertyFieldDefinition` -> `Repo.propertySchemaResolverFor`, which serves the active workspace and the retained previous one and fails CLOSED for any other. Three write-side guards consume them:

- `inlineDeletedBlockRefsProcessor.ts` (~line 131): property machinery is meant to KEEP its dangling ref rather than be inlined. Unrecognized, a field row keyed to a deleted definition is treated as an ordinary referrer and its content is rewritten -- which does not corrupt a value, it detaches the property from its owner entirely. The file's own comment names this as the case that bites.
- `renameProcessor.ts` and `mergeRetargetProcessor.ts` route through the same predicates.

Direction of the failure matters here and runs OPPOSITE to the phantom-page one: recognition SUPPRESSES a rewrite, so failing closed rewrites machinery that should have been left alone. That is a data-shaped outcome, not a cosmetic one.

Reachability, unverified: the definition and its field rows share a workspace, so this needs a definition deletion applied to a workspace that is neither active nor previous -- a sync arrival is the plausible path. Establish that first; if arrival cannot reach these processors for a background workspace, this is latent and should be recorded as such rather than fixed.

Verify it still reproduces before fixing. A flipped workspace is one column value in a test, so this is testable today.

Fix direction, if real: same as the one that dissolved the phantom-page half -- prefer a workspace-capable check that does not go through the scoped registry (the `is_field_form` bit plus a definition probe over the block-types index, matching the SQL twin) over widening the registry's scope.

title: Restore does not re-materialize property children tombstoned by a subtree delete
description:
Split out of the post-flip healing-seams umbrella (item 6). Reachable only in a child-backed workspace — which in a TEST is one column value, so this is fixable and testable today and does not wait on a real flip.

When a block with properties is deleted in a flipped workspace, the subtree-delete paths tombstone its hidden field and value children. A later restore flips only the parent row live and usually leaves its property bag unchanged — and because the materialize-property-children processor watches the PROPERTIES, an unchanged bag schedules nothing. The restored block therefore keeps its local cell value but has lost the child-backed truth, which is the authoritative side post-flip.

FIX DIRECTION: the restore path has to re-materialize property children for a row it brings back, rather than relying on a property-bag change to trigger it. Worth checking whether the same hole exists for any other path that revives a row without touching its bag.

DATA-SHAPED, which is why it should land before the first flip rather than after: post-flip the children ARE the property truth, so a restore that does not rebuild them leaves a block whose properties are silently missing from every reader that has moved to children.
close_reason: Closed on GitHub (issue #778); reconciled by bd-github-sync.

title: Seed field rows written to a background flipped workspace mint alias pages
description:
Split out of the post-flip healing-seams umbrella (item 4). Reachable only in a child-backed workspace — which in a TEST is one column value, so this is fixable and testable today and does not wait on a real flip.

The references processor recognizes a property field row by asking the property-schema resolver for the workspace to resolve the field. That resolver is scoped to the ACTIVE and PREVIOUS workspace, and fails CLOSED for any other. So a code-owned seed field-row write to a BACKGROUND flipped workspace is not recognized as machinery: its schema-reference content is parsed as an ordinary wikilink, which mints an alias page and records a backlink from a row the user cannot see.

Same root cause as the cross-workspace deferral in derive-at-arrival: a recognizer that depends on registry scope cannot answer for a workspace that is not loaded.

FIX DIRECTION, as recorded when found: a workspace-capable recognizer that does not go through the scoped registry — either a deterministic seed-id check, or a probe over the block-types index that matches the SQL twin of the same rule.

USER-VISIBLE POLLUTION, which is why it should land before the first flip: the artifacts are minted pages and backlinks in real data, and nothing sweeps them afterwards.
close_reason:
DOES NOT REPRODUCE against master (05c012f5). Verified by running the scenario, not by reading it. PR: https://github.com/Stvad/knowledge-medium/pull/785

The mechanism has two halves and both are gone:

1. There is no registry-scoped recognizer left in the parse path to fail closed. Parse-level property-machinery suppression (isPropertyMachineryRow + suppressContentMarks) was removed from the references processor in cada335f8 (2026-07-17) -- the same slices-A+B work whose review filed this item. buildSourcePlan consults no resolver; the only content gate left is the extension-source one.

2. A field row carries no wikilink to mint from. propertyFieldContent is the sole producer of field-row content across src/, packages/ and agent-extensions/, and emits the by-id form. referenceBlockContentForLabel (the label form this report assumed) has no writer at all -- only a round-trip self-check. The guarantee is therefore the addressing FORM, which is workspace-independent in a way a recognizer is not.

MEASURED in a workspace flipped to children with the active workspace elsewhere: resolveField there really does return identity-unavailable / registry-not-workspace-keyed, so the fail-closed this report names is real -- and the row still parses to exactly the by-id definition reference, minting nothing. Separately, setProperty with a seed handle into such a workspace writes the cell only and skips the eager dual-write, so that path produces no field row there at all.

Pinned by a regression test in the background-workspace case (the active-workspace case was already covered), asserting the fail-closed precondition, the rows that exist, and the reference values. Mutation-checked: rendering field-row content as a wikilink mints the seat and fails it.

Adversarial review confirmed the verdict and traced every writer that could put a field or value row into a background workspace -- each fails closed or refuses to run outside the active workspace.

TWO RELATED FINDINGS FILED, so closing this does not retire them: km-2lhc (P1, the surviving half of the same root cause -- the write-side guards still resolve through the scoped registry, and there the direction is the dangerous one: unrecognized machinery gets INLINED rather than retained; blocks the slice-C umbrella in this one's place) and km-uako (P3, the same phantom-page failure reachable by id SHAPE rather than workspace scope, held off today only by the canonical block-id policy).

title: A definition rename that syncs while a workspace is inactive never triggers the migration pass
description:
Split out of the post-flip healing-seams umbrella (item 2). Reachable only in a child-backed workspace — which in a TEST is one column value, so this is fixable and testable today and does not wait on a real flip.

The facet bridge diffs the previous property definitions against the next to schedule the definition-migration pass and the added-name rederive. On switching BACK to a workspace, the previous registry is null or belongs to a different workspace, so the same-workspace diff sees no change. A definition rename that synced while the workspace was INACTIVE therefore never triggers the pass: field rows keep their old title and cells stay keyed by the old name until the next local touch of that definition.

Pre-flip this is moot — that pass is flip-gated, and cell-era renames go through the existing reprojection-marker machinery.

FIX DIRECTION, as recorded when found: persist a per-workspace definitions baseline (fieldId to name and codec type, e.g. in the client schema state table) and diff against THAT on registry prime, rather than against whatever the previous in-memory registry happened to be. The alternative is folding a field-row-title and cell-key reconcile into the flipped-workspace open path, mirroring the per-open reference-target sweep.

DATA-SHAPED, which is why it should land before the first flip rather than after: post-flip it leaves real rows mis-titled and real cells keyed by a name nothing resolves.

title: A durable materialization gap has no operator remedy, and 1,127 benign rows are holding one open
description:
MEASURED ON THE PRODUCTION GRAPH, 2026-08-23. A device reports a DURABLE materialization gap of 1,127 rows on a plaintext workspace — rows the drain reached and did not apply, with nothing in flight and no queue entry. Every one-way pass gates on this predicate, so on that device the properties-migration flip, the backfill and the orphan mint all refuse, and nothing available to an operator changes the answer.

WHAT THE ROWS ACTUALLY ARE. All 1,127 share one shape: the live row exists with `updated_at = 0` (the speculative-mint sentinel) while the staged row carries a nonzero server stamp. Content, properties and parent are BYTE-IDENTICAL between the two — 0 differences on all three across all 1,127. So nothing is visibly wrong and no user-facing data is missing; what the staged row would add is the mint metadata a 0-stamped row lacks (created_at, created_by, user_updated_at).

WHY THEY NEVER CLEAR. The one-time seed deliberately does not clear a stamp-0 local row: equal stamps at 0 do not imply equal content (invariant I2), so it cannot prove the row is applied. The runtime drain WOULD clear these — by applying them, since I2 makes a 0-stamped local row yield — but nothing re-delivers them, the queue is empty, and the one-time reconcile rescan is marker-gated per (workspace, client) and has already run. So the flag is correct by its own rule and permanently stuck.

THE REAL HOLE: there is no operator remedy for a durable gap. The queue-less workspace rematerialization is internal to the sync observer, reachable only from a key paste, an encryption-mode confirmation, or that one-time rescan. An operator who reads a refusal has no way to act on it.

TWO FIX DIRECTIONS, not exclusive:
1. Expose a rematerialization the operator can run for a workspace, so a durable gap has an answer. This is the general fix and also covers gaps that are NOT benign.
2. Let a repair pass clear the flag for a row whose stored columns are byte-identical to the staged row, which is exactly the population above. This is a content comparison the seed does not do — too expensive for the hot predicate, fine for a one-time pass.

Direction 2 alone would clear this instance; direction 1 is what makes the next one survivable. Note the sibling issue about a refusal naming a count but no way to find the rows — same operator experience, one step earlier.

title: Property value rows are exposed to rename's content rewrites; only the deleted-ref processor guards them
description:
Found reviewing the #688 fix (PR #751).

A property VALUE row is an ordinary block whose content IS the property value.
Two reference-maintenance processors rewrite block content in place, and they
disagree about whether value rows are fair game:

- inlineDeletedBlockRefsProcessor.ts:131-132 SKIPS them, via isPropertyValueRow
  / isPropertyFieldRow. Its header states the reason: rewriting such a row
  corrupts a typed value or detaches it from its owner.
- renameProcessor.ts does NOT. It imports isPropertyFieldRow only (for the
  marked-name-row tier) and has no isPropertyValueRow guard anywhere.

Consequence: a string-typed property value containing an inline [[Alias]] span
is rewritten when that alias is renamed, silently changing the stored value.
The owner cell is then reprojected from the rewritten row, so the change is
authoritative rather than cosmetic.

Reachable for any value whose text mentions a page, not just pathological ones:
  tx.setProperty(block, noteSchema, "see [[Project X]] for the rationale")
then rename Project X.

NOT the same as the #688 escape. That escape covers values that are WHOLLY a
span; PR #751 additionally neutralizes the span grammar inside the escaped
envelope, so an escaped value is now inert. Neither touches a span embedded in
prose, which is never escaped because the value is not misread on write -- it
is correctly stored, and then edited afterwards by rename.

The real question is a DESIGN one, which is why this is filed rather than fixed
in PR #751: should a string property value support inline references at all?

- If YES (a property value that links to a page is a feature, and following a
  rename is correct behaviour), then nothing is broken for prose values and the
  only issue is the inconsistency with the deleted-ref processor, which refuses
  to touch the same rows.
- If NO (a property value is typed data, and its text belongs to the codec),
  then renameProcessor needs the isPropertyValueRow guard its sibling already
  has, and the two processors stop disagreeing.

Pre-existing; not introduced by PR #751 and not made worse by it. Unreachable
today because no workspace is flipped, so it belongs to the same must-decide-
before-the-first-flip set as #688.
close_reason:
Not a bug. The two processors' asymmetry is correct, not an oversight.

inlineDeletedBlockRefsProcessor guards value rows because inlining DESTROYS identity: ((targetId)) becomes prose, the derived column clears, and the owner's key drops irreversibly. Its own comment states the principle -- prose wants readable TEXT preserved, a typed value wants IDENTITY preserved.

Rename does the opposite: it PRESERVES identity. [[Roadmap]] -> [[Roadmap 2026]] still points at the same page, which is what a wikilink is for, and a property value row is a normal block so it gets that like every other block.

The guard proposed here would make things worse, not better: a value row skipped by rename would keep saying [[Roadmap]] after the page was renamed -- now a dangling reference resolving to nothing, or minting a phantom alias seat. It would convert working behaviour into breakage.

Filed on my own containment reflex (see feedback_normal_block_behavior_is_the_goal): I saw property machinery visibly behaving like a normal block and read that as the defect. Vlad applied the tenet and it resolves immediately.

title: mutationObserverGc.test.ts red = happy-dom 20.11.0 installed; fix is pnpm install
description:
src/test/mutationObserverGc.test.ts fails with:

  AssertionError: expected 0 to be greater than 0
  src/test/mutationObserverGc.test.ts:42

RESOLVED 2026-08-22 — NOT A FLAKE, NOT A TEST BUG, AND NOTHING TO FIX IN THIS
REPO. The test is correct and is doing exactly its job: it detects that the
happy-dom actually loaded has the 20.11.0 MutationObserver regression. Every
observed failure came from an environment running 20.11.0 while its checkout
said ^20.11.2.

That regression was already fixed on master by d0bf45596 (2026-08-19), which
bumped happy-dom to ^20.11.2. In 20.11.0 the per-target callback is an inline
arrow held only by a WeakRef, so any GC collects it and the observer stops
firing; 20.11.2 assigns it to a strongly-held private field first.

THE FIX IS `pnpm install`.

Measured 2026-08-22 (same machine, only variable is the installed version):
- happy-dom 20.11.0: 6/6 runs fail, with the exact assertion above
- happy-dom 20.11.2: 12/12 runs pass
- full gate on the corrected install: green, 645 files / 8303 tests, 70.7s

WHY IT LOOKED LIKE A MACHINE/LOAD-DEPENDENT FLAKE. Agent worktree directories
are recycled across sessions: a new session mints a new branch off current
master inside an existing directory. Git updates the tracked files —
package.json and pnpm-lock.yaml both become current — but node_modules is not
tracked and keeps whatever the last install in that directory produced, which
can be weeks old. From inside the session everything looks new and clean: new
branch, clean tree, current lockfile. The only stale thing is the one
directory git does not manage. A checkout is therefore NOT evidence about the
installed dependency tree.

TWO EARLIER CLAIMS IN THIS ISSUE WERE WRONG, both from sampling one
environment rather than checking the install:
- 'fails deterministically' — it is deterministic per installed version, not
  per machine.
- 'machine/load dependent' — load is irrelevant. Forcing gc() changes nothing
  on 20.11.2 and makes 20.11.0 fail every time.

The GC-premise control was never the problem and must stay: on 20.11.2 the
callback cannot be collected, and a failure of the premise itself would report
at line 36, not line 42. A report naming line 42 is diagnostic of 20.11.0.

DIAGNOSTIC FOR NEXT TIME, before suspecting the test:
  grep '"version"' node_modules/happy-dom/package.json
  pnpm install --frozen-lockfile   # idempotent, ~0.4s when already correct

Same root cause as the PanelFocusRecovery debounce issue — one bug, two
symptoms, not two flakes.
notes: Filed while working on PR https://github.com/Stvad/knowledge-medium/pull/735
close_reason:
Not a test bug and not a flake. The test is correct and was doing its job:
detecting that the loaded happy-dom carried the 20.11.0 MutationObserver
regression. Every observed failure came from an environment running 20.11.0
under a checkout asking for ^20.11.2 — already fixed on master by d0bf45596
(2026-08-19). The fix was `pnpm install`; no test was changed.

Root cause of the confusion: agent worktree directories are recycled, so a
session can hold a genuinely clean checkout at current master over a weeks-old
untracked node_modules. A clean checkout is not evidence about the installed
dependency tree.

Recurrence now prevented: `pnpm run check` reconciles the install first
(`pnpm install --frozen-lockfile --config.confirm-modules-purge=false`), merged
via PR #741.

title: Block merge silently deletes a source field row that has no cell value, with its values and user notes
description:
Reproduced end-to-end through the core.merge mutator on a flipped workspace (2026-08-21). Pre-existing; unchanged by the multi-claimant merge work, which only widened where it can be reached from.

## Repro

1. setProperty('from', <a number property>, 42) — mints a field row plus a value child.
2. The user retypes the value as free text ('about forty-two'). PROJECT unsets the cell key and DELIBERATELY keeps the rows: reprojectParentField does delete nextProperties[schema.name] 'while the rows stay visible/fixable' (src/data/internals/propertyChildrenProcessor.ts).
3. The user adds a child note under that value.
4. repo.mutate.merge({intoId, fromId}) — an ordinary backspace-at-start gesture.

Result: the field row, the value, AND the user's note all come back deleted=1, still parented under the 'from' tombstone, so they are not reachable under the survivor either.

## Where

src/data/blockMerge.ts, the adopt branch's deleteSubtreeInTx call. The branch fires when the merged property bag lacks the key. Its comment claims that only happens for 'a custom mergeProperties strategy [that] deliberately drop[s] a source-only key' — that is wrong. The default mergeProperties copies every key of from.properties, so the branch fires exactly when the source has a field row with NO cell key, which is a state the property system produces on purpose.

## Two candidate fixes

- Adopt the row unconditionally when the target lacks the field. The branch's own last sentence says an unresolvable field row 'rides along harmlessly'.
- Or narrow the drop to the case the comment describes: the key was present in from.properties and the strategy removed it (Object.hasOwn(from.properties, name) && !Object.hasOwn(merged, name)).

Pick deliberately — this is property-system semantics, not a mechanical fix.

## Related

With several sources the outcome is also ORDER-DEPENDENT: folding [A, B] deletes A's value while [B, A] preserves it as a peer. Fold order is created_at ascending, i.e. arbitrary from the user's point of view. That ordering sensitivity is new, the deletion is not.
close_reason: Closed on GitHub (issue #728); reconciled by bd-github-sync.

title: Alias-seat block ids are a page-name oracle on e2ee workspaces
description:
computeAliasSeatId derives an alias seat's block id as uuidv5("<workspaceId>:<alias>:<index>") under ALIAS_NS, a constant in the public client repo (src/data/targets.ts). Block ids sync in PLAINTEXT — e2ee seals content/properties_json/references_json only — so an untrusted server can hash a guessed page name and probe for the row, confirming that an encrypted workspace contains a page called that.

Same oracle shape the properties work just closed for synthesized property definitions, and a wider one: page/alias names are more sensitive than property keys, and the references processor mints these seats for every [[link]] on every workspace, with no encryption-mode gate.

The primitive to reuse already exists: deriveWorkspaceIdNamespace(K_id, label) in src/sync/crypto/derivedIdNamespace.ts. An e2ee workspace would derive its own ALIAS_NS from K_id under a distinct label; plaintext keeps the constant.

Two things make this harder than the property-definition case, and are why it is filed rather than folded in:
 - the derivation is async (SubtleCrypto) and computeAliasSeatId is sync and called on hot reference-resolution paths, including inside transactions; it needs a namespace resolved once per workspace and cached, not re-derived per call.
 - seats ALREADY minted under the public namespace in any live encrypted workspace stay where they are. Re-deriving orphans them, so this needs a migration story or a deliberate accept.

Worth checking whether any other derived-id kind has the same shape (the daily-note and roam-import namespaces key off dates and foreign uids, which leak much less).
close_reason: Closed on GitHub (issue #719); reconciled by bd-github-sync.

title: Daily notes: stop restore renaming into a withheld alias, move identity off the alias
description:
The merged duplicate-name work covers KERNEL PAGES only. The daily-notes half was written, reviewed, found broken, and reverted out — it is not on master. Two things must land together for daily notes.

## 1. BLOCKER — restore re-triggers the original collision

Reproduced mechanically, three consecutive attempts, the page null each time.

A seat minted from a `[[2026-04-28]]` wikilink has `content` = the ISO text (`ensureDailyNoteTarget` sets `freshContent` to the alias). `getOrCreateDailyNote`'s restore branch sets `content` to the long-form label. The same-tx `alias.sync` processor reads the tx's **net** diff, sees the old content is still in the alias list, applies its rule 1 ("content changed, old value in aliases -> replace that entry with new content"), and swaps in the long-form name. If another live page owns that name, the preflight rejects with `alias.collision` (`collisionOrigin: 'content-rename'`, from `assertNoAliasCollision`), the whole tx rolls back, the row stays tombstoned, and every retry repeats. The day is permanently unopenable — the original bug, through a different door.

Withholding the contested alias does not help: rule 1 fires on the value the partition deliberately KEPT. Not reachable via `getOrCreateKernelPage`, whose restore sets content to its own canonical alias.

**Fix direction:** do not rewrite `content` during restore. Resurrecting a tombstone should not rename it — set the title only when the row's content is empty. That removes the rename trigger at the source.

**Sibling bug the same change fixes** (pre-existing, minor): with NO squatter, rule 1 still collapses the two aliases to one, so a restored seat comes back without its ISO alias. Self-heals on the next call.

## 2. MAJOR — a daily note's identity lives in a user-editable alias

`dailyNoteIsoFromAliases` answers "which day is this?" by parsing the alias list, and is documented as deliberately NOT a type check. So withholding a contested ISO alias silently breaks navigation: `DateNavDecorator` renders no date arrows, and prev/next computes `addDaysIso(anchor?.iso ?? todayIso(), offset)` — navigating relative to **today** rather than the day on screen. The picker opens on the wrong month.

The row already carries `DAILY_NOTE_TYPE` and `dailyNoteDateProp`, written on BOTH creation paths (`getOrCreateDailyNote` and `ensureDailyNoteTarget`) — verified. No read path uses them.

**Fix direction:** move identity reads onto `dailyNoteDateProp`, with the alias as a fallback for old rows. Three consumers: `DateNavDecorator`, prev/next in `actions.ts`, the picker. Once identity is a typed property, yielding either alias is purely cosmetic and the whole ISO/long-form asymmetry disappears.

Rejected alternative: "never yield the ISO alias". No read-path changes, but an ISO collision then aborts exactly as before — and the wikilink-seat path is precisely how a rival comes to own `2026-04-28`. It preserves the bug for the likeliest case.

## Also carried

- Read-only viewers reaching the daily-note repair get `ReadOnlyError` instead of the live handle, because a contested alias keeps `needsRepair` true forever. `getOrCreateKernelPage` has the early return; daily notes need the same.
- The banner detects a duplicate by page TITLE, so it cannot see a contested ISO alias (the alias differs from the title). The principled fix is to route the contested set from the claiming code to the banner rather than re-deriving it.

## Ground rules learned the expensive way

- Any test MUST install `aliasDataExtension` (plus `referencesDataExtension` for wikilink seats). The daily-notes harness builds its repo with only `dailyNotesDataExtension`, so `alias.sync` never runs — this is why an earlier repro of the blocker "passed" and why the reverted code had ZERO coverage (a full revert stub passed 7330/7332, identical to baseline).
- Mutation-test every guard: revert it and confirm a specific named test fails.

title: Alias claimant listing: unblock multi-claimant banner, merge and reclaim
description:
`repo.query.aliasLookup` returns only the OLDEST claimant of an alias, and there is no claimant-**listing** query — only `aliasClaimantCounts` (counts, keyed by alias) and `tx.aliasClaimants` (transaction-scoped). A reactive UI cannot use either to answer "who else claims my name, and is it free now?".

Two live blocks legitimately co-owning an alias is an accepted state: the uniqueness trigger deliberately skips sync-apply (`src/data/internals/clientSchema.ts` — "V1 leaves cross-client alias merges as latent"), so two devices creating the same name offline produce it.

That single gap makes three separate defects unfixable in isolation. All three were found on the merged duplicate-name work and confirmed by running, not by reading:

**1. The banner cannot see a rival when this page is the oldest claimant.** `DuplicateNameBanner` looks up the alias and discards the result if it is itself — so in the co-ownership state it renders nothing while links still resolve ambiguously. Note the symptom differs from the case the banner was built for: the page DOES still own its name here.

**2. The merge is a permanent dead end with two claimants.** Only the oldest is ever offered, so `alias.mergeCollision` rejects on the uniqueness trigger, the button re-enables, and every retry fails identically. Measured: target ends `alias: []`, both rivals still live, tx rolled back cleanly (no data loss — just unusable). This is the stuck-button shape already fixed once for the descendant case; there is precedent for treating it as worth fixing.

**3. "Free again" is indistinguishable from "unowned by the oldest".** When the rival releases the name while the canonical page is open, the banner disappears but the page still has no alias, and nothing re-runs the repair until the next `getOrCreateKernelPage` — `Repo.ensureSystemPages` at workspace bootstrap. Typing the name inside that window mints a fresh alias-seat page and recreates the collision. Not a permanent loss (`needsRepair` compares against the full canonical set, so it stays true and reclaims on the next call) — a timing gap.

## Shape

One PR: a claimant-listing read path, the banner consuming it, the merge handling N claimants (fold them in one tx, or refuse with a message that explains why rather than a generic failure), and reclaim-when-free. Do NOT patch these one at a time — each half-fix leaves a banner that appears and then cannot complete.

Deliberately NOT justified by fleet size. Small-fleet reasoning is a migration consideration only, never a design justification.

## Ground rules learned the expensive way

Any test here must install `aliasDataExtension` (and `referencesDataExtension` where wikilink seats matter). A repo built with only the owning plugin's data extension silently omits the `alias.sync` processor, and tests then pass because the mechanism under test is absent.
close_reason: Closed on GitHub (issue #716); reconciled by bd-github-sync.

title: Alias-collision merge replaces adoption: keep the deterministic id as identity (#378)
description:
Alias-first adoption (issue #378, PR #466) fixed a real bug: with the canonical row deleted and a user page claiming the date alias, get-or-create used to collide on the alias-uniqueness trigger and abort — the day was permanently unopenable. Binding to the claimant fixes that.

It also changed "which block is this identity" from a pure function — `uuidv5(workspace, key)`, total, synchronous, no failure modes — into **a query over mutable user data**. Every consumer now has to know five things:

| dimension | failure it produces |
|---|---|
| staleness | claimant deleted between the predict read and the write tx → `ParentDeletedError` aborts the whole seed pass, every retry, registries stay empty (observed) |
| eligibility | a typed block merely aliased 'Journal' was treated as the Journal → user could not delete their own block |
| placement | adopted page left nested → deleting an unrelated ancestor cascades through the system page and everything filed under it |
| self-reference | Journal aliased with a date adopts itself → `CycleError`, date unopenable |
| durability | alias edited away → identity lost, second page created, original content stranded |

Seven review rounds on the stack were this surface arriving one consumer at a time. Six consumers were fixed by routing them through one resolver; the findings then moved to the contract itself, which is the signal that patching consumers is not converging.

## Options

These are issue #378's own three, plus a fourth.

**A. Keep adoption as a derived query, guard per consumer.** Status quo. Fixes the bug; the five dimensions stay live forever and every new consumer is a chance to miss one.

**B. Store the adoption as an explicit fact, decided once.** At adoption time write down that this block IS the workspace's Journal/Types/etc. Afterwards identity is one field read, not an alias query plus guards. Eligibility decided once; durability survives alias edits; staleness shrinks to one site. Costs a migration, and makes adoption explicit rather than a side effect of typing an alias.

**C. Skip the contested alias.** The app keeps its own page at the deterministic id and does not claim the alias while a user block holds it. No collision, page reachable — but two pages then share a name and `[[Name]]` resolves to the user's, so references silently point at the wrong block. Trades a loud failure for a silent one.

**D. Surface a merge/confirm flow at collision time.** Ask once: use this page, or rename it. Costs UI and a decision point in a bootstrap path. Composes with B as its trigger.

## Recommendation

**B, with D as the trigger.** Adoption is the right behaviour; what is expensive is re-deriving it from aliases on every call forever. If that is too big now, **A** — and take the self-reference bug first, since an unopenable date is the same symptom class as the original bug. **C ranked last**: this codebase generally refuses trades that convert a loud failure into a silently wrong one.

## Correction on the record

An earlier claim that the merged bag-strip PR alone fixes the reported bug was **wrong**. Issue #378 states the opposite: a bag-strip does not help when a live block owns the *canonical* alias, because the follow-up alias re-claim still collides. Discarding adoption would leave the original repro live.
close_reason: Decided option D (merge, not adoption) and shipped for kernel pages in #713, merged. Identity stays uuidv5(workspace, key). Remaining work is tracked in km-tgdi (claimant listing) and km-b2v1 (daily notes), which are consequences of the decision, not the decision itself.

title: E2EE workspaces: derive the synthesized-definition namespace from workspace key material
description:
Orphan-definition synthesis currently refuses e2ee workspaces (PR #686). Vlad's
call: supporting encrypted workspaces is required, not optional; this is the
follow-up PR.

WHY THE REFUSAL EXISTS. A synthesized definition's block id is
uuidv5("<workspaceId>:<key>", NS) with NS a constant in this public repo. Block
ids sync in PLAINTEXT (e2ee encrypts content/properties_json/references_json,
not id/workspace_id). So the server can compute the id for a GUESSED property
name and probe for the row - confirming "this workspace has a property called
health". Same content-oracle shape §10 already solved for asset paths.

DESIGN, from reading the key layer (all verified against source):

- The WK is stored as a NON-EXTRACTABLE AES-GCM CryptoKey, so it cannot be used
  for HMAC and its bytes cannot be recovered. Raw bytes are in scope only at
  import/unlock.
- There is already a WK-derived HMAC subkey in the record: `contentKeyHmac`
  (K_id), HKDF-SHA256 from the raw WK bytes with info "km/asset-content-key/v1",
  stored non-extractable alongside the WK (src/sync/crypto/contentKey.ts,
  src/sync/keys/keyStore.ts). It exists for exactly the analogous reason: to stop
  a raw sha256 asset path being a content oracle.
- resolveWorkspaceEntry treats an e2ee workspace whose record lacks K_id as
  LOCKED. So if an e2ee workspace is open, K_id is present - no new gate, no new
  migration.

Cheapest sound derivation, and the recommended one:

    namespace_bytes = first 16 of HMAC-SHA256(K_id, "km/property-definition-ns/v1")
    force UUID version/variant nibbles, format as a UUID string
    id = derivedBlockId({namespace, key: `${workspaceId}:${key}`})

Reusing K_id as a PRF rather than deriving a third subkey avoids touching the key
store, the unlock flows and the entry gate. Domain separation is sound and
checkable: K_id's only other use signs a 32-byte sha256 digest, and the label is
28 bytes, so the two input sets cannot collide.

MEASURED CONSTRAINT: uuid@14's v5() THROWS "Invalid UUID" on a namespace string
whose version/variant nibbles do not conform (verified: 'abcdef01-2345-6789-cdef-
0123456789ab' throws). The version/variant bits MUST be forced. That costs 6 of
128 bits, leaving 122 bits of secret.

SHAPE CHANGE THIS FORCES: synthesizedPropertyDefinitionBlockId is currently sync
and pure. Deriving from key material is async (SubtleCrypto), so it becomes a
resolved-once factory - e.g. resolve the namespace at the start of
applyPropertyDefinitionSynthesis and pass a (key) => id closure down. Plaintext
workspaces keep the constant namespace; their keys are server-readable anyway.

ALSO IN SCOPE:
- drop the e2ee branch of propertySynthesisWorkspaceRefusal. KEEP the absent-row
  branch: an unknown encryption mode must still refuse rather than fail open.
- the successor Supabase trigger migration permitting an e2ee workspace to
  advance 'cell' -> 'children'. The current trigger
  (20260820120000_allow_owner_properties_migration_flip.sql, lines 69-77) refuses
  e2ee outright, for every role including service_role. Per the design that
  migration lands WITH this, not before it.
- decide whether a WK rotation is possible in this design; if it is, rotating
  would make previously synthesized ids underivable and a re-run would mint
  rivals. Check before shipping.

This is the last piece of §8's "option 2". §11's column drop needs every
workspace at 'cell-off', e2ee included.
close_reason: Landed in PR #718, merged as d94f7759b. Supabase migration 20260821120000 applied to the hosted project and verified live (e2ee refusal gone; owner-only, client-step and forward-only rules intact).

title: String property values shaped like field-row content are silently deleted after the flip
description:
In a child-backed (flipped) workspace, writing a STRING property whose value is
itself field-form content silently deletes the property.

Reproduction (passes today, node env, workspace at 'children'):

  await tx.setProperty(blockId, someStringProp, '::((22222222-2222-4222-8222-222222222222))')

Result: the owner's properties_json is {} and the value child was minted with
is_field_form = 1.

Mechanism. encodedValueToContent (src/data/propertyChildren.ts) writes a
string-codec value into the child's content VERBATIM. core.deriveReferenceTarget
then stamps is_field_form from that content, because the content is a genuine
marked exact-reference span. isFieldValueChild filters the bit OUT of the field
row's value set (the §9 binding selection discipline), so the projection finds no
values and unsets the owner's cell key. Nothing errors; the value is gone.

Not currently reachable in production: no workspace is at 'children' yet. It is a
must-fix before the first flip.

Likely fix, and the reason it looks small: encodedValueToContent already has this
exact mechanism for a different collision — needsEscape JSON.stringify()s a
string value that would collide with the bare 'null' sentinel, and
contentToEncodedValue parses the quoted form back. Widening that predicate to
cover a grammar-shaped string (isGrammarShapedLabel) is symmetric with what is
there. Two things to settle before doing it: it changes value-content semantics
for every string/url property, not just synthesized ones; and value rows already
written in the broken shape would need a repair pass rather than being fixed by
the new encode path.

Adjacent: PR #686's orphan-definition synthesis hands a `string` preset to keys
written by raw writers and importers, whose contents nothing has vetted — so it
widens the set of properties this can bite, without being its cause.

Found while building #679.
close_reason: Closed on GitHub (issue #688); reconciled by bd-github-sync.

title: Orphan-definition synthesis for cell keys with no definition block
description:
Orphan-definition synthesis: mint a definition block for every definition-less
cell key, so "every cell key resolves a definition" is an INVARIANT rather than
a branch every consumer carries.

STATE (2026-08-21): implemented in PR #686, open, gate green, zero unresolved
review threads. Closes on merge via "Fixes #679".

WHAT SHIPPED
- `src/data/internals/propertyDefinitionSynthesis.ts` — plan (read-only) + apply
  (one transaction), at a deterministic id so re-runs and concurrent devices
  converge instead of minting rivals.
- `src/data/internals/propertyKeyScan.ts` — the "which keys does the registry not
  resolve" scan, shared with `audit-properties` so the report and the writer
  cannot disagree.
- wired into the palette gesture BEFORE the flip; refuses the flip on a key no
  definition can ever back.
- `Tx.livePropertyDefinitionNames` — the only way to ask that question
  authoritatively inside a write lock.

DECISIONS (owner's, do not re-litigate)
- the preset is PROVEN, not inferred: read the key's distinct values and run the
  real child round trip, narrowest preset that survives, `raw-json` when none
  does. Sized on production first: ~360k cells / 559 keys, of which 8
  unregistered covering 32 cells and 23 distinct values.
- definitions are minted VISIBLE — a hidden property is one nobody is prompted
  to triage, which is the whole job they exist for.
- e2ee is refused, gated on the durable MODE PIN, as an allowlist.
- a hopeless key (empty, reference-shaped, containing U+FFFD) blocks the flip; a
  merely BROKEN definition does not.
- only the workspace owner may start a flip (the server trigger refuses everyone
  else, permanently).

TRAPS FOR WHOEVER TOUCHES THIS NEXT
- see [[reference_property_definition_identity_sources]] — four authorities
  answer "does this key have a definition?" and they disagree by design. Most of
  this PR's ~40 review findings were picking the wrong one.
- see [[reference_test_raw_writes_bypass_projections]] for why several tests
  here look roundabout.
- the sweep-side half of §9 was deliberately NOT built (#689).

FILED, NOT FIXED — all linked, and the first three gate flipping a real graph:
#688 field-form string values; #690 e2ee namespace from workspace key material;
cross-client undo (km-32mk); km-ew48 block_types vs runtime on duplicate keys;
km-dsel a restored definition's own property children stay tombstoned (blocks
cell-off); km-6sm7 schema renderer trims on blur.
close_reason: Closed on GitHub (issue #679); reconciled by bd-github-sync.

title: Make the properties migration flip-then-backfill, and the command do both
description:
DECISION (Vlad, 2026-08-20): the runbook is flip THEN backfill, and the palette command does both. At 'children' the cell is still dual-written and still the synchronous read surface, so flipping a workspace with zero children hides nothing and loses nothing: reads keep coming from cells, new writes grow children, and the backfill fills in history.

DECISION (Vlad, 2026-09-18): this fleet is three or four users who can be told what to do. "What if someone does X during the run" cases are runbook lines, not machinery. Accepted on that basis, each with the reason on its own issue: #1050, #1049, #1042, #1064, #1066, #1067, #605, plus #1023 and #1031 as post-flip repair cases. Earlier accepts: #684 and #1007 (a peer's or another tab's pre-flip undo entries survive; reload clears them).

RUNBOOK

Before:
- Desktop Chromium, normal (not private) browser profile: the client id must survive a reload for an interrupted run to resume (#1066), and the pass holds one block snapshot per created row until reload, a few hundred MB on the largest graph (#605). Non-Chromium browsers run a single-connection storage pool that nothing has exercised end to end (#1069).
- The workspace OWNER's account: the cell -> children step is an owner-only server write.
- The device fully synced. The gesture checks the view gap before the dialog and again after it; a durable materialization gap is repaired with `pnpm agent rematerialize-workspace` first (#807 would automate that).
- Every other user told: do not create, edit, rename, re-type or delete property definitions on any device until the operator says the migration is clean, and reload afterwards. The gate dialog (#1059) says wait on every device holding the claim and pauses undo there; it does not reach an offline device.
- No pre-flip `audit-properties` run is required any more: the gesture runs the same scan, refuses an un-flipped workspace over every hazard it finds, and names the keys (#1119). Run it anyway when you want the uncapped list, or a key's provenance and fix.
- First run on a SMALL workspace and read the report before the large one.

Run: the palette action "Migrate properties to child blocks (one-time)". It plans orphan-definition synthesis, shows the confirmation (blocks to visit, and the keys per category — gets a definition / this device will not mint for / definition is broken / nothing can ever define — named rather than only counted, #1119), takes the graph-wide claim, mints the definitions, flips the column, clears this device's undo history, and runs the backfill: create-only, resumable from the data, batches budgeted by rows.

After:
- Read the report: rows created, values that could not convert. Repair those and re-run. Re-run the gesture until it reports nothing left; an interrupted run resumes from the same browser profile; a stranded claim is released from the gate dialog on any device that may write.
- `pnpm agent audit-properties` with syncGap null.
- Reload every other device and tab.
- Only then may anyone touch property definitions again.
- The CLI verb `run-backfill properties:cell-to-children` deliberately refuses an un-flipped workspace; the palette is the only flip surface.

AFTER THE FIRST FLIP: #626 (per-row SQL cost) if the small-workspace run says so; the consistency sweep (#1011); sweep-side orphan synthesis (#689); the cell end-state (#1012).
notes: 2026-08-23: unblocked on the "seed field rows mint alias pages" side -- that blocker closed as DOES NOT REPRODUCE (verified by running the scenario in a background flipped workspace). Note the related P1 filed in its place, km-2lhc: the phantom-page symptom is gone but the write-side property-machinery guards still resolve through the scoped registry, which fails closed for a background workspace. That one's failure direction is the dangerous one -- unrecognized machinery gets rewritten rather than retained -- so weigh it before the flip, not after.

title: bd github sync's pull reverts newer local edits and closes (measured, reproducible)
description:
A full `pnpm bd:sync` / `bd github sync` silently overwrites LOCAL bead state with an OLDER GitHub issue, despite the documented `--prefer-newer` default. It reverts both text edits and CLOSES, so work marked done can quietly reappear as open.

Measured 2026-08-20 on two beads (GitHub issues 637 and 640):

1. bd update <id> -d '<new text>' at 00:23:01Z. GitHub issue's last change: 2026-08-19T20:43:30Z, i.e. ~3.5h OLDER.
2. bd close <id> --reason '...'  (bead now closed, description carries the new text).
3. pnpm bd:sync -> 'Pulled 2 issues (0 created, 3 updated); Pushed 1 issues'.
4. After: the bead is OPEN again, the description is GitHub's older body, the appended text is gone, and the GitHub issue is untouched (still updated 20:43:30Z, still open).

So the pull applied GitHub's stale state over a strictly newer local version, and the push did not carry the local version out. Both directions of loss in one run.

Earlier instance of the same thing, same day: a bd update rewriting a bead's title + description was reverted by a later sync; only the title/description were affected, while COMMENTS added to other beads in the same session survived. That fits a pull that rewrites the issue-backed fields wholesale.

Not the discriminator: `synced_at` is NULL on all 247 beads, so it does not separate affected from unaffected ones. What did separate them: closes that had already been PUSHED to GitHub survived (a later pull re-adopts 'closed'), while closes not yet pushed were reverted.

Workaround that works (verified): after any bd update/close, immediately run `bd github sync --push-only --issues <ids>` — GitHub then matches, and a subsequent full sync leaves the bead alone.

Fix directions to investigate: whether `--prefer-newer` is actually being applied on the pull path; whether the wrapper should push local changes BEFORE pulling (it currently adopts GitHub closes first, then syncs); or whether the wrapper should snapshot locally-modified beads and re-apply them after the pull. Note the hazard is worst for agents, which routinely close a bead and then end the session — the SessionEnd sync is exactly when the revert lands.
close_reason: Closed on GitHub (issue #647); reconciled by bd-github-sync.

title: Recents, search and empty-query pickers have no property-machinery exclusion
description:
BLOCKS THE PROPERTIES FLIP (km-6qkc), and blocks running the cell->children backfill on a real graph.

Three block-enumeration statements in src/data/internals/kernelQueries.ts filter no property machinery at all:
- SELECT_BLOCKS_BY_CONTENT_SQL (core.searchByContent)
- SELECT_RECENT_BLOCKS_SQL (core.recentBlocks)
- SELECT_RECENT_USER_BLOCKS_SQL (core.recentActivity)

These never had a properties_migration gate, which is why the PR #628 sweep did not find them: a grep for the flip column finds sites that BRANCH on it, not sites that never filtered. They are equally wrong after the flip, so this is a pre-existing defect of the properties-as-blocks design rather than something the backfill introduces - the backfill only makes it start sooner.

Backfilled rows are plain tx.create with no systemMint, so they carry fresh updated_at / user_updated_at and sort to the TOP of every recency-ordered list. Field-row content is non-empty (the marked form), so the content != '' filters do not drop them. The three exclusions in SELECT_RECENT_USER_BLOCKS_SQL (state-root descent, seed key, system block types) all miss.

Consequences once machinery exists (measured scale on a real graph: 107,690 owner blocks / 360,105 property values, so roughly 720k machinery rows):
- the Recents page becomes about two machinery rows per property-carrying block, all newer than any real user edit
- empty-query (( and [[ autocomplete, and the ref-property picker, list marked field rows
- search / quick-find / find-replace / the 'Merge into...' picker match property VALUE rows on their own value text. blockMerge.ts already documents this one as a live hazard: picking a value row as a merge target relocates the source's values under an unrelated block.

Fix is a SHAPE decision, not three patches, and that is the point:
(a) apply the shared recognizedFieldRowSql (now exported from treeQueries.ts) inside each statement before the LIMIT - but note that fragment recognizes FIELD rows; excluding VALUE rows needs the parent's bit, so it is a different, more expensive predicate at each site; or
(b) invert the default so block enumeration EXCLUDES machinery unless a caller opts in, instead of today's opt-in-to-exclude (hidePropertyChildren: true). Every future query is then correct by construction.

(b) is what ends the class. Recognition is currently owned by six sites plus these three, and each review round has found more.
