title: syncViewGap is blind to materializeWorkspace, the queue-less materialization path
description:
Repo.syncViewGap() answers 'is my view of blocks incomplete' by reading the blocks_synced_changes QUEUE. observer.materializeWorkspace rewrites blocks straight from blocks_synced and stages nothing, so while that pass runs the queue is empty and syncViewGap returns null even though blocks is being rewritten under the reader.

The codebase already states the general form of this at clientSchema.ts (~line 1194): that is the BIG path, and every cheap probe for 'still materializing' is wrong.

Reachable at the moment it matters: workspaceBootstrap schedules scheduleWorkspaceBackfills and scheduleReconcileRescan (-> drainSyncWorkspace -> materializeWorkspace) on the SAME deep-idle tier with no ordering between them, and the rescan is marker-gated to the first open after upgrade - which is exactly when an operator opens the app and runs the properties migration. materializeWorkspace commits per 1000-row window, so a backfill batch can interleave between windows and read a row the next window corrects.

Severity note, measured against the CURRENT pass rather than the generic seam: propertyCellBackfill never writes properties_json - it reads cells and creates child blocks - so the classic #237 hazard (uploading a whole bag built from a stale row) does not apply to it, and its convergence loop plus the run-again-before-flip discipline repair children built from a stale cell. A future WorkspaceBackfill that assigns bags would be exposed directly.

Fix direction (recommended by clientSchema.ts for the sibling problem): have drainSyncWorkspace / materializeWorkspace maintain an in-memory in-progress flag that syncViewGap consults. Note a naive 'observer is busy' flag is wrong - ordinary queue drains would make the gate refuse constantly, which is the bug PR #628 just removed. It must count only the queue-blind materializeWorkspace path.

Found by round-2 adversarial review of PR #628; the predicate's doc there now names the limitation.

title: Between the backfill and the flip, property field/value rows render as ordinary outline rows
description:
Field-row recognition is gated on the workspace already being child-backed: the recognition SQL requires properties_migration IN ('children','cell-off'), and the children-hiding short-circuit in the tx engine does the same. Backlink filters carry comments stating that an un-flipped workspace has no property value children and therefore nothing to exclude.

The cell->children backfill makes that false. It creates the field rows and value rows while the workspace is still reading cells, so until the flip lands: every field row shows up in the outline as an ordinary child with '::((uuid))' content, every value row shows up beneath it, a ref-typed value row duplicates the owner's backlink edge, and all of them land in the full-text index.

The runbook (backfill -> verify -> backfill again -> flip) keeps the window short in principle, but it is open for as long as the operator takes, and the obvious user response to unexplained rows appearing throughout their outline is to delete them.

Decide between: making recognition independent of the migration column (is_field_form is stamped pre-flip by the reference-target processor, so the data is there), or stating the window explicitly in the confirmation dialog and the runbook so nobody deletes the rows.

The confirmation dialog currently says 'Existing values are not changed or moved', which a user reads as 'nothing visible changes'.

Found by the round-3 adversarial review of the cell->children pass (PR #596). Related: km-6qkc.

title: Cell->children backfill aborts on its own sync echo, so it cannot finish on a connected device
description:
The operator backfill runner calls assertBackfillMayWrite inside EVERY batch transaction. One of its preconditions is 'SELECT 1 FROM blocks_synced_changes LIMIT 1' — refuse while synced rows are staged and undrained.

The cell->children pass uploads on the order of 700k rows over several minutes. Those rows come back down the sync stream as echoes, land in the PowerSync-managed table, and its AFTER INSERT trigger stages them into blocks_synced_changes. So for most of the run the staging queue is non-empty *because of the pass's own writes*, and the precondition fires. The run then aborts as TRANSIENT: the claim is released, the outcome is 'deferred', and the operator is told 'Not started - synced rows are still draining into blocks. Try again shortly.' for a pass that in fact wrote tens of thousands of rows and already cleared the undo history.

Over ~1000 batches the probability of never hitting it is negligible, so on a connected device the pass very likely cannot reach completion at all. Derived resumability means nothing is lost and a re-run continues, but each re-run hits the same wall, and the report is wrong about what happened.

The precondition is correct in principle (do not materialize children from a cell whose latest value has not arrived yet) and correct as a START-of-run check. What it cannot currently do is tell an arrival apart from the pass's own echo. Options to weigh:
- narrow the staged-rows check to rows that carry properties (the pass's own creates have empty bags), so its own echoes stop tripping it;
- keep the per-batch check but make a mid-run abort a distinct, resumable outcome that reports what was written and says to re-run, instead of 'Not started';
- run the check only at the run boundaries and accept a wider staleness window.

Found by the round-3 adversarial review of the cell->children pass. Related: km-b014 (the pre-claim gate's staging branch), km-6qkc (slice C).
close_reason: Closed on GitHub (issue #599); reconciled by bd-github-sync.

title: [bug] Backfill pre-claim gate misses the staging branch, so tryClaim can still write from a stale view
description:
The pre-claim gate in `Repo` (src/data/repo.ts, the `if (!this.backfillSyncSettledNow())` before `claim.tryClaim`) samples only ONE of the two ways this device's view of `blocks` can be incomplete. It checks whether the device is caught up with the server, but not whether synced rows are still staged in `blocks_synced_changes` awaiting the observer's throttled drain.

The comment directly above that gate explains why the gate exists: `tryClaim` itself WRITES (it ensures the Migrations page and creates the claim row), so on a stale device the old ordering wrote a claim, hit the in-transaction sync assertion, and released it — leaving both the create and the `deleted=1` tombstone in the upload queue, where on reconnect the create can conflict with an unseen server completion while the tombstone frees later operators to repeat the migration.

That exact hazard is still reachable through the unchecked half:

1. Device connected and not downloading, so the sync gate reads settled.
2. Rows sitting in `blocks_synced_changes`, not yet drained into `blocks`.
3. Pre-claim gate passes (it only samples the gate).
4. `tryClaim` writes the Migrations page + claim row.
5. `assertBackfillMayWrite` then aborts on the staged-rows clause.
6. The claim is released — create + tombstone both queued.

A currently-passing test demonstrates step 4 happening with rows staged: 'releases the claim when a run aborts, so it is not blocked forever' in src/data/internals/workspaceBackfillRunner.test.ts stages a row, opens the gate, and asserts the backfill id was released — a release only occurs after a successful `tryClaim`.

FIX DIRECTION: PR #595 extracted `Repo.syncViewGap()`, which is exactly this two-clause predicate (staged rows, then caught-up), already shared by `assertBackfillMayWrite` and the audit verb. Convert this third site to it:

    const gap = await this.syncViewGap()
    if (gap !== null) { console.warn(`[workspaceBackfills] \"${backfill.id}\" deferred: ${gap}, so claiming would write from a stale view.`); continue }

Note the gate is currently synchronous and `syncViewGap()` is async — check the surrounding loop already permits an await (it does; `tryClaim` is awaited on the next line).

The test above will likely need its assertion changed from 'claim released' to 'no claim taken', since with the fix the staged-rows case should never reach `tryClaim`. Verify by deleting the new clause and confirming a named test fails.

Found during adversarial review of PR #595. Pre-existing, not introduced by that PR.
close_reason: Closed on GitHub (issue #600); reconciled by bd-github-sync.

title: Slice C: the cell->children pass (first consumer of the backfill seam)
description:
The properties-as-blocks migration's one-time per-workspace cell -> children
pass. Everything it needs now exists; this is the pass itself.              
                                                                            
## Ready for it — ALL MERGED to master 2026-08-19 (PR #583)                                 
                                                                            
• WorkspaceBackfill seam with trigger: 'workspace-open' | 'operator'. An    
operator pass is never scheduled automatically; Repo.                       
runWorkspaceBackfillNow(workspaceId, backfillId) is its only entry point and
returns ran / already-done-or-held / already-running / not-found / read-    
only.                                                                       
• The production BackfillCompletionClaim: one claim BLOCK per (workspace,   
backfill), deterministic id under a workspace-scoped Migrations page,       
systemMint, workspace-scoped so a SHARED workspace works. It RECORDS; it    
does not arbitrate — see the memory                                         
reference_exactly_once_over_lww_has_no_fixed_point before trying to make it 
decide.                                                                     
• Sync gating before any write, per-transaction preconditions, BlockDefault 
scope, skipUndo, a registry-readiness guard against vacuous completion, and 
single-flight per (workspace, backfill).                                    
• ctx.resolveNameSchema for resolving cell KEYS (which are names) — Tx only 
resolves by fieldId.                                                        
• materializePropertyChildrenForExistingRow (propertyChildrenProcessor.ts)  
is the per-row engine, exported for exactly this.                           
                                                                            
## Open decisions, in the order they block                                  
                                                                            
1. ORPHAN KEYS — DECIDED, not open. Backfill/mint the definitions; do not   
have the pass synthesize them. For the matrix keys specifically that is PR  
#585 (ensurePromotedPropertySchemas — mints a definition at promotion time, 
the streaming counterpart to the roam importer's schemaReconciliation pass),
which fixes #501. Content promotion invents names from block text, so no    
code seed can declare them ahead of time; the definition has to be minted at
write time.                                                                 
RESIDUE STILL TO CONFIRM, and the only part that is genuinely open: #585    
registers on the NEXT promotion of a key, and states it does no data        
migration. So existing definition-less cells become migratable once their   
key is promoted again — which needs (a) the extension reinstalled (pnpm     
agent install-extension; the running copy lives in the DB), and (b) that key
to actually recur. Check audit-properties after #585 lands and is installed;
whatever remains has no future promotion coming and needs a one-off         
registration rather than a design decision.                                 
2. IN-RUN CHECKPOINTING. A crash currently re-scans from scratch; the claim 
is all-or-nothing. Fine for a small repair, expensive for ~650k creates.    
Accept, or checkpoint?                                                      
3. THE OPERATOR SURFACE. Nothing calls runWorkspaceBackfillNow yet. Palette 
action, bridge verb, or both.                                               
                                                                            
## Must ship WITH the pass, not after                                       
                                                                            
• km-e4aa (undo stack): skipUndo cannot reach entries already on the stack, 
and undo replay restores a whole before-row snapshot — so a user edit made  
BEFORE the pass, to a row it rewrote, reverts the migration on Cmd-Z while  
the claim stops it re-running. The notification is the load-bearing half:   
silently clearing someone's undo history is its own surprise, and the       
operator is not necessarily the person whose history goes.                  
• PER-ROW ERROR CATCH. materializePropertyChildrenForExistingRow THROWS on a
cell whose value does not decode under its codec — its own docblock warns   
this caller must catch per row and report the block, or one pre-existing    
junk value aborts the entire flip.                                          
• The #389 flip-day items, especially reprojectParentField's missing pre-   
backfill guard.                                                             
                                                                            
## Should precede trusting the numbers in (1)                               
                                                                            
km-51iw — audit-properties can report clean mid-download, and it is the     
advertised pre-flip check.                                                  
                                                                            
LABELS: data-layer                                                          



LABELS: data-layer



## Status 2026-08-19

The foundation is merged. Nothing runs yet: no backfill is registered, so the seam is idle and every workspace still reads properties_migration = 'cell'. The Migrations page is created lazily by the first claim, so a workspace that never migrates never grows one.

Prerequisite chain before the pass can be written:
1. #585 (mint definitions for promoted property keys) merges — it is clean and open
2. the matrix extension is reinstalled, since the running copy lives in the DB (pnpm agent install-extension)
3. km-51iw (audit-properties can report clean mid-download) — fix before trusting the re-run
4. audit-properties re-run; register whatever tail has no future promotion coming
Then the pass itself.
close_reason: The pass exists and is wired. propertyCellBackfill is registered as a kernel workspace backfill, runs on both sides of the flip and is create-only past it, catches per row so one undecodable value cannot abort the whole run, and has two operator surfaces (the palette gesture that flips then backfills, and the run-backfill bridge verb with --wait). All three open decisions were settled: orphan keys are minted at promotion time rather than synthesized by the pass; in-run checkpointing dissolved because the candidate query asks the data what still owes children, so a killed run simply finds less work; the operator surface is the bridge verb. Its 'must ship with the pass' items are done too — the undo-stack clear plus notification landed with it, and the per-row catch is in the pass. Two things deliberately do NOT close with this: the operational re-audit residue, carved out as its own issue and made a blocker of the flip issue, and the post-flip healing seams, which have always been their own issue. Verified against the code 2026-08-23.

title: audit-properties can report clean while sync is incomplete — the pre-flip check that can lie
description:
Found by Codex on PR #583; the code is PR #500's, already merged.

src/plugins/agent-runtime/propertyRegistrationAudit.ts builds its histogram by scanning the currently materialized `blocks` rows. If it runs during an initial download, or while the sync observer still has a staged backlog in `blocks_synced_changes`, rows that have not landed yet are simply not scanned.

## Why this one matters more than a normal stale read

`audit-properties` is advertised — in AGENTS.md — as THE workspace-wide pre-flip check: 'Use it when a property isn't migrating or before any properties-as-blocks flip.' Its whole job is to enumerate the keys a flip cannot carry.

So the failure is: operator runs it on a device mid-download, gets a clean report, concludes the graph has no unregistered keys, and flips. The keys that were in the un-arrived rows stay cell-only forever — property migration skips unregistered keys silently (propertyChildrenProcessor: no schema -> continue), and after a later cell-off cutover a fresh device has no synced representation of those values at all.

A report that says 'nothing to fix' is acted on. An empty result and an incomplete scan are indistinguishable to the reader.

## Fix direction

Refuse rather than report while either queue is outstanding: connected-and-not-downloading AND `blocks_synced_changes` empty (the runner already has both checks — see Repo.assertBackfillMayWrite, which gates writes on exactly this pair). A refusal the operator retries is cheap; a clean-looking report that is wrong is not.

Worth stating the coverage in the output either way, so a future reader can tell a complete scan from a partial one.
close_reason: Fixed, in a different shape than this description proposed. PR #595 added the refusal, and commit d81d6e7d1 then deliberately reversed it: 'a guard belongs on the act, not on the report'. The scan now STATES its basis — syncGap plus syncedThrough in the output, so an empty unregistered list from a half-materialized graph is distinguishable from a clean one — while the refusal lives on the write path, where the backfill runner gates on it. Verified 2026-08-23: propertyKeyScan.ts reads repo.workspaceViewGap per workspace, which the staging-flag work made honest about the queue-less materialization path and about rows a drain reached and could not apply.

title: Implement BackfillCompletionClaim (synced, once-per-graph)
description:
HANDOFF from PR #508 to slice C. The WorkspaceBackfill seam is complete and safe EXCEPT for this: no production BackfillCompletionClaim exists, so Repo refuses every registration. Slice C's cell->children pass cannot run until this lands.

## What to build

`BackfillCompletionClaim` (src/data/facets.ts):
  isDone(workspaceId, backfillId): Promise<boolean>
  markDone(workspaceId, backfillId): Promise<void>

Inject via `RepoOptions.backfillCompletionClaim` at the composition root (src/context/repo.tsx, where the Repo is constructed).

The record MUST live in synced data, not `client_schema_state`. That is the whole point: every pass on this seam uploads, so N devices each running it independently is N chances to write from a stale local row and overwrite concurrent edits (apply_block_patches assigns properties_json wholesale). A local marker cannot express 'already done for everyone'. Design docs call this 'operator-run-once per workspace' (properties-as-blocks-migration.html §11).

Shape is yours to choose — a workspace-scoped record block, a column, a synced table. Watch out: whatever you pick, the claim itself is a synced write, so two devices can race to claim. Decide whether that needs to be atomic or whether a duplicate run is tolerable.

## What is already done, so don't rebuild it

The runner enforces, each pinned by its own test in src/data/internals/workspaceBackfillRunner.test.ts:
- sync gating (onSyncSettled: connected, not downloading, no downloadError) armed BEFORE the idle deferral, so an offline session schedules nothing rather than parking a promise
- preconditions asserted in THREE positions: before the scan, inside every transaction, and before recording completion. A chunked pass writes over minutes, so a single check only ever covers the first batch; and a run that finds NO candidates never calls tx, which is exactly what a partially materialized graph looks like
- staged-sync-queue drain check (blocks_synced_changes empty) — 'downloaded' is not 'materialized'
- workspace generation token, so an A->B->A revisit doesn't let an earlier visit's job write
- skipUndo, so the pass is not on the user's undo stack
- scope pinned to BlockDefault so assertNoSeedDefinitionWrites keeps applying — do NOT move it to a maintenance scope, that would hand the pass the ability to rewrite code-owned seed rows

## Still owed, tracked separately

- clearing the workspace undo stack when a migration writes (see the sibling bead). skipUndo cannot reach entries already on the stack.
- progress checkpointing INSIDE a chunked run: a mid-run abort currently re-scans from scratch on the next open. Fine for a small repair, expensive for ~650k creates.

## Testing

createTestRepo injects a local stand-in claim so the machinery stays exercised; it deliberately does NOT model cross-device visibility. Pass `backfillCompletionClaim: undefined` to exercise the refusal path.
close_reason:
Implemented on the slice C branch (PR #583), commit 8dea5ca20.

Shape: one claim BLOCK per (workspace, backfill), deterministic id under a workspace-scoped Migrations page (getOrCreateKernelPage, same as Properties/Types; tagged into SYSTEM_BLOCK_TYPES so Recents skips it). Injected at the composition root in src/context/repo.tsx via a lazily-bound repo reference.

Workspace-scoped rather than per-user is load-bearing: a shared workspace with a user-anchored claim is invisible to the other user's devices, which reintroduces the duplicate upload-carrying pass. I built the per-user version first and it was wrong for exactly that reason.

The seam's three questions, answered with measurements from a new two-DATABASE harness (real upload loop -> fake server -> deliver -> materialize), which the single-DB suites could not reach:
1. Atomicity: convergence is by STAMP. Ordered clocks -> both DBs agree on one owner and the loser backs off. Indistinguishable stamps -> neither adopts the other's row and each keeps its own claim. Duplicate runs are reachable, not theoretical. Both cases pinned in graphBackfillClaimRace.test.ts.
2. Crashed device: the claim stays held, no lease, deliberately — a lease expiring under a slow-but-alive run would re-arm the duplicate pass. Recovery is deleting the visible block. releaseClaim covers every abort the runner can see.
3. Duplicate tolerable: it has to be, given 1. Every pass on this seam must stay idempotent per row.

Also fixed while wiring: the claim's own fields are declared as kernel property seeds, not raw keys — an unregistered key is precisely what property migration skips silently, so a migration's bookkeeping must not be the one thing a migration cannot carry.

Still owed, unchanged and tracked elsewhere: undo-stack clearing (sibling bead) and in-run progress checkpointing.

title: Fuzz pack: props-as-blocks bounded suites (codec, MATERIALIZE/PROJECT, rejection sweep, convert-guard, metadata parity)
description:
Part of #430. Branch `claude/fuzz-props-children` exists (empty, at origin/master). The bounded slice of the props-as-blocks explorer findings (the stateful dual-write oracle and N-way rename permutations are tracked as heavyweights in #430). title: Pre-flip correctness: property-machinery containment gaps (movement, ref-deletion, unguarded raw writes)
description:
Found by a 5-agent special-casing audit run during PR #386 (properties-as-blocks slices A/B).

These are **pre-flip correctness** items, filed separately from #389 on purpose: #389 tracks post-flip *healing* seams that land **with** the flip tooling, whereas these should be fixed **now, or before slice C starts**. Different phase, different urgency.

## Severity framing

Two items are **live today in every workspace** (not flip-gated). The rest are dormant until a workspace is child-backed — but they are **flip blockers rather than deferrals**: several are silent data loss, and the flip is precisely what arms them.

---

## Live today

### 1. The raw-write bug class is unguarded — `guardSyncedTableWrites` covers only the bootstrap handle

`guardSyncedTableWrites` is wired only to the bootstrap `LocalSchemaBackfill` db handle (`src/data/repoProvider.ts:405-417`). The general `repo.db.execute` surface — including the agent bridge's raw `sql execute` verb (`src/plugins/agent-runtime/commands.ts:173`) — has **no guard at all**: no chunking/CAS discipline, no audit row, no processor pipeline.

This is live in **every** workspace, not only flipped ones: `typeify` (properties → `block_types`) and `NORMALIZE` (references) are not flip-gated, so a raw `UPDATE blocks SET properties_json = …` desyncs derived state today.

**Why this is the highest-leverage item in the issue:** every other entry here is a fixable instance; this is the only one that stops the *class* from regrowing. Three independent reviews have now each found a *different* missing cell in the hand-audited #402 matrix — hand-auditing is demonstrably not converging. This is the same move as the `callback-set` lint that made `CallbackSet` reinvention impossible instead of sweeping instances.

Worth noting the bridge is documented in AGENTS.md as the sanctioned way for agents to inspect and edit a live client, with nothing warning that a raw write silently desyncs all four kernel derivations.

### 2. NORMALIZE never runs on sync arrival

The Phase-2 upsert in `src/data/internals/syncObserver/materialize.ts` trusts arrived `references_json` as already-canonical and never re-verifies it locally. Currently benign *only* because every writer normalizes before upload — i.e. a latent cross-device invariant dependency with no local enforcement. Not flip-gated.

---

## Flip blockers (dormant now; silent data loss once armed)

### 3. ~~Movement mutators can relocate a property onto an unrelated block~~ — WITHDRAWN, replaced by a much smaller item

**This was filed wrongly and is corrected here.** The original claim was that `outdent` on a field row makes the owner lose a property and the grandparent gain it, framed as data loss. Two problems with that:

1. **That transfer is intended behaviour**, not a defect. Moving a field row moves the property — the coherent everything-is-a-block semantics. The PR #285 spike documents it as consistency case 7 and pins it with a test named *"reprojects both parents when a property child is moved."*
2. **The destructive mechanism I described is not reachable in the current code.** `indent` (`src/data/mutators.ts:521`) reads `visibleChildrenOf`, so a hidden field row yields `ix === -1` and it no-ops. `moveVertical` (`:647-649`) has a `findIndex(...) === -1 → return false` guard covering both branches. `outdent` (`:570`) uses the raw `childrenOf` for grandsiblings, so `parentIx` is found and the stale-read `-1` fallback — the thing that makes the spike's version genuinely destructive — is never hit.

**What actually remains is an asymmetry, not data loss.** `indent` and `moveVertical` no-op on property machinery, while `outdent` acts on it. That is harmless while field rows are hidden, but once the two-tier display makes them visible, a user will be able to outdent a property row and not indent it. Resolve it as part of designing movement semantics for visible property rows (see the #288 divergence note), not as a correctness fix.

Separately, and still worth doing: **movement semantics for property rows are undesigned in both implementations.** In the spike, `outdent`/`moveVertical` on a *value* row hits a `-1` fallback that silently deletes the property, untested. The current branch avoids it by accident of using a raw sibling read rather than by an explicit rule. Whatever the two-tier display lands on should state the intended rule and test it, rather than inheriting either implementation's accident.

### 4. Deleting a ref-target silently deletes the property

`inlineDeletedBlockReferences` rewrites every live `((id))` referrer into inlined prose when the target is deleted, with no property-child exclusion. A ref-typed value child **is** `((targetId))`, so it becomes prose and its `reference_target_id` clears. PROJECT has already run by then (kernel processors precede plugin ones, single pass, no fixpoint), so the owning cell stays stale until some later unrelated edit re-triggers PROJECT — at which point the property vanishes with no visible cause.

**This is a behavioural regression versus the cell era**, where deleting a ref target left a dangling reference with the property *retained*. It is the same failure shape as the `next-review-date` incident, where a derived-data pass silently removed ~10.5k cards' projected backlinks.

**Proposal: skip property value children in `inlineDeletedBlockReferences`, leaving `((deletedId))` intact as a dangling ref.** That restores cell-era semantics exactly — deleting a referenced block leaves the property pointing at a tombstone rather than deleting the property. Recognition is the ancestry-aware interior check; flip-gated.

**Why dangling beats inlining, decisively: inlining is irreversible, a dangling ref is not.** Soft-delete leaves the target as a tombstone, so `((deletedId))` can be fully restored — restore the block and the property snaps back. Inlined prose has thrown the id away; there is no recovering which block it pointed at. This repo has direct precedent: the dangling-refs remediation re-pointed and restored refs, which was only possible *because the ids were still there*.

Framed properly, this is not an exception to `inlineDeletedBlockReferences`'s principle but the same principle applied to a different content type. Inlining preserves *readable text*, which is right for prose; for a typed value the thing worth preserving is *identity*, and inlining destroys exactly that.

(Correction to an earlier draft of this issue: it cited `mergeRetargetProcessor`'s "rewrite the id in place" as the pattern to copy. That does **not** transfer — merge has a surviving id to point at, deletion does not. It is only useful as the contrast showing that inlining prose over a typed value is the wrong instinct.)

**Durability note.** Verified: `deriveReferenceTargetId` resolves a `((id))` block-ref purely textually with no existence or `deleted` check (`src/data/internals/referenceTargetProcessor.ts:60`), so the stamp survives the target's deletion, the value child stays parseable, and the property survives a full re-materialization from children. Worth naming the real asymmetry versus the cell era though: there, a dangling id was *inert data* nothing re-derived; here the cell is a projection, so the id's survival is a live derivation chain — only as durable as the set of passes that might rewrite or delete a value child. That is an argument for items 5 and 1, not against this fix.

### 5. Find-and-replace writes content with no codec validation

`applyContentReplaceMutator` (`src/plugins/find-replace/dataExtension.ts:138-196`) writes straight to `content` via `tx.update`. Replacing text inside a `number` / `date` / `boolean` value child can make it fail its codec; PROJECT's `firstProjectedFieldValue` then silently skips the unparseable child and drops the property key, with no error surfaced to the user who ran the replace. A programmatic-scale version of the "users type arbitrary text into typed properties" case.

### 6. ~~Sync-driven hard-delete never reprojects the old parent~~ — DOCUMENTED ASSUMPTION, won't-fix (Vlad, 2026-07-20)

`DELETE_BLOCK_SQL` (`syncObserver/materialize.ts`) removes a hard-deleted row without reprojecting its owner. If the removed row was a property field/value child in a flipped workspace, the owner's projected cell keeps the now-orphaned key.

**Decision: don't fix on the arrival path.** Reprojecting on arrival means writing `properties_json` — a SYNCED column — from the sync path, which is a categorically different move than the local-only derivations that path is allowed to make (deriving it locally would never reach the server and every peer would recompute its own; see the `arrivalProcessors.ts` invariant). Not worth taking that on for a case that isn't reachable in normal operation.

**Why it's not reachable normally.** A user delete is a SOFT delete (`deleted = 1`, an UPDATE) — it arrives as an upsert, not a `removed`, and the deleting device already ran PROJECT and uploaded the corrected cell, so peers converge. A `removed` is a physical row disappearance: either a **stream-exit** (scope-granular — it takes the parent too, so nothing local is left to reproject) or an **out-of-band individual-block hard delete** (manual server SQL / admin op / a hypothetical block-level GC — none exist as a normal path today). Only that last case strands a cell.

**Recovery if it ever happens:** the parent's next content edit re-triggers PROJECT locally, or a manual reproject. **Revisit if** a routine server-side individual-block hard-delete is ever introduced. Recorded as a code comment at the `DELETE_BLOCK_SQL` site.

### 7. ~~Recognition divergence: SQL and JS disagree on unmaterialized seed definitions~~ — MOVED to #389 item 7

**Not a pre-flip item.** Re-triaged 2026-07-19: this is dormant until a workspace is child-backed, and what it actually breaks is the **invisibility half** that *gates* the slice-C flip (§11) — the blanket hide that keeps C's backfill from dumping raw `((fieldId))` rows into production outlines before slice D's tree UI exists. That is flip-gated containment, which is #389's bucket (it sits directly alongside #389 item 4, whose proposed fix — a deterministic seed-id check instead of the registry resolver — is the same mechanism).

Two refinements found while auditing, both carried over:

- **There is a second window.** Besides boot-before-materialization (closed operationally by the slice-C runbook), a field row can arrive over sync *ahead of its definition block* on an already-warm device — which no boot-time ordering rule covers. That window is what makes this worth fixing rather than documenting.
- **Only the SEED half is a divergence.** For user-authored definitions neither side knows the definition until the block arrives, so both answer "not a definition" — consistent and self-healing, not a divergence.

Also recorded there: converging the *other* direction (making the tx layer forget seeds) is not an option, because that same checker is the write-side positional gate (`txEngine.isInsidePropertySubtree` / `isProspectiveFieldRow`), where under-recognizing lets the `setProperty` dual-write nest machinery that recognition can never reclaim.

### 8. Smaller items

- **Copy drops user content nested under a property value.** `serializeBlock` (`src/utils/copy.ts:17`) builds the clipboard from `subtree({hidePropertyChildren: true})`; because the filter excludes the field row, nothing in its subtree is visited — including ordinary user content under a value child.
- **`src/data/repo.ts` (~2830)** hand-rolls `sibling.referenceTargetId !== change.fieldId` instead of calling `isPropertyFieldInstance`.
- **SQL ancestor walks lack a visited-guard.** The "up" walks in `treeQueries.ts` and `backlinks/query.ts` lack the cycle guard their descendant-CTE siblings have (see #183) — classification still converges, but it spins to the depth cap on a cyclic DB.

---

## Suggested order

1. **Item 1 (the guard)** first — the only item that prevents regrowth, and live today.
2. **Item 4** before slice C — silent, irreversible data loss.
3. Items 2, 5, 6 alongside.
4. Items 7, 8 opportunistically. Item 3 is withdrawn as a correctness item; its residue belongs to the two-tier display design.

## Related

- **#389** — post-flip *healing* seams (recognition invalidation, background-workspace recognition, backfills). Lands with the flip tooling; different phase from this issue.
- **#402** — same-tx derivation liveness. Item 1 here is its structural sibling: #402 stops a derivation going stale *inside* the pipeline; item 1 stops writes bypassing the pipeline entirely.
- **PR #386** — where the audit was run.

---

## Verified correct

Recorded so the audit reads as complete rather than partial. No gap found in: undo/redo and `repo._replay` (atomic and consistent across property writes); direct delete of a field row or value child (reprojects correctly); outline keyboard navigation (machinery structurally unreachable); block merge (explicitly property-aware); export (`export_document` uses the visible view); and the in-pipeline write paths — `txEngine` primitives, `WorkspaceBackfill` and all its users, the post-commit processors (each opens its own fresh `repo.tx`), `typeTagger`, the local-schema backfills, and the schema migrations.

title: Sync: merged echo can share the author's local stamp — equal-stamp skip hides the other device's concurrent edit
description:
Found by the new two-repo convergence fuzzer (issue #372 Batch 3) on its first deep run. Minimized repro is deterministic; see the suite (`src/data/test/twoRepoConvergence.fuzz.test.ts`) with `FUZZ_SEED=2019987000 FUZZ_PATH="9:4:4:4:6:8:8:2:3:3:3:4:4:4:5:6:6:6:6:7:7:7"`.

## Observed fingerprint

Device A and device B both edit the same row before syncing. After full quiescence (all uploads drained, all deliveries materialized):

- server row = B's content + A's properties, `updated_at = S`
- device B row = same as server ✅
- **device A row = A's stale base + A's properties, `updated_at = S`** — A never materializes the merged row and permanently misses B's edit (until some future write to that row bumps past `S`).

## Mechanism (verified against the real trigger SQL and reproduced through the real upload pipeline)

`blocks_clamp_updated_at` (migration `20260612000000`, UPDATE path) computes, for a content-changing patch:

```
NEW.updated_at := greatest(NEW.updated_at, OLD.updated_at)      -- floor
NEW.updated_at := greatest(NEW.updated_at, OLD.updated_at + 1)  -- content bump
```

The `+1` guarantees the merged stamp strictly exceeds the **old server stamp** — the trigger comment says its goal is that "a peer sitting at OLD.updated_at sees a strictly-greater stamp", and that works (B applies A's merge). But when the client-proposed stamp wins the `greatest` (i.e. the patch author's wall clock is ahead of `OLD.updated_at + 1` — the *common* case for a genuinely-later concurrent edit), the merged row's stamp **equals the author's local stamp**. The author's echo then hits `decideStagingRow`'s equal-nonzero-stamp skip (`reconcile.ts` invariant I1), which assumes equal nonzero stamps ⟺ identical content. That assumption is sound between successive *server* states but false between a device's local row and a server row that merged someone else's change beneath that device's own patch.

Timeline of the minimized case (deterministic clocks; all stamps abbreviated):

1. B patches `content` → server floors+bumps to `002`.
2. A (not yet delivered B's edit) patches `properties` with local stamp `003` → server merges: B's content + A's properties, `updated_at = greatest(003, 002+1) = 003`.
3. Echo to A: staging `003` == local `003`, no pending upload → skip-stale. A's disk keeps the pre-merge content forever; the cache LWW never sees it either.

Note this is a *strict generalization* of the documented I1 blind spot (`reconcile.ts:108-121`, same-deterministic-id/same-ms mints): it needs no id or millisecond coincidence — just two devices editing one row concurrently with the later editor's clock ahead of the earlier server stamp + 1 ms.

## Candidate fixes (each has a real cost — needs a design call)

1. **Server: bump strictly past the proposed stamp on content change** — `NEW.updated_at := greatest(NEW.updated_at, OLD.updated_at) + 1` (or `greatest(NEW+1, OLD+1)`). Restores "newer stamp ⟺ changed content" globally, so the author's echo always applies. Cost: *every* edit's echo now re-materializes on its author's device (today the clean-edit echo equal-stamp-skips) — disk rewrite + FTS/alias trigger churn per edit, fleet-wide. This is the same echo-amplification concern that made the create-touch path deliberately NOT bump (see reconcile.ts's I2 discussion), though here it's once per real edit, not per retry.
2. **Client gate: equal-stamp skip only when content columns are byte-identical.** Directly conflicts with the 429fd4b2 protection this skip exists for (a stale in-flight server read carrying different content under the same ms stamp must NOT clobber the local row) — same fingerprint, opposite correct actions, indistinguishable without provenance. Probably a dead end.
3. **Protocol: send the client's base row-version in the PATCH** (expected `OLD.updated_at`). Server bumps past the proposed stamp *only* when applying onto a drifted base (`OLD.updated_at != base`). Precise — the author echo re-apply cost is paid only on genuine merges — but it's an upload-envelope + RPC + trigger change.

The two-repo fuzzer's convergence property is left strict, so nightly deep runs will stay red on this seed until a fix lands (per the red-nightly-is-a-real-bug posture in docs/fuzzing.md).

title: Matrix messages diverge on different clients
description:
So what I observe is that I have two different clients that both independently synchronize the matrix messages.
 And then sometimes when it happens and then I edit one of the messages on one client and then another one brings it from matrix independently before
 the edit propagates. There is a staleness that happens. So we get the old original message on one of the clients.
 And a new one elsewhere. I think server still has the correct new updated one.

title: Field-level merge: concurrent edits silently lost (whole-row LWW)
description:
Surfaced by the extension-seam audit — `docs/extension-seam-gaps.md`, gap **D2**. This is a standalone data-loss issue, independent of the extensibility work.

## Problem
Incoming synced rows are accepted/rejected **whole-row** by `updated_at` in `applyIfNewer` (`src/data/blockCache.ts:~173-177`: `snapshot.updatedAt <= existing.updatedAt` gate). There is no per-field / per-property merge.

Impact: when two devices concurrently edit the **same block** — even different properties, or both appending to a `refList` like `tags` — the row with the higher `updated_at` wins wholesale and **silently drops** the other side's change. Most painful for list/counter-style properties where a union/additive merge is the intuitively-correct outcome.

`docs/field-level-sync-merge.md` designs a per-key shallow merge but is **on hold**, and even as designed it's a fixed shallow merge, not pluggable per property.

## Suggested direction
A `fieldMergePoliciesFacet` (keyed by property name / codec type) consulted **before** the default LWW gate, returning `{value, accepted}`; default stays LWW so behavior is unchanged unless a property opts in. Pairs with the conflict-resolution/reconcile policy (audit gap D9).

## Severity
Silent data loss on concurrent edits. The small device fleet limits how often this fires, but doesn't eliminate it — and the fix is additive (default-LWW preserved).

title: [meta] Codify & enforce "derived data is add-only / retain-on-source" across all derive paths
description:
**Type:** invariant / architecture · **From:** the 2026-06-18 correctness audit (`docs/correctness-audit-2026-06-18.md`) (meta thread #2: derived data replace-written, lost on error/absence)

## Problem
Derived data (backlinks, references_json, SRS intervals) is recomputed and **replace-written**; any error or absence during recompute loses it instead of retaining. You already learned this once and fixed the **reprojection** path (add-only, retain-on-absence) — but the principle didn't propagate to siblings:
- #189 — one bad `refList` element throws → projection contributes nothing → the whole field's backlinks are replaced with `[]`.
- #194 — SRS interval isn't recomputed when its sibling date field shifts → stored interval diverges from reality.
- #187 — undo replay re-derives and clobbers the restored value.
- the historical ~10k `next-review-date` backlink wipe.

## Recommendation
Codify **"derived data is add-only / retain-on-source"** as a named, documented contract, and enforce it everywhere it's derived — not just reprojection. Provide a shared assertion helper ("recompute never reduces the derived set when the source value is present/unchanged") and apply it to the projection processor, the importer reference rebuild, and the refList decode path. Decoding/recompute that partially fails must retain prior derived data, never strip to empty.

## Acceptance
- [ ] A short principle doc (or section) stating the contract + why (link the incident history).
- [ ] A shared test helper asserting the add-only property, applied across all derive paths.
- [ ] Audit the derive sites against it (relates to #189, #187, and the importer).

title: SRS scrub-shift diverges stored interval from realized due date → corrupts interval + snapshot-history
description:
**Severity:** High · **Area:** plugin (SRS rescheduling) · **Status:** confirmed (traced + 2 verifiers) · **Audit:** `docs/correctness-audit-2026-06-18.md` (C1)

## Summary
Scrub-shifting a staged SRS reschedule date diverges the stored interval from the realized due date, permanently corrupting the interval property + snapshot-history and drifting the SM-2.5 curve off the real schedule.

## Where
- `src/plugins/srs-rescheduling/index.ts:366-377` (`shiftPlanDate`)
- `src/plugins/srs-rescheduling/index.ts:198-206` (`basisFromPlan`)
- `src/plugins/srs-rescheduling/index.ts:284-310` (`applySrsReschedulePlan` write)

## Scenario (traced)
Card `interval=10, factor=2`, today 2026-05-05. Stage GOOD → `newInterval=20`, iso=2026-05-25. User scrubs date −10d: `shiftPlanDate` updates the date to 2026-05-15 but leaves `newInterval=20` → commit writes `interval=20` + next-review-date=05-15 (a 10-day gap) + `snapshot{interval:20}`. Worse, regrading the shifted draft: `basisFromPlan` seeds `interval=plan.newInterval(20, UNSHIFTED)` but `scheduleFrom=dateFromIso(nextReviewIso)(05-15, SHIFTED)` → `schedule(40)` → stored `interval=40` against a realized 50-day gap.

## Proposed fix
Recompute the interval from the shifted date on `shiftPlanDate` (or deliberately decouple them and pin which is intended). The committed interval + snapshot must be consistent with the gap between the reviewed date and the next-review date.

## Acceptance criteria (C1 + C1b test)
- [ ] Test: stage GOOD on `interval=10/factor=2`, `draft.shiftDate(-10).commit()`, assert the stored interval + snapshot.interval are consistent with the realized gap.
- [ ] Test: regrade off a shifted draft computes interval from a basis consistent with the shifted `scheduleFrom`.
- [ ] `yarn run check` green.

title: PostgREST errors carry no status field → dead 4xx classification → upload queue jams forever
description:
**Severity:** High · **Area:** sync (PowerSync upload edge) · **Status:** confirmed (vs SDK source + 2 verifiers) · **Audit:** `docs/correctness-audit-2026-06-18.md` (B2)

## Summary
PostgREST error objects carry no `status` field, so the upload-error classifier's "permanent on 4xx" branch is dead. An unrecognized permanent 4xx is classified `transient`, PowerSync retries the same batch forever, and the **upload queue jams permanently**.

## Where
- `src/services/powersync.ts:318,333,353` (upload sinks `throw error`, dropping HTTP status)
- `src/services/uploadErrorClassifier.ts:52-54` (`err.status` 4xx branch — never present)

## Why (verified against postgrest-js)
`PostgrestError` exposes only `{message,details,hint,code}`; HTTP `status` is a sibling of the response tuple, not on `error`. For a non-JSON 4xx body, postgrest-js sets `error = {message: body}` with no `code` at all. All three upload sinks destructure `{error}` and re-throw it, so `status` is lost → the classifier's status branch is dead → an unrecognized permanent 4xx (401/403 expired JWT, 413, generic 400, non-JSON body) falls through to `transient` → infinite retry → queue jam. (Code-based classification at `uploadErrorClassifier.ts:38` still catches known codes like `23xxx`, so only codeless/status-only errors jam.) The existing classifier test builds synthetic errors *with* `.status` — a shape production never produces (false confidence).

## Proposed fix
Thread the HTTP status through the throw (e.g. `throw Object.assign(error ?? {}, {status})`) and classify on it; add a test that feeds a codeless permanent-4xx-shaped error and asserts record-then-complete (not retry).

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Test: a PostgrestError-shaped error `{message, code:undefined}` with NO `status` for a permanent 4xx is classified permanent (recorded+completed), not transient.
- [ ] `yarn run check` green.

title: refList with one malformed element silently strips ALL of a field's backlinks (cross-device data loss)
description:
**Severity:** High · **Area:** sync/codecs + reference projection · **Status:** confirmed (probe + 2 verifiers) · **Audit:** `docs/correctness-audit-2026-06-18.md` (B1)

## Summary
One malformed element in a `refList` property silently deletes **all** of that field's backlinks. `refList.decode` maps every element through `stringCodec.decode`, which throws on a non-string; the throw aborts the whole `map`, the projection catch contributes nothing, and the references processor then *replaces* the references column with the empty set. Same structural class as the historical ~10k `next-review-date` backlink wipe, and it propagates cross-device.

## Where
- `src/data/api/codecs.ts:170-173` (`refList.decode` = `j.map(stringCodec.decode)`)
- `src/plugins/references/referenceProjection.ts:34-52` (try/catch → `[]` on any throw)
- `src/plugins/references/referencesProcessor.ts:188-189,234` (replace-write of `references_json`)

## Scenario (probe-proven)
`['valid-1','valid-2',42]` → `refList.decode` throws on `42` → projection yields `[]` → processor replaces references → both valid backlinks lost, triggered by the next unrelated content edit (the processor watches content+properties). `setProperty` does not validate on write (`stringCodec.encode` is identity), and the `copy` sync path copies `properties_json` verbatim — so a wrong-shape value written by a buggy plugin / schema skew on device A syncs to device B and strips backlinks there. `retainedAbsentRefs` does not help: it only retains refs whose schema is *absent*, and here the schema is present.

## Proposed fix
Decode `refList` element-wise and drop only the bad element (or reject the write), so a recoverable list never strips the whole field's derived refs to `[]`.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Test: a `refList` value with one bad element keeps the good elements' backlinks (no whole-field strip).
- [ ] `yarn run check` green.

title: Latent cross-client alias dup wedges all property edits and restore of the affected block
description:
**Severity:** High · **Area:** data kernel (alias schema/triggers) · **Status:** confirmed (sqlite repro + 2 verifiers) · **Audit:** `docs/correctness-audit-2026-06-18.md` (A4)

## Summary
Two blocks that arrived via sync can both hold the same alias in one workspace (the uniqueness trigger is source-gated OFF for sync — documented intended-until-V2). Any later **local** edit touching the affected block's `properties_json` re-inserts its aliases, trips the uniqueness trigger, and `RAISE(ABORT)`s the **entire user transaction** — making the block uneditable and un-restorable through no fault of the user.

## Where
- `src/data/internals/clientSchema.ts:762-772` (`blocks_alias_update`: DELETE + re-INSERT aliases)
- `src/data/internals/clientSchema.ts:821-840` (uniqueness trigger, `WHEN source IS NOT NULL` at :824)
- surfaced at `src/data/repo.ts:1039-1051` (whole tx rolls back → `ProcessorRejection('alias.collision')`)

## Scenario (sqlite repro)
Sync seeds live blocks `X` and `Y` in one workspace, both with alias `foo` (source=NULL bypasses the uniqueness gate). A later local `setProperty` on `X` that merely adds a type (keeps `foo`) runs `blocks_alias_update` → `DELETE block_aliases WHERE block_id=X` then re-INSERT → the re-insert of `foo` (local ⇒ source set) sees `Y` still claims `foo` → `RAISE(ABORT)` → whole tx rolls back. Every property/type/alias edit on `X` fails; **restore of `X`** (deleted 1→0 re-inserts `foo`) also aborts → `X` is un-restorable while `Y` lives. Content-only text edits survive (they don't fire `alias_update`).

## Proposed fix
Make the local alias re-insert tolerant of a pre-existing cross-client claim (the self-reclaim mitigation currently only covers the block's *own* prior alias, not another block's), or reconcile duplicate aliases on materialization so the latent dup is resolved before a local edit hits it.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Test: two live blocks sharing an alias with `source=NULL` (sync), then a local `setProperty`/type edit on one does NOT throw `alias.collision`.
- [ ] Test: restore of the affected block succeeds.
- [ ] `yarn run check` green.

title: Self-merge (core.merge intoId===fromId) silently tombstones + doubles content + orphans children
description:
**Severity:** High (latent — unguarded public mutator) · **Area:** data kernel (merge) · **Status:** confirmed mechanism, reachability-gated (2 verifiers) · **Audit:** `docs/correctness-audit-2026-06-18.md` (A3)

## Summary
`core.merge({intoId: x, fromId: x})` (block merged into itself) silently soft-deletes the block AND doubles its content AND orphans its children under the tombstone. No data corruption today *only* because every current UI caller happens to exclude self — but `core.merge` is a **public mutator** (agent bridge / macros / plugins) with no guard.

## Where
- `src/data/blockMerge.ts:49-65` (`mergeBlocksInTx`)
- `src/data/mutators.ts:723` (`core.merge`)

## Mechanism (probe-proven)
`tx.delete(x)` writes an `after=tombstone` snapshot; `tx.update(x,…)` then reads that tombstone via `requireExisting` (no `deleted` filter → no throw) and writes `content = x.content + x.content` while the row stays `deleted=1`; `from`'s children re-home under the tombstone. Probe output: `deleted=TRUE, content="foofoo"`, child orphaned under a tombstone parent.

## Why it's currently unreachable via UI (verifier note)
`MergePicker` excludes the source (`excludeBlockIds:[sourceBlockId]`); the alias path self-excludes (`claimant.id===plan.id→continue`); backspace `previousVisibleBlock` never returns current. So this is defense-in-depth for the public mutator, not a live UI bug.

## Proposed fix
One line in `mergeBlocksInTx`: `if (intoId === fromId) return` (no-op self-merge). Add a test.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Test: `core.merge` / `mergeBlocksInTx` with `intoId === fromId` on a block with children + content leaves the block intact (not deleted, content not doubled, children not orphaned).
- [ ] `yarn run check` green.

title: move() cycle guard bypassed by a soft-deleted intermediate → durable structural cycle
description:
**Severity:** High · **Area:** data kernel (tx engine / tree CTE) · **Status:** confirmed (probe + 2 verifiers) · **Audit:** `docs/correctness-audit-2026-06-18.md` (A2)

## Summary
`move()`'s cycle guard filters `deleted=0` in its ancestor walk, so a soft-deleted node on the ancestor chain makes the guard miss a real cycle. A move can create a **durable structural cycle** that is invisible to reads, uploads to the server, and propagates fleet-wide — surfacing as a live cycle when the deleted node is restored.

## Where
- `src/data/internals/txEngine.ts:406-418` (move cycle preflight via `IS_DESCENDANT_OF_SQL`)
- `src/data/internals/treeQueries.ts:119-137` (`deleted=0` at base case :125 and every hop :132)
- `src/data/internals/txEngine.ts:828-841` (`requireParentInWorkspace` — no deleted filter)
- `src/data/internals/txEngine.ts:328-359` (`restore()` — no cycle recheck)

## Scenario (reproduced byte-for-byte)
Tree `root→A→B→C`. Soft-delete `B`. `move(A, {parentId: C})`. The ancestor walk from `C` hits `B(deleted)` and stops, never reaching `A` → `hit=null` → move proceeds. Result: `A.parent=C, B.parent=A(deleted=1), C.parent=B` — closed cycle `A→C→B→A`. All tree reads filter `deleted=0` so it's invisible until `B` is restored (which runs no cycle check → live 3-cycle). The `cycleScanSql` telemetry shares the same `deleted=0` blind spot, so nothing detects or repairs it. The corrupt `parent_id` routes to `ps_crud` and uploads.

## Dominant real-world trigger
Concurrent sync: one device soft-deletes `B` while another moves/outdents `A` under `C` through a still-visible surface. `move()` is a public primitive (indent/outdent/move/setOrderKey, blockMerge, dailyNotes, roam-import).

## Proposed fix
Make the descendant walk traverse `parent_id` **regardless of `deleted`** — cycle-freedom is a structural invariant independent of soft-delete. (Consider the same for `cycleScanSql` so the detector stops sharing the blind spot.)

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Test: `move(A under C)` with the intermediate link `B` soft-deleted MUST throw `CycleError` and roll back (currently does not).
- [ ] Test: restoring a node never exposes a live cycle.
- [ ] `yarn run check` green.

title: Tied order_key siblings make Enter-split / reorder / outdent throw and silently drop the edit
description:
**Severity:** High · **Area:** data kernel (mutators / order-keys) · **Status:** confirmed (adversarial verify + probe) · **Audit:** `docs/correctness-audit-2026-06-18.md` (A1)

## Summary
Two adjacent siblings sharing an `order_key` is an explicitly *supported* on-disk state, but the mutators that insert between neighbors call `keyBetween(equal, equal)`, which throws `"X >= Y"` and rolls back the whole transaction — **silently dropping the user's edit**. This hits the core editing surface (Enter-to-split, reorder, outdent, insert).

## Where
- `src/data/mutators.ts:95,99` (`orderKeyForInsert` after/before)
- `src/data/mutators.ts:396` (`insertChildren` → `keysBetween`)
- `src/data/mutators.ts:531` (outdent)
- `src/data/mutators.ts:685` (split)
- `src/data/orderKey.ts` (`keyBetween`/`keysBetween` wrap `fractional-indexing-jittered`, which throws on equal bounds)

## Why this state is reachable (not contrived)
- The sibling index `(parent_id, order_key, id)` is **non-unique** (`src/data/blockSchema.ts:97-99`).
- `orderKey.ts:5-8` documents that concurrent same-slot inserts collide and are resolved by the `(order_key,id)` secondary sort — i.e. ties are a designed, supported state.
- `treeQueries.test.ts:89-97` seeds two siblings at `'a0'` on the **read** side and asserts the tiebreak. The **write/mutator** side has zero coverage.
- Ties arrive via import, `setOrderKey` (no collision check), and concurrent sync.

## Impact (proven by probe)
With two siblings both at a valid library key, `createSiblingBelow`/`createSiblingAbove`/`split`/`insertChildren(before|after)` all throw `"<key> >= <key>"` and roll back (5 of 6 structural ops; only `moveVertical`'s adjacent-swap dodges it). The Enter handler (`src/shortcuts/defaultShortcuts.ts:630-701`) has **no try/catch**, and it dispatches the after-cursor suffix into the editor *before* calling `split` — so on rollback the editor shows the split text while SQL keeps the original: **editor/SQL divergence + a silently lost edit**.

## Proposed fix
Add an equal-bounds re-key fallback in `orderKeyForInsert` / `split` / `outdent` / `insertChildren`: when the computed neighbor bounds are equal (or `lower >= upper`), generate a key against the next *distinct* neighbor, or re-key the tied run, instead of calling `keyBetween` with equal endpoints.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] A mutator-level test that raw-inserts siblings with identical valid `order_key`s, then drives `createSiblingBelow`/`moveVertical`/`split`/`outdent`/`insertChildren` across the collision and asserts each **succeeds** (currently throws) — written red-first.
- [ ] Enter-to-split across a tied block preserves the typed text (no editor/SQL divergence).
- [ ] `yarn run check` green.

title: Move agent-runtime tokens from localStorage to user-page blocks
description:
## Problem

Agent tokens live in `localStorage` keyed by `(userId, workspaceId)`, managed by `AgentTokenStore` (`src/plugins/agent-runtime/tokens.ts`, storage key `agent-runtime:tokens:{userId}:{workspaceId}`). localStorage isn't actually more secure than a block on the user page — same-origin is the boundary either way — and a block fits the "everything is a block" model better (undoable, exportable, manageable inline on the user page).

## Current state (verified)

- Tokens are still in `localStorage` via `AgentTokenStore`.
- Only scopes today are `BlockDefault` (synced), `UiState` (ephemeral `local-ui`), `UserPrefs`, `References` (`src/data/api/changeScope.ts`). **No** persistent device-local (OPFS, non-syncing) scope.
- **No** `kind: agent-token` renderer.

## Blockers to land first

1. **A persistent device-local block scope.** Existing `local-ui` is per-session-ephemeral; tokens need persisted-but-non-syncing. New scope must (a) write to OPFS, (b) never enqueue into `ps_crud`, (c) avoid `row_events` if that audit is also gated to local. Add an engine guard so `kind=agent-token` blocks can't have their scope upgraded by an `update_block` tx (defends against an edit flipping a token into a synced row).
2. **Renderer for `kind: agent-token`.** Read-only display of label + createdAt + a Revoke button. Hide from QuickFind / autocomplete / outline rendering.
3. **Multi-device sanity check.** Confirm a synced user page on Device B doesn't crash when its child set is partially device-local on A.

Once #1 lands, the migration is small: swap `AgentTokenStore` for a thin wrapper around `repo.tx({scope: DeviceLocal})` + `repo.query.children({parentId: userPage.id, kind: 'agent-token'})`. Bridge handshake and CLI stay identical.

_Triaged from `docs/follow-ups.md` (P1)._

title: Tx-bound read guards for reference processors (close TOCTOU windows)
description:
## Problem

`parseReferences` and `cleanupOrphanAliases` do their expensive reads **before** opening a write transaction, to avoid the PowerSync queue deadlock documented in `tasks/processor-tx-deadlock.md`. That leaves two narrow TOCTOU windows:

1. Alias ownership can change between "alias missing" and deterministic target creation.
2. A newly inserted alias target can gain a reference between the orphan precheck and the cleanup delete.

## Current state (verified)

- `src/plugins/references/referencesProcessor.ts` builds its plan via pre-tx reads (`ctx.repo.query.aliasLookup`, `resolveAliasSeatId(aliasSeatReaderFromDb(ctx.db))`), then applies it inside a single `ctx.repo.tx(...)`.
- A **tx-bound** `aliasLookup(alias, workspaceId)` helper already exists on the Tx path (`src/data/api/tx.ts`).
- **Missing:** a tx-bound "does any block reference this id?" helper. The cleanup processor's reference check runs the `block_references` `SELECT` against `ctx.db` (pre-tx), so the orphan window stays open.

## Fix shape

Add narrow tx-bound read helpers for the final guards on the `Tx`/`TxImpl` path (using the active write-transaction lock context): re-check alias ownership and "does any block reference this id?" **inside** the tx, immediately before creating the fallback alias target or deleting a cleanup candidate. Keep the broad prefilter reads outside the tx. Do **not** call bare `ctx.db` from inside `repo.tx` — that reintroduces the queue deadlock.

_Triaged from `docs/follow-ups.md` (P1)._
close_reason: Closed on GitHub (issue #69); reconciled by bd-github-sync.

title: React identity contract for extensions (host-provided peer deps + jsx-runtime transform)
description:
## Problem

Extensions that render into the app's React tree must share the host app's React module identity. Today that's partly enforced (react / react-dom externalized through the page import map) and partly accidental: the in-browser Babel transform uses the `react` preset, which emits `React.createElement(...)`, so extension blocks rely on `window.React` unless they import React explicitly.

## Current state (verified)

- `src/extensions/compileExtensionModule.ts` runs `Babel.transform()` with presets `['react', 'typescript']` → emits `React.createElement(...)`, **not** `jsx()` from `react/jsx-runtime`.
- `index.html` import map externalizes `react`, `react-dom`, and includes `react/jsx-runtime` + `react/jsx-dev-runtime` entries — but the compiler doesn't target them.
- No docs for extension authors describe React/ReactDOM as host-provided peer dependencies.

## Fix shape

- Document React and ReactDOM as host-provided peer dependencies for extension authors and bundled extensions. Bundled extensions must externalize `react`, `react-dom`, `react/jsx-runtime`, `react/jsx-dev-runtime` and resolve them from the host environment.
- Tighten the in-browser compiler so JSX uses an explicit host import (`react/jsx-runtime`, or an injected `import React from 'react'`) instead of the global `window.React`.
- Keep import-map entries exact where possible, and integrity-pin any CDN-hosted host React modules.

_Triaged from `docs/follow-ups.md` (P1)._
close_reason: Closed on GitHub (issue #68); reconciled by bd-github-sync.

title: Harden synced extension-block trust: content-hash re-approval on source change
description:
## Context

A `type = extension` block is **application code, not inert content** — it is compiled and its top-level module code runs on the client. Before this is relied on in shared/collaborative workspaces, extension execution must be safely gated per user.

## What already exists (verified)

The acute "executes by default" risk is **already mitigated**:
- User extensions default to `defaultEnabled: false` (`src/extensions/togglable.ts`).
- `dynamicExtensionsExtension` checks `isEnabled(...)` **before** compiling — disabled extensions never run their module code (`src/extensions/dynamicExtensions.ts`).
- Enablement is stored device-local in `localStorage` keyed `extensions.overrides.{workspaceId}` (`src/extensions/overridesCache.ts`).

So the baseline "available but disabled until enabled" behavior is in place. This issue is the remaining **hardening**, not a greenfield build.

## Remaining gaps (the P0 part)

1. **No re-approval on source change.** Enablement is not bound to the extension's source. Once a user enables extension block `X`, a workspace writer can later **edit `X`'s source** and the new code executes on every member who previously enabled it — with no re-approval. This is a collaborator → collaborator code-execution vector.
2. **`system:disabled` is not a security control.** It is a synced, writer-editable property, so it can't be the trust boundary.
3. **Enablement granularity.** Today's key is `(workspaceId)` device-local; it is not bound to `(blockId, contentHash)`.

## Fix shape

Keep the trust decision outside synced block properties so a collaborator cannot force-enable (or silently re-enable) code for other members. Store an allowlist keyed by `(workspaceId, blockId, contentHash)` in device-local or user-owned settings, and **require re-approval when the extension block's source changes** (content hash differs from the approved one). `system:disabled` can remain an authoring/convenience switch, but is explicitly not the security boundary.

_Triaged from `docs/follow-ups.md` (P0 — Security). Reframed: baseline default-disabled opt-in already shipped; this tracks content-hash pinning + re-approval-on-change._

title: Reschedule (and similar multi-helper actions) emit 2–4 txs — one undo entry doesn't cover the whole action
description:
## Problem

`rescheduleBlock` → `applySrsReschedulePlan` (`src/plugins/srs-rescheduling/index.ts:319`) calls `getOrCreateDailyNote` **twice** (today + next-review date) before its own `tx.update`, and each of those opens its own `BlockDefault` tx — plus a third for `getOrCreateJournalBlock` if the workspace's journal block doesn't exist yet (`src/plugins/daily-notes/dailyNotes.ts:172`).

On a fresh workspace day a single user-perceived "Good" tap is therefore **2–4 entries on the undo stack**, and cmd-Z (or the toast's Undo button — same `repo.undo()` target) only reverts the property write, leaving the newly created daily notes / journal page behind.

The same shape applies to any action that opens N tx-emitting helpers before its own write — originally flagged on PR #31, but the daily-note coupling means it surfaces in **most SRS first-touches**.

## Current state (verified)

- `applySrsReschedulePlan` calls `getOrCreateDailyNote` twice, then opens its own `repo.tx` afterward (`src/plugins/srs-rescheduling/index.ts`).
- `getOrCreateDailyNote` opens its own `repo.tx` (scope `BlockDefault`) and may call `getOrCreateJournalBlock`, which opens another (`src/plugins/daily-notes/dailyNotes.ts`).
- No `getOrCreateDailyNoteInTx` variant exists; the Tx is not threaded through.

## Fix shape

Thread an optional `Tx` parameter through `getOrCreateDailyNote` / `getOrCreateJournalBlock` so callers already inside a tx can co-opt it. `rescheduleBlock` opens one outer `repo.tx`, calls a `getOrCreateDailyNoteInTx(tx, …)` helper for both daily notes, then performs its own update — collapsing to a single undo entry. Keep the standalone `repo`-only signature as a thin wrapper for existing call sites so this isn't a forced migration.

Wrinkle: `getOrCreateDailyNote` reads outside the tx, then opens a new one to write; the in-tx variant must do its existence check via `tx.get`, which matches the pattern already in `srsBlockDateAdapter.setIso`.

Worth doing before any future surface that needs single-entry undo (e.g. "duplicate card with new schedule", calendar drag-to-reschedule).

_Triaged from `docs/follow-ups.md` (P1)._

title: Copy/paste: carry block structure on the clipboard so a multi-line block pastes back as one block
description:
In-app copy -> paste changes the outline when a copied block has more than one line. `serializeBlock` (src/utils/copy.ts) writes continuation lines indented under the bullet (`- a\n  b`), and `parseMarkdownToBlocks` (src/utils/markdownParser.ts) reads every indented non-blank line as a child. So a copied ["a\nb" with child "c"] pastes back as a -> b -> c: the block is split and its real children drop a level.

Same class, all measured or read from the code (2026-11-05):
- quotes, tables and fences inside a multi-line block break the same way (`> quote\n> more`, table rows each become children; a copied fence followed by a child merges the child into the fence);
- a block's leading/trailing whitespace is lost (the parser trims each line);
- reasoned, not measured: on the shell surface even a single-line paste is parsed (src/paste/decision.ts), so copying one leaf whose content is `- foo` and pasting it there gives `foo`.

Text is not lost; structure is. Ordinary copy/paste reaches it.

Decided direction: put the structured blocks on the clipboard and, when the paste came from this app, rebuild from them instead of re-parsing the text, so the text/plain form stays what other apps get. copy.ts already has the TODO for an `application/json` item. Constraint to check first: `ClipboardItem` accepts only a few standard types (text/plain, text/html, image/png); a custom type needs Chrome's `web ` prefix and Safari has no web custom formats, so the payload may have to ride in the text/html item (e.g. a data attribute on a wrapper element) and be verified against the text/plain twin before it is trusted.

Pins to keep: src/utils/test/copyPasteRoundTrip.fuzz.test.ts restricts its generator to single-line, edge-trimmed content because of this; lift that restriction as part of the fix.

title: Undo after a split or merge drops text typed in the last 300ms
description:
## Observed (2026-11-04)

Production build, local-only workspace, headed Chromium driven by Playwright with real key events. 2 trials per cell.

- A block holds "first". Type " typed", press ArrowLeft, press Enter straight away, then Cmd+Z. The block goes back to "first". With a 450ms pause before Enter, it goes back to "first typed".
- Same result for Backspace-merge: type, jump to the line start, press Backspace, Cmd+Z. "first" without a pause, "first typed" with one.

## Reasoned, not measured

- The split or merge transaction's undo snapshot reads the stored row, which lags the editor by the 300ms content debounce. The live text goes into the transaction, but the `before` row predates it, so undo restores the older text.
- Delete-merge at the end of a block goes through the same path. Not tried.
- Redo should bring the text back. Not tried.

## Fix direction

Save the pending text before the structural transaction: call `flushPendingEditorContent()` at the top of `writeWithEditorRearmed` and before the merge transaction in `delete_empty_block_cm` (both in `src/shortcuts/defaultShortcuts.ts`). The helper arrives with the focus-ordering PR for this editor. It adds one undo step, the same as pausing before the gesture. A review agent tried this for Backspace-merge and undo then restored the typed text. Check multi-line paste for the same mechanism, and the refusal paths that roll the editor back.

title: Text typed within the content debounce is lost when the page reloads
description:
## Observed (2026-11-04)

Production build, local-only workspace, headed Chromium driven by Playwright. Click into a block, press End, type a few characters 3ms apart, then call page.reload() straight away. After the reload the stored block held the text from before the typing in 5 of 5 trials. The typed characters were gone.

## Reasoned, not measured

- BlockEditor debounces content by 300ms and flushes on blur and on unmount. A reload runs neither, and nothing in the editor listens for pagehide or beforeunload, so up to the last 300ms of typing is lost.
- A tab close, or a mobile OS killing the app, should behave the same. Neither was tried.
- A human hits this only by reloading or closing within 300ms of the last keystroke, so the loss is small and rare, but it is user text.

## Fix direction (not verified)

Flush pending content on pagehide. Whether the write transaction can finish during page teardown is the open question: the database runs behind an async worker, so it may need a synchronous local journal of the pending text that the next load replays. Measure a pagehide flush first, including on iOS.

title: Clipboard: block copy and cut may be refused on Safari, since they write after awaited reads
description:
Block copy and cut (`copyBlockToClipboard`, `copyBlockIdsToClipboard`, `cutBlockIdsToClipboard` in `src/utils/copy.ts`, called from `src/shortcuts/defaultShortcuts.ts`, `src/shortcuts/blockActions.ts`, `src/components/renderer/DefaultBlockRenderer.tsx`) serialize the blocks with an awaited subtree query before they call `navigator.clipboard.write`. WebKit allows a clipboard write only while it is handling a user gesture. A write that starts after awaited database round trips, which go through a worker, has probably lost it. If so, block copy and cut fail on Safari and iOS with `NotAllowedError`.

Not measured yet: Playwright's installed WebKit build does not match the Playwright version here, and the iOS Simulator needs an Xcode component install that asks for a password. (Annotations' Copy reference had the same shape. It now starts its write before the await. Same reasoning, also unmeasured.)

To check: on an iPhone or iPad, select a block, copy it, paste it into another app. Or run a probe page on the device: a button whose handler awaits a worker round trip and then calls `navigator.clipboard.writeText`.

Fix direction if it fails: start the write at the call with a promise-backed `ClipboardItem`. `writeTextToClipboard` in `copy.ts` now accepts `Promise<string>` and does this for plain text. `createClipboardItem` would take a promise of the serialized data the same way. Arm the cut only after the write resolves, as now.

title: Comments: retarget threads when a block split moves their quoted text
description:
Splitting a block leaves a comment thread stale when its quoted text moves to the new sibling.

Today: `core.split` keeps the text after the cursor on the original id and moves the text before it to a new sibling (a scope-root split does the opposite). A thread's `annotation:target` still points at the original id, so a thread whose quote left that id resolves as stale (the resolver finds no match), and its highlight disappears until someone reselects the text by hand. Nothing in `src/plugins/annotations` handles a split today; the design doc ("Anchoring against changing text", split row) records this as the v1 behaviour. No data is lost: the root keeps the quote.

Fix direction: in the split gesture's own transaction, retarget each thread whose exact anchor fell in the half that moved: rewrite `annotation:target` to the new block and shift `annotation:quoteStart` by the split offset. Branch on which split shape ran (ordinary vs scope-root). Threads that straddle the split point stay on the original id and go stale as today. Undo of the split then reverts the retarget in the same step.

Test: split before and after a highlighted span, in both split shapes, and assert the thread resolves exact on the right block; a straddling quote stays stale; undo restores the original target.

title: Read-mode selection gestures do nothing from the command palette
description:
Text selected in a rendered (not edited) block can be commented on, highlighted or quoted (Copy reference) through the read-mode gestures in src/plugins/annotations/actions.ts (readSelectionGestures, generated into actions in the annotations.read-selection context). Each handler reads document.getSelection() when it runs.

Opening the command palette focuses its input (Radix DialogContent focuses CommandInput), which collapses the document selection. Measured in Chromium 152: after setBaseAndExtent on paragraph text, focusing an input leaves getSelection() collapsed (type Caret). locateReadSelection then returns null, so the action is either hidden from the palette (isVisible) or, if the list was computed before the focus moved (reasoned, not measured), runs on a null target and does nothing, silently (runOnReadTarget ignores null).

Comment and Highlight have default keys, and a keypress does not move focus, so this only shows from the palette. Copy reference has no default key, so the palette is its only keyboard route and it never works there; the right-click menu does.

Fix direction: capture the read-mode SelectionTarget when the palette opens (before focus moves) and hand it to read-selection handlers; or restore the selection range when the palette closes before dispatching. Test in a real browser: happy-dom does not collapse the selection on focus, so a vitest test would pass without the fix.
