title: Preserve reference component instances across markdown sibling insertions
description: Inserting an unrelated same-kind reference ahead of an existing embed can remount its editor even when occurrenceId and render scope stay stable. Reproduced with the real reference component harness: begin with one page embed, focus its child editor, and prepend another unresolved page embed. The old EditorView DOM disconnects. hast-util-to-jsx-runtime currently assigns keys from tagName plus sibling ordinal. Fix direction: let stable reference identity participate in React reconciliation through an appropriate markdown-renderer seam, rather than a parser-specific workaround. Keep this separate from source-offset occurrence numbering; moving containers or wrappers may need an explicit preservation boundary.

title: Reference property fields targeting the same block share a render scope
description: ReferenceEmbed derives its occurrence id from the owner and target, without the property identity. Two ref or refList fields on one owner pointing to the same target therefore supply identical embedRenderScopeId inputs; field rendering does not introduce a separate scope. This collision is established by tracing the scope inputs; its effect on an open editor has not been measured. Reproduce with two reference fields targeting one block and compare their data-render-scope-id attributes. Include the field identity in the scope and add a component regression proving the copies remain independently focused while refList reordering preserves each entry identity.

title: Reference occurrence ids are source offsets: an edit before an embed remounts it, and ids collide
description:
Reference occurrence ids are source offsets: `text:<offset>`, `link:<offset>` and `cross:<offset>`, built in `remark-blockrefs.ts` and `remark-wikilinks.ts`. `BlockEmbed` and `BlockRef` derive the embed's render scope from them (`embedRenderScopeId`). Two problems follow.

**1. An edit before a reference remounts the embed's subtree.**
- Any change that shifts the reference's offset triggers it: typing earlier in the host block, a synced edit, or a rename that rewrites an earlier `[[Old]]`.
- The embed gets a new render scope, so its block context changes. Every `DefaultBlockRenderer` inside it then memoizes its slots afresh, and the subtree remounts. An editor open inside the embed loses its caret and focus.
- **Reproduced** (2026-10-30): a component test that prepends text to a block with two embeds. The `.blockembed` boxes stayed connected; the embedded rows were replaced.
- **Reasoned, not measured:** the focus location stores a render scope id, and `isFocusedBlock` matches on it. The embedded editor may therefore drop out of edit mode entirely, not just remount.

**2. Ids can collide.**
- Text that `remarkWikilinks` splits off has no position. `remarkBlockrefs` then falls back to an offset local to that text node.
- Example: `![[A]] !((E)) ![[B]] !((E))` gives both `E` embeds `text:1`, so the two share one render scope. **Reproduced** by running the remark plugins directly.

**Fix direction.**
- Derive the occurrence id from the reference's ordinal among the block's references to the same target (for example `E#2`). That stays stable under any edit that doesn't reorder references to that target, and it cannot collide.
- First, find everything that stores state keyed by render scope (the focus location, and per-scope expansion state, if any), and decide what a reordering should do to it.

**Context.** Two related remount causes were fixed in the "Keep reference components mounted" PR and the markdown input seam PR; this is the remaining one.
notes: Ready for review in https://github.com/Stvad/knowledge-medium/pull/1515 at head 20a686d771e86d72acaeba30f218ac5fa98507f6. Final gate: check: PASS (12,817 tests across 882 files). Two adversarial reviewers plus quality completed; the hidden-child ordinal finding was fixed and rechecked. No stored rows rewritten; old embedded focus scopes can stop matching once after deployment. Separate existing scope issues are tracked in #1514 and #1516. PR remains open and unmerged.

title: Multi-select indent/outdent/move treat the selection block by block: edge groups scramble, out-of-panel rows move
description:
The multi-select structural actions (indent, outdent, move up, move down) run the single-block action once per selected block (`applyToAllBlocksInSelection`, `src/shortcuts/utils.ts`). That loop has no notion of the selection as a group, which shows in three ways. All are reachable today with Shift+Arrow and Tab / Alt+Shift+Arrow, and with one tap on the touch selection toolbar.

1. A group at the edge scrambles. Select the first two children [r1, r2] of the panel root and move up: r1 can't move, then r2 swaps above it, giving [r2, r1, ...]. Moving down on the last two does the mirror image. Indent splits a group the same way when its first block has no previous sibling: r1 stays, and r2 nests under it.
2. Rows outside the panel's subtree are edited in their own page. The fan-out passes the panel's top-level block as every block's scope root (`PanelRenderer`'s multi-select context), while a backlink row or embed belongs to a surface whose boundary is the entry's shown block. A backlink row in the selection is outdented, indented or moved among siblings in its own page, where nothing on screen shows it.
3. A selection not stored in tree order misapplies. The fan-out applies in stored order. Spatial navigation's visible-DOM-order ranges (embeds interleave), the agent-runtime writer, and selections stored before toggles kept document order can all store another order; indent then nests blocks into each other.

Measured 2026-10-29 by running the real `multiSelectModeActions` handlers on the test DB. The probe file was in a review session's scratchpad.

Fix direction: make the structural fan-out group-aware, in one owner and ideally one `repo.tx` (which also fixes the one-undo-entry-per-block problem in #1479):
- sort the selection into tree order at the point of use;
- skip blocks not under the panel's scope root;
- treat a block whose adjacent sibling in the direction of travel is a selected block that didn't move as blocked too. Processing indent and move-up forwards, and move-down backwards, a block whose previous (or next) sibling is still a selected block keeps its place, so the group stays whole.

title: Multi-select indent/outdent/move leave one undo entry per selected block
description:
Indent, outdent, move up and move down over a multi-block selection leave one undo entry per selected block, so one Undo (Cmd+Z, or the touch selection toolbar's Undo button) reverts only the last block it touched.

Cause: `applyToAllBlocksInSelection` (`src/shortcuts/utils.ts`) runs the per-block action once per selected block, and each run commits its own `repo.tx`. The TODO above its loop names this.

Reproduce: select two or more sibling blocks, indent them, press Undo once. Only the last block returns. Measured 2026-10-29 on the iOS Simulator with the touch selection toolbar: after indenting two selected blocks, one Undo reverted only the second.

Fix direction: run the fan-out inside `repo.undoGroup`, which folds several txs into one undo entry. Wrapping the loop is not enough on its own: the per-block structural handlers in `getDefaultActionGroups` close over the outer `repo`, so their writes would not carry the group. They need to write through the grouped repo (from deps, or a grouped repo passed into the fan-out). The delete and cut paths are already one batch and are unaffected.

title: GitHub Actions schedule triggers hours late or dropped since late Aug 2026: dispatch the monitors externally
description:
GitHub Actions `schedule` triggers have been hours late and mostly dropped since 2026-08-26/27. The scheduled monitors rely on them. Research only so far; no workflow, routine or setting was changed.

## Measured (2026-10-28, gh run list --event schedule)
- fuzz-nightly (cron 23 6 * * *): 25-60 min late until 2026-08-26, then a step change. Since 2026-08-29 it starts 10:42-15:41 UTC (4-9h late).
- supabase-health (hourly, 17 * * * *): about 24 runs/day until 2026-08-23 (minutes drifting up to ~30 late). Now 4-6 runs/day, so ~75% of ticks are dropped.
- attachments-ciphertext-audit (37 */6 * * *): 3-4 runs/day, starting ~3-5.5h late.
- remove-pr-previews (23 5 * * *): starts ~4-6h late.
- No repo-side event lines up: repo is public, Actions enabled, no visibility/settings change; the fuzz-nightly cron line is unchanged since it was added.

## Hypothesis (not measured)
The cause is GitHub's scheduler, not our workflows. Off-peak minutes (:17, :23, :37) are affected too, and workflow_dispatch starts normally.

## Outside evidence
- Widespread, same onset (2026-08-26), unresolved, no GitHub staff reply: https://github.com/orgs/community/discussions/206019
- Hourly gaps and ~5.5h-late dailies, Oct 4: https://github.com/orgs/community/discussions/209514
- Multi-hour delays and missing slots since Oct 1: https://github.com/orgs/community/discussions/210111
- githubstatus shows no incident for the schedule trigger. October Actions incidents concern runner assignment or result reporting (seen via third-party mirrors, not confirmed on githubstatus).
- Docs say schedule "can be delayed during periods of high loads" and queued jobs "may be dropped"; high load is heaviest at the start of each hour: https://docs.github.com/en/actions/reference/workflows-and-actions/events-that-trigger-workflows
- schedule now accepts an IANA timezone; it changes how the cron is read, not the lateness. Auto-disable after 60 days without repo activity is not our case.

## Fixes considered
1. Off-peak minutes: free, but reported ineffective and we are already off-peak. Skip.
2. External clock calling workflow_dispatch / repository_dispatch (Cloudflare Workers cron, cron-job.org, a Claude routine). Most-cited workaround. Needs a fine-grained PAT (Actions: write, this repo only) or a GitHub App token held by the clock. Cloudflare Workers cron is the pick: free, secret in Workers secrets. Cost: one more moving part and an expiring token.
3. Self-hosted runner: does not help, the delay is in creating the run, not in runner pickup.
4. Dead-man's switch (alert when no run lands in a window): detects, does not fix. Pair with 2.
5. Keep the schedule line as a fallback alongside dispatch: needs a concurrency group or an already-ran-in-this-window check against duplicates.

## Recommendation per workflow
- supabase-health: hourly dispatch from a Cloudflare Worker cron, plus a dead-man's switch alerting if no run lands in ~2h. Make the job idempotent so a late schedule run does not double-alert. This is the one that matters.
- attachments-ciphertext-audit: same Worker, every 6h. Lateness is tolerable (backstop behind the post-deploy run).
- fuzz-nightly: leave the schedule. The triage routine moves to fire on the fuzz run's failure event, removing the clock dependency.
- remove-pr-previews: leave as is; a late sweep costs nothing.

## Done when
supabase-health fires hourly (and a missed hour alerts) without relying on the schedule trigger.

title: sync: enqueue uploads through PowerSync's powersync_crud vtab instead of writing ps_crud directly
description:
Our block upload triggers (`CREATE_BLOCKS_UPLOAD_INSERT_TRIGGER_SQL` / `..._UPDATE_...` in `src/data/internals/clientSchema.ts`) insert upload envelopes straight into PowerSync's queue table `ps_crud`. The data-layer redesign doc says they "forward to `powersync_crud`". That is the SQLite core's virtual table in front of the queue, available since core 0.4.2. The first implementation wrote the table instead, apparently treating the two as the same thing.

Writing through `powersync_crud` makes the core do its own local-write bookkeeping. Bypassing it has cost us three times:
- **#1226 (1.x):** the download hold was never raised, so a server checkpoint cut before our upload landed was applied over the newer local row. Fixed with our own `ps_crud_hold_downloads` trigger.
- **PowerSync 2.x (#1443):** core schema 14 moved that bookkeeping and dropped the column the trigger wrote, so the trigger had to be retired. The 2.x SDK now raises the hold at upload completion.
- **The last-seen checkpoint id is never cleared on our writes.** So if the service's write-checkpoint counter restarts (instance storage wiped, or the app moved to a new instance), a stale checkpoint can be applied. #1443 adds a stopgap trigger that clears it by writing core-internal `ps_kv` keys.

Routing through `powersync_crud` would retire the stopgap and stop us depending on core-internal state. It is a design change, not a swap. To work out:
- **Transaction grouping.** The core assigns `tx_id` per SQLite transaction from its own counter (`ps_tx`). Today we stamp our own `tx_context.tx_seq`, and the upload path groups by it. Confirm a `repo.tx` is always exactly one SQLite transaction, and check every reader of `tx_id` (upload compaction, the rejected-upload quarantine and retry).
- **Locally edited rows during sync.** The simple vtab also records the row in `ps_updated_rows`, and the core then re-applies server state to locally modified rows during sync. Our Layout B syncs into `blocks_synced`, while `blocks` is local-only and not a raw table in the PowerSync schema. Work out what the core does with `ps_updated_rows` entries for `blocks` before trusting it.
- **Conflict clauses and flags.** A `blocks` write that carries `OR IGNORE` / `OR ABORT` reaches the vtab through a trigger, so check how the vtab behaves under each. Also check the `IGNORE_EMPTY_UPDATE` flag, and the envelope shape (`op`, `id`, `type`, `data`, `old`, `metadata`) against what `src/services/powersync.ts` parses.
- **Every other direct writer of `ps_crud`**, e.g. the rejected-upload retry in the system-status dialog.

Done when:
- every enqueue goes through `powersync_crud`;
- the stopgap trigger is retired (added to `RETIRED_TRIGGER_NAMES`);
- `writeCheckpointGate.test.ts` passes against the real core, including the "write-checkpoint ids restart" case;
- one upload still carries one `repo.tx`.

title: On mobile, target:'main' resolves to the first panel row, not the pane the user sees
description:
`src/utils/navigation.ts` resolves a navigation `target: 'main'` to the first panel row. The same class of bug surfaced while building pane maximization (#549): the 'main' read path feeds `resolveDailyNoteAnchor`, so prev/next-day notes were created anchored on an invisible pane. A layout fact reaching live-data creation is the shape to look for.

Fix direction: resolve 'main' to the visible pane on mobile, the same way the maximized case does. Pre-existing; recorded 2026-08-15 and still present 2026-10-22.

title: gh-pages is ~1.8 GB from open-PR previews; decide on preview sourcemaps and idle-preview expiry
description:
After pruning closed-PR previews, the GitHub Pages site on gh-pages is still about 1.8 GB, almost all of it previews of open PRs at about 56 MiB each. That is over GitHub's documented 1 GB Pages limit, which isn't enforced as a hard failure, and every build re-uploads the whole site, so build time, and the window in which a newer push can cancel a deploy, grows with it.

Two levers, measured 2026-10-21:
1. Sourcemaps are 33.6 of 58 MiB in a current preview build (vite.config.ts has build.sourcemap: true for every build). Turning them off for preview builds only (APP_BASE_PATH under pr-preview/) roughly halves each preview, at the cost of readable stack traces in previews.
2. 16 of the 30 open PRs with previews had no activity for 30+ days. The scheduled sweep (scripts/sweep-pr-previews.ts) could also expire previews of PRs idle longer than N days; a push to the PR redeploys its preview.

Either one alone brings the site under 1 GB. Needs a decision on which to apply.

title: E2EE conversion: verify reads re-seal records through an owner-only RPC
description:
Verify's read of re-seal records (`readContentSealHistory` in src/sync/conversion/conversionServer.ts) goes through PostgREST with RLS. For each of a chunk's history rows the planner runs the membership policy function (`private.is_workspace_member`) and detoasts `after_diff` for the content LIKE before it can drop the row. On a block with tens of thousands of history rows, one chunk costs seconds: 7.8 s measured for about 27k rows, so verify hits the app role's 8 s statement_timeout.

**Fix direction:** an owner-only SECURITY DEFINER RPC, like `conversion_workspace_counts`. It checks ownership once, takes the chunk's block ids, returns only the rows matching the re-seal record test, and filters on the cheap columns (op, changed_columns) before touching after_diff. Optionally size chunks by history rows rather than block count.

Done when a workspace with a block holding about 30k history rows verifies under the default 8 s timeout, pinned by a stack test (check:db).

title: E2EE conversion runbook: lessons from the first production run
description:
Fold what the first production run (km-y4q1.7) showed into docs/workspace-e2ee-conversion.md §8.

- **ANALYZE again after the re-seal, before verify.** The re-seal adds one history row per block (here about 60% more history), so the statistics from the pre-run ANALYZE are stale when verify pages the history. The first verify attempt timed out (57014) on a history read.
- **Verify on a workspace with very busy blocks.** Verify reads re-seal records 100 block ids at a time. A chunk holding a block with about 27k history rows took 7.8 s on the server, against the app role's 8 s statement_timeout, so verify failed at the same chunk twice. The run was unblocked by raising `authenticated`'s statement_timeout to 30s (`alter role authenticated set statement_timeout = '30s'; notify pgrst, 'reload config';`), then reverting to 8s after the purge. The runbook should give that step, and a preflight check for the busiest block's history size, until the read moves server-side (the sibling bead).
- **Disk headroom counts whole rows.** The "6x content bytes" rule undercounted about 3x: every re-sealed block also gets a new full row version, index entries and a history row. Measure `sum(pg_column_size(b.*))` over the workspace's blocks and history, and add the VACUUM FULL peak (one table copy plus its WAL).
- **The agent bridge loses the user once the flow's gate closes the workspace,** so a monitor has to follow the server (phase, sealed count, history count), not the tab.

Done when the runbook says each of these, with the measured figures marked measured.

title: Restoring a page should take its name back from a seat minted while it was dead
description:
Follow-up from the restore-and-alias cluster (#883, PR #1366).

## The gap

After a page is deleted, the next re-parse of any block that links one of its names (`[[Name]]`) finds no live claimant and mints an alias seat for that name. Two ordinary ways this happens:
- **During the delete itself.** A block that holds both `[[Name]]` and a `((block-ref))` to the page (or to one of its children) is re-parsed as part of the delete's own cascade.
- **Between the delete and the undo.** Any edit to a `[[Name]]` referrer re-parses it.

With #1366, restoring the page (restore, or undo of the delete) yields the name to that seat instead of aborting. So delete-then-undo is not an exact round trip:
- the page comes back without the name;
- `[[Name]]` keeps resolving to an empty seat;
- if the name is the page's title, the duplicate-name banner offers a one-click merge;
- if it is a secondary alias, nothing tells the user.

Reproduction: `src/data/test/aliasReclaim.test.ts`, the describe block "when the delete's own cascade mints a seat for the name". It currently asserts the yield.

## Fix direction

On revival (both `core.restore` and the undo replay's yield), check every other holder of a contested name:
- **All holders are pristine machine seats** (`matchesAliasSeatSeed`, at their slot id): fold each seat into the revived page with `mergeBlocksInTx`, and keep the name. Children move with the merge, and the merge event retargets inbound references.
- **Any other holder:** yield the name, as now.

One question to decide in the same piece of work: should a yield that remains, because a real page took the name, tell the user? For example, a notice naming the yielded alias and its holder, with the merge action attached.

title: A failed operator re-run of a completed backfill deletes the workspace's completion record
description:
Re-running an operator backfill whose claim is already complete takes the claim with reclaimCompleted, which rewrites the claim block as in flight and drops its completedAt. If the pass then fails, withOperatorBackfillClaim's finally releases the claim it minted, and releasing deletes the block. The workspace's record that the migration finished is then gone, although the failed run wrote nothing else.

Observed while running the #1265 repair: the first run of kmagent run-backfill properties:cell-to-children was refused because the bridge requires a write contributor, and that refusal came after the claim write. The claim block was left tombstoned with no completedAt. A second run with --contributor none succeeded and wrote a fresh completion, so no harm persisted. Today every reader treats an absent claim the same as a completed one: the pass is operator-only, and the gesture only checks for an in-flight claim. So the loss is latent, and it becomes real for anything that later relies on the recorded completion.

Directions: put the bridge's write preconditions (contributor attribution, among others) before the claim is taken, as the gesture-guard checklist says (refuse before the expensive step). And/or have the release of a reclaimed completed claim put its previous completion back instead of deleting the block.

title: CI doesn't run pnpm check:db, so its pgTAP and stack tests can go red on master unnoticed
description:
No workflow in .github/workflows runs `pnpm check:db`. That is the pgTAP suites plus the `*.supabase.test.ts` stack tests against Postgres, GoTrue, PostgREST and Storage. They only run when someone runs them locally.

It has already bitten: `src/plugins/attachments/attachmentCleanerIO.supabase.test.ts` (#1334) failed on master from the moment #1332 merged. #1332 added `bundleFault` to the cleaner's report while #1334 was in review, so the test's exact `toEqual` no longer matched. Nobody noticed until #1345 ran the stack. The conversion's production run leans on these tests: they are the only end-to-end check of the conversion RPCs, the flow and the attachment cleaner against real servers.

Fix direction: a GitHub Actions job that runs `node scripts/check-db.mjs` on Docker. The script already starts an isolated stack, with the hosted images pinned in the script.
- Run it at least on PRs touching `supabase/`, `src/sync/conversion/`, `src/plugins/attachments/` or `src/test/supabaseStack.ts`, and nightly.
- Check the job's runtime and image pull cost first. The stack is four containers; locally the whole run takes a few minutes.
- The stack test files run in parallel. Tests that take the flip's NOWAIT table lock must keep tolerating 55P03 from each other's block writes (#1345 does).

title: A non-open encrypted workspace whose key goes missing stalls every workspace's sync with no explanation
description:
When this device stops holding the key for an encrypted workspace that is NOT the open one, and that workspace still has writes queued for upload, the upload connector cannot seal them. It treats the missing key as transient and retries. The queue drains in order (complete() is a prefix checkpoint), so every later write, for any workspace, waits behind them, and downloads stall with the queue. Nothing tells the user.

Since #1347 the key read signals `onWorkspaceKeyUnavailable` for that workspace, but App only acts on the open workspace (`useCloseOnKeyLoss`).

Repro: in encrypted workspace A, make an edit while offline; switch to workspace B; delete A's record from the `km-e2ee-keys` IndexedDB store; go online. B's edits never upload, and no message says why.

Fix direction: surface the signal for a non-open workspace, for example a banner naming the workspace whose key is missing with a way to open it into its key gate. Skipping a key-less workspace's transactions in the connector is not possible with prefix completion.

title: Inline backlink badges issue ~4 statements each after the flip and queue on render
description:
Once a workspace holds any property machinery, backlinks.countForBlock stops using the core.typedBlockCount SQL aggregate and instead resolves backlinks.forBlock and takes its length, so property-machinery sources are excluded with badge/list parity. Each inline badge then issues about four statements where it issued one: the machinery check (twice — once in the count, again inside backlinks.forBlock), core.typedBlockIds, and the machinery-source ancestry walk.

Measured on a local-only copy of a large graph after the migration (1.1M live blocks). Serially and cache-cold, each badge is still cheap: 1.5-6 ms for typical targets, 18 ms at about 230 references, 96 ms at about 2,000 (the aggregate path: 1-36 ms). But a page with many visible blocks fires them all at once: on a daily note with grouped references, 115 badge resolves and 117 child-id reads in the first minutes queued to p50 471 ms and 278 ms, with pool depth reaching 167, and DB getAll p50 for that session was 227 ms against 9.5 ms on the same graph before the flip. A slow-statement trace during a re-render showed 122 statements over 200 ms, every one of them queued and none slow on its own.

Directions, cheapest first: (1) ask workspaceHasPropertyMachinery once per badge resolve rather than twice; it is also monotone in practice, so a per-workspace cached true needs no re-asking. (2) Batch the visible badges into one statement rather than one resolve each. (3) Express the exclusion in SQL so the count stays an aggregate. The badge must still equal the expanded list's length, which is why the id-list path exists; any change keeps that parity test green.
close_reason: Fixed by PR #1338; real-graph check still to do (see comment)

title: E2EE conversion: answer the open platform-retention items (Supabase, PowerSync)
description:
docs/workspace-e2ee-conversion.md §9.5 lists what the retention spike (km-y4q1.6) could not settle from docs or code. None blocks the conversion run. Items marked (gates the date) name a copy or retention window the "safe from" date waits for; the date stays provisional while any of them is open. The rest bear on the live-systems claim, or on what lies outside the date's boundary.

Owner-side: V1–V4 are answered and recorded in §9 (2026-10-20): no Log Drain, the plan is Pro, the hosted logging settings are recorded, and `postgres` can vacuum all of step 11's tables.

Supabase support:
- S1 (gates the date): is WAL archived while PITR is off, and for how long?
- S2 (gates the date): is a backup deleted from storage when it leaves the listing; do off-schedule backups follow the same retention; are backups encrypted at rest?
- S3: does the S3 bucket behind Storage keep versions of deleted objects; are keys with no storage.objects row (failed delete or upload) ever swept?
- S4: is the instance's own Postgres log file ever pruned by age, rather than only rotated by size; who can read it?

PowerSync support:
- P1: the instance's storage version and backend; the memory limit Cloud's daily compaction uses; when a run does a full compaction vs a chunk merge.
- P2: does the storage engine keep old bytes after a MOVE or a dropped stream; is S3 object storage on for the instance?
- P3 (gates the date): does PowerSync Cloud back up bucket storage, and for how long?
- P4 (gates the date): do Cloud logs, diagnostics or traces ever hold row data, and for how long?

Done when each answer is recorded in §9 (with its source) and §9.4's rule is adjusted where an answer moves it.

title: E2EE conversion: key-loss recovery by re-keying in place from a plaintext snapshot
description:
**Status: needs its own design doc and review before it's built.** Key-loss recovery drew findings in about six consecutive review rounds on the conversion doc. It is a second state machine, and it should be designed as one, reusing the conversion's phase and gate rather than being specified one review comment at a time.

Key-loss recovery for a converted workspace, by **re-keying it in place** from the newest recovery point. Nothing is deleted, so no workspace or block id is ever free for another caller to claim.

This bead is the single home for recovery's requirements. The conversion doc (docs/workspace-e2ee-conversion.md §8) keeps only what recovery promises and what the conversion owes it.

**Recovery points.** Each is a folder, like the conversion bundle, holding `blocks.jsonl` (every block row, read from the server), the plaintext attachment bytes and a manifest. Newest first:

- a periodic one taken from an unlocked device after the conversion (runbook step 14). Its `blocks.jsonl` is read from the server and opened under the key, and it holds the PLAINTEXT of every media block, soft-deleted ones included (from the local byte store, or downloaded and opened under the key, each hash-checked). Take it while other devices are idle, since paging isn't a transaction;
- the conversion's recovery bundle.

A device that still defers is not a source: its `blocks` hold nothing the conversion's bundle lacks.

A raw SQLite export alone isn't one. Attachment bytes live outside the database, and their remote copies are sealed under the lost key.

**Pieces:**

- **Owner-only re-key RPC.** It replaces `wk_canary` on an e2ee row, admitted by the same transaction-local mechanism as the flip. It takes its locks in the flip's order: the workspace and conversion rows first (NOWAIT), then `LOCK TABLE blocks IN SHARE MODE NOWAIT` LAST, so nothing waits while it holds the shared lock; retried on lock-not-available. That way an old-key write in flight commits before the canary changes and can't land after the restore: the ciphertext trigger checks envelope shape, not which key sealed it. It is the only canary change ever admitted on an e2ee row, and it gives an owner nothing that `delete_workspace` doesn't already. The new key is minted, revealed, retyped and stored durably before the RPC, as in the conversion's key step.
- **Whole-row restore.** One `apply_block_patches` patch per row, with the base taken from the server row. It carries the snapshot's content columns sealed under the new key, **and** `parent_id`, `order_key`, `deleted`, `created_at`, `user_updated_at`, `created_by` and `updated_by`, so moves, reorders, deletes and undeletes since the snapshot are undone too. It never carries `updated_at`. That's the row version: `blocks_clamp_updated_at` floors it at OLD and bumps it on a content change, and it must advance so every device takes the restored value. Rows the snapshot lacks were created after it. They're tombstoned: content sealed empty UNDER THE NEW KEY, marked deleted, so a device that still has the row live can open and apply the tombstone. The equality check covers that form.
- **Completion by whole-row equality.** A row counts as restored only when it opens under the new key AND its whole row, `updated_at` excepted, equals the chosen recovery point's. Opening alone proves only which key sealed it. A resume, even with a different recovery point, compares every row again, so the result is never a mix of two points. History then holds only ciphertext under the lost key, so the purge is optional.
- **Attachments rebuilt under the new key.** Each media block's plaintext from the recovery point is sealed under the new key, uploaded to its new keyed path and verified with the shared helper. Objects under the old `K_id` are kept.
- **Entry checks the cached key against the canary** (and so does any change of the synced canary). `resolveWorkspaceEntry` today only checks that a key record with `K_id` exists, and the resolver decrypts whenever one does. So a device still holding the old record would go `ready` and quarantine every row. Entry must open the current server canary with the stored key and treat a failure as locked, so the device prompts for the new key.
- **Deferring devices** take the one-way pin upgrade (#1293). No pin changes direction, so there's no retirement gesture.

**Further requirements:**

- **Entry checks the key against the server's canary**, from the same PostgREST read as the phase (#1293's single-statement read already returns `wk_canary`), never the synced row alone. A device that sees the recovery phase cleared before the new canary syncs would otherwise open with its old key, and the server's shape-only trigger would accept its old-key envelopes.
- **Fence uploads at the connector, not only at entry.** PowerSync uploads in the background before the user opens the workspace, and today `encryptUploadOps` and the resolver consult only the local pin and key. So before sending a workspace's queued writes, the connector checks that its key opens the server's current canary (cached, re-checked when the canary changes or a write is refused), and holds them if it doesn't. The entry-time quarantine below then moves them aside.
- **Fence old-key writes on the server too.** The connector's pre-send canary check isn't atomic with the write: a request delayed past the re-key would still land, since `blocks_require_ciphertext_for_e2ee` checks envelope shape, not key. So each write carries the key generation it was sealed under, as `apply_block_patches` already carries `base_updated_at`. The server refuses a stale one inside the write transaction, and the re-key bumps the generation.
- **Quarantine pre-recovery upload backlogs.** `ps_crud` is durable, and uploads are sealed at send time, so an offline device's old backlog would be sealed under the new key and overwrite the restore. On its first entry after a re-key, the device moves that backlog to the rejection quarantine, user-visible and retryable. It quarantines BEFORE storing the new key: the old key no longer opens the canary, so a crash in between re-enters this path. Storing the key first would let a crash erase the only sign that this was the first entry after a re-key (`WorkspaceKeyStore.put` overwrites the sole record).
- **Recreate rows hard-deleted after the recovery point.** `apply_block_patches` raises `P0002` for a missing id, so the restore recreates such rows under the same id through a create path such as `apply_block_creates`, parents before children, and refuses an id that exists in another workspace. Hard deletes happen only outside the app (clients soft-delete), but the history trigger records them, so they are reachable.
- **Bind the recovery point to the workspace.** The manifest's workspace id and every `blocks.jsonl` row's `workspace_id` must equal the target, checked before the canary changes. A point from another workspace would tombstone every target row, and since `apply_block_patches` addresses rows by global id, it could patch the other workspace's rows with ciphertext sealed for the wrong one.
- **Phase transitions:** none or `cleaning` → the recovery phase (re-key upserts the row); `sealing` stays `sealing`, because that row already gates every device and the conversion still needs its purge; finishing the recovery phase → none.
- **Gate every device for the whole recovery.** A recovery in progress is a server fact from before the canary changes until the equality check and the attachment proof pass. The candidate shape: the re-key RPC inserts a `workspace_conversions` row in a third phase, which the client gate treats like `sealing`, and a finish step clears it. Otherwise a crash after the canary change reloads into a workspace that looks ready and holds a mix of new-key and old-key rows.
- **Synthesized-definition tombstones survive the re-key.** Synthesis honours a deletion by finding its tombstone at the derived id, and the derived id moves with `K_id`. Re-iding is out, because field rows point at definition ids. The candidate rule is that synthesis on a re-keyed workspace looks up existing definitions, tombstones included, by name before minting. Media-block re-captures minting a second block is accepted.
- **Key loss during `sealing` is covered too.** The re-key RPC is admitted while the phase is `sealing`.
    - Before the first re-sealed row, no row is sealed: re-key, take the bundle if missing, and continue the conversion.
    - After it, restore from the conversion's bundle exactly as here. If that bundle is lost too, re-take it: before the purge, its `blocks.jsonl` comes from the server (unsealed rows verbatim, sealed rows from their re-seal records' `before_diff`) and needs no key. Either way the bundle is a complete plaintext copy, since nothing but the re-seal writes during `sealing`. The restore's equality check stands in for verify. The conversion's purge then runs as usual, with `through` and the counts from the bundle's verified manifest.
- **Verify the recovery point before using it.** Its hashes must match and its `blocks.jsonl` must hold exactly its manifest's block count with no id repeated, since every row it lacks is tombstoned.
- **Keep what can't be got back.** Old-`K_id` objects and old key records are kept, in case the old key turns up. The cleaner's "neither" deletion must not apply to them in recovery.
- **Restore from the recovery point's `blocks.jsonl`, never from a device database.** A device database holds only what it downloaded and applied, and `workspaceViewGap` reads clear in the reconnect window `firstSync.ts` documents. A server read can't be stale that way, so rows the point lacks really were created after it.
- **The single-client contract applies to recovery.** A device already open with the old key would keep sealing under it, because the server checks envelope shape only. So the canary check runs whenever the synced `wk_canary` changes, not only on entry.
- **Handle or accept what a new `K_id` re-namespaces**, per the rotation note in `src/sync/crypto/derivedIdNamespace.ts`:
    - synthesized property definitions: a deleted one would resurrect under a new id;
    - post-conversion media block ids: a re-capture mints a duplicate.
- **Don't overwrite an existing key record** when storing the new key.

**Added 2026-10-19, from review of the conversion doc:**

- **Clear undo before admitting edits.** The recovering device's workspace undo and redo stacks hold full pre-recovery snapshots. A later Cmd-Z would replay one, sealed under the new key and accepted by the generation fence, silently overwriting the restore. Clear them and tell the user before recovery finishes or admits an edit (AGENTS.md's rule for migrations that write). Every other device does the same on its first entry after a re-key.
- **Fence restore writes by recovery attempt, not just by key generation.** A delayed restore batch from point A can commit after a resumed attempt with point B has passed its equality check, since both carry the same new generation. Each selected attempt gets its own server token, required inside every restore write, and the finish step invalidates it in the same transaction as the final check.
- **Rematerialize after quarantining the backlog.** A device with queued edits can hold local rows whose `updated_at` exceeds the restored server row's, because recovery advances the version from the server's value. The cache's `applyIfNewer` then rejects the restored snapshot, and the next edit overwrites the restore. After the quarantine, force an authoritative rematerialization and cache replacement, or reset the local workspace image, before admitting edits.
- **Unrecoverable media carries forward.** The conversion's approved-missing set (its manifest) is copied into every later recovery point's manifest. Recovery's attachment proof has the same terminal outcome as the conversion's: "passed, with these blocks unrecoverable". Otherwise a workspace that finished with such a block could never take a valid recovery point.

**It's point-in-time, not lossless.** Everything written after the recovery point is lost. The UI must say so before it starts.

**Done when:**

- pgTAP pins that the re-key refuses non-owners, plaintext rows and calls outside the admit;
- the recovery runs end to end on a scratch workspace: every block id is kept, every derived id resolves, and moved, deleted and undeleted rows return to the snapshot's state;
- a crash between the canary change and the first restored row resumes and completes;
- a device holding the old key record prompts instead of quarantining;
- rows absent from the snapshot end up tombstoned, and decrypt cleanly under the new key on every device.

**Fleet gate:** this piece's client half must be on every device before the first production conversion, alongside #1293 (runbook step 1): the canary check on entry, the upload fence including generation stamping, the backlog quarantine, the undo clear and the rematerialization. A device without generation stamping would either be refused by the server fence or bypass it.

**Recovery points carry the no-server-copy list** (2026-10-19). A step-14 point copies the conversion's list. An *archived* entry's bytes come from the conversion bundle or the device's byte store; if neither has them, the entry becomes *absent*. Recovery's attachment proof treats both kinds like the conversion's.

title: uploadErrorClassifier: treat 25006 (read-only database, e.g. disk full) as transient
description:
When a Supabase project's disk fills, the database goes read-only and writes fail with SQLSTATE `25006` (`read_only_sql_transaction`). `classifyUploadError` (`src/services/uploadErrorClassifier.ts`) has no entry for 25006. PostgREST maps it to a non-retryable 4xx (verify the exact status; the PostgREST docs list 405), so it classifies as `ambiguous`. After `AMBIGUOUS_RETRY_BUDGET` passes, every device's edits in every workspace would be quarantined, not retried.

A full disk is a transient, operator-fixable condition: raise the disk and the database becomes writable again. So 25006 belongs in the transient set.

This is a general robustness fix. It's filed now because the in-place e2ee conversion (`docs/workspace-e2ee-conversion.md` §7) is the first operation that deliberately consumes several times a workspace's size in transient disk.

**Done when:**
- a classifier test maps a 25006 error to `transient`, whatever HTTP status accompanies it;
- the exact PostgREST status for 25006 is confirmed and noted.
close_reason: Closed on GitHub (issue #1300); reconciled by bd-github-sync.

title: row_events: don't log version-only updates (every device would store full snapshots of a whole-workspace bump)
description:
`row_events`: skip version-only updates. The local `blocks_row_event_update` trigger logs full OLD/NEW snapshots for every update, so the conversion's whole-workspace version bump would write hundreds of MB of redundant history on every device.

Design: `docs/workspace-e2ee-conversion.md` §5.6 (Local history).

**Change:** compare the logged projection (`blockJsonObjectSql`) minus `updatedAt`, with `userUpdatedAt`'s `coalesce` fallback neutralized.

**Done when:**
- a version-only sync-applied update writes no row;
- any content, property, structure or `user_updated_at` change still does;
- removing the WHEN clause fails the first test.

Must reach every device before the first conversion.

title: First reload after the cell-to-children migration spends ~3 minutes in repo init
description:
Measured on a local-only copy of a large real graph (about 354k blocks before, 1.12M after; 2.9 GB database; Chrome, OPFS write-ahead VFS; dev server). The palette migration completed in 632 s and a re-run converged in about 20 s, so the migration itself is fine. The FIRST page reload after it is not.

Startup-metrics record for that boot: repoReady 186,957 ms. Workspace resolve, bootstrap and first paint each followed within 0.3 s, so the whole cost sits inside repo initialization — the VFS open plus the local schema and one-shot backfill steps in repoProvider. The UI shows only "Loading..." for the full three minutes, and page opens issued in the minute after it took 50-60 s. The next reload: repoReady 1.4 s, interactive 4.0 s. Boots before the migration: repoReady 0.7-1.0 s. After the slow open, the write-ahead sidecars were drained (about 1 MB and 0 bytes).

Which init step took the time is NOT determined. Candidates: (a) the VFS replaying or checkpointing a large write-ahead log accumulated during the ten-minute bulk write; (b) a one-shot local schema or backfill step in repo init whose cost scales with the new field rows. Distinguishing them needs startup marks around powerSyncDb.init() versus initializeClientSchema and the backfills, plus the sidecar sizes recorded at boot, then one reproduction.

Why it matters for the flip: the device that runs the migration sits on "Loading..." for minutes on its next reload, which reads as a hang and invites killing the tab mid-open.

Related observation, not shown to cause slow plans in this run: sqlite_stat1 stays at pre-migration values afterwards (blocks recorded at 354k rows, idx_blocks_field_form at 0 rows against 369k actual). PRAGMA optimize does not re-analyze a table that grew about 3x, so the planner keeps believing the field-form index is empty until something else triggers ANALYZE. Settled page opens measured 17-554 ms on the heaviest property pages, so this is a watch item, not a known regression.
close_reason: Stats: fixed in #1343. The migration records a refresh as owed before the pass and refreshes after it; every boot repays anything still owed. Slow first reload: diagnosed in #1343 as PowerSync init() replaying a write-ahead log that grew while a held read blocked checkpoints. Fix is tracked in km-hjzl; stats on devices that receive the migration through sync are km-s6lv.

title: E2EE: re-id blocks minted under public namespaces from user-text or externally-known keys
description:
On an e2ee workspace, block ids are plaintext. A uuidv5 id derived under a public namespace from a key that is user text, or a value someone else knows, stays a guess oracle after encryption: anyone holding the key can hash it and probe for the row. #719 fixes the namespace for NEW alias seats. This issue is the migration for blocks already minted under public namespaces, on every e2ee workspace: those created as e2ee and those converted in place (see `docs/workspace-e2ee-conversion.md` §6, which explains why the conversion itself doesn't re-id).

**Kinds in scope**
- **Alias seats**: page name; rename-stale too.
- **Media blocks**: sha256 of the file. Dedup also mints a second block at the keyed id on re-capture.
- **Synthesized property definitions** minted while the workspace was still plaintext. A workspace that switched to properties-as-blocks before its conversion keeps property-name-derived ids, and the switch is forward-only.
- **Extension-derived ids** whose key is sensitive. Each owning extension decides; the kernel can't classify them. Known today:
  - Readwise `user_book_id` / highlight ids (`agent-extensions/readwise.tsx`);
  - Matrix event ids (`agent-extensions/matrix-chat-client.tsx`);
  - Strength Tracker dates / group keys (`agent-extensions/strength-tracker/src/km/store.ts`).

Explicitly NOT in scope, recorded as accepted:
- **daily notes**: dates, enumerable;
- **Roam import**: foreign uids;
- **code-owned kernel, seed and state ids**.

**Requirements surfaced while reviewing the conversion design**

Each would bite this migration.

1. **Locked peers must not lose blocks.** `materializeStagingRows` hard-deletes a removed id once its staging row is gone, even when the replacement upsert is deferred because the device hasn't unlocked (`src/data/internals/syncObserver/materialize.ts`). For a workspace the device can't decrypt, removals must be held and replayed together with the upserts.
2. **Old ids need a durable old→new lookup.** Saved `#<ws>/<old id>` links and every device's `row_events` under the old ids need one: a sealed property on the new block, never a plaintext mapping. A plaintext old→new pair would re-link the new id to the guessable old one.
3. **The leftover can't be counted exactly.** A seat whose original name appears in no history can't be told apart from any other uuidv5 id. So report "matched N, unknown remainder", never an exact count.
4. **Rewrite every pointer** to a re-id'd block: content refs, ref / refList values, `references_json`, `parent_id`, and derived ids keyed on a re-id'd parent (transitively).

title: In-place plaintext → E2EE workspace conversion
description:
Convert an existing plaintext workspace to E2EE **in place**, from inside the app, without privileged access.

- **Single-client contract:** the user converts from one device and tab, with every other client closed. Breaking the contract fails closed for blocks and is detectable for attachments.
- **The conversion keeps:** the workspace id, every block id, timestamps, and device-local history.
- **Afterwards:** no plaintext of the workspace's content remains on the backend, once the operator vacuum and the retention clean-up are done.

Design: `docs/workspace-e2ee-conversion.md`. These beads carry scope, acceptance and order only; the doc wins on any disagreement. A multi-client design is summarized in the doc's appendix (§11).

title: agent-dispatch: spawned claude runs inherit user and project permission allow rules
description:
## Problem

`buildClaudeArgs` in `packages/agent-dispatch/src/runner.ts` passes `--allowedTools` and `--strict-mcp-config`, but no `--setting-sources` and no explicit settings file. So `claude -p` loads the allow rules in the user's `~/.claude/settings.json` and in the project settings of the run's `cwd`.

The README's security posture says Claude runs get no Bash unless a watcher opts in through `runner.allowedTools`. That isn't true when the inherited settings allow Bash. For example, this repo's `.claude/settings.json` allows `Bash(pnpm run *)`, and `pnpm run agent eval ...` reaches the bridge with the daemon's token. A watcher whose `cwd` is such a project, or whose default `cwd` (`$HOME`) picks up permissive user settings, gets shell access that nothing in its watcher config shows.

Found while reviewing the graph agent-memory design (PR #1240), where the trusted-class boundary depends on which runs can execute code.

## Fix direction

Pass `--setting-sources` (or an explicit, minimal settings file) from `buildClaudeArgs`, so a spawned run's permissions come only from the watcher config. Pin it with a test that asserts the argv.

title: Agent todos view: list open/done todos by page or subtree, bounded
description:
## Problem

The agent surface has no answer to "what is still open?", the question `bd ready` / `bd list --status open` answers for beads. Backlinks of a tag page are now bounded and contextual, but on a real graph a reading-list tag has ~6k backlinks with done and open items mixed, and neither `backlinks` nor `search` can filter by completion. Completion lives in two encodings (`status: open|done` for native todos, a `{{[[TODO]]}}` / `{{[[DONE]]}}` marker or `roam:todo-state` for imported ones), so an agent falls back to hand-written SQL over `properties_json` and content, which is exactly the path the bounded views exist to replace.

## Direction

A `todos` view (CLI verb + MCP tool) in the same bounded, breadcrumbed shape as the other views: open/done/all, scoped to a page (references it) or a subtree (under it), optional due-date window via daily-note refs, ordered by due date then recency. One owner for "is this block done", shared with whatever the UI uses, covering both encodings.

## Done when

"Open items on my reading list" and "open todos under page X" are each one call returning a few KB, and the eval gains a task for it.

title: Budget stamp-zero reconciliation fuzz test for contention

title: Track recovery of a staged-newer content row with needs_apply cleared and an empty drain queue
description:
Repeated read-only production health probes found one ordinary live content row classified as syncDivergence.stranded.staged-newer, with needs_apply=0, no pending upload and materialization backlog zero. Local content is empty, while the already downloaded staged row has nonempty short text and a timestamp 463 ms newer. The ordinary workspaceViewGap probe reports null. It is not a property field or value row. No private text or identifiers are retained here.

The current diagnostic detects this correctly; this is not evidence that the recently fixed equal-stamp sync defect is still present, because this row is staged-newer and its original cause is unknown. Preserve the old/new distinction when reporting it. The existing remedy is a deliberately run local rematerialization with scope all, after checking settled sync and reviewing the staged value; scope unapplied will not reach a row whose flag is already clear. That repair was not run during the inspection. Recheck divergence and property consistency afterwards. No new per-transaction gate or automatic full scan is requested.
acceptance_criteria: Review the local/staged discrepancy, apply the existing local-only recovery if appropriate, verify syncDivergence clears, and retain a reproducible regression only if an active origin is established.
close_reason: Duplicate of existing issue #1226. Its recorded diagnosis identifies the same live specimen and two combined causes: stale-checkpoint publication and interleaved drains. The drain-side fix merged in PR #1224; the checkpoint fix PR #1232 is still open when checked. The specimen is intentionally preserved for investigation, so do not run the previously suggested cleanup incidentally.

title: Audit detects type value children containing a whole JSON array as one list member
description:
A read-only audit found two existing metrics record owners whose types cell is a list containing one type id, but whose single type value child contains the entire JSON array spelling as text. Generic example: cell ["example-record"] versus child text ["example-record"], which the list member codec correctly projects as ["[\"example-record\"]"]. Thus every value decodes, yet the child projection disagrees with the cell. Both field rows and their owners are present; no duplicate field groups were found. No private identifiers or user content are included here.

This affects two internal metrics records in the observed data. Their stored app version identifies the writer as build 5903e6ab (2026.09.14-0559); row history shows the whole-array child spelling arriving from sync. That build predates the list-member encoding change and emitted JSON.stringify(encoded) as one child. This is confirmed old-client output, not a current decoder defect. Current typed setProperty reconciles children ahead of cell equality (#1209), so a narrow re-save of the known correct types values under the active target registry is a repair candidate. No live repair has been run. Verify all writing devices have refreshed before larger rollout; historical writer metadata does not establish which devices are stale today. Do not change a string/list decoder to automatically unwrap arbitrary JSON-looking member text: that would reinterpret legitimate strings. Add an explicit semantic consistency diagnostic and investigate the record writer/history; make any data repair narrow, reviewed and separate from the read-only audit. Related to #1011.
acceptance_criteria: A local fixture pins the cell/child type mismatch; the audit reports it despite successful codec decoding; any repair has an explicit unambiguous match condition and preserves legitimate JSON-looking string members.

title: Agent token revoke can be undone by the legacy-key fold
description:
AgentTokenStore (src/plugins/agent-runtime/tokens.ts, from #1244) folds tokens stored under the old per-(user, workspace) keys into the per-user key on every read, and deletes the old keys only when the merged list reads back whole. When that write fails (a full localStorage quota), the old keys stay.

revoke() filters the token out of list() and writes the per-user key (or removes it when the list is now empty) but never touches the old keys. If the revoke's write succeeds while the old keys still hold the token, the next list() re-adopts it: the revoked token is registered with the bridge again. Fail-open for a security control.

Reproduction (unit): a ClientLocalSettings double whose set() throws once for the per-user key; seed a token under an old key; list() (fold fails, old key kept); revoke(token); list() — the token is back.

Fix direction: revoke removes the token from every old key of that user too (or records revoked tokens so the fold skips them). Flagged by an automated security review on a push that carried the merge; the same review called old tokens being adopted as all-workspace credentials over-broad, which #1244 decided deliberately (a token's workspace was never an access boundary).

title: Agent ergonomics eval: a full-shell surface, run from outside the checkout
description:
The eval measures two surfaces: mcp (the km MCP tools) and cli (Bash allowed only for kmagent and a few filters). Agents in daily use run the CLI with unrestricted shell access, which neither arm measures: under the cli allowlist a command that mixes a shell variable, a pipe and a newline is refused as needing approval, and an agent cannot write a scratch file or use other tools.

Direction: add a third surface, full, with Bash unrestricted. The fixture generator (scripts/agent-eval/fixture.ts) holds the answers, so the agent must not be able to reach the checkout: copy the built agent CLI and its runtime dependencies to a scratch directory outside the repository (or bundle it into one file), point the kmagent shim there, and run the agent's shell in a directory that does not contain the repository. Check whether Claude Code's sandbox settings can deny reads of the checkout as a second line. Record the surface in the report conditions like the others, and record a baseline before the read and write slices land.

Done when: pnpm agent-eval run --surface full works with no path into the checkout reachable from the agent's shell, and a baseline is recorded.

title: Agent ergonomics eval: measure the CLI surface, host the graph in node, run tasks in parallel
description:
## Why

Agents mostly reach the graph through the agent CLI with full shell access, not through the km MCP tools, but the eval (#1233) measures only MCP. Each run also needs a paired, seeded local-only dev tab, runs tasks one at a time, and undoes every task by diffing the live graph, which was the main source of review churn on the eval PR.

## Direction

1. Host the graph in node. Each run builds a template PowerSync SQLite file by importing the fixture in-process, as `scripts/agent-eval/testGraph.ts` already does. Each task gets a copy of that file and is scored by diffing the copy against the template. No undo, journal, lock or tab check.
2. The host joins the bridge as a client, with a token it mints itself (it holds the bridge secret), so the real `kmagent` and `dist/mcp.js` reach it with no pairing step. Extract the register / long-poll / post-result loop from `src/plugins/agent-runtime/bridge.ts`, which is tied to the browser, into a module both the tab and the host use.
3. `--surface mcp|cli` as a run condition. `cli` = Bash allowed only for the agent CLI. A later `full` arm (unrestricted shell) must run from a scratch directory outside the checkout, because the fixture generator holds the answers.
4. N parallel workers. Record host, surface and worker count in the report's conditions.
5. Record baselines for both surfaces before the read/write slices land, or the CLI before/after delta is lost.

## Measured (2026-10-16)

- The 10 output probes give identical character counts in node and in the dev tab, and the fixture state matches line for line.
- SQLite is 3.53.2 in node and 3.53.0 in the tab. Their extra function sets differ (node: pow, ln, mod, percentile, rtree; tab: stdev, variance, reverse, padl), and none of 300 recorded sql_query calls used one.
- The serial baseline run took 10.3 min, of which agents took 7.7 min.

## Known gaps

- `eval` in node runs data code only (no DOM).
- The node graph lacks the app's onboarding and system pages, which raw SQL scans in the tab also saw.

## Done when

`pnpm agent-eval run --surface cli|mcp --workers N` needs no browser and no pairing, and baselines for both surfaces are recorded. The undo-path cases left open on the eval PR no longer exist.

title: Agent ref resolution: an exact stored id beats an id prefix, so a planted short id can capture a printed ^prefix
description:
resolveBlockRef (src/plugins/agent-runtime/agentViews/resolveRef.ts) tries a ref as an exact block id before reading it as an id prefix. Sync and restore admit non-canonical ids, so a workspace member can sync a block whose id is literally the 8-character prefix the agent views print for another block (e.g. 3f2a9c1d).

shortIds already avoids printing a prefix that resolves to some other block, so a row planted BEFORE an agent reads is harmless. A row planted after the read, before the agent pastes the printed ^3f2a9c1d back, captures that ref: a read returns the planted block, and on the write path (update/move/delete targets in the write-tool PR) the write lands on it.

Same threat as the wrapper-shaped ids (`[[Inbox]]`, `^x`, `((x))`) that #1241 decided not to probe exactly before unwrapping; that case is pinned by the test "keeps a wrapped ref meaning its target when a stored id spells the ref itself".

Fix direction, pick one:
- When an exact non-UUID id match coexists with prefix matches of OTHER blocks, refuse as ambiguous and list the candidates (keep shortIds resolve-back consistent with it; prefer live over deleted as prefixMatches does).
- Or refuse prefix-shaped / wrapper-shaped ids at sync and restore (data-layer invariant, wider change).

Reachability is low (a malicious workspace member plus a timing window), blast radius a misdirected agent write.

title: agent-cli: detect and restart a bridge older than the CLI's protocol
description:
The local bridge is a detached process that outlives agent-cli upgrades. ensureBridgeRunning (packages/agent-cli/src/cli.ts) accepts any process that answers /health, and /health reports no version, so a CLI and app that changed the bridge protocol keep talking to the old server until someone restarts it by hand.

Concrete case: user-bound tokens (km-1imd.3) make every app tab register every token. A pre-change bridge keeps one client per token and overwrites it on each registration, so with two tabs open in different workspaces calls (including ones naming a workspace) flap between tabs until the bridge restarts. Writes fail closed, but the fix is invisible: nothing tells the user to restart.

Fix direction: /health reports a bridge protocol version; ensureBridgeRunning (and the agent-dispatch preflight) compares it with the CLI's own and either restarts the bridge (needs a way to stop it: a secret-gated shutdown endpoint, since the current server has none and no pidfile) or prints a fact-stating message naming the running version and how to restart. The tab can read the same field from the registration response. A bridge too old to report a version reads as older than any versioned CLI.

title: Re-run the agent-ergonomics eval after the read/write slices land; lower the output budgets
description:
## Why

The agent-ergonomics eval (scripts/agent-eval, issue #1233) recorded a baseline on master before the bounded read views (km-1imd.1) and markdown-native writes (km-1imd.2) landed. The point of the baseline is the delta, so the eval has to be re-run once each slice merges.

## Steps

1. Reload the paired dev tab (`pnpm agent reload --profile km-eval`); `run` rebuilds packages/agent-cli itself.
2. `pnpm agent-eval run --repeat 3 --compare scripts/agent-eval/results/baseline-2026-10-16-sonnet.json`; commit the report. Watch the "capped" and "bytes returned" columns: on master several calls exceed Claude Code's MCP output cap, so the agent saw only a notice, and a bounded tool can legitimately raise "bytes seen".
3. Lower `maxBytes` in `scripts/agent-eval/outputBudgets.ts` to the new sizes (`pnpm agent-eval sizes`): the budgets are a ratchet.
4. If a tool's inputs changed, update its probe and the MCP reference solutions in `fixtureGraph.test.ts` rather than deleting them.

## Done when

A post-slice report with the comparison is committed and the budgets reflect the new sizes.

title: Agent tokens: a graph-only capability tier, enforced in the tab
description:
## Problem

Agent tokens have two scopes: `read-only` and `read-write`. `read-write` includes `eval` (arbitrary JS in the tab), `sql execute`, and extension lifecycle. The `km-mcp` server deliberately exposes only structured graph verbs, but that is a property of the MCP server, not of the token: the same token runs `eval` through the CLI. So there is no way to hand an agent "structured graph writes, but not a JS interpreter in the app". agent-dispatch runs agents steered by untrusted input, and those are exactly the agents that should get that.

Scope is also judged in the bridge relay (`packages/agent-cli/src/server.ts`, from per-verb `readOnly` metadata in `protocol.ts`), while the tab mints and stores the tokens and executes whatever the bridge forwards. The verb classification already drifts (#1037).

## Direction

- Add a middle tier, e.g. `read` / `graph` (structured verbs only: no `eval`, no `sql execute`, no extension lifecycle, no raw-write opt-ins) / `full`, and have agent-dispatch and the MCP setup mint `graph` tokens.
- Make the tab the one owner of "may this token run this command": the bridge forwards the token identity with each command, and the tab checks it against its own token record. The bridge stays a relay. One classification table, in one place.
- Per-workspace confinement is NOT part of this (see #1234 for why tokens are moving to user-bound). If it is ever built, it rides on the `graph` tier, since arbitrary JS and raw SQL cannot be confined.

## Done when

A `graph`-tier token is refused `eval` / `sql execute` / extension verbs BY THE TAB, even if the bridge forwards them; each refusal is pinned by a named test, and the existing read-only behaviour is unchanged.

title: Agent ergonomics eval: realistic graph tasks with token and tool-call budgets
description:
## Why

"Comfortable" needs a measurement, or improvements to the agent surface are judged by feel. Build a small, reproducible eval of realistic graph tasks and record tokens and tool calls per task, so each change to the read/write surface can be compared against a baseline.

## Shape

- ~10 tasks covering the common jobs: find what was noted about a topic in a time window; summarize a page; answer "where is X referenced and in what context"; list open todos under a page; append a structured note to today's daily note; edit one phrase in an existing block; create a page and link it.
- A seeded FIXTURE graph (imported from a checked-in fixture into a local-only dev server), never personal data, so runs are reproducible and writes are free.
- A runner that drives an agent with only the `km` MCP tools allowed, captures per-task tool calls, bytes returned, tokens and pass/fail (by checking the resulting graph state for write tasks), and writes a comparable report.
- Run on demand, not in CI (it costs model usage). A deterministic sub-check — byte size of representative tool outputs on the fixture — can run in CI.

## Done when

A baseline run against current master is recorded, and the runner can be re-run after the read/write slices land to show the delta.
