title: Agent tokens: bind to the user, not the active workspace (access drops on workspace switch)
description:
## Problem

Agent access is bound to one browser tab and to that tab's ACTIVE workspace. `register` in `src/plugins/agent-runtime/bridge.ts` posts only the tokens stored for `repo.activeWorkspaceId`, so switching workspace in the paired tab un-registers the agent's token: every call then fails with "Agent token is not registered …", which reads like a dead bridge. Closing the tab has the same effect. For an agent that should treat the graph like a file system, access disappearing because the user navigated is the opposite of what files give.

Not yet verified: the exact error an MCP call gets when no tab is connected at all, and how long a call waits before it.

## Options to weigh

- Register tokens for every workspace the signed-in user has paired, not just the active one, and route by audience to a tab that can serve it (or have the tab load that workspace's repo on demand).
- Make the failure self-explaining: name the workspace the token is for, what the tab has open, and the fix (switch back / open the app), optionally offering to open the app URL.
- A dedicated long-lived agent tab or window as the documented setup.
- (Long-term, large) a headless client. E2EE rules out server-side reads, so this would have to be a full local client.

## Done when

Switching workspace in the paired tab no longer silently cuts off an agent working in another workspace, or the agent gets an error that tells it exactly what happened and what to do.
close_reason: Closed on GitHub (issue #1234); reconciled by bd-github-sync.

title: km agent writes: markdown append, exact-match edit, conflict-safe update
description:
Give agents write tools that feel like Write/Edit on files, in `km-mcp`, the CLI, and `src/plugins/agent-runtime/commands.ts`.

## Today

`create_block` writes one block and requires `parentId`; `update_block` replaces whole content with no concurrency check, so an agent can overwrite an edit made on another device since it read the block; `daily_note` reports `exists: false` but cannot create; nothing shows what an agent session changed. `reconcile-markdown-subtree` already parses markdown with the app's paste parser, but is keyed for dispatch reply streaming.

## Direction

1. `append_markdown(target, markdown, position)` — target is an id, page name or date expression; one tx; parsing shared with `reconcile-markdown-subtree`.
2. `edit_block(id, old, new)` — exact replacement that must match once, applied inside the tx against current content.
3. Compare-and-set on `update_block` (expected content or edit timestamp); refuse if the block changed since the read.
4. Page creation by name and daily-note creation through the existing alias-seat minting path; top-level creates where intended.
5. `recent_changes` / `block_history` over `command_events` / `row_events`, so a session can report and the user can review/revert what an agent changed.
6. Document todo writes (`types: ['todo']`, `status: open|done`) in tool descriptions / the guide.

## Done when

Each refusal is pinned by a named test (mutate the guard away and watch it fail); verified against a local-only dev server, never the live graph.
close_reason: Closed on GitHub (issue #1235); reconciled by bd-github-sync.

title: km agent reads: bounded, context-rich views for search, backlinks and subtree
description:
Make the agent READ surface usable at real-graph scale: `km-mcp` (`packages/agent-cli/src/mcpServer.ts`), the matching CLI verbs, and the app-side handlers in `src/plugins/agent-runtime/commands.ts`.

## Problems (see epic for measurements)

Unbounded `search` / `backlinks` / `subtree`; hits without breadcrumbs; outline output dominated by raw property JSON and full UUIDs; no MCP orientation or guide; CLI and MCP surfaces drifting.

## Direction

1. Build agent views app-side, where the property registry can decode values, resolve type ids and ref properties to titles, and hide system/import-metadata properties. CLI and MCP pass through.
2. Every list-returning read is bounded: default limits, per-block truncation with a marker (char count + how to fetch the rest), explicit "N more"/cursor.
3. Each hit carries a breadcrumb (page › parent); reference-only blocks include their parent's text.
4. Outline view reads as markdown (`- content  key:: value  ^shortid`), depth limit, "+N children" for deep/collapsed branches; raw JSON mode kept.
5. Accept unique id prefixes (git-style; ambiguous → candidates) and page names / date expressions wherever an id is accepted.
6. MCP `instructions` + a `guide` tool + `grouped_backlinks`; generate MCP tools and CLI verbs from one command table.
7. Search snippets, filters (type, under-page, exclude extension source), dedupe.

## Done when

Representative probes (a daily note's subtree, a 10-result search, backlinks of a heavily-linked page) each return a few KB with enough context to answer without follow-up calls; tests pin limits, truncation and prefix resolution. Output-shape changes for existing consumers (agent-dispatch prompts) are named in the PR.
close_reason: Closed on GitHub (issue #1236); reconciled by bd-github-sync.

title: Agent ergonomics: make the graph as comfortable for agents as files and beads
description:
## Goal

An agent should be as comfortable reading and writing a Knowledge Medium graph through the agent CLI / `km-mcp` as it is with markdown files (Read/Grep/Edit) and beads (`bd`). Files are comfortable because every read is bounded, carries its own context, and the read format is the write format; beads because of short ids, compact listings, and memory injected at session start. The KM agent surface currently has none of those properties.

## Findings (dogfooding pass, 2026-10-15, read-only, real ~340k-block graph)

- `search` with `limit: 10` returned 1.9 MB: one hit was an extension source block returned in full. No snippet, no page/parent context per hit, seeded help blocks duplicated, `total` only echoes the returned count.
- `backlinks` has no limit (most-linked target: ~13.5k) and no context: a page's backlinks that are bare `[[page]]` blocks come back as N identical lines carrying no information.
- `subtree` has no depth/size limit (largest page: ~4.3k direct children). With the default `includeProperties`, ~60% of a daily note's outline was importer-metadata JSON, plus a full 36-char id per line.
- The MCP server has no `instructions`, no data-model guide, and no `grouped_backlinks` (the CLI has `data-model` and `grouped-backlinks`); README, CLI and MCP tool lists disagree.
- Writes are one block at a time with whole-content overwrite, no conflict check against edits made elsewhere since the read, no markdown append, and no page/daily-note creation from the MCP.
- Access is bound to the paired tab's ACTIVE workspace (`register` in `src/plugins/agent-runtime/bridge.ts` lists tokens for `repo.activeWorkspaceId` only).

## Slices

Children of this epic: bounded read views, markdown-native writes, access/availability, an eval set, and the docs pointer. Graph-stored agent memory (the "CLAUDE.md for the graph") is the existing design issue linked here.

Non-goal: moving beads or repo memory into the graph.

title: sync: a strictly-newer staged row can be left unapplied with needs_apply cleared
description:
Found while checking a live client for #1163-shape divergences (none found). One row in a shared plaintext workspace is stranded in a different shape:

- `blocks_synced` holds a STRICTLY NEWER version than `blocks`: staged `updated_at` is 463 ms above local; content is 10 chars staged vs empty locally. All other columns match except the two stamps. Both writes carry the same `updated_by`.
- `needs_apply = 0`, no `blocks_synced_changes` entry, nothing in `ps_crud` or `ps_crud_rejected` for the id. The device is otherwise fully drained (blocks == blocksSynced, backlog 0).
- Both writes date from 2026-09-27, 19:19 UTC.

Why it is not #1163: the stamps differ. Neither the old drain nor the fixed one leaves a strictly-newer, non-pending row unapplied. A pending upload at the moment the drain judged the staged row would explain it (skip-stale clears the flag and consumes the queue entry on the premise that the upload's echo re-delivers). But the local stamp never advanced past the older write, so that premise needs a window where PowerSync stages a download while the crud entry for an already-committed upload is still in `ps_crud`. Not confirmed; PowerSync normally holds checkpoints while local changes are pending.

Reproduce / investigate: find rows where `blocks_synced.updated_at > blocks.updated_at`, the two rows differ, `needs_apply = 0`, and the id has neither a queue entry nor a crud entry. Then work out which drain decision could have cleared the flag (Phase 1/2 skip-stale on pending is the only one that clears without writing).

Heals with an `'all'` rematerialize of the workspace (the row is newer and nothing is pending, so the drain applies it). Detection belongs in the same place as the needs_apply gap reporting: a strictly-newer resolved row is a gap the flag hides.
close_reason: Cause found and fixed. The upload triggers never raised PowerSync's $local hold, so a checkpoint predating an acknowledged upload was published and the drain wrote it over the newer local row; two interleaved drains made one such revert permanent. Fixed in #1232 and #1270; the specimen is healed. The drain-lag follow-up stays open on its own bead.

title: setProperty is a no-op over a stale cell a deleted definition left, so the new definition never gets a field row
description:
In a children-backed workspace, `tx.setProperty` writes nothing when the owner's cell already holds the same value under the property's name — even when that cell value was left behind by a DELETED definition and the definition now answering to the name has no field row on the owner. The write is short-circuited as a no-op, so the new definition never gets a field row: the value the user just set exists only in the derived cell.

REPRODUCTION (measured):
1. A `beta` definition `old` (boolean). Set `beta = false` on block `h` — `h` gets a field row `::((old))` with value `false`, cell `{beta: false}`.
2. Delete `old`. Create a new `beta` definition `new` (boolean).
3. `tx.setProperty(h, beta, false)` — nothing is written: `h` still has only the `old` field row. The same call with `true` creates a `::((new))` field row as expected.

CONSEQUENCE. `h` is not a consumer of `new`, so nothing that works from field rows sees the value: renaming `new` leaves `h`'s cell keyed under the old name (the value does not follow the rename), and any reprojection from children drops it. Found by the definition-rename fuzz suite's value model (seed 1526463238); carved out there with a KNOWN ISSUE (fuzz) comment.

Same family as the stale-cell residual (a name's cells outlive the definition that owned it) and the cell-vs-field-row reconcile, which would detect this shape. Fix directions: let the no-op short-circuit in the eager dual-write consider whether the resolved definition has a field row under the owner (materialize when it does not), or retire a departing definition's cells so there is no stale value to equal.
close_reason: Closed on GitHub (issue #1209); reconciled by bd-github-sync.

title: Outline SQL and the tx layer disagree on whether an unbuildable property-schema block is a definition
description:
Found by the visible-children differential fuzz suite (`src/data/test/visibleChildren.fuzz.test.ts`).

The outline SQL and the tx layer decide "does this field row's target name a definition" (§9 condition 3) with different rules:

- SQL (`recognizedFieldRowSql`, used by `core.children` / `core.childIds` / `core.subtree` with `hidePropertyChildren`, and by the backlinks machinery filter): any block carrying a `property-schema` tag in `block_types`, in the row's workspace.
- JS (`tx.childrenOf(..., {hidePropertyChildren: true})`, so `visibleChildrenOf` and every gesture built on it): `isResolvableFieldDefinition(resolver.resolveField(id))`, which needs the user-schemas projector to have parsed the row's metadata (non-empty name, a real change scope) AND, for a name winner, a buildable schema (a loaded preset whose config decodes).

So a block tagged `property-schema` that the registry cannot build a definition from is a definition to the outline and not one to the gestures. Its field rows are hidden on screen while structural gestures resolve against them as ordinary siblings. Two reproductions, both deterministic:

1. Unloadable or missing preset. Create a definition whose `property-schema:preset` names a preset nothing registers (a peer with the plugin installed syncs it, or the plugin is uninstalled here), then a `::((defId))` child under some block. `VISIBLE_CHILDREN_SQL` omits the child; `visibleChildrenOf` returns it. The resolver reports `identity-unavailable / definition-unavailable` for the definition.
2. Unparseable metadata. Same, with `property-schema:change-scope` set to a value that is not a change scope (or an empty name). Same split.

Which side is right differs per case, which is why this is one bug and not two. §9 says classification needs the definition, not the owning plugin (an uninstalled plugin's definitions sync like any block), so for case 1 the JS side is wrong. For case 2 the registry cannot read the block as a definition at all, and §9's "an unresolvable marked row degrades to a visible unknown-field row" argues the SQL side is wrong.

Fix directions:

- (A, recommended) One owner for definition-ness: bind the set of ids the registry classifies into the SQL predicate in place of the `block_types` leg, the way the seed ids are already bound (`registrySeedParams`). Both views then read one decision and the class cannot recur. It also removes the occupied-seed-slot divergence (#670), and gives the dependency work for mounted handles (#667) a single thing to depend on. Cost: binding the classified set per query, and a registry lag that now applies to both views equally rather than only to the tx side.
- (B) Keep two legs and align their rules: drop the buildable-schema requirement from the tx checker (needs care, since the project/materialize processors share `isResolvableFieldDefinition` and need a codec), and teach the SQL leg the metadata rules (a second copy of the parse, which is the drift this bug is an instance of).

When fixed, flip `GENERATE_UNBUILDABLE_DEFINITIONS` in the fuzz suite to cover these shapes.
close_reason: Closed on GitHub (issue #1202); reconciled by bd-github-sync.

title: Edit-mode paste glues a whole heading or code block onto the text before the caret
description:
## What happens In edit mode, pasting a whole block element after existing text merges it onto that text. The elements affected are a heading, code block, table, quote or ordered item copied from a web page; rich paste produces a one-node outline for each of these. Examples, with the caret after the existing text: - `

Getting started

` after `Read: ` gives `Read: ## Getting started`. Before rich paste it gave `Read: Getting started`. - A `
` block after `See ` gives a fence that no longer starts its line. The block renders with literal backticks.
- A table after `Data: ` no longer parses as a table.
- Any non-blank text after the caret is appended after the closing fence or the last table row, which breaks those too.

`planEditModeMultilinePaste` (`src/paste/operations.ts`) merges the absorbed root onto the prefix. Markdown-text paste already merges this way on master, and `operations.test.ts` pins `note: ```js…``` ` as the expected result. Rich paste makes the case common, because any whole-heading or code-block copy from a page now reaches it.

## Proposed rule (needs a decision)

When the text before the caret is non-blank, a heading, code block, table or quote root starts its own block instead of merging. Paragraph and list-item roots keep merging at the caret, as Roam does.

This needs the pre-built tree to say which roots are block-level, either a kind on `OutlineNode` or a flag on the edit-mode plan. It should apply to the markdown-text path too, which would change the pinned `note: ```js` behaviour.

Alternative: leave the merge as is, and have rich paste produce inline markdown for a lone heading when pasted into the editor (losing heading-ness in an empty block).

title: Rich paste: capture Google Docs images instead of hotlinking expiring URLs
description:
Follow-up to the rich-paste plugin (#1188).

**Problem.** Pasting from Google Docs emits images as `[alt](https://lh7-rt.googleusercontent.com/…)`. Those are short-lived signed URLs, so the image renders at paste time and silently breaks later — the note looks fine until it doesn't. Any other web image is a hotlink too (less likely to expire, but it can disappear and it leaks a request to the origin on every render).

**Direction.** After the paste decision returns a tree, fetch `http(s)` image URLs and capture them through the attachments plugin's `captureMediaVerb` (content-addressed media blocks), rewriting each `[alt](url)` to the captured `((id))` reference. Constraints:
- The paste decision is synchronous (`runSync`), so capture has to happen in the async apply step (like `resolvePasteWithMediaCapture` does for clipboard files), not in the converter.
- Cross-origin fetches will often fail on CORS — fall back to keeping the hotlink, and report the failure the way upload failures are reported.
- Gate it on the attachments plugin being enabled (the capture verb's default is a no-op), so rich-paste keeps no hard dependency on it.
- At minimum do it for `googleusercontent.com` (known to expire); whether to capture every web image is a product call (storage cost vs link rot).

Code: `src/plugins/rich-paste/htmlToOutline.ts` (image handling in `sanitize`), `src/paste/operations.ts` (`resolvePasteWithMediaCapture`).

title: Upgrade hosted Supabase Postgres from 17.6 to 17.11
description:
The hosted project runs supabase-postgres 17.6.1.121 (upstream PostgreSQL 17.6). Upstream 17.11 (2026-08-13) fixes 28 security vulnerabilities, including a regexp heap overflow (CVE-2026-14664) and a tsvector/tsquery allocation bug (CVE-2026-14662). Supabase ships it as the 17.11.0.x image line.

Checked 2026-10-13:
- All migrations and the pgTAP suite pass on public.ecr.aws/supabase/postgres:17.11.0.004 (CHECK_DB_POSTGRES_IMAGE=... pnpm check:db).
- None of Supabase's upgrade caveats apply: no deprecated extensions, no ltree/btree_gist/pg_cron, no pgcrypto PGP-encrypted data, no custom login roles.

Supabase upgrades same-major projects with the same flow as major ones: the project goes offline, and logical replication slots must be dropped first. PowerSync recreates its slot on reconnect and replicates from scratch; its docs don't say whether clients then do a full re-download.

Steps:
1. Pick a quiet window. Make sure every device has finished uploading.
2. Confirm a recent backup.
3. Stop PowerSync replication and drop its slot.
4. Dashboard > Settings > General > Upgrade project.
5. Verify select version() reports 17.11, PowerSync recreated its slot and caught up, and a client syncs.
6. Bump the CHECK_DB_POSTGRES_IMAGE default in scripts/check-db.mjs to the new hosted tag.
close_reason: Closed on GitHub (issue #1199); reconciled by bd-github-sync.

title: CI does not run the pgTAP suites in supabase/tests
description:
None of the SQL behaviour tests under supabase/tests/*.test.sql run in CI. run-tests.yml runs pnpm run check, and scripts/check.mjs has no check:db step. attachments-rls-contract.yml runs only the rls:verify-* scripts. So the suites covering the block upload RPCs, the updated_at clamp trigger, the history trigger, patch-base drift and the anon-write refusal trigger are only ever run by hand (pnpm check:db). A migration that regresses any of them stays green.

Fix direction: attachments-rls-contract.yml already starts a real local Supabase stack. Add a step there that runs supabase test db (or the check:db steps: apply supabase/migrations in order, run each .test.sql, fail on any 'not ok' / 'Bail out!' / '# Looks like'). Optionally add one anon-key PostgREST probe, POST /rest/v1/rpc/apply_block_patches with patches [{id: <nonexistent>}], expecting HTTP 401 and code PT401. That pins the SQLSTATE-to-HTTP mapping the client's retry classification relies on, end to end.

title: cors-proxy: verify on the hosted edge runtime after the first deploy
description:
Two behaviours of the cors-proxy edge function were verified locally under Deno 2.9 and in the edge-runtime source, but not on the hosted platform:

1. Deno.resolveDns resolves at runtime there. The edge-runtime exposes it (ext/runtime/js/denoOverrides.js), but a sandbox could still block DNS. If it fails, every hostname target is refused as 'unresolvable' (fails closed, visibly).
2. The functions gateway passes HEAD requests through. If it doesn't, consumers should use GET and cancel the body.

Also worth one look: the allowHost HttpClient pins http hops to the vetted IP. The edge-runtime's vendored deno_fetch has allow_host, but confirm an http:// target loads the right site (wrong-vhost content would mean Host was dropped).

Check: deploy, then with a signed-in session fetch an https short link (HEAD and GET), an http:// target, and http://localtest.me/ (expect blocked-address).

title: Nightly fuzz failure (2026-09-26)
description:

title: Pin the bd version that cloud sessions install
Sync: reopening a bead locally does not stick while its GitHub issue is closed
description:
`planCloseReconciliation` in `scripts/bd-github-sync.mjs` adopts every GitHub-side close onto its bead: any bead that is not closed but whose issue is CLOSED gets closed, with no comparison of when each side last changed. A bead reopened locally is therefore closed again by the next sync for as long as its issue stays closed.

AGENTS.md says GitHub-side reopens do not stick and to "reopen the bead instead" — but that only works if the GitHub issue is reopened too, which makes the advice circular for anyone following it.

Fix direction: adopt a GitHub close only when it is newer than the bead's last local status change (or push a local reopen out before reconciling closes), and correct the AGENTS.md advice to match whichever rule ships.

title: Sync: an unpushed bead edit is reverted when its GitHub issue is touched
description:
The beads↔GitHub sync decides a record's direction by timestamps (`updatedAt` vs the bead's `updated_at`). A GitHub-side touch — a comment, a cross-reference from another issue or PR, a label change — moves the issue's `updatedAt` past the bead's even though the issue's synced fields are older. So a local edit that has not been pushed yet can be taken over by GitHub's older copy: once GitHub is the newer side the bead is handed to the pull, and bd's skip-locally-modified guard stops covering the edit as soon as any sync (the wrapper's own pre-pull push included) stamps `last_sync` past it.

How an edit ends up unpushed on bd 1.3.0: the push PATCH failed (bd only warns), or bd's clone-local push cache skipped the bead because its content equals what it last pushed. The wrapper now detects both after the pre-pull push and holds back its own comment mirror for such a bead (and for comments naming it), so the wrapper no longer triggers this itself; a GitHub-side touch by anyone else still does. The header of `scripts/bd-github-sync.mjs` lists this under Accepted.

Fix direction: decide per field by content against a last-synced base (local vs base, remote vs base), not by timestamps alone, so a touch that changed no synced field can never outrank a real local edit.

title: Pre-PR gate: refuse a --body-file that this session did not write
description:
Publishing a PR or issue body with gh --body-file from a shared temp path has shipped another session's text six times. The recurring path: a compound 'write payload with heredoc && gh pr create --body-file' is refused by the pre-PR gate (a compound publish is not post-verifiable), so the heredoc never runs; the compliant retry, a lone gh pr create --body-file, then publishes a stale file another session left at the same path. The post-publish verifier catches it only after publication, by echoing the titles of referenced issues. A memory describes the trap and has not prevented it.

Fix direction: in scripts/bd-github-sync.mjs --hook-pre-pr, for a covered publish with --body-file / -F / --body-file=, refuse when the file's mtime is older than a short window (a few minutes) or when the path is not under the session's own scratch directory (the hook payload carries session_id, and the Claude Code scratchpad path contains it). Print the facts (path, mtime age, session id) and the opt-out, per the facts-not-diagnoses rule for hook output. Tests beside the existing pre-PR gate tests; mutation-check each clause with pnpm mutate.

title: Perf monitor: most queries never produce a comparison-eligible sample, so their p95 is never judged
description:
The per-query p95 comparison reads only uncontended resolves and needs MIN_CALLS (20) of them in a session. Measured on one desktop client's 64 stored sessions (21 distinct queries): 15 queries NEVER reached 20 uncontended samples in any session, including groupedBacklinks.forBlock, backlinks.forBlock, backlinks.countForBlock, core.ancestors, core.children, core.aliasClaimants and core.typedBlockCount. Only core.subtree (18 sessions), core.typedBlocks (17), core.childIds (12), core.aliasMatchesFuzzy (7) and core.aliasLookup (5) ever did. A mobile client's 21 stored sessions never judged anything at all (no eligible query, and fan-out never reached its 100-write floor).

So the query half of the monitor is blind to the queries most likely to regress (backlinks on a large graph). The series.ts doc already names the mechanism (a query that only runs inside a render fan-out, or only through the batcher, rarely resolves with the pool to itself), so this is expected behaviour of the filter, not a recorder bug.

First step: measure, per query, how many resolves were rejected and for which reason (competing traffic vs coalesced/batched vs counter reset), to see whether the fix is a looser eligibility rule for batched/fan-out queries, a different comparable measure for them (e.g. per-statement SQL time rather than caller wall-clock), or accepting that these queries are covered by some other signal.

title: Perf monitor: the 'could not be judged this session' note is permanently on, so it carries no information
description:
queryRegressions pushes one aggregate insufficient result (no-current-sample / never-uncontended) whenever ANY query in the current session lacks MIN_CALLS uncontended samples, and unjudgedReason then reports 'partly-judged' whenever anything else was judged.

Measured on one desktop client's 64 stored sessions: a session measures a median of 14 queries, of which a median of 0 have MIN_CALLS uncontended samples; no session ever had every query eligible. The note therefore appeared in all 32 sessions that judged anything. A note that is always present cannot tell a reader that something changed, which defeats its stated purpose (a query the comparison could not judge is where a regression can hide).

Direction to decide: make the note name a CHANGE in coverage rather than its standing level. For example, report a query as unjudged only when it has a usable baseline (it was comparable before) but this session gave it no comparable sample, and stay silent about queries that have never been comparable (the separate never-eligible issue tracks those). Keep the scheduler's recheck behaviour (awaitingCurrentSample) independent of what the note says.

title: Fit properties migration confirmation on short screens
description: The migration consent dialog extends beyond short viewports, hiding its title or actions. Bound its height, keep the header and actions visible while the details scroll, and shorten the consent copy without losing operational warnings.

title: Add commit-pinned manual previews for fork pull requests

title: The KEY-level flip gate still reads a pre-dialog plan snapshot
description:
Found while fixing the cell-level twin (km-a2rt): the same staleness, one gate over.

The migration gesture re-takes the cell survey under the claim now, immediately before the one-way flip. The KEY-level gate does not. `flipBlockedBySynthesis(plan, result)` is asked a second time before the flip, but with the SAME `plan` object built before the confirmation dialog — so only `result.skipped` is fresh. Its other four hazards are all pre-dialog snapshots:

- `plan.blockers` — a key that can never be given a definition
- `plan.unreadableBlocks` — a property bag this device cannot read
- `plan.scanSyncGap` — the survey taken over a partial graph
- `plan.refusal` — the namespace this device may mint under

A sync arrival landing any of those while the dialog sits open is carried into the flip. The blast radius is the same one the cell fix addressed: the workspace is switched one-way with a key that can never resolve a definition, and at the cell end-state (#1012) that value loses its only synced representation.

Not fixed alongside the cell gate on purpose. `ClaimedMigration` carries an explicit decision that the plan and the counts are NOT re-derived under the claim, because they are what built the confirmation and re-deriving them would ask a different question than the user answered. The cell survey sidesteps that because it can only REFUSE — it changes nothing the dialog promised — whereas re-planning changes which definitions get minted. So this needs a call on the shape, not just a second call site.

Two candidate shapes:
1. Split the plan into the part that is CONSENT (candidates to mint, counts) and the part that is a SAFETY GATE (blockers, unreadable bags, sync gap, namespace refusal), and re-derive only the second under the claim. Keeps the recorded decision intact.
2. Re-scan keys under the claim and refuse if the hazard set grew, without touching what gets minted.

Cost of either is a second `scanPropertyKeys`, which is a SQL aggregation rather than a per-cell decode, so cheaper than the cell survey that is already re-taken there.

title: Migration consent screen shows key COUNTS but never names the keys
description:
The migration gesture already runs the same survey `audit-properties` does (`planPropertyDefinitionSynthesis`), and on an UN-flipped workspace `flipBlockedBySynthesis` already refuses on all four hazards — unreadable property bags, a scan taken during a sync gap, keys that can never get a definition, and keys still undefined after synthesis — naming the keys and reasons in the refusal toast.

What it does not do is name anything on the path where it does NOT refuse. `ConfirmMigrationDialog` takes only counts: `synthesizedKeys`, `unfixableKeys`, `repairableKeys`. So a user consenting to a ONE-WAY change is told "N keys cannot be migrated" with no way to learn which, and no remedy. On an already-flipped workspace the same hazards are downgraded to a non-blocking advisory (deliberately — refusing there would withhold the backfill from every other key), which makes that the case where naming matters most and where the CLI audit is currently the only way to find out.

The remedy text is the other half. The audit gives per-key ordered instructions (enable the owning extension FIRST, then run, because synthesising a definition first and enabling the owner later strands field rows on the loser fieldId). Nothing in the UI says this, and it is the one ordering mistake that is expensive.

Fix direction: pass the key names (capped) and the remedy through to the dialog and to the already-flipped advisory, instead of counts alone. The plan already carries `candidates`, `blockers` and `brokenDefinitions` with their per-key reasons — this is presentation, not detection. Once it lands, the runbook pre-flip `audit-properties` step is optional for the un-flipped case rather than load-bearing.

Context: the pre-flip audit step in the migration runbook exists largely because this surface does not name things. Raised while planning the first small-workspace flip.
close_reason: Closed on GitHub (issue #1119); reconciled by bd-github-sync.

title: Config-editor seam gives an editor no way to know whether its change landed
description:
Surfaced by four consecutive review rounds on #1112's fan-out gate, each fixing a real defect and each revealing the next layer of the same one.

`ValuePresetConfigEditorProps.onChange` returns `void`. An editor that keeps optimistic state — the enum options editor does, because committing per keystroke is now a whole fan-out — therefore cannot know when its request landed, whether it landed, or what the stored value was when it did. Every hazard found so far is that one gap:

- an acknowledgement of the editor's own write read as an external change and wiped the draft
- a blur caused by the confirmation's focus trap queued a second, conflicting write
- a cancelled or refused change left the editor showing options the definition never got

Those three are fixed in #1115, the last by the HOST remounting the editor when a change does not land — which needs no contract and reaches editors this repo did not write, but is a blunt instrument: it also throws away state that was newer and valid.

The one left is two in-flight requests. Blur one option, then edit and blur another before the first sub-threshold fan-out finishes: the second request replaces the first's pending marker, the first's acknowledgement then reads as external and restores its own snapshot over the newer draft, and the second write is refused as overtaken because the baseline it was planned against predates the first commit. The typed label is lost.

Every mitigation tried inside the editor bottoms out in the same place. Sequencing requests needs to know when one settles. Re-aiming the second needs to know what the stored value is now — and the renderer's copy of that lags by exactly the window in question. Whether a config payload can even be re-aimed depends on the editor: one holding a cumulative draft can, one rendering straight from its prop cannot, and the host cannot tell them apart.

So the fix belongs at the seam. Roughly: let `onChange` return a promise that says whether the change landed, so an editor can serialise its own requests and roll back precisely; and give the host a way to hand the editor the current stored value at the moment a request is planned, so a queued request is composed against something true. Then the remount can go, along with the pending-marker bookkeeping it papered over.

Small blast radius today — two implementors in this repo, both first-party, and a widening is backward compatible for anyone else. Worth doing deliberately rather than as the eighth round of a PR about rename freezes.

title: Merging two blocks that share a scalar property leaves two value children
description:
Measured 2026-09-21 on a migrated (child-backed) graph, driven through the real gesture.

REPRO
 1. two sibling blocks, both carrying the SAME scalar (non-list) property, with different values
 2. put the caret at the start of the second and press Backspace, merging it into the first

RESULT: the survivor's single field row for that property ends up with TWO value children — the target's and the source's. The cell projects the first, so the block READS correctly; the second value is invisible in the UI but present in the data and syncs like any other row.

It is not transient and it does not self-heal:
  - still there after 8 s
  - still there after a full reload
  - still there after writing the property again through tx.setProperty — the rewrite replaces the FIRST child and leaves the stray untouched (value children become [new, stray])

SCOPE, measured by trying each case:
  only the TARGET carries the property  -> 1 value child, correct
  only the SOURCE carries it            -> 1 value child, correctly relocated
  BOTH carry it                         -> 2 value children

So it is specifically the contested case. A scalar's field row is supposed to hold exactly one value child; the merge relocates the source's value under the survivor's field row without reconciling it against the one already there.

NOT A MIGRATION ARTEFACT — the migrated graph is clean on this invariant. Graph-wide there were 23,080 field rows holding more than one value child, and splitting them by whether the definition is list-shaped gives 23,076 lists (legitimate: one child per member) and 4 scalars, all four of which were blocks these very tests had just merged. Before the tests, zero.

WHERE TO LOOK: the merge mutator's property handling (mergeBlocksInTx in src/data/blockMerge.ts and the property-children processors it runs through). reconcileSingleValueChild already has a primary-plus-duplicates branch, which is presumably why nothing downstream complains — but it means the stray is tolerated rather than folded.

Found while QAing the properties-as-blocks migration; the merge path is not touched by that work.
close_reason:
Not a defect — this is the documented design, and I filed it against evidence I had already read.

reconcileSingleValueChild folds only EXACT duplicates of the projected cell value (concurrent dual-writes of the same value). Its comment names this case directly: 'DIVERGENT siblings are a surfaced conflict — from a merge or divergent concurrent write — and are kept as peer values, not silently collapsed onto the winner.' Discarding the source's value on merge would be the data loss; keeping it as a peer is the point.

The read semantics, which is what has to hold, do: the value set is ordered (order_key, id) so every device projects the same member, the cell read target-value after the merge, and a later write to the property read back correctly. My 'it does not self-heal on a later write' observation is the same documented behaviour seen from the other side — the fold is not supposed to collapse a divergent sibling.

Two process notes for whoever hits this next. The graph-wide survey in the original description is still worth keeping: 23,080 field rows hold more than one value child, of which 23,076 are list definitions (legitimate) and 4 were created by the tests themselves, so the migrated data has no unexplained instances. And the mistake was mine in a specific way — I quoted the duplicates branch in the description as 'tolerated rather than folded' without reading the rationale immediately below it, which states the intent.

title: The enum options editor commits on every keystroke, and each commit is a full definition fan-out
description:
`EnumOptionsConfigEditor` calls its `onChange` from the raw `onChange` of each option's value and label inputs, so one character typed is one committed write of `property-schema:config` on the definition row.

That write is not cheap. `core.migratePropertyDefinition` treats a preset-config edit as a codec-inputs change (deliberately wider than it needs to be — it re-parses rather than assuming), so every keystroke visits every consuming block of that definition and re-reads its value children. It writes nothing when the encoding did not move, but it holds the single SQLite writer for the whole walk either way. On a property with tens of thousands of owners that is the same tens-of-seconds freeze measured in #1112 — once per character.

The input is also controlled from the persisted config, so while a write is in flight the typed character is restored away; the editor is close to unusable at that scale even ignoring the freeze.

The confirmation added in #1112 now stands in front of it, which turns a silent freeze into a dialog the user can decline — an improvement, but a dialog per keystroke is not the answer. The fix is for this editor to commit on blur (or on an explicit action) the way the name field already does, so one edit is one write.

Small and self-contained; the ref picker next to it is already discrete and needs nothing.
close_reason: Closed on GitHub (issue #1116); reconciled by bd-github-sync.

title: Undoing a large property-definition rename freezes the app with no surface at all
description:
Sibling of the rename freeze (#1112), and NOT covered by the confirmation and progress surface added for it.

A definition rename is one undo step by design: the edit and the fan-out to every consumer land in one transaction. Undo therefore replays the whole thing — `Repo._replay` opens one tx and `applyRaw`s every snapshot in the entry, a SELECT plus an UPDATE per row, over the same tens of thousands of consumers. Same single SQLite writer, same duration, and this time no confirmation and no progress: the gesture is a global shortcut, not the property editor, so nothing sizes the replay or says the app is busy.

Same-tx processors are gated off during a replay (#187), so there is no second fan-out on top — the cost is the raw row restores, the topological ordering of the snapshots, and the post-commit walk.

Not yet timed. The rename itself measured 24.8s at 10,048 owners and 56.5s at 40,180 on a migrated ~1.1M-block graph, and the replay does comparable per-row work, so the same order is the expectation until someone measures it.

What a fix probably is NOT: a copy of the rename gate. The entry already knows its own size (`entry.snapshots.size`), and a replay big enough to stop the app is not specific to properties — an import undo or a bulk move has the same shape. The surface this wants is likely a general one over `replayGesture`, which is why this is not folded into #1112.

title: Renaming a widely-used property definition blocks the app for ~1 minute with no progress
description:
Measured on a migrated graph of ~1.1M blocks.

Renaming a property definition fans the new name out to every owner's cell in the SAME transaction (core.migratePropertyDefinition). That is the right design — one undoable step, ordinary synced rows, nothing to claim or re-detect — but it is not free at scale:

  10,048 owners  ->  24.8 s
  40,180 owners  ->  56.5 s

Both correct: every cell moved to the new key, none kept the old, field rows still resolved. The problem is purely what the user sees. It is a single repo.tx, so it holds the one SQLite writer for its whole duration, with every other write and the sync drain queued behind it — and the rename gesture has no banner, no progress, no confirmation that a large fan-out is about to happen. From the outside the app is frozen for up to a minute.

Worth considering, roughly in order of cost:
  - tell the user before starting when the fan-out is large (the owner count is cheap to query), the way the one-time migration already asks for confirmation
  - a progress surface for the duration
  - only then, whether the write should be chunked at all — note chunking costs the single-undoable-step and same-tx-fanout properties, which are load-bearing, so it should be the last resort

Found while QAing the properties-as-blocks migration on a full-size graph.

title: Value preset presentation is resolved by codec type against a preset-id map
description:
Five display sites resolve a value preset with presets.get(schema.codec.type),
against a map keyed by PRESET ID:

  PropertyPicker.tsx (the suggestion entry, and its label)
  BlockTypeBlockRenderer.tsx (the property list's glyph, and its label)
  defaults.tsx resolvePropertyDisplay (Editor and Glyph, twice)

A codec type is not a preset id and does not have to be unique. Two presets
already build a codec whose type is list, and a plugin can register a third:
memberCodecOf's docblock in api/codecs.ts says exactly this about the type
string being an open, non-unique discriminator. So every schema on the text
list preset is presented by the JSON one, because its id happens to equal the
shared type. Editor and Glyph coincide today, so only the LABEL can show it.

FOUND BY: a review of the PR that made the text list the pickable one. That PR
wanted to qualify the JSON preset's label so the two are pickable apart, and
the qualifier would have appeared on every text-list schema — including the
kernel's own types and alias. It settled for keeping the plain label on the
JSON preset (true of both) and putting the qualifier on the offered one, with
the constraint written down at both declarations and pinned by a test. That
workaround is why this is a latent defect rather than a visible one, and it
is also a trap: the next person to reach for a clearer label for either
entry will reintroduce it.

THE FIX is to resolve a presentation from the definition's stored preset
identity, through ONE helper the five sites share, falling back to the codec
type only where no definition is in hand (the unknown-schema path in
resolvePropertyDisplay genuinely has none).

WHAT IT NEEDS, and why it was not done inline: PropertyDefinitionMetadata
carries fieldId, name, changeScope, hidden, origin and seedKey, but NOT the
preset id, so the registry snapshot cannot answer the question today. The
definition BLOCK has it — PropertySchemaBlockRenderer reads presetId straight
off the row — so parsePropertyDefinitionMetadata can decode it, but that is a
new field on a core snapshot type. Note the hazard there: that parser returns
null for a row whose metadata does not decode, and a null drops the definition
from the registry, so a missing or malformed preset id must degrade to
undefined rather than reject the row.

PINNED MEANWHILE: a test asserts that the preset reached by the text list's
codec type is the JSON entry and that its label is still the unqualified one.
It will fail on a relabel, which is the trap above, and can be deleted with
this issue.

title: Successful migration reports "Migrated properties on 0 blocks"
description:
A migration that converted 108,255 blocks and minted 760,821 rows ended with:

  "Migrated properties on 0 blocks. Undo history for this workspace was cleared."

CAUSE
`runPropertyCellBackfill` resets the per-sweep counters at the top of every
sweep, and convergence is "a sweep that materialized nothing" — so the LAST
sweep always materializes nothing. The action reads `blocksMaterialized` from
the most recent progress notification, which is that sweep, so the number is 0
on every successful run by construction.

That also makes a real run indistinguishable from a no-op re-run, which is the
inverse of #1082.

CORRECTION to this issue as first filed
It also claimed the repair worklist never appears. That is WRONG and I withdraw
it. A rejected cell value never gets a field row, so every sweep re-attempts it
and re-records the failure — the converging sweep included. `failureCount` is
therefore non-zero at the end, and `describeOutcome`'s `followUp` (gated on
`unmigrated > 0`) does fire. Only the block count is broken.

FIX
In https://github.com/Stvad/knowledge-medium/pull/1106: `blocksMaterializedTotal`
alongside the existing `valuesMaterializedTotal`, with the action reading the
run-wide total and the per-sweep counter left for the progress line. Pinned by a
test asserting `blocksMaterialized === 0` and `blocksMaterializedTotal === 5`
after a converged run. Close when that merges.

title: Repoint the definitions still on the JSON list preset to the text list
description:
Split out of km-lvxz, which made the text list the one the picker offers and
left the JSON one registered and hidden. 84 definitions still point at the
hidden preset. This is the "decide separately whether to repoint them, and
how" half.

NOTHING IS BROKEN WHILE THEY STAY. Every workspace is still at cell, where
both presets encode a string array identically, so the preset id is the only
difference until a definition has field rows. The cost arrives with the
properties flip: post-flip a member of the JSON list is a value child spelling
"foo" with the quotes, and that is the spelling km-lvxz exists to stop.

EVIDENCE, measured before km-lvxz: every member of every definition on that
preset is a string — 32907 of them across the 84 — and the only object members
belong to one code-declared seed (srs snapshot history), which stays on the
JSON list deliberately and is not part of this.

TWO ROUTES.

1. By hand, per definition, through the UI. No migration code at all. The
   picker now shows List next to their List (JSON), and each pick is an
   ordinary preset change: the fan-out converts that definition's value
   children inside the editing transaction, so it is one undoable step and
   reaches other devices as ordinary synced rows. 84 picks.

2. A one-shot pass. Reaches all of them at once and carries the full
   data-migration discipline: once per graph, claim in synced data, never from
   a stale device, clear the workspace undo stack and tell the user, and put
   the safe-to-write check inside each writing transaction rather than at
   scheduling time.

Route 1 is the recommendation while the count is this small and the flip has
not happened: it needs nothing built, and a pass that re-derives a change the
user could make in a tx is the shape to be suspicious of.

DO NOT REBUILD THE CONVERSION. It is the issue 1024 path, covered in both
directions in propertyDefinitionChange.test.ts — including escaping a member
the target would otherwise store as a live span, and keeping quotes a person
typed. Whichever route is picked, it drives that same preset change.
close_reason: Repointed the 83 user definitions to the text list before the large workspace's flip; verified lossless (see last comment).

title: Make the Options/list preset a list of strings, carrying its already-materialized children
description:
Split out of the PR for issues 1080 and 1088, where it was attempted in place and reverted. The concept is right — confirmed by the maintainer, and by the data: every member of every list-preset property in every synced workspace is a string, 32907 of them across 84 definitions, the only object members belonging to one code-declared seed. A list of strings is also the common case the type system should serve without quoting.

WHY IT CANNOT BE DONE BY NARROWING THE SHIPPED PRESET IN PLACE
Reproduced, pure, no DB:

  members written by the OLD list codec -> children ["foo", "bar", "baz"] (each with literal quotes)
  those children projected by the OLD codec -> [foo, bar, baz]
  those children projected by list-of-string -> ["foo", "bar", "baz"] (quotes now part of each value)

Every member silently gains literal quotes. Touching one member reprojects the whole field, so editing one corrupts every untouched sibling in the owner cell. The definition ROW never changes — only the kernel's meaning of the preset id it already names — so propertyDefinitionChangeProcessor never fires and the conversion machinery that exists for exactly this (convertValueChildContent, which reads a child under the codec that WROTE it) is bypassed.

The both-spellings trick used for enum in that PR is not available here. Enum reserves the whole quoted form forever and escapes any option value shaped like it. The list member codec is the shared string codec, used by string-list, alias, types and every scalar string, where a quoted value the person typed must be preserved verbatim — there is a test asserting exactly that. Reserving the quoted form for one consumer of a shared codec is not expressible.

Not currently reachable in synced data: zero field rows exist and every workspace is still at cell. It IS reachable on a flipped scratch workspace, which is where the two bugs above were found in the first place.

THE ROUTE THAT WORKS
A NEW preset id built on a list of strings, user-pickable, with the old list preset left alone and hidden from the picker. Repointing a definition to it is an ordinary preset change, so the existing fan-out converts its value children correctly in the editing transaction — the issue 1024 path, already tested between the json-member list and string-list in both directions.

Then decide separately whether to repoint the 84 existing definitions, and how. Per-definition by hand through the UI is one option and needs no migration code at all; a one-shot pass is the other and carries the full data-migration discipline.

DEPENDS ON the properties flip only in the sense that the conversion has nothing to do before it — the fan-out is dormant until a definition has field rows.

Naming, already landed in the PR above: the picker entry was relabelled from Options to List, because Options read as pick-from-a-set and that is what Choice does. See the multi-select gap filed alongside.

WHAT LANDED IN #1098 THAT THIS WORK NOW DEPENDS ON (added 2026-09-21, after the merge)

- The value route KEEPS text that already reads back as the value it holds, instead of canonicalizing it. Good for this work rather than an obstacle: repointing a definition from the old list preset to a string-list one DOES respell, because the stored quoted member does not read back as the bare member under the string codec. But it means the fan-out no longer rewrites rows for cosmetic reasons, so do not expect a repoint to normalize anything the new codec already reads correctly.
- enforcesWriteSide walks the whole member chain, so a list whose member is an enum has its write side enforced at every depth, and at every storage grain. That is what makes the multi-select preset filed alongside this one safe by construction.
- The find-replace guard and the value-child reader now both know about the enum spelling. Neither knows anything about list members, which is untouched by that PR.

EVIDENCE FOR THE NARROWING, not repeated in the PR: ListPropertyEditor has only ever been able to write strings. It renders a member as String(v) and writes the whole stringified array back on every mutation, so a non-string member was already destroyed by any edit through the UI. Narrowing the codec makes honest what the editor already did.

ALREADY PROVEN, so do not rebuild it: the conversion this work needs is the issue 1024 path, and propertyDefinitionChange.test.ts covers it in both directions between a json-member list and string-list, including escaping a member the target would otherwise store as a live span, and keeping quotes a person typed.
close_reason: Closed on GitHub (issue #1101); reconciled by bd-github-sync.

title: Properties migration pass is read-bound: ~24 reads per block visited
description:
The properties-as-blocks pass is READ-bound, not write-bound. Measured over a 30 s
window mid-run on a ~350k-block graph (108,456 property-carrying blocks, 364,844
cells, 761,137 rows to mint):

  per block visited   7.6 execute   10.6 getAll   13.5 getOptional
  time in window      10.0 s write  20.2 s getAll  18.8 s getOptional

24 reads per block against 7.6 writes, and roughly 4x as much time in reads as in
writes. (Read totals exceed wall clock because they overlap — the connection is
queueing.)

WHERE THEY COME FROM
Within ONE batch transaction, the same owner is read repeatedly:
  - `namesPendingMaterialization` reads `tx.childrenOf(row.id)` and
    `tombstonedPropertyFieldRows`
  - `materializePropertyChildrenForExistingRow` then reads `tx.childrenOf(row.id)`
    AGAIN for the same row, with no write in between
  - `reconcileFieldValueChildren` reads `fieldValueChildren` per field
  - PROJECT then reads the owner and its children a THIRD time
    (`collectAffectedProjection` -> `reprojectOwner` -> `childrenOf` +
    `fieldValueChildren` per field) to re-derive a cell that the materializer built
    those very children FROM moments earlier. `propertiesEqual` short-circuits the
    WRITE, but only after every read has been paid.

WHY IT MATTERS
Confirmed by elimination: a change that removed 32% of the pass's block writes
(references pre-filled at create time, 1,851 updates -> 197) produced no measurable
change in throughput. Writes are not the limiting resource.

DIRECTIONS (not yet designed)
  - Pass the children the backfill already read into the materializer instead of
    re-reading them.
  - A per-transaction `childrenOf` cache in the tx engine, invalidated on writes
    that change a parent's child set. Invalidation correctness is the whole risk.
  - Let the backfill tell PROJECT that the owners it just materialized cannot have
    moved — during a backfill the projection is a no-op by construction.
The last one touches property truth and the same-tx processor pair, so it wants its
own PR and review rather than an in-passing patch.

FLOOR
Separately, a single `blocks` INSERT costs 1,470-2,862 us in-browser against a
667 MB OPFS database versus 60 us for the identical SQL with every trigger natively;
call overhead is only ~55 us. So 761k rows have a hard floor around 19 minutes
whatever else changes. WAL is unavailable (no wa-sqlite VFS implements xShmMap), so
the database runs journal_mode=delete with synchronous=FULL.
close_reason: Closed on GitHub (issue #1103); reconciled by bd-github-sync.

title: Properties migration is starved by the running tab's own queries
description:
On a ~350k-block graph, starting the one-time properties migration from the
default landing page (a daily note rendering grouped backlinks) left the pass
committing ZERO batches for 90 seconds, twice. Navigating to a block with no
backlinks took live query handles from 136 to 7 and the pass began committing
within a second.

WHAT THE UI WAS DOING IN THAT WINDOW (`repo.metrics()`):
  groupedBacklinks.forBlock    6 calls   mean 13,906 ms   max 51,053 ms
  backlinks.countForBlock     51 calls   mean  1,849 ms
  core.childIds               65 calls   mean  1,144 ms
  dbContention maxDepth 52, concurrentIssues 317 of 389 calls

MECHANISM
Each committed batch invalidates the handles those queries back; they re-run;
they hold the single writer connection the next batch needs. The pass writes
~761k rows, so the loop runs for the whole migration. The gesture's own banner
says "Leave this tab open", which is also what keeps the expensive panes
subscribed.

Every OTHER device gets a blocking modal for the duration. The device actually
running the pass gets a toast and keeps its outline live — it is the one client
that cannot afford to.

SUGGESTION
Put the running device behind the same gate it puts every other device behind,
or otherwise suspend outline query handles while the pass runs.

HOW MUCH OF THE SLOWDOWN THIS IS — read this before acting
Partly confounded, and the honest split is not yet established:
  - A separate defect, km-279i, wedges the connection outright for minutes at
    a time regardless of what the UI is doing, and it reproduces with an idle
    page. Some of the "0 batches in 90 s" above is likely that, not contention.
  - The host was at load average 28-76 during these samples.
What is NOT explained by either: a single `groupedBacklinks.forBlock` taking
51 s, and the handle count dropping 136 -> 7 exactly when the pass started
moving. Hands-off on a quiet page the pass holds ~26 blocks/s, so the UI is
real cost on top of that, but this issue should be re-measured against a build
that has the wedge fixed before sizing the fix.
close_reason:
Filed on evidence from a hidden automated browser tab, which starves requestIdleCallback / requestAnimationFrame / IntersectionObserver while setTimeout keeps firing. The 'zero batches in 90 seconds' and the multi-second backlink query times are not separable from that starvation, and the same starvation is what made the pass itself crawl (see the close on km-279i).

In a headed, visible Chrome the pass holds ~200 blocks/s. I have NOT re-tested the specific claim here — that landing on a daily note with grouped backlinks slows the run — in a visible browser, so there is no evidence left that stands on its own. Re-file with a visible-browser measurement if it reproduces there.

The one piece worth keeping is independent of this and is already its own issue: the backlink queries are slow on a large graph (km-snup).

title: A strict-enum option set that moves in code unsets the blocks holding the old value
description:
Narrowed from the original filing after measuring what actually happens. The original claim — that removing a Choice option unsets it on every block that used it — is FALSE for a user-driven edit, and the tests that establish so are in src/data/propertyDefinitionChange.test.ts under 'narrowing a Choice option set'.

WHAT ACTUALLY HAPPENS FOR A USER-DRIVEN EDIT
A definition's preset config is part of codecInputsChanged, so editing the option list fans out over every consuming parent in the editing transaction. The fan-out refuses when a value will not convert, so removing an option that blocks still hold rolls the whole edit back with 'the blocks using it would lose N stored values. Fix or remove those values first, or choose a type that can hold them.' The value, its row and the option set itself are all left as they were. Adding an option writes nothing at all: the spelling does not move and the fan-out skips a row whose converted content equals its current content.

WHAT IS ACTUALLY OPEN
The refusal needs a definition ROW edit to fire on. A strict-enum's option set lives in a code declaration, and seed materialization is create/restore-only — it never writes a changed payload back to a live definition row. So a release that removes or renames an option of a code-declared Choice fires no fan-out and gets no refusal, and post-flip every value child holding the old value stops projecting. The declaration wins over the stale stored config, so the new option set is what the membership check uses.

Reasoned from verified mechanics rather than reproduced: the fan-out gate is codecInputsChanged over the definition row's before/after, and the no-repair rule is the pending filter in src/data/definitionSeeds.ts. Worth an actual reproduction before building anything.

Not urgent while every workspace is still at properties_migration = cell: the pre-flip read path decodes the cell directly and that decode is lenient on membership, so a stale value still reads. This becomes reachable at the flip.

SECOND, SMALLER CASE
A stale value already sitting in a cell before the flip. The flip materializes it, because the cell decode that gates materialization is the lenient one, and the projection that reads the new value child back then refuses it. Also unreproduced.

FIX DIRECTIONS
1. A release-time check that a code-declared option set only ever widens, in the same family as the seed identity ledger.
2. Teach the flip to report a key whose cell decodes but whose value child would not read back, rather than silently materializing it.
3. Accept both and document, on the grounds that changing a shipped option set is already a frozen-identity-adjacent act.

title: A narrowing loses list members silently when the old preset does not build
description:
PRE-EXISTING, and deliberately left alone by PR #1060 after three attempts to fix it in place each shipped a worse defect. Measured 2026-09-20.

WHAT HAPPENS. A property whose preset no longer builds (extension missing on
this device) holds a list of three members. The user repairs the definition by
re-typing it to a scalar preset. The transaction COMMITS and the cell keeps
only the first member. No refusal, no report.

WHY IT IS NOT FIXED IN #1060. valuesLostBy needs the before-count to be a
LOWER bound on what the property held, or its slack becomes a phantom refusal.
With no old codec there are only two candidate records and both are UPPER
bounds:

  - the CELL's length: an array cell is N members of a list, or ONE value of a
    scalar holding an array (any identity codec). Cannot say arity.
  - the ROW count: a divergent peer row or a duplicate field row was never in
    the cell, so it over-counts; and a row this device has not received, or
    one stamped out of the value set, is missing, so it under-counts.

Combining two upper bounds does not produce a lower bound. Three successive
attempts in #1060 demonstrated this the expensive way - counting the cell's
length refused repairs that lose nothing; bounding it by the row count let the
count reach zero and SILENTLY UNSET a populated cell. The rule now shipped is
the sound weak one: claim a loss only where the projection comes out empty
over a cell that held something.

THE REAL FIX is #1077 - when there is no old codec, rebuild the value children
FROM the cell under the new schema instead of re-reading their text. Then
'what was lost' is a comparison of two cells and needs no row counting at all.
This bead is the symptom; #1077 is the cause. Close this one with that one.

WHERE. heldValueCount in src/data/internals/propertyDefinitionChangeProcessor.ts.
close_reason: Closed on GitHub (issue #1090); reconciled by bd-github-sync.

title: A strict-enum property accepts an off-menu value written through its value child
description:
Found while investigating the spelling defect on the same code path (km-3ovd).
Verified live on a flipped local scratch workspace.

REPRODUCTION
1. Take a todo. Its `status` is a `strict-enum` declared with exactly two options.
2. Edit its `status` value child's content to `"bananas"` (valid JSON, not a declared
   option).

OBSERVED
The write is accepted. The owner's cell becomes `{"status": "bananas"}` — a value outside
the property's declared option set, in source-of-truth data, with no error.

MECHANISM
`codecs.enum` puts the membership check in `encode` (`requireMember`) and leaves `decode`
as `requireString`, which accepts any string. The value-child path goes content ->
encoded, so it lands on the permissive half and never asks whether the string is an
option. Contrast the number, date, boolean and ref presets, where an unreadable value
child correctly unsets the key and leaves the text visible to repair.

This contradicts the standing rule for this model: every content -> encoded path must
refuse garbage into the graceful path rather than coerce it.

MITIGATING, and why this is P2 rather than P1
The app surfaces the bad value honestly rather than hiding it. The property panel renders
the select with a synthesized `bananas (unknown)` entry alongside the real options, so the
value is visible and one click repairs it, and the todo renderer treats the unknown status
as not-done rather than throwing. Nothing is lost and nothing crashes. What is wrong is
that the value got in at all, and that a consumer switching on the declared option set now
has a case it was promised could not occur.

FIX DIRECTION
The content -> encoded path for an enum should validate membership, which is what
`where.encode` / `requireMember` already does. Refusing takes the existing graceful path:
key unset, text left on the value child for the user to fix. Check the same question for
any other codec whose validation is asymmetric between encode and decode before fixing
just this one.
close_reason: Closed on GitHub (issue #1088); reconciled by bd-github-sync.

title: Every content edit costs about twice as much on a child-backed workspace, including on blocks with no properties
description:
Every content edit on a child-backed workspace costs roughly twice what the same edit
costs on a cell workspace, INCLUDING on a block that carries no properties at all. This is
an always-on cost the whole fleet starts paying at the flip.

MEASURED, two local scratch workspaces, median of 9 warmed `setContent` calls, reproduced
over two rounds:

                      cell      children
  0 properties        8.3 ms    16.0 ms
  1 property          8.3 ms    18.5 ms
  6 properties       11.4 ms    22.6 ms

WHERE THE TIME IS
Inside the write statements, not around them. Both modes issue exactly 4 `execute` calls
and 1 `writeTransaction` per edit. On a block with NO properties:

                      cell      children
  4 execute calls     0.6 ms    10.8 ms
  getOptional         2 calls   4 calls
  getOptional time    0.1 ms     0.3 ms

So the same number of write statements costs about eighteen times more, and the two extra
point reads are a rounding error rather than the cause.

RULED OUT
- Row count. The control was padded to the same block count and the gap persisted.
- Reference-index size. The control was then padded to MORE `block_references` than the
  flipped workspace (1780 against 1468) and the gap persisted, unchanged across two
  rounds. The flip does inflate that table by construction, since every field row's
  `::((defId))` content is a reference, but it is not what costs the time.
- Schema drift. `sqlite_master` for `blocks` is identical in both: same 12 indexes, same
  22 triggers, same VFS.

NOT ESTABLISHED
What inside those four statements is expensive. Candidates, none confirmed: trigger work
proportional to something the flip inflates other than references, per-statement cost
scaling with the number of `is_field_form` rows, or page-cache and file-layout effects
from the migration's bulk insert. An `ANALYZE` comparison would separate the last one
cheaply and was not run here because the bridge's SQL verb could not execute it.

INSTRUMENTATION NOTE for whoever picks this up: monkey-patching `repo.db.execute` captures
nothing, so the counted `execute` calls go through the transaction's own path. Find the
call site behind `queryMetrics.record` in `repo.ts` and instrument there.

The two extra reads are real and worth understanding even though they are not the cost.
`PROJECT_PROPERTY_CHILDREN_PROCESSOR` watches `content`, so on a child-backed workspace
every content edit enters `reprojectOwnersForRowStates`, and `collectAffectedProjection`
fetches the changed row's parent to decide whether the row is a value child. It runs for
both the before and the after side of the change, hence two fetches for one edit. The
parent fetch cannot be skipped from row-local data as the code stands, because
`isFieldValueChild` is true for every ordinary block; deduping the before/after pair by
parent id would halve it.

CAVEAT ON THE ABSOLUTE NUMBERS: they drifted between runs as the machine got busier. The
cell-versus-children ratio held in every round.
close_reason:
Not reproducible. The reported cost is not caused by properties_migration,
and the fleet does not start paying it at the flip.

The original measurement compared two separate workspaces, which leaves the
mode confounded with everything else about those two databases. Three
controlled runs, each comparing a workspace against ITSELF:

1. Mode toggled against one database (same rows, same file, same page cache,
   same tab, arms alternated): no effect.
2. One workspace grown 351 -> 1,480 -> 7,504 -> 9,372 rows: statements stay
   flat and both modes drift together.
3. The REAL migration (repo.runWorkspaceBackfillNow; 1,178 -> 5,812 blocks,
   2,297 field rows, undo cleared), measured in all three states:

     edited block   cell pre-mig   cell post-mig   children post-mig
     0 properties      8.3 ms         9.3 ms            9.1 ms
     1 property        8.3 ms         8.6 ms            8.6 ms
     4 properties      8.5 ms         8.2 ms            9.3 ms

   The pre-migration arm reproduces this issue's cell column exactly (8.3 ms,
   0.6 ms across the four statements). The post-migration children arm is
   where the 16.0 ms should be and it is not there. Mode-at-identical-data and
   data-at-identical-mode are both nil.

The four write statements measured 0.5-0.8 ms in every arm of every run,
never within an order of magnitude of the reported 10.8 ms. A node harness
over the same production schema and triggers agrees. Post-migration
background work is out too: the first post-migration arm ran within seconds
of the pass returning, and the reprojection counters stay at zero.

What the flip DOES cost is the extra parent point read the projection
processor makes, which the earlier correction comment already identified and
correctly judged too small to explain an 8 ms gap. PR #1095 halves it (2
reads -> 1 per edit, and 2N -> 1 for an N-row tx over siblings) and is merged.
That is the whole of the always-on cost: about 0.07 ms saved on a ~9 ms edit.

Closing as not-reproducible rather than fixed. What is NOT explained is what
made the original run read 16.0 ms — but it is not the mode, not the row
count, not the field rows and not the migration, so there is no defect here
to hold open. If it shows up again, the one thing to check first is that the
mode gate actually engaged on each arm: the getOptional count per edit (2 in
cell, 3 in children after #1095) proves it per-arm. An early version of this
investigation silently did not engage, because the target block had no
parent, and that counter is what caught it.

Full measurement and method notes: #1095.

title: A schema handle from addSchema stops resolving after the next addSchema, and the error blames shadowing
description:
Found during exploratory QA of the cell-to-children flip, but NOT caused by it: reproduced
deterministically on an unflipped control workspace, so this is pre-existing.

REPRODUCTION (one turn, no concurrency)
1. `await repo.userSchemas.addSchema({name, presetId: 'string'})` three times, keeping
   each returned schema.
2. `await block.set(returnedSchema[i], value)` for each, in order.

OBSERVED
The first two writes throw:

    cannot write property "r3-0": schema identity is unavailable (shadowed)

The third, whose add was the most recent, succeeds. Interleaving add-then-write one at a
time succeeds for all three. Awaiting `whenPropertyDefinitionsReady` or a macrotask before
writing does not help. Re-reading the schema by name from `repo.propertySchemas` before
each write succeeds for all three, and afterwards all three names resolve normally.

MECHANISM
`resolveBoundary` accepts a plain schema only on exact OBJECT identity with the snapshot's
entry (`snapshot.schemas.get(name) === schema`). Each `addSchema` rebuilds the snapshot
with fresh objects, so every handle handed out before the last one stops being identical
to its own entry. The fallback branch then compares the snapshot's behaviour object with
the caller's, finds them different, and reports `shadowed`. A probe confirms it:
`repo.propertySchemas.get(name) === returnedSchema` is false for the first two and true
only for the last.

WHY IT MATTERS
The reported reason is wrong, and expensively so. `shadowed` means "another definition
owns this name", which sends whoever hits it looking for a duplicate definition that does
not exist. The real condition is "your handle is stale". Anything that registers several
properties and then writes them — an importer, an extension's setup, a seeding script —
hits this on the first try; the panel's add-one-then-type-a-value rhythm happens to avoid
it.

FIX DIRECTION
Two independent halves. Either make a returned schema keep resolving (resolve a plain
schema by name-plus-behaviour equality rather than object identity, or have `addSchema`
return a resolved handle that carries its `fieldId`), or at minimum stop reporting a stale
handle as `shadowed` and give it a reason that names what happened.
close_reason: Closed on GitHub (issue #1079); reconciled by bd-github-sync.

title: Copy drops ordinary blocks nested under a property value child
description:
Found in exploratory QA of the cell-to-children flip on a local scratch workspace.
Unreachable before the flip, because value children do not exist there.

`serializeBlock` (`src/utils/copy.ts`) loads the subtree with
`hidePropertyChildren: true`, which prunes each recognised field row AND everything under
it. Its own comment already names this: the predicate "prunes EVERY recognized field row
today, which is correct only while all workspaces read 'cell'".

REPRODUCTION
1. On a flipped workspace, open a block that has a string property, navigate into its
   value child (reachable by its own deep link) and add an ordinary child block under it
   with some text.
2. Copy the owning block.

OBSERVED
The serialized result is one block and the owner's own text. The ordinary child block
under the value child is gone from the clipboard with no indication. Pasting reproduces
neither the properties nor that content.

EXPECTED
Property machinery being pruned matches the outline (which hides it), so copy is WYSIWYG
and consistent today. The part that is a defect regardless of tier policy is that ORDINARY
user content nested under a value child is dropped along with the machinery.

FIX DIRECTION
This is the copy half of the pending display-tier work: once the predicate is tier-aware,
a non-hidden property row travels with its subtree and the nested user content stops being
collateral. Until then the narrower fix is to keep descendants that are not themselves
machinery.

title: A Choice property's value child is JSON-spelled, so retyping the label the UI shows unsets it
description:
Found in exploratory QA of the cell-to-children flip on a local scratch workspace.

`encodedValueToContent` (`src/data/propertyChildren.ts`) gives a plain, unquoted spelling
to `ref`, `string`, `url`, `date`, `number` and `boolean`, and falls through to
`JSON.stringify` for everything else. `enum` and `strict-enum` encode to a plain string but
take the fallback, so their value children are stored and displayed quoted.

REPRODUCTION
1. On a flipped workspace, take a todo (its `status` is a `strict-enum`).
2. Look at the `status` value child: its content is `"open"`, with the quotes.
3. Edit that value child to `done` — the label the checkbox, the panel dropdown and the
   type definition all show.

OBSERVED
The `status` key is removed from the owner's cell. The todo silently reverts to its
default (open) while the value child still reads `done`. Typing `"done"` instead works
and sets the property.

Same for the user-facing `list` ("Options") preset: its members render as `"red"`,
`"green"`.

Contrast: a `string`, `number`, `date`, `url` or `ref` value child shows exactly the text
you would type, and retyping it round-trips.

EXPECTED
The unset-on-undecodable half is the designed graceful path and is correct. What is wrong
is the SPELLING: the text the UI shows for a Choice value is not the text that reads back
as that value, so the obvious correction is the one that loses the property.

Recoverable: the typed text is preserved on the value child and retyping valid JSON
restores the cell, so no data is destroyed.

FIX DIRECTION
Extend the plain-spelling branch to codecs whose encoded form is a plain string, which
covers `enum` and `strict-enum`. Note that a member-wise list already gets this for free
when its member codec is `string` (the `alias` property's members are stored unquoted), so
only the non-member-wise and non-string cases are affected.
close_reason: Closed on GitHub (issue #1080); reconciled by bd-github-sync.

title: Block-reference picker ranks a page's alias value child above the page under the same label
description:
Found in exploratory QA of the cell-to-children flip on a local scratch workspace.
Does NOT reproduce on an unflipped control workspace seeded identically, because the
value child does not exist there.

REPRODUCTION
1. On a flipped workspace, take any page whose title equals one of its aliases (every page
   bootstrapped with an alias qualifies, including the kernel's own system pages).
   The migration gives it an `alias` field row with one value child whose content is that
   same title.
2. On some other block, add a `refList` (or `ref`) property and open its "Add block" picker.
3. Type the page's title.

OBSERVED
Two options with the identical visible label and no other distinguishing mark — the page,
and the page's `alias` value child. The value child ranks FIRST, so it is the highlighted
default. Picking it stores the value child's id as the property's target:

    cell before: ["<pageA>", "<pageB>", "<pageC>"]
