    cell after:  ["<pageA>", "<pageB>", "<pageC>", "<alias value child of the page>"]

The stored reference now points at a machinery row, the property panel renders it with the
same label as the page, and nothing in the UI says the target is wrong.

NOT AFFECTED: the alias index. Only the real page claims the alias, so `[[Title]]` still
resolves correctly. The defect is confined to the content-search picker.

EXPECTED
A value row surfacing in search is accepted behaviour and is not the complaint. The
complaint is that in a picker whose whole job is choosing a target, two candidates are
presented as indistinguishable and the wrong one is preselected.

FIX DIRECTION
Disambiguate rather than suppress: show the owning block (breadcrumb / "alias of …") on a
machinery row, and rank a page above its own machinery. Suppressing property rows from the
picker would contradict the normal-block tenet and is not what is being asked for here.
close_reason: Closed on GitHub (issue #1081); reconciled by bd-github-sync.

title: A no-op re-run of the properties migration still reports 'Migrated properties on N blocks'
description:
Found in exploratory QA of the cell-to-children flip on a local scratch workspace.

REPRODUCTION
1. Flip a workspace to `children` and run the palette action "Migrate properties to child blocks (one-time)" to completion.
2. Run the same palette action again with nothing left to convert.

OBSERVED
The confirmation dialog still says "this fills them in across 248 blocks", and the
completion banner still says "Migrated properties on 248 blocks. Undo history for this
workspace was cleared." Row counts before and after the second run are identical
(3045 blocks, 1227 field rows), so it created nothing.

The same pass over the CLI verb reports the numbers the banner does not:

    "outcome": "ran",
    "blocksScanned": 249,
    "blocksMaterialized": 249,
    "valuesMaterialized": 0,
    "valuesMaterializedTotal": 0,
    "failures": []

`blocksMaterialized` counts blocks the pass accepted, not blocks it changed, and that is
the only number the banner renders (`src/plugins/properties-migration/action.ts:166`).

EXPECTED
A run that materialized zero values says so. The runbook's stop condition is "re-run the
gesture until it reports nothing left"; as built there is no report an operator can read
as "nothing left", and a completed migration is indistinguishable from one that has just
started over.

Secondary: the no-op run clears this device's undo history again and says so, which costs
the operator their history for no work done.

FIX DIRECTION
`describePassOutcome` already receives `valuesMaterializedTotal`; it only consults it on
the all-failed branch. A `valuesMaterializedTotal === 0 && unmigrated === 0` branch gives
the missing "nothing left to migrate" message, and the undo clear can be skipped on that
same condition.
close_reason: Closed on GitHub (issue #1082); reconciled by bd-github-sync.

title: The unconvertible refusal names no block, and its blockIds have no consumer
description:
MEASURED 2026-09-19 reviewing PR #1060. Pre-existing.

The property.definition-change.unconvertible rejection carries
meta.blockIds: [...lostParents] so a surface can offer the blocks whose values
would be lost. Nothing renders it. rejectionToastFacet has exactly one
contribution in the tree (alias.collision), so this code takes the raw-message
fallback in src/extensions/processorRejectionToast.ts and the user sees only
the sentence.

That sentence ends 'Fix or remove those values first', which is not actionable
without knowing which blocks. Property value rows are children of a field row
and are not obviously the thing being talked about.

ALSO, for whoever builds that surface: lostParents is one set across ALL
changes in the transaction while the message is per-field, so a rename+retype
of two properties in one tx would show the wrong blocks for one of them. Fix
that at the same time - make it per-change, or say in the message that the
list spans the whole edit.

WHERE. The throw in src/data/internals/propertyDefinitionChangeProcessor.ts;
the toast routing in src/extensions/processorRejectionToast.ts.

title: Reads starve for tens of seconds under migration load on a single-connection pool
description:
On the coop-sync VFS (one SQLite connection: every browser but Chromium) a long write-heavy pass starves reads badly enough to look like a hang.

Observed repeatedly while verifying the properties migration on WebKit pinned to coop-sync. While the cell-to-children pass commits batches back to back, an ordinary read cannot win a slot for tens of seconds: agent-bridge commands time out at their 25s limit, and the app's own contention counters showed a high-water queue depth of 16 with busy time climbing in real time while the completed-call count barely moved. Reloading the tab clears it.

Not the deadlock fixed in #1072 — nothing holds a connection it will not return, and every read is eventually served. This is pure queueing on one connection, the shape described in the slow-read-starves-writes memory.

Why it matters: this is the storage shape real non-Chromium users have. During a migration the UI's own queries are behind the same queue, so the app is effectively unresponsive for the duration rather than merely slow, and there is no signal distinguishing it from a hang.

Worth measuring before designing: how long a read actually waits at p50/p99 during a pass, whether the batch budget (TARGET_INSERT_ROWS) is the right knob, and whether yielding between batches would let reads through without materially slowing the pass.

title: [BUG] re-typing text holding an alias to a Reference mints a span whose id is the alias text
description:
MEASURED 2026-09-18 during review of the #1055 conversion change. PRE-EXISTING - the same answer comes out on master - so it was not changed there.

A value row under a verbatim codec (string/url/optional-string/string-list)
holding a whole-content alias like [[Page]] converts to a ref/refList/
optional-ref property as the span ((  [[Page]]  )) - written without the
spaces: a reference span whose ID IS THE LITERAL TEXT '[[Page]]'.

That is arguably the exact thing the mint decline next to it exists to
prevent: an identity nobody wrote, pointing at a seat that does not exist. The
decline is gated on the STORED text already carrying a reference, and an alias
IS one, so it waves this through - but what it produces is not the alias
resolved, it is a ref whose id is unparseable as an id.

The alternative is to let it decline, which makes the conversion unreadable
and so refuses the whole re-type (loud, keeps the data). Resolving the alias
properly needs a lookup the pure conversion function cannot do.

WHERE. respellUnderTargetCodec in src/data/propertyChildren.ts, the
isWholeContentReference conjunct. It is now pinned by the test 're-spells a
reference the stored text ALREADY carried' in src/data/propertyChildren.test.ts,
so whichever way this is decided, that test states the current answer.

RELATED: the reverse trip is a dead end too - a Reference re-typed to text now
writes the bare id, which LOOKS convertible back (it is a valid block id) but
refuses, with a message saying the type cannot hold it. Worth fixing the
message even if the conversion stays refused.

title: [BUG] re-typing a property to Choice always refuses, because the picker resets its options to empty
description:
MEASURED 2026-09-18 during review of the #1055 conversion change. Pre-existing.

writePresetId in src/components/renderer/PropertySchemaBlockRenderer.tsx resets
'preset config' to the target preset's defaultConfig. For enum ('Choice') that
is {options: []}, so every stored value is unconvertible and the #1024 refusal
fires on any property that already holds values. Choice IS in the picker, so
this is a selectable option that cannot succeed on a non-empty property.

The user sees a refusal naming values they would lose, with no hint that the
cause is an option list the picker just emptied on their behalf.

FIX DIRECTION. Either carry the existing values into the new option set when
re-typing to enum (they are exactly the options the user already uses), or
refuse earlier with a message about configuring options first. The first is
what a person means by the gesture.

ALSO, same area: the comments at src/components/propertyEditors/selectablePresets.ts
and in PropertySchemaBlockRenderer.tsx both give 'enum' as the example of a
preset hidden from the picker. It is not - strict-enum is. A comment that
contradicts its code.

title: [BUG] the raw-json preset has no presentation, so it renders as an unloaded plugin
description:
MEASURED 2026-09-18 during review of the #1055 conversion change. Pre-existing, unrelated to that change.

rawJsonValuePresetCore exists in src/data/kernelValuePresetCores.ts but has no
entry in kernelValuePresetPresentations, so the join in readValuePresetRegistry
drops it. Two consequences:

- it is absent from the type picker, so no user gesture can select it. Only the
  frozen seeds agent:cancel and property-schema:default use it.
- a property-schema block sitting on it renders 'raw-json (unknown)' plus the
  message 'The plugin contributing preset raw-json is not loaded.' That is
  FALSE - the kernel owns this preset. A user looking at one of those seeded
  definitions is told their install is broken.

FIX DIRECTION. Either add a presentation entry (with hideFromPicker, matching
how json and optional-json are handled - they ARE hidden but DO have entries),
or make the not-loaded message distinguish 'no presentation registered' from
'no core registered'. The first is smaller and matches the neighbours.

title: Verify the migration's view-gap probe on a single-connection VFS
description:
The cell-to-children backfill used to read its view-gap probe through the
Repo's block handle from INSIDE its own write transaction. On a
single-connection pool that read cannot be served while the write is held,
so the batch hangs instead of refusing — and it hangs holding the graph
claim, which now puts a blocking modal on every device for as long as it
lasts.

The probe was moved out of the transaction (PR #1059, merged). The fix has
only ever run on Chromium, where the pool does not have the single
connection that produces the hang, so the bug it fixes has never been
observed and neither has the fix.

HOW TO CHECK
  - Safari, or any browser on the coop-sync VFS:
    localStorage.setItem('km.local-db-vfs', 'coop-sync'), reload.
  - Run the properties migration on a scratch workspace with enough blocks
    to take several batches.
  - Expect: it completes, or refuses with a named reason. A hang with the
    migration dialog up on every device is the failure.

WHY THIS AND NOT THE REST OF THE PR: the rest is React state and synced
rows, which behave the same everywhere. This one is specifically about how
the storage layer serves a read during a write, which is the thing that
differs per browser.
close_reason: Closed on GitHub (issue #1069); reconciled by bd-github-sync.

title: The migration claim's identity does not travel with the run that took it
description:
A run knows THAT it took the claim (a boolean on the local run snapshot) but not WHICH claim. The claimant id is per browser profile, so everything keyed on it cannot separate two tabs of one browser, and three separate defects fall out of that:

1. markComplete refuses to stamp another CLIENT's claim, but two tabs share a claimant, so whichever finishes first can still record a completion over the other's live run — ending the blocking dialog and the undo pause on every device while the other tab is still writing.

2. The migration dialog's holderOf reads a sibling tab's claim as this tab's own, so a tab whose claim was released and re-taken by a sibling is still told 'Leave this tab open. Closing it stops the run' — false, the run is in the other tab.

3. withOperatorBackfillClaim releases only a claim it MINTED, precisely because an inherited one may be a sibling tab's live claim. That is the same missing fact, worked around.

The fix is for tryClaim to return the claim it wrote or inherited — claimantId plus claimedAt is enough, and claimKey already exists in the dialog for exactly this comparison — and for the runner to carry it to markComplete and to the local run snapshot. Then 'is this our claim' is a question about the run rather than about the browser profile.

Duplicate runs from one profile are an accepted residual (the seam header says so). This is not about preventing them; it is about each run knowing which claim is its own so it cannot end another's protection.

title: Three toggle-driven dialogs render Dialog directly and never shadow the keyboard
description:
quick-find (QuickFind.tsx), find-replace (FindReplaceDialog.tsx) and the shortcut-help overlay (ShortcutHelpOverlay.tsx) are all app mounts that render a Radix Dialog directly off a toggle store, rather than through openDialog. None of them activates ActionContextTypes.DIALOG — grep finds zero useActionContext references in all three.

That activation is the only thing that makes a modal shadow the keyboard. Radix makes the app pointer-inert and traps focus, so the leak is keyboard-only and looks completely correct until a bare key press reaches the surface underneath: with a CodeMirror editor mounted, Enter matches the editor's split binding, which both writes a block and preventDefaults the key the dialog's own button was waiting for. Tab indents the block behind. src/shortcuts/test/HotkeyReconciler.test.tsx already documents the hazard.

useModalShadowing (src/shortcuts/useActionContext.ts) is the one-line fix per call site; it was extracted when the properties-migration gate hit the same problem. Whether each of the three actually leaks depends on what is focused when it opens, so each needs checking rather than a blanket edit.

title: Properties migration can be started from a browser whose client id will not survive a reload
description:
The cell-to-children migration's claim is keyed on getClientId(), which graphBackfillClaim.ts calls LOAD-BEARING: a value that does not survive a reload leaves a claim nobody can ever match.

In a storage-blocked browser (private mode, blocked or partitioned storage, a full quota), getClientId falls back to a per-process uuid — see the catch in src/utils/clientId.ts, which says so. After a reload the operator can neither resume the pass (decideClaim returns back-off, because the live claim names an id this process no longer has) nor release it through releaseClaim (which matches on claimant id). The blocking dialog every device shows then reports that another device is converting the workspace, and the manual release inside it is the only exit.

src/utils/clientId.ts already exports isClientIdPersistent() for exactly this question, and the migration gesture does not ask it. passIsUnfit() in src/plugins/properties-migration/action.ts checks read-only, workspace ownership and the sync gap; adding this check there refuses the run before the one-way fleet-wide flip rather than after.

Pre-existing, not introduced by the dialog work — but the dialog leans on the claimant id harder than the old toast did, since it now decides which device is told it is holding the workspace.

title: Value preset cores registered imperatively from an appEffect are invisible to the install-time check
description:
The install-time preset-identity check (`src/plugins/agent-runtime/presetIdentity.ts`) compares the effective value-preset registry before and after an install. It reads the app's contribution list and the candidate's isolated resolution, which covers every core contributed DECLARATIVELY (`valuePresetCoresFacet.of(core)`).

A core registered imperatively — an `appEffect` that calls `runtime.setRuntimeContributions(valuePresetCoresFacet, someSourceId, [core])` — escapes it on both sides:

- the live contribution carries the effect's arbitrary source id, not `block:<id>`, so the diff does not recognize it as the extension's and treats it as an unrelated surviving contribution;
- the isolated resolution collects declarations and never starts effects, so the candidate's replacement is never seen.

An update that changes such a core therefore installs with no refusal, and the changed codec becomes live on reload, re-typing stored values.

Two directions, and the first is probably right:

1. REFUSE a runtime bucket on `valuePresetCoresFacet` from a dynamic extension. A preset core is a storage-identity declaration — the seed ledger, the definition projector and this check all assume it is declared, not computed at runtime — so an imperative one is outside the model rather than a case to support. Cheap, and it makes the gap impossible instead of detected.
2. Carry block ownership on runtime buckets and evaluate the candidate's effects, which means running effect code at install time (the approval gate forbids that for source that is not going live) and predicting what an effect will register.

Raised by review on the install-time check. Related: the same check cannot see the enable path either.

title: Preset-identity check does not cover the enable/approve path
description:
`install-extension` now refuses when a value preset core the extension registers builds a different codec under an id already registered on that device (see `src/plugins/agent-runtime/presetIdentity.ts`). That closes the install gesture, but not the other two ways a new core becomes live:

- `enable-extension` approves the CURRENT source and refreshes. An extension that was enabled, then disabled, then re-installed with a changed core passes the install check (its old core is no longer registered, so there is nothing to compare against) and re-types every value on re-enable.
- the Extensions settings UI's "Enable here" / "Update" buttons take the same approve path with no check at all, and a refusal there needs a UI answer (a confirm dialog naming the definitions and cells, presumably) rather than a thrown error.

Both run through `approveExtension`, which only TRANSPILES — it never instantiates the module — so the cores are not available there for free; the check would need the same isolated resolution install now does.

Worth deciding together, because the UI half is what makes this a design question rather than ten more lines: what does a refusal look like when the user clicked a button, and is "approve" the right place for a data-safety gate at all.

The install-time check's own limits are stated at its declaration.

title: Deleting a property definition during the cell-to-children backfill strands its cell-only consumers
description:
Noticed while building the refusal for #1029 (option (a): refuse definition renames and re-types while a properties:cell-to-children claim is active).

THE SAME HAZARD, A DIFFERENT GESTURE. The backfill resolves each cell key against the CURRENT registry and materializePropertyChildrenForExistingRow skips an unregistered key by design. Deleting a definition block un-registers its name. So every parent the chunked backfill has not reached yet keeps its value under a key that now resolves to nothing, and no later batch will visit it — exactly the permanence #1029 describes for a rename.

WHY #1029's REFUSAL DOES NOT COVER IT. core.migratePropertyDefinition's collectChanges skips a row whose after-state is deleted (`if (after === null || after.deleted || before === null) continue`), so a deletion collects no change and the migration-running refusal — which is gated on a rename or re-type having been collected — never sees it. The gating is deliberate: without it, the materializer's own field-row bookkeeping writes would be refused too.

WHERE IT WOULD GO. The schema editor's "Delete schema" button (PropertySchemaContentRenderer in src/components/renderer/PropertySchemaBlockRenderer.tsx) is deliberately left enabled by the #1029 UI guard, which locks only the name field, the preset picker and the config editor. The guard's own comment points here.

NOT DECIDED. Refusing deletes for the length of a backfill is a wider lock than #1029's and was not part of that decision, and the deletion gesture already has its own semantics ("their values stay; the editor falls back to an inferred type") which a reader may consider the same outcome. Worth deciding before the first flip on a large graph, since the backfill window is long.

title: PR 507 (agent-dispatch retryable-failure deferral) — ready, awaiting merge decision
description:
STATE as of 2026-09-17. Branch claude/dreamy-kilby-4c894d, head dc249e3700. Merged with master (not rebased — Autofix required a merge). Full gate green: 9884 tests. All 65 review threads replied to and resolved. NOT merged; merging is Vlad's call.

WHAT IT DOES: an infrastructure failure (out of credits, expired login, rate limit, network, missing executor binary, dead bridge/channel listener) no longer marks a task agent:status=error. It goes to agent:status=queued + agent:retry-after and retries itself, the attempt and the runsPerHour slot are handed back, and the failing LANE (one executor, or 'channel') backs off. Plus Retry affordances: Retry task, Retry now / Stop retrying, and a bulk Retry-all in the command palette.

REVIEW HISTORY: 20 Codex rounds, ~65 findings. Rounds 1-7 mapped the design; the refactors that closed two whole clusters were (a) one createRunWatch answering 'did the model respond' for both the mention and query paths, replacing four inline predicates, and (b) classifying failures where they are BORN (withRunFailure / classifyThrown, the channel sender, the bridge client marking a command the app ANSWERED) instead of regex-matching rendered error prose. No findings in either cluster since.

OPEN DECISIONS for Vlad — none block merging:
1. Whether to do the two structural follow-ups before or after merge: run identity rolled backward (km-1nyy) and the lane cooldown duplicating agent:retry-after (km-6334). Both are correctness-neutral today.
2. Channel auto-retry ambition. Exactly-once over that boundary has no fixed point; the receiver dedup is best-effort and lost on restart. Offered option, not taken: stop auto-retrying an AMBIGUOUS channel failure and park it for a person to decide, keeping auto-retry only for a connection that never opened. That reduces what the feature promises, so it wants a decision.
3. Whether to add a conditional (compare-and-set) write to the bridge. Two races are NARROWED and cannot be closed without it: a deferred-stop overwriting a concurrent Retry (km-ievn), and a claim overwriting a completion the ambient session wrote (same primitive).

FOLLOW-UPS FILED: km-1nyy, km-6334, km-ievn, km-k0ww, km-cbks, km-a21w. All deliberately not fixed in the PR, each with its reasoning on the review thread and in the issue.

TRAPS worth knowing before touching this again are in [[feedback_fixes_spawn_regressions_stop_looping]] (what made the rounds recur), [[reference_check_gate_load_flakes]] (the diff-driver trap that breaks grep-based diff checks in this repo) and [[reference_gh_publish_bare_command]].

title: agent-dispatch: Retry clears a failure the daemon can no longer rediscover
description:
If the triggering backlink is removed after a task fails, its error chip still offers Retry. retryAgentTask clears agent:status, agent:watcher and the rest of the terminal state, but the daemon derives backlink work only from backlinkSources — so nothing ever claims the block again. The failure record is destroyed, the optimistic queued chip expires, and no retry happens. The bulk sweep does the same to every such stale task and reports them all as re-queued.

Root cause is the same one behind the Stop-on-a-deferred-task issue: the APP cannot know what the daemon can discover. Watcher targets live in daemon config, so the app has nothing to revalidate discoverability against.

Two directions, and the choice is a product call rather than a bug fix:

1. Do not clear the terminal state at the gesture. Retry writes only agent:asked-at; the DAEMON clears status/error when it actually claims. A block nothing can discover then keeps its failure visible, which is the honest outcome — but the chip no longer flips to 'queued' optimistically, so a normal retry looks unresponsive for up to one poll interval. That UX change is the whole cost.

2. Route the retry through the daemon (it owns watcher config and could answer 'nothing scans this block'). Larger, and needs a request path the app does not have today.

Option 1 is small and fixes the data loss; it trades the optimistic chip for correctness. Worth deciding rather than defaulting.

Surfaced by review on the retryable-failure PR; not fixed there because it is a deliberate UX trade, not a defect in that PR's own logic.

title: Assess the cells under the retired property names for data loss, and clear them
description:
The 2026-09-16 re-audit (#750) left 8 unregistered keys / 32 cells, none user content. Its correction comment established what happens to them at the flip: §9 orphan synthesis mints a VISIBLE, user-origin definition for every definition-less cell key before the flip (the retired-names list has no runtime consumer on that path), and the backfill then materializes those cells into field and value children like any other key.

For the two example-extension gating keys that is correct: they register with their owner when it is enabled. For the retired names it is not what anyone wants: focusedBlockId (16 cells) and focusedVisualTargetKey (3), superseded by render-scoped focus; backlinks:filter (4), whose values were deliberately discarded when the filter shape changed; video:playerView (4), superseded by the pane view mode; and system:disabled (2), superseded by the extension overrides map. Minting definitions for them puts five dead names into the property picker as user definitions and grows machinery rows under 29 blocks for values no code reads.

The same call was already made for the singular type key: PR #1009 (add it to the retired-names ledger) was closed unmerged in favour of deleting the one inert cell from the graph, because the right fix for a freed key is the data, not the list. This bead is that decision applied to the other five, before the flip: delete the dead cells, verify the audit reports only the two owner-gated keys, and only then run the migration gesture.

How, safely: the cells live in live blocks' properties_json, so the edit is a per-block property unset through the normal write path (setProperty / update through repo.tx, which uploads and is undoable), never a raw UPDATE; scope to the active workspace; re-check inside the writing transaction that the key is still one of the five. About 29 cells, so a one-off script or bridge eval is fine; no backfill machinery needed. Re-run the property audit afterwards with syncGap null.

Related: #1017 (replace the hand-maintained retired-names constant with a check against the data), #750.
close_reason: All 29 cells under the five retired names cleared; the workspace property audit is down to the 2 owner-gated example-extension keys, with syncGap null and the upload queue drained. The two comment corrections this produced are in an open PR and stand on their own.

title: A stale cell reorders a list that a peer reordered while the owner was deleted
description:
Sibling of #1021 (the scalar content overwrite), same root cause, different
dimension: ORDER rather than content.

Revival re-materializes every UNTOUCHED property name from the owner's cell.
For a multi-valued property, reconcileMemberValueChildren permutes the member
rows into the CELL's order — it matches members by value, collects the order
keys the kept rows occupy, sorts them, and moves each member onto the i-th
slot. On the additive (revival) path that cell can be stale, so a reorder a
peer made while the owner was deleted is reverted.

MEASURED (probe, not shipped), in src/data/propertyChildren.test.ts against
setupWithLists:
  1. flipped workspace, block p with tags = ['alpha', 'beta']
  2. delete p
  3. raw UPDATE swapping the two member rows' order_key — the shape a sync
     arrival has; children then read ['beta', 'alpha']
  4. restore p
  5. children read ['alpha', 'beta'] again — the cell's order

Narrower than #1021: no row is removed and no content is rewritten, so nothing
is destroyed, only reordered. #1021 deliberately did not widen into this.

THE QUESTION TO ANSWER FIRST, because it may be by design: is member ORDER
truth that crosses sync, or is it derived from the cell? The normal path treats
the cell's order as authoritative ('Members permute among the order-key SLOTS
the value children already occupy'), so 'the additive path should too' is a
defensible answer and this is then not a bug.

IF it is to be fixed: skipping the tx.move under `additive` is NOT sufficient
on its own. Created members draw their slots from `[...freed, ...fresh].sort()`,
and with the moves skipped every `freed` key is still held by its own row — so a
member created in the same pass can be handed a key another row already owns.
The additive shape has to allocate created members from `fresh` only (appended
after the last existing row) and leave every existing row's key alone.

`additive` is the option formerly named `mayNotRemove`; it now reads 'may only
ADD rows: never remove one, never rewrite one's content'. Extending it to order
would want that sentence extended too.

title: A definition edited while unpublished re-enters with consumers in a forgotten encoding
description:
A property definition stops being published by the registry two ways: it is
deleted (tombstoned), or it loses the metadata that made it a definition (the
property-schema type tag). Its consumers' field rows and value children survive
both. If the row's CODEC INPUTS (preset id / preset config) are then edited
while it is in that state, and it later re-enters — a restore, or the type tag
coming back — nothing anywhere remembers the encoding the consumers are
actually in, and the rebuilt registry immediately publishes the new codec over
them. Values then decode wrong or throw.

WHY THE SAME-TX FAN-OUT DOES NOT COVER IT. core.migratePropertyDefinition
decides what changed by diffing the definition row's before/after within one
transaction. Both edits above happen in a transaction where the row is NOT a
published definition on either side, so the processor correctly does nothing --
and the later re-entry transaction has no before-state to diff against. The
information is not on the row.

REPRODUCTION (tombstone arm):
1. A `status` definition with preset `string` has consumers holding text values.
2. Delete the definition block.
3. Edit the tombstone's preset id to `number` (a script, or the agent CLI --
   the properties UI does not list deleted definitions).
4. Restore the definition.
Consumers' value children still hold the string text; the registry publishes
`number`.

The metadata arm is the same with the type tag removed and re-added in place of
the delete/restore.

WHY IT IS NOT HANDLED SPECULATIVELY. Re-encoding every revival was tried and
reverted: re-parsing a value child under an UNCHANGED codec is not the identity
for editable representations. A ref value child written as a labelled block
reference decodes to a bare id and re-encodes without the label, and `1.50`
re-encodes as `1.5`. So a blanket re-encode on revival rewrites every plain
restore of an untouched definition, losing ref labels and emitting a
"could not convert to the new type" report when no type changed. That trade is
worse than the hole it closes.

THREE DIRECTIONS, none obviously right:
(a) REFUSE the codec-input edit at the point it is made -- while the row is
    unpublished and has consumers. Cheapest, puts the check where the divergence
    is created, and leaves restore lossless. Costs a refusal on a path that is
    already unusual, and cannot cover a bag that arrives by sync.
(b) RECONCILE at re-entry, content-driven: compare each consumer cell against
    its field rows rather than re-encoding blindly (#389 item 8). Correct for
    every arm including sync, and the same machinery several other stranding
    cases want.
(c) RETIRE the departing definition's cells when it stops publishing, so there
    is nothing stale to re-enter over.

The same three choices as the departing-definition question; picking one should
probably settle both.

Raised by review on the #1013 work.

title: A bare null in stored value text is ambiguous across a required-to-optional widening
description:
Value-child content is TEXT, and the re-encode converts by re-parsing that text under the new codec. One token is ambiguous between codecs: a bare `null`. To a codec that rejects null it is the literal three characters; to one that accepts null it is the UNSET sentinel. `needsEscape` already knows this — it escapes `null` when writing for a null-accepting codec, and does not otherwise.

So widening `string` to `optional-string` silently turns a user's literal "null" into absence. The value was stored unescaped, because the required codec had no sentinel to disambiguate it from; the optional codec reads the same bytes as unset. AGENTS.md classifies that widening as SAFE, which makes this the documented-good path rather than an exotic one.

NOT A REGRESSION. The pre-#1013 deferred batch converted the same way — `propertyChildContentToEncodedValue(schema, value.content)` with the NEW schema — so it lost the same value.

FIX DIRECTION, narrow. The ambiguity is exactly one predicate wide: the before-codec rejects null AND the after-codec accepts it AND the content is a bare `null`. In that case the old bytes were a literal, so disambiguate before re-parsing — escape the content the way the writer would have, which `escapeContent` / `isEscapedEnvelope` already implement for the write side. `codecAcceptsNull` is private to `propertyChildren.ts` today and would need exporting.

WHAT NOT TO DO. Converting semantically instead — decode with the old codec, encode with the new — is the tempting general answer and it breaks the main case: ` 42 ` under `string` decodes to the string, which the number codec then refuses, so every cross-type conversion stops working. Text re-parsing is what makes those work; only this one token needs a before-schema hint.

Raised by review on the #1013 work.

title: Decide whether a contested definition rename should refuse the transaction instead of skipping its fan-out
description:
`withoutContestedRenames` DROPS a rename whose destination or vacated name belongs to another definition, and the definition row's rename commits anyway. The consumers of that definition keep cells keyed under the old name — which is the "mass silent unset" the fan-out exists to prevent, arriving by a different door.

CONCRETE. B renames `beta -> gamma`, refused because another definition holds `gamma`. B's row commits as `gamma`; every B consumer still reads `beta`. If anything else takes `beta` in the same transaction, those blocks now expose B's stored values through the new owner's schema.

THE CHOICE. Two coherent positions, and the current one is neither stated nor chosen:

(a) SKIP, as today. A contested rename is a shadowing situation, and shadowing is a modelled state — the registry permits two definitions under one name. The repair belongs to the content-driven reconcile that compares a cell against its field rows (#389 item 8). Cost: the window between the rename and that reconcile is silent.

(b) REFUSE the whole transaction, the way an unbuildable rename with consumers and an unjudgeable workspace already do in the same processor. A rename whose consumers cannot be re-keyed is exactly what this pass exists to prevent, so committing it is committing half a change. Cost: renaming onto a name another definition holds becomes a hard error, which the data layer currently permits, and shadowing mostly arrives by SYNC rather than by local rename — so the refusal would fire on a state the user did not create.

(b) is more consistent with the rest of the processor and gives a much better message than silence. It is also a product decision about what the schema editor allows, not a data-layer detail, which is why it is filed rather than picked.

NOT A REGRESSION, and measured rather than assumed: the pre-#1013 refusal dropped MORE. Replaying its exact algorithm over the scenario above (A renames `alpha -> beta` while B renames `beta -> gamma` into a contested `gamma`) keeps NOTHING — its vacating set was derived from the surviving batch, so refusing B un-vacated `beta` and cascaded into A. Both consumer sets were left stale. The current code keeps A, so only B's is. Whichever way this is decided, it is a decision about a long-standing behaviour.

Raised by review on the #1013 work.
close_reason: Closed on GitHub (issue #1028); reconciled by bd-github-sync.

title: A plugin same-tx processor can undo a kernel one's content rewrite, reading a tx-start registry
description:
Same-tx processors run kernel-first, then plugins. Every one of them resolves property schemas against `ctx.propertySchemas`, which is frozen at TX START. So a KERNEL processor that rewrites content to match a definition change made in the same transaction can be overwritten by a PLUGIN processor that runs afterwards and still believes the old schema.

CONCRETE PATH. One transaction re-types a ref property and merges a block that property references. `core.migratePropertyDefinition` runs last among kernel processors and canonicalizes the consumer's value children under the new codec. `references.retargetMergedBlockReferences` then runs, resolves the OLD ref codec from the tx-start snapshot, and rewrites the consumer bag with an id-encoded reference under a definition that is no longer a ref. The bounded MATERIALIZE/PROJECT rerun resolves the same stale snapshot, and the definition-change processor declares `settledWrites` and never reruns, so nothing corrects it before commit.

WHY THIS IS NOT JUST THAT PROCESSOR'S PROBLEM. The same shape applies to any kernel processor whose writes depend on a definition edited in the same transaction. The ordering contract says plugins run last so they can see settled kernel output; the schema snapshot contract says everyone reads tx-start. Those two are fine apart and contradict each other exactly when a transaction edits a definition AND touches its consumers through a plugin path.

OPTIONS, none obviously right:
- Give the definition-change processor a facet PRECEDENCE so it runs after plugin same-tx processors, the way `references.renameProcessor` already does for its own ordering reasons. Smallest change; moves one processor without addressing the contract.
- Let a same-tx processor opt into a re-resolved schema snapshot mid-pass, for the processors that actually need post-change identity.
- Declare the combination out of contract and refuse it.

REACHABILITY. Needs ONE transaction that both re-types a definition and drives a plugin path over its consumers. No UI produces that — the schema editor and the merge gesture are separate flows — so it is a scripted or agent-bridge shape today.

Raised by review on the #1013 work, where the definition-change processor is the first kernel processor to rewrite consumer content on behalf of a same-transaction definition edit.

title: A tx queued behind a definition change can still write through the old codec
description:
`repo.tx` captures the property-definition registry BEFORE it waits for the SQLite write lock. So a transaction that starts while a definition-change transaction holds the lock carries the pre-change registry, and when it acquires the lock after that commit it can create or update a consumer encoded under the OLD codec. The definition-change pass re-encoded the consumers visible during its own transaction; this row was not one of them.

WINDOW. Between the queued transaction capturing its registry and the definition change committing. Narrow, and it takes a concurrent writer touching the same property, but SQLite serializes writers so the queue is real whenever anything else is writing.

WHAT IT COSTS. The value child's text is written under the old codec. Readers afterwards parse it under the new one, so the value either fails to decode or is silently reinterpreted. One block per racing write.

WHY IT SURFACED NOW. The deferred per-device re-encode used to cover this incidentally: it ran ten to thirty seconds later and scanned every consumer, so a row written milliseconds after the definition change was inside its sweep. #1013 made the re-encode synchronous and initiator-only, which is the right shape for everything else and removes that incidental cover.

FIX DIRECTION. The general problem is that a property write validates its schema against a registry snapshot taken before the write lock. `PropertySchemaScopeMismatchError` already re-resolves the change SCOPE inside the writing transaction for the same class of reason — a definition edited after the caller captured its schema — so the seam exists; the codec is simply not part of what it re-checks. Extending that to refuse (or re-encode) a write whose resolved codec moved since capture would close this for every writer, not just this pass. That is a data-layer change on the hot path for every `setProperty`, which is why it is filed rather than folded in.

Raised by review on the #1013 work.

title: Give repo.tx a pre-commit validation seam, so an eligibility check can be last
description:
A precondition checked inside a repo.tx callback is never the last point before the commit: runTx still awaits the same-tx processors, the command_events insert and the tx_context clear after the callback returns. A workspace switch or a role revocation landing in any of those passes every check the caller can write.

Three review rounds on one PR each found a check one step too early, and each fix moved it a few awaits closer. Patching cannot terminate, because there is always another await between the caller's last statement and SQLite's commit.

SHAPE: a synchronous validator on RepoTxOptions, invoked by runTx after its final statement and before the writeTransaction callback returns. There is no await between that point and the commit, so it is the last point that exists. Throwing there rolls the transaction back.

CONSUMERS, both of which currently hand-roll an end-of-callback check that is a few awaits short:
- the workspace-backfill runner's per-batch session check (generation, active workspace, role)
- the undo replay's clear-epoch re-check

A related second seam: the tx engine pins its workspace on the first write, and a caller that needs to sample per-workspace state at that moment has no hook, so it samples after the callback instead. A pin callback would close it.

Residuals are accepted and labelled in the code today; this is the shape that would let those labels be deleted rather than maintained.

title: Reproject a restored block's properties against the current definition registry
description:
A block soft-deleted BEFORE a property definition is renamed or re-typed is revived under the old key. Its property bag still reads `status`, the registry now answers `state`, and materialization skips a key it cannot resolve — so the restored block looks like it lost the property, while the value sits in the cell under a name nothing reads.

WHY THE FAN-OUT DOES NOT COVER IT. `core.migratePropertyDefinition` finds consumers through their LIVE field rows (`deleted = 0`), and skips a tombstoned parent even when its field rows are live. Both predicates are deliberate. `tx.update` would accept a tombstone — it refuses only on create — so this is a choice, not a limitation: a deleted block's bag is history, and the live consumer set is bounded by current usage while the tombstoned set is bounded by ALL-TIME usage. Re-keying it would put an unbounded write inside the user's own editing transaction, which is the one thing that pass must not do.

NOT A REGRESSION. The same `deleted = 0` filter is on the pre-existing same-tx rename path and on the deferred batch that preceded it, so this predates the work that removed the deferred pass.

FIX DIRECTION — do it at RESTORE, not at definition-edit time. Reproject the restored block's property bag against the current registry as part of the restore: O(1) per restore, paid exactly when the block comes back, and it covers every definition change that happened while the block was deleted rather than only the ones some pass happened to witness. A pending-repair record would need durable per-device state for a case the restore path can answer from the registry it already has.

Worth checking while there: whether a subtree delete tombstones a consumer's field rows, since that changes which of the two predicates above is doing the excluding, and the restore path has to revive them either way.

Raised by review on the #1013 work.

title: Detect a value preset whose codec type changes under the same preset id, at install time
description:
A value preset's id and the codec type its `build` returns are keys user data is STORED under. `seedIdentityLedger.ts` freezes both for in-repo seeds and its test fails on any change with the remedy on the line. A preset core registered by a DYNAMIC extension gets no such check: the extension is stored in the database, the ledger never sees it, and installing a new version whose `build` returns a different codec type under the same preset id silently re-types every definition using it.

WHAT THEN HAPPENS. No definition ROW changed, so `core.migratePropertyDefinition` never fires — it watches definition-block writes, which is the whole point of #1013. The projector publishes the new codec immediately. Existing cells stay in the old encoding, so a read either throws or returns the default, and the cell and its value children disagree. Before #1013 a registry diff noticed the codec type change and scheduled a deferred re-encode; that pass is gone, and re-adding one for a case the repo's own doctrine says must not happen is the wrong trade.

WHY INSTALL TIME IS THE RIGHT PLACE. The change is deliberate and has an author standing at it. `install-extension --verify` already lints extension source for data-grain mistakes at declaration level and names the catalog pattern that fixes each one. Comparing a preset core's codec type against the one currently registered under that id is the same kind of check, made where someone can act on it, instead of a background sweep that has to guess what the old encoding was.

SHAPE. At install, for each preset core the extension registers: if a core with that id is already registered and `build(config).type` differs, refuse or warn loudly, naming the definitions that use the preset and how many cells are affected. `pnpm agent audit-properties` is the closest existing reporting surface for the second half.

RESIDUAL UNTIL THEN: the divergence is the same cell-versus-children one the content-driven reconcile (#389 item 8) is meant to detect, and it is recorded in the accepted-residual section of `propertyDefinitionChangeProcessor.ts`.

Raised by review on the #1013 work.
close_reason: Closed on GitHub (issue #1022); reconciled by bd-github-sync.

title: Restoring a deleted owner overwrites a scalar property value that arrived while it was deleted
description:
Restoring a deleted owner re-materializes every UNTOUCHED property name from
its cell (`materializePropertiesForChangedRow`'s revival branch: a restore
usually leaves the bag identical, so a diff-only rule would schedule nothing).
That cell can be STALE against the children, because sync-apply skips the
parent-liveness trigger and is free to land a peer's edit under a tombstoned
field row while the owner is deleted.

For a SCALAR, the revival then overwrites the primary value row's content back
to the cell's, destroying the arrived text.

This is the same hazard `reviveTombstonedFieldRow` already refuses to step into
("Restoring the field row hands that value to the caller's cell->child
convergence, which overwrites its content with the local cell's: measured, the
arrived text is destroyed"). That guard covers the TOMBSTONED-FIELD-ROW revive
path only. The owner-subtree restore reaches the same convergence by a
different route, where the field row comes back with its owner's subtree and no
guard applies.

REPRODUCTION SHAPE (the list twin of this was measured and fixed in PR #1019;
this scalar twin was seen but not fixed there, being pre-existing and out of
that issue's scope):
  1. flipped workspace, block P with a scalar property, one value row V
  2. delete P (P, its field row and V are tombstoned)
  3. raw UPDATE of V's content — the shape a sync arrival has
  4. restore P
  5. the revival's untouched-name materialize rewrites V back to the cell

FIX DIRECTION, and the seam already exists: the revival path splits its names
by WHO WROTE THEM, and the untouched half already carries
`MaterializeOptions.mayNotRemove` (added in #1019) saying "this call did not
observe user intent". The scalar branch wants the same statement one step
stronger: it may not OVERWRITE a value row whose content differs from the cell
either. Both are the cell->children twin of the projection's `additive` mode.

Worth checking while in there: whether the same staleness reaches the field
row's own content rewrite, and whether the write half should simply be skipped
for untouched names rather than made conditional per branch.
close_reason: Closed on GitHub (issue #1021); reconciled by bd-github-sync.

title: awaitSeedMaterialization() does not resolve while the test's workspace is pinned
description:
Calling `repo.awaitSeedMaterialization()` inside a test hangs until the test times out. The failure points at the test body with a bare "Test timed out", which reads as a slow assertion rather than as a drain that never settled.

REPRO (12 lines, fails at any timeout, flipped or un-flipped workspace):

  const {repo} = createTestRepo({db: sharedDb.db, user: {id: 'user-1'}})
  repo.setActiveWorkspaceId(WS)
  await repo.tx(async tx => { await tx.create({id: 'b1', workspaceId: WS, parentId: null, orderKey: 'k', content: 'x'}) },
                {scope: ChangeScope.BlockDefault})
  await repo.awaitSeedMaterialization()   // never resolves

MEASURED, instrumenting both ends:

- `PendingIdleJobs.drain()` is NOT spinning — a counter in its `while` loop never fires. One pending job's promise simply never settles.
- The await resolves only AFTER the global scope teardown runs. Logging `endTestRepoScope` shows the order: scope end -> flush -> stopSyncObserver + setActiveWorkspaceId(null) -> and only THEN does the test's own `await` return. So the pending job settles on unpin (or on the observer stopping), not on its own.
- `awaitDeferredWork()` inherits it, since seed materialization is one of the families it drains. Every other family drains clean in the same fixture.

WHY IT IS NOT CAUGHT TODAY: `definitionSeeds.test.ts` calls the same method and passes, so something about its setup lets the pass complete. The difference has not been isolated.

IMPACT: a test that wants to wait for deferred work cannot use either method and gets no clue why. Worth either making the pass settle under a pinned workspace with no observer, or making the drain fail loudly with what it is still waiting on.

Found while rewriting the property-definition change fan-out (#1013) — a test there tried to drain deferred work and hit this.
close_reason: Closed on GitHub (issue #1015); reconciled by bd-github-sync.

title: A poll-driven writer that holds its cursor on a failed write stalls forever on any non-retryable failure
description:
Split out of the promoted-value stall: that bead fixed the one KNOWN cause, this is the shape underneath it.

A poller that must not lose an event holds its sync cursor when a write fails, so the event is retried rather than dropped. That is right for a transient failure and wrong for a permanent one: if the write can never succeed, the same event is re-delivered forever and ingest stops for good. Nothing distinguishes the two today — the retryable/non-retryable split is applied to the FETCH error, not to the write.

The promoted-value case is now refused before the write, so the known trigger is gone. Anything else that makes one event permanently unwritable brings the stall back: a definition edited into a narrower preset between promotion and the write, a workspace invariant the row violates, a processor rejection from any other guard.

Symptom is the bad kind: silent. The cursor simply stops advancing. There is a diagnostic and a one-per-streak toast on the fetch path, but a write that keeps failing looks like a quiet room.

Directions, roughly in order of appetite:
- count consecutive failures for one event id and, past a threshold, quarantine it: skip it, advance the cursor, and record the event somewhere recoverable (a block under the day's container) so nothing is lost silently. The 'somewhere recoverable' part is the whole design.
- surface a loud, persistent diagnostic naming the stuck event as soon as the same event fails twice, and leave the policy alone. Cheaper, keeps the no-loss guarantee, still needs a human.
- do nothing and accept it, now that the known cause is refused upstream.

Not blocking the properties flip: with the promotion guard in, no known input reaches it.

title: Post-flip consistency sweep: recompute child-backed cell keys from children and report or repair divergence
description:
The design doc (§5, §11 slice C) specifies a background CONSISTENCY SWEEP, "fsck for the projection": for each block with child-backed keys, recompute the cell keys from the field/value children, byte-compare against the stored cell, repair divergence with children winning, and report a nonzero divergence counter as the correctness alarm. It is also named as the backfill-verify harness and the "free backfill retry" for stragglers, and as the third maintainer of the "every cell key resolves a definition" invariant (sweep-side synthesis, tracked separately as #689). Verified 2026-09-16: nothing of it exists in the code; grep for a sweep / consistency / divergence pass under the data layer finds nothing. The only cell-vs-children reconciliation today is per-write (the same-tx PROJECT processor) and on sync arrival.

WHAT IT IS FOR, post-flip: any path that writes a cell without the same-tx processors (a sync-applied row from a device whose children have not arrived yet, an undo replay on a peer that kept pre-flip entries, a raw write in a script, a partial pass) leaves a cell that disagrees with the children. Each of those is individually argued away today; the sweep is the one mechanism that catches the class and says how big it is.

SHAPE TO DECIDE FIRST: this is a per-device DERIVATION pass while it only re-projects the local cell (the cell is a derived projection past the flip, so a local rewrite is not a source-of-truth edit), and becomes a DATA MIGRATION the moment it uploads or synthesizes a definition. Keep the two apart per the one-shot-passes doctrine: a read-only divergence report first, then the repair as a separate, deliberately gated step. Build it flip-agnostic and test it on a flipped test row; it is reachable in production only past the flip, which is not a reason to wait.

Reusable pieces: the projection helper the PROJECT processor already uses, `scanPropertyKeys` for enumeration, the partial index the backfill's candidate query uses, and the backfill's progress and operator reporting.

Not a blocker of the first flip. #689 (sweep-side orphan synthesis) depends on it. The cell end-state work depends on it, since "sweep divergence reads zero" is the gate for stopping cell uploads.

title: bd-codex-session-end test fails locally: detached sync output never reaches the shared log
description:
scripts/bd-codex-session-end.test.ts > launchSessionEndSync > "returns before the detached sync finishes and writes its stdout/stderr to the shared log" fails deterministically on a macOS dev machine — on a clean master checkout and in a fresh worktree alike (5 runs, 5 failures) — while CI is green on the same test.

What the log shows: the launcher starts and writes `starting bd-github-sync --quiet`; the fixture writes `fake sync ready`; `fake sync success` never appears within the 5 s `vi.waitFor` budget.

Repro: `pnpm vitest run scripts/bd-codex-session-end.test.ts`

Fix direction: compare what the detached child inherits on macOS vs CI (cwd, stdio handles, env), and whether the fixture sync is being killed with the parent before it writes its second line. Filed directly on GitHub because the beads database was unavailable on the reporting machine; a sync from a machine that has it should adopt this into beads.
close_reason: Closed on GitHub (issue #1004); reconciled by bd-github-sync.

title: Type label: readLabel trims but parseTypeDefinitionMetadata does not, so stored padding diverges
description:
Two separate defects in one review came from the same split, and a third is latent.

The type-name reader used by the typeify processor trims the stored block-type label; the registry builder that publishes the type reads it raw. So a stored label of ' Book ' is treated as the name 'Book' by the processor while the registry publishes ' Book ' — and only the trimmed spelling resolves as an alias.

Two instances hit so far, both fixed locally at the processor:
- a rename that normalized padded content skipped the label write, because the trimmed read already equalled the new name, leaving the padded spelling stored and published.
- un-naming a type with a whitespace-only label released the alias and returned, leaving the row published as a type named whitespace with nothing resolving to it.

Both were fixed by making that one processor compare and write the stored spelling. That does not close the class: any other writer of the label, and any legacy or sync-applied row, can still store a padded value that the registry then publishes under a name nothing resolves to.

Candidate shapes, in rough order of preference:
1. normalize on write — trim in the label property's codec, so no writer can store padding. Does not repair existing rows.
2. normalize on read — trim in the registry builder, matching how the color field beside it is already read. Repairs published output for every existing row, but stored data stays divergent.
3. both, plus a one-shot derivation pass over existing rows.

Worth deciding deliberately rather than continuing to patch each site: the processor now compares the stored spelling in two places specifically because of this, which is a duplicated decision that will drift.

title: Alias plugin claims a derived name when an unrelated gesture rewrites an aliased block's content
description:
Observed while verifying the type-rename work, both in tests and in a live browser.

Setup: a block-type block whose label and alias are 'Tome', with a legacy body that embeds a block reference ('Prefix ((uuid))'). Deleting the referenced block makes the references plugin inline the target's text into that body, inside the DELETE's own transaction, rewriting the content to 'Prefix Foo'.

The kernel typeify processor now correctly leaves the type alone — the label never matched that body, so the rewrite is not a rename. But the alias plugin's additive heal then appends the NEW content to the alias bag, leaving ['Tome', 'Prefix Foo']. So '[[Prefix Foo]]' now resolves to that block, under a name no user ever chose for it, produced by deleting a different block entirely.

This is not type-specific: it is the plugin's general content-to-alias parity for any block that already claims an alias. Any gesture that rewrites content on an aliased block mints a new claim for whatever the content became.

Worth deciding: should the additive heal fire for a content rewrite the user did not author? The kernel side now distinguishes 'this content was the name' from 'something rewrote this text'; the plugin has no such distinction.

Reproduce: plant the row with a raw write (trigger-backed indexes maintained, no post-commit processor — the sync-applied shape), then update content through a normal transaction and read the alias bag.

title: DEV console.error: page and block-type layouts mount Shell without spreading shellProps
description:
Running the app against a local dev server (`pnpm dev`, local-only login), the DefaultBlockRenderer DEV diagnostic in src/components/renderer/DefaultBlockRenderer.tsx fires repeatedly for two core layouts:

- the daily-note page block
- a block-type block (the type editor view)

Message: `Block <id>: its layout mounted Shell without spreading shellProps. Pass shortcutsOnly if that is deliberate.`

The diagnostic's own comment says dropping shellProps costs the block its identity in the DOM — its boundary, focus and edit tagging, the shell click, and (through ref) the spatial-nav row — and that consumers then silently resolve to an ancestor instead.

So one of two things is true and neither has been decided:
1. those layouts genuinely lose shell identity, and focus/edit tagging plus spatial-nav on a page header and the type editor are degraded; or
2. the omission is deliberate and the layouts should pass `shortcutsOnly`, which is exactly what the message asks for.

Either way the console is noisy in dev for every page view, which trains readers to ignore a diagnostic that was added to be noticed.

Found incidentally while doing browser verification of an unrelated data-layer change; the renderer files are untouched by that branch, so this is pre-existing. Not yet checked whether it reproduces in a production build (the diagnostic is `import.meta.env.DEV`-gated, so the WARNING is dev-only, but the underlying missing props would not be).

title: The property-definition codec migration is a data migration driven off per-device local state
description:
The deferred property-definition migration writes and uploads source-of-truth block rows, so by the one-shot-passes doctrine it is a DATA MIGRATION. It is driven per-device off a local unsynced baseline, and does not follow the doctrine's rules for one. Three gaps, in rough severity order.

1. NO GRAPH-SCOPED CLAIM, and it can run from a stale device. Before the durable baseline landed, only the device that made a codec change ran the pass. The baseline's whole purpose is to let a device that did NOT make the change run it too, which is the 'never from a stale device' case the doctrine warns about. The per-row work is idempotent and convergent (already-canonical content compares equal and writes nothing), so the residual is narrower than a general migration: a stale device re-encodes its own older copy of a row and uploads it with a fresh timestamp, clobbering a newer edit it has not yet received. Each device also marks its own baseline complete independently.

2. THE WORKSPACE UNDO STACK IS NOT CLEARED, and the user is not told. The pass writes at References scope, so its own writes are off cmd-Z — but an undo entry recorded BEFORE the migration replays whole pre-migration rows over the re-encoded ones, and the baseline then records the migration as applied, so no later prime repairs it. The doctrine's rule is to clear the stack and surface that.

3. THE 'AM I SAFE TO WRITE' CHECK IS AT SCHEDULING TIME ONLY. The read-only check happens when the migration is scheduled and reads a mutable flag; the batch chunks over parents and runs minutes later. It re-checks the flip gate at run time but nothing about access, so a workspace that became read-only in between is still written. The doctrine asks for that check inside each writing transaction.

A smaller related symptom, already self-healing: the app pins a workspace before resolving its role, and the read-only setter is a bare flag assignment with no re-prime, so switching in from a viewer workspace can race and drop the migration. Because un-applied drift is deliberately not recorded, the next prime re-detects it — so values read unset until then rather than staying stale.

Raised on the PR that added the baseline (#788) and declined there as a decision rather than patched, on the grounds that three guards for a narrow case argued for dropping the feature instead. It merged, so the gaps are live and this records them.

Related: km-81z9 is a different gap in the same pass (its re-key is an unsettled write, so the materializer re-derives from it).
close_reason: Closed on GitHub (issue #995); reconciled by bd-github-sync.

title: A block whose alias is co-claimed cannot be edited at all
description:
Measured on a PLAIN page, no types involved: give a block the alias 'Book' through a normal tx, then land a second block claiming 'Book' with a raw write (the shape sync-apply has — the uniqueness trigger only fires when tx_context.source is set). Now ANY local write to the first block aborts with alias.collision, including the rename that would resolve the duplicate.

Mechanism: a tx.update writes properties_json, the blocks_alias_update trigger deletes and re-inserts that row's whole alias bag, and the uniqueness trigger fires on the re-insert of a name the other block also holds. The row is not claiming anything new — it is re-stating a claim it already had — but the trigger cannot tell the difference.

Consequence: a cross-client duplicate makes both blocks effectively read-only, and the user-facing way out (rename one of them, or merge) is refused by the same rule. Today this is latent because cross-client alias merges were deferred to V2.

Directions, not yet weighed: have the uniqueness trigger ignore a re-insert that does not increase the claimant count for that alias (this row already held it); or route the collision into the existing merge flow on the write rather than aborting.

Found while measuring a review finding on PR 985 that assumed the abort came from an intermediate alias write in the kernel type-rename path — it does not, it comes from the user's own write, and it predates that work.

title: An Automation-scope tx cannot rename anything that carries a name
description:
Measured, on an ordinary ALIASED page with no type involved: a repo.tx with scope ChangeScope.Automation that changes the block's content throws PropertySchemaScopeMismatchError and rolls the whole tx back. The throw comes from alias.sync reconciling content into the alias bag with setProperty — ChangeScope.Automation is {undoable: false, readOnly: 'allow'} while the alias property is BlockDefault {undoable: true, readOnly: 'reject'}, and scopePoliciesEquivalent refuses the pair. The kernel's type naming (block-type:label, also BlockDefault) hits the same wall, which is why the typeify processor already exempts seed-owned definitions with a comment about exactly this clash.

Consequence: automation and import code cannot rename a page or a user-defined type through repo.tx at all. Not specific to types, and not new — reproduced with the type path out of the picture.

The tension to resolve: these are DERIVED writes reconciling a change the tx itself just made, not independent user edits, so the policy axes (undoability, read-only behaviour) arguably should be inherited from the triggering write rather than compared against it. Options, roughly in order of scope: give same-tx processors a derived-write seam that carries the tx's own policy; make Automation policy-equivalent to BlockDefault (changes undo bucketing — needs a decision); or have each processor skip when the scopes are incompatible, which trades the throw for silent drift and is the worst of the three.

Found while reviewing the type-rename work in PR 985; declined there because the fix spans alias.sync, the references processors and the kernel naming path, and because it is a pre-existing constraint rather than a regression from that change.

title: A type block's label goes stale when its content is edited directly
description:
A type block's `content` and `block-type:label` are two spellings of ONE name —
the page title `[[name]]` resolves to. Three writers maintain that: the typeify
processor (on the transition INTO `block-type`), the label editor in
`BlockTypeBlockRenderer` (writes both to the new value), and `typeExtraction`.

Nothing maintains it when `content` alone changes on a block that is ALREADY a
type. `BLOCK_TYPE_TYPEIFY_PROCESSOR` fires only on the transition into
`block-type` (`if (!addedTypes(row).includes(BLOCK_TYPE_TYPE)) continue`), so a
later content edit leaves the label behind.

Measured (kernel-only harness, `createTestRepo`): create a `block-type` block
with content "Dancer", let processors settle (label and alias both become
"Dancer"), then `tx.update(id, {content: 'Ballerina'})`. Result:

    content:          "Ballerina"
    block-type:label: "Dancer"      <- stale

Consequence: the type shows under its old name in the picker and the property
panel header while its page title reads the new one.

The alias in that probe also stayed "Dancer", but that half is NOT confirmed —
`createTestRepo` wires only `kernelDataExtension`, and `aliasSyncProcessor` is a
plugin, so it was never loaded. Re-probe with the alias plugin wired before
concluding anything about the alias.

Direction, not yet decided: either push content -> label (drop the
`addedTypes` early-return for the label step, or a small dedicated processor
watching content on type blocks), or decide content is not an editable surface
for a type block and route every rename through the label editor. The first
looks right — content is the page title, so it is the name the user edited.

Found while fixing the master CI failure that PR #983 addresses: the same
one-name invariant, broken on the merge path instead.
close_reason: Duplicate of km-8hav (GitHub #926), filed 2026-09-10 and in progress — PR #985 implements it. My measurement was correct (the label is stale on master today) but the finding was already tracked; I failed to search before filing. The mirror half is km-44td (#980).

title: A label-only write on a block-type block leaves the type unlinkable by its new name
description:
core.blockTypeTypeify now follows a CONTENT rewrite on a block that is already a type — the label and the claimed alias move with it (#926). The MIRROR write is still unreconciled: a write that changes only block-type:label leaves content and the alias on the OLD name while the type registry publishes the NEW one. [[NewName]] then resolves to nothing (or mints a duplicate seat page), and [[OldName]] still resolves to the type.

Reachable from the property panel, which offers block-type:label as an editable field on any block (#927), and from the agent bridge or an import writing the property directly. The type editor's own writer (writeBlockTypeLabel) is unaffected: it writes label and content together, so the content leg reconciles the alias.

Fix direction: same processor, same one-name invariant — when only the label changed, content follows it, and aliasSync then moves the alias by matching the old content exactly as it does for the content direction. Left out of the #926 change to keep that scope as asked.

Trap: src/components/renderer/nameFieldBlur.test.tsx builds its divergent-type fixture with a label-only write precisely because this hole exists. Fixing this breaks that fixture — rework it to a raw db.writeTransaction (fires no processor, and is the sync-applied shape) rather than weakening the test.

title: Recents query still scans the whole workspace per open
description:
`core.recentUserBlocks` / `core.recentActivity` resolve in ~2s on a ~350k-block workspace even after the descent-index fix (commit "index the user-state descent", PR #977).

The recursive user-state CTE is now cheap (~1900 rows, index-served). What is left is the outer statement: a full scan of every live row in the workspace with a per-row `json_extract(properties_json, '$."seed:key"')` and a correlated `block_types` NOT EXISTS, then `USE TEMP B-TREE FOR ORDER BY` over the whole result before `LIMIT`. The plain `core.recentBlocks` does the same scan+sort without the two per-row tests and costs ~425ms, so the extra ~1.5s is those.

Why it cannot use an index today: the sort key is `coalesce(user_updated_at, updated_at)`, which no index expresses, so SQLite cannot stop early at `LIMIT`.

Directions worth measuring: an index on the coalesce expression (or on `user_updated_at` with the fallback handled in a UNION), and hoisting the seed-key test onto a derived column or a partial index instead of a per-row `json_extract`.

Matters because both queries are on interactive paths — the ref/refList property picker and the `((` picker both await one on focus.

## How to measure it (against a real graph, not a test DB)

A seeded test DB shows none of this; the costs only appear at real row counts. Drive the live client through the agent bridge:

1. `pnpm agent sql all "select count(*) from blocks"` to confirm you are on the large graph.
2. Get the two user-state roots the CTE starts from — they are derived, not stored:
   - `pnpm agent sql all "select block_id as id from block_types where workspace_id=? and type='user'" '["<active ws>"]'`
   - `pnpm agent eval "const {userStateRootBlockIds} = await import('@/data/derivedIds.js'); return userStateRootBlockIds('<user page id>')"`
3. Paste `SELECT_RECENT_USER_BLOCKS_SQL` into `pnpm agent sql all <sql> <paramsJson>` with `recentUserBlocksParams`' bind order (state-root JSON array, workspaceId, …SYSTEM_BLOCK_TYPES, limit) and time the CLI call.

Subtract a baseline: a trivial `select 1` through the same bridge costs ~1.2-1.5s of round-trip, so read the delta, not the wall clock. Time these separately to attribute the cost — the CTE alone (`SELECT count(*) FROM user_state`), the outer statement with the CTE replaced by an empty `json_each('[]')`, and the whole thing.

`EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN` is answerable on a test DB and is the right pin for any fix (see `recentUserBlocksPlan.test.ts`), because the query's own results cannot tell a fast plan from a scan.

**Caution:** a slow variant of this query holds the client's DB connection for as long as it runs, so every later probe times out too and the user's tab is unusable meanwhile — that is the failure PR #977 fixed, and it is easy to re-inflict while benchmarking. Do not run a suspected-bad variant against a live client someone is using.
close_reason: Closed on GitHub (issue #978); reconciled by bd-github-sync.

title: Verify the db-mirror plugin against the real File System Access API
description:
## Why

The db-mirror plugin shipped with every code path tested against a fake File
System Access API (`test/fakeFileSystem.ts`). Nothing has ever exercised the
real one: `showDirectoryPicker` needs a genuine user gesture and opens a native
dialog, so no automated check — unit, integration or browser-driven — can reach
the write, prune or restore paths.

That leaves the seam between the plugin and the browser unverified, in a
feature whose entire value is that the file it writes is usable. If the fake is
wrong about the API anywhere, every test still passes.

## What to check

On desktop Chrome, with mirroring enabled against a scratch folder:

1. A copy actually appears, and its size matches the database.
2. The folder handle survives a reload — the app still mirrors without
   re-prompting, and the settings dialog still names the folder.
3. Lowering the keep count prunes older copies, and only ones this device
   wrote for the database it holds now.
4. A copy imports back through "Replace database with an uploaded SQLite file
   or recovery archive" and the restored database opens.
5. Revoking the folder permission in site settings produces the paused state
   and the "Grant access again" button recovers it.

## Notes

Worth doing on a cloud-synced folder too (OneDrive/Dropbox), since several
guards exist specifically for entries such a client leaves unreadable or
evicts, and that behaviour has only ever been simulated.

title: Pool occupancy is unobservable from inside one tab
description:
Found while instrumenting the DB adapter (km-buse). Corrects a premise that
bead carried, and names a ceiling on what the contention metric from km-8pik
can ever claim.

THE PREMISE THAT WAS WRONG: km-buse said wrapping the DBAdapter would put every
user of the connection pool through one counter, letting the sync-status bracket
and its syncObserved caveat be deleted. It does not, and cannot.

WHY, verified in @powersync/web 1.38.4: with enableMultiTabs set - which this
app sets unconditionally - PowerSync selects SharedWebStreamingSyncImplementation.
That calls the adapter's shareConnection() to obtain a MessagePort and hands it
to a SharedWorker, which builds its OWN client against the database worker. The
sync engine's reads and writes reach the same SQLite connections without passing
through this tab's adapter at all. Instrumenting the adapter covers everything
running IN the tab and none of that.

THE SAME SHAPE, MORE GENERALLY: the connections belong to the database, not to
the tab. A second tab of the same workspace opens its own adapter and its own
counters while using the same pool. So "did this query have the connections to
itself?" is structurally unanswerable from inside one tab whenever another tab
is open, independent of sync.

WHAT THAT MEANS FOR THE FIGURE: the uncontended subset is filtered by observable
occupancy, and unobserved occupancy fails in the direction that INFLATES it - a
read queued behind another context is admitted as a clean sample. So this is not
merely a coverage limit, it is the reason the metric is not simply conservative.

DIRECTIONS, none cheap, in rough order of reach:
  - measure at the database worker, which both sides already talk to. It is the
    only place that sees the whole pool. Needs a channel back to the tab.
  - measure inside the shared sync worker and report its intervals over the
    existing status channel, replacing the flag-derived bracket with real
    occupancy. Fixes sync, leaves other tabs.
  - detect the multi-tab case and say so beside the numbers, rather than fixing
    it. Cheapest, and turns a silent inflation into a stated caveat.

WORTH DOING WHEN: km-kfu9 says the uncontended subset is large enough to matter,
or a session's numbers look implausibly clean. Until then the caveat is recorded
at the declaration in timingMetrics.ts and in watchSyncOccupancy.

title: Coalesced-read sharing is attributed by window count, not participation
description:
Follow-up to km-8pik, and a deliberate approximation rather than an oversight.

A coalesced read that answers several observation windows must not let any of
them record its wall-clock as a clean measurement - N callers awaiting one
statement is one observation reported N times. The batcher is the only place
that fact is known, and it reports it while more than one observation window is
open.

THE APPROXIMATION: window COUNT is not window PARTICIPATION. A resolver that
deliberately batches many ids for its own single resolve (core.manyAncestors,
core.recentActivity) is still marked shared if any unrelated window happens to
be open at the time, even though that other window had nothing to do with the
batch. It costs those queries clean samples they were entitled to.

WHY IT IS NARROW: the unrelated window only escapes the concurrent-issue check
if it issues no database call of its own while this one runs - a window that is
open but touching nothing. So the cases this gets wrong are ones where the other
window is doing pure CPU work for the whole overlap.

WHY IT ERRS SAFELY: the mistake marks a clean window contended. It never admits
a queued sample as clean, which is the failure that would make the metric wrong
rather than conservative.
