THE EXACT FIX: the coalescer has to be told WHO is asking, so it can compare the
set of windows a batch answered rather than the global count. That means
threading an observer token from the resolve into ancestorWalk, which is a
change to the query context every resolver sees - a public-ish surface, for a
narrow gain. Worth doing if the exemption turns out to matter in practice, or if
the query context is being reshaped for another reason anyway.

title: Instrument the DB adapter so every pool user passes one counter
description:
Follow-up to km-8pik. The contention tracker accounts for database work by
assembling signals from OUTSIDE the connection pool, and each signal covers
only part of it. Three review rounds each found a different gap in that
account, which is the shape problem rather than three bugs.

CURRENT STATE: our own calls are timed through the Repo's proxy (complete); the
sync engine's are bracketed from its status channel (a FLOOR, not complete).

THE KNOWN GAP, verified in @powersync/common 1.55.0
(AbstractStreamingSyncImplementation, the _uploadAllCrud path): the upload
routine reads the CRUD queue via adapter.nextCrudItem() BEFORE it sets
uploading: true, and calls adapter.updateLocalTarget() with the flag still
clear when the queue is empty. Both are real database operations on the same
connections. A read landing in one of those gaps is currently recorded as
having had the pool to itself.

THE FIX: wrap the DBAdapter that PowerSync opens, rather than watching its
status. WASQLiteOpenFactory implements SQLOpenFactory with openDB(): DBAdapter,
so a wrapping factory can return an instrumented adapter. Then every user of
the connections - ours, the sync engine's, anything added later - passes one
counter, there is no second channel to trust, and the whole foreign-bracket
mechanism plus its syncObserved caveat can be deleted.

WHY NOT DONE IN THE ORIGINAL PR: it changes how the local database is
constructed, which is the most data-loss-sensitive path in the app, and it
cannot be verified in a worktree - only against a real client. That is a
deliberate separation, not an oversight. The narrower status bracket is a
strict improvement over no bracket and errs towards marking clean windows
contended.

WORTH DOING WHEN: someone is already working in repoProvider, or the residual
turns out to matter. Related: the canary idea on the steady-state-latency issue
measures TOTAL pool occupancy including traffic no instrument here can see, and
would say whether this gap is large.
close_reason: Closed on GitHub (issue #965); reconciled by bd-github-sync.

title: Uncontended query samples are censored in proportion to their duration
description:
Known limitation of the contention work on km-8pik, accepted deliberately and
recorded at the declaration in src/data/internals/timingMetrics.ts.

THE BIAS: a query resolve is admitted to the comparable reservoir only if
nothing occupied the connection pool for its whole life. A long resolve has
more exposure to a stray arrival than a short one, so it is censored more
often. The surviving distribution therefore leans fast, and a p95 computed over
it under-states the tail it exists to report.

CONSEQUENCE: the trend under-reports a regression confined to a slow path. It
does not invent one - the direction is conservative - but a genuine slowdown
that only affects slow resolves can stay invisible.

WHY IT WAS ACCEPTED: the alternative is to judge a resolve on its entry
conditions alone. That admits the sample shape the whole change exists to
exclude - a resolve that opens just before a burst of reads and is billed for
the entire burst - which makes the figure wrong rather than merely
conservative. Single DB calls already use entry conditions, which is both
unbiased and correct for them, because a call issued into an empty pool never
waits: later arrivals queue behind it.

WHAT WOULD ACTUALLY FIX IT: per-resolve service time, which needs attribution
of DB calls to the resolve that caused them. Not available today - request
coalescing means a statement can belong to several resolves, and there is no
async context to attribute through. Measuring service at the pool boundary is
also unavailable: the pool is two connections on one VFS and one on the others,
so there is no serial-FIFO decomposition to take.

WORTH REVISITING IF: the censoring rate turns out to be high enough to matter
in practice. The stored record carries the counts needed to estimate it.

title: Measure how often query resolves run with the DB pool free
description:
Follow-up to the contention work on km-8pik.

The per-query comparison now trends the p95 measured only over resolves that
ran with the connection pool to themselves, gated at 20 such resolves per
session. That figure is concurrency-independent by construction, but the whole
approach rests on those resolves EXISTING in useful numbers, which has not been
measured.

THE RISK: if nearly every resolve happens inside a render fan-out wave, heavy
queries never clear the gate and go permanently unjudged. That is better than a
number that moves with render order, but it is a monitor with reduced reach,
and it would be silent - 'insufficient' reads the same whether history is still
building or no comparable sample will ever arrive.

WHAT TO ANSWER: per query name, what share of resolves are uncontended over a
few minutes of ordinary use, and how many sessions it takes for common queries
to clear the gate.

The data is now stored: each session's record carries the uncontended call
count per query alongside the total, plus pool occupancy and the count of calls
issued while another was in flight. So this is answerable from recorded history
once a few sessions exist, without new instrumentation.

WHAT MIGHT COME OUT OF IT: a lower threshold for thin distributions; reporting
'no comparable measurement for this query' distinctly from 'history still
building'; or evidence that coverage is fine and nothing needs doing.

title: Navigation latency is dependency depth (~5 serial read waves), not main-thread stalls
description:
Split out of the interaction-metrics investigation, then REWRITTEN on
2026-09-13 after direct measurement disproved its original premise. The
original text said the recorded ~580ms was the main thread being blocked and
proposed a long-task recorder as the first step. Both are wrong — see the
measurement comment on this issue. Do not build that recorder.

WHAT IS MEASURED AND TRUE (live prod client, Chrome 152)

One page navigation settles in ~620ms, spending it in ~5 SERIAL WAVES of
reads (37 / 88 / 178 / 203 / 206 / 207 cumulative reads at 106 / 210 / 317 /
418 / 520 / 620ms). Across that window the main thread is ~10% busy and
produces ZERO long animation frames; 4ms-timer lateness is p50 4.1ms, p95
5.5ms. The DB read channel is strictly serial at ~0.1ms per request, so a
concurrent fan of N reads bills item k for k x 0.1ms plus everyone's SQL.

So the per-query p50/p95 the monitor stores is dominated by how many other
queries were in flight — queue depth, not work. A query in flight across the
settle records roughly the whole settle, which is why several unrelated
queries cluster at the same magnitude.

THE WORK

Latency is set by WAVE COUNT, not by round-trip count: ~5 waves x ~100ms.
Each wave is one render -> resolve -> render hop. Cutting reads helps only
where it removes a wave. So the job is to find the dependency chain that
forces five hops and flatten it — e.g. resolving what a row needs before it
renders rather than after, or hoisting a per-row query to one per-surface
query.

Not yet identified: which five hops they are. That is the next measurement,
and it wants per-wave attribution (what was issued in wave 3, and what had to
render first), not more aggregate counters.

RELATED

The measurement defect is tracked separately and is worse than that issue
currently states: the figure tracks concurrency, so any verdict from it moves
when render order changes.

title: Bring Codex repository hooks to parity with Claude
description: Wire the existing command guards, publication verification, compact Beads context and session-end sync into Codex. Adapt lifecycle and tool-result differences without duplicating policy logic; verify hook behavior and document activation.
close_reason: Configured and trusted all ten Codex hooks; shared Claude policies, compact lifecycle context, and detached session-end sync verified. Full repository check passed.

title: Backlinks: retaining an ancestor chain also fetches it, for every backlink
description:
Found by review on the backlinks render-path change (#946).

WHAT IS TRUE

The flat Linked References panel calls useRetainParents(backlinks) so
the per-id core.ancestors handles survive a COLLAPSE: collapsed, the
entries unmount, the store disposes an unobserved handle after its GC
window, and LazyViewportMount remembers which rows were mounted and
brings them straight back — so a reopen otherwise paints every row
without its breadcrumb and then grows a line under each.

The catch is structural: the first subscriber to a cold LoaderHandle
starts its load (handleStore, "First subscriber kicks off a load if
we're idle"). So for this store, retaining a chain and fetching it are
the same act — the retention walks every backlink, including ones
nobody has scrolled to. One coalesced statement per chunk of 500 ids,
and it is what the panel already did before that change, so it was
accepted there rather than narrowed.

THE NARROWER SHAPE

Retain only the handles the surface has ALREADY resolved. A cold handle
is left alone (the entry loads it when it mounts); a resolved one is
held so the collapse cannot GC it. Neither ensureLoaded nor the
subscribe self-load fires for a handle that is already ready, so this
costs no walk.

CHECK BEFORE BUILDING

- the retained SET changes as chains land, so the handle array's
  identity churns and useHandles resubscribes. Bound that before
  building — a naive filter-per-render tears down and reopens N
  subscriptions on every resolution.
- on first render nothing is resolved, so nothing is retained. That is
  correct (the entries load them on mount) but means the guard cannot
  be pinned by a first-render assertion.
- measure before and after on a page with many backlinks. The current
  cost is one statement per 500 ids, so the saving is in handles,
  subscriptions and row deps, not in round trips — worth confirming it
  is real before adding the machinery.
close_reason: Closed on GitHub (issue #956); reconciled by bd-github-sync.

title: bd github sync: a pull re-apply clears assignee, restamps closed_at, and lets the enhancement label override type::chore
description:
bd 1.2.2's pull re-applies a GitHub issue onto its bead once per GitHub-side touch that is not bd's own push (a comment, a label edit). Measured 2026-09-11: an issue touched by a mirrored comment was re-applied on the next sync; a bead restored and pushed afterwards survived two further syncs, so bd's own push does not trigger a re-apply and hand repairs are stable until the next foreign touch.

The applied copy loses what GitHub does not carry:
- assignee: cleared (issues minted by bead pushes carry no GitHub assignee)
- closed_at: restamped with the pull time, not GitHub's closedAt
- issue_type: re-derived from labels with the hand label `enhancement` beating the machine label `type::chore` (chore became feature)

Priority flattening from the same re-apply is already restored by the wrapper (guard 2). The #647 guard covers only local-newer rows, and a re-applied row is local-OLDER by construction, so nothing restores these three.

The comment mirror (#954) touches every issue that gains a bead comment, so every new bead comment now costs one such re-apply on the following sync. Backfill measurement: 100 comments over 54 beads produced 7 rows with a visible field change (6 closed: assignee cleared + closed_at restamped; 1 open: issue_type flipped); repaired by hand the same day. Tracker-wide, only 13 of 445 beads still carry an assignee, so the loss has been running for a while through Codex comments and label edits.

Fix direction (scripts/bd-github-sync.mjs): before the pull, snapshot the fields GitHub cannot carry for beads whose GitHub copy is newer than local — the assigned set is cheap via `bd list --assignee`; closed_at and issue_type need `bd show` or `bd sql` — then detect the re-apply after the pull (its rows get updated_at stamped with the pull time), restore, and push back, i.e. widen the existing suspect/restore machinery. Alternative shape: make the pull selective — pull only issues that have no bead yet (new GitHub-filed issues), since beads is the source of truth and GitHub-side closes are already adopted via gh.
close_reason: Closed on GitHub (issue #955); reconciled by bd-github-sync.

title: bd-github-sync pre-PR gate: escape hatch ignored on the blind-publish path
description:
CORRECTED after measuring — the first version of this issue overstated the bug.

The env-prefix escape DOES work for local commands. Measured: a bd dependency-link command blocked for naming bead ids, and the same command with KM_ALLOW_BEAD_IDS=1 prefixed succeeded. So the prefix mechanism is fine in general, and a leading NAME=value run is not universally read as a shell operator.

What actually fails is the escape on a BLIND-PUBLISH gh command. The gate's message for that branch ends with:

    ... after checking every reference and bead id in it yourself, re-run with KM_ISSUE_REFS_OK=1 KM_ALLOW_BEAD_IDS=1 prefixed.

Measured twice in one session, both still blocked WITH that exact prefix applied:
- a pull-request body edit via --body-file (a COVERED publish shape by the gate's own description)
- a read-only GraphQL query listing review threads

So the blind-publish branch advertises an escape it does not honour, while the bead-id branch honours the same escape. Whatever disqualifies the prefixed form is specific to that path.

Separate, smaller issue in the same area: read-only GraphQL through the CLI is gated at all. A GraphQL document's variable syntax (dollar-prefixed names) reads as shell expansion, and jq filters using jq variables trip it too, though nothing is published. Workaround: inline the literal values and avoid dollar signs in the jq filter — awkward and easy to get wrong.

One more data point on over-matching: creating this very issue with an inline description blocked, because the prose names CLI publishing verbs and the escaped dollar signs and backticks defeat the quoted-span skeleton. Routing the body through --body-file was the way in. That direction is the cheap one by design, so it is noted rather than filed as a defect.

Fix direction: find why the blind-publish branch rejects the prefixed form when the bead-id branch accepts it, and make the two consistent; and consider exempting read-only GraphQL queries (no mutation keyword) from the expansion check.

title: Deleting a type definition with live members silently un-types them
getBlockTypes has no malformed-value tolerance, unlike getAliases
description:
`getBlockTypes`/`hasBlockType` (src/data/properties.ts) decode the `types` cell and THROW on a malformed value. `getAliases` right beside them wraps the same decode in try/catch and degrades to `[]`.

Consequence: one malformed synced `types` cell bricks its row against every LOCAL properties write. The kernel typeify processor watches `properties` and calls `addedTypes` -> `getBlockTypes` on the row's BEFORE snapshot, so any write to that row throws inside the same-tx pass and rolls the whole transaction back — including a write that would have fixed the cell.

Reachable because sync-applied rows bypass the same-tx pass while the trigger-maintained `block_types` index still indexes them. `json_each` over a SCALAR yields that scalar, so even `types: "some-id"` (a bare string, not a list) is indexed as a real membership.

This forced two separate local workarounds while building the merge membership retarget: `wellFormedTypeTokens` and the raw-cell path in `rewriteTypeToken` (src/data/internals/mergeTypeMembershipProcessor.ts), both of which exist only because the shared helper cannot be called safely.

Fix direction: give `getBlockTypes` the same tolerance `getAliases` has (ignore what it cannot decode), then delete the two local workarounds. Decide separately whether a malformed cell should be normalized on the next write or left alone.

title: Grouped backlinks: sourceParents carries a payload nothing reads
description:
Fallout from the backlinks single-render-path change (#946). The bead
for that one asserted that grouped-backlinks needs the ancestor chains
for GROUPING, so passing them down to entries was free there. That
premise is false, checked at the source.

WHAT IS ACTUALLY TRUE

resolveSourceParents runs core.manyAncestors over every source id and
returns {sourceId, parentIds} per source. Grouping does NOT read
parentIds: buildGroupedBacklinks builds from `candidates`, and the
candidate rows come from the grouping SQL, which walks the context
chain itself. parentIds had exactly one reader — the entries'
breadcrumb prefetch — and that reader is now gone.

So sourceParents has two remaining jobs, neither of which is its name:

1. the WALK declares a context-node dep on every ancestor, which is
   load-bearing (a page moved out from under a source re-groups).
2. sourceId is read by currentSourceIdsForGroupedResult, which the
   sticky-group claim pass uses as the current source set.

THE SHAPE

Replace sourceParents with the source-id set the resolver already has
in scope, and turn resolveSourceParents into a dep declaration that
returns nothing. That also collapses
currentSourceIdsForGroupedResult's two-branch fallback to one read.

CHECK BEFORE BUILDING

- the fallback branch (`parentSourceIds.length > 0 || total === 0`,
  else derive from groups) needs its reason established before it is
  dropped. It looks like defence for a result shape that no longer
  occurs, but sticky claiming is visible UI state and getting it wrong
  silently re-shuffles groups.
- the ancestor context-node deps must stay pinned. Mutation-test them
  by deleting the per-ancestor loop, not by substituting.
- test/query.test.ts asserts the sourceParents payload directly and
  GroupedLinkedReferences.test.tsx fabricates it; both need updating.

Filed rather than folded into the render-path PR: the sticky-claim
input is a separate concern with its own tests, and the stale docs
that claimed grouping reads this payload are already corrected there.
close_reason: Premise no longer holds. The bead said parentIds had no reader left, which was true of the PR's first shape (entries fetching their own chains with no seed). Review on #949 found two callers that shape broke — the readwise backlog, which DERIVES each highlight's chain from its section's rather than prefetching, and the grouped panel, whose entries lost their first-frame breadcrumbs and reflowed every row. initialParents is restored as a pending-window seed, so grouped's parentIds has an honest reader again and there is nothing to collapse. What survives is the factual half, already corrected in the code: grouping does NOT read this payload (buildGroupedBacklinks builds from candidates, whose rows come from the grouping SQL's own context walk); its readers are the entry seed and the sticky-claim pass' source-id set. The docs say that now.

title: Backlinks entry: drop the dual render path, now that per-id handles made the prefetch free
description:
Fallout from the per-id ancestor work (PR #934). Found by the quality
review agent; the largest single deletion that change unlocks.

WHY IT IS NOW DEAD WEIGHT
`BlockEntry` has two render paths, and the comment at its declaration
says exactly why: to "avoid a `useParents` query per visible entry in the
*initial* state". With one `core.ancestors` handle per id, an entry's own
`useParents(shownBlock)` acquires THE SAME HANDLE KEY the panel already
warmed. There is no second query to skip any more — only a second
subscription to an already-resolved handle. The premise the split was
built on is gone.

WHAT IT DELETES
- the `BlockEntryContent` / `BlockEntryDynamicContent` split (~45 lines)
- the `initialParents` prop and its doc, plus the `undefined` vs `[]`
  hint distinction that exists only because a missing prefetch used to
  silently disable breadcrumbs
- the threading through `LinkedReferences` and `BacklinkGroup`
- the branch flip on promote, which currently remounts the body

CHECK BEFORE BUILDING
- grouped-backlinks is the case that is NOT obviously free: it gets its
  chains inside its own query payload (`resolveSourceParents`, with
  `deps: 'none'`) because it needs the ancestors for GROUPING, not just
  for breadcrumbs. Passing them down is genuinely free there. Decide
  deliberately whether entries under it should re-acquire per-id handles
  (uniform, one path, N extra subscriptions) or whether `initialParents`
  survives as a hint for a caller that already holds the chains. The
  first is the simplification; the second keeps a prop with one honest
  consumer.
- `LinkedReferences` currently calls `useManyParents(backlinks)` over the
  WHOLE list while `LazyViewportMount` mounts only what is on screen.
  Moving to per-entry `useParents` means only mounted entries query,
  which is strictly less work — but entries then mount in bursts as the
  user scrolls, so confirm the burst still lands in one coalesced
  statement.
- `src/plugins/backlinks/test/linkedReferencesRefresh.test.tsx` captures
  the stubbed entry renderer's props, so it needs rewriting to observe
  the rendered breadcrumb instead. Its sibling
  `linkedReferencesBreadcrumbs.test.tsx` already drives the real
  renderer and is the model.
close_reason: Closed on GitHub (issue #946); reconciled by bd-github-sync.

title: Statically registering a repo extension for dev crashes with useRepo outside RepoContext
description:
## Observation

While verifying a strength-tracker UI change, I registered the repo extension
`agent-extensions/strength-tracker` into `src/extensions/staticAppExtensions.ts`
so a `pnpm dev` tab would load it without the agent-bridge pairing (which needs
two human steps). Its page renderer crashed immediately:

    Error: useRepo must be used within a RepoContext
    The above error occurred in the <StrengthLogContent> component

## What was ruled out

Module duplication was the obvious suspect (`vite-plugins/unifySrcJsUrls.ts`
exists precisely because kernel modules and extension blobs can end up keyed at
different URLs). Three registration shapes were tried and ALL failed
identically:

1. relative import from outside Vite's root
   (`../../agent-extensions/strength-tracker/src/index`)
2. a symlink at `src/__strength_tmp` (Vite resolves through it, so same as 1)
3. a real COPY under `src/`, with every `@/x.js` specifier rewritten to `@/x` so
   it resolved exactly as an app module does

If it were duplication, (3) should have worked. `performance.getEntriesByType`
showed a single `/src/context/repo.js` URL, but that reading is not sound — the
resource-timing buffer was at its 250-entry cap, so entries were missing.

Reproduces on unmodified master (checked by restoring the renderer from HEAD),
so it is not from the change that was being verified.

## Why it matters

The documented dev loop for driving an extension (`local-dev-loop` skill) is
bridge-pairing + `install-extension`, which needs a human to approve pairing and
paste a token. There is no documented way to exercise a repo extension against a
dev server unattended, and the obvious shortcut fails with a misleading error.

An agent hitting this loses a chunk of a session, as this one did.

## Unknown, deliberately

Whether the crash is specific to static registration or would also hit a
DB-installed extension in production was NOT determined. The extension is
reported as working in the live client, which suggests harness-only, but that
was not tested — a fresh preview origin has an empty DB, so the production path
could not be exercised either.

## Fix shape (one of)

- Make static registration of a repo extension work, and document it as the
  unattended dev path; or
- determine why it cannot work and say so in the `local-dev-loop` skill, so the
  next person does not spend the same time on it.

title: Repo-wide isReadOnly authorizes workspace-scoped writes
description:
RESOLVED, the open question this was filed with: there is NO plaintext leak.
The encryption angle that briefly raised this to P1 does not hold, and the
issue is back at P2. Three independent reasons, each sufficient alone:

1. The upload hook is already per-workspace. `encryptUploadOps`
   (src/services/powersync.ts) reads `op.payload.workspace_id` off each op and
   resolves the mode for THAT id. It never consults the Repo's active
   workspace, so a row written while the pin is moving is still encoded under
   its own workspace's mode.
2. That mode comes from the durable mode pin for the same workspace
   (src/sync/keys/resolver.ts). The pin is set-once and locally immutable; it
   does not move with the App effect and has no analogous window.
3. The residual client path — an unpinned workspace resolves mode 'none' and
   would upload plaintext — is refused server-side by the blocks ciphertext
   trigger, which checks the row's own workspace and rejects non-envelope
   content with errcode 23514. The upload classifier treats 23xxx as permanent,
   so it is quarantined rather than retried. The server never stores it.

WHAT REMAINS, and its true size:

`Repo.tx` captures `isReadOnly` at tx-open time and that flag is a single
Repo-wide boolean moved by an async App effect, not a property of the workspace
being written. So a transaction's authorization can describe a different
workspace than the rows it writes. The switch window is real and deliberate —
the workspace switcher flips the pin before the hash on purpose so synchronous
consumers do not lag the click, and the UI stays mounted throughout.

But the read-only half reduces to the existing flag-lag issue. A switch inside
a read-then-write window can only swap in a flag that REFUSES: a spurious
failure, retried on the next gesture. An unauthorized write additionally
requires the flag to be wrong about the pinned workspace already, which is the
lag issue rather than anything this one adds.

The one novel harm is not about read-only at all: a write into a workspace
unpinned on this device creates a local row whose upload is then permanently
rejected and quarantined, in a workspace whose other rows are all still
deferred. Narrow — it needs a workspace never opened on this device, encrypted
server-side, and a gesture inside the window — but it loses that write.

DIRECTION: do NOT do the kernel change originally filed here. Making runTx take
a per-workspace read-only value touches every writer and, with the leak gone,
buys only the lag-shaped half. If the remaining harm is worth closing, the cheap
shape is to treat "this workspace's gate has not spoken yet" as read-only rather
than defaulting editable during the window — a UX trade against the flag-lag
issue (more spurious refusals on every switch), so a deliberate call rather than
a fix to land quietly.

title: LoaderHandle: make a failed load observable — consumers cannot tell failed from slow
description:
A handle whose FIRST load fails is indistinguishable from one that is still
loading, and it never self-corrects while mounted and current. Any consumer that
serves stale or placeholder data during load therefore serves it indefinitely on
failure, with no way to notice.

MECHANISM (all verified against the code, PR #488)
- `LoaderHandle`'s error path (src/data/internals/handleStore.ts, ~715-725) sets
  `status_`/`error`, leaves `value` untouched, and fires NO notify — the comment
  says so explicitly: "Failed loads contribute no notify".
- It rolls `deps` back to `priorDeps`. For a FIRST-load failure that is empty,
  and `matchesAgainst` returns false for an empty dep list, so no commit can
  ever invalidate it.
- `useHandle` ensure-loads only from `'idle'`, and `subscribe()` only loads from
  `idle || stale`. So `'error'` is terminal.
- Net: no notify (nothing re-renders), no invalidation, no retry. Recovery is
  only `dispose()` — refCount 0 plus `gcTimeMs` (5s) — or the caller changing
  the args to a different key.

WHY IT MATTERS NOW
`useManyParents` carries the last resolved ancestor chains while a handle loads.
On a failed load it carries them forever. PR #488 tried to guard that with
`handle.status() === 'error'` and the guard was DEAD CODE: the React Compiler
memoized the expression on `[carried, handle]`, neither of which changes while
the handle is errored, so the status was read once while still `'idle'`. vitest
runs without the compiler, so every test passed. The guard was removed and the
behaviour documented instead. See memory `reference_react_compiler_test_prod_gap`.

Reading `status()` during render cannot fix this in general — it is a read of
mutable external state and the compiler is entitled to cache it. The state has
to be observable through the subscription.

PROPOSED
Give failure an epoch the handle notifies on, so `useSyncExternalStore`
consumers re-render and can branch on it; and decide a retry policy for a
first-load failure (today there is none). This reverses a deliberate decision
for every handle in the app, so it wants its own review rather than riding along
with a consumer fix.

REACHABILITY
Not the SQLite variable cap — measured at 32766 in this toolchain, and the panel
would render 32k rows first. The real paths are DB-level: OPFS corruption, a DB
closed during workspace switch or reload, worker teardown. Low frequency, but it
hits every consumer of that handle at once.

title: A content rewrite on an existing block-type block leaves it unlinkable by its own name
description:
core.blockTypeTypeify fires only on the type-ADD transition, so a content write to a block that is ALREADY a type runs no reconciliation. aliasSyncProcessor then applies rule 1 on its own: the old content matches the claimed alias, so the alias is REPLACED with the new content while block-type:label is untouched.

End state: label 'Widget', content and alias 'Type body text'. [[Widget]] no longer resolves to the type, and the type registry still publishes it as 'Widget' — so the type is unlinkable by the name the picker shows for it.

Not reachable through the outline (BlockTypeBlockRenderer swaps the content editor for the type editor) — the paths are the agent bridge's update-block, an import that updates an existing row, and anything else writing content directly.

Distinct from #757, which is the strand on RENAME and is fixed by refusing the divergent TAG. This is the residual hole on the other side: divergence created after the block is already a type.

Fix direction is an open question with the same shape #757 had — refuse the content write, reconcile it, or accept and label it. Note the rejected precedent: repairing at rename time inside writeBlockTypeLabel was implemented and declined (it contradicts alias.sync rule 2's deliberately additive drift heal, and cannot distinguish the type's own name claim from a user-added alias equal to the label).
notes:
TRAP for whoever fixes this: src/components/renderer/nameFieldBlur.test.tsx DEPENDS on the divergent state being constructible. Its fixture builds a type then rewrites content in a second tx precisely because the tag-time refusal (#584) blocks building it directly. Any fix here that refuses or reconciles a content write on an existing block-type block breaks that fixture again — rework it to a raw db.writeTransaction (fires no processor, and is the sync-applied shape) rather than weakening the test.

Adjacent context from the #584 session:
- The UI-layer coping mechanism is the writeLabel no-op guard added by #748 — its comment states the position this issue has to respect: repair belongs to a processor, not to whoever last tabbed through the field. That guard also REMOVED the incidental healing a bare focus-and-leave used to perform, so the drift now persists instead of being silently repaired.
- Rejected precedent, do not re-derive: reconciling inside writeBlockTypeLabel's rename branch was implemented and dropped before #508 merged (contradicts alias.sync rule 2's deliberately additive heal; cannot tell the type's own name claim from a user-added alias equal to the label). See the note on #757.
- Verification discipline that worked on #584: probe first (tag, rename, read the alias set back) to measure the real end state before choosing a direction — the measured damage was worse than the issue described in both cases so far.
close_reason: Closed on GitHub (issue #926); reconciled by bd-github-sync.

title: Sleep Lab: automatic watch-data ingestion
description: Sleep Lab (agent-extensions/sleep-lab) imports Galaxy Watch sleep data by hand today: the Samsung Health export folder or a pasted Health Connect webhook payload. Health Connect is on-device only, so automatic ingestion needs a relay. Two candidate routes, both need a sample of the format before a parser can be fitted: (1) the Health Data Export app auto-exporting Health Connect to a Google Sheet every 12-24h, with the sheet published as CSV and a 'Sync from sheet' action pulling it on open (no backend); (2) Health Connect's built-in scheduled export, a daily zip on Google Drive holding an unencrypted SQLite database, read by a Mac-side job against an undocumented schema. A third, most complete option is the Health Connect Webhook app posting to an ingest endpoint (Supabase edge function + RLS-locked table, extension pulls on open). Pick one, get a sample, fit the parser, add the sync gesture.

title: Detect and explain a local DB that vanished at boot (browser wiped the OPFS store)
description:
## What happened

On a Chrome desktop profile, minutes after a Chrome update relaunch (152.0.7977.82), the app booted and found no local database. It silently created a fresh one, re-downloaded the whole workspace set (~350k rows, ~6 min), re-ran every one-shot derivation pass recorded in `client_schema_state`, and re-fetched media assets on demand. The user experienced this as "the local DB was wiped and is re-synchronizing" with no explanation from the app.

The forensics store (`km-db-forensics` in IndexedDB) survived and holds the whole story: the previous session recorded `dbSizeAtStart` of ~2.0 GB and a clean `pagehide`; the next session recorded `dbSizeAtStart: 0`. Nothing in the app deleted the file.

## Root cause (below the app)

Chrome recreated the profile's ENTIRE OPFS store — every origin's data — while IndexedDB, localStorage and CacheStorage were untouched. The on-disk `File System/Origins` LevelDB was brand new (`Creating DB … since it was missing`, `MANIFEST-000001`) and every numbered origin directory had the same fresh ctime. Chromium's `SandboxOriginDatabase::Init` (`storage/browser/file_system/sandbox_origin_database.cc`) does exactly this when the `Origins` LevelDB fails to open with Corruption or IOError: repair, and on failure `DeletePathRecursively(file_system_directory_)` — the whole directory — then recreate. Chrome's QuotaManager bucket for the origin was NOT recreated and `navigator.storage.persisted()` was already true, so this is not quota eviction or a site-data clear. No web-content-side change can prevent it.

## What the app should do (this issue)

1. **Detect it at boot.** In the DB-open path we already record a forensic session (`recordForensicSessionStart`). When the current boot finds the `.db` missing or 0 bytes AND the archived previous session for the same user has a non-trivial `dbSizeAtStart`, that is a "local storage was reset" event, not a first install. Capture a forensic snapshot with a distinct reason (e.g. `opfs-store-missing`) so the next investigation starts from evidence instead of a bridge dig.
2. **Tell the user, once, honestly.** A non-blocking notice on that boot: the browser removed this device's local database; it is being re-downloaded from the server; local undo history and any edits that had not yet uploaded are gone; media will re-fetch on demand. Distinguish the local-only mode, where there is no server copy and the loss is total (mirror the branch in `LocalDbCorruptionFallback`).
3. **Do not treat it as corruption** — there is nothing to export and Reset is meaningless. This is a separate branch from the existing Export + Reset flow, not an extension of it.

Out of scope here (file separately if wanted): holding back pre-sync `user`-source writes on such a boot. In this incident only 3 blocks were minted before sync caught up (device-install record and similar get-or-create rows), all legitimate and round-tripped, so the current behaviour did no harm.

## Evidence trail for whoever picks this up

- App-side signature: `session:current.dbSizeAtStart === 0` with the previous archived session at multi-GB and `cleanShutdown: true` (readable via `window.__omniliner.forensics.dump()` or the agent bridge).
- Chrome-side fingerprint (macOS): `<profile>/File System/Origins/LOG` first line "Creating DB … since it was missing"; all `<profile>/File System/NNN` dirs share one ctime; `<profile>/WebStorage/QuotaManager` still has the origin's old bucket row.
- Memory with the full write-up: `bd recall reference_chrome_opfs_store_wipe`.
notes: Follow-up from the investigation (2026-09-04): the trigger inside Chrome is unproven. The only Chrome-side proof (chrome://histograms/FileSystem.OriginDatabase) is per browser process and was read after a Chrome restart, so it showed nothing. What IS established: only the profile's `File System/` directory was recreated (all other storage dirs kept their mtimes), which matches Chromium's SandboxOriginDatabase recovery and rules out quota eviction, site-data clears and cleanup tools. Nothing web content does can prevent the class; the app-side levers are (1) this issue's detect-and-explain, (2) an IndexedDB mirror of pending uploads (ps_crud) so the un-uploaded window survives an OPFS-only loss (IDB survived this incident), (3) an opt-in periodic export to a user-chosen directory via the File System Access API. (2) and (3) are separate issues if wanted.

title: Flaky gate test: bd-github-sync chunked-mint mapping test fails in CI only
description:
`scripts/bd-github-sync.test.ts` > `runSync process behavior` > 'prints the mappings an earlier chunk minted when a later chunk fails' failed once on CI (Run Tests, actions run 33794266991) and has not reproduced locally.

Evidence:
- Passed on the immediately preceding commit's CI run and on the following one.
- Locally: 3/3 in isolation, 177/177 for the whole file, and green in three full `pnpm run check` runs the same afternoon.
- NOT a timeout: the enclosing describe carries `{ timeout: 20_000 }` and the failure was reported at 238ms, so an assertion failed.

Unknown which assertion. `check.mjs` runs the suites in parallel and the CI log kept the per-test tick list but not vitest's 'Failed Tests' section, so the assertion text never reached the log. That is itself worth fixing — a gate failure whose reason is unreadable costs a full re-run to diagnose.

The test spawns the real script via `spawnSync` into a mkdtemp git repo with a PATH-fronted `bd` shim, drives 250 rows across two push chunks with `failPushCall: 2`, and asserts on exit status plus two `minted: … → #N` lines in stdout. Suspect the process-level harness under CI load rather than the logic under test.

Next steps: make check.mjs preserve vitest's failure section for the failing suite, then re-run this test under CPU pressure to try to reproduce.
close_reason: Root cause was stdout truncation from process.exit on a piped stdout, not a harness race. Fixed by setting process.exitCode on the failed-sync path. Linux CI green on the fix (run for sha 1084ea824). Caveat on the record: one green run is weak evidence for a load-dependent bug, but the remedy is the measured one — 200/200 lines with exitCode vs 171-176 with exit under load.

title: repo.ts is a 4,599-line god class: the comment density is the symptom
description:
`src/data/repo.ts` is **4,599 lines** and was, before PR #897, **2,287 comment lines against 2,136 code
lines** — the worst file in the repo by both measures. The comment audit's finding is that the density is a
symptom of the class, not of the commenting.

The mechanism, observed directly: with no smaller unit to hang a rule on, every rule gets re-typed at each
call site that needs it. Counted in this one file — four sites for "capture the resolver, never re-resolve",
three for the view-gap predicate, three for the add-only/retain-on-source contract, two for the query epoch,
two for the workspace-schema ternary, six near-identical idle-lane docs, six drain methods that say "Mirror
of ..." at each other. The copies then drift, and three drifts were verified rather than suspected.

PR #897 compressed the prose. It did not and could not fix the cause: the class owns the mutator/query/
processor registries, the handle store wiring, the sync-observer lifecycle, workspace backfills and claims,
the idle-job lanes, and the metrics surface. Several of those are separable seams that could own their own
rules.

This is a design task, not a cleanup task — it wants a plan and Vlad's agreement on the seams before any
code moves, and it should not be attempted as part of a comment sweep.

title: Comment-as-symptom refactors: plugins, UI and utils (64 findings)
description:
The **priority-A** half of the comment-cleanup audit outside the data kernel: findings where the comment is a
symptom and the fix is a code change.

- `src/plugins` — 30 findings (~20 files). The `references/` parser+processor pair is the densest non-kernel
  code in the repo and the strongest candidate.
- `src/components`, `src/extensions`, `src/shortcuts` — 18 findings.
- `src/utils` — 16 findings.

Same shapes as the kernel bead: extract a named predicate for a paragraph-explained boolean; name a magic
sentinel; encode an implicit call-order protocol in a type instead of a warning comment; give a rule one
owner instead of restating it at N call sites; split a function whose comment enumerates its three phases.

Each is behaviour-preserving in intent but is a real code change — land per subsystem, verify each with
`pnpm run check`, and revert-test any guard you touch (delete the clause, confirm a named test fails).

Prepared agent tasks under `.comment-audit/tasks/` (worktree-local): `plugins-code-00` .. `plugins-code-09`,
`ui-code-00` .. `ui-code-05`, `utils-code-00` .. `utils-code-05`.
Each is blocked by the comment-only pass for the same area, since both touch the same files.

title: Comment-as-symptom refactors: data kernel (57 findings)
description:
The **priority-A** half of the comment-cleanup audit for the data kernel: findings where the comment is a
symptom and the fix is a code change. **57 findings across ~25 files in `src/data`.**

The audit's premise: if code needs a lot of comments, that is usually a smell and the code should improve.
PR #897 removed the rot; this removes the cause.

The dominant shape the audit found, stated once because it recurs everywhere: **the same rule re-typed at
every call site instead of given one owner.** In `repo.ts` alone — four sites for "capture the resolver,
never re-resolve", three for the view-gap predicate, three for the add-only/retain-on-source contract, two
for the query epoch, six near-identical idle-lane docs. With no smaller unit to hang a rule on, the rule gets
re-typed wherever it is needed, and the copies then drift. Verified drift: a metrics doc listing 10 of 12
counters and attributing a call site the same file contradicts 400 lines later; a comment saying "these
three" for six lanes.

Representative fixes proposed:
- give each metrics class a typed snapshot return instead of `Readonly<Record<string, number>>`, so the
  counter names stop needing a hand-maintained prose copy
- extract named predicates for multi-clause booleans that currently carry a paragraph each
- turn the five loose derivation-liveness locals in `commitPipeline.ts` into one object with a named protocol
- collapse the source-gate SQL fragment spelled out at 7 sites and re-explained in prose at 5
- rename `backfill*IfEmpty` helpers whose names contradict their marker-gated bodies and are currently
  patched by three separate comments arguing "marker, not emptiness"

These are behaviour-preserving refactors, but they are real code changes in the kernel — land them in small
per-subsystem PRs, not one sweep, and verify each with `pnpm run check`.

Prepared agent tasks: `kernel-code-00` .. `kernel-code-16` under `.comment-audit/tasks/` (worktree-local).
Blocked by PR #897 because it touches the same files.

title: Comment cleanup: apply the agent-cli, agent-dispatch and core-module findings
