title: Comment-cleanup audit: repo-wide comment bloat (32.5% of non-test source)
description:
A repo-wide comment-cleanup audit measured non-test source at **57,712 comment lines against 119,691 code
lines (32.5%)** and produced **440 findings across ~210 files**, worth roughly **6,400 comment lines**.

The rule applied is the one already in `AGENTS.md`: keep a comment only if a competent editor would DO
something different for having read it. Two failure modes dominate, and the second is the priority:

1. **Content that rots or restates** — design-doc stage labels, accounts of how a bug was found, measured
   figures/dates/shas quoted in comments, restatement of the line below, stale claims that contradict their
   own code, and orphaned JSDoc attached to nothing.
2. **Comment-as-symptom** — a long comment paying rent for code that does not say what it means. 121+ findings
   propose a code change (extract a named predicate, name a sentinel, encode an implicit protocol in a type,
   give a rule ONE owner instead of restating it at N call sites).

The single strongest structural signal: **the same rule re-typed at every call site instead of given one
owner**, because there is no smaller unit to hang it on. The copies then drift — one metrics doc listed 10 of
12 counters and attributed a call site the same file contradicts 400 lines later; one comment said "these
three" for six lanes.

Chunk 1 (the data kernel, comment-only) shipped in PR #897.

Child issues cover the remaining chunks. Findings artefacts are worktree-local and untracked under
`.comment-audit/` (per-chunk task JSON with disjoint file ownership, plus per-area scratch notes); if that
worktree is gone, the audit has to be re-run rather than recovered.
notes: 2026-09-04: PR #899 merged — AGENTS.md comments section rewritten on the audit evidence; two lint rules now gate the mechanical half (comments/no-invisible-jsdoc, comments/no-review-provenance), so the remaining comment-only chunks can skip the PR/reviewer-provenance class entirely (already cut tree-wide) and shadowed JSDoc (also cut). Measure progress with node scripts/comment-density.mjs (working tree) and --added <range> (what a PR adds). The finder/implementer briefs live in the bd memory reference_comment_cleanup_briefs; method notes in feedback_comments_state_the_invariant_not_the_understanding.

title: Content search matches inside generated property value rows
description:
Where properties are blocks (properties_migration = 'children'), a property write materializes a VALUE block whose content is the serialized property value. Those rows are live and non-empty, so find-replace's content search selects them: SELECT_CONTENT_CANDIDATES_SQL in src/plugins/find-replace/dataExtension.ts filters only on deleted = 0 AND content != '', with no exclusion by location.

Consequences: a search matches text inside a serialized payload rather than inside anything a person wrote, and offers a generated row as a result. For plugin ui-state that also means internal payloads are searchable.

The block-ref pickers were fixed by switching to core.recentUserBlocks, which excludes descendants of the user-state roots. Content search needs the same treatment, but the call is broader than the pickers: value rows for a user's OWN properties on ordinary pages are arguably legitimate search hits, so the exclusion probably wants to be the state-root subtree rather than all generated rows. Decide that before implementing.

Repro: flip a test workspace to 'children', write any property, then query for a substring of the value.
close_reason: Duplicate of km-2jjb — same class (content search has no location exclusion), same open decision. Folding the props-as-blocks value-row evidence into km-2jjb instead.

title: Test teardown cannot cancel an armed delayMs processor or idle callback
description:
The per-test Repo release (src/data/test/testRepoScope.ts) drains every deferred-work family via Repo.awaitDeferredWork, but a drain only awaits work whose deferral timer has ALREADY fired. ProcessorRunner schedules a delayed job with a bare setTimeout and keeps no handle (src/data/internals/processorRunner.ts, around the delayMs branch), and PendingIdleJobs likewise only adds a promise to its pending set once the scheduler callback runs.

So a test that ends with an armed-but-unfired callback leaves it armed. It fires later, during another test, against a database resetTestDb has since emptied — the same hazard class as the parked seed passes, reached by a different route.

Reachable, not theoretical: the references processor schedules a recompute with delayMs 4000 (src/plugins/references/renameProcessor.ts / referencesProcessor.ts), which no test waits out.

Mitigations already in place: the release unpins the workspace, so any pass gated on the active workspace refuses when it eventually fires; and awaitIdle's own doc already states that delayed jobs which have not started are not pending. This is a documented property of the job frameworks, not a regression.

Fix direction: give PendingIdleJobs and ProcessorRunner a cancel — track the timer handle at schedule time and clear it on dispose — then have the per-test release cancel rather than only drain. That is new cancellation surface on two core classes, which is why it was scoped out of the release change rather than bolted onto it.

Found by review on the per-test Repo scope work; the boundary is stated at Repo.awaitDeferredWork and in testRepoScope.ts.

title: Exclude user-state rows from content search
description:
Every plugin ui-state root is created by getPluginUIStateBlock with the type label as its block content, so rows titled like "Interaction metrics", "Startup metrics", "Recents" and so on are FTS-indexed and returned by core.searchByContent. The block-reference picker sends a typed query through searchBlocksAcrossSources to that query, so app bookkeeping competes for its twelve results.

Not specific to any one plugin: the titles come from the shared helper, and blanking them would remove the only legible identifier those containers have.

The rule already exists in the kernel. The recent-user-blocks statement excludes everything descending from a user state root, walking down from a set bounded by the UI surface rather than by document size. The same exclusion applied to content search fixes the class.

Decision needed before implementing: whether the exclusion belongs in core.searchByContent (so every consumer, quick-find included, stops offering state rows) or only in the block-reference picker. The former is probably right and is a user-visible behaviour change.

The empty-query half of the picker is already fixed: it reads user-authored recents.

title: Hook scripts still exit via process.exit() after printing, which can truncate output
description:
Follow-up to the #881 fix: process.exit() drops queued writes to a piped stdout/stderr (measured on Linux node 24: 172 of 200 lines survived when the reader was slow to drain). The #881 PR converted the ones whose output is unbounded or is the whole point of the script (scripts/bd-github-sync.mjs sync entry point, scripts/check.mjs, scripts/bd-prime-hook.mjs, scripts/bd-publish-verify.mjs).

Still on process.exit(): the hook control-flow escapes, where exit() doubles as 'stop checking and answer now' -- allow() and the deny sites in scripts/bd-github-sync.mjs, scripts/check-stash-worktree.mjs and scripts/check-staged-pii.mjs. Their payloads (deny messages, issue title tables) are smaller than the ~6.5KB where truncation started to bite in the measurement, so this is a latent gap rather than an observed loss -- but a truncated deny message is a gate that blocks with half an explanation.

Fix direction: give those scripts a single exit seam that sets process.exitCode and returns, rather than converting call sites one by one; the escapes are deep in the control flow, so this is a restructure and wants its own review.

title: Send email invites for workspace collaboration
description:
## The gap

Inviting a collaborator writes a DB row and nothing else.
`inviteMemberByEmail` (`src/data/workspaces.ts:370`) calls the owner-only
`invite_member_by_email` RPC, which upserts into `workspace_invitations` keyed
`(workspace_id, email)`. The invitee discovers it only by signing in with that
address, at which point `list_my_pending_invitations` matches on `auth.email()`
and the dropdown in `src/components/workspace/PendingInvitations.tsx` renders it.

So an invitee who has no account, or who does not happen to open the app, never
learns they were invited. The settings dialog says as much:
"They'll see it next time they sign in."
(`src/components/workspace/WorkspaceSettingsDialog.tsx:156`)

## Approach

Make a Supabase edge function the single entry point for inviting. It calls the
existing RPC with the caller's JWT — so the owner-only authorization stays
exactly where it is today — and then sends the mail. `inviteMemberByEmail`
becomes a `functions.invoke`. There is then no state where an invitation row
exists but no email was attempted.

Considered and rejected for now: a `pg_net` DB trigger on insert. More robust
against a client dying mid-flow, but it adds a shared secret and silent failure
modes to a path that currently has exactly one writer. Revisit if a second
writer appears.

## Work

- Edge function (`supabase/functions/` — the directory does not exist yet, so
  this also establishes the deploy path: `supabase functions deploy` plus a
  workflow step and a repo secret).
- Migration: `last_email_sent_at` on `workspace_invitations`, plus a throttle
  check evaluated **inside** the function.
- Client: `inviteMemberByEmail` swaps the direct RPC call for the function.
- UI: a resend affordance, and an honest partial-success state — today the
  dialog reports success unconditionally, but with mail in the loop "row
  written, send failed" is reachable and must say so.

## Guardrails

The abuse surface is new, not inherited. Today the blast radius of a hostile or
mistyped invite is a DB row nobody sees; with email it is mail to a stranger's
inbox, and the RPC's upsert means an owner can hammer it. So the throttle is
load-bearing, not polish: cap per `(workspace, email)` and per inviter per hour,
checked inside the writing path rather than at the call site. The
`last_email_sent_at` column is what makes both the throttle and a "resend"
button decidable instead of guesswork.

## Email content

Workspace name (plaintext metadata even under E2EE), inviter identity, role, and
a link to the app. Note the deployed base path is not `/`, so the app URL must
be configuration rather than a hardcoded string.

Worth preserving deliberately: acceptance is authorized by `auth.email()`
matching, so the link carries **no secret** — it is just "open this and sign in
as this address". Do not add an accept token to the mail.

For E2EE workspaces the mail must say the key arrives separately from the
inviter, out of band, or the invitee accepts into a workspace they cannot read.

## Blocked on

The sending-domain and provider setup issue. The code can be written and
unit-tested against a mocked provider without it; it cannot be verified end to
end or deployed until the domain is verified.

title: Provision sending domain + transactional email provider
description:
Prerequisite infra for emailed collaboration invites. No sending domain exists
today, and the project has no transactional email path at all: the only mail it
sends is the Supabase Auth OTP code, via Auth's own SMTP, which cannot be used
for arbitrary sends.

A new domain is needed (decision made 2026-09-02 — no existing domain will be
reused for app mail).

Manual steps, in order:

1. Register a domain dedicated to the app.
2. Host its DNS at a provider with a usable API (Cloudflare or Route53), so the
   record creation is scriptable rather than hand-pasted. This choice is the one
   that decides how much of the rest can be automated.
3. Create the transactional provider account and mint the first API key.
4. Publish SPF/DKIM (and DMARC) for the sending subdomain; verify the domain.
5. Store the API key as a Supabase edge-function secret (`supabase secrets set`).

Provider recommendation: **Resend**.
- Sending from a Deno edge function is a single `fetch` with a Bearer token — no
  SDK, no request signing.
- Domain setup is a REST API (`POST /domains` returns the records to publish,
  `POST /domains/{id}/verify`, `GET /domains/{id}` to poll), so steps 2/4 can be
  driven by a script once DNS has an API.
- No manual approval queue.

Rejected alternatives:
- **AWS SES** — the most IaC-native option (identity + DKIM + DNS records in one
  Terraform plan if DNS is Route53), but the sandbox exit is a human-reviewed
  support ticket, which is a larger manual step than everything Resend asks for
  combined. Also needs SigV4 signing from Deno.
- **Postmark** — best deliverability of the three, but new accounts go through a
  manual questionnaire before they can send to arbitrary addresses.
- **Cloudflare** — Email Routing is inbound-only, and the free
  MailChannels-via-Workers path was withdrawn in 2024. Not a send path.

Shape the automatable remainder as an idempotent `scripts/setup-email-sender.mjs`
with `--dry-run`, matching the existing idiom (`scripts/bd-label-colors.mjs`,
`scripts/ensure-pages-published.sh`). Not Terraform: there is zero IaC in the
repo and this is three resources, so a state file and toolchain would cost more
than they carry.

Two things to settle while in here:
- Check whether custom SMTP is already configured for Auth on the hosted
  project. If it is, a verified domain may already exist and this shrinks
  considerably.
- If Auth is still on Supabase's built-in sender, consider moving the OTP mail
  to the same provider. The built-in sender is rate-limited to a handful per
  hour and documented as non-production, which makes it a live constraint on the
  *login* path, independent of invites.

Blocks the implementation issue: the code can be written and unit-tested against
a mocked provider without any of this, but cannot be verified end to end or
deployed until the domain is verified.

title: Telemetry-induced loader reruns are timed into the interaction query series
description:
The interaction record's 'queries' field copies repo.metrics().queries wholesale — page totals — while 'writes' and 'fanout' beside it come from the excludingTelemetry counters.

A telemetry transaction still invalidates mounted query handles, and the loader reruns that follow are timed unconditionally in queryMetrics (repo.ts, the dispatcher's resolve wrapper). The 'telemetry' transaction option excludes the write and the synchronous fan-out counters only; a rerun happens in a later microtask with no provenance about which transaction invalidated it.

Consequence: stored per-query p95 partly measures the app reacting to its own bookkeeping. Against a busy session that is noise. On a nearly idle session — which is exactly when the recorder samples — telemetry-induced reruns can be a large share of all query activity, so a comparison could read self-induced load as an interaction regression.

Fix direction: carry the invalidating transaction's provenance through to the loader runs it causes, so query timings can be split the way the counters already are. That is HandleStore-to-dispatcher plumbing in the hottest path in the app, which is why it is not folded into the perf-monitoring PR.

Currently ACCEPTED and labelled at the field declaration in interaction-metrics/record.ts.

title: bd-sync chunked-push test is load-dependent and flakes on CI
description:
The test 'prints the mappings an earlier chunk minted when a later chunk fails' (scripts/ bd-github-sync tests) failed once on CI under full-gate load and passed on the next commit with no relevant change. Standalone it passes 8/8 locally, so it is load-dependent rather than broken — the same shape as two timing races found in the perf-monitoring PR: a fence on something that is observable BEFORE the state the assertion actually depends on.

Not related to the perf-monitoring work; noticed because that PR's CI run surfaced it.

Fix direction: find what the test fences on and whether that precondition actually precedes the asserted effect; give the test an explicit timeout budgeted for the ~6x wall-clock stretch the gate imposes (one worker per core), per the timeout guidance in AGENTS.md.
close_reason: Closed on GitHub (issue #881); reconciled by bd-github-sync.

title: Decide where the shared metrics-record machinery lives
description:
Three plugins depend on interaction-metrics for machinery that is not about interaction metrics:

- recordStore.ts owns the shared record write path (appendClientRecord, clientSeriesQuery, clientGroupId); its own docblock calls itself 'the one way a metrics record reaches the graph' — a claim about all recorders, made from inside one of them.
- sessionContext.ts owns the shared eligibility and attribution rules.
- startup-metrics imports awaitRecordingAllowed, NoLongerEligible, appendClientRecord from it.
- perf-monitor imports sessionContext, recordStore and record from it.
- The composition root registers observeWorkspaceEffectContribution from it, deliberately OUTSIDE both plugin toggles — an effect that must run whether or not the plugin is enabled, living inside that plugin's module.

Plugin-to-plugin imports are legal here, so nothing is broken; this is about which module owns a rule. A shared module (metrics-records or similar) holding recordStore + sessionContext would let each plugin depend on the shared thing rather than on a sibling's internals, and would let the always-on effect be registered from a module that is not behind a toggle.

Judgement call: a move of two files and ~20 import lines, at three consumers.

title: Share the diagnostics ref-stability memo instead of hand-rolling it per source
description:
The diagnostics facet requires a source's snapshot to be referentially stable while unchanged (it feeds useSyncExternalStore). Three contributors each implement the same cachedKey/cachedSnapshot dance themselves:

- src/plugins/perf-monitor/diagnosticsSource.ts
- src/plugins/data-integrity/diagnosticsSource.ts
- src/plugins/attachments/uploadLaneStatus.ts

A memoizedDiagnosticSource({id, label, subscribe, key, build}) helper in the diagnostics facet would remove ~8 lines per source and, more to the point, remove a trap: a source that forgets the memo renders an infinite loop rather than a wrong number.

Needs a decision because it adds to the diagnostics facet's public surface and touches plugins outside the PR that found it.

title: Extension-only apiCatalog exports are tree-shaken out of the deployed build
description:
`apiCatalog.ts` promises an extension API surface the production build does not ship. Any cataloged export that no core/plugin module imports is removed by Rollup, so an extension importing it gets nothing.

**Measured against the live deploy just now — 4 of 116 cataloged exports are missing:**

```
src/facets/facet.js            :: resolveLastContributionResult
src/paste/decision.js          :: defaultPasteDecision
src/context/backgroundSubtree.js :: BackgroundSubtreeContext
src/context/backgroundSubtree.js :: BackgroundSubtreeProvider
```

Two of these predate the background-subtree work, so this is a standing hole rather than a new regression.

Concretely, the deployed `src/context/backgroundSubtree.js` is 230 bytes:

```js
import{createContext as e,useContext as t}from"react";…
var n=e(!1);function r(){return t(n)}
export{r as useIsBackgroundSubtree};
```

`useIsBackgroundSubtree` survives only because `useActionContext.ts` imports it. The provider and the context — the only two an extension needs — are gone. Net effect: the seam is unusable from an extension, which is the one consumer it was built for.

**Why nothing caught it.** `preserveModules: true` keeps the file at the right path, which makes the import resolve, so the failure is silent rather than a 404. `extensionApiRuntimeExports` is only a list read by `describeRuntime`, not a retention mechanism — nothing references these exports at build time. And `apiCatalog.test.ts` cold-imports each module and asserts every listed export exists, but it runs under vitest against **source**, where tree-shaking hasn't happened. It passes while the deploy is broken.

**How it presents to an extension.** A feature-detecting extension (`'X' in mod`, or a dynamic import behind a try/catch) degrades to "seam absent" and silently does nothing — no error, no console warning, the feature just never engages. A direct named import gets `undefined`, typically surfacing later as `undefined is not a component` inside whatever subtree mounted it.

**Fix shape.** Two halves, and the second is the one that matters:

1. Force retention — e.g. generate a barrel from `extensionApiCatalog` that references every listed export and pull it into the entry graph, so Rollup sees a live reference.
2. Verify against **built output**, not source. Whatever the fix, a check that reads the emitted files (or fetches them post-deploy) is what keeps it fixed; a source-level test structurally cannot see this class of bug.

Repro without a browser — reads the catalog from the repo and fetches each deployed module:

```js
for (const {importPath, exports} of extensionApiCatalog) {
  const rel = importPath.replace('@/', 'src/')
  const text = await (await fetch('https://stvad.github.io/knowledge-medium/' + rel)).text()
  for (const name of exports) if (!new RegExp('\\b' + name + '\\b').test(text)) console.log(rel, '::', name)
}
```

Note the running app's own module cache will lie to you here: importing `@/extensions/apiCatalog.js` in a live tab can return a stale instance, which made an earlier version of this audit report clean. Fetch the files.

title: Flaky CI: UNIQUE constraint failed: command_events.tx_id — an abandoned test Repo's write outlives resetTestDb
description:
Filed from a cloud session (no `bd` available), so this needs adopting into beads on the next sync rather than being filed there directly.

## Symptom

A CI `test` run failed in `agent-extensions/readwise.aliasConflict.test.tsx:502` with:

```
AssertionError: promise rejected "SqliteError: UNIQUE constraint failed: co…" instead of resolving
Caused by: SqliteError: UNIQUE constraint failed: command_events.tx_id
  ❯ src/data/internals/commitPipeline.ts:702
  ❯ runTx src/data/internals/commitPipeline.ts:461
```

Intermittent: the file passes 3/3 locally and the full gate passes locally; `master` is green. It surfaced on a PR whose diff touches only markdown rendering and CSS — nothing in the readwise extension, the commit pipeline, or the test harness — so what the PR changed is almost certainly *scheduling* (it adds a test file and a devDependency, which shifts which files share a worker), not behaviour.

## Mechanism

1. `command_events.tx_id` is UNIQUE, and `tx_id` comes from `newTxId`, which is `repo.newId` (`commitPipeline.ts` `newTxId: this.newId`).
2. `createTestRepo`'s default `newId` is a **deterministic counter** that restarts at `gen-1` for every Repo. Its own header already warns about this: *"each `createTestRepo()` call gets its OWN fresh `newId`/`newTxSeq` counters … Two Repos sharing one db in the same test will therefore mint COLLIDING block ids and tx-seqs."*
3. The shared-db pattern (`createTestDb` in `beforeAll`, `createTestRepo` per test, `resetTestDb` in `beforeEach`) builds a new Repo — counter back to `gen-1` — over a db whose `command_events` was just cleared.
4. So a collision needs two writes carrying the same `gen-N` between two resets: the previous test's **abandoned** Repo landing a commit after the reset, against the new Repo's restarted counter.

That is the class #813 describes (test files leaving a previous test's Repo alive on the shared db). #813 judged it harmless because "only two test files INSERT `workspace_members` rows, so the parked passes stay parked instead of waking and writing", explicitly flagged as "a property of the current test set, not a guarantee". This looks like that guarantee expiring: the readwise sync path does write, and the collision surfaces as a hard `UNIQUE` failure rather than the stderr noise #813 anticipated.

The same two earlier fixes (#812, #828) are the precedent — both were an abandoned test Repo writing into the next test's database.

## Why it is a real bug, not just flake

`resetTestDb` clearing `command_events` while ids restart at `gen-1` makes the shared-db pattern depend on no Repo ever outliving its test. Nothing enforces that. It will keep failing on whichever PR happens to shift worker scheduling, and it will point at an innocent diff each time — the expensive failure mode, since the first instinct is to look at the PR.

## Fix directions

Roughly in order of how much they buy:

1. **Dispose the Repo when its test ends**, so nothing can write after `resetTestDb`. Addresses the root cause and also #813; the blocker #813 names is that `createTestRepo` has no per-test teardown hook.
2. **Give `tx_id` a generator that cannot collide across Repos** (a per-Repo random prefix, or `uuid` for tx ids specifically while block ids stay readable `gen-N`). Cheap and narrowly targeted; readable block ids — the reason the counter exists — are unaffected, since no assertion reads a `tx_id`. This removes the *symptom* class without fixing the leak.
3. **Have `createTestDb`'s cleanup cancel in-flight passes** before closing (also listed on #813).

(2) is the smallest change that stops innocent PRs being blamed, and does not conflict with doing (1) properly afterwards. Not fixed in the PR that surfaced it, since it is unrelated to that diff and touches data-layer test infrastructure.

title: Recovery backup writes an invalid archive above 4 GiB and reports success
description:
getRawSqliteDbBackup bundles the .db and its siblings with fflate's streaming Zip, which emits no ZIP64. Past 4 GiB it writes member sizes and central-directory offsets into 32-bit fields that wrap modulo 2^32, producing a malformed archive — and then reports the backup as captured.

Measured: a 4,294,968,446-byte archive records its central directory at offset 1076 instead of 4,294,968,372, and the member's uncompressed-size field as 1024 instead of 4,294,968,320.

This is the dangerous direction. The user is told the backup succeeded, resets the local database on that basis, and is left holding an archive no tool can read correctly. Reachable as databases grow: a 2 GB database plus an uncheckpointed sidecar is already half the budget.

The restore side now refuses such an archive by size with a message naming the limit, so it fails loudly rather than mis-extracting. That does nothing for a user who already reset.

Fix directions, in rough order of preference:
1. Emit a valid ZIP64 archive (ZIP64 EOCD + locator + per-entry extra fields). fflate can READ zip64 but its writer does not produce it, so this means writing the trailer ourselves.
2. Above the limit, fall back to one download per file instead of a bundle. The bundle exists because a single download is the only reliable way to deliver several files on iOS — but a 4 GiB+ database is not an iOS case.
3. At minimum, refuse to report success: tell the user the backup could not be written and why, before they reset anything.

title: Recovery and handoff fallback screens offer no reset
description:
LocalDbHandoffFallback offers Reload and Export a backup. Several refusals route there with no database worth keeping, and reload just repeats the failure — the app never mounts, so the import action is unreachable and the only exit is clearing site data, which also takes the IndexedDB e2ee workspace keys.

Give the screen a reset action (the corruption fallback already has one), gated the same way: export first, then reset.

Pre-existing; surfaced while reviewing the recovery-restore work.

title: Deploy 2: flip MOVE_NEW_DATABASES to start moving databases to the write-ahead VFS
description:
Deploy 1 shipped in PR #851: every build now reads the record (a database with `-wa0`/`-wa1` sidecars opens with OPFSWriteAheadVFS) but creates none — `MOVE_NEW_DATABASES = false` in `src/data/localDbVfs.ts`. Only the `km.local-db-vfs=write-ahead` pin moves a database.

Deploy 2 is flipping that constant. Two named tests fail when it flips, so the change is deliberate by construction; update their expectations with it.

## Precondition

Deploy 1 must have been deployed and running before Deploy 2 goes out. Not a soak for coverage — OPFS is per-device, so a database can only have sidecars if that device ran a build that creates them — but so that there is always a safe build to roll back to.

## The rule this exists to make possible

Once Deploy 2 has run on a device, never serve that device a build older than Deploy 1. Reverting the flip is safe. Reverting the whole change is NOT: it removes the sidecar branch, and a build without it opens a moved database with CoopSync, which reads an intact but older database and silently drops whatever is still in the log (integrity_check reports ok).

## Before flipping

Run pinned on a real database first. Changing the pin, and flipping this constant, are reload boundaries: the VFS is resolved once per tab at boot, so a live change leaves two tabs on different VFSes, which cannot safely share the file. Close every tab, then change it, then open one.

## Expected benefit

Measured on a 2 GB / 350k-block database through the app: concurrent reads ~2x faster (10 concurrent 3.7ms -> 1.0ms, 40 concurrent 8.9ms -> 4.2ms). Raw per-query cost is unchanged; the win is removing queueing on PowerSync's single connection, which is what additionalReaders buys.

Full design + measurements: docs/opfs-write-ahead-vfs.md
close_reason: Shipped in PR #860, merged 2026-09-01 (dd5d5ea3b). MOVE_NEW_DATABASES is true; databases without sidecars move to OPFSWriteAheadVFS on capable browsers at next boot.

title: Readwise alias: an emptied bag is ambiguous, and a contested re-title drops backlinks
description:
Two findings from review round 13 of the alias-fallback PR, filed rather than fixed. Neither is data loss or a permanent failure; both are real.

1. AN EMPTY BAG MEANS TWO DIFFERENT THINGS. `isSyncOwnedAliasBag` is `bag.every(...)`, so an empty bag is vacuously the sync's. A user who removes every alias from an imported document has it recreated on the next sync, and cannot prevent it: the ownership marker that would say otherwise is a hidden property.

Why the fix is not one line. THREE paths empty the bag and all three currently expect to reclaim afterwards: `releaseSyncOwnedAlias` (contested re-title), `releaseCoClaimedFallback` (a co-claimed fallback before a property write), and `ensureDocumentAlias` itself when no suffix slot is free. Making "empty bag + recorded claim" mean "the user cleared it" requires each of those to clear its own claim record as it goes, or they stop being able to rename. That is three interacting edits to paths whose interactions this branch has already gotten wrong twice in consecutive rounds.

2. A CONTESTED RE-TITLE DROPS ITS BACKLINKS. `releaseSyncOwnedAlias` empties the bag so the content rewrite can commit, but an empty bag is the one shape `alias.sync` rule 1 skips — so `references.renameBacklinks` sees no old-to-new diff and every `[[Old Title]]` keeps pointing at a name this document no longer holds. The uncontested path carries them across and is tested; the contested path was always the trade for the book landing at all, but nothing says so at the call site and nothing tests it.

Fixing 2 properly means the extension retargeting backlinks itself, duplicating what `references.renameBacklinks` does. Cheaper honest option: state the trade where the release happens, and pin it with a test so it is a decision rather than an accident.

title: SRS review: derive on-screen key hints from effective bindings
description:
Every keyboard hint in the review session is a hard-coded default: the "Show answer" button's `space` label and the four grade buttons' hints in `GRADE_BUTTONS` (`1`, `2`, `3 · space`, `4`) in `src/plugins/srs-review/ReviewSession.tsx`. If the user remaps or unbinds `srs-review.reveal` or the `srs-review.grade.*` actions (`src/plugins/srs-review/actions.ts`), the buttons keep advertising keys that no longer work.

Codex flagged the Good-button hint on PR #852; it was declined there because making one hint binding-aware while its neighbours stay hard-coded doesn't close the gap — the fix should cover the whole surface at once.

**Direction**: the override-reactive source already exists — `useActionDiscovery` (see `src/plugins/shortcut-help/ShortcutHelpOverlay.tsx`) returns effective actions with effective bindings, and `formatChord` (`src/plugins/keybindings-settings/keyCapture.ts`) formats chords for display. Derive each hint from its action id's effective binding; omit the hint when the action is unbound. Weigh the cost of mounting the full discovery pass per session — a narrower lookup keyed on the five action ids is fine as long as it reacts to keybinding overrides.

**Done looks like**: remapping `srs-review.reveal` or a grade action updates the session's hints without a reload; hints for unbound actions disappear; a test pins at least one of these.

title: Restoring a recovery zip drops outstanding write-ahead frames
description:
The recovery backup (`getRawSqliteDbBackup`) bundles the main `.db` plus its sibling files, which now includes OPFSWriteAheadVFS's `-wa0`/`-wa1` write-ahead sidecars. But the restore path (`importRawSqliteDb`) takes a single `.db` file and deletes every sibling before writing it.

So a zip captured while committed transactions were still in the sidecars restores an intact-looking database that is missing those transactions. The database opens, `PRAGMA integrity_check` reports ok, and the loss is silent.

The recovery path cannot checkpoint on capture — it runs precisely when the database will not open, with no working connection.

Fix direction: teach the restore path to accept the zip (write the sidecars back alongside the `.db` so the next open replays them), or checkpoint-on-capture when a connection happens to be available and mark the zip as complete/incomplete so restore can warn.

Context: docs/opfs-write-ahead-vfs.md
close_reason: Closed on GitHub (issue #849); reconciled by bd-github-sync.

title: scheduleDeepIdle drops minDelayMs when requestIdleCallback is absent
description:
scheduleDeepIdle drops minDelayMs when requestIdleCallback is absent

`src/utils/scheduleIdle.ts`: `scheduleDeepIdle` opens with

    if (typeof ric !== 'function') { setTimeout(fn, 0); return }

so in any runtime without `requestIdleCallback` BOTH guarantees the function
exists to provide are gone: the `minDelayMs` wall-clock floor and the
genuine-idle gating. The job runs on the next macrotask, i.e. inside the
cold-start window — which is precisely what `scheduleDeepIdle` was introduced to
prevent (it exists because `scheduleIdle`'s 2s cap fired during first paint).

The docstring frames this as the "Test / Node path", and that is the intent, but
the branch keys on the ABSENCE OF AN API rather than on being under test. Every
LAZY_DEEP_IDLE and CATCHUP_DEEP_IDLE consumer inherits it: the data-integrity
audit, prefs bootstraps, the update indicator, the workspace catch-up passes, and
(as of the #833 work) a multi-second exact-stats ANALYZE.

Reachability: Safari gained `requestIdleCallback` in 16.4, so current Safari and
iOS are fine. Older iOS WebViews and any embedded webview without it are not.
Worth checking what the app's supported floor actually is before sizing this.

Possible shapes, roughly in order of appetite:
- honour `minDelayMs` in the no-rIC branch (`setTimeout(fn, opts.minDelayMs)`)
  and, for options with no `fallbackMs`, decline to run at all rather than
  force-running. Care needed: the current `setTimeout(fn, 0)` is load-bearing for
  test drain helpers (`vi.runAllTimersAsync`, real-timer `setTimeout(0)`), so the
  test path probably wants to key on an explicit test signal rather than on the
  missing API.
- ship a tiny `requestIdleCallback` shim for the browsers that lack it.
- accept and document, if the supported-browser floor makes it unreachable.

Found while reviewing the #833 warm-boot fix. Pre-existing; that PR only makes it
more consequential by putting a heavier job on the tier.

title: Alias merge has no seam for blocks a sync would restore
description:
`DuplicateNameBanner` offers to merge any live claimant of a contested name. For a block whose owner recreates it from a deterministic id — a Readwise document, keyed on user_book_id — that merge is not durable: it tombstones the rival, and the next sync of that record restores it, recreating the collision with half the merge applied.

The Readwise conflict dialog already refuses this case (`managedRival`), so the two entry points to the same merge now disagree. That inconsistency is the immediate problem; the deeper one is that the check lives in the extension, where only one of the two callers can see it.

WHY IT NEEDS A SEAM: `src/plugins/alias/` cannot import a user extension — extensions live in the DB, and the dependency runs the wrong way. So the knowledge "blocks of this type are restored by their owner, do not offer to absorb them" has to be declared where core can read it and contributed by whoever owns the type.

Sketch: a facet listing block types that must not be merge SOURCES. The banner filters rivals through it and explains when it cannot offer a merge; the Readwise extension contributes its document type; the extension's local `managedRival` computation is deleted in favour of reading the same facet. Net effect is one rule with two readers instead of two rules with one reader each.

REACHABILITY NOTE: two Readwise records sharing a title could not coexist before the alias-fallback work — the second one's sync aborted rather than creating the document. So that branch is what makes this reachable, which is worth weighing when deciding whether it blocks landing.

title: Replace the ANALYZE arming probes with PRAGMA optimize(0x10002)
description:
Replace the ANALYZE arming probes with PRAGMA optimize(0x10002)

`PRAGMA optimize`'s stale-stats rule only considers tables the CONNECTION has
planned a query against, which is why `ANALYZE_ARMING_PROBES` exists: four
EXPLAIN-free `SELECT`s issued purely to announce interest before the optimize.

SQLite's own documented advice for long-lived connections is `PRAGMA
optimize=0x10002`. The `0x10000` bit ("analyze all tables") satisfies that
determination rule for EVERY table, removing the precondition the probes exist
to satisfy, while still dropping `0x10` (the built-in 2000-row sample cap we
must keep off).

Measured on the production wa-sqlite build:
- settled 300k-row fixture: `optimize(0x10002)` 0.1-0.3ms, against 10.1ms for
  the current four probes + `optimize(0x02)`
- degenerate "0 0" stats on a 300k-row table the connection had never planned
  against: `0x10002` with NO arming repaired it in 56ms — precisely the case the
  arming test says only the probes can fix

It also closes a standing gap rather than only being faster. The four probes arm
`blocks`, `block_references`, `block_types`, `block_aliases` only. `row_events`,
`blocks_synced`, `command_events`, the FTS shadow tables and every future
plugin-contributed table can currently be re-analyzed ONLY via the missing-stat-
row rule — once they hold any stat row (including a "0 0" written while empty at
boot 1) they are frozen forever. And it removes a plugin table name
(`block_references`) hardcoded into a core constant.

Dry run would become `0x10003`.

Trade to weigh: `0x10000` makes never-queried tables eligible for drift-triggered
re-ANALYZE. That is the point, and it measured free on a settled database — but
it widens what a stale-stats boot can decide to do, so it wants its own
measurement on a large client before shipping.

Found during the #833 warm-boot fix. Deliberately not done there: it changes a
pre-existing documented mechanism with its own tests and doctrine, which is a
different change from fixing the regression.
close_reason:
Declined after measurement. The cost side was fine; the BENEFIT is what failed to hold up.
Full evidence is in the comment above — the short version, so nobody re-opens this from the
description alone:

1. **The gap it was meant to close is empty.** On a live 350k-block client, settled:
   `PRAGMA optimize(0x03)` proposes `[]` and `PRAGMA optimize(0x10003)` proposes exactly one
   thing — `ANALYZE "main"."ps_crud"`, a permanent no-op on an empty table. The tables the
   description called frozen carry exactly-current stats (row_events 482526 vs a live 482526,
   ps_oplog 349909 vs 349909, blocks_synced 349898 vs 349898).

2. **Arming is satisfied by ordinary traffic, not only by the probes.** With row_events and
   ps_oplog drifted >10x and no probes at all, one ordinary indexed SELECT against a table
   repairs it under plain `optimize(0x02)`. So a table the app queries is already corrected;
   a table it never queries has no plan on that connection for stale stats to harm. The
   missing-stat-row rule needs no arming either. Sharpest case: nothing in `src/` ever SELECTs
   from row_events (the events tail is deferred, so it is write-only) — it is the largest
   table 0x10000 would newly authorize work on, and no query reads it.

3. **It has a cost that was not on the original list.** An EMPTY table carries no
   sqlite_stat1 row, so the missing-row rule fires on it forever and "a settled boot proposes
   nothing" stops being true permanently. On a real client the residue is `ps_crud`, which is
   empty precisely when sync is HEALTHY — so repoProvider would log an ANALYZE line every
   boot for the life of the app, which is exactly the signal that log line exists to carry.
   Cheap (0.8ms, writes nothing) but it is signal loss, and filtering it is new surface.

4. **Two of the three failing tests would have to be weakened, not re-pointed.** With the
   change applied: 93 pass, 3 fail. `does not repair them without the probes` is the
   revert-test and could legitimately be inverted into a pin on the 0x10000 bit; but
   `leaves a settled database alone` and `reports the tables it decided to re-analyze` would
   have to be relaxed to tolerate permanent phantom entries, which gives up a real contract.

Measured cost side, recorded so it does not need redoing: worst new case on the forcing
catch-up tier is ~270ms warm (~1.8s at the cold ratio) against ~200ms today, and only above a
>10x drift on tables that grow monotonically with nothing pruning them. Fresh device — the
true worst case — is unchanged (614ms vs 619ms). Both original claims reproduce on the
shipped wasm: `0x10002` repairs degenerate `"0 0"` unarmed, and keeps the 2000-row sample cap
off.

The one piece of the rationale that survived is tracked separately as km-ne6x: core hardcodes
`block_references`, a plugin-owned table, in `ANALYZE_ARMING_PROBES`. That is a real
kernel/plugin leak and it does not need a mask change — plugins can contribute their own
probes through the existing `LocalSchemaContribution` seam.

Revisit only if one of these changes: a query path starts reading row_events or another
unprobed large table, or a SQLite upgrade changes what `0x10000` means.

title: Perf monitor: consolidate the 'what can this session honestly say' state
description:
Five review findings from the fifth round on the perf-monitoring PR, plus the
diagnosis of why rounds keep producing them. Filed rather than fixed inline: the
fifth round crossed the "the fixes are generating the findings" line, so the
open question is the SHAPE, not these five patches.

## The five findings (all verified real)

1. The trend dialog ignores per-series readiness and says "No slowdowns against
   the last 0 sessions" -- the day-one state for every existing user, who has
   startup history and no interaction history. The chip was taught this; its
   sibling consumer was not.
2. The recorder and the monitor are independent toggles. With the recorder off
   and the monitor on, nothing observes workspace activation, so the monitor
   treats page-global counters blended across workspaces as attributable.
3. Readiness counts ROWS, not usable samples. Seven records with no writes, or
   startup records missing their paint marks, satisfy the check while every
   comparison returns null -- a clean verdict from nothing judged.
4. The startup comparison takes the three newest records as "current" even when
   none of them is from this boot (write failed, recorder disabled, read-only,
   or the analysis raced the fallback write), so it can repeat a stale verdict.
5. The startup recorder's deferred write is not cancelled on effect teardown, so
   it can fire against the old workspace after a switch. Pre-existing, not
   introduced by the PR.

## The diagnosis

Nineteen findings across four rounds, and the recurring defect is ONE class:
**two or more consumers must agree about a piece of session state, and each
checks it independently.** Six instances so far -- recorder vs analyzer on
attributability; effect-start vs write-time on workspace observation; chip vs
dialog on readiness; alarm vs table on the fan-out metric; recorder-enabled vs
monitor-enabled on who observes workspaces; idle-scheduler vs plain timer on the
sampling floor. Each fix moved a rule to the right place for ONE pair and left
the next pair to be found by the next round.

Root cause: there is no single owner of the question "what can this session
honestly say?" The facts (persistent client id, read-only workspace, more than
one workspace seen, the recorder's own writes, per-series usable samples) are
scattered across the modules that happen to need them.

## The shape that would end the class

One session-context module owning every can-we-measure / can-we-compare fact,
computed once and consumed by all: the recorder asks "may I write?", the
analyzer asks "may I compare?", and the chip and dialog render the SAME verdict
object rather than each deciding. Workspace observation belongs to that module
rather than to whichever plugin happens to be enabled.

Mostly moving existing code, not new code. Would collapse findings 1-3 above
into one place and prevent the next batch.

## The alternative worth weighing

The verdict/alarm logic is where essentially all nineteen findings live. The
recorder and the trend table have produced almost none. A narrower feature --
keep recording, provide the read path, drop the automated verdict -- deletes the
entire surface. Noted because it is a real option, not because it is
recommended: the automated alarm is the thing that was actually asked for.

title: Static gate tests for the two performance-regression classes
description:
Complement to the runtime monitor (see the metrics/monitoring issue): two
assertions that run in `pnpm run check` and need no telemetry at all. Both
catch their bug class at authoring time rather than after it ships.

1. **No workspace-wide invalidation channel on an expensive query.** A query
   that registers a dep keyed on the workspace alone re-resolves on every write
   in the graph. The grouped-backlinks regression would have failed such a test
   the day it was introduced. The runtime monitor catches this class only after
   several sessions of history; a static test catches it in the PR.

2. **Query-plan assertions for the hot statements.** Seed enough rows, ANALYZE,
   assert `EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN` contains no `AUTOMATIC COVERING INDEX` over a
   CTE. Proven cheap -- reproduces from ~2k rows in ~2s. The pattern already
   exists at `src/plugins/grouped-backlinks/test/candidatesJoinOrder.test.ts`;
   this is about deciding which other statements deserve one and adding them.

Note for whoever picks this up: `scripts/bench/` is NOT a usable substrate. It
was quarantined as non-compiling dead code (it predates the Layout B sync
redesign -- raw-maps `blocks` instead of `blocks_synced`, drives the removed

title: Flip & migrate should repair a durable materialization gap before refusing
description:
The properties migration refuses when `workspaceViewGap`'s durable arm fires: rows this device downloaded, could not apply, and consumed the queue entry for. Since the rematerialization verb landed, the remedy for that refusal is a local, safe, idempotent derivation pass — but the operator has to know the verb exists, leave the dialog, run it, and come back.

Wanted: at the migration's PRE-DIALOG eligibility check (the cheap early exit, before the count and the consent dialog), when the unfitness is the durable materialization gap specifically, run the narrow-scope rematerialization once and re-take the predicate.

Constraints, each load-bearing:
- Narrow scope only. The wide scope is a full pass over the workspace and can leave the gap larger; that stays a deliberate operator choice.
- Once, not looped. If the repair does not clear it, the remaining causes are deferred (workspace not materializable) and quarantined (ciphertext that will not decode), and neither is fixed by running again.
- The gate keeps its veto: re-take the predicate after the repair, so the flip still proceeds only on a clean view. This removes a manual step, not a check.
- Not silently: report how many rows were repaired, and when it does not clear, surface the residual deferred/quarantined counts.
- The per-transaction re-check must NOT gain this. It runs inside every writing transaction; a minutes-long repair there is categorically wrong. Pre-flight repair and per-tx veto are different layers.

Known cost: auto-running inherits the short ack-to-echo revert window without the operator choosing it. It is already gated behind nothing being in flight on the download side, and self-heals on the echo.

Follows from the PR that added the verb.
notes: PR 1135 merged at 2026-09-23T04:46:38Z as 4ab8f8e5e79e7f1166f0723b68da872518641e0b. Shipped one narrow pre-dialog recovery with fresh snapshot eligibility and claim ordering. All review threads resolved; ack-to-echo limitation explicitly retained per scope. Latest head CI passed and local full gate passed 733 files, 10161 tests. PR monitor stopped after merge. Task closure left to merge reconciliation.

title: The deferred property-migration batch re-keys cells with an unsettled write, so MATERIALIZE re-derives from it
description:
A same-tx processor can declare settledWrites, which stops the derivation re-run from treating its writes as user intent. The deferred property-definition migration batch cannot: it writes through an ordinary repo.tx, so MATERIALIZE runs on its consuming-cell re-key and re-derives the children from it.

Two consequences have already had to be patched individually:

1. Dropping an old name that an un-shadowed peer now answers to made MATERIALIZE read the missing key as a user deletion and tombstone that peer's field rows and value children. Patched by refusing the contested rename outright.

2. An applied rename re-materializes its value children canonically, so value text that is parseable but not canonical is normalized (measured: 1.50 becomes 1.5; a ref written as a labelled span comes back as a bare id span). Low impact today, because nothing in the app writes non-canonical value content and every other cell write normalizes it the same way. The same-tx rename path does NOT do this, and that asymmetry is the tell.

Both are symptoms of the same gap. The same-tx rename processor's own justification for settledWrites applies verbatim to this batch: the cells it writes are projected FROM the field rows, so they are convergent with the children by construction and re-deriving from them buys nothing.

Fix direction: a settled-write mode a plain repo.tx caller can opt into, so the batch can declare what the processor already declares. That is a commit-pipeline change with real subtleties (see the settledFieldPaths and maskSettledPaths reasoning there), which is why it is filed rather than folded into the rename work.

Found while reviewing the durable property-definitions baseline.

title: Seed-provenanced property definitions have no migration path when their declared name or codec changes across a client upgrade
description:
A property seed's declared name and codec are code-owned. If a release changes either, existing workspaces hold cells keyed by the OLD name (and values encoded under the OLD codec) and nothing migrates them: the same-tx rename processor only fires for a definition-block edit made through repo.tx, and the definitions baseline (issue 780) deliberately excludes seed-provenanced definitions.

The exclusion is correct as far as it goes. A seed's effective name flips with whether the seed is currently registered — the registry answers the DECLARED name while it is loaded and the STORED row name otherwise — so a build that catches a dynamic extension mid-load would diff a phantom rename and re-key every consuming cell onto a name the app stops resolving a moment later. Including seeds in the baseline trades a missing migration for graph-wide corruption, which is the wrong trade.

What is missing is the deliberate version: a seed change should carry its own declared migration (old name -> new name, old codec -> new codec) that runs once per graph, rather than being inferred from a diff that cannot tell an upgrade from a load-order artifact.

Not urgent: it bites only when a seed is actually renamed or re-typed, which has not happened yet. File before it does.

title: changedPropertyDefinitions compares codec.type only, so a string to optionalString swap schedules no migration
description:
Found by an adversarial review of PR #751, verified against master; predates that PR and is not in its diff.

src/data/internals/propertyDefinitionMigrations.ts computes codecChanged by comparing .codec.type. codecs.string and codecs.optionalString BOTH report type "string" (src/data/api/codecs.ts), and a fieldId derives only from the seedKey (propertyDefinitionBlockId) -- not from preset or revision. So widening an existing required text property to be clearable keeps the same fieldId, reports no codec change, and never schedules runPropertyDefinitionMigrationBatch. The stored values are left to lazy re-decode under the new codec.

That matters because the two codecs disagree about one specific content string. A value literally typed as the 4 characters "null" stores VERBATIM under the required schema, correctly -- there is no sentinel to protect, so no escaping applies. Swap the preset to optional-string and the next projection re-decodes the same untouched content through the branch content.trim() === "null" AND codecAcceptsNull(schema), which is now true, and reads it as the UNSET sentinel. The property silently reads empty. No error, no unconvertible count.

Reachable in principle rather than through a known UI path today, but the repo already declares 10+ optional-string properties, and widening a required field to optional is an ordinary thing for a plugin author to do.

Fix direction: broaden the codecChanged comparison so it also fires on a codecAcceptsNull difference, not just .codec.type -- then the batch runs and re-encodes the value, which escapes the literal "null" under the new codec and preserves it.

Worth a test either way: there is currently NO cross-schema decode coverage anywhere (a value written under codec A and read under codec B), which is why neither the fuzz suite nor PR #751 caught it.
close_reason: Superseded by #1013 (PR #1018): the deferred detector this described, the codec.type comparison in propertyDefinitionMigrations.ts, was deleted with that file. The same-tx definition-change processor keys 'did the encoding change' on the definition row's preset id and preset config, which does see a string to optional-string swap. Verified on master 2026-09-17.

title: A repair that turns a row into a field row leaves its stale content backlink
description:
Split out of the post-flip healing-seams umbrella (item 5). Reachable only in a child-backed workspace — which in a TEST is one column value, so this is fixable and testable today and does not wait on a real flip.

The reference-target stamping path (the per-open sweep and the added-definition rederive) updates only the local reference-target column and fans out handle invalidations. It does not re-run reference parsing. So when a repair turns an existing exact schema-reference child INTO a recognized field row, any stale content backlink that row carried from its pre-machinery life stays intact — the machinery-row suppression only runs at parse time.

FIX DIRECTION: schedule a references reconcile for rows whose stamp transitions them into a property field target, or fold that cleanup into the repair path itself.

RELATED, and belongs with this work rather than its own issue: the added-definition and rename rederive only ever RE-STAMPS, never CLEARS. A row referencing a name that, after a rename, resolves to nothing keeps its stale field-id stamp instead of clearing to null. Benign in practice — root rows are position-exempt, and genuine field rows get retitled by the definition-migration pass — but the clear-to-null transition is the same reconcile.
close_reason:
Verified against current code: the primary claim does not reproduce, and the sibling has been split out.

PRIMARY — 'a repair that turns a row into a field row leaves its stale content backlink'. The premise was that machinery-row suppression runs at parse time. That suppression (isPropertyMachineryRow + suppressContentMarks in the references processor) was deleted in cada335f8 on 2026-07-17, the day after the review that filed this item, and is on master. Today buildSourcePlan reads content, properties, references, the alias index and the property-schema registry and nothing else — never is_field_form, reference_target_id or the parent chain — so parse output is recognition-independent and a recognition change cannot make it stale. The suppression that replaced it, propertyMachinerySourceIds, is a live recursive query over the current parent chain, evaluated per backlinks query.

Measured across the catch-up sweep in a child-backed workspace, with the row's references pre-seeded as an upgrading device holds them: the machinery filter over [field row, value row] answers {} before the stamp and {value row} after, while both rows' stored references are unchanged. The stored edges staying put is deliberate — they are what definition merge and rename retarget reach; what changes is how they read.

Pinned by a regression test in the derive-pass suite, mutation-checked against every clause it depends on. PR #784.

SIBLING — 'only ever re-stamps, never clears'. The rename half was fixed in 0f2eca6f7 on 2026-07-30 (the processor recomputes both derived columns from the rewritten content and clears on an unresolvable alias). The remaining half is REAL, not benign as this issue guessed, and not covered by the same-device pinning path: a row that was not local when an alias release was processed keeps a stamp the releasing device never pinned, and no repair revisits an already-stamped row. Split out with its reachability chain and fix direction rather than left on this issue — see the related issue.

Adversarial review also turned up a pre-existing read-side coverage gap in the recognition predicate, filed separately.

title: Loaded children handles keep their pre-flip visible set when the flip arrives over sync
description:
Split out of the post-flip healing-seams umbrella (item 1), which was filed as one issue because all six share a cause: the flip changes which side of the cell/children pair is the truth, so every repair rule has a different answer on each side of it. Reachable only in a child-backed workspace — which in a TEST is one column value, so this is fixable and testable today and does not wait on a real flip.

`core.children` / `core.childIds` default to the visible-children query, whose predicate reads the workspace's properties_migration column — but the handles declare only a parent-edge dependency. A properties_migration change arriving via sync while the app is running invalidates nothing, so already-loaded handles keep their PRE-FLIP visible set until some child under that parent changes, or the app reloads.

Recognition changes driven by definition adds and renames are NOT affected: those stamp the rows' reference_target_id, and the stamping processor fans out parent-edge invalidations.

THIS IS A DECISION MORE THAN A BUG. Two options were recorded when it was found: (a) the flip tooling requires or prompts an app reload on each client — a flip is a once-per-workspace coordinated operator event, so this may be all that is wanted; or (b) a workspaces-table observer that triggers a broad handle invalidation when properties_migration changes, which is permanent machinery for an event that fires once per workspace ever.

Cheap to settle, and it should be settled before the first flip because the runbook has to say one or the other.
close_reason:
The mechanism this described no longer exists. The visible-children predicate does not read properties_migration — it is recognition-based (is_field_form set, plus a reference target that is a property-schema block or a registry seed id), and the treeQueries docblock states the removal deliberately: not gated on the column, so it answers the same for a backfilled pre-flip workspace as for a flipped one. So a flip arriving over sync cannot stale a loaded handle: the flip is not an input to the query.

Checked every other reader of the column for cached state that could survive the arrival, and found none. isPropertyChildBackedWorkspace — the gate behind dual-write, projection, materialize and the seat reaper — is cached per repo.tx only and re-read every transaction, which its own comment states is deliberate because the column is synced-only and never written through the engine. The workspaces hook is a reactive PowerSync query whose docblock notes changes reach subscribers without a reload. The backlink inline-count gate was rewritten to ask the rows whether machinery exists rather than asking the column.

So no reload is required on other clients for this reason, and there is no runbook item here. Verified 2026-08-23.

Note for whoever works the pre-flip retirement: the two gates removed above were removed BECAUSE the pre-flip backfill breaks the premise that an un-flipped workspace holds no field rows. That is backfill-then-flip reasoning, and under flip-first the premise holds again. The code is right either way — asking the rows beats asking the column — but the stated rationale at those sites is now obsolete.

title: Merge catch-up materializes property children with no flip check
description:
blockMerge's pre-backfill catch-up calls materializePropertyChildrenForExistingRow with no properties-migration gate, so it can mint field and value child rows in a workspace that has NOT flipped to child-backed properties.

WHERE. src/data/blockMerge.ts, the pendingByName loop and the materialize call after it. Grep confirms the file contains no isPropertyChildBackedWorkspace / isChildBackedRow / properties_migration check anywhere. Reached from the plain merge mutator and from alias-collision merge, neither of which gates on flip state.

WHY IT IS REACHABLE PRE-FLIP. The catch-up fires when the source block has a property field row whose fieldId the target does not have a row for, and the target's CELL already carries that key. Un-flipped, a source can hold such a field row because is_field_form is stamped from CONTENT by the derive pass, not by the migration state: a hand-written property-field block has the shape. Merge that block into one whose cell already carries the key and the catch-up mints children on the target, in a workspace still reading cells.

WHY IT MATTERS. That is the state the whole flip-then-backfill runbook exists to avoid: children that no live processor maintains, because the projection is dormant until the flip. They are correct at creation but diverge from the cell on the next edit, and at flip time the children become authoritative, so a stale child silently wins over the value the user can see. It also means the comments asserting no machinery mints these rows pre-flip are only true of the backfill and the dual-write.

CONTEXT. The catch-up's own comment describes the window it was written for as 'between a workspace flipping and the backfill reaching into' — i.e. it assumes a flipped workspace. Nothing enforces that assumption.

NOT URGENT: no workspace has flipped, and the precondition needs a hand-authored property-field block. Worth settling before the first real migration, since the damage lands at flip time.

POSSIBLE ANSWERS, not yet chosen: gate the catch-up on the flip the way the dual-write does; or decide the catch-up is safe un-flipped because it writes only what the cell already says, and record that with the reason.
close_reason: Closed on GitHub (issue #773); reconciled by bd-github-sync.

title: Setting a property overwrites a value row the user retyped as free text, in place
description:
Split out of the block-merge reaping fix (GitHub #728), which is only about merge DELETING a field row. This one is a separate mechanism with a wider blast radius, and it needs no merge at all.

## Repro (flipped workspace, number property)

1. setProperty(x, count, 42) — mints a field row plus a value child "42".
2. The user retypes the value as free text ("about forty-two"). PROJECT unsets the cell key and deliberately keeps the rows visible/fixable (reprojectParentField, src/data/internals/propertyChildrenProcessor.ts).
3. The user adds a child note under that value.
4. setProperty(x, count, 7) — no merge anywhere.

Result: the value block's content is rewritten in place from "about forty-two" to "7". The user's typed text is gone with no tombstone to recover it from; the note survives but now hangs under a value that reads "7".

Verified with a standalone probe against a real test repo, no merge involved.

## Where

materializePropertyChildrenForExistingRow, the primary-value update:

    const [primaryValue, ...duplicateValues] = values
    if (primaryValue) {
      if (primaryValue.content !== content) {
        await tx.update(primaryValue.id, {content})
      }

Cell-wins on the FIRST value child. That is the right rule for an ordinary setProperty over a value the cell already agreed with; it is questionable when the cell key is UNSET precisely because the user's text does not decode, which is a state the property system produces on purpose to keep the text fixable.

## Why it matters beyond setProperty

It also makes a multi-source fold order-dependent: folding a keyless-row source together with a source holding a decodable value for the same property loses the keyless source's text when it folds FIRST (its row becomes the survivor's primary and materialize rewrites it), and keeps it as a peer value when it folds SECOND. Fold order is created_at ascending — arbitrary from the user's point of view.

## Options, not yet decided

- Treat an undecodable primary value as a DIVERGENT sibling rather than a slot to overwrite: append the new value and keep the user's text as a peer, the way collapseDuplicateFieldRow already handles divergent values.
- Or accept it and say so at the declaration, on the grounds that setProperty is an explicit overwrite gesture and history covers recovery. Note history does NOT cover it the way a tombstone would — this is an in-place content edit.

The deliberate-divergence comment in reprojectParentField ("rows stay visible/fixable") is the intent this is in tension with, so whichever way it goes should be stated in one of the two places.
close_reason: Working as intended. One undo restores the overwritten text (same-tx processor write, same undo entry); setProperty is an explicit overwrite gesture and a value row is a normal block. Severity was imported from the adjacent merge-reaping bug without checking the mechanism. Rationale on GitHub issue #768.

title: bd-github-sync mints a duplicate issue for a bead created in the same session
description:
OBSERVED (2026-08-22, one `pnpm bd:sync` run): four beads created earlier in the session were pushed, and two of them got TWO GitHub issues each.

  run output:  minted: km-m2li -> #757, km-iow1 -> #759, km-406m -> #761
  after the run, bd show:  km-iow1 External -> #762,  km-406m External -> #763

#759 and #762 are byte-identical issues for km-iow1; #761 and #763 likewise for km-406m. The bead points at the SECOND one, so the first is orphaned — no bead references it, and close-adoption (which matches on external_ref) can never see it. I closed #759 and #761 by hand as duplicates. km-m2li and km-xgnp came through the same run with one issue each.

HYPOTHESIS (not verified — the run is not reproducible without minting more public issues): the wrapper pushes before the pull (trap 4), so the pre-pull push mints the issue and stamps external_ref. The pull then reverts those fresh rows, and step 2.5 restores the PRE-SYNC snapshot — which predates the mint and therefore carries external_ref = null. The final push sees a bead with no external ref and mints a second issue. planMintedRefs already reasons about refs appearing between two listings for the id-map; the restore path appears not to protect the ref it just gained.

WHY IT MATTERS: every duplicate is a public issue on a public repo, and the orphan is invisible to every subsequent sync — it will never be closed, relabelled or adopted, so it sits open forever unless someone notices. The failure is silent: the run reports success and prints a minted mapping that is then wrong, so an agent following the documented 'read the number from the mint output' path writes the WRONG issue number into a PR body or a commit message.

FIX DIRECTION: exclude external_ref from what the restore replays (or re-stamp the post-mint ref after the restore), and make the minted-mapping line print the ref as it stands at the END of the run, so the number an agent copies is the number the bead actually holds.

Related: the id-map reasoning at scripts/bd-github-sync.mjs planMintedRefs / planMintedNonOpen.

title: Renaming a block-type whose content diverges from its label leaves the old alias claimed
description:
Renaming a user-defined type through the type editor can leave the OLD name's alias claimed, so [[OldName]] keeps resolving to the renamed type and the old name is permanently unusable for any other block (block_aliases_workspace_alias_unique).

MECHANISM (read at the source): writeBlockTypeLabel's rename branch writes the label and mirrors it into content in one tx, then leans on aliasSyncProcessor to reconcile the alias set. planSync (src/plugins/alias/syncProcessor.ts) only REPLACES when `afterAliases.includes(before.content)` (Rule 1); otherwise it heals additively by APPENDING the new content (Rule 2). So whenever content != label before the rename, the replace never matches and the old alias survives alongside the new one.

MEASURED (repo with aliasDataExtension registered):
  content 'Type body text', label 'Widget', alias ['Widget'] -> rename to 'Gadget' -> alias ['Widget','Gadget'], [[Widget]] still resolves to the type
  content ' Padded ', label ' Padded ', alias ['Padded'] (typeify trims the alias, not the label) -> rename to 'Gadget' -> alias ['Padded','Gadget']

Note the second shape: a PADDED label diverges from its own trimmed alias, so this does not need an exotic fixture.

WHY IT SURFACED NOW: an untouched blur used to normalize content := label, which happened to restore the content == label == alias invariant that blockTypeTypeifyProcessor's own comment says a later rename depends on. PR #748 stops the editor writing on a blur nobody edited, which removes that accidental healing. The rename bug itself is older and is reachable without it — a user who renames such a type directly never gets the healing pass either.

FIX DIRECTION: reconcile in the rename branch of writeBlockTypeLabel the way the blank branch already does — read the stored label/content inside the tx, drop alias entries matching them, ensure the new name is present — instead of relying on aliasSyncProcessor's content match. Needs its own tests WITH the alias plugin registered: the existing BlockTypeBlockRenderer tests build a repo without it, which is why nothing caught this.

Found by an adversarial review agent on PR #748.
notes:
FIX DIRECTION SUPERSEDED. The direction recorded above — reconcile inside writeBlockTypeLabel's rename branch — was implemented and declined. It contradicts alias.sync rule 2's deliberately additive drift heal, contradicts the existing test 'does not overwrite an existing alias when the label is renamed' (whose comment puts rename reconciliation in aliasSyncProcessor), and cannot distinguish the type's own name claim from a user-added alias that happens to equal the label — so it would silently delete the latter. PR #508 merged without that part.

Taken instead: prevent the divergence at its source in core.blockTypeTypeify. The explicit-label branch was the only TAGGING path that could mint content != label != alias; it now refuses (ProcessorRejection 'blockType.nameConflict') when both are non-empty and differ, and ALIGNS content to the label when content is blank or whitespace-only (lossless). That covers both shapes measured above, including the padded-label one this issue calls the non-exotic case: content is aligned to the trimmed name the alias carries, so the rename hits rule 1 and replaces.

Residual, filed separately: divergence created AFTER the block is already a type (a content rewrite runs no reconciliation) — km-8hav.
close_reason: Closed on GitHub (issue #757); reconciled by bd-github-sync.

title: Flaky: stagingNeedsApplyMigration backlog test has no headroom under gate load
description:
`src/data/test/stagingNeedsApplyMigration.test.ts` > 'seeds a backlog larger than one chunk' measures 1637ms solo and runs under vitest's 5000ms default. Per AGENTS.md's timeout-budget rule (~3x at p99, ~6x at p99.9 under one-worker-per-core gate load) that is ~4.9s at p99, so it times out in the full gate. Observed once on 2026-08-22: the test timed out at 5000ms, and its sibling 'is a no-op on a table that already has the column and the marker' then failed with 'no such column: needs_apply' because the timed-out test left rewindToPreMigration half-applied on the shared DB.

Fix per the house rule: give it an explicit `it(..., 20_000)` with a comment naming the measured cost. Do not raise the global testTimeout.

The file passes when run alone.
