title: Restoring a tombstoned definition leaves its own property children tombstoned
description:
In a child-backed workspace a definition block's own metadata (its name, preset,
config, visibility, change-scope, any custom default) is stored as property
CHILDREN of that block, like every other property. Deleting the definition
through the normal subtree delete tombstones those children along with the root.

Orphan-definition synthesis (#686) restores a tombstoned definition with
`tx.restore(id, patch)`, which restores the ROOT ROW only. The same-tx
materializer then diffs the tombstone's stored bag against the patch, so any
metadata key whose value is unchanged produces no replacement child — and the
cell→children backfill deliberately refuses to recreate a key whose field target
is tombstoned (`Tx.reapedPropertyFieldTargets`, added in the same PR).

Net effect: the definition resolves and behaves correctly at
`properties_migration = 'children'`, because the cell is still the authoritative
read surface for a key with no children (§5's pending-materialization rule). The
loss only becomes real at `cell-off`, where the cell stops carrying the value —
at which point the definition loses metadata and stops resolving.

Not fixed in #686 because the consequence is gated behind a migration step that
does not exist yet, and the fix is not small: there is `deleteSubtreeInTx` but no
restore counterpart, so it means either restoring the tombstoned property-child
subtree alongside the root, or forcing rematerialization of the definition's own
metadata children after the restore.

Two things to settle when picking it up:
- whether a subtree RESTORE primitive is worth having generally (this is
  unlikely to be the only caller that wants one)
- whether the simpler answer is for synthesis to mint a fresh definition at a
  new id instead of restoring, and let the tombstone lie — which trades the
  deterministic-id convergence property #686 relies on, so probably not, but it
  should be ruled out deliberately rather than by omission.

Should be resolved before any workspace reaches 'cell-off'.
close_reason: Deleted by construction: PR #686 no longer restores tombstoned definitions. A definition the user deleted is reported and the flip refuses, so there is no restore path to leave property children behind.

title: block_types disagrees with the runtime for a bag with a duplicated types key
description:
`block_types` is maintained by triggers that read `json_each(NEW.properties_json,
'$.types')`. SQLite resolves a duplicated object key to the FIRST occurrence;
`JSON.parse`, which `parseBlockRow` uses, resolves it to the LAST. Verified
against sqlite3 3.51:

  bag: {"types":["property-schema"],"types":[]}
  json_each('$.types') -> property-schema
  JSON.parse(...).types -> []

So for any bag with a duplicated `types` key, the `block_types` side index and
the runtime disagree about what the block IS. Every consumer that joins
`block_types` sees a type membership the app itself does not recognise.

Reachability: `JSON.stringify` cannot produce a duplicated key, so this needs a
raw SQL write or an import that hand-builds the JSON. The same shape is already
acknowledged for property KEYS elsewhere in the codebase ("a stored bag CAN
repeat a key: JSON.stringify cannot produce one, but a raw SQL write can, and
the types trigger sees only one row so nothing rejects it").

Raised during review of #686 as a synthesis concern — the property-key scan
joins `block_types` to find definition blocks, so a phantom definition there
classifies an orphan key as a repairable broken definition instead of a
mintable one. Declined as a local patch precisely because the divergence is not
that consumer's: fixing one join leaves every other consumer of `block_types`
reading a membership the runtime disagrees with. The property-NAME half of this
class was fixed in #686 by reading the last occurrence via json_each document
order; the type half cannot be fixed the same way from a consumer, because the
side index is what is wrong.

Options worth weighing:
- reject a duplicated key at the write boundary (the blocks triggers already
  run json_each over the bag, so they are positioned to detect one)
- change the type triggers to resolve `$.types` with last-occurrence semantics,
  matching JSON.parse
- accept it and say so at the trigger's declaration, if hand-built bags are
  considered out of contract

Whichever way it goes, the two should not silently disagree.

title: agent-dispatch: run identity is rolled BACKWARD to fake a re-run, which collides with real re-runs
agent-dispatch: a deferred task can be re-claimed by a different watcher
description:
decidePending (packages/agent-dispatch/src/watchers.ts) treats a due 'queued' (deferred) task as pending without comparing the scanning watcher's name to the persisted agent:watcher. A block that links more than one watched target can therefore have its deferred task claimed by whichever watcher scans it first — running it with a different executor, prompt, and allowedTools than the watcher that originally claimed it. The permissions difference is the part that matters: a task deferred by a narrow watcher can be resumed by a broader one.

Pre-existing in the deferral design; surfaced by review of PR 507. Not fixed there because the obvious fix has a stranding failure mode that needs deciding:

- rule: a due 'queued' task is claimable only by the watcher named in agent:watcher;
- but if that watcher has since been renamed or removed from config, the task is then claimable by nobody and sits deferred forever. So the rule needs a fallback — e.g. any watcher may claim it when the stored name matches no CONFIGURED watcher — which means decidePending needs to know the configured watcher names, not just the current one.

The app side already cooperates: an explicit Retry clears agent:watcher (REQUEUE_CLEARED_PROPS), so deliberate reassignment keeps working without a special case.

Note the base case is deliberately unchanged: an UNCLAIMED block linking two watched targets is racing by design, and claim-verify resolves it. Only a task with established ownership is in scope here.
close_reason: Fixed in PR 507: decidePending keeps a claimed task with the watcher named in agent:watcher, enforced only while that watcher is still configured so a renamed one releases its tasks rather than stranding them.

title: Journal aliased with a date adopts itself as that day's note — CycleError makes the date unopenable
description:
Give the Journal block either canonical alias for a date — long-form or ISO — and it becomes eligible to be adopted as that day's daily note. It carries only `PAGE_TYPE`, so `dailyNoteAdoptionGuard` accepts it.

`getOrCreateDailyNote` then resolves the same block as **both the note and its Journal parent**, applies the daily-note shape, and calls `tx.move` with `id === journalId`. The engine raises `CycleError` and rolls the transaction back, so **that date cannot be opened at all** until the alias is removed — and the error gives no hint that an alias is the cause.

Found by review on #466 ([thread](https://github.com/Stvad/knowledge-medium/pull/466#discussion_r3827427919)). Reasoned from the code, **not reproduced**.

## Fix

Treat a claimant that also owns `JOURNAL_ALIAS` as an ambiguous identity and refuse the adoption, the way the guard already refuses a claimant carrying a foreign type. One clause in `dailyNoteAdoptionGuard`.

## Why it is filed rather than fixed

Not because it is hard — it is a one-liner. It is the fifth distinct thing that guard has had to learn (foreign type, wrong day, canonical-vs-fallback, eligibility-vs-recognition, and now self-reference), and that accumulation is the subject of the open design question on the #378 stack: whether adoption should keep being a query over aliases guarded at each consumer, or become an explicit stored fact decided once.

If the decision is to keep adoption as-is, this is the first thing to fix.

title: Adopted page identity does not survive removing its canonical alias
description:
## The question

After alias-first resolution ADOPTS a user's page as a daily note, that page's **canonical aliases are the only durable record of the adoption**. The block keeps `DAILY_NOTE_TYPE` and its `daily-note:date` property, but nothing reads those to find it.

So if the user removes or renames those aliases, the next `getOrCreateDailyNote` for that date falls back to the deterministic id and creates a **second** live daily note. Two notes for one day; the original still holds the user's content but nothing navigates there any more, so it reads as data loss.

Found by review on #466 ([thread](https://github.com/Stvad/knowledge-medium/pull/466#discussion_r3679409546)). Reasoned from the code, **not reproduced**.

## Why this wasn't just fixed

The two obvious repairs are both real design choices, not refactors:

1. **Resolve by type + date before minting the fallback.** Makes identity survive alias edits — but adds a *third* identity signal (id, alias, and now typed-date), and the type and date property are themselves user-editable, so it relocates the mutability rather than removing it. It also means a query on `DAILY_NOTE_TYPE` + date becomes load-bearing for correctness.

2. **Retire the adopted identity when the aliases go.** Strip `DAILY_NOTE_TYPE` and the date property when a canonical alias is removed, so the block cleanly stops being the day's note. Honest, but it mutates a user's block in response to an edit they may not connect to it.

There is also a third answer: **accept it** and let the deterministic note be recreated, on the grounds that a user removing a page's date alias has arguably said it is not that day's page. That is defensible and costs nothing.

Related: the same "which block is this identity" question drove four separate bugs on #466 (the deletion guard, the landing recovery guard, the agent command, and the import alias prediction), all fixed by routing through one resolver. This issue is the remaining piece that a shared resolver does **not** answer, because it is about what happens when the thing the resolver keys on disappears.

## Adjacent

The kernel-page equivalent has the same shape: an adopted Properties/Types page that loses its alias is re-created at the deterministic id, orphaning whatever was filed under the adopted one. Worth deciding both together.

title: Post-publication read-back: unverified substitution advice, slashed release tags, wrong 'already acted' claim
description:
Three correctness bugs in the post-publication read-back, all found by review after the pull requests had merged. Unlike the gate-coverage gaps tracked separately, these are in what the hook does once it has an object — so they are self-contained fixes rather than a design question.

### 1. It recommends substituting a number it has not verified

A published bead id is reported as `km-abc → #12` under an unconditional "replace them now". The mapping comes straight from the bead's `External:` field; if that target was deleted or transferred, or the lookup failed transiently, nothing in that line says so. The reference table printed below it does verify the number and would show `NO SUCH ISSUE` or `COULD NOT VERIFY` — but an agent acting on the instruction without reading the table publishes a number nobody read, which is the exact failure this whole mechanism exists to prevent.

Fix: make the substitution advice conditional on a successful lookup, or state on that line that the number must be confirmed against the table.

The earlier pre-write validation covered this and was removed with the write path; the recommendation stayed. That is the seam to watch when deleting a guard — its *reason* can outlive the code it guarded.

### 2. Release tags containing a slash build a broken API path

`releases/tags/release/1.0` is assembled by string concatenation, so a valid tag with a `/` in it (`git check-ref-format refs/tags/release/1.0` accepts one) addresses the wrong endpoint. The GET then misses, and every bead id and `#N` in that release's name or notes is skipped silently.

Fix: URL-encode the tag as a single path parameter when building the endpoint, decoding what was parsed out of the URL first if needed.

### 3. It claims close keywords "ALREADY acted" when they may not have

The merge-commit read-back warns that close keywords in a merged pull request's commit have already acted, and tells the agent to reopen anything closed wrongly. GitHub only applies closing keywords when the merge lands on the repository's **default branch** — so for a pull request merged into a release branch, or into the branch below it in a stack, nothing was closed and the advice is wrong in a way that invites a pointless reopen.

This is not hypothetical for this repo: the two pull requests that introduced the read-back were themselves stacked, and the upper one carried close keywords while based on the lower.

Fix: gate both "acted" warnings on `pr.base.ref === pr.base.repo.default_branch`. The fetched pull request already carries both fields, so no extra request is needed. The existing merge-strategy qualifier is a separate condition and does not cover this.
close_reason: Closed on GitHub (issue #696); reconciled by bd-github-sync.

title: Publish gate: four shapes are 'covered' but produce nothing for the read-back to check
description:
Four publish shapes pass the pre-publish gate as "covered by the post-publication read-back", while the read-back then finds no object to fetch. A reference in the published text is therefore checked by neither side, which is exactly the failure the two hooks exist to prevent.

All four verified 2026-08-21 against the merged gate (probe: feed each command to `bd-github-sync.mjs --hook-pre-pr`, then check what `publishedTargets` returns for the response shape). The three that already had a matching case are included to show the boundary.

| shape | gate | read-back |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `gh api … -f body="Fixes #N" -t '{{.id}}'` | allows | no target (output is a template) |
| `gh api … -f body="Fixes #N" --template '{{.id}}'` | blocks | — |
| `GH_REPO=owner/other gh pr edit 12 --body="Fixes #N"` | allows | no target (URL pattern is repo-pinned) |
| `gh -R owner/other pr edit 12 --body="Fixes #N"` | blocks | — |
| `gh api …/contents/probe.txt -X PUT -f message="Fixes #N" …` | allows | no target (URLs sit under `content`/`commit`) |
| `gh api "${FLAGS:---input=payload.json}" …/comments` | allows | no target (no literal mutation flag to re-match) |
| `gh api $FLAGS …/comments` | blocks | — |

Causes, one per row: `-t` is missing from the response-hiding flag set, which lists only the long `--template`; the `GH_REPO` environment selector is not in the foreign-target test, which reads `-R`/`--repo` only; an api publish is treated as covered wholesale, though only endpoints answering with a top-level `html_url` actually are; and a quoted parameter expansion is blanked out of the command skeleton, so the shell-operator test misses it while the raw-text expansion test still counts the command as an api publish.

### The fix worth making first

Adding each spelling makes the flag list longer without making it complete — the same treadmill the whitelist inversion was meant to end, just moved from shell syntax into the flag vocabulary.

The structural answer is cheaper and covers all four at once: **make "claimed covered, produced no target" loud.** The read-back already knows this — it returns silently today when a publish yields nothing to fetch. One note there ("this publish was treated as covered but named no object; check its references yourself") converts every shape in the table, and every shape not yet discovered, from a silent gap into a visible one. It also removes the need for the gh-vocabulary list to be exhaustive, since a miss there now surfaces after the fact instead of vanishing.

Cost to weigh: genuinely blind publishes (merge/review/close/reopen, graphql, response-hiding flags) were already pre-gated, so a post-note on those is noise. Either recompute coverage in the read-back and note only the mismatch, or accept one extra line on pre-gated commands.

### Worth taking anyway

`-t` and `GH_REPO` are one-line additions to a closed, documented vocabulary, and cheap over-matching is safe in a whitelist. They should land regardless of the structural change — but they are not a substitute for it.

Found by review on the two pull requests that introduced this shape; both had already merged when the findings arrived.
notes:
Closed 2026-08-21. All four shapes re-verified against the merged gate.

Three are now UNCOVERED and therefore pre-gated: the -t short form joined the response-hiding flag set, GH_REPO joined the foreign-target test, and the quoted parameter expansion is caught because the expansion test reads a command with only SINGLE-quoted spans blanked (the full skeleton was the wrong string, the raw command the wrong string in the other direction).

The fourth — a contents-API PUT — is still classified as covered and still yields no fetchable target, which is the case this bead said should be made LOUD rather than enumerated away. It is: the read-back now reports a coverage claim it could not honour instead of returning silently, so that shape and every shape not yet discovered surface as one manual check rather than a silent gap. The cost this bead flagged (noise on genuinely blind publishes) was avoided by recomputing coverage in the read-back and noting only the mismatch, and by asking whether the command carried text at all before warning.

The predicate-level residue that remains is tracked separately, on the bead for adopting shell-segments in these hooks.
close_reason: done

title: An extension can silently replace a kernel value preset, changing the codec of every definition using it
description:
`valuePresetCoresFacet` is a `keyedMapFacet` keyed on the preset id, and
`keyedMapFacet`'s combine is last-wins with only a console.warn
(src/facets/facet.ts). So an extension contributing a core with id `string`,
`number`, `boolean`, `date`, `ref`, ... REPLACES the kernel one for the whole
app.

Blast radius: a property definition block stores only the preset ID. Both
`tryBuildSchema` (src/data/userSchemasService.ts) and the seed path resolve
behavior through `repo.valuePresetCores.get(presetId)` on every projector
rebuild. So a shadowing contribution silently changes the codec of EVERY
definition using that id — user-created, seeded, and synthesized alike — at the
next subscription tick or app restart. Values already stored under the kernel
codec are then decoded, and in a child-backed workspace re-encoded, by
different behavior.

This is not specific to any one caller; it is a property of the shared
registry. Raised during review of #686 as a synthesis concern, but synthesis
stores a preset id exactly the way `addSchema` and every seed do — giving one
caller a private un-overrideable identity would make it the odd one out
without fixing the class.

Options worth weighing:
- reserve the kernel preset ids: refuse (or namespace-prefix) a contribution
  whose id collides with `kernelValuePresetCoresById`. Cheapest, and matches
  how seed keys already reserve `system:`.
- promote the warn to a loud error at facet resolution, so a colliding
  extension fails to load rather than silently reshaping stored data.
- leave it, and say so at the facet's declaration, if deliberate override is a
  feature someone wants.

Extensions live in the DB where no sweep reaches them, so whichever way this
goes it wants deciding before more extensions exist rather than after.

title: Property-schema renderer renames a definition on blur when its name has surrounding whitespace
description:
The property-schema block renderer trims the name on blur, unconditionally:

  src/components/renderer/PropertySchemaBlockRenderer.tsx:224
    onBlur={() => { void writeName(draftName.trim()) }}

`writeName` early-returns only when `next === propertyName`. For a definition
whose committed name has leading or trailing whitespace, the trimmed draft is
NOT equal to the committed name, so merely focusing the field and leaving it
renames the definition — without the user typing anything.

Why it matters beyond tidiness: a property definition's name is the cell key its
values are stored under. Renaming it re-keys (or collides with) live property
data. In a child-backed workspace the rename processor rewrites the cells; in a
cell-backed one it does not, so the original key is orphaned again.

Reachable independently of orphan synthesis: any definition created before the
name-hygiene rules, or by an import, can carry such a name. Synthesis (#679)
makes it more likely, because it deliberately stores a definition-less cell key
VERBATIM — trimming at the mint would create "padded" for the cell key
" padded " and leave the original still definition-less, which makes the
migration's "no definition-less keys" gate unsatisfiable.

Fix direction: preserve the committed name when the user has not actually edited
it. Trim on COMMIT of a real edit rather than on every blur, or compare
`draftName` (untrimmed) against `propertyName` before deciding to write. Worth
checking the type-label renderer for the same shape — the two mirror each other.

Found while building #679.
close_reason: Closed on GitHub (issue #691); reconciled by bd-github-sync.

title: Sweep-side orphan synthesis for definition-less keys that arrive after the flip
description:
The design makes "every cell key resolves a definition" an invariant with three
maintainers: established before the flip by orphan synthesis, maintained by
addSchema, and "repaired by the sweep, which synthesizes on encountering a
definition-less key from a raw writer or import".

PR #686 built the first. The sweep half does not exist, so a definition-less key
that arrives AFTER the flip — an import, a raw properties_json write, a plugin
enabled and then removed — rides the cell with nothing to promote it, and the
only cure is an operator re-running the migration command.

Depends on a decision this issue should settle first: whether the repair belongs
in the consistency sweep at all, or whether the cheaper answer is to close the
paths that can still mint a definition-less key. Synthesis is a WRITE that
invents a schema; doing it automatically from a background sweep is a different
risk profile from doing it from an operator gesture that shows a confirmation.

Reusable pieces already in place: planPropertyDefinitionSynthesis /
applyPropertyDefinitionSynthesis and keyCannotBeDefined
(src/data/internals/propertyDefinitionSynthesis.ts), and scanPropertyKeys
(src/data/internals/propertyKeyScan.ts).

title: Undo entries recorded before a flip survive on other clients
description:
The properties-as-blocks flip is a synced, fleet-wide, one-way transition. The
client that performs it clears its own workspace undo stack, because undo replay
drives each row to a whole restored snapshot and SKIPS the same-tx processors -
so a cmd-Z of a pre-flip edit restores a cell without the materializer syncing
its children, and past the flip the children are the property truth.

No such clear happens on the OTHER clients. Nothing watches the flip column's
arrival, so a client that was open continuously across the transition keeps its
pre-flip entries, and a cmd-Z there restores cell-only state over authoritative
children. The visible effect is a confusing one rather than a destructive one:
the undo appears to work, the cell diverges from the children, and the next
change that touches those children re-projects over it - so the user's undo
silently evaporates.

Bounded by the undo stack being IN-MEMORY only (plain arrays on the manager, no
persistence), so it needs a second client open continuously across the flip with
entries already recorded. A reload clears it.

Shape if it is worth doing: clear the workspace's undo manager when a sync
arrival advances properties_migration, the same way the flipping client does.
The alternative shape is a replay-time refusal - undo declining an entry
recorded before the workspace flipped - which needs a flip generation marker the
client does not currently keep.

Declined during PR review rather than built: it needs new machinery in the sync
arrival path, and the outcome is a self-correcting local divergence.
close_reason: Closed on GitHub (issue #684); reconciled by bd-github-sync.

title: Decide the pre-publish gate's coverage boundary for opaque publish channels
description:
The pre-publish gate's 'unrepairable/opaque' carve-out (merge/review/close text, opaque-output api calls, graphql mutations) does not converge under review: rounds 3-6 on PR #678 each surfaced findings naming the previous rounds' guards, ending at four-for-four pairwise guard interactions in round 6 (sibling GET disabling the opaque block; the verifier's look-gate minting on explicit-GET reads; the opaque block offering its escape without echoing refs; boolean mode flags consuming the value flag in the restored expansion guard). Fixing stopped at round 6 per the review-treadmill doctrine; those four threads are left open on PR #678.

Why it cannot converge: the carve-out re-imports command-string parsing — the exact layer #672 removed — and the interaction space among its own predicates (two escapes x GET-veto x opacity x verb classes x flag grammar) is quadratic. The post-publish verifier, by contrast, has been quiet since its round-4 single-object shape fix.

The decision (Vlad's): where does the pre-gate's coverage boundary sit?
A. Freeze exactly as-is: residuals + the four round-6 findings documented; all further findings declined. Harm is bounded (nothing in the residual set reaches an auto-close surface; mint-on-read is early scheduled behavior).
B. SIMPLIFY the carve-out to one coarse rule (the doctrine's 'simplify so it cannot arise'): any publish command carrying text the gate cannot fully read from the raw command (any -F/--body-file/--input/@/expansion/output-hiding flag) => one fail-closed block, both escapes to proceed. Deletes the verb taxonomy, the opacity set, and most pairwise interactions; costs more confirm rounds on legitimate file-fed publishes.
C. Opacity fail-close per channel (round-5/6 status quo direction) — demonstrated non-convergent; not recommended.
D. Post-merge detection: after gh pr merge, fetch the merge-commit message via the API and echo its close-keyword refs ('this closed #N — reopen if wrong'). Ground-truth by construction; composes with A or B.

Recommendation: B + D, with A as the low-effort fallback. Full context: PR #678 review threads (rounds 3-6).
close_reason: Closed on GitHub (issue #683); reconciled by bd-github-sync.

title: roam-import: drop a failed daily page's descendants so the import can continue
description:
When `getOrCreateDailyNote` fails for one ISO, roam-import's per-ISO catch logs and continues — but the page's descendants keep their planned parent, which was never materialised, so the descendant write phase throws ParentNotFoundError and the WHOLE import fails. That defeats the per-ISO failure isolation the loop explicitly intends ("a single bad iso shouldn't sink an otherwise-successful import").

This is pre-existing behaviour, not a regression: before alias-first resolution, a failed daily page's `finalId` was the raw deterministic id, equally unmaterialised, and the descendant phase threw the same way.

Fix direction: on failure, exclude the page's descendants from the write set transitively (descendants are emitted leaves-first, so a reverse walk propagates ancestor to descendant correctly), record a diagnostic naming how many blocks were skipped, and adjust the summary's blocksWritten so it does not overcount.

Note the coupling: PR #468 added a `materializationFailed` guard that refuses the frontmatter alias/promoted-attribute writes for such a page. That guard is currently unreachable precisely BECAUSE the import throws first. Dropping the descendants makes the import continue, which makes those writes commit — so the guard becomes load-bearing at exactly the moment this issue is fixed. Do not remove it as dead code while doing this.

title: Workspace-trigger migrations have no contract test (infra exists)
description:
CORRECTED 2026-08-20: the infrastructure EXISTS and is already wired to
migration changes; what is missing is COVERAGE. The original description
claimed there was nothing at all, which was wrong.

.github/workflows/attachments-rls-contract.yml brings up an ephemeral Supabase
stack (db + gotrue + postgrest + storage + kong), applies every migration,
creates REAL gotrue users per role, and runs scripts/attachments-rls-verify.ts
against it. It triggers on supabase/migrations/**, so it already runs on any
migration change. That is a strictly better harness than a stubbed auth.uid()
over a fixture table: real auth, real PostgREST, the actual schema.

What it verifies is only the attachments Storage RLS contract. The workspace
triggers are untested:
- properties_migration: who may write it, which transitions are permitted,
  forward-only, the e2ee refusal, and that every refusal raises a PERMANENT
  SQLSTATE (23514) rather than the default P0001 — a non-permanent code makes a
  stale client PATCH retry forever instead of quarantining.
- encryption_mode / wk_canary immutability.
- the ciphertext requirement on block writes in e2ee workspaces.
- the patch base-version drift bump.
- the user_updated_at monotonic clamp.

The properties_migration half is being added as part of the owner-flip work; the
rest of the list is what remains. A sibling verify script plus one more step in
the existing workflow is the shape — no new infrastructure needed.

title: Replace the pre-publish reference gate's parsing with post-publication verification
description:
The PreToolUse reference gate reconstructs published text by regex-parsing shell command strings — the wrong layer. It must re-implement shell semantics (quoting, expansion, concatenation, stdin, control keywords) times the gh CLI's argument grammar (attached values, aliases, global options, file/template/recover flags), an unbounded input space: PR #652 absorbed ~9 review rounds of coverage findings there, each real, none final.

The class-ending shape: verify the PUBLISHED text, which exists exactly once — in the GitHub API object after gh composes it. A PostToolUse(Bash) hook on publishing commands reads the created/edited PR/issue URL from the command output, fetches the body via gh api (ground truth, no shell parsing), runs the existing reference verification, and on a bad reference repairs (gh pr edit to fix or annotate the body) and feeds the finding back to the agent via additionalContext. Close keywords only ACT at merge, so post-hoc correction before merge loses nothing versus pre-publish blocking.

Plan: (1) PostToolUse verifier + repair, reusing the verify/echo code from scripts/bd-github-sync.mjs; (2) freeze the PreToolUse gate's parsing surface — keep it as a coarse fail-closed nudge, decline further coverage findings there once the verifier owns correctness; (3) optional later: a structured publish wrapper (verify literal argv/file contents in-process, no shell reconstruction) for a zero-friction happy path.
close_reason: Closed on GitHub (issue #672); reconciled by bd-github-sync.

title: Pre-flip drift is invisible, so any pre-flip machinery rule is guesswork
description:
Now a CLEANUP task. The decision this was filed to force has been made and implemented; what remains is retiring the machinery it obsoleted.

ORIGINAL ROOT CAUSE, kept because it explains what is being retired. The cell->children backfill created a state that did not exist before: a workspace holding field/value rows while still reading cells. In that state the projection processor (children -> cell) is dormant, so any edit a user makes to a generated row leaves no trace anywhere else, and every rule that wants to know "is this machinery, or has a user touched it" has nothing to consult. Three instances, five review findings, three rounds:

  1. seat reaping vs an edited value row — a shape check passed it.
  2. seat reaping vs an edited property bag — a shape-plus-content check passed it. At that point the whole tolerance was reverted to flip-gated.
  3. a generated ref-value row edited from one target to another: the owner's cell still names the first, so the value row is the only source of the second edge, yet the machinery filter drops it and a real backlink is silently lost. Display-only, still wrong.

SETTLED (2026-08-23 verification). Flip-then-backfill was confirmed and shipped. The pass's own docblock now states the runbook as fact — the palette gesture flips first, and the CLI verb refuses an un-flipped workspace — and the pass is registered with an operator trigger, so nothing schedules a pre-flip run. Item 3 above was explicitly conditional on the runbook KEEPING backfill-then-flip, so it is moot: the state it needs is no longer produced.

WHAT IS LEFT — one question. The pre-flip machinery is all still in the tree and is now unreachable through either operator surface: the pass's reconcile branch and its pre-flip-only sweeps, the sticky child-backed flag that exists to skip them, and the flip-gated tolerance in the alias-seat reaper. RETIRE IT, or keep it as unreachable weight?

The case for retiring is this issue's own proposed shape fix — do not have the state — and it deletes a class that produced five findings. Keeping it means every future edit in that area still reasons about a state that can no longer occur.

The case for care: this is the code that performs an irreversible, fleet-wide, one-way migration, and that migration has not run yet. Whether the retirement lands before or after the first real flip is a sequencing call worth making deliberately.

ALSO FOUND, and part of the same cleanup: a comment on the seat-seed predicate in the targets module says the reaper tolerates a seat's generated property children "in any workspace, since the backfill mints them before the flip". The guard does the opposite — it gates on whether the workspace is property-child-backed — and the rationale is doubly stale, because under flip-first the backfill mints those rows after the flip, not before.

RELATED: the accepted-cost record for the reaper standing down during the pre-flip window describes a cost that, under flip-first, is no longer payable.
close_reason: Cleanup shipped and merged (PR closed issue #669 via Fixes). The remaining blocker km-7ykr is stale for this bead's rewritten scope: km-tvd7 became the cleanup task — retire the pre-flip machinery flip-then-backfill made unreachable — which landed independently of km-7ykr's outstanding correctness work. Retired: the reconcile branch, the orphaned-owner deletion leg, the row-count convergence query, the sticky child-backed flag, and two progress fields. The per-batch flip check now refuses an un-flipped workspace instead of selecting a mode. The alias-seat reaper's flip gate was KEPT: its stated cause is gone, but is_field_form is content-derived so a hand-written property-field block reaches the shape, and blockMerge's catch-up mints it un-gated (km-g5ev). Stale comments in targets.ts and workspaces.ts fixed.

title: Recognition predicate deps are undeclared across outline and backlink queries
description:
Second instance of the same class as the backlink-ancestry gap (see the related bead): a query filters on state it never declares a dependency on, so a mounted view goes stale.

INSTANCE A (already tracked): the backlink machinery post-filter walks each candidate SOURCE's ancestry while declaring a dependency only on the TARGET.

INSTANCE B (new): the outline recognition predicate resolves definition-ness through block_types, but core.children / core.childIds / core.subtree depend only on the owner's parent edges and the rows already returned. Adding or removing the property-schema type from an organic definition changes whether every field row targeting it is hidden - and the edit emits invalidations for the DEFINITION's row and type, not for the owners' parent edges. So a mounted outline keeps showing a newly-recognized row, or keeps hiding a no-longer-recognized one, until reload or an unrelated structural edit.

Both are pre-existing - the predicates always read this state - and both became reachable in every workspace rather than only child-backed ones when the flip gate came off (PR #628).

Shared fix direction: whatever declares these dependencies should be one mechanism, not per-query bolt-ons, since the same predicate is now shared between the outline SQL and the backlink walk. Worth doing with slice D, when the hide decision becomes tier-aware and the dependency set changes anyway.

Found by Codex review on PR #628.

title: [bug] propertyCellBackfill tests are load-flaky — 3 of 21 fail under full-suite contention
description:
Under machine load, `src/data/internals/propertyCellBackfill.test.ts` fails a VARYING subset of these, while passing 21/21 in isolation:

- migrates past a batch boundary instead of stopping at the first page
- revisits a block edited behind the cursor, which one sweep can never see
- repairs a value edited behind the cursor, not just a key added there
- converges while a property is rewritten under it

EVIDENCE IT IS LOAD, NOT LOGIC: an independent review pass measured it failing 5/5 in a contended copy while the SAME tree passed 5/5 in isolation, and — decisively — the failures flipped to passing when an unrelated line was mutated, i.e. purely CPU-driven timing rather than anything about the code under test. Separately observed failing 3/21 during a full gate whose test step took 158s against a normal ~60s, with another agent session running concurrently on the same machine.

This is the shape AGENTS.md's timeout-budget guidance describes: a test measured comfortably in isolation has no headroom once the gate runs one worker per core, where wall-clock stretches ~3x at p99 and ~6x at p99.9. The fix is not to weaken the assertions — measure each test's solo cost and give the file explicit timeouts sized for the 6x, with a comment recording the measured cost, per the convention. Do not raise the global testTimeout.

Impact: reddens CI on unrelated PRs and trains reviewers to re-run rather than read failures, which is how a real regression gets waved through.
close_reason: Fixed. src/data/internals/propertyCellBackfill.test.ts:168 now declares describe('property cell → children backfill', {timeout: 30_000}, ...), which covers all four named tests plus the rest of the file — the explicit budget this asked for. No recurrence in the last 400 CI runs (2026-08-19 to 08-24).

title: Backlink machinery post-filter declares no dependency on what it filters on
description:
The property-machinery exclusion in backlinks.forBlock (and the independently-resolved grouped-backlinks query) walks each candidate SOURCE's ancestor chain to decide whether that source is interior to a field row. The query's only declared structural dependency is on the TARGET.

So membership can change with nothing to invalidate on:
- a source moved out from under (or in under) a field row keeps its references unchanged, and a parent change emits the structure key for the SOURCE, not the target
- editing an ancestor's content between ((definition)) and ::((definition)) flips is_field_form, which is also undeclared

Either way the backlink list and the composed inline count stay stale until an unrelated reference change or a reload. No data is at risk; the list is wrong until then.

Pre-existing - the filter had the same gap while it was flip-gated - but un-gating it (PR #628) makes it reachable in every workspace rather than only child-backed ones.

Not fixed in #628 deliberately. The direct fix is a dependency per candidate source plus per walked ancestor, and this query is composed by the inline badge on every visible outline block, so that is a large dep set on a hot path. A coarse workspace-level channel would over-invalidate badly during a backfill. Worth revisiting with slice D, when the hide decision becomes tier-aware and this filter's shape changes anyway.

Found by Codex review on PR #628.

title: Focus-recovery path: six legs still unpinned after the PR #646 audit
description:
A 65-mutation audit of the spatial-navigation focus-recovery path (2026-08-20, during PR #646) found 39 mutations fail a named test and 26 do not. Most of the 26 are provably equivalent or now labelled. Six are real coverage gaps, listed with the cheapest fixture that closes each:

1. walker.ts findRecoveryAnchor — the clamp's BOUNDS. Deleting clamp(…, 0, candidates.length-1) is not equivalent: when the panel shrank below surfaceIndex the clamp names the LAST candidate, while without it candidates[i] is undefined and pickViewportFallback answers FIRST VISIBLE. Fixture: remember at surfaceIndex 3 in a 4-row panel, rebuild with 2 rows both visible; clamp names row 2, mutation names row 1.

2. walker.ts findSameDepthSibling — the PREV branch's same-ancestor clause. The symmetric NEXT clause is pinned by three tests; deleting the prev one makes prev mean DOM-flat previous. Fixture: panel > parent > [c1 > [g1], X]; remove X; make c1 and g1 visible, parent not. Correct lands on c1, mutated on the grandchild g1.

3/4. walker.ts panelInstances' locationOf filter, and locationOf's own blockId && renderScopeId guard. data-render-scope-id is OPTIONAL in BlockShellProps and ShellDecorator deletes it, so a scope-less nav item is a real production shape: without the filter it enters instances, shifts every index, and can be returned as an anchor with renderScopeId undefined. Fixture: one nav item with data-block-id and no data-render-scope-id; assert it neither shifts the clamp nor is returned.

5/6. PanelFocusRecovery.tsx observer-effect cleanup — observer.disconnect() and the clearTimeout. Neither is pinned. A leaked observer can arm a recovery for a panel whose watchdog is gone; an armed timer surviving unmount writes focus after the panel is gone. The panel-swap test's own comment leans on this cleanup. Fixture: unmount with a recovery armed, assert vi.getTimerCount() is 0 and a later panel mutation opens no repo.tx.

Context: PR #646 pinned the tiers (next, prev, ancestor closest + walk, clamp position, surfaceIndex, same-depth NEXT, location-match, the two component-side guards) and labelled the unreachable legs. This is the remainder. Filed rather than folded in because the PR had already run four review rounds and the surface is the whole walker module, not the flake it started from.
close_reason: Done in PR #658. All six legs pinned, each verified by deleting that clause alone: the clamp's bounds, findSameDepthSibling's prev branch, panelInstances' locationOf filter and locationOf's own guard (one fixture covers both — a scope-less nav item, which ShellDecorator really does produce), and both halves of the observer effect cleanup. pnpm run check green: 631 files, 7829 tests. That closes the audit — every tier, guard and hint field on the recovery path now has a named test behind it or a label saying why it cannot.

title: Tab-indented markdown pastes as a FLAT list — getIndentationLevel counts a tab as zero levels
description:
`src/utils/markdownParser.ts`, `getIndentationLevel`: `Math.floor(indentMatch.length / 2)` over a leading-whitespace match. One TAB is length 1, so it floors to **zero** indent levels — a tab-indented outline parses as an all-roots flat list and its depth is silently destroyed on paste.

Repro (found while reviewing the paste placement work):

    - Project
    \t- Task 1
    \t- Task 2
    - Notes

parses to FOUR roots. Pasted into a block with children this yields `[Task 1, Task 2, Notes, Kid]` — `Notes` indistinguishable from a task, which is exactly the defect the paste-placement guard was added to prevent. The guard cannot help: by the time it runs the parser has already flattened the tree.

Tab indentation is what many editors and several outliner exports emit, so this is a common clipboard shape.

There is no tab case anywhere in `markdownParser.test.ts`. The fuzz arbitrary does generate tabs but asserts no depth oracle over them, so nothing catches it.

Fix direction (unverified): expand tabs to a tab stop before measuring, or count a tab as one level. Needs a decision on mixed tabs+spaces, and tests over both. Worth checking what the roam importer relies on before changing shared parser semantics.
close_reason: Closed on GitHub (issue #644); reconciled by bd-github-sync.

title: PanelFocusRecovery's debounce re-verify block is unpinned by any test
description:
src/plugins/spatial-navigation/PanelFocusRecovery.tsx: the block that re-verifies at the moment of write (the stillFocused identity check plus the instanceAt re-check inside the RECOVERY_DEBOUNCE_MS timer) can be DELETED WHOLE and the entire spatial-navigation suite stays green — 96/96. Measured 2026-08-19 during the flake work on km-40x1.

Its comment asserts it is load-bearing ('anything could have changed during the debounce window'), and it plausibly is in production: a user moving focus during the 250ms window would otherwise get their new focus overwritten by a recovery aimed at the old one. So per AGENTS.md this needs a real test, not a defence-in-depth label.

Test shape: arm a recovery (yank the focused instance), then inside the debounce window set focus to a different MOUNTED block, then let the window elapse and assert focus is still the newly-set block. Prime the positive case first (the existing tests show recovery DOES fire) so the assertion is not an absence that passes trivially.

Found by an adversarial review of PR #635; deliberately left out of that PR to keep it scoped to the flake fix.
close_reason: Done in PR #646 — both guards now pinned by a test that fails when only that clause is deleted (churn-extends-debounce for the cancel-and-re-arm; panel-element-replacement for the write-time instance re-check). The third clause, the focus-identity check, is unreachable (any in-process focus change re-enters runRecoveryCheck and cancels above it) and is labelled defence in depth at its declaration. Both tests assert on repo.tx, not the focus value.

title: Flaky under load: propertyCellBackfill tests fail on a varying subset
description:
`src/data/internals/propertyCellBackfill.test.ts` fails intermittently under machine load, on a VARYING subset of: 'migrates past a batch boundary', 'revisits a block edited behind the cursor', 'repairs a value edited behind the cursor', 'converges while a property is rewritten under it'.

Measured during review of PR #625: 1-of-5 runs in a normal worktree, 5-of-5 in an isolated copy under concurrent load. Confirmed NOT caused by that PR — it reproduces identically at origin/master, and under an unrelated source mutation it passed 5/5 while the pristine tree failed 5/5. Purely CPU-contention driven.

This is the timeout-budget shape AGENTS.md describes: a test measured comfortably in isolation stretches ~3x at p99 and ~6x at p99.9 when the gate runs one worker per core. It can redden CI for unrelated PRs.

FIX DIRECTION: measure each of the four named tests alone, then give the file explicit timeouts budgeted for the 6x tail (`describe(name, {timeout: N}, ...)`) with a comment recording the measured cost — rather than raising the global testTimeout, which would make every genuine hang cost that much before reporting.
close_reason: Closed on GitHub (issue #639); reconciled by bd-github-sync.

title: propertyCellBackfill batch-boundary test times out locally while master CI is green
description:
src/data/internals/propertyCellBackfill.test.ts > 'migrates past a batch boundary instead of stopping at the first page' fails at ~5.04s against vitest's 5000ms default — solo AND under the full gate — on a dev machine, while run-tests.yml is green on the same commit (master 3e3b22668, 2026-08-19).

Two threads to pull:
1. The test's stderr shows 'getaddrinfo ENOTFOUND proj.supabase.co' (the placeholder VITE_SUPABASE_URL host) surfacing under this test — some code path issues a real network request during a unit test, and the test's wall time then depends on how fast local DNS fails a nonexistent host. Nothing in a unit test should resolve DNS; find the fetch and stub it.
2. Independent of that: the test does 250 creates plus a full backfill sweep and sits at the 5000ms default. Per the AGENTS.md timeout-budget doctrine (budget for 6x under load), it needs an explicit it(..., 20_000) with the measured solo cost in a comment.

Found while running the gate for an unrelated change; pre-existing on the branch point.
close_reason: Closed on GitHub (issue #633); reconciled by bd-github-sync.

title: Backlink machinery walk missed the :: bit, dropping real backlinks
description:
FIXED in the same PR that un-gated it (PR for km-1zsj), recorded because it is independently reachable today.

propertyMachinerySourceIds (backlinks plugin) classified a source as property machinery when ANY ancestor had a non-null reference_target_id resolving to a property-schema type. It never checked is_field_form, although its own doc claimed 'same recognition as VISIBLE_CHILD_PREDICATE_SQL', which does check it.

Consequence in a flipped workspace, no backfill involved: an ordinary block that links to a property definition page, with ordinary children, made every one of those children's backlinks disappear from Linked References, the inline count, and grouped backlinks. Root ancestors are exempt via 'parent_id IS NOT NULL', which is why every existing one-level fixture passed.

Root cause in the tests: the field-row fixtures used unmarked content '((D))' instead of the marked field form '::((D))', so they were never field rows and the missing bit could not show up.

Fix: the walk now requires COALESCE(is_field_form, 0) = 1, matching the doc's parity claim.
close_reason: Fixed in PR #628 alongside km-1zsj, which it blocked.

title: Beads↔GitHub sync triggers: pre-PR bead-id gate + SessionEnd sync
description:
Automate the beads↔GitHub sync at the moments it matters, with the two documented sync traps guarded in one script (scripts/bd-github-sync.mjs):

1. Reconcile GitHub-side closes into beads BEFORE pushing — an open bead otherwise clobbers a GitHub-side close (hand-close or a merged 'Fixes #N') and re-opens the issue.
2. Re-derive priority from P0-P4 / priority::* labels for beads left at the flattened default by a pull.

Triggers: a Claude Code PreToolUse(Bash) hook that gates gh pr create/edit/comment — it mints issues for referenced beads that lack one and blocks bead ids (km-*) in public PR/issue text with a km→#N substitution table; a SessionEnd hook running the full sync; and pnpm bd:sync for manual/Codex runs.

Measured constraint that shaped the split: a converged full sync still costs ~60s (per-issue GET compare), so the pre-PR hook only does a selective --issues push (seconds) and the full sync runs at session end.
close_reason: Closed on GitHub (issue #631); reconciled by bd-github-sync.

title: Port the spike's batched reads and bulk insert to the cell->children pass
description:
The pass issues about 31 SQL statements per candidate row in a writing sweep: one row read, two children reads, then per registered key a parent-validation read plus an insert. Measured on an instrumented run: 44,000 getAll + 64,080 getOptional + 56,240 execute for 8,000 row-visits.

The earlier properties-as-children spike solved exactly this and the helpers are still readable on its branch (commit 66f9a981e, 'Speed up property child backfill'): liveRowsForKnownIds and livePropertyFieldRowsForKnownParents replace two reads per ROW with two batched IN (...) reads per BATCH, and insertKnownValidRowsForBackfill does a multi-row INSERT ... VALUES at 200 rows per statement, skipping tx.create's parent SELECT. Its own test assertion flipped from parentChildrenReads=1 to parentChildrenReads=0.

Not ported in PR #596 deliberately: the bulk path bypasses tx.create's parent-in-workspace validation, and this pass writes source-of-truth rows that upload. That validation is what a later review found the orphan leg needed a workspace term for. Porting it means deciding what replaces the per-row check — a batched equivalent, or an argument that the ids are known-good by construction.

Rough size of the prize: this is where most of the remaining wall-clock lives once the candidate-scan index (landed) is in. Projection for a large graph put the row work at about 5.5 of 8 minutes.

title: Cell->children backfill does not report how many keys it skipped as unregistered
description:
The materializer skips a property key with no registered schema (no schema -> continue), the block still counts as materialized, and no counter anywhere records it. So an operator running the migration is never told that some keys will NOT be carried into the child representation.

The runbook is backfill -> verify -> backfill -> flip, and the verify step's only automatic input is the migration's own report, which is structurally blind to this. audit-properties is the tool that finds them, and the confirm dialog now names it — but a count from the pass itself would be better, since it knows exactly which keys it skipped on which blocks.

Shape: an optional callback on the materializer's lookups (the branch already exists), a distinct-name set plus an occurrence count on the progress struct, and a sentence in the completion toast. The reason it was not done in PR #596: the callback changes a signature shared with the live dual-write processor, and the cheap half (naming audit-properties in the dialog) covers the operator's next action.

Found by the round-3 adversarial review of PR #596.

title: Cell->children backfill leaves ~700k block snapshots in the in-memory cache
description:
The commit pipeline publishes every committed row into BlockCache post-commit. BlockCache.snapshots is a plain Map with no eviction — deleteSnapshot and trackedIds have no non-test callers and there is no size cap or prune anywhere in src/.

So the one-time properties backfill grows the JS heap by one deep-frozen block snapshot per created row — on the order of 700k objects for a large graph, none of which the user would otherwise have loaded, held until reload. Measured shape suggests a few hundred MB; on a phone that is an OOM.

Cheapest fix is for the backfill's transaction wrapper to drop its own created ids from the cache after commit — they have no subscribers by construction, since nothing renders unbuilt property children before the flip. Alternatively accept it and tell the operator to reload after the migration.

Found by the round-3 adversarial review of PR #596.

title: agent-runtime: an asserted --workspace that does not exist is answered, not refused
description:
Follow-up from PR #590 (empty --workspace assertion). That PR made an EMPTY workspace assertion fail. An assertion naming a workspace that does not exist still succeeds and returns a wrong-but-plausible answer.

The five read verbs (page, search, daily-note, backlinks, grouped-backlinks) do no existence check on an asserted workspace id:

- page / search -> candidates: [] / results: [] (reads as 'no such page')
- daily-note (src/plugins/agent-runtime/commands.ts, runDailyNoteCommand) -> computes dailyNoteBlockId(bogusWs, iso), returns exists: false plus a FABRICATED deepLink
- backlinks / grouped-backlinks -> resolveBlockWorkspaceId returns the override without checking the block is in it; hydration reports the target with empty content and 0 backlinks

Reachable shapes: a stale or typo'd id from a script; a space-padded expansion (--workspace " $WS" survives cac as ' abc ' and passes the trim-only guard verbatim).

Same wrong-answer class the empty-value guard closes, one notch subtler: the caller cannot distinguish 'the graph you named has no such page' from 'you named a graph that does not exist'.

Fix direction: an existence check inside the two shared resolvers (commandWorkspaceId, resolveBlockWorkspaceId) when an override is present -- audit-properties already refuses a workspace whose definition registry is not loaded, so the precedent and the shape both exist. Deliberately out of scope for #590: pre-existing, and not reachable from the shell shape that motivated that PR.

Found by adversarial review 2026-08-18.
close_reason: Closed on GitHub (issue #606); reconciled by bd-github-sync.

title: Content promotion destroys page references: [[X]]:: / key:: [[X]] loses its backlink when the source bullet is dropped
description:
Raised by Codex during #585 review and split out, because it predates that PR and needs a product decision rather than a fix in it.

## The problem

A promoted attribute whose value is a page reference loses the reference entirely.

For a Matrix message containing `topic:: [[Alpha]]`:

1. Promotion hoists it to the parent as `matrix:topic` = `[[Alpha]]` (a plain token string).
2. Matrix promotion is **subtractive** — it drops the source bullet once hoisted, deliberately (`matrix-chat-client.tsx`: *"chat ingest wants the literal bullet gone"*, explicitly diverging from the roam importer, which preserves attr blocks for fidelity).
3. That bullet's `[[Alpha]]` was a real reference producing a real backlink. It is now gone.
4. What survives is a property value holding the *text* `[[Alpha]]`. Only `ref` / `refList` codecs project into references — a `string` or `list` codec does not — so nothing replaces the backlink.

Net: a reference the user wrote becomes untyped text, and `Alpha`'s backlinks silently lose an entry.

## Status

**Latent, not currently firing.** Checked production: zero `matrix:*` cells contain `[[` today, so no references have actually been lost yet. This is about the next message that uses the form, not a cleanup.

## Not caused by #585, and not fixed by it

Before #585 the promoted key had no definition at all; after it, it has a `list` one. Both are equally non-referential, so #585 is neutral here. It is visible in that PR only because classification *does* correctly infer `refList` for these values — and `ensurePromotedPropertySchemas` deliberately downgrades that to `list`, since the importer earns `refList` by building an `aliasIdMap` and rewriting tokens to ids (`normalizeRefPropertyValues`), which a streaming consumer has no equivalent of.

## Options

1. **Decline promotion when the value contains a page token.** Cheapest and loses nothing — the bullet survives untouched, so the backlink survives with it, and the attribute simply isn't hoisted. Fits the existing `PromotionOptions.acceptKey` seam, except that seam currently decides on the key NAME before values are known, so it would need to see the value (or a post-finalize withdrawal, which needs promotion to track key→uids — same prerequisite as #594).
2. **Resolve the token and keep `refList`.** Best end state: `matrix:topic` becomes a real typed pointer with backlinks and target types. Requires resolve-**or-create** for `[[Alpha]]` from arbitrary chat text, which is a product decision — should a message mentioning a page in an attribute mint that page? The importer answers yes for an explicit import; a chat firehose is a different question.
3. **Keep the source bullet whenever its value is reference-bearing** — a narrower version of (1): promote AND keep, accepting one duplicated line for the reference's sake.
4. **Accept.** The form is rare (zero instances today) and users can write the reference in the message body instead.

## Related

- #585 — where this surfaced; contains the `refList`→`list` downgrade and its rationale.
- #594 — the other case wanting promotion to track key→uids so a value can be withdrawn after finalization without losing the source bullet. If both are fixed, that mapping is the shared prerequisite.
- #501 — the parent "promoted keys need definitions" work.

title: Post-flip: a promoted value that cannot decode under a narrow existing schema aborts the write and can stall ingest
description:
Dormant today (no workspace is child-backed) — this bites at the slice-C flip. Split out of #585 rather than patched there.

## The hazard

`MATERIALIZE_PROPERTY_CHILDREN_PROCESSOR` decodes each cell value during the write and **throws** on failure, by design:

> Reject the write instead — a processor throw propagates out of the writeTransaction and rolls the whole tx back atomically, so the bad cell value never lands (PR #386 review, F2)

That is correct for a raw `tx.update` mistake. It interacts badly with *content promotion*, which manufactures property values from arbitrary user text:

1. A promoted key has a narrow pre-existing schema — `url`, `number`, `boolean`, `date`, `enum`.
2. A message supplies text that does not decode under it (`audio-url:: see below`, `count:: many`).
3. Post-flip, the materialize processor throws → the whole ingest transaction rolls back.
4. Matrix's poll holds its sync cursor when a write fails (deliberately — see #585, so a failed message is retried rather than lost). So it retries the same event forever and **ingest stops permanently**.

## Why #585 does not fix it

`ensurePromotedPropertySchemas` normalizes values to fit their schema, which closes the common cases: `string` (arrays get JSON-encoded) and `list` (scalars get widened). No reshaping can make `not-a-number` fit a `number` codec, so narrower schemas stay exposed. #585 reports these loudly in its diagnostics but does not block the write — blocking would trade a recoverable state for a stalled caller.

## Options

- **Decline the promotion for that key on that message.** Cleanest: the text stays on its own bullet, nothing undecodable is written. Blocked today because `computePromotedFromChildren` returns `promoted` keyed by property name and `bubbled` keyed by uid, with no mapping between them — so a key cannot be withdrawn after finalization without also un-bubbling its source block (needed, or a subtractive consumer has already dropped the bullet and the text is lost). Wants promotion to track key→uids.
- **Make the flip's own backfill tolerant** and treat this as one more orphan class. The processor comment already anticipates a related need: *"slice C's backfill … must catch per row and report the offending block, not let one bad value throw the whole pass."*
- **Refuse narrow schemas for promoted namespaces**, so promoted keys can only ever carry codecs that accept text.

## Why it is worth fixing before the flip

The failure mode is not a bad cell — it is a silently dead ingest loop, and the same shape applies to any poll-driven writer that holds a cursor on failure.
close_reason: Closed on GitHub (issue #594); reconciled by bd-github-sync.

title: agent-extensions: flat extensions with esm.sh imports are untestable (matrix ingest guards are unpinned)
description:
Split out of #585 review round 8, where three load-bearing guards in `agent-extensions/matrix-chat-client.tsx` ended up shipping without tests.

## The blocker, verified

A probe test that merely imports the module fails:

```
Error: Only URLs with a scheme in: file and data are supported by the default ESM loader. Received protocol 'https:'
```

Cause: `matrix-chat-client.tsx:43` does `import * as matrixSdk from 'https://esm.sh/matrix-js-sdk@38.0.0?bundle'`. That resolves in the app (the page importmap + Babel-standalone handle it) but Node/vitest refuse it outright.

Secondary: `appendMatrixMessage` and `pollLoop` are module-private, so even with the import resolved there is nothing to drive.

## What is currently unpinned

Three guards in the ingest path, all added during #585, none mutation-testable:

1. The workspace check **before** schema registration — deleting it lets promoted definitions land in a workspace the message is not written to.
2. The workspace check **before** the write — same class.
3. The `'done' | 'deferred'` outcome and the poll loop's cursor hold — deleting it makes a deferred message advance `next_batch` and be **permanently lost** (this was a real P1, fixed in 3e494a26f).

The repo's own rule is that a guard clause and its position must fail a named mutation test. These fail nothing; the gate stays green with any of them removed.

## What a fix needs

- A vitest alias (or `server.deps` / resolver plugin) mapping the `https://esm.sh/...` specifier to a stub, and a decision about whether that applies repo-wide or only to `agent-extensions/`.
- Exporting the ingest internals, or restructuring so the poll loop is drivable through a seam (an injected sync transport would also let the cursor behaviour be tested directly).

Both are shared-config / structural calls, which is why they were not made inside #585.

## Wider point

Every integration bug found in #585 — including two P1s that were data loss — was caught by review, not by tests, precisely because this layer has no harness at all. Worth deciding whether flat extensions are meant to be testable; if not, that argues for keeping their logic thin and pushing anything load-bearing into `src/` where it can be covered.

title: Flaky under load: PanelFocusRecovery 'refreshes the positional hint'
description:
src/plugins/spatial-navigation/test/PanelFocusRecovery.test.tsx > 'refreshes the positional hint as the user navigates between blocks' fails under full-gate load and passes in isolation.

Measured 2026-08-18 on PR #583 (which changes nothing under spatial-navigation):
- isolation: 8/8 pass, fast
- full `pnpm run check`: failed at 3029ms, then 3024ms on the next run, then passed on an earlier run the same day

The duration is the tell. It lands within ~30ms of 3000ms, which is the global Testing Library `findBy*` / `waitFor` timeout configured in src/test/setup.ts. So the test's async wait is fine alone and exceeds the default once the suite runs one worker per core — the p99 stretch AGENTS.md describes.

## Fix direction

Per the AGENTS.md timeout-budget guidance: give the awaited assertion an explicit budget sized from its MEASURED cost times the load factor, with a comment stating the measurement. Do NOT raise the global testTimeout or the global TL timeout — the tail is a handful of tests and a global raise makes every genuine hang cost that much before it reports.

Worth checking first whether the wait is on a one-shot event: if the hint refresh is dispatched rather than polled, a longer timeout will not help and the test needs to fence on the observable precondition instead.

## Related

km-kqxu is the same class in clientSchema (three tests, 15-29s). Two independent flake families now reddening unrelated PRs suggests the load budget wants a sweep rather than one-off fixes.
close_reason: Duplicate of km-40x1 — same test, same root cause. The load-budget diagnosis in this issue was wrong: happy-dom 20.11.0 held the MutationObserver callback in a WeakRef with no other referent, so a GC killed the observer and the waitFor could never settle — which is why it always died at ~3000ms, the global Testing Library cap, regardless of load. Fixed by upgrading to happy-dom 20.11.2 in PR #635.

title: Workspace backfills can run twice per open — scheduleWorkspaceBackfills has two uncoalesced callers
description:
Surfaced while deflaking workspaceBackfillRunner.test.ts (PR #588). The test flake was the symptom; this is the underlying behaviour.

`Repo.scheduleWorkspaceBackfills` is called from two places:
- `src/bootstrap/workspaceBootstrap.ts` — the normal per-open path
- `Repo.setActiveWorkspaceId`'s error re-arm path — added because the switch path disposes the outgoing workspace's gate, so a failed pin would otherwise leave the restored workspace never backfilling for the session

Nothing coalesces them. `PendingIdleJobs.schedule` enqueues unconditionally (no dedupe by key), so a workspace whose bootstrap partially failed can run every registered backfill TWICE in one open.

## Why it matters more than it used to

Harmless for a small idempotent repair, which is all the seam carried when it was written. It stops being harmless for the properties-as-blocks cell->children pass: roughly 650k creates, each one an upload. Running it twice per open doubles that cost and widens the window in which two passes are in flight against the same rows.

Note this is orthogonal to the completion claim. The claim stops a SECOND DEVICE running the pass; it does not stop one device scheduling it twice within a single open, because both schedulings see the same local claim state and the second can re-claim after the first releases.

## Fix direction

Coalesce per (workspace, generation) at the schedule site — the runner already has a `workspaceGeneration` token it checks per transaction, so the same key can dedupe the job. Alternatively give `PendingIdleJobs` an optional dedupe key; several other callers there are also idempotent-but-repeatable.

Whichever, add a test: two `scheduleWorkspaceBackfills` calls in one open must run each backfill once.

title: Flaky: workspaceBackfillRunner claim-release test fails ~1 in 5
description:
`src/data/internals/workspaceBackfillRunner.test.ts` > 'releases the claim when a run aborts, so it is not blocked forever' fails roughly 1 run in 5, both in isolation (`npx vitest run <that file>`) and inside the full gate. Not load-dependent — it reproduces alone.

Failure: `expect(released).toEqual(['probe-backfill-v1'])` gets `[]`, i.e. the drain barrier returns before the release round-trip lands.

Suspected shape: the test drives fake timers (`vi.runAllTimersAsync()` inside the `drain` helper at line 54) while the runner's claim/release path goes through async DB calls. `runAllTimersAsync` flushes microtasks between timers, but a continuation that only schedules its timer after enough awaits can be missed, so `awaitWorkspaceBackfills()` resolves while the release is still in flight. Poll the outcome (`vi.waitFor` on `released`) rather than assuming the drain covers it, or make the runner's release observable to the drain barrier.

Pre-existing, not introduced by the ensureSystemPages isolation work — confirmed by stashing that change and reproducing on the clean tree.
close_reason:
Fixed in PR #588 (branch claude/deflake-backfill-release-test).

Found by the #589 session; it is a SECOND, distinct flake on the same assertion, not the one #588 started from. Mine was `released` containing the id twice (a double arming); this one is `released` EMPTY. The balance-assertion fix did nothing for it — `toContain` fails just as hard on an empty array.

Root cause is the drain barrier, as diagnosed in the bead: `awaitWorkspaceBackfills` can return while work is still in flight, because `runAllTimersAsync` flushes microtasks between timers but misses a continuation that only schedules ITS timer after enough awaits. `drain` now loops to a fixpoint, which settles it without depending on how many awaits deep the runner is.

Worth recording for the next person: polling the assertion does NOT work here. `vi.waitFor` under fake timers does not advance the timers the pending job needs, so a second arming's claim sits unreleased for the whole timeout and the test fails a different way. The wait has to drive the clock, not watch it.

Verified: 8 filtered runs and 6 full-file runs green (previously ~1 in 5 red), plus a green gate.

title: Clear the workspace undo stack when a data migration writes
description:
Deferred from PR #508 — the shape is agreed, it just has no consumer yet.

`RepoTxOptions.skipUndo` keeps a WorkspaceBackfill's own writes off the undo stack, but cannot reach entries already on it. Undo replay restores an entry's whole `before` row snapshot rather than a field delta, so a user edit made BEFORE the pass, to a row the pass later rewrote, reverts the migration when they hit cmd-Z for their own edit — and permanently, since the completion marker is already recorded.

Agreed shape (with the repo owner): when a migration actually writes, call `UndoManager.clear()` for that workspace and surface it to the user. The entries at risk are exactly the ones unsafe to replay, so dropping them costs recent undo and buys not silently reverting a migration. Rejected alternatives: reloading the page (heavy, doesn't explain itself) and a toast alone (visible, but the loss still happens).

Not built in #508 because deleting `dailyNoteDateBackfill` left zero registered backfills, so it would have shipped as dead code. It should land with slice C of the properties-as-blocks migration — the first real consumer, and the one where it matters most (~650k creates).

The rule itself is in AGENTS.md under 'one-shot catch-up passes'; this issue carries the state (not built, who builds it).
close_reason: Built, with slice C as the first consumer exactly as this issue anticipated. The properties-migration action clears the workspace undo manager when the pass actually writes and surfaces it to the user in the result banner, which is the agreed shape (clear plus tell them, not a toast alone and not a reload). Verified in the migration action 2026-08-23.

title: Flaky: clientSchema 'samples rather than fully scanning'
description:
