4. Better still, the fix comes back as a merge proposal, reviewed in the same view as an upstream update to the extension.

## Why

- Errors are the moment you most want an agent, and the app already knows exactly which extension failed and on what. Asking you to retype that is waste.
- It's safe by construction: nothing changes until the device-local approval, so a bad fix costs a review, not a broken graph.

## Cost and trigger

Low to medium. The button and the brief are small. The review flow is the shared part: design it together with upstream tracking for extensions, since both end in a "proposed new source for this extension" that you accept or decline.

title: Crystallize an agent run into a durable tool: an extension, saved query or watcher
description:
## Problem

A `[[claude]]` run that does something useful leaves only its reply behind. Doing it again means writing the mention again, with the same context, and paying for the same run. Nothing turns "that worked" into a durable tool.

## Idea, borrowed from Imbue Studio

Imbue's workspace template has a `crystallize-creation` skill. When something the agent did is worth keeping, a background worker rebuilds it on a branch as a proper app, skill or routine, with tests and a review, and it merges only once the user approves.

Sources: https://imbue.com/blog/studio-announce and https://github.com/imbue-ai/default-workspace-template (`.agents/skills/crystallize-creation/SKILL.md`).

## Sketch

1. An action on an agent-dispatch reply block: "Make this a tool".
2. It starts a background run with a brief that carries the original request, the run's reply and the blocks it touched. The run picks the right durable shape:
   - an extension block (a renderer, an action, a processor),
   - a saved query,
   - or an agent-dispatch watcher, when the work needs a model every time it runs.
3. The run writes the result as a **disabled draft**: an extension block that isn't approved or enabled. It checks it with `kmagent install-extension --verify` and `kmagent audit-extension`, and puts the findings in its reply.
4. You read it and approve it the way you approve a hand-written extension. Nothing runs without the existing device-local approval.

Example: you ask `[[claude]]` to pull this week's sleep numbers into a table. It works, so you crystallize it. Next week the table is an extension that renders on its own, with no run.

## Why

- It moves work from "ask the agent every time" to "the agent built you a tool once". That's the malleable-software loop, and it gets cheaper each time.
- Almost everything already exists: agent-dispatch runs (`packages/agent-dispatch/README.md`), `--verify` and `audit-extension` (`packages/agent-cli/README.md`), and the approval gate (`src/extensions/compileExtensionModule.ts`). What's new is the action and the brief.

## Cost and trigger

Medium. The hard part is the brief: how a run decides between extension, query and watcher, and how it reproduces the original run's context. A draft that was only checked by lint still needs a human read before approval, and that's intended.

Related: once merge proposals exist (upstream tracking for extensions), a crystallized draft can arrive as one more kind of proposal.

title: Capability-scoped extensions: declare what an extension may read, write and fetch, and sandbox ones you didn't write
description:
## Problem

User extensions run in the page with the app's full authority. An extension can import any app module (`src/extensions/apiCatalog.ts` is for discovery, not a gate), hold the `Repo`, read and write any block in the workspace, fetch any host, and touch the DOM. Trust is all or nothing: a per-device approval pinned to a SHA-256 of the source (`src/extensions/compileExtensionModule.ts`).

That works while people run extensions they wrote or read. It stops working when extensions pass between people, or when an agent writes and installs one that nobody reviews line by line. This is a missing level of trust between "trusted" and "not running", not a hole: nothing runs without approval.

## Idea, borrowed from Cloudflare OS

- Agents and apps start with access to nothing.
- The user "introduces" them to one specific resource, and the code receives a typed binding (for example `env.REPO`) that stands for one resource under one policy. Credentials stay outside the code.
- App server code runs in a Dynamic Worker (a V8 isolate) with outbound networking disabled. App UI runs in a sandboxed iframe. The two halves talk over Cap'n Web, Cloudflare's open-source object-capability RPC.

Sources: https://blog.cloudflare.com/cloudflare-os/ and https://github.com/cloudflare/cloudflare-os (README).

## Sketch

1. **Declare needs** in KM's own terms:

   ```ts
   export const needs = {
     read:  {types: ['habits:habit', 'habits:check-in']},
     write: {under: 'own-page'},
     fetch: [],   // no network at all
   }
   ```

   Which block types it reads, where it may write (its own subtree, or blocks of its own types), which facets it contributes to, and which hosts it may fetch.
2. **Show needs at approval.** The prompt reads "reads habit blocks, writes under its own page, no network" instead of only "approve this source".
3. **Enforce in tiers.**
   - Advisory, cheap: `--verify` and `audit-extension` compare what an extension actually touches with what it declares. This is a lint, not a security boundary.
   - Enforced, expensive: extensions you didn't write run in a sandboxed iframe or worker with no direct `Repo`. They receive capability handles over RPC (Cap'n Web, or `postMessage`) that filter inside the query to the declared types. Your own extensions keep running in the page as now.
4. **Network as a capability.** A per-host fetch grant routed through the proxy. That also answers the per-extension consent question in #1181.

## Why it's interesting

- It's what makes sharing extensions safe: the step from "my malleable tool" to tools people remix and pass around.
- An agent could install a capability-limited extension unattended, since what it can do is bounded and visible.
- The policy is written in KM's data model (block types, subtrees), which is more precise than Cloudflare's wall between app databases. KM has one shared graph, so walls between databases wouldn't work here anyway.

## Cost, and why P3

- The data layer (`query` / `tx` / `mutate`) needs an async RPC surface, and so does every facet a sandboxed extension may contribute to. Most facets resolve synchronously today.
- Renderer contributions are React components mounted in the host tree. That's the hardest part: sandboxed extensions may get a restricted set of facets, or render inside their own frame.
- Scoping reads to declared types has to happen inside the query, before any LIMIT, not by filtering afterwards.
- Trigger: extensions start being shared between users, or agents install extensions unattended.

## Suggested first step

A design spike. List the facets the extensions in `agent-extensions/` actually use and which of them could cross an async boundary, then prototype enforced mode for one data-only extension that contributes no renderers.

title: Stage outward actions from agents and extensions as approvable proposal blocks
description:
## Problem

Writes inside the graph can be undone. Actions that leave it can't: posting through `agent-extensions/social-media-publisher`, sending mail, calling an API that writes or costs money. Today such an action happens the moment the code calls it, and nothing standard says "do this once a person approves". agent-dispatch makes this sharper, because its runs act while you may be away from the keyboard.

## Idea, borrowed from Cloudflare OS gatekeepers

In Cloudflare OS every external service sits behind a gatekeeper Worker. For an action with side effects, the gatekeeper simulates the result so the agent can keep working, and queues the real action. The user approves or rejects queued actions one at a time or in bulk. Source: https://github.com/cloudflare/cloudflare-os (README, "Gatekeepers").

## Sketch

- A core, namespaced **pending outward action** type. Each proposal is a block that records what will happen (kind, target, payload as typed properties or child blocks), what proposed it (an extension or an agent run), and a status: pending, approved, rejected, done or failed.
- A small API for extensions and agent runs: propose an action and get its block back. The executor runs only after the block is approved.
- The proposal renders with Approve and Reject, and a query view lists everything pending. It's ordinary synced data, so you can approve from your phone.
- An agent-dispatch run that wants to post or send writes a proposal next to its reply block instead of acting.

## Why

- Unattended agents are where an irreversible mistake costs most. A review step before anything leaves the graph is the cheap guard.
- As blocks, proposals get sync, queries, backlinks and history for free.
- It gives extension authors one standard way to ask for confirmation instead of each one building its own.

## Example

You write `[[claude]] post the weekly summary`. The reply arrives as a child block holding the draft and a pending post. Nothing is published until you tap Approve.

## Open questions

- Which device executes an approved action. Trust in an extension is per device, so the executor must be a device where the proposing extension is approved. Executing exactly once across devices over last-writer-wins sync has no general answer; for a small, coordinated fleet, "the approving device executes, if it can" is probably enough.
- Whether the proposing code receives a simulated result (Cloudflare's approach) or just a pending handle. A handle is simpler and is probably enough here.

## Related

#1287 narrows which tools a dispatch run can use. This is the complement for the actions it is allowed to take.

title: Extensions: remember where an installed extension came from, and merge upstream updates with local edits
description:
## Problem

An installed extension is one block whose content is its source. Updating it (`kmagent install-extension` again, or pasting new source) replaces that content. Editing an installed extension is exactly what the malleable model invites, but once you have, an update either overwrites your edits or you keep a stale copy. Nothing records where the extension came from or which upstream version your copy is based on, so there is no base to merge against.

## Idea, borrowed from Cloudflare OS blueprints

Cloudflare OS records `upstream = {blueprintId, commitId}` on every app created from a shared template. Nothing updates automatically. "Update from blueprint" opens a proposal that the user previews and then accepts or discards, in one of three kinds:

- **follow**: the copy already has the release's changes; only the upstream pointer moves.
- **fastForward**: no local edits since the last release taken; the files become the release's.
- **merge**: a three-way merge against the common base. Only this kind can conflict, and an agent reviews it.

Source: https://github.com/cloudflare/cloudflare-os/blob/main/docs/blueprints.md

## Sketch

- On install, record on the extension block where it came from (a repo file, a URL, or a block) and keep the installed source as the merge base. Per the record-grain rule the base is its own block (for example a typed child of the extension block), not a JSON property.
- On update, compare three versions: base, local, upstream.
  - local == base: fast-forward.
  - upstream == base: nothing to do.
  - otherwise: a three-way text merge, optionally with an agent pass over conflicts, shown as a proposal to accept or discard.
- Accepting writes the merged source in one tx. The existing content-hash pin (`approveExtension` in `src/extensions/compileExtensionModule.ts`) then asks for approval again as it does today, so the user approves the merged source and the trust model doesn't change.
- New property and type ids are frozen seed identity once shipped (`src/data/seedIdentityLedger.ts`), so namespace them and pick names deliberately.

## Why

- Editing an installed extension shouldn't make it un-updatable. Today you choose between customising and staying current.
- It's cheap: install metadata, a merge step and one proposal dialog. No new runtime mechanism.
- It fits the current trust model without changes.

## Example

You changed how the Readwise extension (`agent-extensions/readwise.tsx`) surfaces highlights, and upstream later fixes a bug in its sync loop. Today you pick between losing your change and keeping the bug. With lineage you review one merge.

## Acceptance

- Installing records the upstream location and the base source.
- Updating an extension with no local edits fast-forwards.
- Updating an edited extension produces a merge proposal. Accepting it requires approval again, as any source change does today.
- Conflicts are shown to the user and never resolved silently.

## Open questions

- Which upstream kinds to support first: a repo file and a URL are simple; a block in another workspace needs a cross-workspace read.
- Whether "publish my edited copy as a new upstream", Cloudflare's derived blueprint, is in scope.

title: workspaceBackfillRunner sync-gating retry test times out at 5s under concurrent gate load
description:
src/data/internals/workspaceBackfillRunner.test.ts, 'workspace backfill runner — sync gating > still tells the operator a transient blocker IS worth retrying', timed out with `Error: Test timed out in 5000ms.` on vitest's default budget. It failed in one of two pnpm run check gates at the same commit while three gates shared the 12-core Mac (2026-10-23, load average up to ~190). The gate's verdict: failed only under load, passed alone. One sample so far.

Not diagnosed. Fix direction, the method from #1311: measure it alone and count its DB round trips (repo.metrics().db per phase, plus event-loop utilization). Check for an inner budget, such as a vi.waitFor, racing the 5s. Then either cut the setup's round trips or give the test an explicit budget with its measured cost in a comment.
close_reason: Closed on GitHub (issue #1418); reconciled by bd-github-sync.

title: agent-cli compiled contributor CLI tests time out at 30s under concurrent gate load
description:
packages/agent-cli/test/contributorCli.test.ts, describe 'compiled CLI contributor commands' (30s budget): two tests timed out with `Error: Test timed out in 30000ms.` in both of two pnpm run check gates at the same commit while three gates shared the 12-core Mac (2026-10-23, load average up to ~190). The gate's verdict for both: failed only under load, passed alone.

Failing tests:
- creates human profiles without selecting them and refuses selecting them
- uses the CLI flag before the environment and the environment before the saved selection

Not diagnosed. From the describe's name, each test runs the compiled CLI as child processes, so it is probably a chain of sequential cold node starts. That shape stretches with load the way serial worker round trips do (memory testing_serial_db_roundtrips_stretch_past_6x). This is reasoned, not measured.

Fix direction: count the spawns per test and measure each test alone and under three gates (KM_CHECK_SLOTS=4, two scratch worktrees). Prefer fewer spawns, or running the command in-process where the test does not need the compiled binary, over a bigger budget.
close_reason: Closed on GitHub (issue #1419); reconciled by bd-github-sync.

title: agent-dispatch daemon contributor-selection tests fail under concurrent gate load
description:
packages/agent-dispatch/test/daemon.test.ts, describe 'dispatch contributor selection': three tests failed in both of two pnpm run check gates at the same commit while three gates shared the 12-core Mac (2026-10-23, load average up to ~190). Each failed with `Error: Command failed: node <worktree>/packages/agent-dispatch/dist/daemon.js --config <tmp>/dispatch.json --once` and no stderr. The gate's verdict for both: failed only under load, passed alone.

Failing tests:
- uses the normalized profile for both token lookup and saved contributor selection
- clears disabled watcher registration without a contributor or attributed command
- passes the explicit none choice to the spawned MCP server

Likely cause (reasoned from the code, not measured): the `runDaemon` helper spawns the compiled daemon through `execFileAsync` with `timeout: 5_000`. A cold node start plus module load under heavy load can exceed 5s, so the child is killed with SIGTERM, well inside the describe's 20s budget. An inner budget racing load, not the test's own budget.

Fix direction: measure runDaemon's cost alone and under three gates (KM_CHECK_SLOTS=4, two scratch worktrees). Confirm the kill (`err.killed` / `err.signal`). Then give the inner timeout a load-sized value strictly below the enclosing test's budget, per AGENTS.md testing rules, with the measured cost in a comment.
close_reason: Closed on GitHub (issue #1420); reconciled by bd-github-sync.

title: Decouple block layout slot identity from the BlockResolveContext object
description:
`DefaultBlockRenderer` builds each layout slot as a `useMemo` over the `BlockResolveContext` object. So any new context identity is a new React element type, and the CodeMirror editor under Content/Shell remounts mid-typing. Characters since the last commit are lost, autocomplete is killed, and the caret moves. That is why context fields must be stable across ordinary editing (src/extensions/blockInteraction.ts, #548/#553).

The fix has two pieces, and the second must come first:

1. Stop memoizing slots on the resolve context; pass it through React context instead.
2. `blockContentDecoratorsFacet.combine` must guarantee identity-stable composition. Today it mints a fresh wrapped component per resolve unless the author used `cachedContentDecorator`. Piece 1 alone would reintroduce the remount through that door.

This would also let `ctx.aliases`/`types` be honestly reactive. That cannot be restored through a dependency list: a contribution is a structural gate, not a reactive one. `types` churn on its own is not a motivator, since it comes from accepting a dialog.

title: Typing a page title can degrade backlinks into pinned links for intermediate spellings
description:
Editing a page title is the main rename gesture, and it is typed one character at a time. Each debounced commit counts as a completed rename, so `references.renameBacklinks` rewrites every backlink source's content for each intermediate spelling. The comment in src/plugins/references/renameProcessor.ts ("Renames are rare and not on the typing path") is therefore wrong.

The full cascade was accepted on 2026-08-13 and is not the ask here. The remaining failure mode, observed 2026-08-14: an intermediate spelling that cannot render faithfully as a wikilink degrades the source's `[[wikilink]]` into a pinned `[label](((uuid)))` link. It still points at the right block but loses late binding.

Not re-verified since 2026-08-14 (renameBacklinks has run in the same tx since #461, before that observation); reproduce on current master first. Fix direction: an in-progress title edit should not count as a completed rename (commit the rename on blur or settle), or never degrade a wikilink for an intermediate spelling.

Related: #552 (the faithfulness guard does not validate through markdown).

title: Delete the Storage objects of deleted workspaces
description:
Deleting a workspace removes its rows and, since migration 20261019140000_never_reuse_workspace_ids.sql, its `blocks_history`. Its attachment objects under the workspace's Storage folder are never deleted. The workspace id is retired (never reused), so nothing can reach them through membership-gated RLS. They still occupy storage and keep a deleted workspace's bytes around after the owner asked for deletion.

Fix direction: delete the workspace's Storage objects as part of workspace deletion (a server-side job, since the client may never return), or sweep folders whose id is retired with no live workspace. Count first: on 2026-10-20 a count found 0 orphaned attachment objects, so the backlog may be empty and this is about future deletes.

title: Count, then repair, legacy type blocks created without PAGE_TYPE
description:
The retired "New type" button created type blocks without `PAGE_TYPE` ("half-types"), and nothing repairs them. No location or count has been gathered yet.

Step 1: count them, read-only, and see where they come from. Step 2, only if the count is non-zero: a repair. Per AGENTS.md, decide first whether it can fan out in a user tx or is a once-per-graph data migration ("one-shot catch-up passes"). Name the recovery path before writing anything.

title: Strength tracker: layoff records are never re-derived when sessions finish out of order
description:
In agent-extensions/strength-tracker/src/km/store.ts, `refreshLayoff` only DEEPENS a layoff record when it is re-measured worse. It never re-derives the record from a corrected finish order. So when sessions finish out of order (for example, a past session completed late), the recorded layoff can stay wrong. There is no reconcile path. Recorded 2026-08-14; the code still has no reconcile path on 2026-10-22.

Fix direction: re-derive the layoff from the ordered set of finished sessions whenever a session's finish changes, rather than only ratcheting it.

Layoff records use derived ids (`getOrCreateTypedChild`) on purpose: a duplicate layoff is silent and corrupting. A re-derive must keep that identity.

title: Cursor-follows-scroll: decide the edit-mode guard
description:
The scroll re-anchor declines while the panel is in edit mode: `PanelCursorFollowsScroll.tsx` reads the panel's `isEditingProp`, and `resolveSettledAnchor` in src/plugins/cursor-follows-scroll/viewportAnchor.ts returns null when `isEditing` is set.

Why the guard exists: moving focus closes the editor (`focusBlock` preserves edit mode only for an unchanged location), and scrolling with the phone keyboard up is exactly when that would fire.

What it costs: clicking a block enters edit mode, so the cursor does NOT follow scroll until Escape. Measured 2026-08-15: `isEditing: true` before Escape, `false` after, and follow resumes only after.

Flipping it is a one-line change plus a test, but it needs a decision. Is keeping the editor open during scroll worth the cursor not following until Escape?

title: Decide whether to lint raw tx.update({properties}) writes, and the post-flip moveSrsState simplification
description:
Two questions left from the properties-as-blocks work:

(a) Should a lint rule flag raw `tx.update({properties})` (whole-bag property writes) outside sanctioned call sites? It would need a path allowlist for the legitimate whole-bag writers: panel rename/delete, migration re-key, merge retarget, `moveSrsState`, and the importer. The precedent is `no-raw-synced-table-writes`. Raw writers to synced tables are legal in a few places, so the rule is about call sites, which a lint allowlist can express and a runtime wrapper cannot.

(b) Should the post-flip simplification of `moveSrsState` become an item under #389?

title: Property definitions claiming their name as an alias: decide the collision policy
description:
The natural next step after properties-as-blocks is auto-claim: a property definition block claims its name as an alias, as type blocks do, so `[[name]]` resolves through the normal alias index. Recognition is already form-agnostic, so field rows would light up with no recognition change. Not built (checked 2026-10-22).

Open decision, which affects live data: what happens when a definition's name-as-alias collides with an existing page of the same name. Types reject the second claimant, but seeded definitions cannot hard-fail bootstrap. The likely shape is best-effort/skip for seeds and reject for a user `addSchema`; it needs a ruling before anyone builds it.

title: Decide: should `;max` in a shared URL maximize the pane on the recipient's screen?
description:
Pane maximization (#549) stores the state as the `;max` slot-context key in the URL. A shared URL that carries `;max` therefore hides the other panes on the recipient's screen. That matches the design (§4.4 of docs/video-notes-navigation-native.html), but `;max` is the first slot-context key with that power, and the default has not been ruled on.

Options:
- Keep it: a shared link reproduces the sender's layout exactly.
- Strip `;max` when building a share link, or ignore it on arrival from an external link: the recipient keeps their own layout, and a link from the video-notes gesture loses its maximized view.

title: j/k navigation: residual gaps around nested surfaces
description:
Gaps the position rule from #519 left deliberately open in src/plugins/spatial-navigation (walker.ts / actions.ts). Recorded 2026-08-15 and still present in the code.

1. A nested surface inside a COLLAPSED row's still-mounted descendant has its own scope, so it takes the positional path and nothing rejects it. Fix direction: require the neighbour's owning row to be ancestor-or-self of either end of the move. This was declined at the time because the window needs a collapse, a surviving descendant, an embed inside it and a keystroke in the same commit, and nobody reproduced it. It needs a decision: fix it, or record the decline at the declaration.
2. `k` from outside a nested surface skips that surface's DEFERRED trailing rows. The near-side test is bounded only by the current scope's model row. Fix direction: consult `reservedRowBetween` on the main path, not only at the edge.
3. A deferred backlink ENTRY is unreachable: its wrapper mints its scope inside itself, so its slot is anonymous. This is the one reproducible stall left. It may be the same class as #514; check before fixing separately.

Related and tracked elsewhere: #514 (focused-location anchors that can't be re-resolved after a remount, including the scope-edge focus write with no watchdog) and #512 (two fast j/k presses collapsing into one move).

title: Local DB recovery: a standalone reset command and a save-picker backup gate
description:
Two follow-ups to the corrupt-local-database recovery flow (#281: src/utils/localDbRecovery.ts, src/components/util/LocalDbCorruptionFallback.tsx). Neither is built (checked 2026-10-22).

1. A "Reset local database" command reachable from settings, independent of hitting a real corruption. Today `resetLocalDatabase` is only reachable from the corruption fallback screen. The same invariants apply: never auto-wipe, always offer the backup first, and use different copy for local-only workspaces, where a reset destroys the only copy.
2. Where the File System Access API exists, use `showSaveFilePicker` as a real save-completion signal for the backup gate. Today reset unlocks only after the user explicitly confirms the backup saved, because an `<a download>` click has no completion signal. The primary target, iPad Safari, has no File System Access API, so the explicit confirmation must stay as the fallback. `chooseRawSqliteExportFile` in src/utils/exportSqliteDb.ts already wraps the picker for raw export.

title: Attachments: build the §16 reference-counted byte GC
E2EE uploads re-read the workspace key from IndexedDB for every op
description:
`encryptUploadOps` (src/services/powersync.ts) memoizes the upload MODE per workspace per batch, but calls `getCek` once per op. In production that is `requireWorkspaceKeys`, which opens an IndexedDB readonly transaction on every call, so a 10k-entry batch does 10k key reads.

Measured in Chrome on a ~780k-entry upload queue (a properties-as-blocks migration of a large workspace), sealing exactly as the connector does:
- per-op key read: 115 s total, ~148 µs/op
- one key per batch: ~35 µs/op, ~27 s total
- so roughly three quarters of e2ee upload encryption time is the key read, not the crypto

Fix direction: snapshot the key once per workspace per batch, the way `materializeStagingRows` does per window ("one key snapshot per workspace in this window"). It stays fail-closed: a missing key still throws for that batch. Normal edit-sized uploads don't notice either way; this matters for bulk uploads (migrations, imports, long-offline drains).
close_reason: Closed on GitHub (issue #1397); reconciled by bd-github-sync.

title: fixtureGraph.test.ts failed in every concurrent-gate run; cause not captured
description:
scripts/agent-eval/fixtureGraph.test.ts failed in every concurrent-gate run measured on 2026-10-22 (12-core Mac, 1-min load average 170-320, other sessions' gates also running). That was all 4 gates when 4 ran at once, and all 4 when 2 ran at a time. It passed in the one solo gate run.

The cause was not captured: the measuring script kept only failing file names. One gate failed on this file alone with zero 'Test timed out' lines, so that failure was not a test timeout. It may have been the 60s beforeAll hook timing out, or something else. Alone under a synthetic 3x CPU oversubscription (36 busy loops on 12 cores) the file passed in 73s, against 15s unloaded, so plain CPU starvation does not reproduce it.

Cost alone: about 15s. beforeAll imports about 5.8k blocks through the real Roam importer (about 4s), then about 10 write cases each copy the template DB and boot a fresh runtime (0.2-1.4s each). No test has a timeout above the 5s default, though create-linked-page takes 1.4s alone.

Next step: reproduce with two concurrent full gates and keep the full output when this file fails, then fix what the failure text shows. With the check-gate verdict in place, the gate prints 'failed only under load, passed alone' and the file's own failure output when it recurs.
close_reason: Closed on GitHub (issue #1392); reconciled by bd-github-sync.

title: bd-prime-hook: a hung bd leaves session start with no memory index and no reason
description:
`runBd` in `scripts/bd-prime-hook.mjs` passes no timeout to `spawnSync`. If bd blocks, for example while waiting on a store lock, the host kills the hook at its own limit. Codex's limit is 30s per `.codex/hooks.json`. The session then starts with no memory index and no `index unavailable` line. That is the one remaining path where the index goes missing silently.

Fix direction:
- Give the spawn a timeout below the host limit. In the Codex path, `bd codex-hook` and `bd memories` both have to fit inside it.
- Map a timeout to `index unavailable (ETIMEDOUT)`, the same way ENOBUFS is handled now.

Trap: bd 1.3.0 runs auto-push and backup after `memories`, `prime` and `codex-hook`, because none of them is in its read-only command list. A slow push can therefore outlast a timeout after the JSON was already written. Before choosing a timeout:
- check whether `--sandbox` (which disables auto-push) or `--readonly` skips that step;
- or accept a complete stdout despite the timeout.

Not reproduced: no read-only way was found to make bd block on a lock.

title: Publish gate: a gh call inside sh -c / bash -c is invisible to both hooks
description:
The pre-PR publish gate (`scripts/bd-github-sync.mjs --hook-pre-pr`) cannot see a `gh` publish that runs inside a shell string handed to another shell:

```
sh -c 'gh api repos/Stvad/knowledge-medium/pulls/1/comments/2/replies -f body="tracked in km-abcd"'
bash -c "gh pr comment 1 --body 'see #999'"
xargs -I{} sh -c 'gh api …/comments/{}/replies -f body=…'
```

The whole `gh …` call is one quoted word. Both readers miss it: the detectors scan a skeleton with quoted spans blanked, and the call reader keeps the string as a single token. So neither the pre-gate nor the post-publication read-back (`scripts/bd-publish-verify.mjs`) examines the text, and a bead id or an unread #N ships unchecked. This is the same on master; found during an adversarial review of the false-positive work.

The `xargs … sh -c` reply loop is a fairly common agent idiom.

Fix direction: when a segment's command is `sh`/`bash`/`zsh` (after the usual wrappers) with `-c`, feed the `-c` argument back through the same readers as a command of its own, the way a `$(…)` body is lifted today. Fail closed (count the command as a publish) when the argument is not literal (it holds an expansion).

Done when a test pins each spelling above as a publish and `pnpm run check` is green.

title: Extract one helper for projecting a property's cell from its field rows
description: The expression childContentsToEncodedPropertyValue(schema, unionValuesAcrossFieldRows(schema, perFieldRow).map(v => v.content)) is spelled at four sites: src/data/blockMerge.ts, src/data/internals/propertyChildrenProcessor.ts, and twice in src/data/internals/propertyDefinitionChangeProcessor.ts (valuesLostBy and applyToParent). These are the same rule (a property's value is the union across duplicate field rows, projected through the codec), so a change to it has to be made four times. Fix direction: a projectFieldRows(schema, perFieldRow) helper in src/data/propertyChildren.ts, next to the two functions it composes, used by all four. Behaviour-preserving; the existing property-children and definition-change suites cover every site. Found by the quality review of the PR that refuses changes to a definition whose current type does not load.

title: Adding an enum choice commits an empty option, so a widely used enum asks and walks twice per new choice
description:
The enum options editor (src/components/propertyEditors/EnumOptionsConfigEditor.tsx) commits "Add choice" immediately, as a structural act, with an empty value and label. Every write to a definition's config is a full fan-out over the property's consumers, and once PR 1115 lands, a fan-out of 1,000 or more consumers first asks for confirmation.

So on a widely used enum, adding one choice costs two confirmations and two full walks: one for the empty row, and one when its value is typed and blurred. The empty row on its own changes nothing a consumer can hold.

Direction: keep a new row as a draft and commit it on its first non-empty blur. The catch is the editor's render-phase resync, which replaces the whole draft when somebody else changes the committed options. A draft-only row must survive that, or be dropped knowingly, and its interaction with the `pending` marker needs a test.

Found reviewing PR 1115. Not a regression: before that PR the editor committed on every keystroke.

title: Readwise: drop the co-claimed-fallback release that the old alias trigger needed
description:
Follow-up from PR #1366.

The Readwise extension (`agent-extensions/readwise.tsx`) has a workaround for the old alias trigger, which re-inserted the whole bag on every properties write. That made a name a row co-claimed with a synced block abort any write keeping it. #1366 removes the re-insert, so the workaround now does harm:

- **`releaseCoClaimedFallback`** gives up a book's own recorded fallback alias whenever a synced row co-holds it, before the book's properties are written. Its stated reason ("one co-claimed entry rejects the whole transaction") is gone, so it now releases a name for nothing.
- **`pruneContestedAliases`** uses the old every-owner rule. It is only called on tombstones before a restore, and there it is still correct (a tombstone holds nothing). It could call core's `partitionClaimableAliases` instead of keeping its own copy.

Fix: delete `releaseCoClaimedFallback` and its call site, and update the tests in `readwise.aliasConflict.test.tsx` that pin the release. Then reinstall the extension, since source in the repo reaches the live copy only through `pnpm agent install-extension`.

title: Measure whether a large property-definition change leaves a write-ahead log the next open re-reads
description:
A rename or re-type of a property definition re-keys every consuming block inside ONE transaction (core.migratePropertyDefinition, same-tx by design). At 40k consumers that transaction rewrites tens of thousands of rows plus their upload-queue entries in a single commit.

The write-ahead-log upkeep added for bulk writes (writeAheadLog.ts: awaitWriteAheadHeadroom between batches, drainWriteAheadLog after, both via runBulkWrite) does not reach it. The headroom check cannot apply inside one transaction. The post-write drain could, but no definition change runs through runBulkWrite.

Unmeasured: how large the log is after a 40k-consumer rename, and whether it survives to the next page load. Under normal use the next writes after the commit checkpoint it and swap files, so the exposure may only be a tab closed right after the change.

To measure: on a large migrated graph, rename a widely used definition, read PRAGMA wal_checkpoint=noop on the writer connection right after, then reload and check the boot timeline. If it matters, the large-fan-out branch of the definition-change gate in PropertySchemaBlockRenderer (the gate from PR 1115) is where to wrap the write in runBulkWrite, and its progress surface would need a line for the drain.

Found while rebasing PR 1115 onto master.

title: Deleting a workspace leaves its workspace key and mode pin on the deleting device
description:
WorkspaceSettingsDialog's delete calls the delete_workspace RPC and navigates away, but nothing removes this device's local key material for the deleted workspace: the WK stays in the workspace key store (IndexedDB, getWorkspaceKeyStore) and the e2ee mode pin / pin-upgrade marker stay in localStorage (modePin.ts). Applies to every delete path (sidebar switcher, and now the key gate's settings button). Only the conversion flow ever deletes a stored key (conversionKey.ts).

Impact: a decryption key for a workspace that no longer exists lingers on the device indefinitely; stale pins are harmless but accumulate.

Fix direction: after a successful deleteWorkspace on this device, best-effort delete the key-store record and clear the mode pin + upgrade marker for (userId, workspaceId), in one helper the delete UI calls (useLeaveDeletedWorkspace in WorkspaceSwitcher.tsx is the natural owner). Other members' devices are out of reach and keep theirs; that is accepted.

title: Opening a workspace by URL on a device without it shows 'Loading workspace…' with no progress for the whole first download
description:
Seen in the E2EE conversion dry run: a second device whose local database was empty opened a converted workspace of about 50k blocks by URL. It showed only "Loading workspace…" for about 2.3 minutes, then the key prompt. Nothing on screen said a download was running, and the user reported it as stuck.

Cause: `WorkspaceSyncWaiting` in `src/App.tsx` waits for the workspace's row to appear locally. That row arrives with the first complete checkpoint, after every row in the sync stream has downloaded.

Reproduce: clear a profile's local database (or use a fresh one), then open `#<workspace id>` of a large workspace.

Fix direction: show the sync's download progress on that screen (rows or operations received so far), so a long first download reads as progress, not a hang. After a conversion, every other device goes through this screen after the PowerSync Defragment (runbook step 10).

title: Inline badges on a heavy navigation still resolve 0.7-1.3 s late, waiting on the navigation's layout write rather than their own SQL
description:
Measured 2026-10-20 on a local-only copy of a large graph after the properties migration (1.1M live blocks), current master, headed Chrome against the dev server. Sequence: fresh page load on a busy daily note, navigate to a heavily referenced page for 8 s, then back to the daily note. This is the same sequence as the measurement behind #1330.

The batching fix (#1338) holds at the database. That wave's 69 badges resolve through five batched statements of about 1 ms each. Pool depth peaks at 64, against 167 before. Child-id reads are p50 60-71 ms, against 278 ms.

What remains is end-to-end latency. All 69 badge resolves finish together, 0.7-1.3 s after they are requested: p50 1156, 695, 1316 and 1119 ms over four fresh loads. Child-id p95 lands at the same value.

A trace of every worker request shows the batch statements go out only after the navigation's write transaction commits. That transaction is "reconcile panel layout from URL", 1.5-1.7 s as repo.metrics slowestTx. Its wall time spans a 0.7 s main-thread long task, the render of the heavier page (seen with a PerformanceObserver longtask observer). Its BEGIN IMMEDIATE reply is handled 0.86-1.0 s after it was posted, because the main thread is busy rendering; the database is not slow there. Sampling Web Locks every 25 ms showed no write-lock contention: the writer held the lock throughout and nothing was pending.

Not established:
- why the badge batch dispatch waits for the in-flight write transaction: deliberate read-after-write ordering, the batch's microtask timing, or the connection lease;
- whether a small graph shows the same shape. Only the render cost should scale with graph size.

Directions, cheapest first:
1. Find what holds the badge batch until the layout write commits. If it is ordering, a read that does not depend on that write need not wait.
2. Let the layout write commit before the heavy render instead of spanning it.
3. Repeat the measurement on a small workspace to see whether any of this depends on graph size.

Not a blocker for the flip: no data risk, and a plain daily-note load measures the same as before the flip (DB getAll p50 10 ms vs 11 ms).

title: A write-ahead pause stalls every read in the tab whose long read caused it
description:
When a bulk writer (the properties migration, the Roam importer, any WorkspaceBackfill) pauses for the write-ahead log (src/data/writeAheadLog.ts awaitWriteAheadHeadroom, added for the log-growth fix), it holds the writer connection inside a truncate checkpoint until every read in flight ends.

PowerSync sends each read to whichever connection comes free first: the writer mutex or the reader semaphore (@powersync/web AsyncWebAdapter withConnection). With ADDITIONAL_READERS = 1 (src/data/repoProvider.ts), the tab whose long read is holding the log has no free connection at all during the pause, so all of its reads wait too. Other tabs keep their reads, because their readers are free. Writes wait everywhere, which is intended.

Reasoned from the PowerSync source, not measured. To measure: on the big-DB rig, issue a UI read while a pinned read holds a pause and time it.

Fix directions:
- ADDITIONAL_READERS = 2. The page-cache budget is total, so each connection gets less.
- Do the waiting OUTSIDE the writer lease (poll for the readers to catch up, then checkpoint). This needs the VFS's txId lock names, which are internal.
- Accept it: pauses only happen while a bulk write races a long read.

title: Stop setting window.React / window.ReactDOM once no stored extension reads the bare global
description: The in-browser extension compiler now uses the automatic JSX runtime, so extension JSX no longer reads the React global (see #1353). main.tsx still sets window.React and window.ReactDOM as a legacy convenience for stored extension sources that name React without importing it. No source in the repo does this at runtime. Before removing the globals, audit the extension sources stored in a real workspace for bare React or ReactDOM references (an extension that imports react or react-dom is unaffected). If none read them, delete the two assignments in main.tsx and the README note that calls the global legacy. If some do, they need a one-line import fix first. Removal is an extension-surface break: a source that still reads the bare global would throw a ReferenceError at call time.
close_reason: Closed on GitHub (issue #1355); reconciled by bd-github-sync.

title: Re-resolving the open workspace's layout re-applies the hash it was opened with
description:
App's `reResolve` (src/App.tsx) bumps the layout version but keeps `hashSnapshot.hash`, which only changes when the user switches workspace (`onLayoutHashChanged` / the hashchange listener ignore same-workspace changes). So a re-resolution of the OPEN workspace hands `bootstrapWorkspace` the hash the workspace was opened with, and its URL-to-layout step (`applyCurrentLayoutUrl` → `reconcilePanelRows`) appears to rewrite the panel rows to match that old hash.

Paths that re-resolve the open workspace: the server converting it in place (`useCloseOnServerE2ee`), the key-loss lock (`useCloseOnKeyLoss`, #1347) and the key gate's unlock after it, and the sync-waiting screen.

Suspected effect (found by reading, not yet reproduced): open a workspace by a deep link, rearrange or open panels, then trigger one of those paths; when the workspace reopens, the panels revert to the deep link's layout. A workspace opened at an empty hash should be unaffected.

Fix direction: have `reResolve` take `getCurrentHash()` rather than the snapshot's hash, after checking that the layout projection keeps the URL in step with the panels while the workspace is open.

title: Devices that receive the properties migration through sync keep pre-migration planner stats
description:
The device that runs the properties-as-blocks migration now re-analyzes the hot tables when its pass ends. Every OTHER device gets the same growth through sync and never does.

Measured on a local copy of a large graph, after the migration: `blocks` went from about 354k to 1.12M rows, `block_references` from about 228k to 644k, and both field-form indexes went from empty to about 369k rows. `sqlite_stat1` still held the pre-migration values for all of them. The boot check (`runAnalyzeIfStale`, i.e. `PRAGMA optimize`) does not react to this. It re-analyzes a table only when its row count drifts by about 10x, and an index that was empty when last analyzed keeps its `0 0` row. A receiving device therefore keeps pre-migration stats until the manual ANALYZE command runs. The same blind spot applies to any growth under 10x: a large import into an existing graph, or a large sync after the first-sync check.

No slow plan has been shown yet, so this is a watch item rather than a known regression.

Fix direction: a cheap growth detector in the boot check. The signal has to measure net growth, not inserts:
- `max(rowid)` tracks inserts, and without AUTOINCREMENT the top rowid is reused after the max row is deleted.
- `block_references` is maintained by delete-and-reinsert per edited block, so its rowid high-water mark counts ordinary edit churn as well.

Candidates are a bounded `COUNT(*)` of the tables already known to be hot, compared at deep idle against the recorded `sqlite_stat1` row count, or a per-table insert/delete counter maintained beside the existing side-index triggers. Either one also covers the importer.

title: Attachment-cleaner 413 stack test flakes: Storage resets the socket before its rejection arrives
description:
The attachment-cleaner stack test "keeps a raw object whose sealed copy is one byte over the bucket's limit, reporting Storage's 413" (src/plugins/attachments/attachmentCleanerIO.supabase.test.ts) fails intermittently under pnpm check:db. The cleaner reports `errors: [{message: 'upload failed: fetch failed'}]` and `refused: []` where the test expects `refused: [{status: 413, ...}]`.

Cause (measured 2026-10-20, Storage v1.80.2 on Apple container + socktainer): Storage rejects an over-limit upload before the body has finished arriving and closes the socket while the client is still writing it. A probe that POSTs limit+1 bytes straight to Storage, with no other test running and neither GoTrue nor PostgREST on the path, got Storage's rejection (HTTP 400, body statusCode "413") on 18 of 20 uploads; the other 2 threw `fetch failed` with cause `write ECONNRESET` / `write EPIPE`. Whether the client reads the response before the reset is timing.

Rate in the full stack-test run: 1 of 14 on GoTrue v2.189.0 / PostgREST v14.5, 3 of 6 on GoTrue v2.197.0 / PostgREST v14.18. Neither server is on the upload path; the bump can only shift timing through the concurrently running conversion stack test. The flake predates the bump.

Not known: whether hosted Storage, behind its gateway, also resets instead of answering. If it does, the cleaner tells the user "upload failed: fetch failed" (a transient error) where the actionable answer is "raise the upload limit". The raw object is kept either way, so nothing is lost.

Fix directions, undecided:
- refuse before uploading: compare the sealed size against the bucket's file_size_limit and report the refusal without sending ~50 MiB. Deterministic, and the test then pins the pre-upload check. It needs the limit readable by the client; whether an authenticated user can read storage.buckets is unchecked.
- classify a write reset during an upload whose size exceeds the limit as the refusal. This guesses at the cause, so it's the weaker option.
Making the test accept either outcome is not a fix.
close_reason: Closed on GitHub (issue #1339); reconciled by bd-github-sync.

title: E2EE conversion: let adoption tell the purge's bundle from an earlier take
description: A device with no bundle record adopts the recovery bundle by verifying a folder's own consistency only: after the purge the server keeps nothing to compare against (workspace_conversions holds only the phase). An earlier take of the same workspace, one the flow told the user could go after a stale or changed retake, verifies too. Deletes stay safe because the cleaner deletes an archived object only when the bundle entry holds its bytes, but that take's noVerifiedSource list can mark a block unrecoverable that the purge's bundle holds, and a later key-loss restore from it would roll back what the retake added. Fix direction: have purge_workspace_history record the purged through and the archived count (or the manifest sha256) on the conversion row, and require an adopted bundle to match them.

title: E2EE attachment cleaner: report the keyed copy of a converted orphan
description: In the run that converts a raw orphan R(h) (an object named by its own hash that no media block references), or finds K(h) next to it, the keyed copy K(h) is marked 'stays' (placed or keyed) and appears in no left list. The finish screen then says every attachment is encrypted while an unreferenced ciphertext copy stays. A later run reports it as left 'not-archived' with the reason 'the recovery bundle has no copy of it', which is wrong: its plaintext is in the bundle's other-objects/ under the raw path. Design doc section 6.3 step 8 says such objects are kept and reported. Fix direction: report a keyed copy under a hash no media block carries as left with its own reason (for example 'orphan-copy') in the run that places it, and let the finish prompt show it. Ciphertext only, so low severity.

title: check:db pins GoTrue and PostgREST behind the hosted project
description:
scripts/check-db.mjs says its GoTrue and PostgREST images are the hosted project's, as a linked checkout records them in supabase/.temp. Those files only update on `supabase link` and are months stale. `npx supabase services` (2026-10-19) reports the hosted project on GoTrue v2.197.0 and PostgREST v14.18, while check:db pins v2.189.0 and v14.5. Its Storage pin (v1.80.2) was taken from `supabase services` and matches.

Fix: bump both pins, run `pnpm check:db` (the re-seal and attachment-cleaner stack tests run against them), and name `npx supabase services` as the source in the comment. ECR rate-limits anonymous pulls; pull docker.io/supabase/gotrue:<tag> and docker.io/postgrest/postgrest:<tag> and re-tag them under public.ecr.aws/supabase/ if needed.
close_reason: Closed on GitHub (issue #1333); reconciled by bd-github-sync.

title: A post-commit processor that throws loses its event: derived data stays missing until the source is edited again
description:
ProcessorRunner.runOne (src/data/internals/processorRunner.ts) catches a processor's error, logs it and moves on. The event is not kept, so whatever that processor derives for the rows in it is never derived unless one of the watched fields changes again.

Example: references.parseReferences failing for a commit leaves that commit's [[links]] without references or pages. Backlinks stay missing until the user edits the block. The ref backfill does not repair it, because it runs once per workspace behind a marker.

Where it bites on an encrypted workspace: the parse processor cannot mint a page for a new [[link]] when this device holds no key for the workspace while the alias-seat namespace cache is cold. That case no longer drops silently (#1347): the key read locks the workspace into the unlock screen, and the processor's event throws instead of writing the source's references without the new page. The event is still lost, so after the key is pasted back those links stay without references or pages until the block is edited again. That remaining part is the general problem this issue tracks.

Fix directions:
- keep failed events and retry them with backoff, for errors marked transient;
- or a per-workspace re-derive pass that finds rows whose stored references disagree with a fresh parse, run on open after a failure was recorded.

title: Rejection dialog Retry re-queues one row, splitting a refused transaction
description:
The upload path quarantines a refused PowerSync transaction whole: recordRejectionToTable (src/services/powersync.ts) writes every CrudEntry of the transaction into ps_crud_rejected under one tx_id. But RejectionDialog.handleRetry (src/plugins/system-status/RejectionDialog.tsx) re-inserts and deletes only the selected row. Retrying a multi-entry transaction therefore uploads its entries in separate passes, so a create and the patches that depend on it, or a parent and its child, can be re-applied partly.

Fix direction: Retry (and Dismiss) act on every ps_crud_rejected row with the selected tx_id, in one write transaction, in original id order. Show the transaction as one item in the dialog.

Found while designing key-loss recovery (docs/workspace-key-loss-recovery.md), whose adoption step moves a workspace's whole stale backlog into this quarantine, which makes multi-entry retries common.

title: agentViews output-budget test times out at 5s under gate load
description:
src/plugins/agent-runtime/test/agentViews.test.ts, test 'view-outline > the output budget > keeps the breadth-first prefix whose printed lines fit, and continues by offset from there', failed with 'Test timed out in 5000ms' during a full pnpm run check at load average ~280 (the gate took 250s against a ~64s idle baseline). Alone, the whole file passes in about 3.4s (115 tests).

The commit 'test(agent-views): the bulk-tree budget tests fit vitest's default timeout' made these tests fit 5s. That leaves no headroom for the ~6x p99.9 stretch that AGENTS.md budgets for.

Fix direction: measure this test alone, then give it (or its describe) an explicit timeout with the measured cost in a comment, per AGENTS.md 'timeout budgets under load'.
close_reason: Closed on GitHub (issue #1311); reconciled by bd-github-sync.

title: E2EE conversion: integration-test the re-seal and verify engine against a local Supabase stack
description:
The re-seal/verify engine (src/sync/conversion/) is unit-tested against an in-memory server model, and its PostgREST adapter (createSupabaseConversionServer) against an in-memory query builder. Neither proves the adapter's filters behave as assumed on real PostgREST: the JSONB path filter (after_diff->>content like enc:v1:%), the text[] containment filter on changed_columns, keyset paging on id and event_id, and apply_block_patches' history rows carrying the full pre-seal plaintext in before_diff.

Needs the server migration's flip RPC so a test can take a seeded plaintext workspace to e2ee.

Done when: a test against a local Supabase stack seeds a plaintext workspace with history, flips it, runs resealWorkspace then verifyReseal through createSupabaseConversionServer, and shows every row sealed, each record found, and a tampered row repaired from before_diff.
close_reason: Closed on GitHub (issue #1306); reconciled by bd-github-sync.

title: Park a workspace's held or frozen upload transactions so one workspace can't stall a device's whole queue
description:
**Deferred — needed only for the multi-client design** (`docs/workspace-e2ee-conversion.md` §11).

PowerSync uploads a device's transactions in strict FIFO order, so one held or refused transaction for a workspace stalls that device's whole queue. Parking would move such transactions, in order, to a local side table and replay them later.

The single-client conversion doesn't need it: other devices are closed during the run and unlock right after. It stays filed as a robustness improvement for the multi-client case.

title: agent-cli bridge test leaks a server process whenever its worker dies before teardown
description:
## Problem

`packages/agent-cli/test/bridgeServer.test.ts` spawns the built `dist/server.js` as a child process on a random port and kills it in `afterAll`. When the test worker dies before teardown (a killed or interrupted gate, a timeout, a crashed worker), the child keeps running forever. On one development machine, 39 such bridges had accumulated over two months, each still listening on its random loopback port, most of them from worktrees that had already been deleted.

Related, same root: the long-lived bridge on the default port can be a build from a long-gone checkout, so bridge-side fixes silently never run (#1247 covers detecting a version mismatch from the CLI).

## Direction

- Make a test-spawned bridge die with its parent: e.g. the test passes its PID (or keeps a stdin pipe open) and the server exits when the parent is gone. Gate this behind an explicit test-only flag so the real detached bridge is unaffected.
- Or run the server in-process for the test, if the end-to-end wire coverage survives that.

## Done when

Killing a vitest worker mid-run leaves no bridge process behind (checked by a test or a scripted repro), and a normal run still exercises the bridge over the wire.
close_reason: Closed on GitHub (issue #1282); reconciled by bd-github-sync.

title: Measure headless data imports that still load daily-note UI
description: Follow-up to the measured test-only import reductions in PR #1276. Production Roam helpers ids.ts:1, roamMemo.ts:1, srsMarkers.ts:1, import.ts:31 and report.ts:2 import data helpers from the daily-notes UI barrel; all those helpers already live in dailyNotes.ts. left-sidebar/shortcuts.ts:7 and srs-rescheduling/srsBlockDateAdapter.ts:10 do the same. These paths kept the module graphs unchanged in the derivedIds/Roam/SRS test probes despite narrower test imports. Measure source-level leaf imports across all relevant paths before keeping a change. SRS plugin-index tests intentionally load UI; do not pretend a helper import change removes their independent UI path. Preserve runtime contracts and all test coverage.
notes: Ready for merge: PR #1280 at 0950de8714. Production Roam, sidebar shortcuts and SRS adapter use existing daily-note data leaves; coordinated four data-test imports. Focused 152 tests passed; 2,154 to 1,527 per-file module entries (627 fewer, 29%). Local full pnpm run check passed 758 files / 10,847 tests in 165.04s. CI 39014752138 passed the same 758 files / 10,847 tests, build/export and extension checks; preview 39014752119 passed. Automatic review completed with no findings. CI gate 353.44s versus merged baseline 39014265298 at 370.60s; 361 untouched >=100ms files were also median 4.9% faster, so no isolated full-suite timing win claimed. Awaiting user merge; Fixes #1278 will close through sync.
close_reason: Closed on GitHub (issue #1278); reconciled by bd-github-sync.

title: sync: a staged row reached after a later local edit's upload completed reverts that edit
description:
A staged row the drain reaches only after a LATER local edit of the same block has uploaded is written over that edit.

Reproduction (reasoned from the code, not yet observed):
1. A checkpoint publishes normally (queue empty, `$local` hold released) and stages block X at v1, flagged needs_apply.
2. Before the drain reaches X, the user edits X to v2. v2 uploads, and complete() empties ps_crud.
3. The drain runs. Both its Phase-1 read and its Phase-2 re-check of ps_crud see no pending upload for X, so it writes v1 over v2.
4. v2 comes back only with its echo, which the `$local` hold now delays until the write checkpoint covers it. So the revert lasts somewhat longer than it did before the hold.

It needs the drain to lag behind a whole upload round trip. The drain throttle is 100 ms, so steady state is safe. It is plausible during catch-up drains: initial sync, coming back online, or a write lock contended across windows. The doc on decideStagingRow accepts this cost only for rescan paths (drainWorkspace), and this is the queue path.

Fix direction (a design call; NOT the rejected newer-or-equal gate):
- Treat ids that were acknowledged but not yet echoed as still pending while the hold is engaged.
- For example, an AFTER DELETE trigger on ps_crud records the uploaded ids in a local side table.
- The drain adds those ids to its pending set while `$local.target_op > last_op`.
- The table is cleared once the hold releases. By then the echo has replaced the stale staged row.

Measure first: after the hold deploys, count sync update row_events whose after updatedAt is below the before updatedAt. If that count stops growing, this path is too rare to be worth new state.

title: agent-eval fixtureGraph test: shared beforeAll exceeds its 60s budget under heavy gate load
description:
`scripts/agent-eval/fixtureGraph.test.ts`: the top-level `beforeAll` (seed ~5.8k blocks, snapshot, reopen) failed with `Hook timed out in 60000ms` in two consecutive `pnpm run check` gates on macOS on 2026-10-16, at load averages ~150-200 on 12 cores (several parallel sessions' gates). The other 756 files passed in both gates. A third gate at load ~56-130 passed. Alone, the whole file takes ~16 s, and the hook's own comment puts seeding at ~5 s alone, so the 60 s budget is ~12x headroom. It is still the most load-sensitive hook in the suite.

Not urgent: it needs oversubscription well past the 3-6x stretch AGENTS.md budgets for. Fix direction, if it keeps recurring: measure the hook's solo cost precisely. Then either cut the seeding (seed once to a template file and copy it, as the per-case `openGraph` already does), or raise the hook budget with the measured cost stated beside it.

title: bd-codex-session-end tests: launcher reports started:false under extreme load
description:
`scripts/bd-codex-session-end.test.ts`: two cases that call the real launcher, "uses file descriptors and unrefs the child, without probing for a Beads clone" and "captures a failing delegated sync in stderr-backed log output", occasionally fail with `expect(result.started).toBe(true)` receiving `false` after about 2 s.

Observed 2026-10-16 on macOS: one failure in each of two arms of 32 runs, at load average ~280 (8 concurrent copies of the file plus file-system churn plus other sessions' gates). Not seen at lower load. This is separate from the release-file flake fixed alongside it (that fixture now polls instead of using `fs.watch`).

Cause not proven. `launchSessionEndSync` returns `started: false` only when `resolveMainRepoRoot` returns null (its `git rev-parse` probe errors, exits non-zero or hits the 1 s `PROBE_TIMEOUT`), or when `mkdirSync`/`openSync`/`appendFileSync` on the log throws. The ~2 s duration fits the probe timeout, but a direct timing of that `git rev-parse` under similar load peaked at 143 ms.

Fix direction:
1. Make the failure self-describing first: `expect(result.started, result.error).toBe(true)` in both cases, so the next failure names its branch.
2. If it is the probe timeout: the 1 s budget is a production choice (Codex caps the SessionEnd hook at 3 s), so let the tests pass a larger probe timeout (or a probe stub) rather than raising the production value.

title: Agent subtree view: bound its output by characters, not only by block count
description:
## What happens

In the agent ergonomics eval, the MCP `reading-log-filter` task opens with the same call on every run (6 of 6 across two runs): `subtree` on a 2,000-child page with `depth: 4, limit: 300, properties: "full"`. It renders 86.7k characters, which is over Claude Code's MCP output cap (25k tokens). The whole result is replaced by a notice, so the call is wasted, and the agent falls back to raw SQL.

Every agent view caps rows by count, not by characters: outline up to 2,000 blocks, backlinks 500, search 200. So a large enough `limit` can push any of them over the cap. Only `subtree` has done so in the eval.

## Fix direction

The cut has to be made in each view. A cut in the dispatcher would leave the `offset=` continuation wrong.

For the outline: keep the breadth-first prefix of the selected blocks whose rendered lines fit a budget under both clients' caps (about 24k characters; the CLI shell cap is 30k). Then say the budget stopped it, with the ways to narrow: `properties: none`, a lower limit or depth, or search with `under`. The existing "+N children" and "continue with offset" lines stay correct if dropped nodes are removed before the rows are built.

## Measure before building

A budgeted reply puts about 24k characters in front of the agent, where the cap notice cost 1.4k. In this task, 70 of 2,000 entries don't answer the question either, so the task's context may go up. The win is for the class (reading a long page in chunks), not for this task. Measure with `pnpm agent-eval run --tasks reading-log-filter --repeat 3` on both surfaces.
close_reason: Closed on GitHub (issue #1257); reconciled by bd-github-sync.

title: Agent ergonomics eval: output-size probes through the CLI
description:
The eval's deterministic output-size probes (scripts/agent-eval/outputBudgets.ts) call the km MCP tools only, so they budget and report MCP output sizes on both surfaces. The CLI renders some results differently: the 2,000-child Reading Log subtree is about 229k characters through kmagent and 644k through MCP. A change to the CLI renderer alone therefore shows no size delta, and nothing stops CLI output from growing back after the read slice shrinks it.

Direction: give each probe a CLI form (the kmagent verb and arguments that ask the same question), run it in the fixture-graph test through the CLI's own rendering against the in-process graph, and budget it beside the MCP size. Report both columns in the size table, and record CLI sizes for the CLI surface's runs.

Done when the gate budgets CLI output sizes for every probe, and a CLI report shows CLI sizes.

title: Repo-level read snapshot, so a read made of several queries sees one consistent state
description:
The agent read views (src/plugins/agent-runtime/agentViews/) answer each command with several queries in a row: list ids, load rows, count children, walk breadcrumbs, and call shared queries (backlinks, grouped backlinks, search, alias matches) through the repo query layer. Sync can commit between those reads, so one response can disagree with itself by what changed: a child count off by one, a row missing or extra, a breadcrumb one step stale. The next call is correct. #1241 accepts this for the read views and keeps the cheap invariants (a count is never below what is shown, the workspace is bound in SQL, no offset is offered that cannot be read).

The systematic fix is a repo-level read-snapshot scope: one read transaction held for the whole multi-query read, with the query layer routing its reads through that transaction and bypassing its result caches (a cached result from another moment would break the snapshot). It is a data-layer design, not a view change.

Costs to weigh before building it:
- On WAL devices the database has one writer plus one additional reader connection (ADDITIONAL_READERS in src/data/repoProvider.ts). A snapshot held for a whole view occupies that reader, so the UI's own reads queue behind it.
- On non-WAL devices there is a single connection, so a held read also delays writes, including the user's edits.

Measure first: how often a concurrent write actually lands inside a view's read window, and how long the largest views hold the reader.

title: Paginate the backlinks query so a bounded view loads one page
description: The backlinks panel and the agent view-backlinks command both call BACKLINKS_FOR_BLOCK_QUERY, which loads and machinery-filters every backlink id of the target before any page is taken. For a target with hundreds of thousands of backlinks, a 20-row agent page still materializes the whole set. Fix direction: a count plus a paged variant of the same query in the backlinks plugin (one owner for the set, so the panel and the agent view keep agreeing), and switch view-backlinks to it. Raised in review of the agent read views.

title: Agent tokens dialog: 'last seen' never updates (lastSeenAt has no writer)
description:
AgentToken.lastSeenAt in src/plugins/agent-runtime/tokens.ts is shown by the tokens dialog ('last seen …'), but nothing writes it: AgentTokenStore.touch has no caller, and the bridge registration reply carries no per-token usage. So the dialog never shows when a token was last used, which is the one signal a user has for spotting a stale token to revoke.

Fix direction: have the bridge server report, in the registration response, which of the listed tokens submitted a command since the last registration (it already sees every submission), and let the tab call touch() for those. Alternatively drop lastSeenAt and the dialog text if usage isn't worth tracking.

title: Document the graph as an agent working surface (AGENTS.md pointer to km MCP)
description:
Once the bounded read views and markdown-native writes land, tell agents in this repo when and how to use the graph as a working surface — today AGENTS.md frames `pnpm agent` only as a dev/inspection tool for the live client.

- A short AGENTS.md section (or a skill) pointing at the `km` MCP tools for graph work, distinct from the `pnpm agent` dev loop; one line on what not to do (no raw SQL writes, no unbounded reads).
- Keep the MCP `instructions` and `guide` tool as the single source; the repo text points at them instead of restating them.

title: Rich paste fuzz: add a text-preservation oracle to the tag-soup suite
description:
The clipboard-HTML tag-soup fuzz suite (src/plugins/rich-paste/test/htmlToOutline.fuzz.test.ts) only asserts that no block renders nothing. Two silent text losses fixed in #1222 were invisible to it: a link the converter splits around a list ended up inside the list and its item was dropped, and a list item outside a list was dropped by walkFlow.

Add a property: when the result is an outline or an inline paste, every letter and digit of the HTML's text, after normalizeClipboardDom has removed non-content, appears in order in the output markdown. Check it as a subsequence, because URLs, list numbers and image alt text add characters. Expect it to surface more converter losses; per docs/fuzzing.md, diagnose each one (product bug or unsound oracle) before changing anything.
close_reason: Closed on GitHub (issue #1223); reconciled by bd-github-sync.

title: bd auto-push blocks whichever command trips its throttle for 15-22s
description:
bd 1.3.0 runs its Dolt auto-push (`dolt.auto-push=true`, set on the one machine that pushes the beads remote) synchronously, in the post-run hook of whichever bd command is running when the 5-minute push throttle has lapsed and the head has moved since the last push. That command blocks for the whole git+ssh push.

Measured 2026-10-15 against the live tracker (bd 1.3.0):
- one `bd close` inside a bd-github-sync run: 15.6s, with the push-state file rewritten during the call. The same close with no push due: 0.65–0.86s.
- `bd dolt push` that committed and pushed a small delta, then ran its own auto-push: 22.5s. An explicit push with nothing new: 4.2s, which is the git+ssh round trip alone.
- auto-backup, by contrast, adds about 0.3s when it is due.

This is what put bd-github-sync over its 15s budget twice (a 22.9s `bd close` and an 18.3s `bd github sync --push-only`, a single step each time).

What this repo did: bd-github-sync now runs its bd commands with `BD_DOLT_AUTO_PUSH=false`; the env var overrides the yaml setting, checked with `bd config get`. The push now waits for bd's next auto-push outside the sync. The trade: the Dolt remote can lag by the sync's own commits until some other bd command trips the throttle. Nothing is lost: the commits are local, and every change the sync makes is also on GitHub. Every other bd command still pays the full push when it lands on it, including agents' interactive writes.

Fix direction, upstream in bd: take auto-push off the command's critical path. One way is a detached push process that holds the push lock and records push-state when it finishes. Another is a per-invocation "defer maintenance" mode for batch callers. Either way, adopt it through the upgrade checklist in #877, not as a side effect.

title: An extension property name is held by two live definitions with different presets
description:
A read-only audit of a live workspace (2026-10-15, while fixing #1204) found readwise:location held by two property definitions: one with preset optional-string (what agent-extensions/readwise.tsx declares today) and one with preset optional-number. Every stored cell under the name is JSON text.

Which codec reads the cells depends on which definition wins the name. If the number one wins, every cell decodes as a failure, and since #1204's fix (comparators admit only cells of the codec's storage shape) no where comparator on the property matches anything.

To find out: where the optional-number definition came from (an earlier seed revision, a synthesized definition, a user edit), and whether the shared-name refusal (property.definition-change.shared-name) should have prevented it or predates it. Fix direction is the data repair the seed-identity ledger describes for a key two seeds claim, not a query change.

title: pr-reply test flakes: refsCap reads the clock twice, so the echo cap is 4 or 5 by millisecond timing
description:
`scripts/pr-reply.test.ts` › "bounds the reference echo by a cap and a time budget" fails intermittently in CI: it expects 5 issue lookups and gets 4. It passes locally.

## Why

`pr-reply.mjs` computes the cap as `refsCap(Date.now() + ECHO_BUDGET_MS)`, and `refsCap` then calls `Date.now()` a second time:

    Math.floor((deadline - Date.now()) / ISSUE_LOOKUP_TIMEOUT) - 1

The default budget is an exact multiple of the lookup timeout.

- When both `Date.now()` calls land in the same millisecond, `floor` sees exactly 6 and the cap is 5.
- When even one millisecond passes between them (common on a loaded CI runner), it sees 5.9999…, so `floor` gives 5 and the cap is 4.

The assertion is therefore a millisecond-boundary race, not a budget check.

## Fix directions

- Compute the cap from the budget itself, `refsCap` taking a duration rather than a deadline, so no clock read sits between the two.
- Or keep the deadline but make the default budget a non-multiple of the lookup timeout, and assert the cap the budget implies.

Seen failing on a PR whose diff does not touch either file. A re-run of the failed job is the stop-gap.
close_reason: Closed on GitHub (issue #1213); reconciled by bd-github-sync.

title: Restore resurrects a property a peer deleted before the owner went down (stale cell + single-tombstone revival)
description:
Raised in review of the props-as-blocks dual-write fuzz suite; confirmed with a deterministic repro.

## Repro (flipped workspace)

1. Block A has `status: done`, so it has a field row and a value child.
2. A peer deletes the property. Its field-row and value tombstones arrive, but the owner row's cell update does not: it loses last-writer-wins to a newer local edit of A. Arrivals never re-project, so A's cell still says `status: done` over tombstoned children.
3. Locally, delete A (subtree), then restore it, in separate transactions.

**Actual:** A comes back with `status: done`. The restore revives the peer's tombstoned field row and value (#787), so the peer's delete is silently resurrected.

## Why

- `reviveTombstonedFieldRow` revives the single tombstoned field row for a definition. It cannot tell a tombstone the owner's own delete created from one that already existed before the owner died. Its docblock already rejects a clock comparison between rows for the multi-tombstone case: peer clocks make it unsound.
- Not reviving would not be enough on its own. The revival re-materializes every key in the restored bag, and with no live field row for `status` the untouched-key path mints a fresh one from the stale cell, which resurrects the value as well.

The root is the stale cell the arrival leaves behind. The revival then treats that cell as untouched truth.

## Fix directions

- Record deletion provenance: which tombstones the owner's own delete cascade created (for example a tombstone stamp tied to the deleting transaction, or a cascade marker). Revive only those, and for a key whose field row died BEFORE the owner, read "unset" instead of minting.
- Or close the stale-cell gap at its source: let arrivals that tombstone a field row (or its last value) reconcile the owner's cell. That is a synced-column write from the arrival path; see the CRITICAL INVARIANT in `syncObserver/arrivalProcessors.ts`.

Pre-existing (`master`): the single-tombstone revival predates this suite. Reachability is low, since it needs an LWW-lost owner cell update followed by a local delete and restore of that owner. The outcome is a silently resurrected delete.

title: Deleting and restoring a block in ONE transaction silently unsets all its properties
description:
Found by the props-as-blocks dual-write fuzz suite (`src/data/internals/propertyDualWrite.fuzz.test.ts`).

## Repro (flipped workspace)

1. Block A has property `flag: false`, so it has a field row and a value child.
2. In ONE transaction: subtree-delete A (`deleteSubtreeInTx`, as `core.delete` does), then `tx.restore(A)`.

**Expected:** A comes back with `flag: false`, as it does when the delete and the restore are separate transactions (the #778 revival re-materializes the bag).

**Actual:** A is live, its field and value rows stay tombstoned, and the cell no longer has `flag`. Every property of A is silently unset.

## Why

The same-tx processors see the transaction's NET change.

- A's `deleted` is unchanged net (live → live), so MATERIALIZE's revival branch, which keys on a tombstone → live transition, never fires.
- The field rows went live → dead, so PROJECT re-projects A in `'full'` mode, finds no live field row, and unsets each key ("the deletion won").

## Fix directions

- Treat a row whose `deleted` flipped during the tx as revived even when the net value is unchanged. This needs the per-row write log, not just before/after.
- Or have `tx.restore` of a row deleted earlier in the same tx also restore what that delete took.

Reachability is low: no known UI path deletes and restores one block in a single transaction. But the outcome is silent loss of every property on the block.

The fuzz suite carries a `KNOWN ISSUE (fuzz)` carve-out for this shape that should be removed with the fix: it skips the intent check for an owner deleted and restored in one transaction.
close_reason: Closed on GitHub (issue #1211); reconciled by bd-github-sync.

title: Restore + same-tx field-row re-marking leaves a cell key with no field row (MATERIALIZE reads pre-DERIVE bits)
description:
