Found by the props-as-blocks dual-write fuzz suite (`src/data/internals/propertyDualWrite.fuzz.test.ts`).

## Repro (flipped workspace)

1. Blocks A and B both carry the property `related`, so both have a field row and a value child.
2. Delete A (subtree). A's field and value rows are tombstoned.
3. In ONE transaction:
   - restore A;
   - move B's `related` field row under A;
   - edit that row's content to plain text, so it is no longer `::`-marked.

**Expected:** A's own tombstoned `related` field row is revived (or a fresh one is minted from the cell), and the cell agrees with the children.

**Actual:** A's cell still says `related: …` but A has no live field row for it.

## Why

Same-tx processor order is MATERIALIZE → DERIVE → PROJECT.

- MATERIALIZE's revival branch picks A's field rows by the `is_field_form` bit. DERIVE has not re-stamped that bit yet for the edited row, so the moved-in row still counts as A's `related` field row. The revival therefore neither revives A's tombstoned row nor mints one.
- DERIVE then clears the bit.
- PROJECT only re-projects the moved row's OLD owner (B). The moved row is no longer a field row, so A's pair is never touched.
- MATERIALIZE's pass-two re-run covers only rows dirtied after its watermark. That is the moved row, not A, so the revival decision is never revisited.

Low reach: it needs a restore and a tree edit that changes a field row's marking under the same owner, in one transaction.

## Fix directions

- MATERIALIZE's pass two could re-run the revival for the PARENT of any row whose field-form bit or target DERIVE changed after MATERIALIZE's watermark.
- Or classify field rows from content inside the revival branch. This needs care: §9 selection is deliberately bit-based.
- Moving DERIVE ahead of MATERIALIZE is a broader ordering change; check the comments in the kernel processor list first.

The fuzz suite carries a `KNOWN ISSUE (fuzz)` carve-out for this shape that should be removed with the fix: it waives projection for an owner revived in the same transaction as a child edit under it.
close_reason: Closed on GitHub (issue #1210); reconciled by bd-github-sync.

title: Typed query comparators match property cells of the wrong JSON type
description:
`where` comparators in the typed-block query compiler (`src/data/internals/typedBlockQuery.ts`) compile to `json_extract(properties_json, path) <op> ?`, with the operand from `codec.where.encode`. Nothing checks that the STORED cell has the codec's JSON type, and SQLite orders values across storage classes (INTEGER/REAL < TEXT, JSON `true`/`false` extract as 1/0, an array or object extracts as its JSON text). So a cell the property's codec could not have written matches comparators it should not:

| property | stored cell | where | matches? |
|---|---|---|---|
| number | `"abc"` | `{gt: 3}` | yes (TEXT > INTEGER) |
| number | `true` | `1` | yes (`true` extracts as 1) |
| string | `5` | `{lt: "m"}` | yes (INTEGER < TEXT) |
| string | `["a"]` | `{lt: "m"}` / `'["a"]'` | yes (array's JSON text) |
| boolean | `1` | `true` | yes |
| date | `""` | `{lt: <any date>}` | yes (`""` sorts first) |
| date | `"2026-01-01"` (non-canonical) | `{lt: 2026-05-01}` | yes; `eq 2026-01-01` does NOT match |

Measured with a raw-insert probe against the real test DB. Exclude is affected symmetrically (a stale cell can be wrongly excluded).

**Reachability.** Such cells are an accepted residual: `propertyDefinitionChangeProcessor` documents that a re-type in a workspace with no field rows yet fans nothing out, leaving cells in the old encoding; an older client or a hand edit can do the same. The query then silently returns wrong members (e.g. a "priority > 3" view listing every block whose priority is a leftover string). Low frequency, silent effect.

**Fix direction.** A comparator should only match a cell whose `json_type` is the codec's storage type (`text` for string/date/url/enum, `integer`/`real` for number, `true`/`false` for boolean), e.g. `json_type(properties_json, path) IN (…) AND json_extract(…) <op> ?`. That needs `WhereCapability` to declare its storage type(s), since the compiler is codec-agnostic. Check the expression-index plans for the `=` path stay intact. Dates additionally assume canonical `toISOString()` storage; a non-canonical but parseable string compares lexicographically, so either canonicalize at write or compare via a normalized expression.

**Fuzz carve-out.** `typedBlockQuery.fuzz.test.ts` generates malformed cells only for ref / refList / list properties (where no comparator applies); its `KNOWN ISSUE (fuzz)` note on `FOREIGN_CELLS` marks the scalar kinds as excluded. When this is fixed, extend the foreign-cell generator to the scalar kinds and the model (which already says "a malformed cell matches no comparator") becomes the regression test.

The refList half of this class (a non-array cell made every `target` query throw `malformed JSON`) is fixed in the PR that adds the suite.
notes: Same class, date codec: a date outside years 0000-9999 encodes as `+010000-01-01T00:00:00.000Z` / `-000001-…`, which sorts BEFORE every 4-digit year as text, so `{lt: <2026 date>}` matches a year-10000 date. The fuzz suite keeps its date pool inside 0000-9999 for this reason; widen it when the comparator stops being plain text ordering.
close_reason: Closed on GitHub (issue #1204); reconciled by bd-github-sync.

title: Paste: a paragraph between numbered steps splits the list under it
description:
The paste structuring rule nests a list under the paragraph before it (`nestsAtSameIndent` in `src/utils/markdownParser.ts`). One numbered list interrupted by a note therefore lands under two parents: ``` 1. a note 2. b 3. c ``` Pasted, this gives `1. a` at the root, then `note` with `2. b` and `3. c` nested under it. The HTML path does the same for `
  1. a

note

    …`. The pattern is common in LLM answers, which put a paragraph between steps. The rule was asked for ("if it's a list should probably always nest"), so this is a question rather than a bug. One option: a list that continues a numbering (`start > 1` in HTML, a leading number above 1 in text) does not nest under the paragraph before it.

title: Rich paste: handle math and verify CSS line breaks against real clipboard samples
description: ## Math `hast-util-to-mdast` ignores ``, so rich paste's text-loss guard (`keepsAllText` in `src/plugins/rich-paste/htmlToOutline.ts`) makes any paste containing MathML fall back to the browser's plain text, as on master. Each source puts math on the clipboard differently: - KaTeX (ChatGPT, many docs sites): a visually hidden MathML copy with a TeX ``, plus glyph spans that carry the visible text. The MathML half duplicates the glyphs. - MathJax 3: glyphs drawn with CSS, so the assistive MathML is the only text. - Wikipedia: MathML in a `display:none` span, plus a fallback `` whose `alt` is the TeX. Handling them properly (TeX as inline code, or the glyph text) needs real Chrome clipboard captures of each. Drop them into `src/plugins/rich-paste/test/fixtures/`. ## CSS-drawn line breaks `normalizeClipboardDom` turns a newline under an inline `white-space: pre-wrap` / `pre-line` style into a line break. This assumes Chrome serializes that style into copied markup, for example in chat UIs' user messages. That assumption is unverified. A captured copy of a multi-line ChatGPT or Claude user message would confirm it or show what to key on instead.

title: Rich paste: keep the HTML structure when a paste also carries a captured image (Excel/Word copies)
description: Follow-up to the rich-paste plugin (#1188). **Today.** Excel, Word and LibreOffice put a picture of the selection on the clipboard (`image/png`) next to the `text/html` and `text/plain`. With the attachments plugin on (the default), that paste is a media paste: the PNG is captured, its `((ref))` is spliced into the text, and the HTML is dropped before the paste is decided again. The rest of the paste then lands as flat TSV text instead of the table rich paste would build. The HTML is dropped deliberately. Once references are spliced in, it no longer describes the text, and keeping it breaks "Copy image" from a browser, whose HTML is just ``: the converter would paste a hotlink beside the captured copy. **The design question first:** when the HTML already carries the content as a table or structured text, is the picture of it wanted at all? The core comment in `src/paste/decision.ts` treats a spreadsheet copy as "attach the image AND keep the data". That made sense when the data was TSV, and is less clear when the data is a real table. **Possible shapes:** - Decide the paste on the original text + HTML (files stripped), then add the captured references afterwards: as extra blocks when the decision carries a tree, appended to the text otherwise. HTML that is only images (the "Copy image" case) is skipped so it doesn't duplicate the capture. - Or skip capture when the HTML carries structure the image merely renders, and paste only the table. Code: `resolvePasteWithMediaCapture` in `src/paste/operations.ts`; the rich-paste decorator in `src/plugins/rich-paste/pasteDecision.ts`.

title: Paste task lists as todo blocks (markdown `- [ ]` and HTML checkboxes)
description:
Follow-up to the rich-paste plugin (#1188). **Today.** A pasted task list keeps its state only as text. A markdown paste of `- [x] done` creates a block whose content is `[x] done`, and an HTML task item (`
  • done
    • `) produces the same `[x] done`. Neither becomes a todo: in this app a todo is a block of the `todo` type with a `status` property (`open`/`done`), not checkbox text. So the pasted items can't be checked off, filtered or queried as todos. **Direction.** Make a pasted task item a todo block whose status comes from the checkbox, with the `[ ]`/`[x]` prefix removed from its content. That needs a paste tree node to carry more than `content`: - give `OutlineNode` (`src/utils/markdownParser.ts`, part of the extension API via `@/paste/decision.js`) optional type tags / properties; - have `pasteParsedBlocks` (`src/paste/operations.ts`) apply them in the same transaction it creates the blocks in; - have both front ends produce them: the markdown lexer for `- [ ]` / `- [x]` lines, and `src/plugins/rich-paste/htmlToOutline.ts` from mdast `listItem.checked`. The todo type belongs to the todo plugin, so the paste core should take generic types/properties and let the front ends name `todo` (or let the todo plugin rewrite tagged nodes), rather than core importing the todo plugin.

title: Rich paste: recognize Microsoft Word desktop list HTML (mso-list)
description:
Follow-up to the rich-paste plugin (#1188). **Problem.** Word desktop (Windows/macOS) does not emit real `
    /
      ` on copy. Lists arrive as `

      ` paragraphs whose bullet glyph sits in a `<[if !supportLists]>…<[endif]>` conditional span. The generic converter turns these into flat paragraphs that begin with a stray `·`/`o`/`1.` glyph, losing the nesting. **Direction.** A Word normalizer in `src/plugins/rich-paste/normalizeClipboardDom.ts`, gated on Word markup (`xmlns:w="urn:schemas-microsoft-com:office:word"` / `Mso*` classes) the way the Google Docs one is gated on its wrapper: read `level N` from `mso-list`, drop the conditional glyph span, and rebuild nested lists. Bold/italic in Word HTML are real ``/``, so no style-span pass is needed. **Blocked on real samples.** This should be written against actual clipboard captures (Word for Mac and Windows, a nested bulleted list and a numbered list), saved as fixtures next to the existing ones in `src/plugins/rich-paste/test/fixtures/`, not against the format from memory.

title: Rich paste: shortcut/vim paste never sees clipboard HTML
description:
Follow-up to the rich-paste plugin (#1188).

**Problem.** `pasteFromClipboard` (vim normal-mode `p`/`P`, multi-select paste actions) reads the clipboard with `navigator.clipboard.readText()`, so `PasteRequest.html` is always undefined there. The rich-paste decorator therefore never fires for those paths: the same Google Doc pasted with Cmd+V becomes a structured tree, while vim `p` gives the flattened plain text.

**Direction.** Read with `navigator.clipboard.read()` and take `text/html` alongside `text/plain` when the item has it. Caveats to handle:
- `clipboard.read()` can prompt for permission (Firefox, Safari) where `readText()` may not — fall back to `readText()` on rejection rather than failing the paste.
- Safari requires the read to be inside the user gesture; the shortcut handler already is, but verify on iOS.
- Keep the request `surface: 'shell'`.

Code: `src/paste/operations.ts` (`pasteFromClipboard`; its docblock already notes the gap).

title: check:db pins an older supabase/postgres image than the supabase CLI uses
description: scripts/check-db.mjs defaults CHECK_DB_POSTGRES_IMAGE to public.ecr.aws/supabase/postgres:17.6.1.121. supabase CLI 2.120.0 starts public.ecr.aws/supabase/postgres:17.11.0.004 for a local stack. Migration and pgTAP tests should run on the same Postgres image as the hosted project, so check which version the hosted project runs (read-only) and move the pin to match. Consider deriving it from one place, e.g. supabase/.temp/postgres-version if the CLI writes it, instead of a second hard-coded tag.
close_reason: Not drift: the hosted project runs supabase-postgres 17.6.1.121 (checked 2026-10-13 via select version() and supabase projects list), the same tag check:db pins. The CLI's 17.11.0.004 is only its fallback for an unlinked project. A linked checkout uses supabase/.temp/postgres-version. Added a comment at the pin saying it follows the hosted version.

title: Expose proxyFetch to user extensions?
description: proxyFetch (src/services/proxyFetch.ts) is core, so plugins can use it, but it's not in the extension API catalog (src/extensions/apiCatalog.ts). Listing it would let any installed extension make arbitrary GET/HEAD requests with the user's session through the project's proxy. The proxy can't tell callers inside the app apart, so per-extension consent or attribution, and the per-user rate limit, are worth deciding first.

title: cors-proxy: per-user rate limit and quota
description:
The cors-proxy edge function (supabase/functions/cors-proxy) requires a signed-in, non-anonymous session, but sign-up is open (email OTP), so anyone with an email address can use it. Each request is bounded (GET/HEAD, 10 redirects, 10 MiB, 30 s), but nothing bounds requests per user: a determined user can spend the project's egress or use its IPs to hit third parties at volume.

Direction: count requests (and maybe relayed bytes) per user per window and refuse past a limit with a new X-Proxy-Error code (e.g. rate-limited, 429). Needs shared state across isolates, e.g. a small table written with the service role from the function, or a Postgres function doing an atomic upsert-and-check. A migration on the hosted DB is part of it, so it needs a deliberate push.

Not urgent while the user base is tiny; worth doing before proxyFetch is exposed to user extensions.

title: pr-reply test asserts an exact lookup count under a wall-clock budget, flaky under CI load
description:
scripts/pr-reply.test.ts 'bounds the reference echo by a cap and a time budget' expects exactly 5 issue lookups to fit the default echo time budget. Each lookup spawns a shim process, so under a loaded CI runner only 4 fit and the assertion fails (seen on a PR run on 2026-10-08: expected length 5, got 4; master's own run of the same code passed).

Fix direction: make the cap case deterministic, e.g. pin the budget generously (KM_PR_REPLY_ECHO_BUDGET_MS) so the 5-lookup cap, not the clock, is what stops the echo, and keep the out-of-budget case on the existing budget-0 run.

title: pre-PR gate: decide whether the hooks keep recognizing pnpm pr:reply
description:
Since #1157, scripts/pr-reply.mjs checks its own text however it is invoked: it refuses bead ids before posting and echoes every #N in the posted reply with its real title, bounded by the shared refsCap. The publish gate and the read-back verifier also recognize the invocation (matchesReplyCommand in scripts/bd-github-sync.mjs) and treat it as a covered publish of a review comment.

What keeping the hook-side recognition costs, observed while #1157 was in review:
- every recognized reply echoes its #N titles twice, once from the script and once from the read-back;
- each review round found another spelling of the invocation to recognize (quoted script name, npm run, path forms, node --run), and a non-executing run such as node --check is read as a publish and draws the verifier's no-object note.

What dropping it costs: an invocation whose output is redirected away loses the pre-publish block on its #N titles; the script still refuses bead ids itself.

Options: keep the detector as is, or delete it (about ten rules in the gate, plus the verifier's reply branch) and rely on the script. Needs a call from the maintainer before building either.

title: Sync: judge landed pushes with a by-number query instead of a full re-listing
description:
After the pre-pull push, `scripts/bd-github-sync.mjs` re-reads the whole issue listing (`fetchIssues()`, `gh issue list --state all` with bodies) to judge by content which handed beads actually landed (`planUnlandedPushes`). That costs about 5–6s on every run that pushes an already-linked bead — which is most SessionEnd runs in a session that edited beads — and a failure there is only non-fatal by design.

Only the handed issue numbers are needed. A single GraphQL query by number (the same aliasing shape as `fetchIssueComments`) would return title/body/state/labels for just those issues in about a second, and would also remove the listing's size-cap and empty-listing failure paths from this step.

Watch for it first: the slow-sync alarm on the run log will show whether the extra listing pushes typical runs over budget. Test harness note: the mirror tests configure `gh api graphql` responses per call, so a new GraphQL call shifts their fixtures.

title: Sync: adopting a GitHub close makes the pre-pull push overwrite earlier GitHub edits
description:
When the sync adopts a GitHub-side close (`bd close --force` on the bead, step 1 of `scripts/bd-github-sync.mjs`), the close bumps the bead's `updated_at`, so the adopted bead is always local-newer at the pre-pull push. If the issue's title, body or labels were edited on GitHub before it was closed, the pre-pull push then PATCHes the bead's older content over that edit in the same run.

Example: issue body edited to B2 at 10:00 and closed at 10:05; the bead still has description B1 (updated 09:00). The 11:00 sync adopts the close, which makes the bead newer, and the push sends B1 back over B2.

The withheld-bead report does fire for such a bead (a closed bead is never pulled: it would lose its close date), but it says "the bead's next push sends the local value — compare them by hand" while that push happens seconds later in the same run. Behaviour predates the bd 1.3.0 upgrade.

Fix direction: judge an adopted bead by its pre-adoption `updated_at` when selecting the pre-pull push (so GitHub's newer edit is not overwritten), or at minimum say in the report that this run's push is overwriting the GitHub-side value.

title: Prime hook: surface bd 1.3.0's 'memories were NOT injected' banner
description:
bd 1.3.0's `bd prime` no longer drops the memory section silently when it cannot read the store: it renders `Skipped: beads storage unavailable (<error>) — persistent memories were NOT injected this session` (upstream changelog, 1.3.0, "`bd prime` says when it could NOT read the memory plane").

`scripts/bd-prime-hook.mjs` re-renders prime's output to fit the host's inline limit. With no memory bullets, `parsePrimeContext` reports `parseOk: false` and `buildAdditionalContext` falls back to prime's raw output clipped to `MAX_CONTEXT_CHARS` — so the banner reaches the session only if it happens to sit inside the clipped prefix. A session whose memories failed to load can then look like one that simply has none, which is the exact ambiguity upstream fixed.

Fix: detect the `NOT injected` / timeout banners in the prime output and put them first in the rendered context (both the parsed and the fallback paths), with a test that feeds a banner past the clip point.
close_reason: Closed on GitHub (issue #1170); reconciled by bd-github-sync.

title: strength-tracker: plan-root is a block id stored in a string property
description:
The strength settings block's strength:planRoot is declared with the string preset but holds a block id. Since the hardcoded plan-root default was removed, it is the primary way the extension finds the plan outline, so it is now set in real workspaces, and audit-extension flags it (block-id-not-a-ref): the plan's backlinks never show the settings block, and the pointer does not survive a merge or retarget of the plan block.

Fix direction: a new ref-typed property (optional-ref, targetTypes left open or a plan type), read in resolvePlanRoot ahead of the old string one; the seed name and preset are frozen, so this is a new name rather than a preset change on strength:planRoot. Carrying a set value across is a one-off move for the few workspaces that have it (an agent eval, not code the extension keeps), after which strength:planRoot goes on the seed ledger's retired list.

title: One owner for the hook additionalContext size limit
description:
Claude Code inlines one hook command's additionalContext only up to about 10,000 characters and shows a 2K preview past that. Three hook scripts each encode their own clip for it, with different numbers and behaviour: scripts/hook-context.mjs (NOTE_BUDGET 8,000 per note, CONTEXT_MAX 9,500, lists lines until the budget and counts the rest), scripts/bd-publish-verify.mjs clipContext (9,000, surrogate-safe slice plus a clip marker), and scripts/bd-prime-hook.mjs (9,800, adaptive preview clipping). A change to the host limit would have to be found and fixed three times.

Fix direction: make hook-context.mjs own the limit (one exported constant and one clip helper that keeps the surrogate strip and marker bd-publish-verify needs), and point the other two scripts at it. Behaviour-preserving apart from aligning the numbers; each script's existing budget tests should keep passing.

title: pre-PR gate: a number whose title a hook already echoed this session still blocks
description:
The pre-PR gate's session memo (bd-github-sync.mjs, attestationMemo) passes a command whose issue numbers were all attested earlier in the session with KM_ISSUE_REFS_OK=1. Replaying the 2026-09-03..18 blocks, that covered 4 of 24 issue-reference blocks. Of the 19 that remain, 15 had the number surface earlier in the same session, mostly as the post-publish verifier's own title echo after a covered publish (a PR body saying Fixes #N, then every commit repeating it). The heuristic used for that count is loose (an issue URL, a title-table line or an issue view before the block), so re-measure before building on it.

Fix direction: record the numbers bd-publish-verify echoes (it already knows session_id from the payload) into the same memo, as seen rather than attested, and let the gate pass a seen number with its title as context.

Open question before building: whether a title echoed by a hook counts as the agent having read the number. The echo puts the title in context, but nothing confirms it was the number the agent meant.

title: bd-sync: fetch the issue listing by number in parallel chunks (~5s → ~2.3s)
description:
After the sync performance work, a converged `pnpm bd:sync` is ~7s. About 5s of that is `gh issue list --state all`, which is paging-bound: GraphQL pages of 100, fetched one after another, so it grows ~0.85s per 100 issues.

Measured alternative (live repo, ~1150 issue+PR numbers, ~586 issues):
- probe the highest issue number: `issues(first: 1, orderBy: {field: CREATED_AT, direction: DESC})` — 0.9s
- fetch `issue(number: N) { number state updatedAt title body assignees(first: 1) labels(first: 100) }` for 1..max as GraphQL aliases, in 23 concurrent chunks of 50 — 1.4s (12 chunks of 100: 2.4s)
- total ~2.3s against ~5.1s, and flat as the repo grows.

Why this is a judgment call rather than a drop-in: every absence-based decision in the sync (close adoption, close pushes, the pull's unlinked-issue set) trusts this listing to be complete. So the replacement must be strict where gh's pagination was:
- a NOT_FOUND alias (a PR, a deleted issue) is absence; ANY other GraphQL error, or a failed chunk, must abort the run rather than read as a missing issue
- the returned `number` must equal the requested one, so a transferred issue resolving elsewhere never counts
- the existing empty-listing refusal stays
- ~23 concurrent requests per sync; GitHub's secondary limit is 100 concurrent and 2000 points/min, so fine, but worth a bound

The run log (`.beads/github-sync-runs.log`) shows `gh issue list` as the top spawn on every converged run, so the win is directly visible there.

title: strength-tracker: a parenthetical qualifier in a plan line collapses two lifts onto one name
description:
The plan parser strips a trailing parenthetical off an exercise name and folds it into the note, so a cue like 'Waiter carry (one arm, overhead)' keeps the canonical name 'Waiter carry' that defaults and milestones key on. The same rule turns a qualifier into nothing: 'Overhead press (light)', a second, lighter pressing track in another session, parses as 'Overhead press'.

Consequences:
- The start dialog, trend cards and stalled list show two different lifts under one label.
- An entry logged before definitions were linked (no strength:definition) name-matches BOTH definitions in lastEntryFor, so the light track can inherit the heavy track's history instead of its start weight. (Workaround for existing data: backfill strength:definition on such entries.)
- Name-keyed readers (milestones, lift ratios) cannot tell the two apart; liftBalance takes the heavier one deliberately, milestones take the best.

Fix direction: for a TYPED exercise-def, keep the parenthetical in the display name unless stripping it lands on a name the built-in defaults or milestones know; or give the def an explicit name property. Renaming the plan line ('Light overhead press — ...') avoids it today.

title: Flaky under load: agent-dispatch runner test 'retains the session id from a run that timed out'
description:
packages/agent-dispatch/test/runner.test.ts, test 'retains the session id from a run that timed out before the result line', runs a fake claude child with timeoutMs: 300. The child prints its init line (with the session id) and then hangs. Under heavy load (a full pnpm run check at load average ~150, measured 2026-09-24) node's child startup alone exceeds 300ms, so the timeout kills the child before the init line is written, and the assertion sees sessionId null instead of 'sess-timeout'. It passed 3 of 3 runs alone in the same session.

Fix direction: fence the timeout on the precondition instead of racing a fixed budget, e.g. let the fake child write the init line and then signal readiness, or give the run a timeout well above the startup cost (a few seconds) since the child hangs for 60s anyway and the test only needs timedOut true after the init line. Per AGENTS.md testing guidance, budget for the ~6x p99.9 stretch under the gate.

title: Back up dirty files before git reset --hard, git clean and switch --discard-changes
description:
The PreToolUse backup hook (scripts/backup-before-restore.mjs) copies every file that differs from HEAD before a worktree-overwriting git checkout or git restore runs, plus untracked files that a named source commit tracks, and reports it as additionalContext. Three other commands discard uncommitted work the same silent way and are not covered: git reset --hard (every tracked change), git switch --discard-changes / git switch -f, and git clean -f/-fd (untracked files that no commit tracks).

Fix direction: extend restoreInvocations with these verbs. reset --hard and switch --discard-changes map to the whole-tree pathspec the hook already uses for checkout -f (with the target commit as source, so untracked files it tracks are copied too). git clean needs a different file list (git clean -n output, or git ls-files --others --exclude-standard under the pathspec), so it may belong in its own rule. Same never-block, facts-only contract; per-clause mutation checks through pnpm mutate.

title: check-staged-pii scans only the hook cwd's index: misses cd/-C targets and commit -a
description:
scripts/check-staged-pii.mjs runs `git diff --cached` in the hook process's working directory and nothing else. Two commit shapes therefore go unscanned (false negatives):

1. Another repo or worktree: `cd <other> && git commit …` or `git -C <other> commit …` scans the session directory's index, not the one being committed. check-stash-worktree.mjs already resolves the same target via gitInvocations' cdPath/cArgs (effectiveCwd).
2. Content outside the index: `git commit -a` and `git commit <pathspec>` commit working-tree changes that `--cached` does not show.

Fix direction: reuse gitInvocations' cdPath/cArgs to run the diff in the commit's repo; for -a / pathspec, diff HEAD against the working tree for the tracked paths the commit will take.

title: Perf monitor: query comparison windows history before filtering, so one unsampled session voids the recent window
description:
queryRegressions (src/plugins/perf-monitor/series.ts, comparisonWindows) slices history into the recent window (first RECENT_WINDOW-1 sessions) BEFORE dropping sessions with no comparable sample for that query (comparableSamples: fewer than MIN_CALLS uncontended resolves). A single session among the last two that did not exercise the query, or never got a quiet stretch, leaves the recent side short, so the query reports insufficient history for the next two sessions even with ample history behind it.

The fan-out comparison had the same shape and now filters before windowing (fanoutRegression, merged in the PR that reworked the fan-out rate). Unverified whether this is a material cause of the frequent 'some interaction metrics could not be judged this session' note; first step is to replay stored interaction records per query and count how often a query is unjudged because of a gap in the recent window versus genuinely thin history.

Fix direction if it matters: filter each query's samples first, then take recent/baseline windows from the filtered list, keeping the clustered-tail caveat reading the same consumed samples (comparisonWindows is shared with it).
close_reason: Closed on GitHub (issue #1142); reconciled by bd-github-sync.

title: Drop the mandatory pre-flip audit-properties step from the migration runbook
description:
The runbook (GitHub issue 671) tells the operator to run `pnpm agent audit-properties` by hand before every flip, because the migration consent screen reported key COUNTS with no way to learn which keys. The consent screen now names them per category (synthesized / stranded on this device / broken definition / can never be defined), so for the UN-flipped case the pre-flip audit is a cross-check rather than the only source of the list.

What is still only in the CLI, and so still worth a manual run when it matters: per-key provenance (which blocks and types carry a key, which extension likely wrote it) and the per-key reason behind a hopeless key. The consent screen points at the audit for the second.

Update the runbook wording to say the pre-flip audit is optional for an un-flipped workspace and what it still adds.
close_reason: Closed on GitHub (issue #1124); reconciled by bd-github-sync.

title: Collapse ContentReferencePrefill to a bare function
description:
The content-reference prefill seam ships as an object with an `id` field that is written and never read: `exactBlockRefPrefill` sets `id: "references.exactBlockRef"`, and nothing consumes it. The first-wins combiner also sits beside the facet rather than in it.

Collapsing the interface to a bare `(content: string) => BlockReference[] | undefined` is roughly 15 lines lighter and removes a field that reads as meaningful and is not.

Deliberately left out of the PR that introduced it: it changes a published shape in the facet surface and a test, and the PR was already long. Flagged at the time and merged as-is.

Fix direction: drop the interface, have the facet carry the function directly, keep the first-wins combiner as the facet reader. Check `contentReferencePrefillsFacet` consumers first (repo.ts wiring, the references dataExtension, and the facet test that asserts the contributed value by identity).

title: shellProps dev warning fires on blocks whose shell is actually mounted
description:
The DEV-only detector in src/components/renderer/DefaultBlockRenderer.tsx (~line 840, inside the ShellSlot useEffect) reports a false positive.

MESSAGE: 'Block <id>: its layout mounted Shell without spreading shellProps. Pass shortcutsOnly if that is deliberate.'

REPRO (measured 2026-09-21, dev server, headed Chrome, large migrated graph):
 1. open a block that carries a property (its property panel open)
 2. reload the page
 3. it fires twice, naming that block — intermittently, roughly every other reload. A block with NO properties never triggered it.

EVIDENCE IT IS FALSE: catching it in the act and inspecting the named block immediately, the element carries exactly the tagging the warning says is missing — data-block-shell, data-block-nav-item, data-block-surface, tabindex=0 — and double-click still enters edit mode, and the block still takes focus. So the shell IS mounted and spread; only the detector disagrees.

LIKELY CAUSE: the detector is 'shellRef.current is still null when this effect runs'. On some hydration orders the effect fires before the ref is attached, which is a mount-order race rather than a layout that dropped the props. Worth checking whether a layout effect, or a check deferred past paint, sees the ref reliably.

WHY IT IS WORTH FIXING despite being dev-only: the message names real consequences (focus, edit tagging, the shell click, the spatial-nav row), so it reads as a genuine defect and sends the reader looking for one. It cost several rounds of investigation during migration QA before the tagging was inspected directly. A detector that cries wolf also devalues a true instance.

Found while QAing the properties-as-blocks migration on a full-size graph; NOT caused by that work — the renderer path is untouched by it.

title: Backlink queries take seconds on a 350k-block graph
description:
On a ~350k-block graph (~330k live, ~227k reference edges) the backlink queries
looked very slow. Recorded with `repo.metrics()`:

  groupedBacklinks.forBlock    6 calls   mean 13,906 ms   max 51,053 ms
  backlinks.countForBlock     51 calls   mean  1,849 ms
  core.childIds               65 calls   mean  1,144 ms
  core.typedBlockCount         1 call         3,059 ms

MEASUREMENT CAVEAT — read before acting on these numbers.
They were taken in an automated browser tab that was not displayed, which pauses
requestIdleCallback / requestAnimationFrame / IntersectionObserver while
setTimeout keeps firing. That starved the whole app (see km-279i, closed as a
harness artifact), and a write-heavy pass was holding the single writer
connection at the same time, so an unknown share of each figure is scheduling
delay and queueing rather than query cost. Treat them as "something here is worth
looking at", not as the cost of the query.

WHAT TO DO
Re-measure in a headed VISIBLE browser with nothing else writing, on a graph this
size, before sizing any fix. `tmp/bigdb/run-migration.mjs` in the worktree is a
working headed-Chrome rig to copy.

NOT the obvious cause: `block_references` does have
`idx_block_references_target (target_id, workspace_id)`, so the lookup by target
has an index to stand on. If the cost is real it is likelier in the grouping /
parent-resolution half of `groupedBacklinks.forBlock`, which loads parents and
ancestor crumbs per source.

title: Migration dialog's fixed "several minutes" should scale with the block count
description:
The migration confirmation dialog says "It can take several minutes".

Measured on a ~350k-block graph (108,456 candidate blocks, 761,137 rows to mint),
in a headed visible browser, from a pristine copy, 300 s samples:

  before the batching change   108 blocks/s  ->  sweep 1 ~16.7 min
  after                        ~200 blocks/s ->  sweep 1  ~9.1 min

plus a convergence sweep that re-walks the same blocks doing reads only.

So "several minutes" is roughly right on a graph this size once the batching
change lands, and understates it by perhaps 3x before. This is a wording nit
rather than the defect I first filed — the original figures here said 1.6-2.1
HOURS, and those came from a hidden automated browser tab that was starving
requestIdleCallback (see km-279i, closed as a harness artifact). Corrected and
downgraded rather than left standing.

Still worth doing: scale the estimate off the block count the dialog already
computes and shows, rather than a fixed phrase, so it stays honest on a graph an
order of magnitude larger.

Separately and unchanged: the pre-run count (`countPropertyCellBackfillCandidates`)
takes ~1.4 s on the UI thread before the dialog appears on this graph. Its own
comment notes it runs there; worth knowing it is a visible stall at this size.

title: No multi-select property: pick SEVERAL values from a configured set
description:
Noticed while renaming the list preset's label from Options to Text list (PR for issues 1080 and 1088).

The kernel preset picker now reads: Plain text, Number, Checkbox, Text list, Date, URL, Choice, Reference, References. Two axes are covered on their own and their combination is missing.

- Choice (enum) is pick ONE from a configured option set.
- Text list (list) is SEVERAL free-form strings, with no configured set.
- References (refList) is SEVERAL of something, so the multi-valued child shape is already there.

There is no pick SEVERAL from a configured option set. That is the thing the label Options sounded like it meant, which is part of why the label was wrong.

SHAPE
codecs.list(codecs.enum(options)) — member-wise, so it inherits the one-value-child-per-member storage that alias and types already use, and each member spells plainly through the enum member codec that the PR above just added. The config codec is the one enum already has. The editor is the multi-select equivalent of SelectPropertyEditor.

NEW PRESET ID, not a reshape of an existing one. Both list and enum are shipped ids with user data stored under them.

WORTH CHECKING FIRST
Whether the member-grain paths behave with an enum member codec — the PR above added enum to storesContentVerbatim and gave it its own escape and unwrap pair, and every existing member-wise preset has a member whose codec is string or ref. The list member round-trip assertion in encodedPropertyValueToChildContents is the place it would show up.

Low priority: no one has asked for it, and it is recorded so the gap in the picker is deliberate rather than forgotten.

title: Quick-find crumbs drop the property a value row belongs to
description:
`crumbsFromAncestors` (src/utils/blockCrumbs.ts) skips every `isFieldForm`
ancestor, because a field row's content is literally `::((fieldId))` and names
no place a person could go. With properties-as-blocks that leaves a property
VALUE row's crumb line reading as its owner's title alone — so a page's `alias`
value row shows the page's own title, which is exactly the label the row itself
already carries. In quick-find the two rows are then a crumb apart from being
indistinguishable.

The reference picker solved the same ambiguity by saying "alias of <owner>"
(`src/utils/propertyValueContext.ts`, added alongside the fix for #1081).
Crumbs should name the property instead of dropping it: `<owner> > alias`.

Shape: `crumbsFromAncestors` is pure over BlockData and the property name lives
in the workspace definition registry, so the caller would pass a
`fieldId -> name` resolver (`repo.propertySchemaResolverFor(ws).resolveField`,
or `repo.propertyDefinitions.definitionsByFieldId`). A field row whose target
resolves to no definition keeps today's drop — that is the §9 recognition rule,
not a special case.

Same treatment would then be available to every crumb consumer (quick-find,
recents, grouped backlinks) rather than to the pickers alone.
close_reason: Closed on GitHub (issue #1094); reconciled by bd-github-sync.

title: The projection pipeline is written out at four sites instead of having one owner
description:
NOTICED 2026-09-20 during review of PR #1060.

The expression

  childContentsToEncodedPropertyValue(schema,
    unionValuesAcrossFieldRows(schema, rows).map(v => v.content))

appears verbatim at four sites:

  - src/data/internals/propertyChildrenProcessor.ts (the projection itself)
  - src/data/blockMerge.ts
  - src/data/internals/propertyDefinitionChangeProcessor.ts, in heldValueCount
  - src/data/internals/propertyDefinitionChangeProcessor.ts, in applyToParent

The definition-change processor's entire loss-counting argument is 'the before
side is projected exactly as the projection does'. Right now that is true by
inspection and nothing holds it true - a change to the real projection that
missed one of the other three would make the refusal quietly wrong in a way no
test would name.

unionValuesAcrossFieldRows is already generic over Pick<BlockData,'id'|'content'>,
so a single exported owner in propertyChildren.ts typechecks at all four sites.

Not done in #1060 because it is a syntactic extraction across files that PR
does not otherwise touch, and the PR was already carrying four rounds of
review.

title: Enter in a property-panel value editor does not commit the edit
description:
Found during exploratory QA of the cell-to-children flip, but NOT caused by it: it
reproduces identically on an unflipped control workspace, so this is pre-existing property
panel behaviour.

REPRODUCTION
1. Open a block's property panel and put the caret in a text-valued property's editor.
2. Type a change and press Enter.

OBSERVED
Nothing is written. The input keeps the edited text, the cell keeps the old value, and no
field row or value child changes. Blurring the input (Tab, or clicking elsewhere) commits
correctly on both workspaces.

EXPECTED
Enter is the ordinary "I am done with this field" key in a one-line editor, and the panel
gives no other signal that the edit is uncommitted. An edit lost to navigating away
without blurring is silent.

Notes: only single-line text-ish editors were checked. Checkbox, reference picker and
reference-list editors commit on their own gesture and are unaffected.

title: A field row renders block-level markup inside a paragraph, and a link inside a link
description:
Found in exploratory QA of the cell-to-children flip on a local scratch workspace. Unreachable before the flip, because field rows do not exist there. A field row's content is a reference to its property definition, and the definition's renderer emits block-level markup (the schema editor: name input, preset select, delete button). Rendered inside markdown, that lands inside the paragraph the markdown pipeline opens, and React reports: In HTML,
cannot be a descendant of

. This will cause a hydration error. ... MarkdownContentRenderer >

> PropertySchemaContentRenderer >

Navigating into a value child produces a second one, because the breadcrumb renders the field row's reference inside the breadcrumb's own link: cannot contain a nested . ... Breadcrumbs > > ReferenceLink > OBSERVED Both fire on an ordinary flipped workspace, on page load, with no unusual data. No visible layout break was isolated in this session, but a browser closes the open

when a block element arrives inside it, so the DOM does not match what React rendered; and the noise will mask genuine console errors during the rollout. EXPECTED A field row and a breadcrumb render valid HTML. FIX DIRECTION The definition renderer needs an inline presentation when it is reached through inline markdown (the reference layout already distinguishes inline from block elsewhere), and the breadcrumb should render a reference's label rather than mounting the reference component inside its link.

title: Migration confirm dialog warns that synthesis claims a name but never names the properties
description:
Found in exploratory QA of the cell-to-children flip on a local scratch workspace.

The migration confirmation dialog devotes a paragraph to orphan-definition synthesis:

  "2 properties in this workspace have no definition — written by an importer, a raw
   write, or a plugin that is no longer installed. ... If a plugin or extension owns any
   of them, install or enable it before you run this ... Creating a definition here claims
   the name: re-enabling the owner afterwards leaves two definitions competing ... Run
   audit-properties first if you are not sure who wrote them."

OBSERVED
The dialog never says WHICH properties. There is no expander and no list — the only
controls are Cancel, Migrate and Close. The operator is told the decision is consequential
and then sent to a CLI command in another window to find out what the decision is about.

EXPECTED
The plan the dialog is counting from already holds the names. Listing them (with the
inferred preset per name, which synthesis has to choose anyway) is what makes the warning
actionable in the place the warning is given.

Lower bound on effort: the count is already computed and rendered; the names travel with
it.

title: The backfill's view-gap probe can now be asked under its own write lock
description:
Two callers answer one hazard two ways, which is how they drift.

Repo.assertBackfillMayWrite still samples the view gap immediately BEFORE opening each batch's transaction, and accepts the resulting window: a drain committing between the probe and the writer is seen by the next batch's probe rather than this one. That position used to be forced, because the probe read through the Repo's handle and such a read cannot be served while the write lock is held on a single-connection pool.

It is no longer forced. #1072 gave Repo.workspaceViewGap an injectable ViewGapReads and gave Tx the two queries as named methods, so a caller holding the lock can pass its transaction and ask the whole question under it. The synthesis path does exactly that. assertBackfillMayWrite's comment now records the outside position as a deliberate choice rather than a constraint.

The choice is defensible as it stands: the backfill re-probes before every batch and its writes are idempotent per row, so a gap opening mid-batch costs one batch's window instead of an un-undoable write, which is what made the same window unacceptable for synthesis (it mints at deterministic ids and uploads).

So this is not a bug — it is an asymmetry worth either closing or recording as settled. If closing: pass the transaction the same way synthesis does, and note that the in-lock reads refuse once the transaction has written, so the probe has to stay the first statement of the batch.

Whichever way it goes, the decision belongs at the declaration rather than in a merged PR body.

title: codecs.date decodes a bare year in LOCAL time, so two devices write different instants
description:
MEASURED 2026-09-18 during review of the #1055 conversion change. Pre-existing and reachable by typing, not only by a re-type.

codecs.date's decode resolves a tolerant spelling against the DEVICE's
timezone. Observed on a machine at UTC-8: the content '42' decodes and
re-encodes to 2042-01-01T08:00:00.000Z. On a UTC machine the same text gives
2042-01-01T00:00:00.000Z.

So the instant a date property ends up holding depends on which device read
the text - and that instant is then synced. Two devices doing the same thing
to the same property disagree, and neither is flagged.

The #1055 change makes this slightly more visible (a re-type off date now
canonicalizes the row text, so the device-dependent instant becomes the
stored spelling too) but does not cause it; typing a tolerant date has always
gone through the same decode.

FIX DIRECTION. Parse date-only and year-only forms as UTC, the way
Date.parse already treats a full ISO date-only string ('2024-01-02' is UTC,
'42' is not). That makes the decode device-independent for exactly the
spellings where there is no time to be local about.

WHERE. dateCodec in src/data/api/codecs.ts.

title: A migration claim records that a run finished, not that it wrote anything
description:
graphBackfillClaim stamps completedAt when a pass runs to the end, which is not the same as the pass having rewritten rows. A re-run over an already-migrated workspace commits no batch, clears no undo history, and still stamps completedAt — the gesture actively invites such re-runs (its own report says already-migrated blocks are skipped, so run it again).

Two places currently have to work around the gap:

1. MigrationGate's history drop is ABANDONED rather than finished, so a peer keeps pre-migration undo entries a completed run has made stale (#684/#1007). A sound clear needs to know the run wrote; it cannot be inferred from the claim going away, because the claim is equally absent after a release that wrote nothing.

2. The reload toast the gate shows on completion is gated on this device still having undo entries, which is a good proxy but not the question. A device that has entries and watched a run that wrote nothing is told to reload for no reason.

The fix is a firstWriteAt (or a boolean) stamped onto the claim block in the SAME transaction as the pass's first committed write — the flip for a run that flips, the first backfill batch otherwise. Then the gate can finish the drop instead of abandoning it when that stamp is present, which is the peer-side undo clear that #684/#1007 wanted, and the toast can ask the real question.

Not built with the dialog work because it changes what the claim record carries, and the claim's property names are frozen once shipped (seedIdentityLedger rules apply).

title: The shortcut activation funnel resolves a UI-state block even for contexts that carry no dependencies
description:
useActionContextActivations (src/shortcuts/useActionContext.ts) calls useUIStateBlock() unconditionally, to merge into each activation's dependencies. useUIStateBlock is use(getUIStateBlock(...)) — it suspends, it calls useUser(), and it calls requireWorkspaceId.

For an activation whose dependencies are null that work buys nothing, and it makes the cost real: any component that only wants modal shadowing becomes a suspending component that requires an AppRuntime, an ActiveContextsProvider, a signed-in user and an active workspace. The properties-migration gate had to put its dialog behind its own render boundary for exactly this reason — without it, a dialog that could not render took the migration's undo pause down with it, because both sat under one per-mount boundary.

React 19 allows use() inside a conditional, so skipping the read when every activation has null dependencies looks feasible. It is a change to the central funnel every block surface in the app lands in, so it wants its own PR and its own verification rather than riding along with something else.

title: Give the property-definition row read and cell histogram one owner in src/data/internals
description:
Three copies of one SELECT, and the JSON-vs-SQLite duplicate-key rule re-explained in prose at four sites.

The statement: join blocks to block_types on type='property-schema', filter workspace and deleted=0, read the property bag.
  - src/data/internals/propertyKeyScan.ts (uses an ORDER BY j.id DESC LIMIT 1 subselect to get last-duplicate-key semantics)
  - src/data/internals/txEngine.ts (same, over the tx db rather than repo.db)
  - src/plugins/agent-runtime/presetIdentity.ts (reads the WHOLE bag and JSON.parse-es it, which gets the same rule structurally and also survives non-object configs)

The third is the most capable of the three and is the one to keep. Moving it down into src/data/internals as an unfiltered {fieldId, bag} read lets presetIdentity keep only its presetId filter, lets scanPropertyKeys drop ~35 lines of subselect-plus-comment, and leaves txEngine (which reads ctx.txDb) pointing at the owner instead of restating the rule.

Separately, presetIdentity's countCells is propertyKeyScan's own per-key histogram plus one 'j.key IN (...)' conjunct. One exported cellCountsByKey(repo, workspaceId, names?) serves both, and ties together the two definitions of 'a cell' — which currently disagree in comment: one says 'live blocks carrying a cell', the other correctly says one row per (block, key).

Found during review of the install-time preset-identity check; deliberately left out of that PR because it touches modules outside its scope.
close_reason: Done in the PR that found it, not deferred: readPropertyDefinitionBags + cellCountsByKey in propertyKeyScan own both reads now, three SQL copies collapsed to one (the tx-side caller included, via a db-handle parameter), and the fourth prose copy of the duplicate-key rule points at the owner instead of restating it.

title: cadencedIdleJob does not forward a park handle into its role wait
description:
PendingIdleJobs.schedule now hands its job body a ParkHandle so a drain barrier can skip a job blocked on a signal only sync can deliver (see the PR fixing the awaitSeedMaterialization hang). cadencedIdleJob (src/utils/cadencedIdleJob.ts) schedules its run callback without forwarding one, and the interaction-metrics job it backs awaits awaitRecordingAllowed -> awaitLocalMemberRole, which waits for the local membership row.

Consequence: with remote sync active, drainInteractionSamples() (src/plugins/interaction-metrics/schedule.ts) can block for the length of that wait instead of returning past a job that is not progressing. It is BOUNDED, unlike the seed-materialization case: awaitRecordingAllowed wraps the wait in its own AbortController with a ROLE_WAIT_MS budget, so the worst case is a slow drain, not a hang. No test exercises it today (the metrics schedule suite short-circuits because remote sync is inactive).

Fix direction: give cadencedIdleJob a run callback that receives the ParkHandle, and thread it through awaitRecordingAllowed into awaitLocalMemberRole (which already takes an optional onPark). Deliberately left out of the original PR: it is a plugin-facing signature change for a bounded wait, not the unbounded class that PR fixed.

Found by an adversarial review of that PR.

title: matrix promotion test flakes under full-suite load: ingest stalls on the first message
description:
Observed once while running the gate on unrelated work, recorded so it is not rediscovered from scratch.

FAILING TEST: agent-extensions/matrix-chat-client.promotion.test.ts, "matrix ingest into a child-backed workspace > keeps ingesting the next message after one carried an unstorable key".

The assertion that fails is the vi.waitFor whose message is "ingest stalled on the first message" - it waits for the SECOND message's row to appear after the first carried a value the schema cannot store.

EVIDENCE, such as it is. One failure in roughly seven full-suite runs on a branch that does not touch this file or anything it exercises; zero failures in two full-suite runs on master at the same time; zero in five isolated runs of the file alone. So: load-dependent, not deterministic, and not obviously caused by the branch it was seen on.

WHY IT IS NOT AN OBVIOUS BUDGET PROBLEM. The budgets here are already generous by this repo's standards - the waitFor is 10_000ms at 50ms interval inside a test declared at 30_000ms - so the usual remedy of raising a too-tight default does not apply, and a stall that outlasts ten seconds under load is more likely a genuine starvation or a missed wake-up than a slow machine.

WHERE TO START. The test drives matrixIngestEffect.start against a two-page timeline, so the question is whether the effect's advance from cursor-0 to cursor-1 can be dropped rather than merely delayed when the first page's promotion is declined. A one-shot scheduling edge there would look exactly like this: fine in isolation, fine most of the time, and permanently stalled the once.
close_reason: Fixed on master by #1045 (c244d6f757, 'Keep each poll budget under its test's, and fence the matrix cursor read') — the cursor read is now fenced inside the waitFor rather than asserted immediately after it, which is the race this bead described. Not my fix; closing because the code it is about no longer has the shape.

title: unsetProperty can already remove a cell under an undeclared name (checked, no change needed)
description:
`tx.unsetProperty` resolves its schema first and throws
PropertySchemaIdentityError when no definition resolves for the name. That is
right for the typed seam, but it means the API refuses exactly the case that most
needs it: removing a cell under a name nothing declares.

The cost is not that the removal is impossible, it is that the only remaining
path is `tx.update` with a rewritten properties bag. That is a whole-bag replace,
which is precisely what `unsetProperty`'s own contract exists to prevent: its
doc-comment says a TARGETED delete, never a whole-bag replace, so it cannot
clobber a sibling key a peer synced in. Verified in the engine: `tx.update`
writes `properties_json` wholesale and does no child reconciliation. So the
undeclared case is pushed onto the one shape the typed path was built to avoid,
and every caller has to independently re-derive the discipline of doing the read
inside the transaction. A caller who reads the bag before opening the
transaction loses a concurrently synced sibling key, silently.

What the schema resolution actually buys on the unset path is small for this
case. The field-row subtree it would eagerly soft-delete does not exist, because
property migration skips unregistered keys, so an undeclared name has no field
rows to clean up. The scope check has no authoritative scope to check against
either, since there is no definition carrying one.

Sketch of a fix, if wanted: a name-keyed sibling, `unsetPropertyKey(id, name,
opts)`, reusing the existing targeted-delete machinery, skipping schema
resolution, taking its scope from the transaction the way `tx.update` already
does, and reconciling field rows only when a definition does happen to resolve
for the name. Small, and it keeps the typed seam unchanged.

Not urgent, and arguably shrinking: the migration's orphan synthesis mints a
definition for every definition-less cell key, so after the flip these names
resolve and `unsetProperty` works on them. This is a pre-flip maintenance gap.
Filed rather than fixed inline because it is a new primitive on the central write
seam and deserves its own review.

Found while deleting the cells under four retired property names, where the
cleanup had to route around this.
close_reason:
Not a defect. The premise was wrong, and it was reasoned from the doc comment
rather than measured.

`unsetProperty` resolves the caller's schema HANDLE through `resolveBoundary`,
which is not the same question as whether a definition exists for the name.
Measured against the live registry, a plain `defineProperty` schema for every one
of these names resolves `available`, while resolving the same name through
`resolve(name)` returns definition-unavailable. So the supported path was there
all along: hand `unsetProperty` a plain schema for the name and it performs the
ordinary targeted delete, skipping the field-row branch because a plain schema
carries no fieldId, which is correct for a key that has no field rows.

Checked the other direction too, since a gap would have lived there: a name a
live definition CLAIMS resolves `shadowed` for a plain lookalike, so a fabricated
handle is refused. But that case needs no fabrication, because the real
registered handle is available and is the designed path. Between the two there is
no reachable state where a cell cannot be removed through `unsetProperty`.

Implemented a name-keyed `unsetPropertyKey` with tests before running this check,
then reverted all of it. A new primitive on the central write seam has to earn
its place, and this one only saved the caller from constructing a plain schema
for a delete that never uses its codec.

Consequence for the cleanup that prompted this: it used a transactional
read-modify-write through `tx.update` rather than the property primitive. That
was sound, since the read happened inside the serialized transaction and the
workspace is un-flipped with no field rows to reconcile, and the write goes
through the same bag-write and undo/upload recording. But it was not the best
available path, and any remaining cleanup should use `unsetProperty` instead.

title: agent-cli: two prefs-resolving read verbs classify readOnly differently
description:
Noticed while reading packages/agent-cli/src/protocol.ts for the comment-cleanup pass (km-o9fj); not touched there because it is a behaviour question, not a comment one.

Two verbs in knownCommandRegistry reach a prefs block on a read path, and they are classified opposite ways:

- audit-extension is readOnly: false, because resolving the enabled intent goes through getPluginPrefsBlock, which bootstraps the per-user prefs row on a profile that has never had one. The comment says that is a write, so the verb is not classified read-only rather than quietly breaking a read-only token's contract.
- backlinks and grouped-backlinks are readOnly: true, because the backlinks prefs sub-block is bootstrapped at idle on every client by pluginPrefsExtension, so on a warm client the resolve path is a pure read. The comment then concedes the only write either could make is that same one-time prefs-block creation, before the bootstrap has run.

So on a client that has not yet bootstrapped, a read-only-scoped token calling backlinks --filter effective (or grouped-backlinks, whose default grouping is user) can cause a write. Either that is acceptable and the audit-extension classification is stricter than it needs to be, or it is not and the backlinks classification is wrong.

Worth deciding once and recording the decision at whichever declaration owns it, since the read-only allowlist is derived from this single field. Low priority: the window is a cold client, and the write is a benign one-time prefs row.

title: Replace the retired-property-names constant with a data-driven name-collision check
description:
`RETIRED_PROPERTY_NAMES` / `RETIRED_TYPE_IDS` in `src/data/seedIdentityLedger.ts` have exactly ONE consumer: the ledger's own test. Nothing at runtime reads them — not the registry, not property migration, and not orphan-definition synthesis, which mints a user-origin definition for every definition-less cell key whether or not its name is on the list.

WHAT THEY GUARD, and it is real: a NEW seed declaration spelled with a name user data already sits under. Seeds are unshadowable in the registry, so the new seed wins the name; the pre-existing definition row keeps the `fieldId` that field rows are bound to, and the old cells are then read under the new seed's codec.

WHY THE SHAPE IS WEAK: the list is non-exhaustive by construction — its own header says a key qualifies only once someone notices it — and the data it reasons about lives in users' workspaces, where no build-time constant can see it. So it answers a data question with a hand-maintained code constant, and reports "clear" for every freed name nobody happened to write down.

PROPOSED: ask the question against the data. The verdict already exists as `nameHolding` in `propertyDefinitionSynthesis.ts` (seed-reserved / vacant / held / contested). Surface it where a collision would be introduced or found: at seed registration in a dev build, and/or as a check in `audit-properties` and `install-extension --verify` — "this seed declares a name already held by a non-seed definition block in this workspace". That is complete where the constant cannot be, and it fires in the workspace where the collision actually exists.

Then the constant can be kept as plain documentation of which names were freed and why their values were discarded, or dropped entirely.

NOT IN QUESTION: the frozen-seed set-equality half of the ledger stays. That is what catches a rename or codec change stranding stored values, and it is unrelated to this.

Context: came out of the re-audit in #750, where the audited graph's 8 unregistered keys all turned out to be retired names, owner-gated keys, or inert residue — and where the retired list turned out to have no bearing on whether any of them migrates.

title: Cell end-state: stop uploading, then downloading, then drop properties_json, measurement-gated after backfill and sweep
description:
The final phase of the properties-as-blocks migration, per the design doc §11 "Cell end-state: measure first, then stage the sync-off". Nothing of it is filed and nothing of it is built; this bead is the tracker so the phase does not live only in the doc.

The staged sequence, each step gated on the one before:
1. The flip has shipped and the fleet fully dual-writes (the flip bead).
2. The backfill has completed per workspace AND the consistency sweep reports zero divergence for it.
3. Stop UPLOADING the cell for that workspace. The `'children' -> 'cell-off'` transition of `workspaces.properties_migration` stays service-role only in the trigger, deliberately; it is an operator step, not a client gesture.
4. Stop DOWNLOADING it (needs the staging schema to accept a null cell).
5. Deprecate, then drop, the server `properties_json` column.

The doc gates steps 3 and 4 together on a tiered real-database measurement of projection-pass time (the doc names a threshold on the order of ten to fifteen seconds); build the measurement before deciding, not the sync-off. Whether this phase happens at all is a decision the measurement informs: the cell is cheap to keep syncing and is what keeps reads synchronous, so "never" is an acceptable answer if the numbers say so.

Consequences to carry: any key still unregistered at cell-off time loses its only synced representation (the reason the pre-flip key audit blocks the flip); a fresh device past cell-off must project every cell from children before first render, which is the measurement above; and the PowerSync sync rules plus the local staging schema are a three-layer change each.

Depends on: the flip bead and the consistency sweep bead.

title: CI flake: HotkeyReconciler 'hold-fired modal shadowing works with real timers'
description:
One test failed on a master Run Tests job; re-running the SAME commit's job was green, so this is a flake, not a regression.

Failing assertion: src/shortcuts/test/HotkeyReconciler.test.tsx:1894
  expect(modalHandler).toHaveBeenCalledTimes(1)  ->  0 times
Test: HotkeyReconciler > phase > hold > 'hold-fired modal shadowing works with real timers and no extra act wrapping around the keydown'. It failed in 71ms, so no fence timed out.

Shape: a real 20ms hold timer fires outside act() and its handler calls dispatch.activate(MODAL). The test then fences on (1) the handler's own `holdFired` flag via vi.waitFor and (2) a single `await act(async () => {})`, and finally dispatches an UNWRAPPED 'h' keydown. 'h' is one-shot: dispatched before React has committed the activation AND flushed the reconciler's binding-install useEffect, it routes against the pre-activation binding set and nothing re-delivers it.

Not reproduced locally: ~380 runs of that test (isolated, under 16-40 competing busy processes, and with randomized 0-55ms stalls straddling the hold deadline plus stalls inside the waitFor predicate). A forced stall that makes the hold timer and a waitFor poll expire in the same timers phase also stayed green, so `await act()` does flush an update scheduled outside act on this Node/React.

Candidate hardening (unverified, since the failure could not be reproduced): fence on the OBSERVABLE consequence instead of the handler's own flag - a probe component mounted after <HotkeyReconciler/> whose useEffect records that the modal context is active, waited on with vi.waitFor. Passive effects flush in tree order, so that probe firing means the reconciler's install effect for the same commit already ran, and waitFor keeps retrying across macrotask boundaries however many turns React needs. The current fence 1 observes the HANDLER, not React, and fence 2 is a single flush.
close_reason: Closed on GitHub (issue #1005); reconciled by bd-github-sync.

title: db-mirror filename test flakes on a birthday collision in its 200-draw uniqueness assertion
description:
`src/plugins/db-mirror/test/filenames.test.ts` > `dbMirrorFilename` > "gives two runs in the same second different names" draws 200 random filenames and asserts all 200 are distinct. The token is 6 hex characters, so 16^6 = 16,777,216 values; by the birthday bound the probability that 200 draws collide is about 1 - exp(-200*199/(2*16777216)) ~= 0.12%, i.e. roughly one run in 840. Observed failing in CI with `expected 199 to be 200`.

The assertion is an over-strong proxy for the property it names. "Two runs in the same second get different names" is about the token varying per call, not about 200 draws being collision-free — and no amount of tuning the sample size makes a random-token uniqueness assertion permanently green.

Fix direction (needs the owner's call on what the naming actually guarantees): assert the property directly — e.g. that two successive calls differ, or that the token varies while every other segment is pinned — rather than sampling. If a collision-resistance claim is genuinely wanted, it belongs as a statement about the token width, not as a sampled assertion. Widening the token would reduce but never remove the flake.

Noticed while working an unrelated PR whose CI it reddened; the test predates that work and is on master.
close_reason: Closed on GitHub (issue #1003); reconciled by bd-github-sync.

title: bd-sync: planLossyReapplies and pullWouldWrite hold the same four predicates
description:
Deferred cleanup from the /areview pass on PR #981 (the #955 fix). Not a defect — both sites are correct and well covered by ~30 assertions; this is weight.

`pullWouldWrite` and `planLossyReapplies` in scripts/bd-github-sync.mjs each spell the same four non-label comparisons (title, description vs body, trimmed assignee, normalized label sets), and `labelFieldsWhere` is called three times per bead where once would do. They are also at different altitudes: the three label-derived fields go through a four-valued verdict (ambiguous / default / imports / agrees) while the other four are classified ad hoc, twice.

One FIELDS table returning a verdict per field would let all three answers fall out of a single pass — pullWouldWrite = any field not `agrees`; losses = the lossy verdicts; overwrites = the `imports` ones. It would also close a small gap the two-site shape hides: when the bead has no assignee and the issue does, pullWouldWrite is true but neither losses nor overwrites names assignee — a neutral import with no bucket.

Payoff: ~8 duplicated expressions and 2 redundant calls per bead deleted, and the two sites can no longer drift. Cost: it reshapes the implementation (not the signature) of an exported, heavily-tested function, so do it in its own change where the test suite is the safety net.

title: A rename synced from a client without the typeify rename path lands drifted
description:
core.blockTypeTypeify now follows a content rewrite on an existing type: the label and the claimed alias move with it. Sync-applied writes bypass the same-tx pass by design, which is fine when the originating device ran the same code — the finished row replicates as data.

It is not fine under version skew. A peer on a build that predates this path renames a type by writing content alone; that row replicates here with the new content and the OLD label and alias still attached, and nothing on the receiving side reconciles it. End state is exactly the shape the fix is for: the registry publishes the old name while the content and (after that peer's own alias sync) the claim say the new one.

Not fixable by reacting on the receiving side alone — the same-tx pass is deliberately skipped for sync, and re-running naming logic against rows another device authored is how two devices fight over a name. What it needs is a decision: an audit/repair pass that finds label != content on block-type rows and reconciles them once per graph, or accepting the drift until the row is next edited locally (which does reconcile it).

Reachability shrinks to zero as clients update; it matters for the window, and for any repair pass written later, which would otherwise omit exactly these rows.

title: Keyboard shortcuts inert in a local-only dev workspace, with a shellProps layout warning
description:
Observed while driving a local dev server against a local-only (no sync) workspace: the console carried a warning naming shellProps, and keyboard shortcuts did not reach their handlers in that tab — actions that work normally elsewhere did nothing.

Not reproduced by the test suite, and not seen in a synced workspace, so the likely cause is that a freshly-seeded local-only workspace lacks whatever layout/shell block the shortcut surfaces resolve their context from, and the resolution degrades to activating no context at all rather than to a sane default.

Fix direction: find what reads shellProps and what it does when the expected layout block is missing or malformed. A missing layout should still leave the normal-mode shortcut context active; silently activating nothing is the part that makes this look like 'shortcuts are broken' rather than 'this workspace is half-seeded'.

Unverified beyond the single observation — reproduce first (fresh local-only workspace, check whether the warning and the inert shortcuts always travel together) before changing anything.

title: The alias.collision rejection is built in two places
description:
src/data/aliasClaim.ts (assertAliasClaimable, the preflight) and src/data/repo.ts (buildAliasCollisionRejection, the rollback translation of the storage trigger's RAISE) construct the same ProcessorRejection: same message string, same field set, same 80-char title truncation — repo.ts's own comment says the truncation matches the other copy.

A shared factory in aliasClaim.ts taking the claimant would own the message and the truncation, and could export the meta type that src/plugins/alias/rejectionToast.tsx currently redeclares.

Not identical, so the factory has to model the difference rather than flatten it: repo.ts can emit conflictingBlockId: null (the claimant lookup can miss after rollback), and the toast's type guard deliberately routes that to the raw-message branch instead of offering a merge.

title: One owner for the name-hygiene pair: assertWritableLabel
description:
src/data/referenceBlock.ts now exports assertWritableLabel / isWritableLabel — the grammar-shaped check and the round-trip check applied together, which every caller whose name doubles as its [[name]] page wants. Its own docblock already said the two are always applied together.

Four sites still spell the pair out, three of them with a multi-line comment re-deriving the same argument:
- src/components/renderer/BlockTypeBlockRenderer.tsx (writeBlockTypeLabel)
- src/data/typeExtraction.ts (createTypeBlock)
- src/components/renderer/PropertySchemaBlockRenderer.tsx (predicate form)
- src/data/userSchemasService.ts (propertySchemaNameRejection)

Mechanical: each becomes one call, and the shared argument lives once instead of four times. Behaviour-preserving — every site applies grammar-then-round-trip in that order, and the predicate sites compose with || so order is irrelevant. Keep both forms: the throwing one exists for the distinct GrammarShapedLabelError / LossyLabelError the UI catches to revert a draft.

title: A rename cannot rewrite backlinks when the alias bag is malformed
description:
references.renameBacklinks computes what a rename retired by diffing the stored property bag (getAliases(row.before)), while the alias INDEX is maintained from json_each over the same cell and honours shapes the codec refuses — a scalar, an object, an array with a non-string entry. For a row whose cell is one of those, the bag decodes to nothing, so the processor sees no removal and inbound [[old name]] spans are neither rewritten nor invalidated.

Consequence: a block with a malformed alias cell cannot be renamed without silently breaking every link into it by its old name. Any write that heals the cell into a well-formed list makes the SAME tx look like pure additions, so the healing write cannot rescue the removal either — the information about what was claimed before is only in the index, and nothing passes it to the reference processor.

Directions: have the reference processor take the retired set from the index (tx.aliasesOf, snapshotted before the write) rather than re-deriving it from the bag; or give the same-tx pass a way to carry an explicit retirement so the producer of the change names it rather than each consumer re-deriving it.

Found while reviewing PR 985. That PR's kernel type-rename deliberately retires only what the bag shows, so it does not ADD to this class, but it cannot fix it either — the gap is in how the reference processor learns what was retired. See the memory reference_alias_index_vs_bag for the index-vs-bag distinction this sits on.
notes:
Second path into the same class, from the PR 985 review (round 7): a claim moved on a RERUN of a same-tx processor also escapes the backlink owner. references.renameBacklinks is deliberately pass-one and not rerunOnDirtyRows (its header explains why: keeping the kernel's project-property-children re-run downstream of its rewrites), so any alias transition written in pass two is invisible to it. Reachable when some other processor rewrites a block's content mid-pass — references.inlineDeletedBlockReferences retitling a type whose name embeds an inline ref, alias.sync's AR1 content rewrite, or renameBacklinks itself retitling a type whose name embeds the renamed wikilink.

alias.sync documents the same gap for its own non-rerun and leaves it deliberately. So the class now has two entrances — a malformed bag hiding the retirement, and a retirement written after the reader ran — and one exit: carry the retirement explicitly through the pass instead of having each consumer re-derive it from a bag diff.
Third shape in the same class, found by an adversarial review of the type-rename work: a claim MOVED on a pass-two rerun is retired against the merged baseline, which still holds the tx-start name — so the name the processor itself wrote in pass one is never released. It stays claimed workspace-wide and sits at aliases[0], which is what the sidebar displays, so the block renders under a name its own content and label disagree with.

Measured with shipped processors only via a title embedding a wikilink; that instance is now closed by not claiming an unwritable name at all. What remains needs an extension-registered processor that rewrites content mid-pass with a writable name. Same exit as the rest of this issue: carry the retirement explicitly through the pass instead of each consumer re-deriving it from a baseline diff — a consumer that re-derives cannot see a name that only ever existed between passes.
