title: Folding a property schema into another block hands over its name
description:
Measured: merging a property-schema block into a plain block with contentStrategy keepTarget leaves the survivor carrying types: ['property-schema'] and property-schema:name: 'priority' while its own content says something else — the schema silently relocates onto a block whose title is not its name.

Same class as the type-label case fixed in PR 985 (src/data/blockMerge.ts, keepOwnTypeLabel): mergeProperties is deliberately name-agnostic, so an IDENTITY property (a name that addresses the block) rides the union like an ordinary value. For block-type:label the result was a fold the kernel refused outright; for property-schema:name nothing refuses, so it lands quietly.

Open question for whoever picks this up: whether the survivor should keep its own schema identity (the symmetric fix — extend the same keep-own rule to the schema name), or whether a schema should refuse to be folded into a non-schema at all. Worth checking what the schema registry and propertyRenameProcessor do with a name whose block content disagrees before choosing.

Repro: create two child blocks, one plain with content 'Plain page', one with content 'priority' and the property-schema type + name/preset/config properties; merge the schema into the plain block with keepTarget; read the survivor's properties.

title: Insufficient samples reads the same whether the pool tracker is fed or not
description:
Observability gap noticed while verifying km-buse against a deployed build.

DbContention refuses to judge anything when nothing is feeding it - poolWatched
false makes every window contended rather than trivially clean, which is the
right direction. But from the perf-monitor UI that is indistinguishable from a
correctly working instrument on a busy workload: both render an em dash and the
note "queries ran, but none produced a comparison-eligible timing this session".

Measured instance: a local-only session recorded 599 adapter calls, 190 of them
into a free pool, and 59 clean read timings - a healthy instrument - and still
showed the em dash, because the per-query gate is 20 clean resolves and no single
query name reached it. An instrument that was never wired would look the same.

The tracker already knows which case it is. It just does not say.

THE FIX, roughly: carry poolWatched into the stored sample the way syncObserved
is carried, and let the verdict distinguish "no query reached the gate" from
"occupancy is not being observed at all". The second is a bug report, not a
caveat.

Deliberately NOT done in km-buse: the flag was argued there as not worth storing
because repoProvider is the only place the app opens a database and always
instruments, so a record would carry a constant. That argument is sound about
the DATA and wrong about the DIAGNOSTIC - the value of the field is precisely
that it is constant, so a record where it is false localises the break
immediately.

title: Type-membership retarget is event-only, so it cannot cover a merge it did not perform
description:
`core.retargetMergedTypeMembership` watches `CORE_BLOCK_MERGED_EVENT`, which is emitted only by local `foldBlocksInTx`. A device that receives a merge as ROWS rather than performing it sees the source tombstone arrive with no event, so nothing retargets there.

Why this is mostly benign today: the retarget writes the member rows, and those writes sync like any other edit, so a merge performed on an up-to-date device is corrected everywhere. The gap is only when the ORIGINATING device does not run the processor — i.e. a client on a build predating this feature. That is transitional and closes as clients update.

Why it is worth recording anyway: the limitation is structural, not incidental. Any future path that produces a tombstone without going through `foldBlocksInTx` (a server-side merge, an importer writing tombstones directly, a repair that folds rows) would hit it permanently and silently. Nothing does that today, which is the only reason this is P3.

If it ever needs closing, the shape is a reconciliation pass rather than a processor: on sync arrival, look for tombstoned type definitions that still have members and retarget them. Note that is a DATA MIGRATION by the AGENTS.md taxonomy (repairs source-of-truth rows and uploads them), so it needs the per-graph claim, the undo-stack clearing, and the in-transaction freshness check — not a derivation pass's shape.

title: Extension CSS safelist has no viewport-fraction heights for scrolling dialogs
description:
## Gap

`src/extension-utilities.css` safelists a broad utility vocabulary so extensions
get working Tailwind in a client whose CSS was built without them. Its sizing
line covers the numeric scale plus `full/auto/screen/min/max/fit/dvh`, but no
VIEWPORT FRACTIONS — there is no `max-h-[85vh]` equivalent an extension can rely
on.

That matters for the commonest extension UI: a dialog whose content can exceed
the screen. The choices today are

- `max-h-dvh` / `max-h-screen`, which pins the dialog edge-to-edge with no
  margin when it caps; or
- an arbitrary `max-h-[85vh]`, which compiles ONLY while some app file happens
  to use that identical class. Measured 2026-09-11 against the PR preview's
  production CSS: `.max-h-[85vh]` is present, generated by
  `src/plugins/perf-monitor/PerfTrendDialog.tsx` and
  `src/plugins/daily-notes/ReschedulePicker.tsx`. An extension using it borrows
  their rule and loses its height cap silently, with no error, whenever the last
  app-side usage is changed.

Neither is good: one is ugly, the other is invisible coupling to unrelated
files.

## Fix shape

Add viewport fractions to the sizing safelist, e.g.

    @source inline("{max-h,max-w,h,w}-{75,80,85,90,95}{dvh,dvw}");

or a small set of named `max-h-*` values. Weigh against CSS weight — the file is
already ~84KB gz and the header says the base vocabulary is deliberately broad,
so a handful of viewport fractions is in keeping.

## Context

Came up in the strength-tracker dialog fix, which chose `max-h-dvh` and
documented why. Nothing is blocked on this; it is a papercut for every extension
author who writes a scrolling dialog.

title: Restoring a tombstoned page races PanelContentRecovery's debounce and bounces the pane
description:
`PanelContentRecovery` recovers a pane off a confirmed TOMBSTONE after `RECOVERY_DEBOUNCE_MS` (120ms). Any get-or-create that RESTORES a soft-deleted page and then shows it in a panel is racing that debounce: if the restoring transaction takes longer than 120ms, the pane is stepped back to history or the workspace landing page while the restore lands behind it. The user clicks a page, gets bounced somewhere else, and the page they asked for now exists but is not on screen.

Reachable via the Recents header button and the recents command once the Recents page has been deleted (PR #935 navigates first and materializes after, so the panel is pointed at the tombstone while `getOrCreateKernelPage`'s restore path runs — `restorePropertiesStrippingAliases`, `tx.restore`, `partitionClaimableAliases`, `setProperty`, `tagTypes`, several awaits inside one tx).

NOT introduced by that PR: before it, the same click pointed the panel at the same tombstone and got the same bounce, with nothing restoring the page afterwards. The PR strictly improves the outcome (the page comes back, so the next click works) without closing the race.

The debounce already exists for exactly this shape — its comment says 'undo can restore a just-deleted block a tick later' — so the mechanism is right and the budget is what a tx under load overruns. Note `RECOVERY_DEBOUNCE_MS` is deliberately 'well below human-perceptible latency', so simply raising it trades this for a visible delay on every real deletion.

Directions worth weighing: have the recovery notice an in-flight restore for the block it is about to abandon (a pending-restore set the kernel page path registers), rather than lengthening the debounce for everyone; or give the pane a 'restoring' state so the watchdog holds off instead of recovering. Not obviously worth either until someone hits it — deleting a kernel page is already unusual.

Related: the daily-notes landing resolver sidesteps the same interaction by refusing to resurrect a tombstone (`anyBlockTombstoned` in `src/plugins/daily-notes/landing.ts`), which is a different answer to the same question.

title: Global commands materialize their target before the intent policy can veto it
description:
`open_today` and `open_preferences` both await a get-or-create and then call `navigateFromGlobalCommand`:

    const note = await getOrCreateDailyNote(repo, workspaceId, todayIso())
    navigateFromGlobalCommand(repo, {blockId: note.id, workspaceId})

`navigateFromGlobalCommand` resolves `navigationIntentVerb` internally, so a policy returning SUPPRESS for navigator commands stops the navigation but not the write. The command still creates the page and, because `getOrCreateKernelPage` / `getOrCreateDailyNote` are undoable by default, pushes an undo entry — and `UndoManager.record` clears the redo branch on every push, so a vetoed command silently discards a redo the user still wanted.

`openDailyNoteByOffset` has the same ordering, as does the roam-import report path.

The mechanism to fix it already exists: `GlobalCommandNavigateInput` takes an `ensure` callback, which `navigateFromGesture` runs only after the policy resolves to a `navigate` decision and only when the resolved blockId still matches the requested one. The Recents command was converted to it.

The conversion is not mechanical for these two, because both use the RESULT of the ensure as the blockId (`note.id`), where Recents can derive its id up front. So each needs a deterministic id at the call site — `dailyNoteBlockId(workspaceId, iso)` exists; the prefs block would need one — or a variant that lets the ensure supply the target.

No policy in the tree returns SUPPRESS for navigator commands today, so this is latent; `navigationIntentVerb` is a documented plugin seam, so it is reachable by design rather than by accident.

title: A navigation whose target cannot be materialized leaves the panel empty and unexplained
description:
A navigation whose `ensure` cannot materialize its target leaves the panel open on a block that never arrives: `navigateEnsuringTarget` logs to the console and returns, so the user sees an empty panel with no explanation.

(Filed before PR #935's ordering flip, when the failure cancelled the navigation entirely and the button appeared to do nothing. The panel now opens either way, which is more informative but still unexplained.)

Reachable today when the Recents page's derived id is occupied by a row from another of the user's own workspaces: `getOrCreateKernelPage`'s `refuseForeign` throws `DeterministicIdCrossWorkspaceError`. A transient DB error has the same shape, though there the next click retries.

The sibling commands are worse — a rejected `getOrCreateDailyNote` inside `open_today` / `openDailyNoteByOffset` becomes an unhandled rejection in the action dispatcher — so this is one decision for every 'open a lazily-created page' gesture, not a Recents fix.

Direction: decide where a failed navigation target surfaces. A toast from `navigateEnsuringTarget` would put the toast layer inside core navigation, which is the design call to make deliberately rather than by default; routing it through `repo.onUserError` instead keeps core free of the toast dependency. Whichever way, the same answer should cover the command path, which has no gesture to hang it off.

title: List-keyed query handles re-read the whole set when one id enters
description:
Same root shape as the ancestor-queries issue, different blast radius.

WHAT
core.blockTypesByIds({workspaceId, blockIds}) and core.aliasClaimantCounts({workspaceId, aliases}) are both keyed by the whole list, so any change to the set mints a cold handle and the next load re-reads every id — including the ids read a keystroke ago.

Both are called from the link-target autocomplete (src/utils/linkTargetAutocomplete.ts, loadTypeIdsByBlock and searchAliasLabels), whose result set shifts on every keystroke. So a typing burst re-reads the types of every still-displayed row on every key.

NOT the same symptom as the ancestor case: these are reached with .load() from an imperative async search path, not through useHandle, so the caller awaits and paints once. There is no blank frame — the cost is redundant reads, not a layout jump. That is why this is P3.

FIX DIRECTION
The ancestor fix is the worked example: decompose to a per-id query (which is then the cache and invalidation unit), and coalesce concurrent single-id loads into one multi-id statement so the cold case still costs one round trip. src/data/internals/ancestorBatch.ts is ~60 lines and its tests pin the coalescing, chunking and error scoping.

Per-id decomposition is straightforward for blockTypesByIds (per-id row deps already). aliasClaimantCounts is the harder one: it depends on the workspace ALIAS CHANNEL rather than row deps, deliberately — counting claimants among only the displayed rows would miss a claimant ranked below the cutoff. A per-alias handle keeps that channel dep, so every alias handle still invalidates on any alias change in the workspace; check whether that leaves anything to gain before splitting it.

MEASURE FIRST
The ancestor probe measured 30 ids of depth 8 at 1.7ms batched vs 8.2ms serialized on the node harness. Do the equivalent for these two before building: an index-backed lookup keyed (block_id, type) may make the redundant read cheap enough that the coalescing layer is not worth a second owner.

title: Recents header navigates to a derived id it never ensures
description:
`RecentsHeaderItem` (and the recents global command) navigate straight to `recentsPageBlockId(workspaceId)` with no get-or-create and no existence check. Every other system page is re-ensured at its point of use — Properties/Types via the seed materializer's ensureParent, Journal via getOrCreateDailyNote, Locations via createOrFindPlace — so Recents is the only one where a page that failed to materialize at bootstrap stays broken until the next workspace open.

Two outcomes, both from clicking the clock icon:
- the ordinary one: the page was skipped at bootstrap, so navigation lands on a block that does not exist.
- the rare one: the derived id is occupied by a row from another of the user's own workspaces (sync materialization rewrites workspace_id under a stable id), so the panel renders that block instead. Not a data exposure — the local database only holds workspaces the user syncs, and panels showing a block from another workspace is existing accepted behaviour, see the foreign-workspace cases in BlockProperties.component.test.tsx — but it is a confusing render where an unavailable-page state is wanted.

Raised by Codex on PR #589, which declined the proposed fix there: re-raising the cross-workspace error from ensureSystemPages would make workspace open fatal again, which is the failure that PR exists to remove. The fix belongs at the consumer.

Direction: have the Recents consumers get-or-create like their siblings do, or render an unavailable-page state when the derived id does not resolve to a live block in the active workspace. The SystemPage interface doc already states the rule this violates.
close_reason: Closed on GitHub (issue #931); reconciled by bd-github-sync.

title: Property panel offers block-type:label as a field on any block
description:
The property panel's `+ Field` picker offers `block-type:label` on ordinary blocks. `isPropertyPanelHiddenProperty` (src/components/propertyPanel/visibility.ts) keys on the property NAME, and `block-type:label` neither starts with `system:` nor carries `hidden: true` at its `seedProperty` declaration (src/data/properties.ts) — while the TYPE picker does filter `block-type` out of its options.

Consequence: setting that field on a prose block and then tagging it `#type` is a pure-UI route into a block-type block whose content and label are two different names. The kernel now refuses that tag (core.blockTypeTypeify), so this is no longer a correctness hole — it is a picker offering a kernel type-definition field on blocks that can never be types, whose only outcome is a refusal later.

Fix direction: mark the block-type:* definition fields hidden, the way the other kernel internals are, so they only surface on the definition block itself.

title: Sleep Lab: blinded per-night mode (capsule bags, unblind at the end)
description: Design adopted from a LessWrong self-blinding method, done with POWDER, at 5 g morning + 5 g evening (10 g/day, the repletion regimen): pre-weighed sachets of glycine (G) and dextrose (P, matched sweetness, no cooling aftertaste) in identical bags, two per day-bag (morning, evening), a folded G/P note in the day-bag; one random draw per day, poured without looking; the note goes unread into a dated envelope; arms are revealed only at the end. The extension needs a per-day experiment kind with no schedule: (1) experiment property design = per-day-blinded (no periods stamped, no pairs) and dosesPerDay = 2 with labels (morning, evening); (2) 'tonight' creates the night with TWO identical dose todos every day and no arm; adherence per dose; (3) morning ratings gain a blinding-check guess (G / P / no idea) and the afternoon set gains energy 1-5 and mood 1-5; guess accuracy against the true arm is reported at unblinding; (4) the analysis stays empty until an Unblind step, a dialog that takes date -> G/P lines and writes sleeplab:arm on each night, after which the free-permutation p and bootstrap CI already in the engine apply, plus an exploratory regression of each outcome on the count of glycine days in the preceding 3; (5) the night decoration, footer and dialog preview show no arm while blinded; (6) extension by 12+12 day-bags. The open-label period design stays as the other kind.

title: Backfill claim: give the operator gesture cross-tab single-flight
description:
The graph-wide backfill claim identifies a browser PROFILE (claimantId is getClientId(), a localStorage value), while the gesture that holds it is per TAB. The in-flight single-flight set is per-Repo, i.e. per tab, so neither layer separates two tabs of one profile: the second tab's tryClaim reads the first's live claim as its own and proceeds.

Two consequences shipped as accepted residuals:
- two tabs can run the same operator gesture concurrently (tolerated — the passes are idempotent per row);
- the release had to be taught not to delete a claim it only INHERITED, because it could not tell a sibling tab's live claim from its own half-written one. That is the 'minted' vs 'inherited' distinction on tryClaim.

The root fix is cross-tab mutual exclusion at the gesture, which would make the per-profile claimant honest: at most one tab of a profile inside the gesture at a time. navigator.locks is the primitive and the repo already wraps it as withLock/runSingleOwner in src/plugins/attachments/laneLock.ts — that helper would need lifting into @/utils first, since core cannot import the plugin layer (boundary/no-core-to-plugin-imports).

If it lands, the 'inherited' branch becomes unreachable for the gesture and the two-tab caveat can come out of the held-by-peer message.

Not urgent: the residuals are documented and the dangerous half (deleting a live sibling's claim) is already closed.

title: Measure how long the mirror's write lock stalls the editor, and gate the run if it is perceptible
description:
The scheduled database mirror copies the local SQLite file under the checkpointed write lock (`withCheckpointedDbLock`), which excludes every other writer for the whole copy. The run is scheduled on a genuine idle window, but an idle window is only "the main thread is free right now" — a user who pauses between keystrokes qualifies, and the copy then holds the lock for however long a multi-gigabyte read/write takes.

What to find out: how long the lock actually holds for a large database on ordinary disks, and whether an edit made during that window is perceptibly stalled (writes queue behind the lock; the UI renders from the block cache, so the stall may or may not show).

If it is perceptible, the fix is a precondition on the run rather than a change to the copy: require some quiet period since the last user input, or a hidden document, before taking the lock. Both have a failure mode worth checking — a tab that is always focused, and background-tab throttling that may never fire an idle callback at all — so measure before choosing.

title: Opt-in scheduled mirror of the local database to a user-chosen directory
description:
## Why

The local SQLite database lives in the browser's OPFS, and the browser can delete that store wholesale without any app-side cause (see the sibling issue about detecting a vanished DB at boot). Everything uploaded survives on the server; what is lost is local-only state (undo history, the local event log) and any edit that had not uploaded yet. Today the only copy outside OPFS is a manual export.

## What

An opt-in, scheduled mirror of the local database to a user-chosen directory on disk, so OPFS becomes expendable on desktop.

- **Opt-in from settings.** The user picks a directory once via `showDirectoryPicker`; the handle is persisted in IndexedDB (which survives an OPFS wipe) and re-checked with `queryPermission` / `requestPermission` on each run. Chrome grants persistent permission for installed web apps and, with the user's "allow on every visit" choice, for tabs. Unsupported browsers (no File System Access API) simply don't show the option. Off by default.
- **Runs on genuine idle, on a cadence.** Reuse the existing cadenced idle-job scheduling rather than a timer. Skip a run when nothing changed since the last mirror (compare a cheap change marker, e.g. the sync state / last local write, before copying 2 GB). One copy in flight at a time; a run that is interrupted leaves the previous good copy intact (write to a temp name in the target directory, then rename or replace).
- **Uses the existing checkpointed export**, which folds the write-ahead sidecars in before copying so the file on disk is a complete `.db`. Do not write the sidecars.
- **Keeps N most recent copies** (small N, configurable) with informative names (app db name + timestamp), and prunes older ones it wrote itself only — never other files in the directory.
- **Surfaces status**: last successful mirror time and any failure (permission lost, quota, target missing) in settings; a lost permission asks once, not on every idle tick.

## Non-goals

Restore UI (the existing "Replace database with an uploaded SQLite file or recovery archive" action already imports a `.db`), syncing local-only tables to the server, and mobile browsers.
