title: Namespace the startupRecord property to match its sibling
description:
The two metrics recorders name their payload properties inconsistently:

- startup-metrics: `startupRecord` (flat, unnamespaced)
- interaction-metrics: `interaction-metrics:record` (namespaced)

Property names share one workspace-wide namespace, so the flat one can collide with an extension's claim — which is exactly the reasoning recorded at the interaction property's declaration, applied to only one of the two.

Cost of fixing is not zero: renaming after records persist orphans the existing history, and the readers match on the container's children rather than on the property, so orphaned rows would go quiet rather than error. Decide whether to rename with a migration, rename and accept losing the pre-rename series, or record the flat name as a deliberate exception at its declaration.

Also a usability wrinkle: anyone writing SQL against these two series has to know they are spelled differently.

title: Comment-block length tripwire lint (runs over 40 lines), after the cleanup epic lands
description: Measured 2026-09-03 during the comment-audit follow-up: 57 contiguous comment runs of 40+ lines in 49 non-test files (11 of 60+), and no area note of the audit defended any block that long (the longest defended blocks are ~30 lines). But 86% of the comment lines a PR adds live in runs under 20 lines, so a length cap catches only the tail, and existing violations would make it noise today. Plan: once the cleanup epic has landed its chunks, add a third rule to eslint-rules/comment-hygiene.js that reports a contiguous comment run longer than 40 lines (JSDoc or //), with the usual eslint-disable escape and a reason. Start it at zero existing hits so it is a lock, not a backlog.

title: Recorder-off is not a RecordingBlocker, so surfaces promise samples that will never arrive
description:
`recordingBlockedBy` reports only two reasons: no durable client id, and a read-only workspace. The interaction recorder is a separately togglable plugin, so with it disabled the blocker is null and every surface reasoning from it assumes recording is merely slow to start.

Two consequences seen on the trend dialog:
- The empty interaction table used to promise the first record 'about a minute into a session'. Removed rather than made conditional, since the surface has no way to see the toggle.
- The verdict headline can still read 'Building a baseline' with the recorder off. Partly hedged today: the unjudged reason is 'not-recording', whose note says 'interaction recording may be off'. 'May be' is doing real work there, and a precise statement would be better.

The clean shape is for the blocker to include 'the recorder is not running'. Note the source of truth should be whether the effect is RUNNING, not the toggle's nominal value — they differ during startup and in safe mode.

Care needed: `recordingBlockedBy` also feeds `metricsSessionContext().canRecord`, which gates the recorder's own writes. A naive 'is the recorder running' clause there is circular and could refuse the first sample of a session that is in fact recording. Get that ordering right before wiring it.

Deferred from the perf-monitor PR review: correct, but it touches the write-eligibility path, where a mistake silently stops recording.

title: Perf monitor: move design rationale out of comments into docs/
description:
PR 832 (reader slice) carries ~30% comment lines even after two trimming passes. Measurement on the perf-monitor plugin: 481 comment lines in 1585 source lines, and 253 of those (53%) sit in ~42 blocks of 4+ lines.

Root cause is NOT verbosity per line. The guard-to-rationale ratio is about 1:1 (21 early-return guards, 26 guard-rationale lines), which is proportionate. The mass is design rationale — why a device is compared against itself, why medians not means, why the trend window is split the way it is, why each staleness mechanism exists — documented at each SITE instead of once.

Per AGENTS.md, docs/ is intent and design; comments are invariants a future editor would violate. That rationale belongs in a design note with one-line pointers at the code.

Plan:
1. Write docs/perf-monitor-design.md covering: the comparison model (device against itself, trend not session, median not mean), the readiness/unjudged model and why the reasons are distinct, the staleness model (monitor run, counter epoch, publication seq, dialog context) and what each answers, and the recorder/reader split.
2. Replace the multi-line rationale blocks with one-line pointers to the doc section.
3. Keep inline only: invariants a future edit would break, why an obvious simplification is wrong, and defence-in-depth labels.
4. Target under 20% comment share without losing a rule.

Do NOT do this as another compression pass — the previous two already took the easy 40%. What is left is material that is worth keeping but is in the wrong place.

title: Comment cleanup: pass over test files (excluded from the first audit)
description:
The comment-cleanup audit deliberately excluded test files, so its 32.5% baseline covers non-test source
only. Tests are a large fraction of this repo and are not exempt from the rule.

Scale: several test files are among the biggest in the tree — `kernelQueries.test.ts` ~87 KB,
`handleStore.test.ts` ~83 KB, `clientSchema.test.ts` ~69 KB, `definitionSeeds.test.ts` ~79 KB,
`txEngine.test.ts` ~60 KB, `mutators.test.ts` ~64 KB.

The rule needs adapting before running this: in a test, a comment explaining **why a scenario is set up a
particular way** is usually load-bearing — the repo has hard-won rules about raw writes bypassing
processors, about ordering by rank rather than recency, and about timeout budgets, and a test whose setup
comment is deleted invites someone to "simplify" the setup and silently destroy what it proves. What is
safe to cut is narration of which bug prompted the test, review-round history, and restatement of the
assertion on the line below.

Reuse `.comment-audit/FINDER_BRIEF.md` with that amendment.

title: Comment cleanup: audit scripts/eslint-rules and agent-extensions (finders died)
description:
Two areas of the comment-cleanup audit never got a completed finder: their agents died on API 529s.

- **`scripts/`, `eslint-rules/`, `vite-plugins/`, root configs.** Known density: `bd-github-sync.mjs`
  685 comment lines / 682 code, `kernel-plugin-boundary.js` 457/336 (58%), `eslint.config.js` 260/192,
  `bd-publish-verify.mjs` 199/286. Be conservative with the `bd-*` script headers: `AGENTS.md` treats them as
  the authoritative description of the publish-gating behaviour, so compress narration rather than delete
  rules.
- **`agent-extensions/`.** Known density: strength-tracker 2745/4450, `readwise.tsx` 567/2417,
  `matrix-chat-client.tsx` 174/1065. This tree is not typechecked by `pnpm run check`, so prefer
  comment-content findings over refactors unless a change is trivially safe.

Partial findings from the killed attempts survive in `.comment-audit/scratch/find-tooling.md` (53 lines) and
`.comment-audit/scratch/find-agent-extensions.md` (132 lines) — read those before re-running so the work is
continued rather than redone. The audit brief the finders used is `.comment-audit/FINDER_BRIEF.md`.

title: Diagnostics sources capture a Repo that lags a swap by one paint
description:
DiagnosticSourceContribution is {subscribe, getSnapshot} with no argument, so a source captures its Repo when the plugin is constructed. AppRuntimeProvider keeps supplying the previous runtime until its passive reconcile effect runs, so for the paint in between, a source answers from the discarded Repo.

For the performance monitor that means the status chip can show the previous user local sign-out verdict for one frame: the captured repo satisfies both the analysis run-owner comparison and the current-run check, because both lag the same effect.

Not specific to this plugin. Any diagnostics source that reads user-scoped data has the same window; perf-monitor is just the one where it was noticed.

No fix available inside a source: there is no live Repo reachable at snapshot time, only the construction-time capture and module state that the same effect updates. Options are to pass a live context into getSnapshot (a change to the facet contract, affecting every source) or to have the host drop snapshots across a runtime swap.

Exposure is one paint of a stale diagnostic line, no data involved.

title: Ephemeral-storage sessions leave unreachable metrics groups
description:
A private/incognito window has a fully functional localStorage that is discarded when the window closes. The client id readback therefore succeeds, both recorders are enabled, and each such session writes records under a freshly minted per-client group. No later session derives that group id, so its retention pass never reaches it and the rows stay in the synced graph.

Bounded in practice — a handful of rows per private session, and only for a signed-in user — but unbounded over time for someone who habitually browses that way.

No good fix identified. navigator.storage.persisted() is the only durability signal a page has, and it is false for ordinary non-installed browsing, so gating on it would disable recording for nearly everyone. Retention across groups is unsafe: a device cannot distinguish its own retired group from another device live one.

Documented as accepted at isClientIdPersistent. Revisit if a cheap durability signal appears, or if a workspace-level sweep that can safely identify abandoned groups becomes possible (for example, groups whose newest record is older than every other group by a wide margin AND whose device label matches this one).

title: Pin the superseded startup collector's teardown
description:
A second startup collector (started while a first was mid-write) now retires itself once the session is recorded, instead of keeping its long-task listener alive for the life of the page and re-arming the interactive mark.

The clause is unpinned. Reaching it needs the fake-PerformanceObserver quiet-window path crossed with a held write: start collector A, hold its transaction, start B, release A so the session records, then drive a long task plus the quiet window so B evaluates again. The existing tests have each half (see the two-collector test and the debounce test in the startup-metrics record suite) but not the combination.

Delete the clause and confirm the new test fails.

title: blockedPerfAnalysis is a second PerfAnalysis constructor for a ~15ms saving
description:
src/plugins/perf-monitor/analyze.ts builds a synthetic analysis so schedule.ts can short-circuit the no-persistent-client case. But runPerfAnalysis already reaches the same verdict in that environment: the derived group id has no children, both loadRecords calls return empty, every comparison is insufficient, nothingJudged is true, recordingBlockedBy is set, and summarize returns the same headline either way.

What the shortcut saves is two index-hit queries returning zero rows plus one countLiveBlocks (~15ms by its own comment), once per session, in private-browsing mode.

What it costs is two constructors for PerfAnalysis that must stay in sync — all ten fields spelled out twice, so every field added to the interface costs an edit here.

Either derive the defaults from one place, or drop the synthetic constructor and let the early return publish a real run.
close_reason: Deleted in 22b4d6d17 — the shortcut only made the same verdict appear one idle delay sooner, so the ordinary pass replaces it and the second constructor is gone.

title: Retention bounds the reader's scan, not storage: soft-deleted records keep their payload
description:
`tx.delete` is a soft delete — `UPDATE blocks SET deleted = 1` — and leaves `content` and `properties_json` intact. There is no hard-purge path in the repo.

So the retention bounds on the two metrics series (interaction, startup) limit how far the READER scans and nothing else: not local storage, not sync volume. Each prune additionally ships one more synced update.

MEASURED on an active device: ~4.2 page sessions/day, ~1.7KB per interaction record, ~439B per startup record. That is roughly 3.2 MB per device per year retained as tombstones, growing linearly and without bound whatever the retention numbers say. Multiple devices multiply it, since each keeps its own client group.

Accepted deliberately for now (2026-09-02) — flagged during review of the perf-monitoring work and confirmed as known and acceptable at this size.

## Why it is not just a metrics question

Soft delete keeping the payload is general. Anything that appends rows on a cadence and prunes them has the same shape; the metrics series is simply where it was measured. A fix belongs at the storage layer or in a shared record-store pattern, not in one plugin.

## Fix directions

1. A bounded set of REUSABLE record slots: rewrite the oldest slot in place instead of appending a new row and tombstoning an old one. Storage becomes exactly `retain` rows, and the sync volume becomes one update per session instead of an insert plus a delete.
2. A synced compaction pass that hard-deletes tombstones past some age. Needs care: it is a data migration in the sense that it must run once per graph and cannot be driven from a stale device.

Option 1 is the smaller change and removes the growth entirely rather than bounding it after the fact. It does change record identity semantics (a slot's id is reused), which the reader currently relies on to exclude the current session's own record.

title: Upgrade beads (bd) from 1.2.2 to 1.3.x once a stable release exists
description: Decision on 2026-09-01: do NOT upgrade to v1.3.0-rc.1 (prerelease, published 2026-08-31); wait for the stable v1.3.0 tag. The speed reason is gone: PR 873 made the converged GitHub sync ~5s on 1.2.2 by pushing only beads bd could update and pulling alone. Why it needs its own task: 1.3.0 is 1,342 commits since the 1.1.2-era code that 1.2.2 re-tags; the first bd command migrates the embedded store in place from schema v53 to v66 (~28 migrations); this store was born on the retracted 1.2.1 at v65 and had its cursor rolled back to v53 with the v54-v65 tables left in place, so the forward migration runs over tables that already exist - a path nobody else exercises; every clone/machine sharing the Dolt remote must move together (a 1.2.2 binary refuses a v66 store with 'schema version mismatch'). Plan: (1) wait for stable v1.3.0 and read the withheld [1.2.1] changelog + 'Breaking changes for v1.2.2 users' (bd update --status enforces close policy; bd search includes closed by default; the no-id last-touched fallback refuses in scripts; BD_NO_REMOTE_ADOPT semantics); (2) back up .beads OUTSIDE the repo; (3) rehearse the migration on a dolt clone of .beads/embeddeddolt in a scratch dir with the new binary; (4) upgrade every machine and clone in one sitting and bd dolt push right after; (5) re-time pnpm bd:sync and re-check scripts/bd-github-sync.mjs's push premise: 1.3.0's push decides by content equality (ContentEqual/ContentHash hooks), not by the strictly-newer timestamp rule 1.2.2 uses, so planPrePullPush's comment and the wrapper's dry-run wording need re-verifying against the 1.3.0 engine source; (6) bd upgrade review before the first session. Rollback if needed is a schema-cursor rollback per beads' recovery runbook (same procedure used here on 2026-08-17, v66 numbers).
close_reason: Done: the store runs on bd 1.3.0 (schema v66, migration verified), the Dolt remote is pushed with auto-push on one machine, the Homebrew formula is pinned, and the sync guards are re-verified (#1161). Remaining follow-ups are tracked in #1166 (pin the cloud-session install) and #1170 (prime-hook banner).

title: CI-only flake: readwise.aliasConflict 'restores a deleted document whose old name was taken meanwhile'
description: Failed once in the run-tests workflow on a PR branch (GitHub Actions run 33580361378, commit 5bd8dfb15, which touched only scripts/bd-github-sync.*), while the same commit passed the full local gate and the file passes 3/3 in isolation locally. Master's last eight run-tests runs are green. The failing test is in agent-extensions/readwise.aliasConflict.test.tsx; the surrounding suite passed. The --log-failed output carries the × line but not the assertion block, so the failing expectation is unknown — next step is to run the file under load (pnpm run check, or vitest with the full suite) until it reproduces, then check for the shapes AGENTS.md lists: a fixed sleep before a one-shot event, an absence assertion before the async precondition resolves, or a same-millisecond rank tiebreak.

title: Database import takes no lock against other tabs
description:
importRawSqliteDb relies on removeEntry throwing to detect a tab holding the database, which only covers a tab already holding it. A tab that BOOTS during the replace window creates a fresh .db and handles; the importing tab's write then fails, and its teardown removals fail too.

The export path serialises via withCheckpointedDbLock and deleteLocalSqliteDb documents the same hazard. A fix is not free: the two VFSes use different Web Lock names (`${zName}#ckpt` for the write-ahead VFS, ahp:/<path> for CoopSync), so serialising against both means holding two.

title: Import staging temp files are never swept
description:
importRawSqliteDb streams the selection into OPFS temps named .<db>.import-staging-<ts>-<uuid>.tmp and removes them in a finally. A tab killed mid-import leaves one behind at full .db size, and nothing ever reclaims it: removeRecoveryBackupTemps matches only the recovery-zip- prefix.

Same reasoning that made removeRecoveryBackupTemps exist, applied to the other temp family.

Caveat for whoever picks this up: a boot-time sweep must not delete a temp another tab is mid-import on. An age threshold, or sweeping only on the reset path, avoids that.

title: Interrupted database restore can strand a rollback journal
description:
importRawSqliteDb writes the restored files one at a time (siblings, then the .db) because OPFS cannot swap a set of files atomically. A caught failure tears the set back down, but process termination cannot be caught.

Terminating between the -journal write and the .db write leaves a journal with no database. The next boot resolves to the write-ahead VFS, sees a hot journal and no sidecars, and does a CoopSync open to roll it back — which creates a fresh database and replays the stale journal into it. Usually surfaces as the corruption screen.

An orphaned -wa0/-wa1 pair is harmless by comparison: the VFS truncates both when it opens a .db that is not there.

ACCEPTED for now, documented in docs/opfs-write-ahead-vfs.md. Nothing unique is at stake: the restore had already deleted the old database deliberately, and the backup file being restored is untouched, so reset-and-retry recovers fully. The window is seconds during an explicit user action.

Fix direction if it turns out to matter: a durable in-progress marker written before deletion and cleared after success, consulted at boot before SQLite opens. Weighed against: it puts a second source of truth beside 'the sidecars are the record', changes the boot path, and has its own window — a marker left behind by a restore that DID finish would wipe a good database, so it needs to record the expected fileset rather than just a flag.

title: Exported and recovery database artifacts carry no integrity check
description:
A raw .db export and a recovery archive are both restored on trust: import verifies 16 magic bytes and, for an archive, that the member set matches the zip directory. Nothing verifies the CONTENT of what is restored.

A corrupted byte inside a restored .db can be entirely silent (SQLite has no page checksums), and a corrupted write-ahead frame fails its own checksum and is skipped — so committed transactions vanish with integrity_check still reporting ok. Same silent-subset shape as the bug fixed in the write-ahead restore work.

Raised by review as 'verify each zip member's CRC'. Declined at that scope: honouring the zip CRC would harden only one of the two restore routes, and fflate exposes neither the member CRC nor a CRC32 helper, so it means a central-directory parser plus a CRC32 implementation for the archive path alone.

Fix direction, if this is worth doing: one checksum over the whole artifact written at CAPTURE time, covering both the plain .db export and the recovery archive, checked on restore. That is one mechanism for both routes instead of zip machinery for one.

Realistic likelihood is low — the common corruption is truncation, which the archive path already refuses.

title: Raw recovery backup has no cross-tab exclusion
description:
`getRawSqliteDbBackup` reads the main `.db` and each sibling sequentially with no exclusion, so another tab can checkpoint or append to the write-ahead sidecars between those reads. The resulting zip can be internally mismatched while the UI reports the download succeeded.

This got more likely with the write-ahead VFS: the sidecars change independently of the main file, and the bootstrap fallback now offers this backup from a screen whose most common cause is another tab holding the database.

Current mitigation is only advisory — the fallback tells the user to close other tabs first.

Fix direction: gate the read on a worker-held exclusive OPFS access handle on the main `.db`. Measured behaviour that makes this work: an exclusive `createSyncAccessHandle()` is refused with NoModificationAllowedError while any other connection holds the file, and succeeds once they close — so it doubles as a liveness check and as the exclusion itself. Needs a worker, since createSyncAccessHandle does not exist on the main thread.

Weigh against: an inconsistent copy is still better than no copy for a user who is locked out, so the refusal must not be absolute.

Context: docs/opfs-write-ahead-vfs.md

title: SRS grade action ids are derived from display labels, orphaning saved keybindings on rename
description:
The four SRS grade actions build their PERSISTED action id from their DISPLAY label:

    const gradeActionId = (label: string): string => `srs-review.grade.${label.toLowerCase()}`

in src/plugins/srs-review/actions.ts. Renaming a button label (e.g. "Hard" -> "Difficult") silently changes the action id, so any keybinding override a user saved for it stops matching and their remap is lost — quietly, since a stored override that resolves to no action is simply inert.

Predates the key-hint work, which only gave the existing template literal a name.

Fix: give each row an explicit id field, decoupled from the label, e.g. {signal, id: 'srs-review.grade.hard', key: 'Digit2', label: 'Hard', icon: Gauge}. Worth checking whether other action tables in the codebase derive ids from labels the same way.

Found by a review pass on the key-hint change.

title: Decide: move SRS deck/tag identity from tag names to refs
description:
A design decision left open from PR #852 (Codex P1 thread on `src/plugins/srs-review/schema.ts`, declined there with reasoning and left for Vlad).

**The problem**: deck/tag identity across the SRS + tagging stack is the bare tag NAME, resolved via `aliasLookup` at query time. Renaming a tag page therefore silently orphans everything holding the old name: the curated Tags list (`blockTagsConfigProp`), the review deck's pointer (`reviewDeckTagProp`), and the new daily-note deck selection (`dailyNoteDecksProp`). The deck resolves to the no-match sentinel and quietly reports zero due cards / disappears from the daily-note hint, while the stale name stays stored.

**Why #852 didn't fix it piecemeal**: making only the new pref a `refList` would rename-proof one of three deck pointers while the other two — including `reviewDeckTagProp`, which actually scopes the review query — keep alias semantics; and `''` (the all-due deck) has no target block to reference, so the selection isn't purely a set of pages.

**If taken, the scope is**: move `blockTagsConfigProp` + `reviewDeckTagProp` + `dailyNoteDecksProp` to refs together (`ref`/`refList` with `targetTypes`, per the record-grain doctrine), keep a non-ref representation for the all-due deck, migrate stored names by resolving through `aliasLookup` once, and decide what a dangling ref shows (vs. today's silent zero). Touches the add-tag flow and the tags config editor too, since they mint pages from free-text names.

**The alternative** is to accept alias semantics as the tagging model's contract (tags-as-names is also how inline `[[name]]` tagging works) and document that renaming a tag page means re-adding it in Tags — in which case this closes as not-planned.

title: Point ANALYZE_REPAIR_TABLES at the contributed analyzeTables
description:
`ANALYZE_REPAIR_TABLES` (the one-shot exact-stats repair's table list) hardcodes
`block_references`, a table owned by the references plugin. The seam that fixes
it is now on master: `LocalSchemaContribution.analyzeTables: {name, probe}[]`,
with `name` carried specifically so this list can read it.

The repair list should drop `block_references` and take the contributed names
from `analyzeTables[].name`, the same way `resolveAnalyzeArmingProbes` takes the
probes. A few lines — the resolver pattern is already there to copy.

State: the repair list exists only on the warm-boot branch, not on master, so
there is nothing to change until that lands. `name` has no reader on master in
the meantime; it is pinned by a test asserting each probe plans to
`SEARCH <name>`, which is worth having regardless.

If the one-shot repair is dropped rather than landed — its own docstring weighs
that as an option — this is moot and should be closed unactioned. Nothing on
master depends on it either way.

Filed rather than left as a note in the merged PR body, since that is where a
follow-up goes to die.
close_reason: Closed on GitHub (issue #847); reconciled by bd-github-sync.

title: Rows a device downloaded but cannot decrypt stay flagged until that workspace is unlocked there
description:
Measured on a device: 26 staged rows with NO local blocks row at all — live rows, not tombstones — in an e2ee workspace that device has never unlocked. They are durably flagged unapplied, and unlike the identical-column population they are a REAL gap: the rows genuinely have not been materialized.

No code change reaches them, and that is correct rather than a shortfall:
- the needs_apply seed's identity arm cannot fire, because there is no local row to compare and a sealed staged row is never byte-identical to plaintext;
- the queue-driven drain cannot reach them, because their queue entries were consumed by a pass that deferred them;
- the operator rematerialization verb runs but reports them deferred, because the workspace is not materializable on that device.

The whole remedy is unlocking that workspace there, which runs the existing key-gate rematerialization (WorkspaceKeyGate.onResolved -> drainSyncWorkspace at the wide scope, whose id set includes rows with no local row).

Filed because the tracking issue for the original investigation was closed when the seed fix merged, and this half was never addressed by it. Two possible endings: unlock the workspace on that device and confirm the count goes to zero, or decide that a workspace a device never opens is expected to keep staged rows it cannot read, and close this saying so.

No action needed unless that workspace's one-way passes are wanted on that device.

title: Let plugins declare the tables the ANALYZE paths need to reach
description:
Let plugins declare the tables the ANALYZE paths need to reach

Core hardcodes a plugin-owned table name in two places in
`src/data/internals/clientSchema.ts`:

- `ANALYZE_ARMING_PROBES` — `SELECT target_id FROM block_references WHERE ...`
- `ANALYZE_REPAIR_TABLES` — `'block_references'` (added by the #833 work)

`block_references` is contributed by the references plugin's local schema
(`src/plugins/references/localSchema.ts`). The ESLint boundary rule is not
tripped (it matches imports, not string literals), so this is a design smell
rather than a build failure — but it is the same dependency direction the rule
exists to prevent: the kernel knowing what a plugin owns, in two places that can
drift from the plugin independently.

Shape: a facet the local-schema contributors already fill — they declare their
tables to core anyway — so the ANALYZE paths read the registered set instead of
a literal list. `resolveLocalSchemaContributions` already collects these at
bootstrap, so the information exists; it just is not reachable from
`clientSchema.ts`, which takes a params-less `ClientSchemaBootstrapDb`.

Worth doing together with km-fw1q if that lands: replacing the arming probes with
`PRAGMA optimize(0x10002)` deletes the probe list outright, which removes one of
the two sites for free and changes what the right seam looks like for the other.
Sequencing them the other way round means designing a seam and then deleting half
its consumers.

Not urgent: the current list is correct today and a wrong entry degrades to a
skipped table, not a failure.
close_reason: Duplicate of km-ne6x, which was filed from the km-fw1q investigation and covers the same kernel/plugin leak with a concrete seam (analyzeProbes on LocalSchemaContribution). The one thing this issue had that km-ne6x did not — the second hardcoded site, ANALYZE_REPAIR_TABLES — is now recorded there as a comment.

title: Let plugins contribute their own ANALYZE arming probes
description:
`ANALYZE_ARMING_PROBES` in core hardcodes `block_references`, a table owned by the
references plugin (`src/plugins/references/localSchema.ts`). Core naming a plugin table is
the kernel/plugin leak the boundary rule exists to prevent; it is invisible to the ESLint
rule because it is a string in SQL, not an import.

`LocalSchemaContribution` already carries plugin DDL, so the fix is additive: an optional
`analyzeProbes?: readonly string[]` on the contribution, resolved alongside the statements,
and the references plugin brings its own probe. Core then names only core tables.

Behaviour-neutral — the same four probes still run, just sourced from where the tables are
declared.

Found while evaluating the `PRAGMA optimize(0x10002)` proposal, which would have removed
the probes entirely. That was measured and declined; this is the part of its rationale that
survived, and it does not need a mask change.
close_reason: Closed on GitHub (issue #843); reconciled by bd-github-sync.

title: Extract the one-shot marker triple in clientSchema.ts
description:
Extract the one-shot marker triple in clientSchema.ts (6th copy now)

`client_schema_state` one-shot markers are hand-rolled as a triple every time:
a `*_MARKER_KEY` const, a `SELECT 1 FROM client_schema_state WHERE key = '<K>'`
const, and an `INSERT OR REPLACE INTO client_schema_state (key, completed_at)
VALUES ('<K>', strftime('%s','now') * 1000)` const. There are five in
`src/data/internals/clientSchema.ts` and one in
`src/plugins/references/localSchema.ts`. The read side is a 5th copy of
`const done = await db.getOptional<{1: number}>(SELECT_X); if (done !== null) return`.

Proposed shape: two SQL factories plus a predicate, with the named consts kept
as one-liners so tests and the references plugin are untouched and the
core->plugin boundary is unaffected (the plugin imports from core, not the
reverse):

    markerDoneSql(key) / recordMarkerSql(key) / isMarkerSet(db, sql)

Removes roughly 30 lines and makes the next marker one line.

NOT the reuse to reach for: `MarkerStore` in
`src/data/internals/idleMarkerJobs.ts`. It serves PREFIXED FAMILIES of
per-workspace keys with an in-memory cache, needs `getAll` (absent from
`ClientSchemaBootstrapDb`), and the cache buys nothing for a single global key
read once per pass. That module exists because this same duplication was
already extracted once for the other marker family; the singleton-key family
never got the same treatment.

Found during the #833 warm-boot fix, which added the 6th copy. Deliberately
left out of that PR to keep a perf regression fix from turning into a refactor.
close_reason: Closed on GitHub (issue #837); reconciled by bd-github-sync.

title: Readwise conflict dialog: stale-gesture windows the current checks do not cover
description:
Two narrow races in the sync-time conflict offer, filed rather than fixed because they are the fourth and fifth iteration of the same guard and the pattern needs a decision, not another clause.

1. `mergeAliasCollision` (src/plugins/alias/mergeCollisionAction.ts) has no workspace recheck between `ensureDeletableThroughUi` and `repo.run`. The Readwise dialog checks the active workspace before calling, but the preflight awaits user-facing guards, so a switch during it leaves the check stale and the mutator merges the first workspace's blocks under the second's context. Affects the duplicate-name banner equally — the helper is shared.

2. `acceptFallbackAlias` validates only that the document still has the displayed title. It does not revalidate the predicate that PRODUCED the offer: that the document lacks its title and a live rival holds it. So a conflict that resolves while the dialog sits open — rival releases the name, a sync reclaims it, content unchanged — still records an acceptance, which then suppresses a genuine later collision on that title.

The fix for 2 is arguably the better shape rather than another window-patch: make the write validate the same predicate the scan uses, so the offer and the answer agree by construction instead of by two checks kept in sync by hand. 1 wants the recheck inside the writing path, per the gesture-guard checklist.

Both need a decision about the dialog's concurrency model more than they need individual clauses. See the review-round discussion on the PR.
notes:
Third case, same class (review round 9): a co-claimed FALLBACK blocks the managed-property write that precedes naming. Another device sync-applies a claimant for the document's fallback; Readwise then changes a managed property (author, category); the content transaction rewrites properties_json while the duplicate alias is present, the uniqueness trigger rejects it, and execution never reaches ensureDocumentAlias to step the document onto a free suffix. That book then fails every run with the cursor pinned behind it. Fix direction per the reviewer: reconcile a co-owned sync alias BEFORE any managed-property write — which means reordering the sync's transactions, not adding a clause.
2c FIXED on the readwise branch (a6cb9303c): releaseCoClaimedFallback gives up the sync's own recorded claim before the managed-property write, when another live row co-holds it and it is not the document's content. Pinned by 'updates a book whose fallback another row co-claims'; deleting the content clause fails the rename test, so the two guards are connected. Cases 1 and 2 (stale workspace check across the deletion preflight; a keep clicked after its conflict resolved) remain open here.
close_reason: Closed on GitHub (issue #831); reconciled by bd-github-sync.

title: Readwise: a co-claimed old title aborts an uncontested re-title
description:
Found while pinning the `aliasClaimants` fix; reproduced, then set aside as a separate case.

Repro: sync a book so the document claims `Title`; land a sync-applied co-claimant of `Title` (a raw insert with a later `created_at`, the shape sync apply produces); sync the book again under a NEW, free title.

The re-title is uncontested, so nothing is released first. `alias.sync`'s A3 rule then heals the content change by appending the new title to the bag, and that write re-inserts `Title` under the uniqueness trigger against the co-claimant. `ProcessorRejection: alias.collision`, and the content rewrite rolls back with it.

Contained but not fixed: per-book isolation means the run continues and the toast reports the failure, but that document never re-titles, and the cursor is held so every later sync re-fetches from the same point.

Why it is filed rather than fixed: the guard that would cover it is `releaseSyncOwnedAlias` firing on a co-claimed OLD name as well as a contested NEW one — a fourth clause in the same predicate family, and the fourth review round in a row to land in it. The shape question comes first.

Same family as the alias-provenance work: both come from single-claimant assumptions in code the kernel lets several rows claim.

title: Readwise placeholder aliases only reconcile for documents the incremental export returns
description:
`runSync` passes `lastSyncedAt` as `updatedAfter` and calls `syncBookToBlocks` only for the records that export returns, so `ensureDocumentAlias` — the thing that re-probes a contested name and retires the placeholder — never runs for a document Readwise has not touched.

Consequence: a document parked on `Title (Readwise)` (or, past the 20 suffix slots, on no alias at all) does not pick the real name back up when the page holding it is renamed or deleted by hand. It stays on the placeholder until Readwise next updates that book, so an ordinary `[[Title]]` link keeps missing it.

Not a silent trap for the intended flow: the duplicate-name banner's merge hands the name back directly, in its own transaction, without waiting for a sync. This is the case where the user resolves the conflict some other way.

Fix direction (either): reconcile every Readwise document once per sync, independent of the export results — a query over the document type, then `ensureDocumentAlias` per row, which is cheap because it writes only when the bag would change; or trigger reconciliation when the conflicting claim is released. The first is simpler and does not need a new hook.

Sits with the alias-provenance work: whichever way this goes, the reconcile is the same call.

title: Readwise alias ownership is inferred from the string instead of recorded
description:
`isSyncOwnedAlias` / `isSyncOwnedAliasBag` (agent-extensions/readwise.tsx) decide whether the sync may overwrite a document's alias bag by matching the strings against what `fallbackAlias` can emit. That is an inference about provenance, and each review pass over this code produces another finding about a case the inference reads wrong:

- a user alias that merely looks generated (`Title (Readwise 2024)`) — fixed by matching the generated set exactly rather than the shape;
- a multi-entry bag combining generated values (`Title (Readwise)` plus a hand-added `Title (Readwise 2)`) — ACCEPTED and labelled at the declaration, because the multi-entry allowance is load-bearing: `alias.sync` appends the new content on a re-title, and reconciling that pair is what retires the placeholder, after both a re-title and a merge.

The shape that removes the class: record what the sync last claimed as a managed property on the document, and reconcile only when the stored bag is explainable from that record. Ownership stops being a guess about strings and becomes a fact the writer wrote down. It also makes the placeholder-retirement rule statable without reference to alias shapes at all.

Cost, and why not now: it needs a property schema plus an adoption path for documents that predate it (no record + a bag the current inference recognises → adopt it, then record). Not worth blocking a fix for a sync that stops importing.

Prerequisite reading before touching this: the two-entry bag is produced by the kernel, not by the sync, and two tests fail the moment that is forgotten.
close_reason: Closed on GitHub (issue #824); reconciled by bd-github-sync.

title: Readwise runSync per-book isolation and cursor-hold are untested
description:
`runSync` (agent-extensions/readwise.tsx) now wraps each book in try/catch, holds `lastSyncedAt` when any book failed, and counts the success toast from highlights that actually landed. None of that is unit-tested — the alias-conflict suite drives `syncBookToBlocks` and `ensureRoot` directly, one level below.

Testing it needs a stubbed `fetch` (export pagination), a token in prefs, and a toast harness. Worth doing if that harness gets built for another reason; the cursor-hold in particular is the only thing that brings a failed book back, so a regression there is silent data loss from the user's point of view (a book that never imports).

title: Readwise re-title into a contested name still fails when the alias is user-set
description:
Accepted limitation of the suffixed-alias work, recorded so it is not rediscovered as a surprise.

`ensureDocumentAlias` overwrites only a bag it recognises as its own (`isSyncOwnedAliasBag`), so a document whose alias the USER set keeps it. When Readwise then renames that document into a name another page holds, `alias.sync`'s A3 rule appends the new content to the existing bag, the append of a contested name is refused, and the content rewrite rolls back with it — that book fails to sync.

Why it was left: the alternative is emptying an alias the user chose in order to force a title through, which is the worse trade. `runSync` now isolates each book, so the cost is one document per sync instead of the whole run, and the failure is reported in the sync toast.

If it ever needs fixing, the shape is probably: keep the user's alias, and skip the CONTENT rewrite for that document rather than the whole book — the title on a page the user has named is the less important of the two.

title: Readwise document create does not strip a tombstone's stale alias bag on restore
description:
`syncBookToBlocks` (agent-extensions/readwise.tsx) creates/restores the document page via `createOrRestoreTargetBlock` WITHOUT `stripAliasesOnRestore`. A document that was deleted while holding an alias, and whose name was then claimed by another page, re-inserts the tombstoned bag on the `deleted` flip and trips `block_aliases_workspace_alias_unique` inside the restore statement.

Same shape as #378 (raw restore call sites resurrecting a stale claim), which fixed the kernel/daily-note seats but left this call site alone. Pre-existing; the suffixed-fallback work deliberately did not touch it.

Blast radius is now one book rather than the whole sync — `runSync` isolates each book — but the document still never restores.

Fix direction: pass `stripAliasesOnRestore` at the document (and highlight/note/meta) create sites, and let `ensureDocumentAlias` re-probe the name afterwards, which is what it already does on every sync.
close_reason: Closed on GitHub (issue #823); reconciled by bd-github-sync.

title: Test files leak parked seed-materialization passes; stderr noise at shared-db close
description:
Follow-up to the definitionSeeds flake (GitHub #806). Any test file using the shared-db pattern (createTestDb in beforeAll, createTestRepo per test) leaves each test's Repo with a scheduled seed-materialization pass parked on awaitLocalMemberRole, holding a workspace_members onChange subscription on the shared db. Nothing disposes it.

Where that bites hardest is fixed (definitionSeeds.test.ts now unpins the workspace in afterEach). The residue is log noise: when the shared db closes in afterAll with passes still parked, the pass fails and logs '[seedMaterialization] workspace <id> access wait failed: Called operation on closed remote'. Seen in CI from src/utils/test/navigation.test.ts among others; it clutters the stderr that a real failure has to be read out of.

Harmless today because only two test files INSERT workspace_members rows, so the parked passes stay parked instead of waking and writing. That is a property of the current test set, not a guarantee.

Options: dispose the Repo in createTestRepo's own teardown (needs a per-test hook the harness does not have today), or have createTestDb's cleanup cancel passes before closing, or leave it and accept the noise. Not urgent.
close_reason: Closed on GitHub (issue #813); reconciled by bd-github-sync.

title: Concurrent delete-vs-edit leaves a peer's property value orphaned under a tombstoned field row
description:
When a peer edits a property value while another device deletes the owning block, restoring that block surfaces the CELL's value and leaves the peer's edited value row live but unreachable under a tombstoned field row.

WHAT HAPPENS
1. Device A deletes block P (subtree delete tombstones P, its field row F, and F's value V).
2. Device B concurrently edits that same property. B's PROJECT runs in the same tx, so B uploads the edited value row and the corrected cell together.
3. B's edited value arrives on A and lands LIVE under A's tombstoned F — sync-apply skips the parent-liveness trigger (clientSchema.ts, the trigger is gated on tx_context.source IS NULL), which is what makes a live child under a tombstone possible at all.
4. A restores P. The revival refuses to revive F, because a live value sits under it and reviving would expose that value to the cell-to-child convergence and overwrite its text (measured; that overwrite was a real regression, fixed before #804 landed).
5. So the caller mints a fresh field row carrying the CELL's value. B's edited value stays live, still parented to the tombstoned F, and nothing lists it — childrenOf is live-only and never returns F, so no traversal reaches through it.

Net: no data is destroyed, but the losing side of a concurrent delete-vs-edit is invisible rather than surfaced. Divergent values are normally kept as PEER VALUES under one field row precisely so a human can see and resolve them; this path does not get that treatment.

Pinned by the test "does not revive a value when sync left a live one under the tombstoned field row" in propertyChildren.test.ts, which asserts the arrived value keeps its own content and stays live while the mint carries the cell value.

WHAT THIS ISSUE USED TO SAY, AND WHY IT WAS WRONG (recorded so nobody re-derives it)
It claimed a revival faces an UNDECIDABLE choice: a field row tombstoned by the owner's own delete looks identical to one deleted independently by a peer whose cell correction has not arrived, so materializing from the cell might resurrect a property the fleet deleted.

That pair is not reachable. The revival only runs on the owner's tombstone-to-live transition, so a peer deleting a property on a block that was never deleted never reaches this code at all. Reaching it needs a compound case: the peer's field-row tombstone arriving WITHOUT its cell correction, plus a local delete and restore of the owner. But core.projectPropertyChildren is a same-tx processor watching `deleted`, so the deleting device writes the tombstone and the corrected cell in ONE transaction and uploads them together. The state was produced in analysis only by a raw UPDATE that tombstoned the field row while deliberately skipping the cell correction — i.e. by bypassing the mechanism that prevents it.

The correct rule is the simple one: if we are restoring, the block was deleted; if it was deleted, its cell is the record of what it had and its children were taken down by that same delete. Materializing from the cell is right, and no causal lookup (row_events tx ids or otherwise) is needed. row_events was considered and rejected as a source — it is long-lived but not a durability guarantee we make.

ALSO ACCEPTED, NOT A BUG
If a peer deletes a property while the owner is tombstoned elsewhere, the peer's cell correction can lose to LWW, because the delete bumped the owner row's updated_at. The restore then brings the property back. That is LWW resolving a concurrent edit in favour of the later action, the same as anywhere else in the system.

POSSIBLE DIRECTIONS
1. Accept. The losing value survives and a determined user can still reach it by restoring F. Cheapest.
2. On refusal, move the live value under the newly minted field row so it surfaces as a peer value, which is how divergent values are handled everywhere else. Makes the conflict visible; needs a rule for which becomes primary.
3. Revive F but preserve the live value's content, minting a separate cell-backed sibling instead of overwriting it.

Reachable post-flip only.

title: Recognition's root leg is hand-rolled in several places; blockCrumbs' copy is wrong
description:
Recognition's root leg ("a workspace-root block is user content whatever its content says", §9 root half) is hand-rolled in several places instead of composed from the shared predicate. `isPropertyFieldInstance`'s own docblock names hand-rolled restatements as the recorded failure mode for exactly this.

THE ONE WITH A BEHAVIOUR DIFFERENCE — `crumbsFromAncestors` (src/utils/blockCrumbs.ts) drops an ancestor's breadcrumb on a bare bit test:

    if (chain[i].isFieldForm) continue

missing BOTH other legs. So a root block whose content is a marked reference (`::((someDefinitionId))`) loses its breadcrumb label even though it is user content — the rename processor has a test asserting precisely that such a row is not machinery — and so does a marked row whose target resolves to no definition. Cosmetic: a missing crumb, no data effect, and it needs a page whose whole content is a bare marked reference.

THE OTHERS, correct today but each a separate copy a future edit to the shared predicate will not reach:
  - src/data/repo.ts (the definition-migration batch) — raw SQL carrying its own `parent_id IS NOT NULL`, self-labelled '§9 root half'.
  - src/data/internals/propertyRenameProcessor.ts (consumingParentIds) — same, same label.
  - src/data/internals/propertyChildrenProcessor.ts — two positional guards (`addAffectedProjection`, `collectAffectedProjection`) that refuse a root candidate before consulting the bit.
Both SQL sites are additionally followed by a JS-level null check on the same column, so their SQL clause is redundant at those call sites — unlabelled defence in depth.

AND ONE THAT CANNOT BE PINNED — `TxImpl.childrenOf` (src/data/internals/txEngine.ts) returns early on `parentId === null` before the predicate is consulted. Measured: deleting that line leaves propertyChildren.test.ts fully green, and no test anywhere calls childrenOf(null, ws, {hidePropertyChildren: true}). Even one that did would not pin it, because `isPropertyFieldInstance` guards the same case one layer down. Per the repo's own rule a clause that fails nothing when deleted must be LABELLED defence in depth at its declaration; this one is not.

FIX: compose the shared predicate where a definition-checker is available; where it is not, keep the hand-rolled leg but label it and say why. Start with blockCrumbs, which is the only one that is actually wrong.

Found by adversarial review while pinning the SQL predicate's root leg.

title: clientSchema 'samples rather than fully scanning' has no timeout budget and flakes on CI
description:
Intermittent CI failure, seen once on a PR whose commit changed only a code
comment in an unrelated file. A re-run of the same commit passed.

TEST: 'samples rather than fully scanning', in the 'runAnalyzeIfStale — arming
(stale-stats axis)' describe of src/data/internals/clientSchema.test.ts.

MEASURED: 214ms locally under full-suite load (vitest --reporter=verbose over
the whole suite), 204ms in isolation. CI recorded 11139ms for the same test on
the failing run. It has no explicit timeout, so it runs under vitest's 5000ms
default.

The describe's beforeEach writes a real SQLite file, inserts 500 rows, runs
ANALYZE, then corrupts sqlite_stat1 to the degenerate '0 0' shape and reopens;
the test runs another ANALYZE. That is file-backed I/O plus two ANALYZE passes,
which is the profile that stretches worst on a contended shared runner. Local
numbers therefore say little about the CI tail — 23x headroom here, apparently
under 1x there.

CAVEAT ON THE DIAGNOSIS: GitHub's log API truncated the run before the failure
detail, so the assertion-or-timeout message was never readable. 'Timed out' is
inferred from the 11139ms duration against a 5000ms default, not confirmed.
Worth re-checking against a fresh failure before sizing anything.

WHAT IT NEEDS: a measured CI baseline for this test (and probably its sibling
'repairs degenerate "0 0" stats', same beforeEach, 238ms locally), then an
explicit it(..., N) budget per the AGENTS.md rule about budgeting for the ~6x
p99.9 load stretch, with a comment recording the measured cost. Sizing it from
local numbers alone would be a guess.

Filed rather than fixed in-flight: the guess would have been mine to make and
the numbers to make it well are not available from a developer machine.
close_reason: Closed on GitHub (issue #799); reconciled by bd-github-sync.

title: Reference-target stamping has no release-side rederive: an alias loss never revisits an already-stamped row
description:
The reference-target machinery repairs the GAIN direction only. `core.aliasClaimRederive` schedules on alias gains; `Repo.drainNameRederives` and the per-open sweep both filter `reference_target_id IS NULL`, so neither ever re-points or clears a column that is already stamped. The sync path is the same shape: the materializer's `onAliasTargetsAdded` hook fires only for arrivals that GAINED alias values, and derive-at-arrival runs only for content-changed arrivals.

Same-device releases are covered by a different mechanism and are not the gap: `renameBacklinksProcessor` enumerates the releasing block's backlink sources and PINS each span (`::[[name]]` -> `::[name](((id)))`), which is a content rewrite, so both derived columns recompute. That enumeration only sees rows already materialized locally.

THE GAP is a row that was not local when the release was processed. Device B releases the alias while row R has not yet synced to B, so B pins nothing. R then arrives on device A ahead of the release and A's arrival-derive stamps R to the definition — correct at that instant, and never revisited. The same row arriving on B after the release derives to null or to a fresh seat. The two devices then disagree permanently about whether R is a recognized field row, with no repair path short of editing R's content.

REACHABILITY IS NARROW, which is why this is P3 and was accepted rather than fixed when found: it needs a definition that claims its own name as an alias (possible only by hand through the generic property panel — nothing in the app does it), an alias-FORM field row (the app writes the id form, and materialize canonicalizes alias-form rows to it, so an alias-form row is transient by design), a multi-device arrival order, and then a release.

FIX DIRECTION: mirror the claim-side machinery for the clearing direction — a deferred batched pass keyed off alias-LOSS events, including sync-applied ones, that revisits rows whose stamp names a definition no longer claiming the alias their content spells. That is a real feature, not a patch, and it should land with the work that makes definitions name-resolvable, which is what decides the semantics it needs.

Found while verifying a neighbouring issue. The declining rationale on that issue originally claimed this case was already covered; it is not, for the cross-device ordering above.

title: referenceBlockContentForId accepts bracket-shaped ids its inline reader would parse as a wikilink
description:
Latent today, recorded from a review of the #779 investigation. Not reachable in production under the current block-id policy; the point is that only that policy stands between this and the exact failure #779 described.

`referenceBlockContentForId` (src/data/referenceBlock.ts) guards the content it emits by round-tripping it through `parseExactReferenceBlockContent`, the WHOLE-BLOCK grammar. Its id filter (`BROAD_BLOCK_REF_ID_SOURCE`) excludes whitespace and parentheses but not brackets, so an id containing `[[`/`]]` composes to a span that round-trips cleanly at that grammar and is accepted.

The references processor does not use that grammar. It runs the INLINE scanner over content, which is a bracket-depth text scan unaware of the enclosing `((...))` -- so it finds an alias mark inside the composed span, mints an alias page named after it, and records a reference from a field row. That is the phantom-page failure #779 reported, triggered by id SHAPE instead of workspace scope.

Why it cannot happen now: `assertCanonicalBlockId` requires a strict UUID and runs at `tx.create` whenever `blockIdPolicy` is 'canonical', which is the Repo default and is never overridden by the app. The agent runtime reaches the same outcome by a different route -- its command layer calls `assertCanonicalBlockId` directly on caller-supplied ids rather than by setting the Repo option. Every `blockIdPolicy: 'any'` in the tree is a test; `createTestRepo` opts out for mnemonic ids.

Fix direction if it is worth closing: have the emitter agree with BOTH readers -- assert the inline scanner finds zero marks in the composed content, the same two-readers-must-agree discipline `spanReplacement.ts` already applies. Weigh that against permanent weight for an unreachable case; ACCEPTING it with a line at the declaration saying the canonical-id policy is what makes it unreachable is a legitimate answer, and probably the cheaper one.

title: Root exemption in recognizedFieldRowSql is unpinned on the read side
description:
`recognizedFieldRowSql` (src/data/internals/treeQueries.ts) has three legs: the `is_field_form` bit, `parent_id IS NOT NULL` (the root exemption), and the definition-ness disjunction. Deleting the `parent_id IS NOT NULL` leg leaves the ENTIRE suite green — 647 files, 8381 tests — so it is genuinely unpinned. No marked (`::`) fixture anywhere in the suite was root-parented before this was filed.

CORRECTION 1 to the original filing, which also claimed the seed-ids disjunct was unpinned: it is not. Neutralizing that leg arity-preservingly fails two tests (the treeQueries visible-children suite and the backlinks machinery-filter suite, the latter asserting both directions). The first measurement was scoped to a single test file and was over-generalized. The block_types leg is pinned too.

CORRECTION 2, to a claim made while fixing this: there are THREE independent root exemptions, not two, and an earlier note conflated them.
  1. SQL — `recognizedFieldRowSql`'s `parent_id IS NOT NULL`. This is the unpinned one.
  2. TS predicate — `isPropertyFieldInstance`'s `if (data.parentId === null) return false` (src/data/propertyChildren.ts). Pinned by the rename-processor suite's 'a ROOT ::[[alias]] row keeps the pinned label' test, which is the only place a root row is both marked AND definition-resolving.
  3. The tx engine's `childrenOf` early return `if (parentId === null) return data`, which exits BEFORE the predicate is consulted at all. Pinned by propertyChildren.test.ts's 'root rows are never filtered (WRITE-side)' describe — whose fixture content is UNMARKED, so it exercises this early return and not leg 2.
Root listings therefore do NOT reach `isPropertyFieldInstance`; an earlier version of this description said they did.

Where leg 1 is actually observable, which is narrower than it appears: the outline paths cannot exercise it, because VISIBLE_CHILDREN_SQL selects on `parent_id = ?` (never true for a root row) and VISIBLE_SUBTREE_SQL applies the predicate only to `child` rows in its recursive term, which have a parent by construction, while never pruning its own seed. The one SQL consumer that can reach it is the backlink machinery filter's ancestor walk — a source whose ANCESTOR is a root-level marked row. Without the leg that source is classified as property machinery and its backlink is dropped.

Found by mutation testing while verifying a neighbouring issue; pre-existing, not introduced by that work.
close_reason: Closed on GitHub (issue #793); reconciled by bd-github-sync.

title: stagingNeedsApplyMigration test has no timeout budget; times out under gate load and cascades
description:
Observed twice while running the full gate on a loaded machine (2026-08-23), and passing 3/3 when run alone.

src/data/test/stagingNeedsApplyMigration.test.ts, "seeds a backlog larger than one chunk": 600 iterations, each doing two sequential db.execute round-trips (deliver + seedLocal), against vitest default 5000ms. Measured 5090ms under load; the gate ran 210s that pass versus ~75s quiet, so the machine was contended.

Two consequences, and the second is what makes it worth filing:
1. the test itself times out;
2. the NEXT test in the file then fails with `SqliteError: no such column: "needs_apply"` inside rewindToPreMigration, because the file shares one DB and the timed-out test left it mid-migration. That second failure looks like a schema bug and is not one.

Fix per AGENTS.md timeout-budget guidance: give it an explicit timeout with a comment naming the measured cost, e.g. it(..., 20_000), rather than raising the global testTimeout. 1200 sequential DB round-trips is a real cost and the 6x-under-load rule applies squarely.

Worth considering as part of it: batching the seed loop into fewer statements would remove the cost rather than budget for it.

Not fixed inline because it is unrelated to the PR that surfaced it (a properties/codec change that never touches this path - the test writes via raw SQL INSERT with properties_json {}).
close_reason: Fixed; duplicate of km-qvuf. The 600-row backlog seed has an explicit }, 30_000) budget with the measured cost recorded. No recurrence in the last 400 CI runs (2026-08-19 to 08-24).

title: Revival re-materializes fresh property children instead of restoring the tombstoned ones
description:
Follow-up to the revival fix for #778 (bead km-6yf5).

When a tombstoned row comes back live in a child-backed workspace, the
materialize direction find-or-creates its field/value rows — and childrenOf is
live-only, so it mints FRESH rows and leaves the tombstoned originals behind.

Two consequences:

1. USER CONTENT UNDER A VALUE CHILD IS NOT BROUGHT BACK. A value child can host
   arbitrary user content (a comment thread under a property value — the case
   collapseDuplicateFieldRow explicitly relocates rather than reaping). The
   subtree delete tombstones that content with the field row, and a fresh
   value child does not carry it. The property comes back; the annotation
   under it does not.

2. IDS DIVERGE ACROSS REPLICAS. Two devices that each restore the same row mint
   different field-row ids for the same definition, so the pair converges only
   through the duplicate-collapse path instead of never diverging.

Restoring the tombstoned field-row subtree instead of minting would fix both
and preserve ids. It needs a deterministic rule for which tombstone to revive
when several generations exist, and has to stay convergent with the cell (a raw
bag write to a tombstoned row could have moved the cell on while the children
were down). Not obviously worth it before the flip — file rather than lose.

Strictly better than the pre-fix state either way: before, the whole property
was missing.
close_reason: Closed on GitHub (issue #787); reconciled by bd-github-sync.

title: A same-tx ancestor content-flip nests property machinery under a descendant
description:
Split out of the post-flip healing-seams umbrella (item 3). Reachable only in a child-backed workspace — which in a TEST is one column value.

The write-side guards (the dual-write in setProperty, and the materialize processor) carry a content-based prospective-field-row twin, so a row that flips its OWN content to a schema reference in the same transaction as a property-bag write stays cell-only. That check is SELF-ONLY. If one transaction changes an ANCESTOR's content to a whole-block schema reference and also writes a property bag on a DESCENDANT, the interior-subtree walk reads the ancestor's not-yet-stamped column (derive runs later in the chain), fails to recognize the descendant as interior, and materializes field and value rows under it. Once derive stamps the ancestor, those rows ARE interior, the visible-children rule stops filtering them, and machinery becomes visible.

CANDIDATE FOR ACCEPT RATHER THAN FIX, and it is filed separately so that decision can be made on its own merits instead of inside a six-item pile. The trigger is an exotic single transaction that both flips an ancestor's content and writes a property on a descendant — not reachable through normal UI, only through raw, bridge, or otherwise programmatic multi-writes. The fix threads a prospective content-aware predicate through the shared interior-subtree walk, which ALSO feeds the read-side children filter: a hot-path primitive change with real regression surface.

Weigh reachability and blast radius against a permanent change to a hot primitive. Accepting it — with a line at the guard saying it is accepted and why — is a legitimate outcome; so is simplifying so it cannot arise.

title: Pre-flip cell/child divergence survives the flip unreconciled
description:
MEASURED, on master, in a workspace at properties_migration = 'cell'.

SHAPE. A block whose cell holds key N, plus a hand-authored child
`::((fieldIdForN))` with a value child holding a DIFFERENT value. Pre-flip the
cell is the truth and the projection is dormant, so the user sees the cell
value; the field row is hidden by the visible-children exclusion, which is not
flip-gated. Nothing reconciles the two.

WHY IT IS REACHABLE. `is_field_form` is stamped from CONTENT by the derive
pass, not from the migration state, so a hand-written marked reference
classifies exactly like a generated field row. No pass mints these pre-flip;
a user has to type one. Deliberate, so rare, but the flip is one-way.

WHAT THE FLIP DOES WITH IT. Nothing, and that is the problem:
- flipping alone does not rebuild any cell (PROJECT watches content changes);
- the backfill is CREATE-ONLY and skips a key that already has a field row,
  so it does not visit the divergence either;
- the first content touch of any value row under that field row then makes
  PROJECT publish the field row's FIRST value into the cell — silently
  replacing the value the user could see. Measured: a cell edited to
  'edited-after-merge' pre-flip reverted to the child's 'target-value' on the
  first post-flip touch of a peer value row.

Direction is arbitrary, decided by which side is touched first: a post-flip
setProperty converges the child to the cell instead.

NOT the merge catch-up. Reproduced with no merge at all — see km-g5ev, where
the same investigation established that gating blockMerge's catch-up makes
the merge case strictly worse rather than fixing this.

POSSIBLE ANSWER, not chosen: the flip gesture already plans and can refuse
(planPropertyDefinitionSynthesis / flipBlockedBySynthesis). A pre-flight scan
for owners that have BOTH a cell key and a field row for it, reported to the
operator before an irreversible one-way migration, puts the check at the one
moment that matters instead of at each writer. Cheap pre-flip, where the set
should be empty or tiny. ACCEPTING the case with a line saying so is also a
legitimate answer given how deliberate the precondition is.
close_reason:
Closed as ACCEPTED — unreachable, not fixed. Vlad, 2026-08-23: nobody is
creating ::((ref)) properties before the flip.

That is the whole precondition. The hazard needs a field row to EXIST in an
un-flipped workspace, and the only two ways to get one are:
- a user hand-writes ::((fieldId)) with a value child — which is what the
  statement above rules out; or
- code mints one, which nothing does pre-flip: the backfill refuses an
  un-flipped workspace, the dual-write is flip-gated, and blockMerge's
  catch-up only fires when the SOURCE already has a field row, so it cannot
  bootstrap the first one.

Zero pre-flip field rows means no block reaches the flip with children, the
backfill builds them all from cells, and there is no divergence to reconcile.
The pre-flight scan this bead proposed for the flip gesture would scan for a
set that is empty by construction.

The mechanism itself is real and stays documented where it matters — the
catch-up's own comment in blockMerge.ts, and the alias-seat reaper's flip
gate, both of which reason about content-derived recognition rather than
about migration state. Reopen if a pass ever mints field rows pre-flip, or
if the ::((ref)) authoring surface ships before the flip does.

title: Expose the workspace rematerialization in the app, not only the agent CLI
description:
`rematerialize-workspace` (the remedy for a durable materialization gap — rows this device downloaded, could not apply, and consumed the queue entry for) is reachable only through the agent bridge. The refusal it answers also reaches a user through the UI: the properties-migration flow surfaces `workspaceViewGap`'s durable reason as a toast, and a user reading it there has no in-app move.

Wanted: a command-palette entry that runs `Repo.rematerializeWorkspace(activeWorkspaceId)` and reports the result the way the migration command reports its outcome — how many rows were unapplied before and after, and, when rows are still unapplied, the pass's own `deferred`/`quarantined` counts. `system-status` is the natural home (it already owns the sync indicator and its queue counts).

The pass is a derivation over local state: no uploads, no per-graph claim, no undo-stack clearing, safe to re-run — so the palette entry needs no confirmation dialog, unlike the migration one.

Follows from the PR that added the verb.
notes: PR 1135 merged at 2026-09-23T04:46:38Z as 4ab8f8e5e79e7f1166f0723b68da872518641e0b. Shipped the in-app recovery command with structured feedback, safe-mode/status-toggle availability and coalesced concurrent calls. All review threads resolved; CI passed, local full gate 733 files and 10161 tests. Ack-to-echo limitation unchanged; no live workspace accessed. PR monitor stopped. Task closure left to merge reconciliation.
close_reason: Closed on GitHub (issue #774); reconciled by bd-github-sync.

title: agent:* property drift between the daemon's PROPS and the companion's AGENT_PROPS is untested
description:
Noticed while verifying #502 (which is otherwise resolved — every `agent:*` key in live data is seed-declared).

## The gap

The chain that keeps a daemon property key seed-declared has two links, and only one is tested:

1. `agentProtocolSeeds` ≡ `AGENT_PROPS` — **tested** (`src/plugins/agent-dispatch-companion/test/schema.test.ts`)
2. `AGENT_PROPS` ≡ the daemon's `PROPS` — **comment only** (`src/plugins/agent-dispatch-companion/chipState.ts`: "keep the two in sync")

So a new key added to `PROPS` in `packages/agent-dispatch/src/config.ts` gets no seed, and nothing fails. That key is then unregistered, which means property migration skips it silently — and `grainAudit.isSystemProperty` blanket-exempts `agent:*`, so the grain audit cannot report it either (#613). That is exactly the three-way blind spot #502 documented, reopened for any future key.

## Why the duplication exists

It is deliberate, not an oversight: the app bundle cannot depend on the daemon's node package (`@knowledge-medium/agent-dispatch` is not a dependency of the root package — only `@knowledge-medium/agent-cli` is), and the daemon cannot import app `src/` either, since it ships as a published npm package. Neither side can import the other today.

## Shapes, none obviously right

- **Move the name table into `agent-cli`**, which both sides already depend on, and have both import it. Cleanest — makes the drift impossible rather than detected — but it widens a published package's surface, which is a call worth making deliberately.
- **A text-level drift test** that extracts the string literals from both files and compares them. No dependency inversion, but it is a test that parses source, which is its own kind of debt.
- **Accept it.** `pnpm agent audit-properties` reports any unregistered key with no exemption list, and #750 already mandates that audit before the flip — so an operator running the documented pre-flip check would catch a drifted key. The comment plus that process may be enough.

Filed rather than fixed because the first option is a design decision about a published package, not a mechanical change.

Priority note: no current instance — all 13 keys are seeded and every one resolves on the live graph. This is a guard against a future addition, and the pre-flip audit is a real backstop, hence P3.

title: Consolidate the draft/committed field state machines onto useTextDraft
description:
useTextDraft + DraftInput in src/components/propertyEditors/defaults.tsx already implement the whole draft-field contract: draft state, render-phase resync from the committed value, Enter-commit + blur-commit, a readOnly/disabled lock, and a dirty flag — including `if (!dirty && text === committedValue) return`, the same do-not-commit-what-nobody-edited rule PR #748 had to add by hand elsewhere.

Three hand-rolled copies of the resync block exist outside it: the property-schema name (PropertySchemaBlockRenderer), and the block-type label AND description (BlockTypeBlockRenderer).

Direction: lift the useTextDraft HOOK (not DraftInput, which is coupled to block + Input) into src/hooks/, and use it for those three pairs. The renderers then get editedness from `dirty` instead of a value comparison.

Does NOT reach the third site: the property panel's field row (PropertyRow) is an UNCONTROLLED input with defaultValue, so there is no draft state and value comparison is the only signal — trimIfEdited stays there.

Worth checking while in there whether the two definition renderers should share more than the draft hook; they mirror each other closely (resync, blur commit, Enter-to-blur, delete affordance).

Found by the quality pass on PR #748.

title: fuzz: fc.string({unit:'binary'}) does not generate unpaired surrogates, contrary to several comments
description:
Measured on fast-check 4.9.0: fc.string({unit: "binary"}) produced 0 lone surrogates in 20,000 samples. The unit emits whole code points, so surrogates only ever appear correctly PAIRED.

At least one comment in the repo still claims otherwise:
  src/utils/test/routing.fuzz.test.ts:77 -- "arbitrary UTF-16 incl. unpaired surrogates"

src/data/propertyChildren.fuzz.test.ts carried the same false claim and was fixed in PR #751 by building the arbitrary from UTF-16 code units instead:
  fc.integer({min: 0, max: 0xffff}).map(c => String.fromCharCode(c))
which yields lone surrogates in ~14% of samples.

Two things to do, in order:
1. Audit every fc.string({unit: "binary"}) use for a comment claiming surrogate coverage. Grep also finds src/shortcuts/test/recoverLogicalKey.fuzz.test.ts:151.
2. For each, decide whether the suite MEANT to cover ill-formed input. Where it did, switch the arbitrary -- and expect real failures: routing and logical-key recovery have never actually been fuzzed against unpaired surrogates, so a switch may surface genuine bugs rather than just widening coverage. That is the point, but it makes this more than a comment fix, which is why it is filed separately.

Left out of PR #751 deliberately: changing another suite generator there would have mixed an unrelated (and possibly failing) surface into a data-loss fix.
