title: Property-panel field-row rename input swallows Tab, so focus cannot leave it
description:
The rename Input in src/components/propertyPanel/PropertyRow.tsx handles Enter and Tab in the same branch:

    if (event.key === 'Enter' || event.key === 'Tab') { event.preventDefault(); onRename(event.currentTarget.value) }

preventDefault on a Tab keydown cancels focus traversal, so neither Tab nor Shift+Tab moves focus out of a field-row name input.

It has looked like it worked in one narrow case: when the rename actually CHANGES the name, the row's React key (`${sectionId}:${row.name}` in BlockProperties.tsx) changes, so the row remounts and the focused input is destroyed. Focus then falls to document.body — that is focus LOSS, not traversal. For an unedited field (the common case, and every field once the padded-name no-op landed) Tab simply does nothing.

Fix direction: keep Enter as commit-then-preventDefault; let Tab commit and fall through without preventDefault, or move focus deliberately (the same row's value editor is the natural next stop). Worth deciding what Tab should mean inside the panel rather than just dropping the preventDefault.

Found via a review comment on PR #748, which attributed the behaviour to that PR's identity no-op. It predates it: preventDefault runs whether or not the rename writes.

title: Properties-page bootstrap inside synthesis records undo, and its excuse covers only the create path
description:
applyPropertyDefinitionSynthesis (src/data/internals/propertyDefinitionSynthesis.ts, the getOrCreatePropertiesPage call before parentId is derived) bootstraps the Properties page in its own transaction with the default skipUndo: false.

The excuse on record in src/plugins/properties-migration/action.ts says: 'its transaction is skipUndo, and its Properties-page bootstrap is a no-op - kernel:properties is a systemPagesFacet entry, so the page exists before this gesture can be invoked'.

That covers the CREATE path only. getOrCreateKernelPage also writes on the REPAIR path, which fires whenever the live page is missing PAGE_TYPE or its marker type or its alias - a row synced from a build predating the marker, or a page a user or extension stripped.

Scenario: user edits, presses cmd-Z (redo now pending), runs 'Migrate properties to child blocks'; willSynthesize > 0 so synthesis runs; the Properties page needs a type repair; that bootstrap tx records an undo entry and clears the redo branch; every candidate then converges so result.created === 0, and the action's undoManagerFor(ws).clear() is gated on synthesized > 0 so it never runs. The user is left with a silently discarded redo and a lone 'repair Properties page' entry that cmd-Z will replay.

Same class as the Migrations-page fix (PR 745), which added the skipUndo option this would use. Narrow - it needs an already-damaged Properties page - but identical in kind.

Fix: pass {skipUndo: true} at that call, and correct the action.ts comment from 'is a no-op' to 'already exists, and the repair path must not record either'. Needs a test: the file has a harness (propertyDefinitionSynthesis.test.ts) with rawCell/planFor helpers, so the case is a damaged Properties page plus a pending redo that must survive an apply.

Not folded into PR 745 deliberately: different file, different gesture, and it needs its own harness work, where the Migrations fix is complete and pinned on its own.

Related but a separate judgement call, NOT covered here: srs-review/index.ts and agent-extensions/readwise.tsx each create a kernel page from a bare open-this-page action, which also leaves a lone entry and drops a redo - but there the user did ask for the page, so whether cmd-Z should revert it is a real question rather than an obvious bug.

title: ensureSystemPages creates kernel pages inside undo history at bootstrap
description:
Repo.ensureSystemPages runs every registered systemPagesFacet ensure at workspace bootstrap (Properties, Types, Recents, Journal, Locations). Each is getOrCreateKernelPage, which records an undo entry by default. Bootstrap is unattended — there is no user operation for the entry to merge into — so on a workspace where any of those pages is missing, the create lands alone on the stack and the user's first cmd-Z of the session deletes a system page instead of doing nothing.

Milder than the Migrations-page case (fixed separately): at bootstrap the undo stack is empty, so there is no redo branch to destroy. The consequence is the phantom step only, and it fires on first-ever open of a workspace or after a page is deleted, not on a warm open (ensureSystemPages opens no tx when every page is present).

Not fixed alongside the Migrations page because the mechanism is different. getOrCreateMigrationsPage could pass skipUndo at the wrapper, since that page has no attended caller by construction. The system pages DO have attended callers — getOrCreateDailyNote and createOrFindPlace deliberately merge the page create into the user operation's undo entry (issue #306, pinned by tests in daily-notes and geo) — so the same wrapper cannot decide. The decision has to come from the CALLER, which means SystemPage.ensure would grow an options parameter that every registration forwards. That is a facet contract change touching plugin-registered entries (daily-notes, geo), and worth its own review rather than riding along.

Check when doing it: whether the option should live on the facet's ensure signature at all, or whether ensureSystemPages should instead be given a way to run a block of work with undo recording suppressed — the latter keeps the decision in one place and stops each registration from having to remember.

title: I1 misreads two same-millisecond deterministic-id mints as identical content
description:
Invariant I1 (in the sync observer's reconcile layer) reads equal NONZERO `updated_at` stamps as proof of identical content, because the server strictly advances the stamp on any content change. That holds for two SYNCED writes to one id. It does not hold for two INDEPENDENT mints of the same deterministic id: two clients that mint the same id in the same millisecond with divergent content produce equal nonzero stamps from different writes. I1 misreads them as identical and skips, so the insert-or-touch echo is consumed and the loser strands.

WHY NOT THE OBVIOUS FIX. Advancing the touch's stamp server-side would force every id collision — including the common fresh-client bootstrap — to re-materialize and reindex on every device, and would break the "newer stamp implies changed content" coupling the whole reconcile gate rests on.

FIX DIRECTION. Creator side: mint deterministic ids at stamp 0 (the speculative-mint sentinel), so both mints yield via invariant I2 and converge on the server row.

KNOWN REMAINING NONZERO-STAMP DETERMINISTIC CREATOR: the matrix-message ingest extension creates its message-tree nodes with a precomputed deterministic id through a plain create, which stamps from the clock. An inventory sweep is needed to confirm whether it is the only one left — the previous note in the code claimed it was, and that claim was never re-verified.

SEVERITY: astronomically rare in practice (same id, same millisecond, divergent content) and accepted as a known gap. Filed so the reasoning has a home outside a source comment, where it was the only record.

title: Bulk-delete confirmation: count and delete should share one traversal
description:
The bulk-delete confirmation (PR #732) counts affected blocks with core.subtree, while the delete itself walks via deleteSubtreeInTx. Three known divergences between the two traversals, all surfaced in review — the class is the point, not any one instance:

1. Machinery rows. The count uses the FULL subtree so authored descendants under a property field row are included (the visible view prunes the whole branch and could drop the total under the threshold, skipping the question entirely). FIXED in the PR. Cost: recognized field/value rows count too, so a property-heavy block reads higher than what is on screen. In an unflipped workspace there are no such rows and the views agree — this starts to bite as properties-as-blocks rolls out, showing up as the dialog asking about deletes that look small.

2. Depth cap. core.subtree stops at depth 100 (a deliberate kernel-wide guard on every tree query); deleteSubtreeInTx is unbounded. A tree deeper than 100 levels is counted low. DECLINED: truncation implies at least 101 counted blocks, so the dialog always appears and only its number is imprecise.

3. Tombstoned anchor. SUBTREE_SQL anchors on deleted = 0, so a root tombstoned by sync counts zero; deleteSubtreeInTx deliberately calls childrenOf even for a tombstoned root and takes its live descendants. Count zero, delete N, no confirmation. DECLINED as an individual patch: it needs a remote tombstone on the parent while children are still live, on a block no longer rendered for the user to act on, and the descendants it takes are ones the incoming cascade is already deleting.

The shape that dissolves all three: one data-layer count that shares the deletion walk — dropping machinery rows without pruning their authored descendants, with no separate depth policy and no separate liveness anchor. That is new kernel query surface, deliberately not built for a confirmation dialog without a decision. Triggers to revisit: the confirmation starts asking about deletes that look small on screen (symptom 1 arriving), or a fourth instance of the class shows up.

Do NOT fix (1) by hand-rolling a field-row classifier in the UI util — restating that predicate is the recorded failure mode; compose the named predicate or do it in SQL.

title: Flaky: VideoNotesRenderer editorFocusRequest waitFor times out under full-suite load
description:
CI failure on an unrelated PR (agent-dispatch only; video-player is not in that diff).

  TypeError: actual value must be number or bigint, received "undefined"
   at src/plugins/video-player/test/VideoNotesRenderer.test.tsx:272

Line 272 is inside a vi.waitFor:

  expect(panel.peekProperty(editorFocusRequestProp)).toBeGreaterThanOrEqual(1)

'undefined' is what waitFor reports when the property never commits within its budget — the assertion never saw a value, rather than seeing a wrong one.

Evidence it is load, not logic:
- the file is untouched by the PR that hit it, and identical to master;
- all 15 tests pass locally in ~2.4s, both before and after rebasing onto current master;
- the full suite (8434 tests, the same set CI runs) passes locally in 64s, where the failing CI run took 200s — the ~3x stretch AGENTS.md describes for p99 under one-worker-per-core contention;
- the comment immediately above the assertion already documents flakiness in this area ('flaky, misattributed to whichever test is mid-flight').

Fix direction per the AGENTS.md timeout-budget rule: the chain here is a sequence of async property commits ending in editorFocusRequestProp, so the waitFor is waiting on the tail of several round-trips. Give this waitFor an explicit budget sized from its measured cost times the load factor, with the measurement stated — not a global testTimeout raise. Worth checking whether the surrounding it() budget is also too tight for a 6x stretch.

Same family as the other load flakes already filed.
close_reason: Closed on GitHub (issue #739); reconciled by bd-github-sync.

title: Write eligibility is a repo-wide flag while kernel-page writes name a workspace
description:
repo.isReadOnly is one boolean for the active workspace, but getOrCreateKernelPage is handed a workspaceId and writes into it. Whenever the two disagree, eligibility is decided against the wrong workspace: an editable target is skipped (the caller then navigates to a page that was never created), and a viewer target is written locally and rejected by RLS on upload.

The commit-time net does not close it. getOrCreateKernelPage's docblock notes the real refusal is CHANGE_SCOPE_POLICIES (BlockDefault is readOnly: 'reject'), but that reads the same repo-wide flag - when it is stale, both checks are stale together.

Known vectors:
1. A navigationIntentVerb policy that retargets the workspace while a caller materialises against it. Reachable only if something resolves a get-or-create from a navigation decision; PR 720 did, and was closed, so this vector is currently dormant rather than fixed.
2. The workspace-switch window. App.tsx calls repo.setActiveWorkspaceId(incoming) BEFORE getLocalMemberRole + repo.setReadOnly and before the access gate, so during that async gap the active workspace (and the hash) name the incoming workspace while isReadOnly still describes the outgoing one. The previous tree is still mounted, so a click can land in it. This window is NOT caused by preferring the URL hash - plain repo.activeWorkspaceId has it too, since its setter runs first.

This is independent of any recents work: every kernel-page caller has the exposure (daily notes, locations, media capture, migrations, types/properties), and it predates all of it.

Partly accepted already, in writing: App.tsx comments that a not-yet-synced membership row defaults to read-only=false and 'any edits attempted in the meantime would be RLS-rejected server-side anyway'. The switch window has the same consequence and is not written down anywhere.

The fix belongs where the write happens - a per-workspace eligibility check inside getOrCreateKernelPage's writing transaction, not per-caller guards. That primitive does not exist today: Repo exposes only setReadOnly/isReadOnly, so this needs a canWrite(workspaceId) style read first.

title: DailyNotePicker gates the click after an await, so modifier routing is lost
description:
In the daily-note picker (src/plugins/daily-notes/DailyNotePicker.tsx), the click handler awaits the get-or-create and only then calls the block opener:

    const note = await getOrCreateDailyNote(repo, workspaceId, iso)
    openBlock(event, {blockId: note.id, workspaceId})

The opener gates the DOM event (stopPropagation/preventDefault) as its first step, which after an await is too late - ancestor handlers have run and the default action is committed, so the shift/alt/native-passthrough routing is nominally lost.

Benign today: the surface is a button in a portal, the sibling overlay closes on mousedown, so there is no ancestor click handler and no native default to prevent. Filed because it is the shape src/utils/navigation.ts documents as wrong, not because it is currently breaking.

Fix direction is OPEN. An earlier note here said this was a one-line conversion using an ensureTarget option on the opener - that option was part of PR 720, which was closed unmerged, so it does not exist. Anything that resolves the target before the gate has the same problem this bead describes, and anything that makes the click create a page inherits the write-on-gesture problems catalogued on the recents bead (undo history, workspace scoping, write eligibility). Worth solving together with those rather than in isolation.

title: Publish read-back: memoize the beads-DB probe, and check the deadline inside a target's prologue
description:
initializedDbRoot() runs a git rev-parse plus a bd --version on every call, and the read-back calls it once per target that carries a bead id. Both are invariant for the process, so the repeats are pure cost — and each probe is bounded by PROBE_TIMEOUT rather than by the report's own deadline, so a slow or hanging git/bd can spend a large share of the 70s budget before the first note is emitted, against a 120s host kill.

Two changes, both small and independent:
- memoize the probe the same way ghJson and fetchIssueInfo are memoized (a null result must memoize too, or a DB-less clone re-probes per target — the exact case the guard exists for).
- check the deadline INSIDE a target's prologue, not only between targets. A single target can currently spend several bounded subprocesses with no chance to stop, which is why the outer loop guard alone is not enough.

Not urgent: the worst case needs a genuinely slow git or bd, and the hook fails silent rather than wrong. Verified unmemoized 2026-08-21 against the merged code.

title: Publish hooks: adopt shell-segments for the predicates that still parse raw command text
description:
The publish hooks resolve a shell command several different ways — a quote-blanking skeleton, the raw text, and a single-quote-only variant for expansions — and each predicate picks one. Picking the wrong rendering is the recurring defect class on these hooks: it produced findings in five separate review rounds, each individually correct, each fixed, each followed by another against the same shape.

`scripts/shell-segments.mjs` already resolves a command properly and is already in this repo: argv tokens per simple-command position, quoted spans resolved into their token, subshell depth, and heredoc bodies flagged as data. It is used by two other PreToolUse hooks and has its own tests. This is an ADOPTION, not a build.

Three uses landed already and are the evidence it fits:
- the commit leg's file read takes command-position evidence from it, so a command that merely carries the tokens in argv cannot make the hook open a file;
- a heredoc body is excluded from command position, which no regex over the skeleton could do;
- the explicit-read exemption is restricted to a single segment, which is what finally made that exemption safe after several rounds of looking unsafe.

### What adopting it further would retire

- **Quoted option TOKENS.** `'-X' PUT`, `'-f' 'k=v'` reach gh unchanged but are blanked by the skeleton, so the api matcher misses them and the command is invisible to both hooks. Same shape as the quoted-VALUE case that was fixed by hand.
- **Escaped apostrophes.** An unquoted escaped apostrophe is a literal character, not a delimiter, but the hand-written quote scanner pairs two of them and blanks everything between. shell-segments tracks quote state, which is the prerequisite here.
- **Message-file attribution.** `bodyFilePaths` scans the whole invocation, so a sibling command's file flag is resolved as a commit message path — a grep with a fixed-string flag beside a commit blocks, reporting the grep's pattern as an unreadable message file. Segments are already computed at that point; attributing flags to the segment that owns them is a loop, not a parser. Narrowing the REGEX instead was tried and reverted for losing two fail-closed cases, so this is the route that remains.
- **Naming the token that matched.** The block for text living outside the command lists three possible causes without saying which one fired, and for a literal inline body with an at-sign in it all three are false. With tokens in hand the message can name the actual one.

### What it would NOT fix, deliberately

Wrapper option arity (`env -u NAME git commit …` leaving one message file unscanned) stays declined. Telling an executing wrapper from an informational one needs a per-wrapper table of flag arities AND modes, complete or wrong, and the failure is an under-match whose only cost is that one file — the command's own text is checked either way.

### Cost to weigh before starting

shell-segments does not currently record whether a token was QUOTED, which is the distinction the predicates encode by hand today (a suppressor reads the skeleton so it under-matches; a detector reads the raw text so it over-matches). Adding that flag is the likely first step, and it changes a module two other hooks depend on — so it needs its own tests there, not just here.

Not urgent. The hooks are correct as merged; this retires a defect CLASS rather than a live bug, and should be done against a stable base rather than stacked on more review rounds.

title: navigate() has no freshness guard: a deferred navigation can land after a newer one
description:
Two overlapping navigations can land out of order. navigate() is fire-and-forget and async (destination resolution + a tx), and nothing tracks which gesture is the newest — so a slow first navigation can commit its panel write after a later one, leaving the user on the earlier destination.

Pre-existing, but the ensureTarget option widens the window on one path: when the target page must be created or restored, the get-or-create runs before the navigation, so the deferred landing is a page-create longer than usual. In practice that is first-use-only (afterwards the resolve is a cached read) and self-correcting with one click, which is why it was accepted rather than special-cased there — a freshness mechanism that exists on one option and not on navigate() itself would read as complete and not be.

If this is worth fixing, it belongs in navigate()/applyNavigation as a generation check covering every async navigation, not in any single caller. applyNavigation already reasons about late-landing writes for the active-panel mark (it awaits them within the navigation instead of firing and forgetting); this is the same class of problem one level up.

title: E2EE: ciphertext length leaks property-name length, and the tradeoff list does not say so
description:
Not a defect in any one change — a gap between what the e2ee threat model documents and what it actually accepts.

AEAD sealing does not pad (src/sync/crypto/aead.ts), and the envelope is 'enc:v1:' + base64url(nonce||ct||tag), so the length of an encrypted column is a deterministic function of its plaintext length. docs/e2ee-design.html §15 lists what the server can see and accepts — tree shape, order key, edit timing, authorship, deletion flag, which-column-changed — but NOT ciphertext length.

That is sharper than generic length leakage for one row shape in particular: a synthesized property definition. The server can single those out without decrypting anything, because parent_id is the Properties page (a uuidv5 of the workspace id under a public constant), systemMint stamps updated_at = 0, and the definition seeds that share that stamp have publicly computable ids and subtract out. The remaining rows have a fully known plaintext template — only the property name and one of four preset ids vary — so the envelope length recovers the name length to roughly a 3-byte bucket. It confirms nothing, but it rules out most guesses before they are made.

The same is true of every hand-declared definition and of block content generally, so this is not specific to synthesis; synthesis just makes an identifiable cohort of it.

What this needs is a DECISION on the record, not necessarily a fix. Padding a column is permanent weight for a channel that is inherent to the scheme, and the likely right answer is 'accepted' — but §15 should say so, so the next person reading the threat model does not infer coverage that was never claimed. If it is instead judged worth closing, the cheapest form is padding properties_json to a bucket boundary before sealing.

title: Properties migration: integers beyond JS safe range lose precision, in the cell before the migration touches them
description:
Accepted rather than fixed, recorded so it is not re-litigated.

A properties cell can hold a JSON integer outside JavaScript's safe range only if something wrote it WITHOUT going through JavaScript — a direct SQL write, or an importer streaming JSON text into the column. Every ordinary path stringifies from JS, so the value is already rounded before it is stored.

Measured on the local SQLite build: with properties_json = '{"k":9007199254740993}', both json_each and json_extract hand JavaScript 9007199254740992. Only CAST(json_extract(...) AS TEXT) recovers the digits. So every reader in the app — rendering, the property panel, the sync upload path, the migration backfill — already sees the rounded value, and no two such values are distinguishable to any JS consumer.

Consequence: migrating such a key writes the rounded form into the child, and past the flip the cell is re-derived from children, so the stored TEXT changes even though no observable value does.

Why it was not fixed: detecting it means parsing numeric tokens out of the raw JSON text, since by the time a value is in JS the information is gone. That mechanism would have to live in the backfill to cover all keys — it is not a property of orphan-definition synthesis, which was where it was reported. It would refuse migration over a difference nothing in the app can observe.

Revisit if a non-JS writer to properties_json is ever introduced.

title: agent-dispatch: the lane cooldown duplicates agent:retry-after — derive it instead
description:
Design follow-up from the PR 507 review, which ran four rounds and 19 findings. Six of the 19 were about the lane cooldown itself, one or more in every round: scope it per executor, reserve the post-cooldown probe, let an explicit retry bypass it, clear it after a channel success, arm it when a query channel delivery fails, and make its gate per-source rather than ending the scan.

Diagnosis: the cooldown is a SECOND clock. The durable per-task agent:retry-after already says 'not before T'. The in-memory lane cooldown exists only to stop the daemon discovering NEW work on a lane during an outage. Because it is a separate mechanism rather than a projection, every path that can launch or succeed must independently answer three questions — arm? clear? bypass? — and there are six such paths (mention spawn, mention channel, query spawn, query channel, explicit retry, probe reservation). That is ~18 individually-invisible decisions, and the six findings above were six of them being wrong. Each fix was correct and none of them reduced the number of decisions.

Proposed shape: derive 'is this lane cooling' from data the tick already reads, rather than storing it. The daemon fetches blockViews for every backlink source each tick, so 'does any task on this lane hold a future agent:retry-after' is nearly free for mention watchers. Then arming is just writing retry-after on the deferred task (already happens), clearing is that stamp lapsing or being cleared (already happens), and an explicit retry bypasses by clearing it (already happens) — no per-path arm/clear/bypass to get wrong. The probe reservation becomes one rule in one place: claim at most one task whose retry-after just lapsed.

It does not vanish entirely: a query watcher has no graph-side task state, so its outage state genuinely lives nowhere else. But the mechanism would shrink from six paths to one, which is the point.

Not urgent — the cooldown is correct and tested as it stands. This is about the cost of the next change to it.

title: Publish hooks: messages that assert more than the code established
description:
Findings from adversarial review of the two publish hooks, reduced to what is still OPEN after the round of fixes merged 2026-08-21. They share a theme worth keeping in the title: **the hooks talk about commands they have not established anything about.** Each is a message asserting more than the code knows, and the cost is the same every time — the reports are only worth having while they are trusted.

### Open: message names a cause it has not established

The block for uncovered text living outside the command lists three possible causes ("a file or payload flag, an @-reference, or shell expansion") without saying which one matched. For a review with a literal, inline, fully readable body that happens to contain an at-sign mention, all three are false. The message then advises publishing literal inline text, which is already the case, and offers a body-file alternative that only works for verbs the read-back covers — for merge/review/close/reopen there is no route but the double escape.

Naming the token that actually matched fixes the whole family, and needs the command resolved into tokens. Blocked on the shell-segments adoption for that reason.

### Open: one suspected case, never reproduced

A command reported as FAILED is assumed to have published nothing, which suppresses the coverage report. Counterexamples would be a tool-timeout kill after the request completed server-side, or a release create failing on asset upload after the release exists. If it needs tightening, softening the wording on the failure event is cheaper than removing the suppression — the suppression itself is right for the common case.

### Fixed, kept for the record

- Cries wolf on commands that publish no text — the report now asks whether the command carries text at all, which covers comment deletions, label changes, reactions and merge-method calls without enumerating flags. A CREATE is text-bearing by its VERB, so the flags that supply a body implicitly (fill, recover, templates, editor, interactive prompt) need no enumeration either.
- Explicit reads classified as publishes — a LONE read is exempt now; a compound that mixes one with a mutation still is not, because the effective method resolves across the whole skeleton. This was the oldest finding here and the single-segment restriction is what made it safe.
- The stdin refusal named merge/review channels that cannot reach it; only the commit leg can.
- Two messages recommending an issue-shaped view command for targets that are not issues, including one branch that has no target at all by definition.

### Moved

Message-file attribution (a sibling command's file flag resolved as a commit message path) moved to the shell-segments adoption bead, which carries the fix route: attribute flags to the segment that owns them. Narrowing the regex instead was tried and reverted for losing two fail-closed cases.

The per-target probe cost has its own bead.
notes:
Update: the 'cries wolf on commands that publish no text' section is FIXED — the coverage report now asks whether the command carries text at all (carriesPublishableText), which covers comment deletions, label changes, reactions and merge-method calls without enumerating flags. The GET-classified-as-publish half of that section stands, as do the message-naming and message-file-scope findings and the unreproduced failure-event case.
Also open, declined on PR #697 round 12 and filed here: quoted option TOKENS ('-X' PUT, '-f' 'k=v') reach gh unchanged but are blanked by commandSkeleton, so matchesApiPublish misses them and the command is invisible to both hooks. Same shape as the quoted-VALUE case fixed in that round. Symptom of the design rather than a spelling to fix: ~10 predicates each read one of several renderings of the command, and picking the wrong one is the recurring defect. Proposed shape: parse the command ONCE into a structure naming quoted spans, comments, escapes, expansions, flags and verbs, and have every predicate read fields off it. See also the aiming rule in memory reference_predicate_match_direction.
Third in the same family (PR #697 round 13, also declined): an unquoted ESCAPED apostrophe is a literal character, not a delimiter, but the quote-span regex pairs two of them and blanks everything between. Quoted values, quoted option tokens, escaped apostrophes — all one root cause, a hand-written quote scanner that does not track quote state. A scanner that does is a prerequisite for the parse-once normalizer above, and is where these three belong.
The parse-once normalizer in the notes above is an ADOPTION, not a build: scripts/shell-segments.mjs already is one. 186 lines, exports shellSegmentsWithDepth (argv tokens per simple-command position, quotes resolved into their token, subshell depth, heredoc bodies flagged as data) and shellSegments. It is already consumed by two other PreToolUse hooks — check-stash-worktree.mjs and check-staged-pii.mjs — and tested in check-stash-worktree.test.ts. Verified 2026-08-21. It tracks quote state properly, which is exactly the prerequisite the three declined findings above share, and its docstring already states the deliberate limits (no expansions; a close-paren inside a double-quoted string nested in a substitution closes early). What it does NOT yet carry is whether a token was quoted, which is the raw-vs-skeleton distinction the gate's predicates encode by hand; adding that flag is the likely first step.

Also fixed by the 2026-08-21 cleanup pass: the stdin refusal now says 'commit text' only, matching the one leg that reaches it.
2026-08-21, on the same branch: the file-read leg now takes command-position evidence from shell-segments (commitsInCommandPosition), after Codex found that a command merely CARRYING the tokens — printf '%s' git commit -F <path> — made the hook readFileSync that path. That was a regression from de-anchoring the detectors: right for gh, where over-matching costs one echo round, wrong for the one leg that opens files.

The 'message-file check fires on another command's flag' finding above still STANDS, and is now a smaller job than when it was filed. Measured just now: for 'grep -F needle src/x.ts && git commit -m chore', commitsInCommandPosition is true (a real commit segment exists) and bodyFilePaths still scans the whole invocation and returns ['needle']. But shellSegmentsWithDepth already splits that into [grep -F needle src/x.ts] and [git commit -m chore], so per-segment attribution — the fix the description called cheaper than shell parsing — is now one loop over segments that are already computed, not a new mechanism. Note that bodyFilePaths itself must NOT be narrowed to achieve it: narrowing its regex was tried and reverted on this branch after it lost two fail-closed cases (a filename containing '=', and process substitution). The change is to pick the segment first, then run the existing breadth inside it.

Also 2026-08-21: TEXT_FIELD_NAME learned 'content', closing the nested-field case (gh api gists -f 'files[a.md][content]=…' was covered by the gate and reported by neither hook).
2026-08-21, round 15 on the same branch — DECLINED and labelled at the declaration (commitsInCommandPosition's docstring): a wrapper option taking a SEPARATE value, e.g. env with its unset flag before git commit with a message file, stops the prefix skip at the value, so that message file goes unscanned. Reproduced. Bounded: the raw command is scanned for close keywords either way, so only a keyword living ONLY in the file is missed. The fix asked for is a table of per-flag arities for env/xargs/command/…, which must be complete to be correct and cannot be — the blacklist shape rejected everywhere else in that file, and the shape that generated the preceding rounds.

Worth keeping straight, because the two get conflated: the round-14 finding was an OVER-match wired to a file read (over-matching is not cheap there); this is an UNDER-match on a check whose miss costs one unscanned file. Opposite directions, different answers. See memory reference_predicate_match_direction.

Fixed in the same round, both one token added to a list that exists to grow: SHELL_OPERATOR learned bash's negating reserved word (it inverts the pipeline status and with it which post-hook event fires — the one input the read-back reasons from and cannot check), and TEXT_FLAG learned gh's fill flags (they name no text in the command because gh derives title and body from the branch commits, close keywords included).

Meta, for whoever picks this up: across rounds 14-15 the pre-gate blocked its own author three times — a read-only graphql query passed via a file reference, the same query with a shell variable in a loop, and a commit whose heredoc message quoted an example command with a message-file flag. The first two are the 'read classified as publish' item above; the third is the accepted heredoc false positive. All three had a cheap workaround, but they are the friction that item is measuring.
2026-08-21, round 16. Both findings landed on the two lines round 15 touched, and both were answered by DELETING machinery rather than adding it. Net surface on the branch went down.

1. The wrapper prefix skip no longer walks past a wrapper's OPTIONS. Round 15 added that skip for a hypothetical (a wrapper invoked with flags) and it reintroduced the round-14 defect: 'command -v <git commit invocation with a message file>' prints a description and runs nothing, but was read as a live commit, so the hook opened the file. Distinguishing that from the env-unset form needs a per-wrapper table of flag arities AND modes, complete or wrong. Stopping at the first option refuses the dangerous form and folds every wrapper-with-options case into the under-match accepted in round 15. The xargs case that motivated the skip is now in that class and its test asserts so.

2. carriesPublishableText asks the VERB about creates instead of listing the flags that supply their text. Round 15 added gh's fill flags to the list; round 16 found the recover flag; templates, EDITOR and the interactive prompt were queued behind them — one review round each, forever. A PR, issue or release cannot exist without a title, so the verb settles it. The fill flags came back OUT of the list, which is now smaller than before round 15. EDIT keeps the flag list, because an edit really can carry no text.

The generalizable half is in memory reference_guard_direction_whitelist_over_blacklist: when even a closed-vocabulary list keeps growing, the answer is the fact one level up, and the ARRIVAL RATE of individually-correct additions is the signal rather than the size of any one of them. Also recorded there: two findings on the same predicate can need opposite answers (an over-match wired to a file read is a defect; an under-match costing one unscanned file is acceptable and gets labelled), so they must not be batched by location.
2026-08-21, round 17 — both fixed, neither added a case. Different in kind from rounds 14-16: these were predicates reading their input WRONG, not lists missing an entry, so the fix is a correction rather than an enumeration and does not set up a round 18 on the same line.

1. The explicit-read suppressor took any read method token in the argv as proof nothing was published. gh keeps the LAST method flag — measured against the installed gh, not reasoned: a POST followed by a GET against the rate-limit endpoint answers as a GET, and the reverse order 404s as a POST. So a mutation whose argv mentioned a read earlier had its coverage warning silenced, with the close keyword in its title acting immediately on merge. Now resolves the effective method. Suppresses strictly LESS than before, so it cannot open a new gap.

2. The read-back failure note handed back an issue-shaped view command for every target kind. A comment target keeps only the comment id and a release only its tag, so for four of six kinds it named a command that cannot reach the text — at the exact moment the agent has been told to go read it by hand. Now hands back the api path the hook just tried, already computed one line above. This is the failure mode this issue is titled after, at its worst position.

Status of the earlier sections after this round: the 'cries wolf on commands that publish no text' section is fixed; the GET-classified-as-publish half of it still stands (matchesApiPublish still counts a field flag as a mutation regardless of the effective method — the same last-wins resolution is now available in the file if that is taken up); the 'message names a cause it has not established' section still stands for the outside-the-command block; the message-file attribution section still stands and is now one loop over already-computed segments.
2026-08-21, round 18 — the READ-CLASSIFIED-AS-PUBLISH section is now FIXED, and this issue's oldest open finding is closed with it.

What unblocked it: the exemption looked unsafe every previous round because the effective method is resolved across the whole skeleton, so exempting a read would exempt a mutation compounded with it. Restricting the exemption to a SINGLE non-heredoc segment settles that — a compound keeps the old behaviour and needs no vocabulary of its own. The harm it removes is concrete rather than theoretical: a lone read's response object was collected as something the command PUBLISHED, so its references were reported against an object the agent never wrote and might be told to go edit.

An existing test, 'echoes refs of a silent mutation even when a sibling segment is an explicit GET', independently pins the compound half — dropping the single-segment restriction fails it. That was written for an unrelated reason rounds ago and turned out to be exactly the guard this change needed.

Also fixed: the no-target note recommended an issue-shaped view command in the one branch that by definition has no target (a second copy of the verifyTarget defect fixed in round 17), and AGENTS.md still promised publishers are recognized only with the verb in command position and that mentions pass — untrue since the detectors were de-anchored on this branch.

PROCESS NOTE worth keeping: the no-target message fix was UNPINNED when first written — mutating the new wording back to the old failed nothing, so the fix was invisible to the suite and would have regressed silently. Caught only by running the mutation, not by the green gate. Message-only fixes are the easiest kind to leave unpinned, because there is no behaviour to assert on unless you assert on the text.

Still open on this issue: the 'message names a cause it has not established' section (the outside-the-command block lists three possible causes without saying which matched), and the message-file attribution section (a sibling command's file flag is attributed to the commit), which is one loop over already-computed segments.

title: agent-dispatch: a Stop on a deferred task is missed once its mention is deleted
description:
The daemon's Stop-on-deferred branch (packages/agent-dispatch/src/engine.ts, tickBacklinksWatcher) only iterates the watcher's current backlinkSources. If the trigger mention is deleted from a block while its task is deferred (agent:status=queued + agent:retry-after), a later Stop from the chip writes agent:cancel that nothing ever observes: sweepCancellations cannot help either, because a deferred task holds no abort controller. The chip then reads 'retry in Nm' with a pending Stop indefinitely.

Accepted rather than fixed when the deferral path landed, and noted at the site. Nothing runs or bills either way — deleting the mention already stops the task re-firing — so the cost is a stale chip on a task the user has already orphaned.

Two fix directions, both more expensive than the symptom today:
- a watcher-independent cancel sweep, which needs a property query over agent:status/agent:cancel that the daemon has nowhere else;
- letting the app write the terminal state directly for a queued task, which moves lifecycle ownership out of the daemon (today every terminal write is the daemon's).

Worth revisiting if the daemon grows a property-query surface for another reason.

title: Rename backfillSyncGate to syncSettledGate — the gate has non-backfill readers
description:
`RepoOptions.backfillSyncGate`, `Repo.backfillSyncSettledNow` and `disposeBackfillSyncGate` are named for the backfill runner, but the gate is now half of `syncViewGap`, which is also read by the per-transaction write assertion and by the `audit-properties` verb. A third caller reading `backfillSyncSettledNow` reasonably concludes the predicate is about backfills rather than about whether this device can vouch for its view of `blocks`.

Proposed: `backfillSyncGate` -> `syncSettledGate`, `backfillSyncSettledNow` -> `syncSettledNow`, `disposeBackfillSyncGate` -> `disposeSyncSettledGate`. Mechanical; ~10 occurrences at time of writing across src/data/repo.ts, src/context/repo.tsx, src/data/test/createTestRepo.ts, src/data/test/repoFacadeGate.test.ts and the agent-runtime tests. `RepoOptions.syncSettledGate` is the only externally visible name and nothing outside this repo constructs a Repo.

Two doc corrections belong with it, because the rename is what makes them wrong:
- `syncSettledNow`'s doc says it is 'the same predicate the scheduler gates on'. That was true when the pre-claim gate sampled it directly; the scheduler now gates on the whole of `syncViewGap`. Leaving it is worth fixing on its own — 'this is the predicate the scheduler gates on' is precisely the belief that produced the bug fixed as km-b014.
- `createTestRepo`'s option doc still says 'Override the workspace-backfill sync gate', while that option is injected by the audit tests for a non-backfill reason.

Context: this was written and reviewed as part of PR #625, then dropped when that PR was reduced to its one novel change after #628 landed the rest independently. Filing so it is not lost. Low priority — naming only, no behaviour.

title: Consider git-layer interception if command-string concurrency guards keep leaking
description:
The two git-concurrency guards (shared-refs stash rules, index-absorbing amend rule)
decide from the Bash command STRING, before the shell runs. That works, but it means
statically approximating both bash (quoting, substitutions, subshell scope, heredocs,
line continuations, reserved words, wrapper commands, assignments, cwd state) and git's
CLI grammar (global repo-location flags, per-subcommand positional grammars, option
arity, clustered short options, pathspec semantics). Six review rounds on PR #654 kept
finding the next divergence between the approximation and the real thing; the last
rounds converged only because the policy became "fix realistic wrong-allows, decline
the rest".

The shape that removes the whole class: intercept at the GIT layer instead of the
command string. A `git` shim on PATH (or a wrapper the agent harness invokes) sees the
ACTUAL argv after the shell has expanded it, in the ACTUAL working directory, at the
ACTUAL moment of execution. Then:

- no shell parsing at all — no quoting/heredoc/continuation/subshell/wrapper handling,
  which is roughly half the current surface and the source of the false-positive class
  (a command that merely MENTIONS a guarded operation in prose or a heredoc body)
- no cwd inference — the shim runs where the command runs
- unresolved-expansion cases disappear; `git -C "$VAR"` is just a resolved path
- check-to-use races shrink to near zero, since validation happens immediately before
  the operation rather than in a separate pre-flight process

Costs / open questions, which are why this is deferred and not queued:
- it intercepts human terminal use too, not only agent calls; needs an escape that
  does not become habitual (a habitual opt-out is how the next incident gets waved through)
- process-level machinery (PATH shim or wrapper) vs a self-contained hook script:
  more install surface, more ways to be silently absent
- must be transparent for every unguarded git command (exit codes, stdout/stderr,
  interactive commands, pagers, stdin)
- it does not subsume the PII commit-message guard, which needs the message content
  and legitimately runs pre-execution

TRIGGER for revisiting: real incidents recurring despite the current hooks, or a third
distinct same-state-concurrency hazard needing a third rule. Absent that, the current
selective guards plus their documented residues are the accepted state; do NOT rewrite
them speculatively.

Context: the guards and their per-clause tests landed in PR #654; that PR's discussion
holds the full shape diagnosis, the coarse-rules alternative that was weighed and not
taken, and the reasons each declined finding was declined.

title: SQL seed leg recognizes a definition slot the tx resolver rejects
description:
Pre-existing divergence, surfaced by Codex review on PR #628.

Recognition's seed leg binds every deterministic definition id the registry computes, so the SQL treats a marked child pointing at that id as a field row. But when the slot is occupied by a live block of different provenance, materializePropertySeeds refuses to claim it and the tx-layer resolver reports definition-unavailable - so the same child is NOT machinery to the tx layer. The SQL then hides it from the outline and drops its descendants' backlinks.

This is the mirror of the divergence already documented at recognizedFieldRowSql (issue #389 item 7), which covers the opposite direction: the registry knows a seed the block_types index does not carry yet. Same seam, other side.

Fix direction: filter occupied non-definition slots out of the seed parameters (registrySeedParams), or have the SQL seed leg verify the slot is unoccupied or genuinely a definition. The first is cheaper - the occupancy answer is already computed when seeds are materialized.

Pre-existing: the seed leg predates PR #628 and was reachable post-flip. Un-gating recognition makes it reachable in un-flipped workspaces too, which is why it surfaced now.

title: Alias-seat reaping is off during the pre-flip backfill window
description:
ACCEPTED COST, recorded so it is not rediscovered as a bug.

The alias-seat reaper tolerates a seat's own generated property children (aliases/types field rows) only in a FLIPPED workspace. The cell->children backfill mints those rows before the flip, so from the moment it runs until the flip lands, every live seat has children and no orphan seat is reaped. Orphan seats squat until their alias is re-typed and re-dropped; normal reaping resumes at the flip.

WHY THIS IS THE CHOSEN TRADE, not an oversight. Post-flip an edit to a generated value row reprojects into the seat's cell, so matchesAliasSeatSeed sees the drift and refuses - that is what makes tolerating machine children safe there. Pre-flip the projection processor is dormant, so the cell cannot vouch for the subtree, and tolerating children means enumerating every way a user could have touched them. That enumeration was attempted and failed twice in two review rounds: first an edited value row passed the shape check, then an edited PROPERTY BAG passed the shape-plus-content check. Each was a silent soft-delete of a user's edit.

Not reaping is the documented safe miss. The cost is bounded by the migration window and self-resolves at the flip; the alternative is an open-ended guard whose completeness nobody has been able to establish.

Revisit only if orphan-seat squatting turns out to matter during a long verify window, and if so prefer comparing the subtree wholesale against a fresh materialization over adding another per-attribute check.
close_reason: Cannot arise under the runbook that shipped. This recorded a cost of backfill-then-flip: the pass minted a seat's generated property children while the workspace still read cells, and the reaper's tolerance for those children is gated on the workspace being child-backed, so from the first backfill batch until the flip landed no orphan seat was reaped. The runbook is now flip-then-backfill — the palette gesture flips first, the CLI verb refuses an un-flipped workspace, and the pass carries an operator trigger so nothing schedules it — which means a seat has no generated children before the flip and the tolerance is never consulted in the state this described. Verified against the pass, the reaper's gate and the seat-seed predicate 2026-08-23. Reopen only if a pre-flip backfill run becomes reachable again; the trade recorded here is still the right one for that state, and the two failed enumeration attempts are still why.

title: Concurrent GitHub syncs can mint two issues for one tracker item
description:
Observed 2026-08-20 while opening PR #662. One tracker item was minted TWICE as separate public issues: #661 at 19:09:06 and #663 at 19:09:29, identical title and body. The second batch minted #664 for a different item in the same second, so it was a batch push, not a retry of the first.

Sequence: the pre-PR hook (scripts/bd-github-sync.mjs --hook-pre-pr) blocked a 'gh pr create' whose body referenced the item, minted #661 for it, and reported that mapping. The re-run with the number substituted contained no ids, so the hook allowed it without minting — the hook did not create the duplicate. 23s later a second push (another session's sync, most likely a SessionEnd run) minted #663 for the same item, so it did not see the external_ref the first mint had recorded.

Consequences: two public issues for one item; the tracker item ends up pointing at whichever mint wrote last (#663 here), silently orphaning the other (#661), which a PR body may already reference. Cleanup is manual — #661 was closed by hand as a duplicate and the PR body repointed.

Worth checking whether the push path re-reads external_ref inside the same transaction as the issue creation, or whether two syncers can interleave read-then-create. A cheap mitigation if that is hard: have the push refuse to mint when an open issue with an identical title already exists.

No fix attempted; filed from the observation.

title: Nothing surfaces a node_modules stale relative to pnpm-lock.yaml
description:
PR #635 bumped happy-dom 20.11.0 -> 20.11.2. Local installs predating that merge kept serving 20.11.0 for days, and nothing surfaced the drift: 'pnpm run check' neither installs nor verifies, and a single-file 'pnpm vitest run' obviously does not either. It only came to light because that particular upgrade shipped a canary test, which then read as a flaky test (#653) rather than as a stale install; a dependency bump without a canary drifts silently or fails confusingly.

Options:
- add a lockfile-vs-installed verification step to scripts/check.mjs. A no-op 'pnpm install --frozen-lockfile' measured 1.7s when already up to date.
- accept it and keep relying on per-case canaries.

Costs of the first: it gives the gate an install side effect (check.mjs currently mutates nothing), and it does NOT help the case that actually bit here — running one test file directly, without the gate. A cheaper variant is a read-only comparison of installed package versions against the lockfile, failing with the pnpm install hint instead of running the install.

Not decided; needs Vlad's call on whether the gate should touch node_modules.
